papers.label: SPORT disc RCT
papers.design: Multicenter randomized trial at 13 US spine centers, alongside a separate observational cohort; no sham control
papers.population: Age 18 or older, surgical candidates with imaging-confirmed lumbar disk herniation matching radicular pain, plus a positive nerve-root tension sign or matching deficit, persisting at least 6 weeks. Prior lumbar surgery and cauda equina syndrome excluded.
papers.endpoint: Change from baseline in SF-36 bodily pain, SF-36 physical function and ODI at 6 weeks, 3 and 6 months, and 1 and 2 years
papers.finding: Both assigned groups improved substantially. Intent-to-treat differences on the primary outcomes were small and not significant on global tests, mostly favoring surgery; sciatica bothersomeness and self-rated progress favored surgery. Crossover in both directions prevented a superiority or equivalence conclusion from the intent-to-treat analysis.
papers.numbers: Surgery by 3 months: 50% assigned surgery vs 30% assigned nonoperative care; by 2 years 60% vs 45%. 1-year ITT effects: bodily pain 2.8 (95% CI −2.3 to 7.8), physical function 1.2 (−4.1 to 6.5), ODI −3.2 (−7.8 to 1.3); global P .74, .71, .21. Sciatica bothersomeness −1.6 (−2.9 to −0.4), global P=.003. Adjusted as-treated 1-year: bodily pain 15.0, physical function 17.5, ODI −15.0.
papers.caveat: Do not call the intention-to-treat result proof that discectomy is ineffective, or the as-treated result proof of a large effect: as-treated comparisons lose randomization's protection, and patients who crossed into surgery were worse at baseline. Nonoperative care was not standardized, there was no sham, and only 25% of eligible patients were randomized.
papers.discussion: SPORT is essential partly because it teaches how crossover changes what a surgical trial can establish.
papers.title: Surgical vs nonoperative treatment for lumbar disk herniation: the Spine Patient Outcomes Research Trial (SPORT): a randomized trial.
papers.review_depth: Full text reviewed, not supplementary appendix
missing_or_discrepant_fields: Results say primary-outcome effects were not significant at any time point, but Table 5 ODI at 3 months is −4.7 (−9.3 to −0.2), which excludes zero (our P about 0.04).

Results say satisfaction and employment changes were not significant, but satisfaction with symptoms at 3 months is 11.3 (1.6 to 20.9), which excludes zero (our P about 0.02). The global P=.17 may be what is meant.

Results say the effect favors surgery for each measure at each point, and the Conclusion says all outcomes at all times; Table 5 work status favors nonoperative care at all three times (−5.6, −0.6, −2.2) and physical function at 2 years is 0. The Results text itself says employment favored nonoperative care.
Table 3 footnote says data were unavailable for 7 surgical patients, but 243 of 247 implies 4.

Table 3 denominators: length of stay and the postoperative rows (4 + 9 + 226) each sum to 239, not the stated 243; the printed percentages fit 239 (226/239 = 95%). L5-S1 145 of 243 is 60%, printed 61%.

Table 3 lists blood replacement 4 (2%), and the text says 2% needed transfusion, yet the postoperative footnote lists blood transfusion as not reported. Possibly intraoperative vs postoperative; not stated.
Table 1 nonoperative column: herniation level, herniation type and health trend each sum to 239, not 240. Table 4 levels sum to 132 for the 133 nonoperative patients without surgery.
Table 2 devices 'None' 216 of 323 is 67%, printed 68%.

Sensitivity analysis paragraph promises 4 methods; the wording names simple means, baseline and last value carried forward, and an adjusted mixed model, and attributes the mixed model to 'the latter' single-imputation method. Ambiguous.

Table 4 is titled as significant characteristics, but several rows are not significant in one arm (for example age P=.21 and leg-raise P=.11 in the nonoperative arm); rows appear significant in at least one arm.

Figure 1 surgery percentages use analyzed denominators (232, 240), not randomized (245, 256); over randomized patients the 2-year figures are 57% and 42% (ours). Stated in the footnote, but the abstract's 50% and 30% inherit it.
The as-treated model adjusted for baseline predictors of missing data or treatment received, but the paper does not list them.
Power: no SD is given for the 10-point target, so 250 per group cannot be checked; our back-calculation implies an SD of change near 33 to 37.

Checks that passed: flow diagram arithmetic in every box; Table 1 percentages and P values (none below 0.05 on our recomputation); Table 4 percentages, pooled means and P values; Table 5 differences within rounding and every interval consistent with the arm SEs; as-treated interval midpoints; Comment figures against Table 5.

papers.label: Peul: timing of discectomy
papers.design: Multicenter randomized trial (nine hospitals); patients and research nurses not blinded
papers.population: Age 18–65 with radiologically confirmed disk herniation and incapacitating lumbosacral radicular syndrome for 6–12 weeks. Cauda equina syndrome, paralysis and strength below antigravity were excluded.
papers.endpoint: Roland Disability Questionnaire, leg-pain VAS and Likert perceived recovery during the first year
papers.finding: Early surgery accelerated leg-pain relief and perceived recovery. Disability over the first year did not differ significantly, and 1-year outcomes were similar to a strategy of prolonged conservative care with surgery if needed.
papers.numbers: Surgery: 89% early (mean 2.2 weeks) vs 39% conservative (mean 18.7 weeks). Roland AUC P = 0.13; leg-pain AUC P<0.001. Median time to recovery 4.0 vs 12.1 weeks; reported HR 1.97 (95% CI 1.72–2.22). Perceived recovery at 1 year: 95% in both groups.
papers.caveat: The comparator was a treatment strategy allowing delayed surgery, and research-nurse support did not reflect usual care. Paralysis and strength below antigravity were excluded, and group results for the repeat neurologic examination are not reported, so these findings do not establish that waiting is appropriate for every neurological presentation. Patients and nurses were not blinded.
papers.discussion: For 6–12-week sciatica, the major advantage of early surgery is faster relief of sciatica, not a better 1-year result.
papers.title: Surgery versus prolonged conservative treatment for sciatica.
papers.review_depth: Full text reviewed, not supplementary appendix
missing_or_discrepant_fields: Table 1 says no significant baseline differences, but ankle reflex is 53% vs 75% (our chi-square P about 0.0001).
Table 1 suspected level, conservative group: 5 + 57 + 83 = 145 with N = 142; percentages add to 102.
Fig. 1: 141 less 1 and 3 lost is 137 but 140 assessed; 142 less 1 and 2 lost is 139 but 141 assessed.
HR 1.97 (1.72–2.22) is symmetric on the linear scale and looks too narrow; our estimate is about 1.55–2.50. Unresolved.
Median recovery CIs differ, text vs Fig. 3 legend: 3.7–4.4 vs 3.7–4.3 early; 9.5–14.9 vs 9.5–14.8 conservative.
Fig. 3 % difference row does not reconcile with counts: 6 vs 8 without recovery, but 6 (0.1–12.0) printed. Censoring may explain part.

Table 2 intervals look misprinted: Prolo functional 8 wk −0.8 (−1.1 to 0.6) despite P<0.001; VAS general health 8 wk −12.0 (−18.8 to 5.3); SFBI frequency 26 wk 1.8 (0.7 to 1.9); SFBI bothersomeness 26 wk 1.2 (0.1 to 1.3).
Table 2 Roland at 2 weeks: 14.4 vs 13.0 gives −1.4, but −1.6 is printed.
Primary outcomes differ: Abstract and Methods name three; Table 2 lists back-pain VAS as a fourth.
Back pain: Fig. 2 AUC P = 0.14 vs Table 2 footnote P = 0.045. Roland: AUC P = 0.13 vs Table 2 P = 0.12. Not reconciled.
Trial powered on 3 Roland points, but the Discussion uses a 4-point MCID.
Power assumes SD 10, while baseline Roland SD was about 4; a simple two-sample calculation with SD 10 needs about 233 per group, not 140 (ours). Reference 11 not reviewed.
Fig. 4 vs Table 1 subgroup proportions: crossed straight-leg raising 59% vs about 50%; L5–S1 61% vs about 53%.
Complications given as 1.6% of surgical patients, but 3 of 180 is 1.7%.
Discussion cites references 22–24 for Weber, but reference 23 is the CONSORT statement.
'Relief twice as fast' follows the hazard ratio, while medians differ threefold; both medians sit on visit weeks (ours).
Methods says nine participating hospitals; the Appendix lists 10.
Fig. 2 title says mean (±SE); legend says the bars are 95% CIs.

papers.label: Bailey: persistent sciatica
papers.design: Single-center randomized trial (London, Ontario); permuted blocks stratified by workers' compensation; blinding not described
papers.population: Age 18–60 with unilateral sciatica for 4–12 months and posterolateral L4–L5 or L5–S1 herniation compressing the matching root. Patients already treated with epidural injection or ongoing exercise-based physiotherapy for the episode were excluded.
papers.endpoint: Leg-pain intensity on a 0–10 visual analogue scale at 6 months
papers.finding: Microdiscectomy produced lower leg pain at 6 months than another 6 months of standardized nonoperative treatment.
papers.numbers: 6-month leg pain: 2.8 versus 5.2; adjusted difference 2.4 points, 95% CI 1.4–3.4. Crossover: 22 of 64 (34%) nonsurgical patients had surgery, median 11 months; 2 before 6 months. Primary-outcome follow-up 80% and 84%.
papers.caveat: Single center, with up to 20% of primary data missing and no description of blinding. Patients who had already had injections or structured physiotherapy were excluded. Secondary and 1-year outcomes had no multiplicity plan. Distinguish this population from Peul's earlier sciatica cohort.
papers.discussion: The evidence for waiting changes when concordant sciatica has already persisted for several months.
papers.title: Surgery versus Conservative Care for Persistent Sciatica Lasting 4 to 12 Months.
papers.review_depth: Full text reviewed, not supplementary appendix
missing_or_discrepant_fields: Table 2 gives 54 nonsurgical patients for 12-month leg pain; Fig. 1 and every other 12-month row give 47.
Statistical Analysis says 'beta level of 0.80'; this should be power 0.80 (beta 0.20).
Fig. 1 excludes 18 for symptoms '>13 mo', while the inclusion window is 4–12 months.
Conclusions say sciatica 'lasting more than 4 months'; the criterion was 4 to 12 months.

Binary secondary outcomes (satisfaction, employment): printed 95% CIs are about 1.6 times wider than the group SEs imply. Satisfaction at 6 mo from SEs is about −35 to −6 (ours), printed −43.4 to 2.2. Unexplained.
Table 1 nonsurgical BMI SD 10.5 against 5.6 surgical; possible outlier or error (ours).
Abstract spells 'Owestry Disability Index'.
Table 3 footnote says the 20 late crossovers were 'included in the primary analysis', but all 64 per group were analyzed by intention to treat.
Results say 34% of screening-visit exclusions lacked an L4–L5 or L5–S1 posterolateral herniation on MRI; Fig. 1 labels those 70 'MRI did not match clinical symptoms or bilateral radiculopathy'.

papers.label: SPORT lumbar stenosis
papers.design: Multicenter study at 13 US spine centers: a randomized cohort plus a concurrent observational cohort of patients who declined randomization
papers.population: Surgical candidates with neurogenic claudication or radicular leg symptoms for at least 12 weeks and imaging-confirmed stenosis; degenerative spondylolisthesis and instability excluded. Mean age 65.
papers.endpoint: SF-36 bodily pain and physical function, and modified ODI
papers.finding: By intention to treat, surgery improved SF-36 bodily pain at 2 years but not physical function or ODI. The adjusted as-treated analysis combining both cohorts favored surgery on all primary outcomes from 6 weeks through 2 years.
papers.numbers: 289 randomized (138 surgery, 151 nonsurgical) plus 365 observational. Surgery by 2 years: 67% vs 43% of randomized groups. 2-year ITT: bodily pain 7.8 (95% CI 1.5 to 14.1), physical function 0.1 (-6.4 to 6.5), ODI -3.5 (-8.7 to 1.7). 2-year as-treated: bodily pain 13.6 (10.0 to 17.2), physical function 11.1 (7.6 to 14.7), ODI -11.2 (-14.1 to -8.3). Reoperation 8% by 2 years.
papers.caveat: The as-treated result is observational: patients who had surgery were worse at baseline and preferred surgery, and the listed adjustment covariates omit treatment preference. Randomized enrollment fell short of the planned 185 per group. This supports decompression for selected symptomatic stenosis; it does not establish a fusion indication or benefit for an incidental narrow canal.
papers.discussion: SPORT supports surgery for a concordant symptomatic syndrome, with the crossover limitation stated explicitly.
papers.title: Surgical versus nonsurgical therapy for lumbar spinal stenosis.
papers.review_depth: Full text reviewed, not supplementary appendix
missing_or_discrepant_fields: Deaths: the text reports 13 deaths by 2 years (7 nonsurgical, 6 surgical), but Figure 1 cumulative deaths sum to 10 (3 + 4 + 2 + 1). Not reconciled in the paper.
The Discussion says the only baseline cohort differences besides treatment preference were nerve-root tension signs and stenosis location; Table 1 also shows non-Hispanic 93% vs 97% (P = 0.03).
The abstract says the as-treated advantage was significant by 3 months; Table 4 shows significant as-treated effects on all three primary outcomes at 6 weeks, as the Discussion states.
The 1.3% 1-year reoperation rate for recurrent stenosis comes from a Table 2 category that also includes progressive spondylolisthesis (5 of 396).

Some Table 1 categorical rows do not sum to their column N, with no missing-data footnote: self-assessed health trend 273 of 278 randomized, 354 of 356 observational, 387 of 394 surgical; treatment preference 277 of 278 randomized, 239 of 240 nonsurgical.

papers.label: SPORT degenerative slip: 8 years
papers.design: Randomized and concurrent observational cohorts
papers.population: Surgical candidates with degenerative spondylolisthesis on standing films, stenosis and at least 12 weeks of symptoms; 304 randomized and 303 in an observational cohort.
papers.endpoint: SF-36 bodily pain and physical function, and ODI
papers.finding: As-treated analyses favored surgery on all primary outcomes through 8 years. Intention-to-treat analysis instead favored nonoperative care on ODI (global P=0.039), with no significant global difference on bodily pain or physical function, a result the authors find hard to interpret given crossover.
papers.numbers: As-treated 8-year effects: ODI -10.3 (95% CI -13.6 to -6.9), bodily pain 11.8 (7.2 to 16.4), physical function 10.3 (5.9 to 14.7). 54% assigned nonoperative care had surgery; 28% assigned surgery did not. 8-year reoperation 22%. Data at 8 years for 69% of randomized and 57% of observational patients; the Results text separately gives 337 of 601 (56%) remaining.
papers.caveat: This compares surgery with nonoperative care, not fusion with no fusion: only 7% of surgical patients had decompression alone. Crossover and attrition limit causal claims, and the authors warn that loss of poorly performing surgical patients may overestimate benefit. Fusion technique was not randomized. Instrumented posterolateral fusion was reported better than 360-degree fusion on physical function (P=0.022). Assuming independent estimates, the printed intervals do not reconcile that with P=0.062 for uninstrumented fusion vs 360, the larger gap; covariance is unknown.
papers.discussion: SPORT addresses whether to operate; NORDSTEN addresses whether to add fusion. Its 8-year as-treated advantage should be quoted alongside the opposite intention-to-treat ODI result.
papers.title: Long-Term Results of Surgery Compared With Nonoperative Treatment for Lumbar Degenerative Spondylolisthesis in the Spine Patient Outcomes Research Trial (SPORT).
papers.review_depth: Full text reviewed, not supplementary appendix
missing_or_discrepant_fields: Retention conflict: Fig. 1 shows 385 seen at 8 years (107+104+104+70), matching the abstract's 69% and 57% and pooling to 63% of 607. Results and Table 2 give 337 of 601 (56%) remaining and 264 lost. Not reconciled.
Deaths conflict: Results give 50 (33 + 17); Fig. 1 8-year boxes give 46 (8+10+17+11).
Fig. 1, observational surgery, 8 years: 104+7+42+17 = 170, not 173. All other boxes sum correctly.

Time-weighted physical function, text and Fig. 3: PPS 24.5 (21.7-27.3) vs 360 18 (11.6-24.4), P=0.022; PLF 26.8 (21.6-32) vs 360, P=0.062. The two P values are hard to reconcile under the printed intervals. Treating estimates as independent, we get about P=0.07 and P=0.04. P=0.022 needs SE about 2.8 vs 3.6 independent, ratio 0.80, inside the 0.77 to 0.88 seen in Table 3, so positive covariance could explain it. P=0.062 needs SE about 4.7 vs 4.2 independent, ratio 1.12, which positive covariance cannot produce. PLF vs PPS (P=0.46) does reproduce. Covariance is unknown; unresolved.
Table 1: leg pain bothersomeness row has XX placeholders for the PLF, PPS, 360 columns and P value. May be limited to the author manuscript.
Abstract says as-treated surgery was better at all time points; Results state years 6, 7 and 8 plus the global test. The rest is in Supplemental Table 1, not reviewed.
Abstract conclusion omits that the ITT global ODI result favored nonoperative care (P=0.039).
Fig. 2 caption says combined cohort, but the panels show randomized and observational cohorts separately.

Methods promise Kaplan-Meier reoperation rates compared by log-rank for randomized and observational cohorts; these are not reported. Results give only 22% (91/406), which is the crude fraction, while Table 4 labels its rates Kaplan-Meier.
Table 4 reoperation reasons sum to 25 for PLF against 20 reoperated, 44 for PPS against 43, and 16 for 360 against 17. Overlap could explain PLF and PPS, not 360.

Table 4 denominators shift and are not stated. 360 column: header n=71, but levels decompressed sum to 68; 17 (26%) and 19 (29%) imply 65, while 65 (96%) implies 68. PPS: 113 (52%) implies about 217, while 216 (97%) fits 222. L4-L5 P=0.77 reproduces only with 68 (P=0.095 with 71).

Adjustment lists differ: Results include osteoporosis, symptom duration and treatment preference; Table 3 footnote omits them and adds stomach problem. Table 3 is the 2-year analysis, so this may be intended, but the paper does not say.
Reference 25, cited for age and sex specific mortality, is a Medicare fusion cohort paper; the citation looks misnumbered (our reading).

Table 1 footnote points to Table 2 for 8-year surgery counts, which are in Table 4. Fusion Technique text reads '10 degrees of rotation of 4 mm' where Table 1 footnote gives '10 degrees of angulation or more than 4 mm'.

Table 3 intervals do not fit the printed SEs if estimates are independent. CI-implied SE vs independent SE: BP 1.33 vs 1.56 and 1.68 vs 1.91; PF 1.28 vs 1.56 and 1.61 vs 1.91; ODI 0.99 vs 1.28 and 1.28 vs 1.49; SBI 0.36 vs 0.42 and 0.46 vs 0.57. All 8 are narrower (ratio 0.77 to 0.88). Positive model covariance is a likely explanation (our reading).

Methods say baseline variables associated with missing data or treatment received were adjusted for. The Results list and Table 3 footnote do not name compensation (9% vs 3%, P=0.008 by treatment; 9% vs 4%, P=0.014 by retention), education (P=0.021 by retention), diabetes (P=0.043) or heart problem (P=0.004). The 'other comorbidities' footnote names neither diabetes nor heart problem.
No baseline table by randomized assignment: Table 1 compares as-treated and fusion groups, Table 2 retained vs lost. Balance of the 159 vs 145 arms cannot be checked in this paper.
Fusion comparisons were hierarchical, pairwise only after an overall test at p<0.10, but the overall results are not given, while Fig. 3 prints pairwise P values for every outcome.

Checks that passed: flow totals (1,164-272=892; 892-285=607; surgery counts 412, 345), Table 1 and 2 P values on our recomputation, Table 3 differences and interaction P values, 8-year effect CIs, surgical percentages.

papers.label: SLIP
papers.design: Randomized trial
papers.population: Age 50-80 with single-level grade I degenerative slip (3-14 mm), stenosis and neurogenic claudication. Excluded motion over 3 mm, surgeon-judged mechanical back pain, prior lumbar surgery and ASA IV or higher.
papers.endpoint: Change in SF-36 physical component score at 2 years; ODI secondary
papers.finding: Fusion improved the primary SF-36 endpoint and reduced reoperation, but the 2-year SF-36 difference was not significant after adjusting for baseline differences. ODI change did not differ significantly.
papers.numbers: SF-36 gain 15.2 fusion vs 9.5, difference 5.7 (95% CI 0.1-11.3, P=0.046); baseline-adjusted 3.9 (-1.9 to 9.7, P=0.19). ODI change -26.3 vs -17.9 (P=0.06). Reoperation 14% vs 34% (P=0.05), all index-level instability after decompression and all adjacent-level after fusion. Blood loss 514 vs 83 mL.
papers.caveat: 66 randomized, 51 from one site, 68% followed at 4 years, and no multiplicity adjustment. Decompression was complete laminectomy with partial medial facet removal, so it does not test midline-preserving surgery. Reoperation was at surgeon discretion.
papers.discussion: SLIP favored fusion on SF-36 and reoperation, but the effect lost significance after baseline adjustment and came from 66 patients.

papers.label: Swedish Spinal Stenosis Study
papers.design: Multicenter open-label randomized superiority trial (seven Swedish hospitals), stratified by slip; per-protocol primary analysis
papers.population: Age 50-80 with pseudoclaudication and back pain (VAS over 30) for over 6 months and 1 or 2 adjacent stenotic levels (dural sac 75 mm2 or less); 135 of 247 had a slip of at least 3 mm. Excluded spondylolysis, scoliosis over 20 degrees and prior surgery for stenosis or instability. No flexion-extension films.
papers.endpoint: ODI at 2 years
papers.followup: 2 years; 5 years in 138 of 144 eligible patients; additional surgery at mean 6.5 years
papers.finding: Adding fusion did not improve 2-year clinical outcomes, including in the stratified slip group, and it increased operative burden and cost.
papers.numbers: 2-year ODI 27 vs 24 decompression (P=0.24); difference in change -2 (95% CI -7 to 3). Slip of 7.4 mm or more: ODI 25 in both arms (post hoc). Stay 7.4 vs 4.1 days. Direct cost about $6,800 higher with fusion. Reoperation by 2 years 17 vs 13, for adjacent-level stenosis 11 vs 1. Additional surgery 22% vs 21% at mean 6.5 years.
papers.caveat: Superiority design, so a nonsignificant result alone does not prove equivalence. Our reading: the CI for the difference in change excludes the 12-point benefit the trial was powered for. Primary analysis was per protocol, leaving out 14 who did not receive assigned surgery (10 fusion, 4 decompression). Techniques were surgeon-chosen, and instability was not assessed. Table 3 P values and Table 2 slip counts do not fully reconcile. The 5-year data in this paper covered only part of the cohort; use the 2024 report for 5-year results.
papers.discussion: The Swedish trial challenges routine fusion for stenosis, including its slip stratum, but it never measured dynamic instability.
papers.title: A Randomized, Controlled Trial of Fusion Surgery for Lumbar Spinal Stenosis.
papers.review_depth: Full text reviewed, not supplementary appendix

papers.label: NORDSTEN-DS: 2 years
papers.design: Open-label multicenter randomized noninferiority trial (16 surgical departments, single country)
papers.population: Age 18-80 with stenosis and single-level slip of at least 3 mm on standing films after 3 months of conservative care, regardless of flexion-extension findings. Excluded grade 3 foraminal stenosis, prior surgery at that level, and fracture or fusion in the thoracolumbar region.
papers.endpoint: At least 30% reduction in ODI from baseline to 2 years; noninferiority margin -15 percentage points
papers.finding: Midline-preserving decompression alone met the noninferiority criterion against instrumented fusion in both required analyses.
papers.numbers: ODI responders 71.4% vs 72.9% fusion (difference -1.4, 95% CI -12.2 to 9.4); per protocol 75.5% each (-11.4 to 11.4); post hoc ITT -3.3 (-14.0 to 7.5). Margin 15 percentage points, about NNT 7. Surgery 104 vs 174 minutes; dural tears 5.3% vs 13.3%. Fusion confirmed in 86 of 100.
papers.caveat: The margin was chosen empirically, and the trial was open label with unblinded outcome assessors. Per-protocol analysis excluded reoperated patients, which may favor decompression. Reoperation was 12.5% vs 9.1% and not powered. Secondary intervals, including dural tears, were not adjusted for multiplicity. About 20% had dynamic instability, but no subgroup conclusions can be drawn.
papers.discussion: NORDSTEN supports decompression alone in its eligible single-level population within an empirically chosen noninferiority margin. It draws no conclusion for the roughly 20% with dynamic instability.
papers.title: Decompression with or without Fusion in Degenerative Lumbar Spondylolisthesis.

papers.label: NORDSTEN-DS: 5 years
papers.design: Randomized open-label noninferiority trial follow-up, 16 Norwegian clinics
papers.population: Age 18-80 with stenosis and single-level slip of at least 3 mm on standing films, regardless of signs of instability. Excluded scoliosis over 20 degrees, deformed nerve root in the foramen, prior surgery at that level, and fracture or fusion in the thoracolumbar region.
papers.endpoint: At least 30% reduction in ODI from baseline to 5 years; margin -15 percentage points
papers.finding: Decompression alone remained noninferior to instrumented fusion at 5 years. Total subsequent surgery was similar. First reoperations were more common after fusion before 3 months and from 2 to 5 years, and after decompression from 3 months to 2 years; no window differed significantly.
papers.numbers: ODI responders 63% each (difference 0.4, 95% CI -11.2 to 11.9); per protocol 65% vs 66% (-1.3, -14.5 to 12.2). Mean ODI change -17.8 in both arms. Subsequent surgery 16% vs 18%. First reoperation by table: 2 vs 7 before 3 months, 13 vs 5 from 3 months to 2 years, 6 vs 11 from 2 to 5 years. Dural tears 5% vs 13%.
papers.caveat: 15-point margin chosen empirically. Per-protocol lower bound of -14.5 sits close to it, that analysis was below its planned sample size, and it excluded all 44 reoperated patients. Open label. Not applicable to multilevel slips, scoliosis, severe foraminal stenosis or prior surgery at that level. Text gives early reoperations as 11 and 15, which conflicts with the table used here.
papers.discussion: At 5 years, NORDSTEN found 63% ODI responders in both arms with similar total reoperation. Timing shifted between windows without a significant difference.
papers.title: Decompression alone or with fusion for degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis (Nordsten-DS): five year follow-up of a randomised, multicentre, non-inferiority trial.
papers.review_depth: Full text reviewed, not supplementary appendix
missing_or_discrepant_fields: Reoperation text gives 11 and 15 by 2 years; the table gives 15 and 12 and matches the 5-year totals of 21 and 23. The table is used here.
PDF is reformatted PMC text: Figures 1 and 2, table footnotes, funding and competing-interest statements are absent. Flow and sensitivity results could not be checked against the figures.

Reoperations by 2 years: text 11 and 15; Table 3 gives 15 (2+13) and 12 (7+5). Only the table sums with 6 and 11 to the totals of 21 and 23, and the Discussion's 'slightly more reoperations in the decompression group during the first two years' agrees with it. The text's 11 and 15 are L08's 2-year counts (15 vs 11) reversed, a possible transposition (ours).
Conclusion says reoperation in about one in five in both groups; Table 3 gives 16% and 18% of participants. The 22% in each group is total operations per participant.
Abstract ODI difference 0.02 (-3.8 to 3.9) has the opposite sign to the text -0.02 (-3.9 to 3.8) and Table 2 -0.02 (-3.85 to 3.80).

Table 3 difference column changes direction: complication rows from dural tear to respiratory, and blood loss, run fusion minus decompression (dural tear +8), while surgery time, neurological and reoperation rows run decompression minus fusion.
Table 3 duration of surgery and stay 'SD' values (4.2, 6.15, 0.21, 0.23) are too small for SDs; surgery SE from them gives the printed interval (ours), so they look like standard errors.
Table 3 blood loss: 429 - 141 = 288, printed difference 292 (235 to 348).
Table 3 deep infection reoperation in fusion: 4/129, while other fusion rows at that stage use 125, and no difference is given.
Table 1 EQ-5D SD printed 3.0 in both groups; impossible on a -0.59 to 1.0 scale. Probably 0.30 (ours).
Table 1 smoker 24/130 is 18.5%, printed 19%.
Table 2 EQ-5D upper limit printed '073'. ODI fusion 39.6 to 21.9 is -17.7 by the printed means, -17.8 printed (rounding).
Results cite Table 2 for clinically meaningful improvement rates; they are in Table 3.
Abstract 230 (88%) uses 262; of 267 randomized it is 86%.

Missing data mostly reconcile, by our reading: 262 - 44 reoperated - 29 missing = 189, the printed per-protocol set (by arm 133 - 21 - 12 = 100, 129 - 23 - 17 = 89), so the text's 29 (3 baseline, 26 at 5 years) are patients not reoperated and its 7 (2 baseline, 5 at 5 years) are reoperated patients. Then 26 + 5 = 31 missing at 5 years vs 32 without 5-year data (7 died, 25 lost; 262 - 230), and 7 vs 6 reoperated missing (44 - 38, Table 3 denominators 18 + 20). Figure 1 needed to resolve those two.
Table 3 first reoperation denominators are 129, 120, 123 and 125, 121, 113. Decompression rises from 120 to 123, so these are not risk sets and the window percentages are not cumulative rates.

Modified ITT interval reproduces exactly from rounded imputed counts over full denominators (84/133 vs 81/129), though about 32 of 262 had no 5-year data. It appears to treat imputed patients as observed and may carry no between-imputation uncertainty, so -11.2 may be too narrow (ours). Imputation method is in the unread appendix.
Fig 1 legend says inclusion started 15 April 2014; Results say 12 February 2014.

Sample size of 116 per group cannot be reproduced: expected responder rate not stated here. With 95% two-sided CI and 80% power it implies about 80%; at the observed 63% it is about 163 per group (ours). Protocol not reviewed.
Discussion lists reference 15 (SLIP) among results recommending decompression alone, though it reports SLIP favored fusion.
Fig 1 legend cites Lee et al as reference 34; Lee is reference 39, and 34 is Shen.
Interim analysis described as 'at two years' when 150 had completed one-year follow-up; wording is unclear.
Swedish reoperation given as 22% vs 21% over five years; library records give that at mean 6.5 years (2016 report) and 22% vs 24% at 5 years (2024 report, not cited).

papers.label: Blumenthal: delayed instability
papers.design: Small prospective single-site cohort
papers.population: Age 50-80 with grade I degenerative slip (3-14 mm) treated by one surgeon with open facet-sparing laminectomy alone. Excluded motion over 3 mm, mechanical back pain, prior lumbar surgery and ASA III or higher.
papers.endpoint: Reoperation for presumed instability
papers.finding: Motion at the slip was the only significant predictor of reoperation. Disc height and facet angle stayed in a permissive stepwise model without reaching significance.
papers.numbers: 15 of 40 reoperated (37.5%). Model: motion in mm OR 2.65 (95% CI 1.08-6.46, P=0.033); disc height over 6.5 mm OR 4.10 (0.75-22.31, P=0.102); facet angle in 3 bands OR 2.83 (0.60-13.29, P=0.187). Reoperation with motion over 1.25 mm 54%, disc height over 6.5 mm 45%, facet angle over 50 degrees 39%. By risk-factor count: 0, 0%; 1, 38%; 2, 35%; 3, 75%. 3 vs 0 factors, P=0.14.
papers.caveat: Small single-surgeon cohort with no fusion arm, a stepwise threshold of P=0.35 and no stated reoperation criteria. Reoperation was for mechanical back pain presumed to be instability. The motion and facet cutoffs were not the variables modeled, and group sizes are not printed; the 75% vs 0% probably rests on 3 of 4 vs 0 of 3 (our reconstruction). Shares SLIP's trial registration, site and period, so patients probably overlap. These cutoffs are not validated fusion indications.
papers.discussion: The instability markers are hypotheses from 40 patients; only motion reached significance, and the combined comparison did not.
papers.title: Radiographic predictors of delayed instability following decompression without fusion for degenerative grade I lumbar spondylolisthesis.
papers.review_depth: Full text reviewed, not supplementary appendix
missing_or_discrepant_fields: Same trial registration as SLIP (NCT00109213), with an overlapping site and period; cohort overlap is likely but not stated.
Fig. 1 legend gives 1.46 degrees of motion, but panels A and B read 9.66 and 11.12 mm, a difference of 1.46 mm. The unit should be mm.

Table 2 enters motion in mm, disc height as a binary and facet angle in 3 bands, while the text reports rates by cutoffs. No test of the 1.25 mm or 50-degree cutoff is printed, and their source is not given.

The Abstract, Discussion and Conclusions call all 3 variables predictors or risk factors, but disc height (P=0.102), facet angle (P=0.187) and the 3 vs 0 factor comparison (P=0.14) are not significant at the paper's own 0.05 level.

Fig. 2 prints no group sizes, and the test behind P=0.14 is not named. Only 4 whole-number splits fit; 0 of 3 vs 3 of 4 gives Fisher P=0.143 (ours), though Methods list chi-square rather than Fisher. Four-group chi-square on this split is about 0.24 (ours).
Fig. 2 is not monotonic: 2 factors 35% is below 1 factor 38%.
Facet angle over 50 degrees gives 39% against an overall 37.5%, little difference for a stated risk factor.
Abstract says pain 'caused by instability'; Results say 'presumably caused'. No radiographic definition of instability is given.
Discussion says 3 risk factors carried a 75% chance of delayed instability; the measured outcome was reoperation.
'No CSF leaks in either group' appears in a single-arm paper.
Methods say 2 independent neuroradiologists confirmed eligibility, then 2 independent radiologists plus the surgeon made the measurements; the roles are not clear.

Results call baseline groups similar apart from motion, but facet angle is borderline: 54.7 vs 61.9 degrees, our t test P about 0.06. Sex also differs: 68.0% vs 86.7% female, no P printed, our chi-square P about 0.19, Fisher 0.27.
Fig. 3 is labeled total population with no numbers at risk and no statement that patients were removed after fusion, so laminectomy durability may be mixed with fusion results (ours).
Error bars in Figs. 3-5 are undefined and visit numbers are not printed. Baseline bars match SE from Table 1, and on that reading Fig. 4's identical ODI P=0.094 at 3 and 6 months is plausible (ours).
'Delayed' instability includes 4 of 15 reoperated within 6 months, which we consider early (ours).
Mean follow-up 3.6 years is called long-term, with no minimum stated; enrollment ran to September 2009 and the paper was submitted May 2012.

papers.label: MRC spine stabilization trial
papers.design: Pragmatic multicentre randomised trial, 15 UK centres
papers.population: Age 18–55 with over 12 months of chronic low back pain, considered fusion candidates, where surgeon and patient were uncertain which treatment was best; 81% chronic low back pain, 11% spondylolisthesis, 8% post-laminectomy.
papers.endpoint: Co-primary: Oswestry disability index and shuttle walking test at 24 months
papers.finding: Surgery (mostly fusion) gave a small Oswestry advantage over intensive rehabilitation at 2 years; the shuttle walking test and SF-36 did not differ, and both groups improved.
papers.numbers: Oswestry difference −4.1 points, 95% CI −8.1 to −0.1, P=0.045 (−4.5 after imputation). Shuttle walk 34 m, 95% CI −8 to 77. 48 of 173 (28%) rehabilitation patients had surgery by 2 years.
papers.caveat: Rehabilitation was a 75-hour programme with cognitive behavioural principles, not routine physiotherapy. About 15% of the surgery arm was planned Graf flexible stabilisation. Assessors were not blinded, crossover was large, and 19% lacked a 24-month Oswestry.
papers.discussion: For chronic axial pain, the quality of the nonsurgical comparator substantially changes the fusion argument.
papers.title: Randomised controlled trial to compare surgical stabilisation of the lumbar spine with an intensive rehabilitation programme for patients with chronic low back pain: the MRC spine stabilisation trial.
papers.review_depth: Full text reviewed, not supplementary appendix
missing_or_discrepant_fields: Discussion says the confidence intervals rule out Oswestry differences of more than 10 points favouring surgery and more than 2 points favouring rehabilitation, but the reported interval (−8.1 to −0.1) rules out more than 8.1 for surgery and any benefit for rehabilitation.
Shuttle walking test numbers at 24 months differ: flow diagram 119 and 127, Table 4 118 and 126.
The sentence that the Swedish trial showed no difference between three fusion techniques cites reference 24 (European guidelines); reference 20 is the Swedish technique trial.

The abstract (Objectives, Intervention) and the 'What this study adds' box describe fusion, but the surgery arm included flexible stabilisation (Graf), planned for 27 of 176. The title correctly says surgical stabilisation.
Discussion gives 20% loss to follow-up at 24 months; that matches the Oswestry (65 of 349, 19%), but about 30% lacked the co-primary shuttle walking test.
Text calls the 19 complications intraoperative, while Table 3 also includes a systemic haemorrhage and further surgery.

No baseline comparisons are reported; our tests suggest imbalance in the four-category DRAM distribution (P about 0.03; distressed-depressive versus the rest alone, P about 0.09), somatic perception score (P about 0.05) and SF-36 physical functioning (P about 0.008, assuming all patients contributed).
Table 5 header reads '(% CI)' for the imputed analyses and gives Oswestry P as 0.04 against 0.045 elsewhere.

Table 1 percentages are slightly off: 66 of 173 (printed 38.1, computes 38.2), 142 of 176 (printed 80.6, computes 80.7), surgery 'had to change job' 19 of 149 (printed 12.7, computes 12.75, so 12.8 by the table's own half-up rounding) and rehabilitation 'had to reduce hours' 12 of 149 (printed 8.0, computes 8.05, so 8.1).
The page header DOI ends .BF while the article footer gives .8F.
Introduction says US fusions rose from about 11 000 a year in 1996 to 37 000 in 2001, 'a 336% increase'; that is a 236% increase (3.4-fold).

Table 2 further-treatment percentages (97, 55.1%; 68, 39.3%) use all randomised patients, although only those who received their allocated treatment (139 and 151) could have further treatment; among them the rates are 70% and 45%. The denominator is not stated.

Table 4 adjusted differences imply implausible baseline slopes (about 1.1 to 1.3) for Oswestry (−2.1 raw at 24 months, +1.7 at baseline, −4.1 adjusted), shuttle (+42, +7, +34) and SF-36 physical component (+1.2, −0.6, +2.0), so completers' baselines must differ from Table 1, and they are not reported.

papers.label: Swedish Lumbar Spine Study
papers.design: Multicenter randomized trial, 19 Swedish centers; three fusion arms pooled against one nonsurgical arm (222 vs 72)
papers.population: Age 25-65, back pain at least 2 years and worse than leg pain, no root compression, at least 1 year of sick leave or equivalent disability, degeneration at L4-L5 and/or L5-S1.
papers.endpoint: Back pain VAS, disability (Oswestry, Million, General Function Score), patient global rating and return to work at 2 years
papers.finding: Fusion reduced back pain and disability more than nonstandardized physical therapy at 2 years in this selected cohort, but rarely cured.
papers.numbers: Back pain VAS 64 to 43 (-33%) vs 63 to 58 (-7%), P=0.0002; Oswestry 47 to 36 vs 48 to 46, P=0.015; much better or better 63% vs 29%. Early complications 17%; reoperation 16 of 211.
papers.caveat: The nonsurgical arm was unstandardized physical therapy, which critics, including the invited commentary, call the same care patients had failed; the authors reply that special rehabilitation was started because of the study in 46% of cases. It was not MRC-style intensive rehabilitation. No blinding was described, 1990s techniques were used, and Acromed, maker of the screws used, helped fund it.
papers.discussion: Apparently conflicting fusion trials can partly reflect the care offered to the control group.
papers.title: 2001 Volvo Award Winner in Clinical Studies: Lumbar fusion versus nonsurgical treatment for chronic low back pain: a multicenter randomized controlled trial from the Swedish Lumbar Spine Study Group.
papers.review_depth: Full text reviewed, not supplementary appendix
missing_or_discrepant_fields: The abstract says 294 patients were randomized; the Results and Figure 1 say 310 were randomized and 16 were excluded afterwards, without stating their arms.
Table 3: nonsurgical leg pain change is printed as -20.5% (text: worsened by 21%), but the printed means 35.6 to 42.6 give -19.7%.
Unintended reoperation is given as 16 of 211 (7.8%); 16/211 is 7.6%.
Early complication rate is 17% in the abstract and Discussion but 18% (37/211) in the Table 7 footnote; 37/211 is 17.5%.
The fusion-definition paragraph refers to Groups 1, 2 and 3, but the surgical arms are 1a, 1b and 1c and Group 2 is nonsurgical.
Work status: the text says the chi-square test was used; the Table 6 footnote says Fisher's exact test. Table 6 prints 57% for 27 of 48 (56%).

Litigation subgroup P values (0.085 surgical, 0.043 nonsurgical) could not be reproduced from the printed counts (47/67 vs 57/98; 10/20 vs 6/34) with Fisher or chi-square tests; the test is not named.
Table 3, 4 and 5 results exclude group changers and dropouts, while their P values include group changers, so the displayed figures are not the intention-to-treat comparison.

Dropout accounting: the Table 8 footnote says dropouts (1 surgical, 1 nonsurgical) were excluded from the group-changer analysis, but the text says all group changers were examined at 2 years, the abstract says 289 were examined including 25 changers, and the Table 3 footnote counts dropouts separately from changers (18+3, 7+2).

Table 2: Fisher P values recompute as NS for all rows and P=0.020 for comorbidity (84/215 vs 16/68), but some percentages cannot come from the stated denominators with no missing values listed: sick leave 58.8% of 222 (130/222 = 58.6%, 131/222 = 59.0%); nonsurgical litigation 64.5% of 72 (46/72 = 63.9%, 47/72 = 65.3%); nonsurgical working 23.6% equals 17/72, not a value from the 56 left after excluding 16 pensioners as footnote requires (13/56 = 23.2%, 14/56 = 25.0%). Surgical working 20.9% = 37/177 follows the footnote.
The abstract gives nonsurgical Zung as 39 to 36, but Table 3 gives 36.7, which rounds to 37.
The Discussion gives 5% (6/121) of surgical patients rating much better or better who would not repeat treatment, but 122/195 rated so (Table 4, abstract).

Work-status exclusion: the Methods exclude only patients on full disability pension; the Results exclude full or supplementary disability pension (47/222, 16/72); Table 2 gives disability pension as 20.3% of 222, which is 45, not 47.

papers.label: AO Spine: when to decompress or fuse
papers.design: Expert-selected literature review and recommendations
papers.population: Degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis literature.
papers.endpoint: Critical appraisal of treatment comparisons and selection
papers.finding: AO concludes that no single statement fits all patients and that both decompression alone and decompression with fusion can be considered, ideally reserving fusion for patients whose instability justifies it.
papers.numbers: Six articles appraised: 3 trials, 2 meta-analyses and 1 radiographic cohort. Evidence rated High for NORDSTEN, Moderate for SLIP and the Swedish trial, and Low for the others. Recommendations for individual papers are conditional.
papers.caveat: Expert selection with no stated search method or single grading framework across the six papers, not a systematic guideline. It omits the full Swedish 5-year report and SLIP's baseline-adjusted result, calls disc height and facet angle significant though only motion was, and says midline structures were not preserved in NORDSTEN fusion cases, though the trial made this optional and 58 of 128 preserved them. Its evidence label for Blumenthal is internally inconsistent. Published erratum corrected the title.
papers.discussion: AO's 2025 synthesis is a useful map of the debate, but its strong statement is only that both options can be considered.
papers.title: AO Spine Clinical Practice Recommendations for the Surgical Management of Degenerative Spondylolisthesis: When to Decompress Alone and When to Fuse.
papers.review_depth: Full text reviewed, not supplementary appendix
missing_or_discrepant_fields: Rates Blumenthal both "very low" and "Low". Says NORDSTEN fusion cases did not preserve midline structures; the trial made this optional.
Blumenthal evidence is called 'very low' in the Methodological Review and 'Low' in the recommendation.
Blumenthal is called prospective in the summary and 'level 4 retrospective' later; AO's reason, a single arm with no control, does not make a study retrospective (ours).
Calls motion, disc height and facet angle 'significant risk factors'; the L10 record shows only motion was (P=0.033 vs 0.102 and 0.187), and all three vs none was P=0.14.
'At least one parameter' giving 39%-54% relabels rates reported for each single factor (ours).

Shukla stable-subgroup reoperation OR 0.53 (0.28, 1.29), P=0.063: the log midpoint is about 0.60 and the printed values imply P near 0.10 or higher. An upper limit of 1.02 would fit (ours). Shukla not reviewed.
SLIP is reported at P=0.046 without the 2-year baseline-adjusted 3.9 (-1.9 to 9.7, P=0.19) in the L06 record.
SLIP sample size is called sufficient, though AO states it was sized for 7.5 points and reports 5.7 (ours).

'51 out of 106' enrolled at one SLIP site; the L06 record ties 51 to the 66 randomized. AO's 66 randomized and 40-patient registry sum to 106, and the L06 paper calls the 51 a majority, which 48% is not, so this is likely a denominator mix-up (ours).
NORDSTEN fusion cases are said not to preserve midline structures; the L13 record notes this was optional and 58 of 128 preserved them.
NORDSTEN: only the per-protocol 75.5% in each arm is given, the analysis AO says likely favors decompression; L08 also has 71.4% vs 72.9%.

Discussion says SLIP and NORDSTEN report higher index-level reoperation with decompression alone. AO's NORDSTEN section gives overall reoperation, 12.5% vs 9.1% with CI -4.6 to 11.5, not significant, and L09 shows 16% vs 18% at 5 years.

Discussion says ODI showed no difference at final follow-up across the trials. SLIP's 2-year change of -26.3 vs -17.9 (P=0.06) is a near-miss in a small trial that this sentence smooths over, not a contradiction (ours).
Six Conditional recommendations become a 'strong recommendation' in the Conclusion, with no method given; the abstract does not use the word.
NORDSTEN first-choice wording (High evidence) and Shukla 'consider equally' (Low evidence) are not reconciled.
Methods describe both meta-analyses as RCTs and prospective cohorts, but AO later faults Shukla for level 4 retrospective cohorts.
Abstract says Shukla found no difference in raw scores and omits its main conclusion, which the Discussion uses.
Gadjradj is said to include all posterior techniques, then to have used 'only three different techniques' performed minimally invasively.
Gadjradj recommendation calls decompression 'non-inferior' with no margin, and cites 'post-operative instability' where the summary reports slip progression (ours).
Swedish 6-minute walk test is described as done at baseline and 2 years, then reported as unchanged at both 2 and 5 years.
Per-protocol primary analysis is praised in the Swedish trial and criticized in NORDSTEN (ours).
Spelling varies: Gadjradi and Gadjradj, Forsth and Försth; D + F and DF.

Swedish recommendation specifies predominant leg pain, but AO describes inclusion as pseudoclaudication plus back pain VAS over 30, reports no leg-predominant subgroup, and says severe mechanical back pain was not described (ours).

SLIP primary is given as 2-year SF-36, but AO later says 1-year and 2-year changes were both primary initially, the analysis strategy was developed after trial completion but before data examination, and 1 year showed no significant difference.
Blumenthal reoperation is printed as 37%; 15 of 40 is 37.5%.
Gadjradj's studies are 'low or unclear risk of selection bias' in the summary and 'relatively high risk of bias' in the review.
SLIP cites 'high dropout rates after 4 years', though follow-up stopped at 4 years.
Blumenthal is one of the six papers but is absent from the numbered reference list.

papers.label: Herkowitz and Kurz: historical fusion evidence
papers.design: Prospective comparative study with alternating allocation, not randomized; one surgeon did all operations
papers.population: Degenerative spondylolisthesis with stenosis at a single level and primary complaints of leg pain.
papers.endpoint: Pain and activity graded excellent to poor after decompression with or without arthrodesis; slip and motion on radiographs
papers.finding: The historical study favored adding intertransverse arthrodesis.
papers.numbers: As reported in the Vaccaro and Garfin 1997 critique, not checked against the primary paper: 25 patients per group; good-to-excellent results 24 of 25 with fusion versus 11 of 25 without; slip increased in 28% vs 96%; slip 4.8 to 5.3 mm vs 5.3 to 7.9 mm; pseudarthrosis on plain films in 36% (9 patients) of the fusion group.
papers.caveat: Historical decompression and noninstrumented fusion differ from modern midline-preserving decompression and instrumented constructs. Per the same critique, allocation was alternating rather than truly randomized, no patient was instrumented, and outcome used imprecise excellent-to-poor categories with no functional measure such as SF-36. The critique gives no complication or reoperation data.
papers.discussion: The original fusion rationale comes from different operations and a much smaller evidence base than today's trials.
papers.title: Degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis with spinal stenosis. A prospective study comparing decompression with decompression and intertransverse process arthrodesis.
papers.review_depth: Abstract plus secondary critique; primary full text unavailable
missing_or_discrepant_fields: The saved PDF is a two-page critique (Vaccaro and Garfin, Spine 1997;22:368-369), not Herkowitz and Kurz 1991. All recomputation below is of the critique's text; the primary paper remains unchecked.

Randomization is described inconsistently. Page 368 says the study is not a true randomized, controlled study and that patients were assigned alternately, yet also refers to the randomization process. Page 369 calls it a prospective, randomized analysis.

Page 368 reports no significant differences only for age and sex, then says the groups were well balanced on age, sex, radiographic variables, degree of stenosis, claudication severity and pain profiles. No baseline data are shown for stenosis, claudication or pain.

The critique calls the clinical advantage statistically significant but gives no P value. The only named test, Fisher exact, is attached to slip. Our Fisher recomputation: 24 of 25 vs 11 of 25, P about 0.0001; 7 of 25 vs 24 of 25, P under 0.00001. The second count is inferred from 96%, since the critique gives no count for that group. Printed percentages and counts are consistent: 7/25 = 28%, 9/25 = 36%.

Page 369 says correlation of slip and motion with pain attests that successful fusion leads to a better outcome, but also says a solid fusion is not necessary for a good result. With 9 pseudarthroses on plain films and only 1 fused patient below good, at least 8 of the 9 had good-to-excellent results. Ours: the first statement therefore cannot rest on radiographic union alone, but page 369 calls plain films a poor indicator, so this does not settle whether true bony union matters.

The grading categories are called narrowly defined and also imprecise, and are said to be not mutually exclusive or completely exhaustive. The example given shows only non-exhaustiveness; no overlap is demonstrated (ours). Poor is not defined in the critique.

Baseline tests cannot be recomputed: no SDs for any preoperative value and no age or sex data. Balance on slip, dynamic motion and angle is untestable from this source. Our bound with 25 per group: a t-test reaches P<0.05 only if SD is under about 0.88 mm for slip, 1.05 mm for dynamic motion and 0.53 degrees for angle.

Fused dynamic motion of 0.1 mm sits beside 4.2 degrees of angular motion and 36% pseudarthrosis. Our arithmetic: if motion cannot be negative, the 9 pseudarthrosis patients averaged at most 0.28 mm. No measurement error is given, so 0.1 mm cannot be distinguished from zero or checked. Other figures are plausible: follow-up mean 3 lies within 2.4 to 4, and a 0.5 mm rise with 7 slippers implies about 1.8 mm each if the rest were unchanged.
Page 369 says the study ideally should be redone with strict randomization and a fixation arm, then says it appears the data are clear on the necessity for an adjunctive fusion.

papers.label: AO Spine/CSRS DCM guideline
papers.design: Clinical practice guideline
papers.population: Mild, moderate and severe DCM; nonmyelopathic cord compression with or without radiculopathy.
papers.endpoint: Treatment recommendations by clinical category
papers.followup: Not applicable (guideline). Review planned at 3 to 5 years after publication.
papers.finding: Strongly recommends surgery for moderate and severe DCM. Weakly suggests surgery or a supervised trial of structured rehabilitation for mild DCM; if managed nonoperatively, recommends surgery for neurological deterioration and suggests it for failure to improve. Weakly suggests against prophylactic surgery for nonmyelopathic cord compression without radiculopathy, and suggests either surgery or nonoperative care when radiculopathy is present.
papers.numbers: Mild mJOA 15-17, moderate 12-14, severe ≤11. Evidence quality: severe and moderate, moderate; mild, very low to low; no radiculopathy, none (expert opinion); radiculopathy, low. mJOA gain after surgery in the one stratified study: severe 4.91, moderate 2.58, mild 1.29. Nonmyelopathic patients with cord compression or canal stenosis: myelopathy in 8% by 12 months and 22.6% at median 44 months. Symptomatic radiculopathy as a predictor of myelopathy: univariate RR 3.0 (95% CI 2.0-4.4).
papers.caveat: Nonmyelopathic compression without radiculopathy is a separate category, and its recommendation has no direct evidence (expert opinion, weak). Surgical effects are change from baseline, only one study stratified by severity, and complication rates were not reported by severity. No study compared surgery with observation in nonmyelopathic patients.
papers.discussion: The recommendation depends on clinical myelopathy severity, not simply the appearance of the MRI.
papers.title: A Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Patients With Degenerative Cervical Myelopathy: Recommendations for Patients With Mild, Moderate, and Severe Disease and Nonmyelopathic Patients With Evidence of Cord Compression.
papers.review_depth: Full text reviewed, not supplementary appendix
missing_or_discrepant_fields: PDF is a reformatted PMC copy with images omitted; published figures or tables, if any, not seen (PMC5684840).
Mild evidence grade conflicts: Summary says very low to low; Part 3 says very low. Part 3 rationale rates the nonoperative question very low or low and the operative question low.
Nurick changes said to exceed reported MCIDs (Parts 1-3), yet Part 3 says the Nurick MCID is not defined.

VAS 'SMDs' (32.74, 32.55, 40.00) look like raw points (our inference). mJOA or JOA figures (1.92, 1.40, 1.92) are SMDs in Part 1 but pooled mean improvements in Part 2; if raw, 1.92 is near the MCID (1.11-2.0), not the large effect cited for the moderate rating (our inference).
OR 0.72 (95% CI 0.66-0.92), reference 20, is well off the geometric center (about 0.78); likely transcription error (our inference).
Citation mismatches in this copy: Fehlings 18 is Tetreault; Tetreault 22 for mJOA MCID is Nouri on MRI; GRADE tool citation 8-11 includes Wu, an epidemiology study. Origin not determined.

Part 5 population allows clinical and/or electrophysiological radiculopathy; the recommendation says clinical evidence with or without electrophysiological confirmation. Isolated electrophysiological finding left unclear.

papers.label: Hills: T4–L1–hip axis
papers.design: Retrospective analysis of a prospective multicenter ISSG registry (15 centers, 2008-2019); targets derived and tested in the same cohort; Level III.
papers.population: 247 of 342 adults with ASD fused from T1-T5 to the sacrum or pelvis, with 2-year radiographs; median age 64, 82% female.
papers.endpoint: Mechanical failure within 2 years: severe PJK, displaced rod fracture, or reoperation for junctional failure, pseudarthrosis or rod fracture. Secondary: C2PA change and 1-year ODI and SRS-22r.
papers.followup: Failures counted to 2 years (median follow-up 3.1 years); PROMs at 1 year.
papers.finding: On 6-week films, failure risk was lowest with L1PA slightly above a PI-based normal and T4 stacked over L1, and rose with distance from those targets in either direction, adjusted for age. Higher 6-week C2PA went with worse 1-year ODI and SRS scores.
papers.numbers: 68 of 247 (28%) failed. Lowest risk at L1PA 0.5 x PI - 19 deg +/- 2 and T4-L1PA mismatch -3 to +1 deg. Failure 2 of 28 (7%) at both targets vs 23 of 46 (50%) with T4 ventral and L1PA undercorrected. aOR 7.0 (2.3-21.6) for L1PA deviation +14 vs +2; 7.2 (2.9-17.9) for mismatch +10 vs -1. Change in T4PA vs C2PA r2 0.96.
papers.caveat: Targets were found and tested in the same 247 patients, with only age adjusted and no validation. Osteotomy, PJK prophylaxis, prior fusion and bone density were not modelled, and 68 patients without 2-year films were excluded. Applies only to upper-thoracic-to-sacrum fusions.
papers.discussion: The T4-L1-hip axis gives two surgeon-controlled targets that fit these data well, but it is a hypothesis to validate, not proof that planning to it lowers failure.
papers.title: The T4-L1-Hip Axis: Sagittal Spinal Realignment Targets in Long-Construct Adult Spinal Deformity Surgery: Early Impact.
papers.review_depth: Full text reviewed, not supplementary appendix
missing_or_discrepant_fields: Figure 2-A caption gives the normal L1PA range for PI 47 as -1.5 to 6.5 degrees; the normal formula (0.5 x PI - 21) gives a single value of 2.5, and the target formula (0.5 x PI - 19 +/- 2) gives 2.5 to 6.5. The caption's range equals normal +/- 4, a tolerance the paper never defines for L1PA.

Methods (aim 2) measure the change in T4PA and L1PA from preop to 6 weeks and the change in C2PA from preop to final follow-up; the Figure 5 caption places the change in T4PA at final follow-up. The Results sentence and the abstract are ambiguous on this.
Discussion cites Figure 6 for T4PA predicting standing alignment; that result is in Figure 5 (Figure 6 shows PROMs).
Figure 3-B caption describes the age contrast as 50 versus 65 years; the plot is labelled 65 vs 50 (aOR 0.7, 0.4-1.2).

Failure-type counts differ: Table I lists pseudarthrosis or rod fracture 46 and junctional/PJK 30 (overlapping, total 68); Figure 4 bars assign one reason per patient, about 41 and 27. The rule for Figure 4 is not stated.

Model details are not reported: number of spline knots, degrees of freedom, interaction terms, discrimination or calibration, and any correction for overfitting. No confidence interval is given for the target bounds.
Number of patients with 1-year PROMs and the amount of imputed data are not reported.
Table III coefficients rounded to two decimals cannot be checked against their P values (e.g., age 0.01 (0.00, 0.02) printed with P 0.20 for Self-Image and 0.003 for Subscore).

Figure 3-B caption describes the aORs as deviation in L1PA or T4-L1PA mismatch 'versus normal alignment', but the plotted reference points are +2 (L1PA deviation) and -1 (mismatch), the target centres, not normal (0 and 0).

Abstract and Results say deviation from a normal L1PA in either direction raised failure risk, but the same sentences put minimum risk at a deviation of 0 to +4 (Figure 3-A minimum near +2), so a small positive deviation from normal lowered risk.

Body Conclusions state that realignment based on the targets 'carried a lower risk of mechanical failure', a stronger claim than the abstract's 'may lead to', tested in the same sample that derived the targets.

papers.label: Copay: MCID
papers.design: Review of prospectively collected PRO data comparing seven MCID calculation methods
papers.population: Lumbar surgery patients (88.5% fusion, mixed diagnoses) from 11 surgeons at three centers; 460 of 948 in the database, retained because they answered satisfaction questions. The abstract's n of 454 matches one analysis subset (see source problems).
papers.endpoint: Change from preoperative to 1 year in ODI, SF-36 PCS and 0-10 back and leg pain; anchors were the SF-36 health transition item and a satisfaction scale.
papers.finding: MCID thresholds varied about fivefold or more by calculation method in the same patients; the two anchors gave similar values. The authors chose the minimum detectable change (MDC) as the MCID.
papers.numbers: MDC adopted as MCID (HTI anchor): ODI 12.8, SF-36 PCS 4.9, back pain 1.2 and leg pain 1.6 (0-10 scales). ODI candidates ranged 2.9 to 15.4 (HTI). About half of patients reached the MDC (ODI 51.7%).
papers.caveat: MDC is a measurement-error threshold that depends on sample SD and borrowed reliability values; for back pain it is below the change of patients reporting no change. Anchors were unvalidated. The authors call MCID a minimum, not a measure of success.
papers.discussion: ODI 12.8 is one sample's MDC chosen as MCID, a minimum change rather than a universal constant or a target.
papers.title: Minimum clinically important difference in lumbar spine surgery patients: a choice of methods using the Oswestry Disability Index, Medical Outcomes Study questionnaire Short Form 36, and pain scales.
papers.review_depth: Full text reviewed, not supplementary appendix
missing_or_discrepant_fields: Table 3: back pain effect-size MCID (HTI column) printed 0.28, but its own 0.5 SD (0.95) and SEM imply 0.38; every other column has 0.5 SD = 2.5 x effect size, and the satisfaction column gives 0.39. The abstract's '10-fold' range for back pain (0.28 to 2.88) depends on this cell; with 0.38 it is about 7.6-fold.
Sample count: abstract says 454 patients with 1-year ODI or PCS; Methods says 460 retained, with 457 paired ODI and 460 paired PCS scores. 454 matches the HTI-by-PCS N in Table 2.

Distribution-based values are said to use the SD of baseline scores, but the SDs they imply (ODI about 14.6 HTI and 13.3 satisfaction; PCS about 6.3 and 5.8) differ from Table 1 (14.06, 6.62) and from each other; the subset used is not stated. With Table 1 SDs, ODI MDC would be about 12.3.
Results: correlation for PCS printed as '-13' (presumably -0.13).

Results paragraph says lower baseline health predicts greater improvement (consistent with the printed r values, including -0.13 for PCS), then says patients with greater ODI and back pain change had lower baseline disability and pain, and 'similarly' that those with the lowest baseline PCS improved less (Table 6); the correlations and the HTI-group pattern conflict for ODI, back pain and PCS.
Discussion mean changes (PCS 6.20, back 2.66, leg 2.43) differ slightly from Table 2 totals (6.11, 2.67, 2.44); Table 1 means give 6.18, 2.66, 2.44.
Methods text describes satisfaction answers as 'Definitively True/False' and then 'Definitely True/False'.

papers.label: Brinjikji: asymptomatic degeneration
papers.design: Systematic review; age-specific prevalence pooled with a mixed-effects model
papers.population: 3110 individuals with no history of back pain in 33 imaging studies (32 MRI, 1 CT).
papers.endpoint: Age-specific prevalence of 8 degenerative imaging findings, ages 20 to 80
papers.finding: Degenerative findings were common in pain-free people and increased with age.
papers.numbers: Modeled prevalence at age 20 and 80: disc degeneration 37% and 96%, bulge 30% and 84%, protrusion 29% and 43%, annular fissure 19% and 29%.
papers.caveat: Model estimates with no confidence intervals. Few people over 60; the 96% at age 80 rests on about 19 people in 2 studies. No symptomatic comparison or severity grading, so it cannot say whether a particular concordant lesion causes pain.
papers.discussion: The authors read incidental findings, or findings at a level that does not match the exam, as normal aging; every finding needs the clinical context.
papers.title: Systematic literature review of imaging features of spinal degeneration in asymptomatic populations.
papers.review_depth: Full text reviewed, not supplementary appendix

Discussion says degenerative findings exceed 90% at age 60 or older; Table 2 at age 60 gives 88% for degeneration and 86% for signal loss (the Discussion elsewhere says 'nearly 90%').

Results say authors 'rarely reported' facet degeneration at ages 20 and 30 (4%-9%), but Table 1 shows 0 people and 0 studies at those ages; the 4%, 9% and spondylolisthesis 3%, 5% are model extrapolations.

papers.label: Depression and lumbar surgery outcomes
papers.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of comparative and correlation studies (29 of 44 retrospective, 36 single center); random effects.
papers.population: Adults having surgery for degenerative lumbar disease, 44 studies (21,452 patients); 2 mixed lumbar-cervical studies excluded from pooling.
papers.endpoint: Change in PROs versus absolute pre/postoperative severity
papers.finding: Patients with depression had worse absolute status before and after surgery, yet a similar magnitude of improvement.
papers.numbers: Change SMD 0.04 (95% CI -0.02 to 0.10; I2 75%; P = .21). Absolute severity SMD -0.52 before (-0.62 to -0.41) and -0.52 after surgery (-0.75 to -0.28).
papers.caveat: Mostly retrospective, single-center studies; depression defined by chart diagnosis or varied scales and cutoffs; high heterogeneity; no data on depression treatment. Neither proves depression harmless nor justifies assuming depressed patients cannot benefit.
papers.discussion: Worse final scores and a similar surgical improvement can both be true.
papers.title: Implications of Preoperative Depression for Lumbar Spine Surgery Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
papers.review_depth: Full text reviewed, not supplementary appendix
missing_or_discrepant_fields: Results: depressed patients had worse preoperative status 'compared with patients with depression'; should read without depression.

Table: publication-year counts 3 + 8 + 34 sum to 45, not 44; 34/44 is 77%, not the printed 75% (33 would fit). Posterior approach 31/44 is 70.5%, printed 71%, which fits neither rounding nor truncation.

Percentages mix rounding and truncation: eg 29/44 printed 66% and 25/44 printed 57% (rounded), but 24/44 printed 54%, 2/44 printed 4%, ODI 35/44 printed 79%, PHQ-9 4/37 printed 10% and SF-MCS 11/37 printed 29% (truncated). Reference 7, cited as a PHQ-9 study, is titled as a PHQ-2 study.
SF-MCS use (11 studies) is attributed to eTable 2 in one sentence and eTable 3 in another.
Results says depressed patients had 'greater improvement' and Discussion 'possibly even larger', although the difference was not significant (P = .21).

The SMD sign convention is not defined. Figure captions say 'Without vs With', and Results reads a positive change SMD as more improvement in depressed patients, but the Discussion reads larger SMDs as more severe depression and smaller SMDs as a diminished role of depression, which is the opposite direction. The number of studies and patients in each pooled analysis is not given in the text.
The Table reports counts of studies that did adjust for age, comorbidities and baseline severity, while the text cites them as studies that did not account for these.

papers.label: CNS: preoperative opioids
papers.design: Evidence-based guideline
papers.population: Adults having elective spine surgery for degenerative disease.
papers.endpoint: Postoperative opioid use, patient-reported outcomes and adverse events
papers.followup: Not applicable (guideline). Literature searched to September 20, 2019; published 2021.
papers.finding: Grade B: any preoperative opioid use, and longer preoperative use, are associated with longer postoperative opioid use and worse outcomes, including complications, length of stay, costs and resource use. Evidence on dose was inconsistent. Grade Insufficient: insufficient evidence (one Level II study) that a preoperative wean improves outcomes.
papers.numbers: 845 relevant abstracts, 78 full texts, 41 included; none Level I, most Level II. Any preoperative use before ACDF: OR 5.7 (95% CI 5.3-6.2) for chronic postoperative use. Long-term preoperative use before lumbar fusion: OR 10.8 (8.2-13.2), as printed; interval asymmetric. Weaning question: one Level II study.
papers.caveat: Observational data, many from claims databases, with varying definitions of chronic use; residual confounding likely. The dose question was answered as any use versus none. The weaning statement rests on one observational study of a prescription-free drug holiday (how it came about is not stated), not a tested taper.
papers.discussion: Preoperative opioid use predicts risk, but the guideline did not establish that preoperative weaning improves surgical outcomes.
papers.title: Congress of Neurological Surgeons Systematic Review and Evidence-Based Guidelines for Perioperative Spine: Preoperative Opioid Evaluation.
papers.review_depth: Full text reviewed, not supplementary appendix
missing_or_discrepant_fields: Question 2 asks about preoperative dose (MME), but its Grade B statement concerns any use (yes/no); the text calls the dose association inconsistent.

Connolly (ref 9): OR 220 (95% CI 149-326) for 250 d or more of preoperative use is implausibly large; log-symmetric, so possibly a decimal shift to 22.0 (14.9-32.6) or 2.20 (1.49-3.26), both equally log-symmetric (our inference, unverified).
Deyo (ref 20): OR 10.8 (95% CI 8.2-13.2) is asymmetric on the log scale in the wrong direction (geometric center about 10.4); one bound or the estimate may be misprinted (our inference).
Weaning study (Jain, ref 17): drug holiday printed as '3- to 489-mo' (up to about 40 years); unit likely wrong. No event rates or effect sizes given.
Wick (ref 39): 'dose increased from 47.8 to 90 mg per day (95% CI 29.0-60.0 mg/day)'; the CI cannot belong to that range, so the sentence is garbled.
Text says 'Five other Level III studies' after Tuna (ref 35) but names four (refs 36-39).
Jain (ref 12): chronic longer-term use defined as 'opioid use ≤1 yr after surgery'; direction looks reversed.
Rosenthal (ref 18): comparison of prescriptions at 3 and 6 mo versus prescriptions at 3 mo is garbled.
Hockley (ref 14) compares MIS with open TLIF, not a preoperative opioid exposure, but is cited under question 1.
Kanaan (ref 40) is listed among studies agreeing on long-term postoperative opioid use, but its reported result is leg pain at 2 weeks.
Ref 28 is spelled 'Amraghani' in the text and 'Armaghani' in the reference list.
Question 3 is worded 'impact' in the question list (S2) and 'decrease' in the Discussion (S6); abstract says 'insufficient evidence', Conclusions say 'limited data'.
Methods heading reads 'Rating Quality of Diagnostic Evidence' for prognostic and therapeutic questions.

Conclusion calls the literature consistent, yet Ahn (23), Elsamadicy (44) and Mesfin (45) report null or opposite-direction findings on some outcomes (Elsamadicy and Mesfin users started from worse baselines).
Disclosure table has no entry for coauthor Basma Mohamed.

papers.label: CNS: preoperative osteoporosis
papers.design: Evidence-based guideline from a systematic review (modified NASS grading)
papers.population: Patients with suspected osteoporosis undergoing spinal instrumentation.
papers.endpoint: Osteoporosis-related adverse events: nonunion or delayed fusion, screw loosening, cage subsidence, PJK and PJF
papers.finding: Grade B: DEXA T-score < -2.5, CT HU < 97.9 or vitamin D3 < 20 ng/mL predicts postoperative adverse events, so assess suspected osteoporosis before instrumentation and counsel confirmed cases. Grade B: consider preoperative teriparatide. Insufficient evidence for bisphosphonates alone.
papers.numbers: 17 of 281 screened studies, none Level I. Testing: 11 studies (4 Level II, 7 Level III). Treatment: 6 studies (3 Level II, 2 Level III, 1 Level IV).
papers.caveat: The 97.9 HU cutoff is not traced to any study in the text, and T-score cutoffs varied between studies. Teriparatide evidence is small, none described as randomized, mostly radiographic, and the one study with stated timing describes a 1-year postoperative protocol. Clinical outcomes were similar in the teriparatide studies.
papers.discussion: Bone quality belongs in the surgical plan, with evidence for assessment and selected anabolic optimization.
papers.title: Congress of Neurological Surgeons Systematic Review and Evidence-Based Guidelines for Perioperative Spine: Preoperative Osteoporosis Assessment.
papers.review_depth: Full text reviewed, not supplementary appendix
missing_or_discrepant_fields: The CT threshold HU < 97.9 appears in the recommendation but in none of the study summaries in the text; the one CT study with numbers (Sakai) reports screw-trajectory HU means of 147 vs 208.
Grade B is defined as 'suggest', but recommendation 1 says assessment 'should be performed'.
Question 2 and its recommendation specify preoperative treatment, but no teriparatide study summary states treatment began before surgery; Cho 2017 describes a 1-year postoperative protocol.
Abstract says DEXA, CT 'and' vitamin D3; the recommendation says 'or'.
Vitamin D3 < 20 ng/mL is said to be associated with poor bone mineral density, but the only vitamin D study summarized (Ravindra) measured fusion, not BMD.

Cho 2018 (ref 9): cage subsidence and screw loosening attributed to 'low body mass index' in a bone-density comparison, likely low BMD. Text says 268 patients (182 PLF, 86 PLIF) while the reference title is one-level PLIF and the groups total 86. Subsidence 65.4% vs 17.6% fits neither 31 nor 55 (17/26, 3/17 or 6/34 fit), and one-level surgery rules out per-level counting. Fusion with vs without loosening (71.4% vs 93.9%) fits neither 17 nor 69. Loosening P printed as 'P < .029'; 10/31 vs 7/55 gives P = .029 exactly.

Yagi 2018 (ref 11): OR 6.4 (95% CI 1.2-32.3) printed with P < .01; the CI implies P about .03 (our calculation). Groups labeled moderate (T > -1.5) and severe (T < -1.5) osteoporosis; T > -1.5 is not osteoporosis by any definition, and neither matches the T < -2.5 used in the recommendation.

Ravindra (ref 13): groups written as deficient < 20, insufficient 20-30 and nondeficient > 20 ng/mL; > 20 overlaps the insufficient range. Unadjusted nonunion difference (38% vs 20%) was not significant (P = .063).

Puvanesarajah (ref 18): 44.9% described as 'more than one-third'; name misspelled 'Puvansearajah'. Q1 text says CT and DEXA were evaluated in 10 studies, but this study is summarized only as an osteoporosis diagnosis.
Salzmann (ref 19): obese sacral fracture incidence given as 52.4% (11/21), but 21 is the whole cohort.
Ohtori 2012 (ref 20): fusion compared as 82% at 8 months vs 68% at 10 months, different time points; 82% does not fit 29 patients.
Ohtori 2013 (ref 21): loosening 7%, 13%, 15% cannot be patient counts of 20, 20 and 22; denominator not stated.

Cho 2017 (ref 22): percentages imply denominators of 27 and 28, not 23 and 24 patients. 6-month fusion called significantly higher (77.8% vs 53.6%), but 21/27 vs 15/28 gives P about .06 (chi-square) or .09 (Fisher). CT P values .374, .648 and .626 do not fit 3/27 vs 3/28 or 4/27 vs 4/28 (P near 1). T-score gain 0.7 +/- 1.4 vs 0.1 +/- 0.5 with P = .013 recomputes to about .04-.06. Bridging bone 88.9% (24/27) is given to the bisphosphonate group and 87.5% (21/24) to the teriparatide group, suggesting swapped labels. Its authors concluded no significant benefit in fusion rate or clinical outcome.
Kang 2019 (ref 24): described as a retrospective review, but the reference title says prospective comparative study.
Kim 2014 (ref 25): endplate degeneration 91.3% vs 52.4% by nonunion status fits 21/23 and 11/21, the drug-group sizes; only about 13 patients had nonunion by the fusion rates given.
PICO questions cited to Supplemental Digital Content 5, which the supplement list names as the PRISMA flowchart.
Misspellings: keyword 'Denosamab'; disclosure 'Eli Lily'.

papers.label: CNS: diabetes, smoking and BMI
papers.design: Systematic review and evidence-based guideline (CNS, endorsed by AANS/CNS); modified NASS levels and grades; Level II and III studies only.
papers.population: Adults having spine surgery: diabetics (HbA1c, 5 studies), increased BMI (54 studies), smokers having fusion (8 studies).

No study of smoking cessation met criteria.
