papers.label: Teriparatide versus denosumab for PJF
papers.design: Single-center randomized superiority trial with active control (denosumab). Called single-blind, but patients and investigators knew the drug; the radiographic assessor/analyst and PRO administrator were blinded.
papers.population: Postmenopausal women aged 50-85 with untreated osteoporosis (T-score below -2.5) having deformity correction for symptomatic degenerative thoracolumbar deformity; single center, one surgeon, UIV T10 in all.
papers.endpoint: PJK (junctional angle at least 10 degrees and at least 10 degrees above preoperative) and PJF (revision for UIV or UIV+1 fracture, subluxation, fixation failure or neurological deficit) within 1 year.
papers.followup: 1 year (PJK, PJF and PROs at 3, 6 and 12 months).
papers.finding: Perioperative teriparatide reduced PJF versus active-control denosumab in this small trial; PJK difference was not significant.
papers.numbers: 64 randomized, 56 analyzed (29 vs 27). Modified ITT PJF 3.4% vs 22.2% (1 vs 6 events, back-calculated from percentages), P=.034; PJK 17.2% vs 33.3%, P=.165. Per protocol PJF 3.7% vs 22.2%, P=.043. Back pain VAS change -3.7 vs -1.6, P=.008.
papers.caveat: Only 7 PJF events; printed P values are uncorrected chi-square, and Fisher exact gives .048 (mITT) and .10 (per protocol). Powered on PJK, not PJF. 8 of 64 excluded for canceled surgery. Women only, 6-month drug course then bisphosphonate in both arms, 1-year follow-up.
papers.discussion: The positive randomized signal was for PJF, while the PJK comparison was not statistically significant.
papers.title: Perioperative teriparatide for preventing proximal junctional kyphosis and failure in patients with osteoporosis after adult thoracolumbar spinal deformity surgery: a prospective randomized controlled trial.
papers.review_depth: Full text reviewed, not supplementary appendix
missing_or_discrepant_fields: Table 2: postoperative TK values repeat the preoperative row exactly (12.4 +/- 14.2 vs 14.3 +/- 14.4) but carry a different P (0.931 vs 0.638); a t-test on those values gives about 0.62.

Table 1 and Table 3 hip BMD SDs are implausible: teriparatide 0.651 +/- 0.462 at baseline and 0.742 +/- 0.912 at 1 year; denosumab change SD 0.723 is impossible given level SDs of 0.080 and 0.044. Recomputed P for the printed change values is about 0.59, not 0.496.
Table 1: SRS-22r pain baseline SD 2.64 (teriparatide) is impossible on a 1-5 scale; the maximum possible SD with n=29 is about 2.04.

papers.label: SINS
papers.design: Classification built from 2 systematic reviews and a two-round modified Delphi consensus of the Spine Oncology Study Group. No patient cohort.

papers.finding: MIS had fewer intraoperative complications than open surgery (0% vs 25%), mostly blood loss over 4 L. Total and major complications did not differ significantly. MIS bled less but left more PI-LL mismatch.
papers.numbers: Any complication MIS 30%, hybrid 47.4%, open 62.5% (6/20, 9/19, 10/16; P = 0.147). Intraoperative 0%, 5.3%, 25% (P = 0.027). Needing surgery 15.0%, 15.8%, 18.8% (P = 0.952). EBL 669 vs 2322 ml MIS vs open. Postop PI-LL 17, 11, 6 degrees.
papers.caveat: Two databases with different entry rules and collection methods. 20 per group; complication data missing in 4 open and 1 hybrid patient (our back-calculation from Table 7 percentages; the paper gives only 55 complete). Matching left preop SVA 28 mm in MIS vs 61 and 65 mm. The intraoperative signal is 4 open patients, 3 with blood loss over 4 L. MIS vs hybrid intraoperative difference was not significant despite the abstract. 1-year follow-up, no fusion assessment.
papers.discussion: Early matched comparison of approach and complications in adult deformity; hypothesis generating, and does not show MIS is safer overall.
papers.title: Complications in adult spinal deformity surgery: an analysis of minimally invasive, hybrid, and open surgical techniques.
papers.review_depth: Full text reviewed, not supplementary appendix
missing_or_discrepant_fields: Abstract and Results say MIS had significantly fewer intraoperative complications than hybrid; counts 0/20 vs 1/19 give Fisher P = 0.49 (our calculation), and the Discussion says the only significant complication difference was MIS vs open.
Overall mean length of stay given as 8.5 days, but the group means 6.4, 4.5 and 7.4 in three groups of 20 average 6.1.
Discussion says hybrid fused 6.4 posterior levels vs 5.2 for MIS; Table 3 gives MIS 5.6 and open 5.2.
Discussion says MIS implant failure was 8%; Table 7 gives 10.0%, and 8% is impossible with 20 patients.
Discussion says groups were matched on age, ODI and coronal and sagittal parameters; Methods list age, SVA, posterior levels fused and lumbar Cobb.
Discussion says PI-LL correction did not differ between groups; Results and Table 5 report greater correction in open than MIS (-14 vs -3 degrees, P = 0.04/0.035).
Blood loss over 4 L in 3 open patients is called 15% (denominator 20), while Table 7 open complication percentages use 16.
Text says 46% of the 60 patients had a major complication; Table 7 gives 45.5% of 55 with complete data.

Major complication rates equal any complication rates in every group although hybrid and open had minor complications of 21.1% and 25.0%; this requires every patient with a minor complication to also have a major one.

Complications per patient (1.06, 0.84, 0.30, P = 0.04) are attributed to Table 7, which does not contain them; the per-patient minor comparison 0.4 vs 0 is given P = 0.4 within a sentence describing differences.
Postop thoracic Cobb difference given as P < 0.003; Table 5 gives P = 0.031 for open vs MIS.
Table 6 footnote says all changes were significant except MIS leg pain, but hybrid leg pain change has P = 0.057.
Table 4 change values conflict with pre and post means: MIS SVA 28 to 31 listed as -2, hybrid PT 36 to 37 listed as -1, hybrid PI-LL 26 to 11 listed as -12.
Postop pelvic tilt was higher in hybrid than MIS and open (Table 5 P = 0.003 and 0.001), but the text says no other differences existed.
The claim that complications had no impact on ODI appears in the abstract with no supporting data.
EBL MIS vs open is P = 0.001 in the abstract and P < 0.001 in the Results.
Discussion includes percutaneous presacral interbody fusion in the MIS group; the Methods group definition does not.
Pairwise P values in Table 5 (many 1.000) imply an adjustment method that the Methods do not describe.

Table 7 chi-square P values are uncorrected tests on cells with expected counts mostly below 5. Freeman-Halton exact tests (our calculation): intraoperative P = 0.019, DVT P = 0.058 (not significant), minor P = 0.044 (significant, vs chi-square 0.065), any complication P = 0.165.
Results give matched-cohort mean age 63 and ASA 2.2; Table 2 group means average 64.9 years and ASA 2.27 (our calculation). 63 +/- 8.9 is the 280-patient query cohort.
Abstract says all ODI and VAS improvements were P < 0.001; Table 6 gives hybrid ODI 0.004, open ODI 0.001, open VAS back 0.001, open VAS leg 0.005 and hybrid VAS leg 0.057.
Discussion says preop thoracic Cobb was smaller in hybrid (15) than MIS (16) and open (28, P = 0.008); Table 5 gives hybrid vs MIS P = 1.000, open vs hybrid P = 0.005, and 0.008 for open vs MIS.

papers.label: Scheer JK 2015
papers.design: Retrospective review of a prospective multicenter database (International Spine Study Group, 11 US sites); operated vs nonoperated cohorts, unadjusted comparisons
papers.population: Adults over 18 with ASD (Cobb 20 degrees or more, SVA 5 cm or more, PT 25 degrees or more, or TK 60 degrees or more); 421 with 2-year follow-up: 235 of 286 operated (82.2%) and 186 of 403 nonoperated (46.2%)
papers.endpoint: Change in back and leg pain NRS category (none 0, mild 1-4, moderate 5-6, severe 7-10) by at least 1 category; also NRS, ODI and PCS MCID/SCB and SRS-22 satisfaction
papers.finding: Operated patients more often moved down a pain category at 2 years than nonoperated patients (back 68.2% vs 25.7%, leg 45.9% vs 21.9%) and less often worsened, but they started with much worse pain and the comparison is unadjusted. Leg pain NRS, ODI and PCS were similar between groups at 2 years.
papers.numbers: Back improvement OR 6.2 (95% CI 4.0-9.7); leg improvement OR 3.0 (1.9-4.8). Back worsening 3.3% operated vs 27.4% nonoperated. Baseline back NRS 7.1 vs 4.4. Among operated patients with preoperative pain, 24.3% back pain free and 37.8% leg pain free at 2 years. New leg pain in operated patients without preoperative leg pain: 17/46 (37.0%) at 6 weeks, 20/60 (33.3%) at 2 years, vs 27.0% in nonoperated patients (P = 0.50).
papers.caveat: Odds ratios, not risk ratios (back about 2.7 as a risk ratio). Treatment by indication, no adjustment, 46.2% nonoperated follow-up, MCID/SCB cutoffs from lumbar fusion. Several table errors (Table 5 ODI SCB above MCID; Table 7 all-patient change row). Subgroup claims on surgery type and curve type rest on small, unadjusted cells.
papers.discussion: A counseling reference for how often pain categories improve, persist or worsen after ASD surgery; not proof that surgery beats nonoperative care for pain.
papers.title: Comprehensive study of back and leg pain improvements after adult spinal deformity surgery: analysis of 421 patients with 2-year follow-up and of the impact of the surgery on treatment satisfaction.
papers.review_depth: Full text reviewed, not supplementary appendix
missing_or_discrepant_fields: Table 2: operated back pain 'no change' printed 60 (25.2%); 60/211 is 28.4%, and the reported OR of 1.9 for staying in the same category only reproduces with 28.4%.
Table 2: back pain new onset 1/1 (100%) vs 7/14 (50.0%) printed with P = 0.0009; a Fisher exact test on these counts gives P = 1.0.

Table 2 lists 41 (25.5%) operated patients whose back but not leg pain improved; the satisfaction paragraph says 27 of 147 (18.4%), citing Table 2, yet its MCID/SCB percentages (39.0%, 34.2%, 62.2%, 54.1%) only work with denominators of 41 and 37.
Table 1: P values for age (0.0934), BMI (0.0001) and CCI (0.0073) cannot be reproduced from the printed means and SDs (t-test gives about 0.14, 0.002 and 0.0002); rank tests may have been used.

Table 5: ODI SCB counts exceed ODI MCID counts in every curve type (e.g., Type N 45 vs 29) although the SCB threshold (-18.8) is stricter than MCID (-15); the SCB row totals 153 vs 95 in Table 8. Text claims that Type N and L more often reached ODI SCB rest on this row.
Table 7: all-operated ODI change printed -8.2 although means fall from 41.3 to 25.8 (-15.5) and every subgroup change is -9.2 to -21.1; PCS change printed 4.1 against 33.4 to 41.6 (+8.2).

Text: pain-free rates by preoperative severity (13.8%, 4.8%, 5.7%) are percentages of all 210 patients, not of each severity group; within groups, mild 12/29 (41.4%), moderate 10/43 (23.3%), severe 29/138 (21.0%), reversing the stated conclusion that severe patients were more often pain free.
Text: leg pain improvement OR for severe vs mild printed 4.5 (1.9-9.7); Table 6 counts (51/67 vs 18/42) give 4.25 with that same CI.
Text: PCS of moderate leg pain patients said to reach MCID and SCB more often than mild; Table 8 shows mild higher (65.9% vs 41.2% MCID; 63.6% vs 41.2% SCB).

Stated significant differences that do not recompute from table counts (Fisher exact, our check): new leg pain osteotomy-only 9/20 vs decompression-only 1/6 (P about 0.35); leg improvement Type L 20/28 vs Type T 31/51 (P about 0.46); leg improvement Type N 26/45 vs Type D 17/43 (P about 0.09); ODI MCID severe 73/145 vs mild 11/30 back pain (P about 0.2); ODI SCB severe 62/145 vs mild 8/30 (P about 0.15). The PCS MCID and SCB differences by back pain severity do hold.

Abstract, text and Conclusions: decompression said to improve leg pain more than Group Other (p < 0.05); Table 3 gives D 19/33 and D+O 50/88 vs Other 8/20, chi-square P about 0.21 and 0.17 (pooled 69/121 vs 8/20, 0.16), not significant.
Text: mild preoperative back pain patients said to have no change more often than severe (p < 0.05, Table 6); 13/29 vs 39/138 gives chi-square P about 0.08 (Fisher 0.12).
Table 2 'leg pain but not back pain improved' 21 (14.3%) vs 20 (21.3%) printed P = 0.6011; chi-square on these counts gives about 0.16 (still not significant).

Table 3 leg pain change percentages use denominators larger than the counts with baseline leg pain (e.g., osteotomy 17/46 = 37.0%), while the text gives 17/28 (60.7%) for the same group; denominators are not explained.
Table 2: baseline back pain > leg pain 124/225 vs 104/181 printed P = 0.7007; chi-square gives about 0.64 (still not significant). The other baseline P values in Table 2 reproduce.
Table 1: operated curve-type percentages mix denominators (N, T, L of 234 classified; D 25.5% = 60/235); trivial.

papers.label: Soroceanu A 2015
papers.design: Retrospective review of a prospective multicenter ASD database (International Spine Study Group, 11 US centers); obese (BMI 30 or more) vs nonobese, multivariable regression and repeated-measures mixed models
papers.population: Adults treated surgically for ASD (Cobb 20 degrees or more, SVA 5 cm or more, pelvic tilt 25 degrees or more, and/or thoracic kyphosis 60 degrees or more) with baseline BMI and complete baseline and 2-year data: 241 patients, 175 nonobese and 66 obese. Neuromuscular deformity, active infection and malignancy excluded.
papers.endpoint: Complications over 2 years (overall, major, minor, infection, implant, radiographic, neurologic, revision); EBL, operative time and LOS; ODI, SF-36 physical and SRS-22 at baseline, 6 weeks, 1 year and 2 years
papers.finding: After adjustment, obese patients had more major complications and more infections. Revision, neurologic, radiographic and implant complications, operative time, EBL and LOS did not differ significantly. Both groups improved; obese patients had worse HRQL at baseline and at 2 years.
papers.numbers: Major complications 53% obese vs 33.7% nonobese, adjusted IRR 1.54 (P=0.021); any complication 78.8% vs 65%, IRR 1.26 (P=0.054). Infection 10.6% vs 3.4%, adjusted OR 4.88 (P=0.02). Revision 22.7% vs 20% (P=0.846). ODI baseline to 2 years: obese 49.3 to 33.2, nonobese 40.3 to 24.2 (group P=0.0035). No confidence intervals for regression estimates; Table 6 gives SEs only.
papers.caveat: Completers only: patients without complete 2-year data were excluded and not described. The infection estimate rests on about 13 events (our back-calculation) with no confidence interval. By our arithmetic on Table 6, ODI improved about 16 points in both groups; the paper's 'less improvement' claim rests on group-level P values, not smaller change. HRQL models adjusted for complications but not smoking or prior surgery. No BMI class analysis.
papers.discussion: Useful for consent: obesity is linked to more major complications and infection after ASD surgery. The authors conclude obese patients improve less; by our arithmetic on Table 6, 2-year ODI change was similar.
papers.title: Impact of obesity on complications, infection, and patient-reported outcomes in adult spinal deformity surgery.
papers.review_depth: Full text reviewed, not supplementary appendix
missing_or_discrepant_fields: Revision rate is 20.7% in Results (20% nonobese, 22.7% obese; about 50 of 241 by our arithmetic) but 20.3% in the Discussion, which is the neurologic complication rate.
Neurologic complication P value is 0.861 in the abstract but 0.88 in the text and 0.881 in Table 4.

Table 4 is headed IRR/Odds Ratio, yet neurologic is 0.03 (P=0.881), radiographic is -0.139 and implant (BMI) is 0.08 (P=0.804); a negative value cannot be a ratio, so the table appears to mix regression coefficients with ratios.

The infection outcome is called wound infection in the abstract and text but labeled only Infection in Table 4; the Table 1 infection category also includes pneumonia, sepsis, urinary tract infection and C difficile.

Table 2 percentages do not fit the stated group sizes: 83.1%, 55.4% and 3.1% fit 54, 36 and 2 of 65 obese (not 66); 86.7% and 38.1% fit 150 and 66 of 173 nonobese, and 11.7% fits 20 of 171. Missing baseline data are not reported.
Surgical approach P=0.34 in Table 2 does not reproduce for posterior-only 61.1% vs 62.1% (recomputed chi-square P about 0.89); it may be a test across approach categories that are not shown.
Overall complication rate for nonobese patients is printed as 65%; 167 total minus 52 obese leaves 115 of 175, or 65.7%.

The abstract and Results describe ODI, SF-36 and SRS group P values (0.0035, 0.0012, 0.022) as the magnitude of improvement, but in Table 6 these are group main effects; the ODI change from baseline to 2 years is 16.1 points in both groups.
Time P values print as 0.0001 for SF-36, ODI and SRS in Figures 1-3, the abstract and Results, and SF-36 group*time P as 0.0001 in Figure 1, the abstract and Results; Table 6 gives 0.00001 for each.
Table 5 regression coefficients (LOS 0.05, EBL 5.99, OR time 23.2) have no units, and no group means for these outcomes are reported.
No confidence intervals are reported for any regression estimate (Table 6 gives SEs for HRQL means only), and the years of surgery and total database enrollment are not stated.

Results say baseline differences were accounted for in all subsequent analysis, but the HRQL models (Results and Table 6 footnote) list only age, comorbidities, magnitude of surgery and major complications, omitting smoking and previous spine surgery, both imbalanced in Table 2.

papers.label: Smith JS 2016
papers.design: Prospective multicenter observational cohort (11 US ISSG sites); patients chose operative or nonoperative care; unmatched comparison plus 97 propensity-matched pairs; not randomized
papers.population: Adults over 18 with ASD: scoliosis 20 degrees or more, SVA 5 cm or more, pelvic tilt 25 degrees or more, or thoracic kyphosis 60 degrees or more. 689 met criteria (286 operative, 403 nonoperative); 246 operative and 223 nonoperative analyzed. 38 nonoperative patients who converted to surgery were excluded.
papers.endpoint: ODI, SF-36 PCS and MCS, SRS-22r total and domains, back and leg pain NRS, and share reaching MCID; complications in operative patients only. No single primary outcome named.
papers.followup: Minimum 2 years (mean 24.7 months operative, 24.8 nonoperative); follow-up 86% operative, 55% nonoperative
papers.finding: Operative patients improved on every quality-of-life measure; nonoperative patients on average stayed at baseline, with small SRS gains only. In 97 matched pairs, operative patients were better at 2 years on all measures except SF-36 MCS. 71.5% of operative patients had at least one complication by 2 years.
papers.numbers: Matched pairs, baseline to 2 years, operative vs nonoperative: ODI 30.1 to 17.1 vs 30.0 to 30.8; SRS-22r total 3.2 to 4.0 vs 3.2 to 3.3; back pain NRS 6.4 to 2.7 vs 5.1 to 5.5; leg pain 3.1 to 1.8 vs 3.2 to 3.7. ODI MCID reached by 53.6% vs 10.3%. Complications: 407 events (217 major) in 246 operative patients; 53.7% perioperative, 43.5% delayed, 71.5% overall.
papers.caveat: Patients chose treatment and were not blinded, so selection and expectation bias remain after matching. Nonoperative follow-up was 55%, crossovers to surgery were dropped, and nonoperative care was neither standardized nor checked for harms. Matched operative patients were 6.6 years younger and had worse baseline back pain. Some table values do not reconcile.
papers.discussion: Operative patients did much better than nonoperative patients at 2 years in both matched and unmatched analyses, at the cost of a high complication rate. It is observational and cannot say what defined, fully followed nonoperative care would do.
papers.title: Outcomes of Operative and Nonoperative Treatment for Adult Spinal Deformity: A Prospective, Multicenter, Propensity-Matched Cohort Assessment With Minimum 2-Year Follow-up.
papers.review_depth: Full text reviewed, not supplementary appendix
missing_or_discrepant_fields: Mean age of the 689 eligible patients is given as 53 (operative) and 55 (nonoperative) in the abstract but 54 and 55 in Results. Table 1 (469 analyzed) gives 55.4 operative and 52.6 nonoperative, reversing which group is older, without comment.
Table 4 flags the matched operative leg pain NRS change as at least 1 MCID, but 3.1 to 1.8 is 1.3, below the 1.6 MCID stated in Methods.

Text says matched operative improvement was at least 1 MCID for every measure with a reported MCID; SRS mental changed 3.9 to 4.1 (0.2) against a stated MCID of 0.42 (Table 4 correctly does not flag it), and leg pain fails as above.

Table 4 matched P values: baseline PCS P = .11 recomputes to about .22 and baseline MCS P = .01 to about .03 by unpaired t test with 97 per group; missing data would only raise these, so they cannot be right as stated. The 2-year MCS P = .06 (the abstract's only exception) recomputes to about .03 with 97 per group, but could reach .06 with unreported missing data, so it is unverifiable rather than wrong. Methods do not say whether matched pairs were analyzed as pairs.
The Conclusion calls the study a 'prospective case-control analysis'; it is a cohort study.
Table 2 category percentage columns are events per 100 patients (for example implant total 64/246 = 26.0%), not percentage of patients affected, and are not labeled as such.

Several Table 1 and Table 3 percentages are not whole-number fractions of the stated group sizes (for example matched operative female 87.4% and nonoperative previous surgery 23.2% of 97), so data were missing with unreported denominators.

Discussion range of 41% to 73.2% of operative patients reaching MCID matches unmatched Figure 3 only; in matched Figure 4 the range is 32% to 75.3%. Likewise, the Discussion says about 25% to 30% of nonoperative patients reached MCID for SRS pain and activity (Figures 3 and 4); Figure 3 gives 28.2% and 25.9%, but matched Figure 4 gives 32% for both.
Enrollment dates and propensity score method (model, caliper, replacement) are not reported, nor how 97 pairs were chosen from 223 and 246 patients.

Table 3 matched baseline pelvic tilt is 21.0 (10.0) vs 21.0 (11.7) with P = .78; with means equal to one decimal, an unpaired test gives P of about .95 or higher, and fewer patients only raises it. It matches the Cobb P of .78 in the same table and may be a copy error.

Table 3 matched 2-year coronal alignment 27.9 (27.6) vs 26.6 (22.5) gives P about .72 (.70-.74 across rounding), not the reported .61, which missing data cannot explain. Baseline coronal alignment (.03 vs about .013), baseline Cobb (.78 vs about .67) and thoracic kyphosis (.15 and .11 vs about .12 and .09) also differ, possibly from missing radiographs.

Figure 3 (unmatched) MCID percentages are often not whole-number fractions of 246 or 223 (for example operative SF-36 PCS 58.7%, back pain 70.6%, leg pain 44.4%; nonoperative ODI 9.2%, appearance 9.5%, activity 25.9%), so those analyses used unreported denominators.

papers.label: Lenke LG 2016
papers.design: Prospective multicenter international observational cohort; Level of Evidence 3
papers.population: Complex adult spinal deformity surgery, age 18-80, 15 sites; 204 normal and 68 abnormal preoperative LEMS
papers.endpoint: Change in ASIA lower extremity motor score (LEMS) from preoperative
papers.finding: LEMS decline in 22.18% at discharge, 17.91% at 6 weeks and 10.82% at 6 months; 83.33% with a preoperative deficit improved by 6 months.
papers.numbers: Decline 59/266 discharge, 48/268 at 6 weeks, 29/268 at 6 months; decline over 10 points at 6 months 1.49%. Six-month decline NML 12.38%, ABNML 6.06%.

papers.title: Neurologic Outcomes of Complex Adult Spinal Deformity Surgery: Results of the Prospective, Multicenter Scoli-RISK-1 Study.
papers.review_depth: Full text reviewed, not supplementary appendix
missing_or_discrepant_fields: 6-week denominator: 272 - 13 missed + 8 imputed = 267, but 268 (98.53%) is reported and Table 4 sums to 268 (202 + 66). The 6-month arithmetic works (272 - 20 + 16 = 268).
Discussion gives the NML discharge decline as 22.17% vs 25.76% in ABNML; Table 4 gives 21.00% (42/200) for NML. 22.17-22.18% is the overall rate.
Text says NML decline at discharge was transitory in about half; counts go from 42 at discharge to 25 at 6 months (about 40% fewer), and individuals are not tracked across time points.
266/272 is 97.79%, reported as 97.80% (rounding).
Missing 6-week values were imputed from 6-month data (LVCB) and 6-month values from 6-week data (LVCF), which blurs the time trend being reported.
No confidence intervals are reported anywhere in the paper.
Table 2 number-of-stages P = 0.7613 cannot be reproduced from 164/204 vs 55/68 single-stage (Fisher 1.0, chi-square 0.93). Other baseline P values reproduce.

Table 4 between-group P < 0.0001 values are driven by improvement, impossible in NML at the LEMS ceiling of 50; decline alone does not differ (Fisher P 0.49, 1.0, 0.18 at discharge, 6 weeks, 6 months), so the Discussion's 'higher rate' with a preoperative deficit is not supported.
83.33% of ABNML described as showing significant improvement counts any gain of 1 point or more (38 of 55 gained 1 to 5 points).

papers.label: Soroceanu A 2016
papers.design: Retrospective review of a prospective multicenter ISSG database (11 US centers); risk-factor cohort, level of evidence 3
papers.population: 448 operative ASD patients (coronal Cobb >20°, SVA >5 cm, PT >25° or TK >60°) with at least 6 weeks of follow-up; mean age 56.8, 75% female, mean 9.7 levels fused
papers.endpoint: Any intra- or perioperative medical complication within 6 weeks (cardiopulmonary, infectious, GI, neurologic, renal), major and minor, no severity breakdown reported; ODI, SRS-22r and SF-36 in a 2-year subgroup
papers.followup: Complications to 6 weeks; HRQL at 6 weeks, 1 and 2 years in 256 of 286 eligible patients
papers.finding: 26.8% had at least one medical complication within 6 weeks, mostly cardiopulmonary. Smoking, hypertension and longer duration of spine symptoms independently predicted them. In a 2-year subgroup the authors found no difference in HRQL improvement between patients with and without one.
papers.numbers: 120/448 patients (26.8%), 185 complications; cardiopulmonary 53% of complications. Multivariate IRR: smoking 2.39 (1.63-3.50), hypertension 2.43 (1.78-3.31), symptom duration 1.24 (1.02-1.50). Operative time 422 vs 372 min (P = 0.0004, unadjusted). 2-year HRQL subgroup: 78 with vs 178 without, no group or group-by-time difference.

Complication lists differ between abstract and Methods (Methods add electrolyte imbalance and cholecystitis).
Funding line names 'Deputy Spine', presumably DePuy Spine.
Discussion quotes Charosky as 40/306 (13.7%); 40/306 is 13.1%.
Table 4 Constant row: IRR 0.1 (95% CI 0.04-0.25) is printed with z = +5.01; since ln(0.1) < 0, z should be about -4.9.
Time effect is P < 0.0001 in Figures 1 to 3 but P = 0.0001 in the abstract and Results text.

papers.label: Strike SA 2017
papers.design: Narrative review with institutional expert practice description (Level V); unstructured PubMed search, no search or selection methods reported
papers.population: No patient cohort. Describes one center's IONM practice for adult and pediatric spinal deformity surgery; two illustrative pediatric cases
papers.endpoint: None; no outcome measured
papers.finding: SSEPs miss motor and anterior cord injury, so the authors pair SSEP with TcMEP and add EMG for roots; DNEP and NMEP are alternatives. After a signal change: exclude technical and anesthetic causes, raise MAP to 90 mm Hg, optimize oxygen, anemia and distraction, then do a wake-up test.
papers.numbers: No original data. Quoted: Quraishi, 102 adult deformity cases, multimodal sensitivity 100%, specificity 84%, SSEP alone 33%. Useful monitoring impossible in at least 10% of neuromuscular patients. Volatile agent 0.3 MAC or less for TcMEP.
papers.caveat: Expert opinion; all accuracy figures are secondhand. Text and Table 1 conflict on SSEP volatile limit; text is internally inconsistent on DNEP versus SSEP alert thresholds; text and Table 3 conflict on lumbar monitoring; at least one clear citation error.
papers.discussion: A practical primer on what each modality sees and how anesthesia affects it, with one center's response sequence; it gives no evidence that monitoring changes outcomes.
papers.title: Intraoperative Neuromonitoring in Pediatric and Adult Spine Deformity Surgery.
papers.review_depth: Full text reviewed, not supplementary appendix
missing_or_discrepant_fields: Volatile anesthetic limit for SSEPs: text says halogenated agents at 0.5 MAC or less; Table 1 gives 0.5-1.0 MAC.
Table 1 footnote '*MAC indicates minimum alveolar concentration' has no matching asterisk in the table.

Table 1 citations do not match the cells they support, by title: the propofol row (TcMEP 50-300 µg/kg/min) cites reference 16, a study of isoflurane and propofol on cortical SSEPs; the remifentanil row cites reference 17, a survey of anaesthetists' practices.
DNEP alert criteria are described as similar to SSEPs but given as an 80% amplitude decrease, while the SSEP criterion is a decrease over 50%.

Kelleher figures as quoted: MEP specificity 96% and PPV 96% cannot both hold at a 3.2% deficit rate; a 96% PPV at 96% specificity implies a prevalence near 50%. One of the quoted values is likely wrong or uses a different denominator.

The 1-in-74 missed DNEP deficit from a 23-year study of 3436 children is cited only to Emerson (reference 21, a 2-page item) as reviewing that study; the study itself is Thuet et al (reference 13), which is not co-cited in that sentence.
Rodriguez-Olaverri (reference 19) is described as placing screws from T6 to T12, but the reference title says T3-T6.

papers.label: AO-GO: ACDF osteobiologics 2024
papers.design: AO Spine (KF Degenerative) guideline using the GIN-McMaster checklist and GRADE Evidence-to-Decision frameworks; 73 panelists from 22 countries; 15 systematic reviews.
papers.population: ACDF for degenerative conditions: primary single- or multi-level ACDF, ACDF-TDR hybrids, and revision ACDF.
papers.endpoint: Fusion, pain, function and complications, plus cost, feasibility, acceptability and equity; GRADE certainty for each recommendation.

papers.finding: Five conditional suggestions. Structural iliac crest autograft, allograft or a cage with an osteobiologic give similar outcomes in primary ACDF, so choose by availability and cost; use osteobiologics other than BMP-2 in common situations; osteobiologics are acceptable at single or multiple levels and at the fusion level of a hybrid. papers.numbers: Certainty low (autograft vs cage, single vs multi-level) or very low (allograft vs cage, BMP-2, hybrid). Autograft vs cage: 2 RCTs (n = 375) and 6 non-randomized studies (n = 392), fusion difference 0-12% favoring autograft; donor-site morbidity 8% (14/172) in RCTs, 22% (24/107) non-randomized. BMP-2: dysphagia or dysphonia 26% vs 21%, other soft tissue complications 27% vs 20%.

curriculum.title: Adult deformity: planning alignment
curriculum.question: How do I choose a target without treating a score as a mandate?
curriculum.case: Defend an age- and anatomy-aware correction plan and explain the newer T4-L1-Hip and L1PA concepts.
curriculum.challenge: Derivation, external validation and association with outcome are separate questions.

curriculum.title: Bone health before reconstruction
curriculum.question: What supports evaluation and treatment?
curriculum.case: Present a bone-health optimization plan for a long fusion and state what trial outcome improved.
curriculum.challenge: Keep PJF separate from PJK; do not describe the matched teriparatide cohort as randomized.

curriculum.title: Junctional complications: prevention under uncertainty
curriculum.question: How do biology, correction and prophylaxis interact?
curriculum.case: Explain a multimodal strategy for a patient at high junctional-failure risk.
curriculum.challenge: The second anchor is an alignment-association study, not a randomized test of PJK prophylaxis. Avoid implying that an ideal angle guarantees prevention.

curriculum.title: Optimization and patient-reported outcomes
curriculum.question: How do opioid use and depression affect counseling?
curriculum.case: Counsel a patient with depression and chronic opioid use while distinguishing baseline burden, absolute postoperative status and improvement.
curriculum.challenge: Association does not prove that a preoperative intervention changes outcome; depression alone is not evidence of no benefit.

curriculum.title: Case defense and evidence literacy
curriculum.question: Can I give a precise 90-second evidence-based answer?
curriculum.case: Give two 90-second defenses: cervical surgery versus rehabilitation and decompression versus fusion. Cite study, population, result and limitation.
curriculum.challenge: Explain crossover, noninferiority and MCID; identify cohort overlap and one claim requiring full-text verification. These anchors deliberately revisit earlier weeks.

curriculum.title: MIS and indirect decompression
curriculum.question: Which selection criteria make a less invasive approach work?
curriculum.case: Defend an indirect decompression case and identify a feature that would make direct decompression more suitable.
curriculum.challenge: Results depend on eligibility and operator experience; a technique comparison is not a universal superiority claim.

curriculum.title: ACDF osteobiologics
curriculum.question: What does a conditional graft recommendation mean?
curriculum.case: Explain graft choice for degenerative ACDF, then contrast the separate fusion-versus-arthroplasty question.
curriculum.challenge: The arthroplasty trial does not directly test graft choice; keep the two questions separate.

curriculum.title: Metastatic spine disease
curriculum.question: How do mechanical instability, neurological compression and systemic disease affect indication?
curriculum.case: Explain why stability and epidural disease can lead to different treatment choices.
curriculum.challenge: This extension remains foundational; a current metastasis evidence refresh is still needed before calling it contemporary-complete.

curriculum.title: Acute spinal cord injury
curriculum.question: What did the 2024 guidelines update?
curriculum.case: Discuss timing of decompression and the current hemodynamic framework.
curriculum.challenge: Quote exact guideline strength and targets only after reviewing full recommendations; timing and perfusion are distinct evidence questions.

curriculum.title: Spine trauma
curriculum.question: Which patterns require stabilization?
curriculum.case: Contrast subaxial cervical injury with a neurologically intact thoracolumbar burst fracture.
curriculum.challenge: These are separate injury populations; do not transfer one trial or classification mechanically to the other.

curriculum.title: Spinal infection
curriculum.question: When do neurological status and infection control change the plan?
curriculum.case: Explain the indication for decompression or stabilization, then discuss antibiotic duration separately.
curriculum.challenge: Older foundational studies retained; current society-guideline update remains a stated gap.

glossary.definition: Fixed morphologic angle between the perpendicular to the S1 endplate midpoint and the line to the femoral head axis. PI = PT + SS.
glossary.usage: "Her PI is 65, so she needs much more lordosis than a formula built on an average patient would give her."

glossary.definition: Positional angle reflecting pelvic retroversion. A high PT usually means the patient is compensating for sagittal malalignment.
glossary.usage: "The SVA looks acceptable, but PT is 32, so that's a compensated deformity."

glossary.definition: Angle between the S1 endplate and the horizontal. It falls as the pelvis retroverts.
glossary.usage: "Sacral slope has dropped as he has rolled his pelvis back."

glossary.definition: Pelvic incidence minus lumbar lordosis. The classic target is within about 10 degrees, though age and morphology shift what is appropriate.
glossary.usage: "She has a 30-degree PI-LL mismatch, and that's what is driving the disability."

glossary.definition: Horizontal offset of the C7 plumb line from the posterosuperior corner of S1 on a standing film.
glossary.usage: "SVA is 11 centimeters; she's pitched forward even with her knees bent."

glossary.definition: Angle combining trunk lean and pelvic retroversion. Less dependent on how much the patient is compensating at a given moment than SVA.
glossary.usage: "TPA is useful here because her pelvis is hiding part of the imbalance."

glossary.definition: Targets that accept more positive alignment in older patients, rather than one fixed goal for every age.
glossary.usage: "At 78 I'd aim for his age-adjusted target, since chasing a 40-year-old's numbers risks overcorrection."

glossary.definition: Pelvic-incidence-based score of relative alignment that sorts patients as proportioned, moderately disproportioned or severely disproportioned.
glossary.usage: "GAP has been used to predict mechanical complications, but external validation has been mixed."

glossary.definition: Sagittal morphotype classification of lumbar shape, based mainly on sacral slope and apex of lordosis.
glossary.usage: "He's a Roussouly type 2, a flat back shape, so I wouldn't give him a generic lordosis."

glossary.definition: Pelvic retroversion, knee flexion, hip extension and thoracic flattening recruited to hold posture upright.
glossary.usage: "Get a full-length film with knees extended so you can see the true deformity past the compensation."

glossary.definition: Alignment concept that compares T4 and L1 relative to the hip axis, using T4-pelvic and L1-pelvic angles.
glossary.usage: "Matching T4 to L1 pelvic angles is one proposed way to reduce mechanical failure."

glossary.definition: Adult deformity classification combining coronal curve type with three sagittal modifiers: PI-LL, SVA and PT.
glossary.usage: "Schwab type L with a ++ PI-LL modifier and a + SVA modifier."

glossary.definition: Coronal curve magnitude, measured between the most tilted end vertebrae.
glossary.usage: "The Cobb is 45, but the sagittal plane explains her symptoms better."

glossary.definition: Radiographic kyphosis above a long construct, commonly defined as at least 10 degrees and at least 10 degrees worse than before surgery.
glossary.usage: "She has radiographic PJK with no pain, so I'm watching it for now."

glossary.definition: Clinically significant structural failure above a long construct, such as fracture, hardware pull-out or neurologic decline, often leading to revision.
glossary.usage: "This is PJF rather than asymptomatic PJK: she has a UIV fracture and new myelopathy."

glossary.definition: Upper and lower instrumented vertebrae. Their choice defines the construct's junctional risks.
glossary.usage: "Where do you stop? I'd take the UIV to T10 and avoid ending at the apex of the kyphosis."

glossary.definition: Extending a long construct to the pelvis, commonly with S2-alar-iliac screws, to protect the lumbosacral junction.
glossary.usage: "Long fusion to the sacrum, so I'd add S2AI fixation."

glossary.definition: Posterior-column osteotomy through the facets that gains a modest amount of lordosis at each level through a mobile disc.
glossary.usage: "Multiple SPOs may be enough, since the discs are still mobile."

glossary.definition: Three-column closing-wedge osteotomy, classically giving about 30 degrees of focal correction through one vertebra.
glossary.usage: "She's fused and flat, so she needs a PSO at L3."

glossary.definition: Any osteotomy crossing all three columns, such as PSO or vertebral column resection, with larger correction and larger risk.
glossary.usage: "I'd plan around the morbidity of a three-column osteotomy."

glossary.definition: Risk measure that counts deficits rather than relying on chronological age.
glossary.usage: "He's 74 but not frail, so his age alone doesn't rule out a big operation."

glossary.definition: Umbrella term for cord dysfunction from degenerative cervical compression. It has largely replaced CSM in the literature.
glossary.usage: "This is moderate DCM with a clear progression."

glossary.definition: 18-point functional myelopathy score. Commonly: mild 15-17, moderate 12-14, severe 11 or less.
glossary.usage: "mJOA is 13, moderate, and I'd offer surgery."

glossary.definition: Six-level (0-5) scale of myelopathy focused on gait and employment.
glossary.usage: "Older series report Nurick grade, so they don't map neatly to current mJOA data."

glossary.definition: Reflex thumb or index flexion when the middle finger's distal phalanx is flicked. An upper motor neuron sign.
glossary.usage: "Bilateral Hoffmann's and tandem gait is off."

glossary.definition: T2 hyperintensity in the cord on MRI. Its prognostic meaning depends on pattern and on other clinical factors.
glossary.usage: "There's focal T2 signal change at C4-5, but the exam is what decides this."

glossary.definition: Posterior motion-preserving expansion of the canal without fusion.
glossary.usage: "Preserved lordosis and little neck pain make her a laminoplasty candidate."

glossary.definition: Posterior decompression with instrumented fusion, often for multilevel disease.
glossary.usage: "With loss of lordosis, I'd favor laminectomy and fusion over laminoplasty."

glossary.definition: Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion.
glossary.usage: "For single-level ventral disease with arm pain, ACDF remains the reference."

glossary.definition: Motion-preserving disc replacement used in selected patients without significant facet disease or instability.
glossary.usage: "She fits the arthroplasty criteria, with no facet arthropathy and preserved motion."

glossary.definition: Motion-preserving posterior decompression of a foraminal root.
glossary.usage: "For a soft lateral disc, foraminotomy avoids an anterior fusion."

glossary.definition: Symptomatic degeneration next to a fusion. Distinguish it from radiographic change, which is often silent.
glossary.usage: "Radiographic adjacent segment change isn't the same thing as symptomatic disease."

glossary.definition: Includes C2-C7 SVA and T1 slope minus cervical lordosis, used to judge cervical deformity and plan approach.
glossary.usage: "T1 slope minus lordosis is large, so she'll drift further kyphotic after a laminoplasty."

glossary.definition: Consensus classification of adult cervical deformity by curve type and sagittal and myelopathy modifiers.
glossary.usage: "By Ames she has a C-type deformity with a major modifier."

glossary.definition: Leg symptoms provoked by standing and walking, relieved by sitting or flexion. Distinct from vascular claudication, which eases with standing rest.
glossary.usage: "He leans on the shopping cart and it settles when he sits. That's neurogenic."

glossary.definition: Dermatomal pain, sensory change or weakness arising from nerve-root compression or inflammation.
glossary.usage: "This is a concordant L5 radiculopathy, and the MRI matches."

glossary.definition: Agreement between symptoms, exam and imaging. The term carries much of the weight in surgical selection.
glossary.usage: "The MRI is striking, but it isn't concordant with her symptoms."

glossary.definition: Slip of one vertebra on another with an intact pars from facet and disc degeneration, classically L4-5.
glossary.usage: "It's a grade I degenerative slip at L4-5."

glossary.definition: Slip severity by percentage: I up to 25, II 25-50, III 50-75, IV over 75.
glossary.usage: "Meyerding I, which is what SLIP required; NORDSTEN accepted any slip of at least 3 mm."

glossary.definition: Abnormal motion on flexion-extension films. There is no agreed definition: SLIP excluded motion over 3 mm, NORDSTEN reported at least 3 mm or 10 degrees, and the Swedish trial took no dynamic films.
glossary.usage: "He has 4 mm of motion, so he'd have been excluded from SLIP, and NORDSTEN can't tell us about him as a subgroup."

glossary.definition: Fluid in the facet joint on MRI, sometimes read as a sign of motion that a supine film may hide.
glossary.usage: "The facet effusions make me wonder about motion, though NORDSTEN enrolled patients with them too."

glossary.definition: Fusion with or without implants. Older comparative studies used noninstrumented technique, which limits comparison to current practice.
glossary.usage: "Herkowitz used noninstrumented fusion, so we can't simply transfer it to pedicle screws."

glossary.definition: Restoring disc height and foraminal volume with an interbody device, without directly removing compressive tissue.
glossary.usage: "I'd pick indirect decompression only when the stenosis is soft and dynamic, not bony."

glossary.definition: Lateral lumbar interbody fusion through the psoas. Selection includes the lumbar plexus and osteopenia-related cage subsidence.
glossary.usage: "L4-5 lateral has plexus risk, and I'd check bone density for subsidence."

glossary.definition: Transforaminal interbody fusion, performed through a posterior approach and available as open or MIS.
glossary.usage: "MIS TLIF cuts blood loss and stay, but long-term results converge."

glossary.definition: Anterior lumbar interbody fusion, giving a large graft and good lordosis at the lower lumbar levels.
glossary.usage: "An ALIF at L5-S1 gives me the lordosis I want."

glossary.definition: Standard posterior removal of a herniated disc fragment.
glossary.usage: "Microdiscectomy remains the comparator for endoscopic techniques."

glossary.definition: Percutaneous transforaminal endoscopic discectomy.
glossary.usage: "PTED was noninferior for leg pain, with a specific learning curve to weigh."

glossary.definition: Saddle anesthesia, bladder or bowel dysfunction and bilateral leg symptoms from compression of the cauda equina. A surgical urgency.
glossary.usage: "Retention with saddle numbness: this goes today, and don't wait for the morning list."

glossary.definition: Provocative disc injection to identify a pain generator. Long-term data raised concern about accelerated degeneration.
glossary.usage: "I don't use discography. Carragee's data show accelerated degeneration in punctured discs."

glossary.definition: Analyzes patients by assigned group regardless of treatment received. It preserves randomization.
glossary.usage: "The ITT result in SPORT is muted by crossover, and that doesn't mean surgery failed."

glossary.definition: Analyzes patients by treatment actually received. It captures real exposure but loses some protection of randomization.
glossary.usage: "As-treated favors surgery, but patients chose to cross over, so confounding is back."

glossary.definition: Includes only patients who followed their assigned treatment, though definitions vary: NORDSTEN also removed reoperated patients. It matters in noninferiority trials, where ITT can bias toward no difference.
glossary.usage: "For a noninferiority trial, I check the per-protocol result too."

glossary.definition: Patients receiving the treatment of the other arm. High crossover dilutes the ITT comparison.
glossary.usage: "With that much crossover, the trial can't answer the question it set out to."

glossary.definition: The largest loss of benefit accepted while still calling a treatment noninferior. It is a judgment: NORDSTEN chose 15 percentage points empirically.
glossary.usage: "The result is noninferior within that margin, so ask whether you'd accept that margin."

glossary.definition: Trial built to show one treatment is better. A non-significant result doesn't prove the treatments are equivalent.
glossary.usage: "Failure to show superiority isn't proof of equivalence."

glossary.definition: Patients who declined randomization and chose treatment, followed alongside the trial. Useful but open to selection effects.
glossary.usage: "The observational arm helps, but those patients chose their treatment."

glossary.definition: Smallest change patients perceive as meaningful. It varies by method, population and baseline, so it isn't a fixed number.
glossary.usage: "The group mean change passed MCID, but I'd want to see how many individual patients did."

glossary.definition: A larger threshold than MCID, representing a change patients consider substantial.
glossary.usage: "MCID is the floor. Substantial clinical benefit is closer to what patients are after."

glossary.definition: Standard 0-100 patient-reported score of low back-related disability.
glossary.usage: "ODI fell by 20 points, comfortably beyond the usual threshold."

glossary.definition: Physical component summary of a generic health-status survey.
glossary.usage: "SLIP's primary outcome was SF-36 PCS, not ODI, and that's part of why trials disagree."

glossary.definition: Neck Disability Index, the cervical counterpart to ODI.
glossary.usage: "Her NDI is 50, severe for arm-predominant disease."

glossary.definition: Deformity-specific patient-reported outcome covering function, pain, self-image, mental health and satisfaction.
glossary.usage: "SRS-22 subscore gains held at two years."

glossary.definition: Number needed to treat for one benefit, or to harm one patient. Both depend on baseline risk and time frame.
glossary.usage: "Quote the NNT, since relative risk flatters a rare event."

glossary.definition: Range of effects compatible with the data. Its width shows precision, and its limits matter more than the point estimate alone.
glossary.usage: "The interval is wide enough to include a real harm."

glossary.definition: Differences created by who enters a study or treatment group, which then distort a comparison.
glossary.usage: "The surgeon picked who got fused, so that comparison has selection bias."

glossary.definition: Sicker or better-selected patients receive a given treatment for reasons that also affect outcome.
glossary.usage: "The fused group had more instability to begin with: confounding by indication."

glossary.definition: Whether a study's result applies to patients outside its eligibility criteria.
glossary.usage: "That trial excluded his kind of instability, so its external validity stops here."

glossary.definition: Loss of patients to follow-up, which can bias long-term results if related to outcome.
glossary.usage: "Long follow-up, but with that much attrition I'd be careful."

glossary.definition: Framework rating certainty of evidence and strength of recommendation separately.
glossary.usage: "It's a recommendation built on low-certainty evidence, so call it that."

glossary.definition: Combines baseline factors to estimate an individual's risk. Needs external validation, and it may not transfer to other settings.
glossary.usage: "Useful for counseling, but I won't treat a model output as a certainty."

glossary.definition: Course of a condition without the intervention. Without it, operated-cohort improvement is hard to interpret.
glossary.usage: "Improvement in an operated cohort says little if we don't know the natural history."

glossary.definition: Thoracolumbar injury score from morphology, posterior ligamentous complex and neurologic status. Commonly: 3 or less nonoperative, 5 or more operative, 4 either.
glossary.usage: "TLICS is 3, so I'd treat this burst nonoperatively."

glossary.definition: Axial load fracture involving the anterior and middle columns, sometimes with canal retropulsion.
glossary.usage: "Neurologically intact burst fracture, and the long-term Wood data support bracing or no fusion."

glossary.definition: Injury severity grade from A (complete) to E (normal).
glossary.usage: "He's AIS C with sacral sparing."

glossary.definition: Surgery within about 24 hours of acute spinal cord injury, where feasible.
glossary.usage: "STASCIS is why I try to get an acute cord injury to the OR within 24 hours."

glossary.definition: Spinal Instability Neoplastic Score. 0-6 stable, 7-12 indeterminate, 13-18 unstable.
glossary.usage: "SINS is 11, indeterminate, so I'd bring surgery into this."

glossary.definition: Neurologic, oncologic, mechanical and systemic considerations for metastatic spine disease.
glossary.usage: "Walking through NOMS: high-grade compression, radioresistant, so separation surgery first."

glossary.definition: Tumor compressing the cord, usually graded by the Bilsky scale.
glossary.usage: "Patchell supports decompression plus radiation in selected patients."

glossary.definition: Epidural infection that can cause rapid neurologic decline. Medical management is selected and can fail.
glossary.usage: "He's diabetic and MRSA-positive, so nonoperative failure is more of a concern."

glossary.definition: Infection of vertebrae and adjacent disc. Duration of antibiotics is a trial question.
glossary.usage: "Bernard's trial is why I'd accept six weeks rather than twelve in pyogenic disease."

glossary.definition: Managing modifiable risk such as smoking, glycemia, weight, opioids, depression and bone health before elective surgery.
glossary.usage: "That's an elective fusion, so I'd optimize her before booking it."

glossary.definition: Glycemic marker used in preoperative risk discussion. Evidence-based cutoffs are guides rather than hard limits.
glossary.usage: "Her A1c is 9, so let's optimize before an elective fusion."

glossary.term: Bone mineral density and Hounsfield units
glossary.definition: DEXA T-score and CT attenuation, both used to estimate bone quality. DEXA can overestimate BMD in degenerative spines.
glossary.usage: "DEXA reads falsely high with her osteophytes, so I'd look at the CT Hounsfield units."

glossary.definition: Anabolic osteoporosis drug used before or after instrumented surgery, including in junctional failure prevention.
glossary.usage: "The question is whether anabolics actually prevent PJF, and how well."

glossary.definition: Antiresorptive RANKL inhibitor. Stopping it can cause rebound bone loss.
glossary.usage: "Don't stop denosumab without a plan, or you'll get rebound bone loss."

glossary.definition: Age-related imaging findings present in people without symptoms.
glossary.usage: "Brinjikji is why I don't treat an MRI: disc degeneration is common without pain."

glossary.definition: Marker of worse postoperative outcomes and prolonged use, and a target for preoperative counseling.
glossary.usage: "She's on high-dose opioids, so we need a plan before surgery."

glossary.definition: Decompression that keeps the spinous process and supraspinous-interspinous ligament complex, used in the decompression arm of NORDSTEN.
glossary.usage: "NORDSTEN preserved the midline, while SLIP did a complete laminectomy with partial medial facet removal."

glossary.definition: Intention-to-treat with defined exclusions. NORDSTEN kept patients treated as randomized who had data after randomization.
glossary.usage: "It's modified ITT, so check who was dropped."

glossary.definition: A surgeon-influenced outcome. In open-label trials the threshold may fall when another operation, such as fusion, remains available.
glossary.usage: "SLIP's 34% is real, but reoperation is also a surgeon decision."

briefs.title: Decompression alone or fusion in degenerative spondylolisthesis
briefs.question: Why do SLIP, the Swedish trial and NORDSTEN-DS appear to disagree, and which patient does each apply to?
briefs.spoken: For single-level degenerative spondylolisthesis with stenosis and leg-dominant symptoms, I'd offer decompression alone first, ideally midline-preserving. NORDSTEN-DS found decompression alone noninferior at five years, with 63% reaching a 30% ODI improvement in both arms, and the Swedish trial found no benefit from fusion at five years. SLIP is the counterweight: 66 patients, a 5.7-point SF-36 advantage for fusion, and 34% versus 14% reoperation. But that SF-36 result lost significance after baseline adjustment and ODI wasn't significantly different. So I'd consider fusion for patients these trials don't cover, such as multilevel slips, scoliosis over 20 degrees, severe foraminal stenosis or prior surgery at that level, and I'd be open that dynamic instability is unresolved.

rows: At least 3 mm, or no slip; 1-2 stenotic levels
Single level, at least 3 mm on standing films
Excluded motion over 3 mm and mechanical back pain
Not excluded; about 20% unstable on dynamic films
ODI score at 2 years, then 5 years
At least 30% ODI reduction at 2, then 5 years
Complete laminectomy with partial medial facet removal
Surgeon's choice: 97 of 120 central, 23 of 120 bilateral laminotomy
Instrumented posterolateral, iliac crest graft, no interbody
SF-36 gain 15.2 fusion vs 9.5; difference 5.7, 95% CI 0.1-11.3, P=0.046
2-year ODI 27 fusion vs 24 alone, P=0.24; 5-year 28 vs 25, P=0.226
Change -26.3 fusion vs -17.9 alone at 2 years, P=0.06
Mean change -17.8 in both arms at 5 years
14% fusion vs 34% alone at 4 years, P=0.05

reasons.title: They measured different things
reasons.text: SLIP's primary endpoint was SF-36 PCS, a generic health measure, while the other two used ODI. All three show no significant ODI difference, though SLIP's point estimate still favored fusion by 8.5 points (95% CI -17.5 to 0.5), under its 10-point MCID.

reasons.title: SLIP's result is fragile
reasons.text: Its confidence interval starts at 0.1. After adjusting for baseline differences, the 2-year effect fell to 3.9 points (95% CI -1.9 to 9.7, P=0.19). No adjustment for multiple comparisons was made, 51 patients came from one site, and only 68% were followed to 4 years.

reasons.title: Reoperation depends on surgeons, not only biology
reasons.text: Reoperation was at the surgeon's discretion in SLIP and unstandardized in the Swedish trial, which like NORDSTEN was open label. Both the Swedish and NORDSTEN authors argue the threshold is lower when a fusion remains available. In SLIP's related cohort, reoperation was for mechanical back pain presumed to be instability.

reasons.title: The decompressions differed, but that isn't the whole answer
reasons.text: SLIP used complete laminectomy with partial medial facet removal, while NORDSTEN preserved the midline. That's the usual explanation. However, most Swedish decompressions were also central, and reoperation there matched the fusion arm. Our reading is that technique alone can't explain SLIP's 34%.

reasons.title: The most stable patients had the most reoperations
reasons.text: SLIP excluded dynamic instability yet had the highest reoperation rate. NORDSTEN allowed instability and had a far lower one. If instability alone drove failure, you would expect the opposite.

reasons.title: Their questions differ
reasons.text: A superiority trial with no significant difference does not prove the treatments are equal. NORDSTEN does make a noninferiority claim, but only within a 15-point margin that its authors say was chosen empirically, equal to accepting a number needed to treat of about 7.

applies.patient: Single-level slip, mainly leg symptoms, no scoliosis
applies.reading: Well covered. All three trials include this patient, and NORDSTEN and the Swedish trial support decompression alone.

applies.patient: Dynamic motion of 3 mm or more
applies.reading: Unresolved. NORDSTEN included about 20% such patients but says no conclusions can be drawn for subgroups. SLIP excluded them.
Unresolved. SLIP excluded it. NORDSTEN reports no treatment-effect modifier in an exploratory analysis, which doesn't settle it.

applies.patient: Slip at more than one level
applies.reading: Outside SLIP and NORDSTEN. The Swedish trial allowed two adjacent stenotic levels but wasn't designed to answer this.

applies.patient: Scoliosis over 20 degrees, grade 3 foraminal stenosis, or prior surgery at that level
applies.reading: Excluded from NORDSTEN, and scoliosis and prior stenosis surgery also from the Swedish trial. The trial results don't apply.
A different question. SPORT compares surgery with nonoperative care, not fusion with no fusion; only 7% of its surgical patients had decompression alone.

misstatements.better: SLIP's primary result was significant unadjusted but not after baseline adjustment, and ODI was not significantly different.

misstatements.wrong: The trials proved fusion is unnecessary.
misstatements.better: They show no added benefit in the patients studied. Multilevel slips, scoliosis, severe foraminal stenosis and prior surgery fall outside them.
It included patients regardless of flexion-extension results; about 20% had dynamic instability.

misstatements.wrong: Reoperation is the same either way.
misstatements.better: The 5-year totals are similar, but the pattern differs: more early after decompression, mainly fusion at the index level, and more after 2 years following fusion, mainly at a new level.

misstatements.wrong: Motion over 1.25 mm, disc height over 6.5 mm and facet angle over 50 degrees are indications to fuse.
misstatements.better: Those cutoffs came from 40 patients with no fusion comparator. Only motion was significant, and the all-three versus none comparison had P=0.14.
AO's individual recommendations are conditional. Its 'strong recommendation' is that both options can be considered.

flags: The Swedish 5-year paper places its leg-pain finding in patients without a slip in the abstract, results and table, but says the slip subset in its discussion. The table is used here.
NORDSTEN's 5-year text gives early reoperations as 11 and 15, while its table gives 15 decompression and 12 fusion. The table matches the reported 5-year totals of 21 and 23.
AO states that fusion-arm decompressions in NORDSTEN did not preserve the midline. The 2-year NEJM paper made this optional, and 58 of 128 patients had it preserved.
AO doesn't include the full Swedish 5-year report, which adds 213 patients at 5 years against the 138 it discusses. AO also rates Blumenthal's evidence both 'very low' and 'Low'.
Blumenthal and SLIP share a trial registration, site and period, so their patients probably overlap. Blumenthal is not independent support for SLIP.

NORDSTEN's mean facet orientation of about 56 degrees and disc height of 7.6-8.0 mm sit beyond Blumenthal's cutoffs, yet reoperation was 16-18%. This comparison is ours, and the two papers may measure differently.
briefs.limits: Reviewed from full text, not supplementary appendices, so some subgroup and protocol details weren't checked. L14 was reviewed only through a 1997 critique. The reasons and patient readings combine the papers' statements with our interpretation.

cases.case: A 68-year-old woman has neurogenic claudication and a 7 mm L4-5 degenerative slip. Flexion-extension films show 1 mm of motion, and her back pain is mild. A colleague says a slip means fusion. Respond.
cases.challenge: Which trial would your colleague cite, and what happened to that result after baseline adjustment?
cases.evidence: NORDSTEN-DS and the Swedish trial support decompression alone. SLIP is the opposing trial: SF-36 difference 5.7, adjusted 3.9 with P=0.19, ODI P=0.06.

cases.case: A 62-year-old has an L4-5 slip with 5 mm of motion on flexion-extension films and significant mechanical back pain. What does the evidence say, and what would you tell the patient?
cases.challenge: Can you cite NORDSTEN here as proof that fusion is unnecessary?
cases.evidence: SLIP excluded this patient. NORDSTEN included about 20% with dynamic instability, but says no conclusions can be drawn for subgroups. Evidence is unresolved, and Blumenthal's cutoffs aren't validated indications.

cases.case: A resident says NORDSTEN proves decompression alone is equivalent. Correct them in under a minute.
cases.challenge: What does the 15-point margin allow, and what was the lower confidence bound in the 5-year per-protocol analysis?
cases.evidence: Noninferiority isn't equivalence. The margin equals a number needed to treat of about 7 and was chosen empirically. The 5-year per-protocol bound was -14.5, close to the margin, and that analysis was below its planned sample size.

decks.not_reviewed: Published figures or tables (the reformatted PMC copy omits images), the appendix with conflict disclosures, the companion methods article, and the underlying systematic reviews.

slides.title: DCM guideline
slides.lead: Managing mild, moderate and severe myelopathy, and cord compression without myelopathy.
points: Journal club: degenerative cervical myelopathy
Fehlings MG, et al. Global Spine J 2017;7(3 Suppl):70S-83S
Bottom line: surgery is a strong recommendation for moderate and severe DCM. Mild DCM and compression without myelopathy get weak suggestions, built on thin or indirect evidence.
slides.notes: This is the AOSpine North America and Cervical Spine Research Society guideline. The question: until this paper, no guideline said how to manage mild (mJOA 15-17), moderate (12-14) or severe (11 or less) disease, or nonmyelopathic patients with cord compression. A multidisciplinary group used five systematic reviews plus clinical expertise. GRADE rated the evidence, and the GRADE Guideline Development Tool recorded how the group weighed benefits and harms. Listen for the difference between "we recommend" and "we suggest". In this paper, recommend goes with a strong rating and suggest with a weak one. What was reviewed: the full article text, in a reformatted PMC copy whose header says images are omitted. So no published figures or tables were seen, and all tables in this deck were built from the text. Also not reviewed: the appendix with conflict disclosures, the companion methods article, and the systematic reviews themselves.

slides.title: The recommendations
points: Mild DCM treated nonoperatively: recommend surgery for neurological deterioration. Suggest surgery if the patient fails to improve.

rows: Suggest surgery or a supervised trial of structured rehabilitation
Suggest no prophylactic surgery. Counsel, teach the symptoms, follow clinically
Counsel on higher risk. Suggest surgery, or close serial follow-up or supervised rehabilitation

slides.notes: This is the slide to memorize. Two rows are strong and three are weak. The mild row has two strengths inside it. The rationale says the group strongly recommended conversion to surgery for deterioration, and formed a weaker recommendation for failure to improve. The headline grade of weak hides that split. The paper is also inconsistent on the mild grade: the summary says very low to low, and Part 3 says very low. The reason for urgency with deterioration is that longer symptoms and worse myelopathy both reduce the odds of reaching mJOA 16 or higher. The paper advises immediate referral for progressive myelopathy, whatever the baseline severity. If a nonmyelopathic patient develops myelopathy, manage by the severity rows above, considering how fast it came on. Not defined anywhere in the text: how long a supervised trial should last, what counts as failing to improve, or how often to see patients. The paper itself says nonoperative care was poorly defined in the source studies. Bring your own protocol to this.

slides.title: Change after surgery, by severity
points: One study, the only one stratified by these cutoffs. Change from baseline with 95% CI. NDI MCID 7.5. Nurick MCID not defined.
No control group here. The pooled mJOA or JOA gain, 1.40 to 1.92, is also change from baseline. Labeled SMD, units unclear.
Complications: 14.1% cumulative. Death 0.3%, worse myelopathy 1.3%, C5 palsy 1.9%, reoperation 1.4%.
Timing: odds of mJOA 16 or higher fall with each longer duration group, OR 0.78 (0.61-0.997).
slides.notes: Read the table in two directions. Absolute gain is largest in severe patients, 4.91 points, but the MCID also rises with severity. The paper says the bigger gain likely reflects the mJOA ceiling effect and more room to improve. In the other direction, each extra preoperative mJOA point raises the odds of finishing at 16 or higher, OR 1.22 (1.05-1.41). Our inference, since the paper gives odds and not final scores by group: severe patients gain most but likely finish lowest. Lower odds at worse baseline is the paper's argument for operating before patients progress. Our reading, not the paper's: mild is the one row where the mJOA lower bound, 0.70, sits below its MCID of 1. The moderate NDI lower bound, 5.90, is below 7.5. The paper says all changes exceeded the MCID, which holds for the point estimates only, and it also says the Nurick MCID is undefined. The evidence base was 32 studies: 9 prospective comparative, 4 randomized and 19 prospective case series. Evidence was rated moderate because of the large pooled effect. Our reading: the size of that effect is unclear. Part 1 calls the pooled mJOA or JOA figures standard mean differences, Part 2 calls them pooled mean improvements, and the Nurick and NDI figures beside them are raw units. If these are raw points, 1.92 is near the overall MCID of 1.11 to 2.0, not a large standardized effect. Our reading: 14.1% is called low by the authors, but it is a pooled figure, not reported by severity, and library papers show other numbers (C02 18.7% treatment-related; C05 48% ventral and 24% dorsal), with definitions that may differ. Timing rests on one study with an upper bound of 0.997; three other studies found no difference by duration, and the paper warns that duration is subject to recall bias. Cost: ICUR of 32,916 dollars per QALY in one model and 11,496 in a lifetime model, Canadian patients only and not by severity.

slides.title: Mild DCM: why it stayed a choice
points: Pulls toward surgery: 20% to 62% lose 1 or more JOA points at 3 to 6 years
Pulls toward surgery: nonoperative change 0 to 2.3, mostly below MCID
Pulls toward surgery: admission for spinal cord injury, HR 1.57 (1.11-2.22), conservative vs operative
Holds it back: Kadanka RCT, no mJOA difference at 1, 2, 3 or 10 years
Holds it back: that RCT used mJOA 12 or higher, not 15 or higher
Holds it back: no nonoperative study of mild patients alone
Holds it back: one study stratified surgical results by severity
The vote: are the desirable effects of surgery large relative to the undesirable? Probably yes 12, uncertain 16.
So decide together: preference, age, comorbidities, symptom duration, smoking.
slides.notes: This is the core of the guideline for a practicing surgeon. None of the left column is mild-specific: every item comes from mixed or unstratified severities, and no study reported nonoperative outcomes in mild patients alone. The 20% to 62% figure is for symptomatic myelopathy in general, from 2 small prospective and 4 retrospective studies. The paper also reports worsening activities of daily living at 1, 2, 3 and 10 years: 6%, 21%, 28% and 56%. The group doubted whether these effects applied to mild disease, since severities were mixed. The group called spinal cord injury rates low and less important for the mild decision, even though the HR favors surgery. Conversion to surgery after failed nonoperative care ranged from 23% to 54%. It is off the left column on purpose: it was a critical outcome, but the group did not count it as an undesirable effect, because it may reflect patient or clinician preference. Kadanka is both the best trial and the awkward one. It also found a slower 10-meter walk after surgery. But the operative arm showed no mJOA improvement, unlike other surgical series, which may partly explain the null result. Nonoperative care ranged across bed rest, traction, immobilization, thermal therapy, physical therapy and NSAIDs. The best gains came with soft disc herniation and dynamic myelopathy, where you would expect them. Static compression did less well. Fukui: 80% improved by 1 or more JOA points with symptoms under 3 months, against 46% with longer symptoms, with nonoperative care. Both options came out closely balanced or uncertain, so both were suggested. Risk markers for progression come from earlier studies: circumferential compression, angular-edged cord, greater range of motion, lower segmental lordotic angle, greater slip, segmental instability and a narrower CSF column. The paper calls for better predictors and gives no scoring rule.

slides.title: Compression without myelopathy
points: 8% myelopathy by 12 months
22.6% at median 44 months
Two cohorts with cord compression or canal stenosis, not split by radiculopathy. These rates mix the two rows of the guideline.
No study compared surgery with observation in either group.
Why the two groups differ: without radiculopathy, expert opinion suggests against surgery. With radiculopathy, risk is higher and benefit unknown, so surgery stays an option.
slides.notes: Both of these recommendations rest on the Wilson review and clinical opinion. No studies after 2013 met criteria when the group tried to update it. Without radiculopathy, the group said benefit was probably not large and the undesirable consequences probably outweigh the desirable ones, especially in patients not at high risk. Note the evidence line is no identified evidence, based on expert opinion. The 8% and 22.6% are for subjects with cord compression or canal stenosis, not compression alone. The 22.6% is called "only" 22.6% by the authors. Our reading: this figure includes radiculopathy patients, so the rate for the true no-radiculopathy group is unknown from this text and may be lower. With radiculopathy, the group said the desirable effect was uncertain, not large. Higher risk alone does not prove surgery prevents myelopathy. Radiculopathy was present in 62.5% of those who developed myelopathy by 12 months and 26.3% of those who did not. On multivariate analysis, radiculopathy (P = .007), prolonged SEP (P = .007) and prolonged MEP (P = .033) were associated with early myelopathy. The four electrophysiologic and clinical RRs on the slide are univariate. T2 signal: 35.6% versus 21.4%. T2 hyperintensity is a significant predictor, RR 1.7, yet for the purpose of this guideline the group chose not to segregate this population by T2 signal, and it says future evidence should be incorporated. Our reading: an MRI bright spot alone does not move a patient to another row of this guideline, but that rests on an expert-opinion, weak suggestion, not on evidence that the signal does not matter. OPLL: progression ranged from 0% to 61.5% across 3 studies, with insufficient evidence. Complication rates come from myelopathic patients; none exist for prophylactic surgery. One wording gap: the Part 5 population allows clinical and/or electrophysiological radiculopathy, but the recommendation says clinical evidence with or without electrophysiological confirmation. So the isolated EMG finding is left unclear.

slides.title: Grading, gaps and possible errors
points: What holds up: GRADE with a documented process
What holds up: multidisciplinary, editorially independent group
What holds up: conflict-free methodologists
What holds up: external review, patients invited
What holds up: gaps stated openly
Evidence gap: pooled surgical effects are before-after
Evidence gap: complications not reported by severity
Evidence gap: nonoperative care poorly defined
Evidence gap: cost data Canadian only, not by severity
Evidence gap: duration of symptoms open to recall bias
Evidence gap: mJOA reliability listed as unknown
Possible error: Nurick "exceeded MCID", yet no MCID defined
Possible error: mild grade, very low to low, or very low
Possible error: "SMD" labels, VAS 32.74 looks raw, mJOA unclear
Possible error: OR 0.72 (0.66-0.92) is off-center
Possible error: citations 11, 18 and 22 mismatch the reference list
slides.notes: Be fair. These authors are candid about their limits, and they list six knowledge gaps and five methodological limitations. The paper does not rank them. Our judgment: most serious for practice are no standard definitions, nonoperative protocols, and studies not stratified by severity. Vote counts vary from question to question. Examples are 25 on the moderate and severe balance, 24 on nonoperative certainty and 28 on the mild surgical balance. The text does not explain why. Severe is a strong recommendation with moderate evidence, and the vote was probably outweigh 16, outweigh 9, with 12 of 26 uncertain on cost. Moderate was probably outweigh 20, outweigh 5. Items in the possible errors column are our reading of this copy. On the SMD label: the VAS values look like raw points, and the mJOA or JOA values are called standard mean differences in Part 1 but pooled mean improvements in Part 2. The mismatch: the text cites Fehlings et al as 18 and Tetreault et al as 22 for MCID, but reference 18 is Tetreault and reference 22 is Nouri on MRI. The GRADE tool sentence cites 8 to 11, but reference 11 is Wu, an epidemiology study. These may be errors from the PMC copy or the reformat, so check the published version before quoting. For the OR, 0.72 sits well off the geometric center of its interval, which suggests a typo, though we cannot tell which number. Our reading again: the appraisal against AGREE II was internal, done by the vice-chair, with external review added. Lead guideline authors also lead the only severity-stratified study and the prediction study. The paper says conflicts were disclosed in an appendix, which we did not see. The paper says randomized surgical trials are largely unfeasible without equipoise. Our reading: 16 of 28 members being uncertain in mild DCM looks a lot like equipoise there, so that claim is weakest where the question matters most. The paper planned review at 3 to 5 years.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: “Moderate or severe DCM: surgery, strong recommendation. Mild: weak suggestion for surgery or supervised rehabilitation. If nonoperative, operate if they deteriorate, and suggest surgery if they fail to improve. Compression alone: no prophylactic surgery, weak and opinion-based. Add radiculopathy: risk is higher, and either path can be offered, also weak.”
points: Badhiwala and the 2026 AO Spine review are quoted from their library records, not this paper. That review is not a formal update of this guideline.

rows: Four selected papers; low or very low
Weigh severity and pain/NDI burden; MRI-only prediction uncertain

slides.notes: Expect three follow-up questions. Should an MRI finding alone make you operate? This guideline does not support it, but the support is thin. It sorts patients by clinical category and, for the purpose of this guideline, chose not to split by T2 signal, even though T2 hyperintensity predicted myelopathy (RR 1.7). The suggestion against prophylactic surgery is weak and opinion-based, and the paper says future evidence on T2 signal should be incorporated. Does surgery beat rehabilitation in mild DCM? The paper cannot say. Its one RCT used a different cutoff, and 16 of 28 members were uncertain. Which approach should I use? Out of scope. The paper lists comparative efficacy of surgical techniques as a separate question. Badhiwala's mJOA gain of +0.87 is inside this paper's 0.70 to 1.87 interval for mild patients, but the two estimates sit on opposite sides of the mild MCID of 1: 0.87 below, 1.29 above. The NDI change of −12.97 is near 12.05. Our inference: the cohorts likely overlap, going by the titles, since this paper's reference 12 is the AOSpine North America study and Badhiwala adds the International study. Follow-up differs: 2 years in Badhiwala, 1 year for the North America study, both per our library records. The Badhiwala figure is abstract-level in our record, so do not overread the match. Read the guideline alongside the later AO Spine work in the library (C10 and C11) rather than alone. The 2026 review (C10) is an expert-selected review of four papers with conditional recommendations, on mild DCM only.
