Nothing in this paper or our records makes it the formal update of this guideline, which planned its own review at 3 to 5 years. It still rests on low or very low evidence and is not a randomized comparison of surgery with observation. The guideline's key message on timing stays useful: progressive myelopathy needs immediate surgical referral, regardless of baseline severity. With radiculopathy, higher risk does not by itself establish that surgery helps. This deck did not review the published figures, the appendix, the companion methods article or the underlying reviews.

decks.not_reviewed: The online Appendix (outcomes by severity adjusted for baseline covariates, and the covariates kept in each model), the linked commentary by Lindsey, and the online conflict-of-interest disclosures. The 8-page article itself was read in full; the paper has tables but no figures.

slides.title: AOSpine North America DCM surgery
slides.lead: Does decompression help patients with cervical spondylotic myelopathy, and does severity change the answer?
points: Journal club: degenerative cervical myelopathy
Fehlings MG, et al. J Bone Joint Surg Am 2013;95:1651-8
Prospective cohort, 12 North American centers, 2005-2007; surgery only, no control group

Bottom line: at 1 year, function, disability and quality of life were better than before surgery in mild, moderate and severe disease. Only the mJOA gain grew with severity. 18.7% had a treatment-related complication.
slides.notes: This is the CSM-North America cohort (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00285337), sponsored by AOSpine North America. It is the source of the mJOA gains by severity (1.29, 2.58, 4.91) that the 2017 guideline (C01) quotes as its one stratified study, so knowing its limits tells you how much weight that guideline row can carry. Why it was done, in the authors' words: the role of surgery in CSM was controversial because natural history reports were mixed. The only RCT they knew of (Kadanka) enrolled mJOA 12 or higher and found no difference between surgery and conservative care. Against that, observational reviews say 30% to 50% of nonoperated patients worsen. Surgery was traditionally done to stop deterioration; the authors wanted to know whether it also improves patients, and whether that holds across severity. Keep one idea in mind for the whole deck: every number here is change from before surgery in operated patients. There is no observed or conservatively treated arm, so nothing here estimates what surgery added over not operating. The journal rates it Therapeutic Level II. What was reviewed: the full article. Not reviewed: the online Appendix with the adjusted analyses, the linked commentary, and the disclosures. The PDF is the complete article, not a critique.

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: 278 operated patients, grouped by preoperative mJOA.
points: Included: age 18 or older, symptomatic CSM, MRI cord compression, no prior myelopathy surgery, no symptomatic lumbar stenosis. No limit on symptom duration or prior nonoperative care.
Surgery: decompression with instrumented fusion; approach and levels at the surgeon's choice. Rehabilitation not set by protocol.
Measures: mJOA (0-18), Nurick (gait), NDI (0-100, MCID 7.5), SF-36v2 (PCS MCID 4.1). No MCID for mJOA or Nurick, per the paper.
Missing 1-year scores: multiple imputation, assumed missing at random. Paired t tests, ANOVA across groups, then ANCOVA adjusted for screened confounders.
slides.notes: Read the groups as three different patient populations, not one disease at three doses. Severe patients were about 9 years older than mild (61.6 vs 52.3) and 6 years older than moderate (55.4), had worse NDI, Nurick and SF-36, more levels operated, and were posterior or circumferential more than half the time (P under 0.01 for each). Sex, smoking (21% to 31%) and symptom duration (mean about 26 months) did not differ. We recomputed the Table I P values from the printed means, SDs and counts: age, NDI, Nurick, PCS, MCS, levels and approach all come out under 0.01, symptom duration 0.94, sex 0.82 and smoking 0.32, all matching. Race printed as 0.61; our Pearson chi-square on the printed counts gives about 0.46. Same conclusion, but not reproduced. The table does not give baseline mJOA by group, so final mJOA by group cannot be worked out. Flow arithmetic checks: 278 enrolled, 17 withdrew and 1 died, leaving 260; 222 of 260 (85.4%) had 1-year data, and the other 38 were imputed. Note what that means. The 18 who left before 1 year are outside the analysis altogether, so the tables say N = 260, not 278. Against enrollment, 222 of 278 (79.9%) had 1-year data. Follow-up fell with severity: 91.0% mild, 84.8% moderate, 80.5% severe (our chi-square P about 0.18). Selection: the authors did not keep data on patients screened but not enrolled, though they say over 90% of those screened at the lead center were enrolled. Mild here means mJOA 15 or higher, which includes 18; the guideline (C01) uses 15-17. Severe here, under 12, matches the guideline's 11 or less. Power: the paper says 80% power for a 1.4-point mJOA difference among groups, using an observed SD of 2.7. Our reading: that is a power statement based on the data, not a stated prespecified sample size, and it covers mJOA only.

slides.title: Primary outcome: change at 1 year
slides.lead: All 260 patients, imputed data, mean (95% CI).
points: Every measure except SF-36v2 general health improved (P under 0.05).
NDI fell 11.28, beyond its MCID of 7.5. PCS rose 5.60, beyond 4.1, and its lower bound (4.33) clears it too.
The authors' word in the Conclusions is associated with improvement. The Discussion's closing line says surgery resulted in it.
slides.notes: We recomputed every difference in Table II from its baseline and 1-year columns; all match (MCS gives 5.59 against a printed 5.58, rounding). Intervals for means should be symmetric. Two are not: baseline NDI, 42.01 (39.30 to 44.47), sits 2.71 above the lower bound and 2.46 below the upper, and 12-month physical functioning, 38.56 (36.98 to 40.08), sits 1.58 and 1.52 from its bounds, more than rounding explains. One number in each is probably a typo; the matching change intervals are symmetric. The baseline mJOA interval implies an SD of about 2.6, close to the 2.7 used for power. Other baseline intervals fit Table I less well (our arithmetic, N = 260): they imply SDs of about 1.23 for Nurick against 0.97 in Table I, 11.0 for PCS against 9.63, and 11.7 for MCS against 10.85; NDI, 21.3 against 20.8, is close. Baseline scores were not imputed, so leaving out 18 patients should not explain the gap, and the paper does not say how the intervals were computed. The SF-36v2 scores are norm-based (population mean 50, SD 10), so this cohort started about 1.4 SD below the norm on PCS and finished about 0.8 SD below (our arithmetic): better, not normal. How to read it. A mean change past the MCID is not the same as most patients reaching it; the paper gives no responder proportions. The paper says no MCID has been established for mJOA or Nurick, so a 2.88-point mJOA gain has no anchor in this paper. The general health domain did not move, which the authors call a trend. Now the fragile part. Without a control, the change from baseline mixes the effect of surgery with natural history, regression to the mean (patients often present at a low point), and expectation; every patient knew they had been operated on (our reading). The mJOA and Nurick are investigator-administered; the paper does not say who scored them or whether the scorers were independent of the surgeon. Imputation assumed missing at random. If patients who did poorly were the ones who missed the visit, the gains are overstated (our reading). The authors call this the largest prospective cohort of its kind and say their results apply to most patients with CSM; the broad entry criteria support that, but surgeon selection of who was operated still applies.

slides.title: Change by baseline severity
slides.lead: Severe patients gained the most mJOA. No other change differed significantly by severity.
points: mJOA gain differed by group (P under 0.0001), and the time by severity interaction held after adjustment (P under 0.01).
Nurick, NDI and all SF-36v2 changes: no significant difference among groups.
Authors' explanation for mJOA: a ceiling effect, as mild patients cannot pass 18.
slides.notes: Check that the groups add up: weighting the Table III changes by 78, 105 and 77 reproduces every Table II overall change, so the two tables agree. All Table III intervals are symmetric. Two cautions on the mJOA gradient, both ours. First, the groups were defined by the same baseline mJOA that the change is measured on. Patients classed as severe on a bad day will drift up, and mild patients classed on a good day will drift down, so regression to the mean pushes the gradient the same way as the ceiling effect the authors cite. Second, a mild patient at 15 can gain at most 3 points, and an 18 cannot gain at all. Bigger gains in severe disease do not mean severe patients end up better; baseline mJOA by group is not reported, so their final scores cannot be computed from this paper. For prediction of final state, see the Tetreault model (C04), built in 272 CSM-NA patients. No difference is not the same as the same. The study was powered for a 1.4-point mJOA difference, not for NDI or SF-36. The NDI intervals are about 8 to 9 points wide, so differences of several points between groups cannot be ruled out. Against MCIDs (our reading): moderate NDI has a lower bound of 5.90, below the 7.5 MCID, and moderate PCS (3.67) and severe PCS (2.36) have lower bounds below 4.1, so for those groups the data do not exclude a mean change smaller than the MCID. Mild PCS (4.15) and mild NDI (7.76) clear their MCIDs only barely. The adjusted model screened covariates by their correlation with the 12-month outcome (P under 0.2), not by association with both group and outcome. The adjusted tables are in the Appendix, which we did not review, so we cannot say which covariates were kept. The Methods also say covariates with a partial correlation above 0.1 were eliminated; as written that would remove the stronger covariates, so it probably means a P value above 0.1. What the authors say: apart from mJOA, the degree of improvement did not depend on preoperative severity. That means no significant difference, not proof that mild patients improved as much as severe ones.

slides.title: Complications
slides.lead: 52 of 278 (18.7%) had a treatment-related complication by 1 year; 78 events in all.
points: Prospective list of 30 expected complications, checked at 6 and 12 months and unplanned visits, verified by external monitors, adjudicated by an independent spine surgeon.
Revision surgery: 6 (2.2%); indications included neck hematoma, deep wound infection and graft malposition.
Worsening myelopathy right after surgery: 3; two were back to baseline at 1 year.
Rate did not differ by severity (P over 0.05).
slides.notes: Table IV arithmetic checks: the 32 rows add to 30, 22 and 26 events by group, 78 in total, matching the text, and every row percentage is the count over 278. Our rates by group: 20.0% mild, 15.5% moderate, 21.7% severe; our chi-square gives P about 0.51, consistent with the paper. Note the denominator: complications use all 278, while outcomes use 260. Read the 18.7% for what it is: patients with at least one treatment-related complication, as judged by one surgeon, within a year. It is not all adverse events, since unrelated events were set aside. The authors argue that careful prospective monitoring should find more events than retrospective series, and that their rate sits within the 11% to 38% reported elsewhere. They also say most complications were transient and without long-term functional impact; the paper gives no data on duration to show this. Mild patients carried 2 of the 3 cases of worsening myelopathy. Small numbers, but in a group with the least mJOA to gain, it is the trade a patient should hear about (our reading). Dysphagia at 3.6% is far below the 41% after ventral surgery in the CSM-S trial (C05), whose any-complication rates were 47.6% ventral and 24.0% dorsal. Those figures are from the C05 record; definitions and ascertainment clearly differed, so do not compare the rates directly. Badhiwala's mild subgroup of the combined cohorts (C03) reports at least one complication in 30.6% by its own definition. Small table problems: hematoma appears as two rows, Epidural/wound hematoma (2) and Wound hematoma (1), and revisions are not a separate row beyond one reoperation not otherwise specified, so the 6 revisions cannot be traced in the table. Complications were not split by approach.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: Strong measurement, weak comparison.
points: Holds up: prospective, 12 centers, broad entry, validated scales
Holds up: externally monitored data, adjudicated complications
Holds up: arithmetic of Tables I to IV mostly reproduces
Fragile: no nonsurgical control, so no treatment effect
Fragile: severity groups defined by the outcome scale
Fragile: 18 dropouts excluded; 38 imputed; worse follow-up in severe
Fragile: screened patients not recorded
Fragile: approach and levels uncontrolled; not analyzed by approach
Fragile: one year only
Source problems: baseline NDI and 12-month physical functioning CIs off-center; baseline CIs imply larger SDs than Table I; race P not reproduced; partial correlation rule; 15% attrition uses 260
slides.notes: Be fair first. The measurement side is good: four instruments, a predefined complication list, more than 80 monitoring site visits, and independent adjudication. The authors state their limits plainly: no control group, 15% attrition, no surgical protocol, nonexperimental adjustment, and no data on screened patients. Their reasons for no RCT: they judged there was no equipoise for symptomatic myelopathy with cord compression, and expected crossover would undermine a trial, citing SPORT. The authors also say Kadanka's conclusions must be tempered by unbalanced groups, an underpowered analysis and substantial loss to follow-up, and they cite an unpredictable natural history and irreversible cord damage from prolonged compression. Our reading: even granting those points, the paper's own account of the literature (Kadanka found no difference; 30% to 50% worsen, so 50% to 70% do not) sits awkwardly with a claim of no equipoise, especially in mild disease. That uncertainty is exactly what later work (C01, C10) still lists. The attrition figure. The authors call it 15%, which is 38 of 260. Counting from 278 enrolled, 56 lacked 1-year data, about 20%, and the 18 who left (17 withdrawals, 1 death) were not imputed. The direction of effect is labeled correctly throughout: higher mJOA and SF-36 are better, lower NDI and Nurick are better, so negative NDI and Nurick changes are improvements. Treatment was heterogeneous: anterior 61%, posterior 34%, circumferential 5%, more posterior work in severe disease. The paper says all cases were decompression with instrumented fusion and does not mention laminoplasty. Approach comparisons are left to future analyses, so any difference by approach is confounded into the severity comparison. One year is short for a degenerative disease; durability is untested here, and Badhiwala's 2-year mild data (C03) are the library's next look. Level II is the journal's rating for a prospective cohort. Our reading: for the question of whether surgery works, a case series without a comparator answers what happens after surgery, not what would have happened without it.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: “Of 278 operated patients, 260 were analyzed. At 1 year, mJOA, Nurick, NDI and the SF-36 summary scores improved, mild to severe; the general health domain did not. Severe patients gained the most mJOA; the other gains did not differ significantly by severity. 18.7% of the 278 had a treatment-related complication. There was no control group, so this is the course after surgery, not proof of benefit over observation.”
points: Numbers to hold: mJOA +2.88 overall; 1.29 mild, 2.58 moderate, 4.91 severe. NDI −11.28. PCS +5.60. Complications 18.7%, revision 2.2%.

rows: Surgery strong for moderate and severe; weak for surgery or supervised rehabilitation in mild

slides.notes: Expect these follow-up questions. Does this prove surgery works for myelopathy? No. It shows patients were better a year after surgery. Without a control, natural history, regression to the mean and expectation cannot be separated from the operation. Why do severe patients gain more mJOA? The authors say ceiling effect; add regression to the mean, since groups were built on the same score. Severe patients gain more but probably end lower; this paper does not report their final mJOA. Should mild patients be operated on? This paper found no significant difference by severity in disability and quality-of-life gains, which is not the same as showing mild patients improved as much. It cannot say they did better than they would have without surgery, and 2 of the 3 cases of worsened myelopathy were mild. The guideline (C01) kept mild as a weak suggestion for surgery or supervised rehabilitation. Badhiwala's 2-year mild figures come from the C03 record, which draws on CSM-NA and CSM-I; our inference is that it overlaps with this cohort, so it is not independent confirmation. Its mJOA gain, 0.87, is lower than this paper's 1.29, and its definition of mild excludes mJOA 18. How safe is it? 18.7% treatment-related complications at 1 year by careful prospective capture, dysphagia the most common (3.6%), then superficial infection (2.9%); revision 2.2%. Which approach? Not tested here; the CSM-S trial (C05) is the library's randomized comparison of ventral and dorsal surgery. What did this deck not see? The adjusted analyses in the online Appendix and the commentary.

decks.not_reviewed: Published figures (the reformatted PMC copy omits images). The full table of baseline SF-36v2 scores against population norms with all SMDs and 95% CIs: the text cites it as Table 3, but Table 3 in this copy is the outcomes table, so only the three SMDs quoted in the text were reviewed. The parent CSM-NA and CSM-I reports, the Canadian normative data source and the other cited studies were not read. The copy is otherwise complete full text; only the last word of the conclusion is cut off.

slides.title: Surgery for mild DCM: Badhiwala 2019
slides.lead: Patients operated on for mild DCM (mJOA 15–17) started with poor quality of life and were better at 2 years, but with no control group the gains cannot be credited to surgery alone.
points: Badhiwala JH, et al. Neurosurgery 2019;84(4):890-897
Design: the mild subgroup of two prospective AOSpine surgical cohorts, CSM-NA and CSM-I
193 patients, all operated; seen at 6, 12 and 24 months
Question 1: how impaired is quality of life in mild DCM compared with population norms?
Question 2: how do function, disability and quality of life change after surgery?
Read from the full text in a reformatted PMC copy with images omitted
slides.notes: Set the context the way the authors do. In their account, guidelines recommend surgery for moderate and severe DCM and nonoperative care with serial follow-up for asymptomatic cord compression. For mild DCM the guidelines suggest either surgery or a supervised trial of structured rehabilitation, and the authors put that softer wording down to a lack of evidence. They frame mild DCM as a conundrum: little to gain and a lot to lose, or the best chance to stop irreversible damage early. They had two hypotheses. First, quality of life would be clearly impaired despite mild disease. Second, surgery would halt progression and improve function and quality of life. Notice that a single-arm surgical cohort cannot test halting progression, because nobody was observed without surgery. The mild, moderate and severe groups were defined in advance in the parent studies to test whether surgical benefit varies with severity, but this paper reports the mild group only and makes no comparison across groups. This is a cohort paper, so the deck covers selection, measurement and validity rather than a trial template. Where to look in the paper: Table 1 for baseline, Table 3 for outcomes over time, Table 5 for complications. The SMD table for baseline quality of life against norms was not in this copy.

slides.title: Patients and methods
points: Included: age 18 or older, symptomatic DCM with at least 1 sign of myelopathy, cord compression on imaging, no prior cervical surgery
Excluded: asymptomatic DCM, infection, tumor, rheumatoid arthritis, trauma, ankylosing spondylitis, concomitant lumbar stenosis
CSM-NA: 12 sites, 2005–2007. CSM-I: 16 sites in 4 world regions (6 Asian, 5 European, 3 Latin American, 2 North American), 2007–2011
Approach at the surgeon's discretion: anterior 143, posterior 46, circumferential 3
Outcomes at baseline, 6, 12 and 24 months: mJOA, Nurick, NDI, SF-36v2, SF-6D, 30-meter walk test. Complications monitored within 30 days
Analysis: pairwise comparison of means with Tukey adjustment; missing data assumed missing at random and left out
slides.notes: Mild by mJOA does not mean trivial. Numb hands in 81 percent, weakness 65 percent, clumsy hands 54 percent, gait difficulty 48 percent, and 40 percent were Nurick grade 3. Hyperreflexia was found in 70 percent and Hoffmann sign in 60 percent. The symptom duration SD is larger than its mean, so the distribution is skewed and a few long histories pull the mean up. The pathology was mostly focal and anterior: disc herniation in 75 percent, and 61 percent had 1 or 2 levels operated. The authors reason that this explains the 74 percent anterior approach; approach was not linked to pathology in the data. Selection: patients were chosen for surgery by experienced surgeons at academic centers, and the authors concede some selection bias despite attempts at consecutive enrollment. Power: the authors claim more than 99 percent power to detect 1 mJOA point, using an SD of 1.8 from an older trial. Our reading: the sample was whatever the parent studies enrolled, and the observed baseline SD was only 0.77 because the range is cut off at 15 to 17. Missing data: 180 of 193 (93.3 percent) had 24-month data, but baseline NDI exists for only 158, and the paper does not give the n for each outcome at each time point. Our recomputation: Table 1 gives a mean Nurick of 2.31 ± 0.81, but its own counts give 2.25 ± 0.73, which matches Table 3's baseline of 2.25. The approach counts add to 192, not 193. Table 3's baseline CIs are wider than the Table 1 SDs imply for the two clinician-scored scales only: about twice as wide for mJOA and about 1.5 times for Nurick. The baseline CIs for NDI, PCS, MCS and SF-6D match their own Table 1 SDs. Our inference: this fits a variance pooled across time points, since later mJOA and Nurick SDs are larger (the 24-month mJOA CI implies an SD of about 1.8), with time points compared as separate groups rather than as paired data. The method is not described fully.

slides.title: Baseline quality of life against norms
slides.lead: The authors report every SF-36v2 domain below Canadian population norms, with effect sizes they call large.
points: Comparator: a Canadian survey of 9,423 randomly selected community adults aged 25 or older
Largest SMDs in the text: Social Functioning −2.33, Physical Functioning −2.31, Mental Health −2.30
Baseline SF-6D utility 0.60
Authors' comparison from another study: asthma 0.76, cancer 0.72, epilepsy 0.71, chronic bronchitis 0.66, depression 0.64, stroke 0.64, heart failure 0.60
Authors suggest hand symptoms and pain help explain why quality of life is poor when mJOA is mild
slides.see: The text sends you to Table 3 for the SMDs, but Table 3 in this copy is the outcomes table. Check the published version for the norms table.
slides.notes: The direction is believable: these patients felt unwell. The size is the fragile part. Our plausibility check, not the authors': SF-36v2 domain scores in the 36 to 46 range look like norm-based scores, which are set to a mean of 50 and SD of 10 in the US general population. The paper does not say which scoring it used. If they are norm-based, these patients sit about 0.4 to 1.4 SD below the norm, which is hard to reconcile with SMDs of about −2.3. On that scale Energy/Fatigue (about −0.50) and General Health (about −0.44) would also fall below Cohen's 0.8 threshold for large, the threshold the Methods say they used, so the claim that every domain difference was large would not hold either (our inference). The rank order also does not fit. Role Physical (35.92) and Bodily Pain (37.92) are the lowest domains, yet the three largest SMDs are Social Functioning, Physical Functioning and Mental Health, and Mental Health (42.47) is one of the better domains. Possible reasons include a different SD in the calculation or norms on a different scale, but we cannot check without the full table. The norms are Canadian adults 25 and older; the paper does not say whether they were matched for age or sex to a cohort with mean age 52. The SF-6D comparison with asthma, cancer, stroke and heart failure comes from a different study and population, so treat it as the authors' framing, not a matched comparison. Our point on selection: these are patients who were selected for surgery at the surgeon's discretion. Mild DCM patients managed without surgery may have better quality of life, so these figures may overstate the burden of mild DCM in general. The authors' explanation: hand function drives daily physical and social life, and pain was present in 44 percent. That is reasonable, but it is their interpretation and was not tested.

slides.title: Outcomes over 2 years
slides.lead: Function, disability and quality of life improved from baseline to 2 years; walking time did not.
points: All changes P < .01 except the 30-meter walk test (P = .62) and General Health (P = .053)
Most of the gain was there by 6 months: mJOA 16.40, NDI 21.05
Authors: mean gains in PCS, MCS and NDI exceed MCIDs of 5, 5 and 7.5; the SF-6D gain is nearly 4 times its MCID of 0.03
No proportion of patients reaching an MCID is reported
slides.notes: Read every number as change from baseline in operated patients, not as benefit over observation. We recomputed each change from the printed means, and all match within rounding, with symmetric intervals. Lower Nurick and NDI are better. mJOA: the gain of 0.87 is small in absolute terms, partly by design. The maximum is 18, and the 39 patients who started at 17 could gain at most 1 point; the authors themselves say ceiling effects may hide improvement. This paper gives no MCID for mJOA. The study claimed its power for a 1-point change, and the interval of 0.42 to 1.33 includes 1. Means against MCIDs: a mean above the MCID does not mean most patients reached it. Our reading: the lower bounds for PCS (3.08) and MCS (3.41) fall below 5, and the NDI bound of −7.76 only just clears 7.5. The authors acknowledge that some patients do not improve or get worse, and 13 had worsening myelopathy recorded as a complication, but no responder analysis is given. Source error: the Discussion says SF-6D reached 0.72 at 24 months, but Table 3 gives 0.71 at 24 months; 0.72 is the 12-month value. Our list of alternative explanations, since there is no control: regression to the mean, expectation effects on self-reported scores, and the treatment that came with surgery. The 30-meter walk did not change. The authors explain that gait impairment was mild and the test responds to change only in more severe myelopathy. The paper does not state the units. Library comparison: the C01 guideline record reports a mean mJOA gain of 1.29 for mild DCM in its one stratified study. That record does not identify the study, so do not try to reconcile it with 0.87 here.

slides.title: Complications
slides.lead: At least 1 complication in 59 of 193 (30.6%); worsening myelopathy was the most common.
points: No deaths
Abstract: the rate of complication was low. Discussion: 30.6% appears high, but fits the 16–41% reported elsewhere
Methods say complications within 30 days were monitored, yet Table 5 lists late events such as pseudarthrosis, deformity and adjacent segment degeneration
All 11 cases of dysphagia followed anterior surgery
slides.notes: For a patient with mild symptoms, harms carry more weight, so this slide matters in counseling. The 6.7 percent with progression of myelopathy is the number to remember. The authors describe the natural history of mild DCM, from other studies, as stable over 3 years in most patients under 75, who rarely improve, while many patients have a slow, stepwise decline. Our inference: progression of myelopathy after surgery cannot be attributed to the surgery without a control, and the cohort does not tell us how often it would have happened with observation. For counseling, set the 6.7 percent against that natural history, not against zero. The paper contradicts itself on the overall rate. The abstract calls it low. The Discussion says it appears high and defends it against reported rates of 16 to 41 percent that vary by approach. The time window is also inconsistent. Methods say complications within 30 days were monitored, but the table includes events that develop late, such as adjacent segment degeneration and pseudarthrosis. So the true observation window is unclear. Our sum: the listed complications total 73 events in 59 patients. All percentages use 193 as the denominator. Dysphagia occurred only after anterior surgery; against the 146 patients with an anterior or circumferential approach it is about 7.5 percent, by our arithmetic. Also listed: new radiculopathy 3, C5 radiculopathy 2, adjacent segment degeneration 2, serious bleeding 2, wound hematoma 2, pseudarthrosis 1 and a cardiopulmonary event 1. Not reported: severity grading, reoperation, return to theatre and complications by approach beyond dysphagia.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: Holds up: prospective, multicenter, across several continents, with external monitoring of data
Holds up: mild group defined in advance in the parent studies; validated outcome measures
Holds up: 24-month data for 180 of 193 (93.3%)
Weakens it: no nonsurgical control, the authors' own main limitation
Weakens it: surgeon-selected patients at academic centers; techniques not standardized
Weakens it: mJOA ceiling; means only, with no responder analysis
Weakens it: available-case analysis; baseline NDI missing in 35
Weakens it: causal wording in the conclusion
Weakens it: baseline SMDs look too large for the scores shown (our reading)
Weakens it: internal inconsistencies in tables and text
slides.notes: Be fair: this is the largest prospective series of surgery for mild DCM that the authors know of, with good follow-up and a broad set of validated measures. The core problem is the design. The conclusion says surgery results in significant gains, which is causal wording for a single-arm cohort. The authors' own limitations section is honest: there was no conservative group because of ethical concerns about withholding treatment, so they compare against natural history studies, which this paper did not measure. The alternative the guideline offers, a supervised trial of structured rehabilitation, was never tested here. Our reading: change from baseline mixes surgery with regression to the mean, expectation effects on self-reported scores and natural fluctuation. The paper reports the mild group alone, so even the parent studies' question of whether benefit varies with severity is not answered here. Selection: the authors concede some selection bias, and we add that patients selected for surgery may be more symptomatic than mild DCM patients in general. Analysis: missing data were assumed missing at random and left out. That is untested, and the number analyzed at each time point is not given. Inconsistencies we found: Table 1 Nurick mean versus its own counts; approach counts adding to 192; SF-6D 0.72 versus 0.71 at 24 months; complication rate called low and then high; a 30-day window that includes late events; the norms table cited as Table 3. Funding: the parent studies were sponsored by AOSpine North America and AOSpine International, and the authors declare no interest in drugs, materials or devices. The authors' own calls for further work: predictors of who improves, since some patients do not improve or get worse, and cost-utility analysis.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: “In 193 patients with mild DCM who were selected for surgery, quality of life started well below population norms. At 2 years, mJOA was up 0.87, NDI down 13 and SF-36 summary scores up 6 to 7, with most of the gain by 6 months. Nearly a third had a complication, and myelopathy worsened in 6.7%. There was no nonoperative group, so this shows surgery is a reasonable option, not that it beats observation.”
points: Guideline and 2026 review entries are quoted from their library records, not from this paper
Expect: should every mild patient have surgery? Is 0.87 mJOA meaningful? What is the risk of making them worse?

rows: Gains in mJOA, NDI and SF-36 after surgery; 30.6% complications
Guideline; mild evidence very low to low
Pain and motor phenotype improved more
Four selected papers; low or very low

slides.notes: Expect three follow-up questions. Should every mild patient have surgery? The authors favor surgery, arguing that impairment is real, gains are meaningful and observation offers stability at best. That last point comes from natural history studies they cite, not from their own data. This cohort cannot show surgery beats observation or rehabilitation, so it supports offering surgery as a reasonable option, consistent with the guideline record's weak suggestion. Is a 0.87 mJOA gain meaningful? It is small, and the scale has a ceiling, since many patients started at 16 or 17. The patient-reported gains, NDI −12.97 and PCS 5.75, are more persuasive, but they are means, the PCS lower bound is below 5, and patient-reported scores move with expectation when nobody is blinded and there is no control. What is the risk of making them worse? Worsening myelopathy was recorded in 13 of 193 (6.7 percent), and 30.6 percent had at least 1 complication, including dysphagia in 11, all after anterior surgery. Say it as a range of harms, not a single low number. On library links: C12 is a later analysis of mild patients from the same AOSpine studies, per its record, and like this paper it includes operated patients only. Our inference: predicting who improves after surgery is not the same as showing who benefits compared with observation. C10 is an expert-selected review of four papers, and its evidence was low or very low. If pushed on baseline quality of life, say the direction is credible but the SMDs of about −2.3 look larger than the printed scores support, and the norms table was not in the copy we read.

decks.not_reviewed: Full 10-page article read end to end, including Tables 1-5 and Figures 1-3; it is the original paper, not a critique. Not reviewed: the 2013 JBJS derivation paper (reference 6), the CSM-NA and CSM-I study protocols, the published comment on this paper (PMID 26526653), and any supplement (none is cited).

slides.title: Tetreault 2015: predicting DCM outcome
slides.lead: Can six bedside facts predict who reaches mJOA 16 or higher one year after surgery for cervical myelopathy?
points: Journal club: degenerative cervical myelopathy
Tetreault LA, Côté P, Kopjar B, Arnold P, Fehlings MG. Spine J 2015;15:388-97
Built on 272 AOSpine CSM-North America patients, tested on 471 CSM-International patients
Bottom line: discrimination held up abroad, AUC 0.77 falling to 0.74. But in the international cohort the model overpredicted good outcomes, observed:expected 0.79.
slides.notes:
This deck comes from the full published article, all 10 pages with five tables and three figures. It is the paper itself, not a commentary. It won the journal's 2014 Outstanding Paper award for surgical science. The model was first published in 2013 in JBJS (reference 6). That paper is not in the library and was not reviewed, so anything about the original seven-predictor version comes from this paper's description only.

What kind of paper it is: a prognostic model study. It answers 'among patients we operate on, who ends up nearly normal at 1 year?' It is not a treatment comparison. Every patient had surgery, so it says nothing about benefit relative to no surgery. Keep that frame the whole way through.

Funding: data collection was funded by AOSpine North America and International. Several authors report AOSpine grants paid to their institutions, and two authors report industry consulting. AOSpine ran both cohorts and supplied the monitoring.

Three messages to carry away. First, the endpoint is a threshold on the final score, mJOA 16 or higher at 1 year, not the amount of improvement. Second, discrimination was fair in both cohorts. Third, in the international cohort the predicted probabilities ran too high, and the paper's conclusion of adequate calibration glosses over that.

slides.title: What the model predicts
slides.lead: The outcome is the final state, mJOA 16 or higher at 1 year. It does not measure how much a patient improved.
points: mJOA runs 0-18. The authors call 16 or higher 'optimal': no or mild residual impairment.
Below 16 they call substantial residual neurologic impairment
Patients with a baseline mJOA of 18 were excluded (6 CSM-NA, 8 CSM-I)
The authors say the cutoff has not been validated, and that the mJOA itself has not been validated and its reliability not tested
slides.notes:
Use Table 3 to make the endpoint concrete. Case 5 went from 8 to 13, a 5-point gain, and counts as a non-optimal outcome. Case 1 started at 17 and would have counted as optimal even after losing a point. So a low predicted probability in a severe patient does not mean surgery will not help. It means the patient is unlikely to finish near normal. This is our reading, but it follows directly from the definition.

The authors highlight case 2. The surgeon predicted the patient would stay the same, and the model gave an 80% chance of reaching 16. The patient reached 18. They use the case to argue that surgeons' impressions and objective prediction differ. The six cases are CSM-NA derivation patients from one centre, Toronto Western, so the model was predicting patients it was built on. Treat them as worked examples, not validation.

We recomputed all six probabilities from Equation 1 (intercept 1.59; psychiatric -0.81; baseline mJOA 0.19; age -0.036; gait 0.91; smoking -0.69; duration -0.27). We got 93.7, 79.5, 72.5, 49.8, 39.4 and 27.4 percent, all within half a point of the printed values. So the equation and the case table agree. To do that, the gait variable has to be coded as the paper defines it, 2 for no impaired gait and 1 for impaired gait. That matters on the next slide.

One small wording point. For case 2 the paper says reaching 16 means 'improving by at least 1 point'. That is true for a baseline of 15. It is not true in general: a baseline-17 patient can reach the threshold without improving at all.

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: Two prospective AOSpine surgical cohorts with identical case report forms
points: Consecutive adults with symptomatic CSM, at least one myelopathic sign, imaging confirmation, no prior spine surgery
Excluded: asymptomatic CSM, infection, tumor, rheumatoid arthritis, trauma, ankylosing spondylitis, concomitant lumbar stenosis
CSM included spondylosis, disc herniation, OPLL, ligamentum flavum hypertrophy and subluxation
Approach and technique left to the surgeon: anterior, posterior or combined
Missing 1-year outcomes filled by multiple imputation, assumed missing at random
Internal check: 200 bootstrap replicates. External check: original equation applied to CSM-I, then refitted.

rows: 16: 6 Asia, 5 Europe, 3 Latin America, 2 North America

slides.notes:
Flow arithmetic. 278 minus 6 is 272, and 217 of 272 is 79.8%, which matches the stated 80%. 479 minus 8 is 471, but 397 of 471 is 84.3%, not the 84.5% printed. Later the paper gives 18% attrition for CSM-I, while 84.5% follow-up implies 15.5%. The numbers do not reconcile. Either way about one in five derivation outcomes and one in six validation outcomes were imputed. The authors state no key demographic differences between dropouts and completers but show no data.

The validation cohort is not purely foreign. Two of its 16 sites were North American, with 123 patients by Table 1 counts, about a quarter of the sample. Enrollment was later, 2007 to 2011. So this is part temporal and part geographic validation. Table 1 itself labels the column 'temporal validation group'.

The groups were similar at baseline on severity, smoking and gait. The CSM-I cohort ended worse: mean 1-year mJOA 14.91 versus 15.69, significant. It was lowest in the European (14.21) and Latin American (14.45) subsamples, which the paper marks as significantly lower; the North American (15.29) and Asian (15.39) subsamples were also below 15.69 but not marked. Psychiatric comorbidity was 24% in CSM-NA but 7.9% in CSM-I, and 31 of the 37 CSM-I cases came from the North American sites. The authors read the low prevalence elsewhere as underreporting, cultural reluctance or selection.

We rechecked Table 1. Smoking and gait counts add up to 471 across regions. The psychiatric denominators sum to 469, and the Asia column gives 146 rather than 148. CSM-NA gait counts, 206/65, add to 271, not 272. The Latin American psychiatric proportion, 1/76, carries the asterisk the footnote reserves for means rather than the dagger used for proportions. The Latin American baseline mJOA SD prints as 0.02, which cannot be right for a range of 4-17. The table marks Asian and Latin American mean ages as significantly younger. Our Welch t-tests give P about 0.06 and 0.11, so we could not reproduce those marks. The test the authors used is not stated. Text and Table 1 also give different CSM-NA enrollment periods.

The paper does not say who scored the mJOA, or whether assessors knew the predictor values.

slides.title: The six predictors
slides.lead: Odds ratios for reaching mJOA 16 or higher, as derived and as refitted in CSM-I
points: Duration has five categories: 3 months or less, over 3-6, over 6-12, over 12-24, over 24
Psychiatric means depression or bipolar disorder (schizophrenia counted as grade 2)
Transverse cord area was in the 2013 model but was dropped: not significant, and the authors cite a systematic review
slides.notes:
Watch the gait row. The tables and abstract label OR 2.48 'impaired gait', which reads as if impaired gait helps. The equation codes gait as 2 for no impairment and 1 for impairment, with a positive coefficient. The Introduction says the absence of impaired gait predicts an optimal outcome, and our recomputation of Table 3 only works with that coding. So 2.48 is the odds ratio for walking normally compared with impaired gait. Say it that way.

How to read the sizes. Each baseline mJOA point raises the odds by about a fifth. Age is per year: using the equation's coefficient, 10 years multiplies the odds by about 0.70 (our arithmetic). Duration is per step across five categories, so the longest compared with the shortest is four steps, 0.76 to the fourth, about 0.33, in the derivation model (ours). These are odds ratios, not risk ratios, and with a common outcome they overstate relative risk.

What replicated. Baseline severity, age, gait and smoking kept similar values in CSM-I. Smoking was not significant in derivation (P = .097, CI crossing 1) and only became significant in the larger international sample. Duration (P = .497) and psychiatric comorbidity (P = .998) lost their effect. The authors attribute both to unreliable data: recall of duration, and underreporting of psychiatric illness outside North America. They keep duration in the model anyway, citing their systematic review. That is a reasonable clinical judgement, but it is a judgement.

The abstract says the duration OR in CSM-I was significantly different from the original. No test of that difference is reported, and the two CIs overlap (0.59-0.99 and 0.80-1.11). The abstract also lists the original values as 1.28, 2.39 and 0.97, which do not match Table 2 (1.21, 2.48, 0.96). We recomputed P values from the published CIs, and they match Table 5 within rounding.

Causality: these are associations in operated patients. Stopping smoking may or may not change the outcome. The authors suggest smoking cessation and earlier surgery, but the model cannot show that changing a predictor changes the result.

slides.title: Discrimination and calibration
slides.lead: Ranking held up. The absolute probabilities ran high in CSM-I.
points: Discrimination: can the model rank who reaches 16 above who does not?
Calibration: when it says 70%, do about 70% get there?
The authors say the CSM-I model 'predicts a slightly better outcome than what is actually observed'
slides.see: Figure 3 puts observed on the x axis and predicted on the y axis. In the bottom (CSM-I) panel most points (each a group of 10 patients) sit above the 45-degree line, so predicted exceeds observed.
slides.notes:
An AUC of 0.74 means that if you take one patient who reached 16 and one who did not, the model ranks them correctly about three times in four. It is fair, not strong. It says nothing about whether the printed probability is right.

Calibration is the clinically important part, because the authors want surgeons to quote probabilities to patients. In CSM-I the observed:expected ratio was 0.79 and its CI excludes 1. On average, about a fifth fewer patients reached 16 than the model predicted (our paraphrase). If the model says 60% for a CSM-I patient, the true figure is probably lower. The paper did not test calibration by region, and the CSM-I cohort includes 123 North American patients. Our guess is that the overprediction sits mostly outside North America, because the European and Latin American mean 1-year scores were lowest, but the paper does not show this. The authors flag the miscalibration in Results, but the abstract reports only the slope and a nonsignificant Hosmer-Lemeshow test. The Conclusions call the calibration adequate, and the Discussion speaks of a 'strong ability' to predict in future populations. That is more than the data support. Hosmer-Lemeshow has low power and missed a 21% overprediction here. The ranges in Table 4 are presumably across imputations (our guess). The paper does not say.

Three technical cautions, all our reading. One: the plotted slope regresses the mean predicted probability of each group of 10 patients on the observed proportion, with axes the reverse of the usual layout. It is not the standard logistic calibration slope, so 0.75 cannot be read by the textbook rule the authors cite. Two: the bootstrap refitted the model in each replicate and reported the mean AUC with a CI of 0.762-0.772. That CI reflects how precisely 200 replicates pin down the mean, not uncertainty in performance, and no optimism correction is reported. The same applies to the very narrow bootstrap OR intervals in Table 2. Three: the only P value comparing external discrimination (.88) compares 0.77 with the refitted 0.76, not with 0.74, the AUC of the original equation in CSM-I. The paper never reports how many patients in each cohort reached 16, so the event rate and events per predictor cannot be checked.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: Holds up: two prospective, consecutive, monitored multicenter cohorts
Holds up: identical case report forms, so no proxy variables needed
Holds up: predictors are cheap bedside facts
Holds up: real external validation in a later, mostly non-North American cohort
Holds up: equation printed, and it reproduces the worked cases
Weakens it: final-state endpoint, mJOA and its cutoff not validated
Weakens it: 20% and about 16% of outcomes imputed
Weakens it: CSM-I miscalibrated, O:E 0.79; summarized as adequate
Weakens it: bootstrap reported as a check, not as optimism correction
Weakens it: event counts not reported
Weakens it: two predictors failed to replicate
Weakens it: no regional validation; psychiatric data too sparse
Source problems: gait OR direction mislabeled; several numbers disagree across abstract, text and tables
slides.notes:
Be fair first. In our view this is careful work: prospective data, consecutive recruitment, external monitoring of data quality, and identical forms in both studies. The model was tested outside the cohort that built it, which the authors rightly say must happen before a prediction rule guides practice. The authors name their own limits. They could not validate by region because of sparse psychiatric data. Attrition was 20% and 18%, which they addressed by imputation. The mJOA's reliability is untested and it has only been translated into Dutch, so language may have affected scoring. The dichotomized endpoint needs validation.

Our additions. The endpoint rewards patients who start mild. Baseline mJOA is the strongest predictor partly by construction, because a patient starting at 15 needs one point and a patient starting at 8 needs eight. That is not a flaw for counselling about the final state. It is a flaw if anyone reads the model as identifying who benefits from surgery. With no nonoperative arm, it cannot.

The numbers that do not agree inside the paper:
- The gait OR is printed as 'impaired gait' but is the OR for no impairment.
- Abstract CSM-I AUC CI 0.69-0.79; text and Figure 2 give 0.69-0.78.
- The abstract's 'original values' (1.28, 2.39, 0.97) differ from Table 2.
- CSM-I follow-up: 397 of 471 is 84.3%, not 84.5%, and attrition is later given as 18%.
- CSM-NA enrollment is December 2005 to September 2007 in the text, September 2005 to December 2007 in Table 1.
- Table 1: CSM-I psychiatric denominators add to 469, not 471, and CSM-NA gait counts add to 271, not 272. Latin American baseline SD prints as 0.02. The Latin American psychiatric proportion carries the means marker, not the proportions marker. Age significance marks for Asia and Latin America could not be reproduced.
- The abstract calls the duration ORs significantly different without a test.
- Table 4 gives the original-model calibration slope as 0.811, but the fitted line on Figure 3 is y = 0.8144x + 0.1067, which rounds to 0.814.
- The only reported external AUC comparison is against the refitted model.

None of these overturns the main result, but together they mean the abstract should not be quoted without the tables.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: “In operated DCM patients, baseline mJOA, age, normal gait and not smoking predicted finishing at mJOA 16 or higher at 1 year. The model ranked patients fairly well, AUC 0.74 in an international cohort, but overpredicted there by about a fifth. It predicts the final state, not improvement, and it says nothing about benefit relative to no surgery.”
points: Comparison rows come from the library records, which are abstract-level for C02 and C12

rows: Chance of mJOA 16+ at 1 year; AUC 0.77 then 0.74
Function, disability and QOL improved across severity groups
A pain and motor phenotype improved more in QOL and disability

slides.notes:
Expect these follow-up questions.

Can I give my patient a number? You can, with care. The equation is in the paper, and it reproduced the worked cases for us. Say it is the chance of ending near normal (mJOA 16 or higher) at 1 year, not the chance of improving. In the international cohort as a whole it read high, observed:expected 0.79. The paper did not test calibration by region; our guess is that the overprediction is mostly outside North America, but that is not shown.

Does a low probability mean I should not operate? No. Cases 5 and 6 had predicted chances of 39% and 27% and both gained 3 to 5 mJOA points. Every patient had surgery, so the model cannot estimate benefit relative to observation. The C02 record makes the same point: improvement after surgery with no control group.

Which predictors can I change? Smoking, and perhaps timing. The authors suggest smoking cessation, earlier management and operating on milder patients. Those are their recommendations. The model shows association, not that changing a factor changes the outcome. Duration did not replicate in CSM-I.

Is AUC 0.74 a 74% chance? No. AUC is ranking ability across pairs of patients. The probability comes from the equation.

Does it work in Japan, or for OPLL? The paper did not validate by region. The authors note more OPLL and congenital stenosis in East Asian patients and did not test cause of compression as a predictor.

How does this relate to C02 and C12? Our inference: the CSM-NA derivation cohort is probably the same AOSpine North America cohort as C02, which has 278 enrolled in our record, and C12 draws mild patients from the AOSpine studies. C12 predicts change in quality of life and disability, which is a different target from this paper's final mJOA threshold. Both records are abstract-level, so do not compare numbers beyond that.

decks.not_reviewed: Supplements 1-4 (trial protocol, statistical analysis plan, eAppendix with eTables 1-9 and eFigures 1-4, data sharing statement), so the mJOA, NDI, EQ-5D, sagittal vertical axis and return-to-work-by-approach results held there were not seen. Also not reviewed: the visual abstract, the CME quiz, the pilot study (reference 13) and the three published comments listed for this paper. The PDF itself is the complete 10-page JAMA article, not a critique.

slides.title: CSM-S: ventral vs dorsal surgery
slides.lead: The authors' description: the first randomized trial, to their knowledge, of surgical approach for cervical spondylotic myelopathy.
points: Journal club: degenerative cervical myelopathy
Ghogawala Z, et al. JAMA 2021;325(10):942-951
Question: in patients who could have either operation, does ventral surgery give better patient-reported physical function at 1 year than dorsal surgery?

Bottom line: no. SF-36 PCS improved 5.9 points after ventral and 6.2 after dorsal surgery (difference 0.3, 95% CI -2.6 to 3.1). Ventral surgery had about twice the complication rate, 47.6% vs 24.0%, driven by dysphagia.

rows: Age 45-80, myelopathy, compression at 2 or more levels C3-C7
Ventral multilevel diskectomy (partial or single-level corpectomy allowed), fusion and plate
Dorsal laminectomy with lateral mass fusion, or open-door laminoplasty, surgeon's choice
1-year change in SF-36 PCS; MCID 5 points

slides.notes: Set the scene. The authors open with the problem: cervical spondylotic myelopathy is the most common cause of spinal cord dysfunction worldwide, more than 112 400 cervical operations are done in the US each year, and the best approach was unknown. Before this trial the evidence was observational. The authors cite their own prospective, nonrandomized pilot study (reference 13), which linked ventral fusion with better quality of life and less neck pain and showed SF-36 PCS gains of 8.7 points after ventral surgery vs 4.0 after dorsal fusion; this is one study, not two. They also cite a Washington State database (reference 14) with a lower 5-year adjusted reoperation rate after ventral fusion, 12% vs 17.7%. So the hypothesis was that ventral would win, and it did not. The trial is CSM-S, run at 14 US sites and 1 Canadian site, enrolling April 2014 to March 2018, final 2-year follow-up April 2020. Registration NCT02076113. Funding came from NIH, PCORI and the Tufts CTSI, and the authors state the funders had no role. Note the comparison carefully: it is ventral vs dorsal, and the dorsal arm mixes two different operations. What was reviewed: the full 10-page JAMA article. The four supplements were not reviewed, and they hold the mJOA, NDI, EQ-5D and alignment results, so this deck cannot tell you those numbers.

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: An equipoise population, chosen case by case by an expert panel.
points: Myelopathy meant 2 or more of: clumsy hands, gait disturbance, hyperreflexia, Babinski, bladder dysfunction, ankle clonus
Excluded: C2-C7 kyphosis over 5 degrees, segmental kyphosis, significant OPLL, prior cervical surgery, ASA class IV or higher

An expert surgeon panel (15 investigators in Methods; 15 plus 9 auxiliary members, 24, in Article Information) saw a vignette plus 4 to 6 images. No equipoise if 80% or more chose one approach, or a majority voted against randomization
2:3 block randomization, site specific, web-generated after consent and panel review
Questionnaires by site coordinators blinded to group, at 3, 6, 12 and 24 months
Baseline: mean age 62, 49% women, mJOA 12.2 vs 12.1, SF-36 PCS 37.4 vs 37.3
slides.notes: Walk the flow. 458 screened, 189 excluded (168 ineligible, 13 unwilling, 8 no surgery or surgery elsewhere), 269 enrolled. Then 91 went to a nonrandomized cohort: 76 because 80% or more of the panel preferred one approach, 13 refused randomization, 2 because the panel did not favor randomization. 15 withdrew before randomization, leaving 163. Our arithmetic: every box in Figure 2 adds up. That 76 is the key generalizability fact. More than one in four enrolled patients (76 of 269, our arithmetic) had anatomy on which the experts agreed, and they are not in this trial. Add the exclusion of kyphosis over 5 degrees and OPLL, and this is a population where laminoplasty and ventral fusion are both reasonable. The authors present it the other way: they randomized about one third of screened patients from many regions, which they say makes the results more likely to generalize. Why 2:3? Surgeons chose fusion or laminoplasty inside the dorsal arm, so the extra dorsal patients were meant to give roughly equal ventral fusion and dorsal subgroups. It worked: 66 had ventral fusion, 69 dorsal fusion, 28 laminoplasty. Crossovers were 5, for patient preference (4) or surgeon preference (1). Power: 90% to detect 5 points, SD 9, minimum 137, inflated 15% to 159. Our check: a 2:3 allocation gives about 142 (normal approximation) or 144 (t test), while a 1:1 allocation gives about 136 or 138. So the printed 137 matches an equal-allocation calculation, not the stated 2:3 design; that is our likely explanation, not the authors'. Neither 137 x 1.15 (158) nor 137/0.85 (161) gives 159. Baseline work status looks uneven: full-time work 27.0% vs 40.8%, unable to work 27.0% vs 18.4%. Our chi-square across the five categories gives P about 0.08, so the authors' statement that all baseline variables were comparable holds at the 0.05 level. Table 1 says 3 dorsal patients had 1 stenotic level, though inclusion required compression at 2 or more levels. The paper does not say whether patients were blinded; the coordinators were. Panel size is inconsistent in the paper: Methods says 15 investigators, but Article Information lists the 15 site investigators plus 9 auxiliary expert members.

slides.title: Primary outcome: SF-36 PCS
slides.lead: No difference, and the interval rules out a 5-point difference either way.
points: Analysis as randomized with a linear mixed model: baseline score, group, time, group by time, surgeon as random effect
No imputation; 5% missing at 1 year
Positive difference = dorsal improved more
slides.see: Figure 3A plots each patient's baseline-to-1-year bar; a visible share in both arms point downward. Figure 3B box plots show the lower quartile of change near zero at every visit.
slides.notes: Read the interval, not just the P value. The 1-year confidence interval runs from -2.6 to 3.1. Both ends sit inside the 5-point MCID. Our inference: in this equipoise population, a 5-point advantage for either approach is unlikely. The trial was designed for superiority, not equivalence, so the authors do not claim equivalence, and you should say 'no meaningful difference was found' rather than 'proven equivalent'. Recompute it: from the printed raw SDs (8.2 ventral, 10.2 dorsal) and the 60 and 95 patients with 1-year data, the standard error is about 1.5 and the 95% half-width about 2.9. That matches the printed interval. The dorsal SD of 10.2 is larger than the 9 assumed in the power calculation, and the ventral SD of 8.2 is smaller. The paper gives no explanation; our speculation is that a dorsal arm mixing two operations could add spread. One inconsistency: at 2 years the printed mean changes, 5.2 and 6.0, differ by 0.8, but the printed difference is 1.1, and its interval centers on 1.15. Model estimates may explain it, but the paper does not say. Also, the Results sentence calls the comparison 'ventral and dorsal fusion groups', which is wrong; the primary comparison is ventral vs all dorsal. The authors say both approaches gave a clinically meaningful improvement. Our caution: 5.9 and 6.2 are group means just above an MCID that is meant for individual change, and Figure 3B puts the lower quartile of change near zero. Our arithmetic: baseline PCS of 37 is about 1.3 SD below the normed population mean of 50. SF-36 PCS is generic. The myelopathy-specific mJOA was a secondary outcome reported only in the supplement, so we cannot tell you whether neurologic function differed.

slides.title: Secondary outcomes and harms
slides.lead: Six of seven secondary outcomes showed no difference; complications did.
points: Return to work by 1 year: 45 of 63 working patients (71%); 69.6% vs 72.5%, P=.80
Health resource use (testing, opioids, physical therapy): no significant difference between randomized groups
mJOA, NDI, EQ-5D and sagittal vertical axis: supplement only
slides.notes: Separate severity from count. The headline difference in complications, 23.6 points (95% CI 8.7 to 38.5), comes from minor events, mostly dysphagia. Major complications did not differ significantly, 22.2% vs 17.0%. Our recalculation of all three risk differences, their intervals and their chi-square P values matches the paper. Definitions matter: minor meant resolved within 3 months; major meant ongoing at 3 months, reoperation within 2 years, or 30-day readmission. Investigators blinded to treatment categorized events, but post hoc. The authors add that coordinators asked patients specifically about swallowing, which may have raised the dysphagia count compared with other studies. Now Table 2. It is by treatment received, not randomized group, so its denominators are 66, 69 and 28. After ventral fusion: dysphagia in 9 (prolonged, major) plus 18 (minor), 27 of 66. After dorsal fusion: motor radiculopathy, all C5 per the footnote, in 8 as a major event and 2 as minor, and 6 readmissions (8.7%), 2 of them for C5 paresis. One laminoplasty patient had a spinal cord injury. The dorsal harms are different in kind: fewer events, but C5 palsy and readmission. Inconsistency: the Discussion says ventral complications were mostly minor, 'including dysphagia that resolved within 1 year', but minor was defined as resolved within 3 months, and 9 ventral patients had dysphagia still present at 3 months. Return-to-work: Table 1 lists 68 patients working full or part time at baseline, but the text says 63 were working preoperatively. The paper does not explain the gap; missing 1-year data is our guess. The 69.6% and 72.5% fit 16 of 23 and 29 of 40, our back-calculation. The authors state that secondary analyses are exploratory because of multiple comparisons.

slides.title: The laminoplasty signal
slides.lead: Nonrandomized, surgeon-selected, and exploratory.
points: Only 8 of 24 enrolling surgeons had laminoplasty skills; 5 of those 8 chose it more often than fusion
Laminoplasty complications 10.7% (95% CI 2.3% to 28.2%) vs 29.0% dorsal fusion and 47.0% ventral fusion, P=.002 across 3 groups
slides.notes: This is the most striking result in the paper, so read it hardest. These are analyses by treatment received. Laminoplasty was not randomized; the surgeon chose it inside the dorsal arm. The authors say so plainly: surgeon selection bias could have occurred, there may have been subtle differences suggesting less severe disease in laminoplasty patients, and the results should be interpreted with caution. Only 28 patients had laminoplasty, and the authors call secondary end points exploratory. Now compare that with the Discussion. It says laminoplasty was associated with significantly better patient-reported function, significantly fewer complications, and significantly less health service use compared with ventral fusion and dorsal fusion, with differences at 1 year sustained and significant at 2 years. Check the table: at 1 year, laminoplasty vs ventral fusion was not significant, P=.06, with an interval that crosses zero. The complication and utilization P values are 3-group tests; no pairwise laminoplasty vs ventral fusion test is reported. So the Discussion overstates its own Results. Our recalculation of the 3-group P values (any complication .002, diagnostic testing .02, opioids .02, physical therapy .03) matches. One more fact to hold beside this: the disclosures state that one author holds a patent for laminoplasty plates issued by Medtronic. That is a fact from the paper, not evidence of bias. The ventral fusion vs dorsal fusion comparison, the closest to the randomized question, showed no difference: -1.1 at 1 year and -0.7 at 2 years. Treat the laminoplasty finding as a hypothesis for a randomized laminoplasty trial, not as a result.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: Holds up: concealed web randomization after panel review; site-specific blocks; surgeon as random effect
Holds up: 95% 1-year follow-up, 5 crossovers, flow diagram adds up
Holds up: blinded questionnaire administrators; prespecified primary outcome; interval excludes the MCID
Weakens it: patient-reported outcome; the paper does not report patient blinding
Weakens it: dorsal arm mixes two operations by surgeon choice
Weakens it: equipoise population excludes kyphosis over 5 degrees, OPLL, and 76 cases with strong expert preference
Weakens it: complications categorized post hoc; myelopathy scores only in the supplement
Discussion overstates the laminoplasty results
slides.notes: Be fair first. This is a well-built surgical trial. Allocation came from a web platform only after consent and after the expert panel confirmed equipoise, which is good concealment. Analysis was as randomized, crossovers were few, and losses were small at 1 year. The equipoise panel is the trial's main design idea; the authors note that sharing panel results with patients has raised consent to randomization in earlier work (their references 16 and 17), but they do not report a consent effect in this trial. Now the limits. The authors name three: laminoplasty was not randomized because only 5 of 15 centers routinely did it, subgroup numbers were limited, and surgeon selection bias may have occurred in the dorsal group. The rest are our reading. The primary outcome is self-reported, and blinding a patient to an anterior vs posterior incision is not plausible; the paper states only that coordinators were blinded. The 2-year data are 80% complete, with 21 of 100 dorsal patients missing, 14 of them missed visits. Source problems to flag: the Results text says 3 dorsal patients were lost at 1 year, but Figure 2 shows 1 lost and 2 missed visits. The mJOA is described as 0-18 in Methods and 0-17 in the Table 1 footnote. The 2-year primary difference (1.1) does not equal the gap between the printed means (0.8). Methods says the panel had 15 investigators; Article Information says 15 plus 9 auxiliary members. The primary Results sentence mislabels the dorsal group as dorsal fusion. The Discussion calls laminoplasty significantly better than ventral fusion at 1 year when P was .06. Our recalculations that did match: baseline percentages, the women count (80 of 163, 49%), crossovers, received-treatment totals (66, 69, 28), the randomized complication risk-difference intervals, 11 of 12 three-group complication intervals (ventral fusion 31 of 66 is printed 34.6%-60.0%; exact gives 34.6%-59.7%, trivial), and the 1-year primary interval from raw SDs. Ask one more question: is SF-36 PCS the right primary end point for a myelopathy operation? It captures what patients feel, but not hand function or gait directly.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "In patients who suit either approach, no meaningful difference was found between ventral and dorsal surgery in 1-year gain in physical function; both groups improved about 6 points. Ventral surgery had more complications, mostly dysphagia; dorsal fusion brought C5 palsies and readmissions."
points: Do not say laminoplasty was proven better: it was surgeon-selected, 28 patients, exploratory
Do not apply it to kyphosis over 5 degrees, OPLL, revision surgery, or cases where experts agree on one approach
slides.notes: C02 and C03 come from the library's abstract-level records, not full-text review here, and they are cohorts, not approach comparisons; they give context for the size of an SF-36 PCS gain and a complication rate. In C01, the DCM guideline, mJOA 12-14 is moderate disease, where surgery is strongly recommended; CSM-S patients averaged mJOA 12.2 (SD 2.7) and 12.1 (SD 2.2). The group means fall in the moderate band, but with SDs that wide many patients were mild or severe, so do not read this as a trial of moderate disease only (our reading). Expect these questions. Does this mean approach does not matter? Within the equipoise population, for SF-36 PCS, a 5-point difference is unlikely (our reading of the interval). It does not test kyphotic necks, OPLL, or cases where experts agreed. Should I switch to laminoplasty? The data are suggestive, not conclusive. The authors themselves urge caution, the surgeons chose who got it, and the authors note laminoplasty patients may have had less severe disease. Isn't ventral riskier? More complications in count, mostly minor dysphagia, and major complications did not differ significantly. The dorsal harms were different: C5 radiculopathy, readmission, and one spinal cord injury after laminoplasty. What about neurologic recovery? mJOA was a secondary outcome reported only in the supplement, which we did not review, so do not quote a number from this deck. What about cost? The authors say laminoplasty had lower outpatient use and call for a formal cost-effectiveness analysis; none is in this paper.

decks.not_reviewed: Nothing beyond the paper. The full 10-page article (pages 519-528) was read, including Tables I-IV and Figures 1-8. No supplement is cited. Cited studies (Bohlman 1993, Gore and Sepic, Lunsford, Henderson, Saal, White and Panjabi) were not reviewed; their numbers are as reported in this paper.

slides.title: Hilibrand 1999
slides.lead: Radiculopathy and myelopathy at segments adjacent to a previous anterior cervical arthrodesis.
points: Journal club: adjacent-segment disease after anterior cervical fusion
Hilibrand AS, Carlson GD, Palumbo MA, Jones PK, Bohlman HH. J Bone Joint Surg Am 1999;81(4):519-28
Bottom line: new symptomatic disease next to an anterior cervical fusion appeared at about 2.9% a year, and a life-table estimate put it at about one patient in four by 10 years.
This is symptomatic disease, not radiographic change and not reoperation. There is no unfused comparison group.
slides.notes: This paper reports the 2.9 percent per year figure. Learn exactly what it counts. The endpoint is new radiculopathy or myelopathy referable to the level next to the fusion, present on two consecutive visits, with compression confirmed on imaging when symptoms persisted or myelopathy was the presenting problem. It is not a reoperation rate and not a radiographic degeneration rate. What was reviewed: the full article text, all four tables and the eight figures. No supplement is cited. The older studies the authors compare against were not reviewed, so their numbers here are as this paper reports them. Set the frame for the room: this is a single-surgeon series from Henry Bohlman's practice, 1973 to 1992, mostly modified Robinson-Smith ACDF with no plating described, and a two-poster brace for six weeks in most patients. It belongs to the pre-plate, pre-arthroplasty era. Our note: arthroplasty trials use adjacent-level surgery as an outcome, while this paper is about symptoms, and only about half of its affected patients had more surgery. Three things to carry out of the room: the 2.9 percent and 25.6 percent figures, the level pattern (C5-C6 and C6-C7 highest), and the authors' argument that the cause is the natural history of spondylosis rather than the fusion. That last claim is their interpretation, not something this design can prove.

slides.title: Question and patients
slides.lead: How often, where and why does new symptomatic disease develop next to an anterior cervical fusion?
points: Consecutive series, one surgeon, one institution, 1973-1992: 383 patients and 418 arthrodeses; 9 who died within 6 months excluded.
Analyzed: 374 patients, 409 procedures. 31 patients had more than one anterior procedure, and each new procedure started a new follow-up evaluation.
Patients: mean age 51 (17-83); 180 men, 194 women. Presentation, counted by procedure (409): 284 radiculopathy, 103 myelopathy, 22 both.
338 ACDF (168 one-level, 131 two-level, 37 three-level, 2 four-level) and 71 corpectomies with iliac (41) or fibular (30) strut.
Hospital and office records reviewed by a second spine surgeon (Hilibrand). Follow-up up to 21 years.
Annual incidence: new cases in a year among those disease-free at its start. Life-table (Kaplan-Meier) survivorship for the 10-year estimate.
slides.notes: Four stated goals: incidence and prevalence over 10 years, which levels are at risk, whether multilevel fusion is a risk factor, and whether preexisting adjacent degeneration predicts later disease. The hypothesis was that multilevel fusion would raise the risk. Selection: these were patients who had failed bracing, therapy and anti-inflammatory drugs, or had progressive myelopathy, with compression on myelography, and after 1980 CT and after 1984 MRI. The operation was done at every level the clinical findings and imaging pointed to. Fractures, tumors and combined posterior fusions were excluded. Measurement: the senior surgeon examined everyone and the diagnosis was made from his records by a second surgeon. The paper does not say whether that review was blinded or whether case definitions were set in advance. Our inference: this reads as a retrospective records review of a prospectively followed practice, but the paper does not use either word, so do not label it. The unit of analysis is the procedure, not the patient. 31 patients contributed 2 to 4 procedures each, so observations are not fully independent. Note what is missing: no mean or median follow-up is reported, only a maximum of 21 years, and patients operated near 1992 could not have had long follow-up. The paper does not say how many of the 409 reached 10 years except through the life table, where 53 entered year 10. Postoperative immobilization (354 two-poster brace, 11 halo, 9 soft collar, counted by patient) made no significant difference with the numbers available, by the authors' account.

slides.title: Primary result: rate over time
slides.lead: About 2.9% a year, steady over 10 years; Kaplan-Meier estimate 25.6% by 10 years.
points: Average annual incidence 2.9%, range 0.0-4.8% by year. The printed '95% CI 1.6-4.2' is the mean plus or minus 1 SD of the yearly rates; a 95% CI is about 2.0-3.8 (ours).
Disease-free survival 86.4% at 5 years (95% CI 82.2-90.6) and 74.4% at 10 years (95% CI 68.4-80.4).
So 13.6% by 5 years and 25.6% by 10 years (95% CI 20-32).
Crude: 58 of 409 procedures (55 of 374 patients) developed disease, 14.2% (95% CI 10.8-17.6), over the whole follow-up.
slides.see: Table III gives all 10 years; Figure 2 plots the survivorship curve with widening error bars.
slides.notes: Read the table from left to right. At risk is the number entering the year minus half of those lost that year, the standard actuarial correction. Incidence is new cases divided by that number. We recomputed every yearly incidence and the cumulative survival products, and they match the table. The 2.9 percent average matches the plain mean of the ten yearly rates (29.1 divided by 10), our check. Its printed 95 percent interval, 1.6 to 4.2, is exactly that mean plus or minus one standard deviation (1.3) of the ten rates, not a confidence interval. A 95 percent interval of the mean is about 2.0 to 3.8; pooled, 51 events over 1781.5 interval-years gives 2.9 percent, about 2.1 to 3.8, our calculation. Two things are fragile. First, censoring is heavy: 357 procedures left follow-up within 10 years and only 53 entered year 10, so years 7 to 10 rest on 5, 2, 0 and 2 events. The 10-year estimate is really driven by a few dozen patients. If those lost to follow-up differed from those who stayed, for example if patients with new symptoms were more likely to come back to the same surgeon, the estimate is biased, and the paper cannot tell us which way. Second, the printed 10-year confidence interval is too narrow. It is printed as plus or minus 6.0, narrower than year 9 (6.2), though an event occurred and fewer remained at risk. Our Greenwood recomputation gives about plus or minus 7.5, so the 10-year incidence is roughly 18 to 33 percent rather than 20 to 32. The point estimate stands. The table's entered column also does not reconcile: from year 3 on, each year's entered count is 2 to 7 higher than the prior year's entered minus lost minus new disease. The paper does not explain this. Prevalence: the paper gives 11.7 percent at 5 years and 19.2 percent at 10 years. Neither can be rebuilt from its own counts: Table III has 38 cases by year 5 and 51 by year 10, which is 9.3 and 12.5 percent of 409, and 19.2 percent is higher than the 14.2 percent quoted for the whole 21 years. The denominator is not stated, but both printed intervals reproduce exactly as binomial intervals with 409 procedures, implying about 48 and 79 cases; 79 exceeds the 58 total cases, our calculation. Quote the Kaplan-Meier 25.6 percent, as the authors themselves advise, and do not quote the 19.2.

slides.title: Where it happens
slides.lead: Risk tracked the mobile lower cervical levels.
points: Levels differed (printed P < 0.0001; from the Table IV counts we get P about 0.001, still significant). Relative risk versus low-risk levels: 3.2 intermediate, 4.9 high.
Prevalence tracked White and Panjabi flexion-extension motion by level (r2 = 0.92).
Multilevel fusion: 31 of 256 (12%) versus single-level 27 of 153 (18%); printed OR 0.64 (95% CI 0.55-0.75), P < 0.001.
slides.see: Figure 5 overlays prevalence by level on segmental motion; both peak at C4-C5 to C6-C7.
slides.notes: The level table mostly holds up. We recomputed each prevalence and both relative risks (low group 8 of 296, 2.7 percent; intermediate 25 of 287, 8.7 percent; high 32 of 241, 13.3 percent), and they match. One small problem: Table IV lists 824 discs at risk, but 409 procedures with one segment above and one below can supply at most 818. Treat the denominators as approximate. Two more: Table IV counts 65 diseased discs against 58 affected procedures, and the text reports two patients with a C6-C7 fusion who had new disease at C5-C6 and C4-C5, yet C4-C5 is not adjacent to C6-C7, which conflicts with the authors' statement that disease was immediately contiguous.
