The overall P value also does not reproduce: a chi-square across the seven levels gives about 21.7, P about 0.001 rather than below 0.0001, our calculation; the pairwise comparisons do reproduce. The motion correlation in Figure 5 is across seven levels, a correlation of group summaries, not of patients. The multilevel finding is the one to challenge. The authors expected multilevel fusion to raise risk and found the opposite. But the printed confidence interval cannot be reproduced. From the counts given, 31 of 256 against 27 of 153, the crude odds ratio is 0.64, as printed, but its 95 percent interval is about 0.37 to 1.13 and a chi-square P is about 0.12, our calculation. The printed interval of 0.55 to 0.75 and P below 0.001 are far too precise for 58 events. The methods mention logistic regression, but no covariates or adjusted model are reported, so we cannot tell whether an adjusted analysis explains the gap. The single-level count of 153 also does not match the 168 one-level ACDFs in the methods, with or without the 20 one-level corpectomies. Bottom line for the room: do not say multilevel fusion protects. At most, the crude data lean that way and are compatible with no difference. The authors' explanation is reasonable but untested: multilevel fusions usually included C5-C6 and C6-C7 and so ended next to the lower-risk levels.

slides.title: Degeneration, age and treatment
slides.lead: Only patients who developed disease had their earlier films graded.
points: 49 of 55 patients (50 procedures) had preoperative films. Higher grade went with earlier onset and older age; mean age 41.5 (grade I) to 64.5 (grade IV).
14 patients aged 50 or less (9% of that age group) had early disease from a new soft disc herniation at a near-normal level.

Of 46 patients followed 2 or more years after onset: 13 settled without surgery, 6 declined or were not offered surgery (fair result), 27 had anterior decompression and arthrodesis at the adjacent level.
The 29 adjacent-level procedures: 11 excellent, 10 good, 8 fair.
slides.see: Figure 3 shows months to onset by grade; the error bars of grades I to III overlap widely.
slides.notes: This is where the abstract overreaches. The abstract calls preexisting adjacent degeneration one of the greatest risk factors. But the radiographs were graded only for patients who developed disease. Nobody graded the adjacent levels of the roughly 350 procedures that stayed disease-free, so the paper cannot show that degeneration raises the chance of disease. What it shows is that among cases, more degenerated levels became symptomatic sooner. That is a timing finding inside the cases, not a risk factor. The grading system was new, built for this study, applied by two authors, with no reliability reported. The correlations are printed as r2 = -0.985 for grade against time and 0.994 for grade against age. A squared correlation cannot be negative, and both are fitted to four group means, one of which has just 2 procedures. Figure 3's bars run from about 20 to about 150 months for grade I. Read these as the direction of a trend, not a strong relation. Treatment of the new disease: the abstract says more than two thirds failed nonoperative care and needed more surgery. From the text, 33 of 46 (72 percent) did not improve without surgery, but only 27 of 46 (59 percent) actually had surgery, and 6 declined or were not offered it. Across all 55 affected patients, 27 (49 percent) had adjacent-level surgery. That gives a crude adjacent-level reoperation of 27 of 374 patients, about 7 percent, our calculation, though follow-up is incomplete. Compare the authors' citation of Saal: 20 of 26 primary radiculopathies did well without surgery. The authors suggest nonoperative care works less well for adjacent disease than for primary radiculopathy, but these are different series and different eras.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: A strong descriptive series; a weak test of causation.
points: Strengths: consecutive, single surgeon, long follow-up, a clinical rather than radiographic endpoint, and an actuarial method that handles loss to follow-up.
No unfused control: the paper cannot separate fusion effect from natural history.
Heavy censoring: 53 procedures entered year 10. Mean follow-up is not reported.

Statistics: the multilevel odds ratio interval, the 10-year survival interval and the level P value do not reproduce; the 2.9% 'CI' is a standard deviation; prevalence figures are not reconstructable.
Risk factor claims rest on films graded only in cases.
Era: 1973-1992 technique, no plating or arthroplasty described; one surgeon's indications.
slides.notes: The authors' causal argument has three legs. One, the level pattern follows the levels that degenerate most in the general population. Two, risk tracks segmental motion. Three, other series report similar new radiculopathy after operations without fusion: they cite Lunsford, with no difference between decompression alone and decompression with fusion, and Henderson, with new radiculopathy after 9 percent of 846 posterior foraminotomies within an average of under 3 years, which they translate into more than 3 percent a year. Note that the paper describes Henderson two ways: earlier as reoperation for radiculopathy at another level after 9 percent of 846 discectomies, later as new radiculopathy in 9 percent (79) of 846 patients. They conclude that adjacent disease reflects progressive spondylosis and is not caused by the arthrodesis. Each leg is indirect. None compares fused and unfused patients in the same cohort, and the Henderson rate is a crude division across a different operation, era and follow-up. The paper itself says the findings suggest natural history; the abstract hedges more than the discussion, which says the disease is not caused by the arthrodesis. Our reading: the data are consistent with natural history but cannot exclude a contribution from fusion. The authors describe the yearly incidence as relatively constant over ten years. Our extrapolation: the risk does not appear to burn out after the early years, at least through year 10. The age pattern also matters: early disease in younger patients came from new soft herniations, and late disease from gradual spondylosis. Their surgical recommendation follows from the level data: include all degenerated levels that are causing radiculopathy or myelopathy, assess degenerative changes at adjacent levels in the lower (caudad) cervical spine carefully, especially in older patients, and do not treat clinical disease at multiple levels with a single-level procedure. Note that they do not advise fusing asymptomatic degenerated levels; the recommendation requires clinical correlation and compression on imaging.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: About 3% a year, about 1 in 4 by 10 years, symptomatic, not reoperation, cause unproven.
points: Spoken summary: in 374 patients after 409 anterior cervical fusions by one surgeon, new symptomatic radiculopathy or myelopathy at an adjacent level appeared at about 2.9% a year. A life-table estimate put it at 25.6% by 10 years. Risk was highest next to C5-C6 and C6-C7. About half of affected patients had more surgery. The authors attribute it to progressive spondylosis, but there was no unfused control.
Expect: is 2.9% a reoperation rate? No. 27 of 55 affected patients had adjacent-level surgery.
Expect: does multilevel fusion protect? The crude data lean that way, but the printed significance does not reproduce.
Expect: does fusion cause it? Not shown; this design cannot answer.
Expect: how many were followed 10 years? 53 procedures entered year 10.
slides.notes: Practice the one-sentence version: about 3 percent a year, about one in four by 10 years, symptomatic disease rather than reoperation, and the cause is unproven. Likely follow-up questions and answers. How does this square with arthroplasty trials? Our library's Mobi-C 10-year follow-up (C09), a postmarket follow-up of a randomized trial at 3 sites, reports adjacent-level surgery of 3.1 percent after arthroplasty versus 20.5 percent after ACDF. That endpoint is reoperation in a selected trial population, not symptomatic disease in a 1970s-1990s series, so do not put the numbers side by side as if they measured the same thing. Is the 25.6 percent the truth? It is a life-table projection resting on 47.5 procedures at risk in year 10, with an interval our recomputation puts at roughly 18 to 33 percent. Why is the crude rate (14.2 percent) lower? Because many procedures had short follow-up, and the life table corrects for that. Should I fuse a degenerated asymptomatic neighbor? The authors do not say so; they say include degenerated levels that are causing symptoms, with confirming imaging. Did the brace matter? No significant difference by immobilization type, with the numbers available. What about age? Older patients had more degeneration at surgery and earlier onset; patients aged 50 or under could still get early disease from a new soft herniation. Where would you push back? The abstract's risk-factor claim about preexisting degeneration, because only cases were graded, and the multilevel P value, which the printed counts do not support.

decks.not_reviewed: Read from a reformatted copy of the full open-access PMC text (main paper complete, references included). Not available: Figures 1 and 2 (images omitted from the copy; only captions read), the online appendix (Tables S1 to S10: post hoc power, time-point results, adjusted and sensitivity analyses, MCID responders, adverse event and reoperation detail), the 2017 protocol with full eligibility criteria and MCID thresholds, the 1-year JAMA Neurology report and the short-term neck pain paper.

slides.title: FACET at 2 years: foraminotomy versus ACDF
slides.lead: Posterior foraminotomy met noninferiority against ACDF for Odom success and arm pain at 2 years in single-level, one-sided radiculopathy; reoperations were 8% versus 6%.
points: Simões de Souza NF, et al. J Bone Joint Surg Am 2024;106(18):1653-1663
Foraminotomy ACDF Cost-Effectiveness Trial (FACET), 9 Dutch hospitals
Investigator-blinded, multicenter, randomized noninferiority trial, 265 randomized
This report: final 2-year clinical and safety results; cost-effectiveness is promised for a later paper
Read from the full main text. Figures and the online appendix were not available.
slides.notes:
This deck was built from the full main text of the JBJS paper, in a reformatted copy of the PMC version. It is the complete article, not a commentary. The two figures were stripped from the copy, so only their captions were read, and the online appendix (Tables S1 to S10) was not available. Several claims in the text point to that appendix: the post hoc power, the per-time-point results, the adjusted and sensitivity analyses, and the reoperation detail. Where a statement rests only on the appendix, the deck says so.

This is the 2-year follow-up of a trial whose 1-year result was already published in JAMA Neurology in 2023. The authors say noninferiority was reported at 1 year; this paper presents the concluding clinical and safety results. Expect the same primary conclusion, with more reoperations by 2 years.

Abbreviations used: posterior surgery means posterior cervical foraminotomy; anterior surgery means anterior cervical discectomy with fusion (ACDF). The paper uses posterior and anterior throughout, and so does this deck.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: For single-level radiculopathy needing surgery, is foraminotomy no more than 10 points worse than ACDF?
points: Both operations are common; the choice is still argued and many surgeons prefer anterior
Prior evidence: mostly retrospective series and one low-quality randomized study
Claimed posterior advantages: fewer vital structures, no implant, motion kept, lower cost
Hypothesis: posterior is noninferior to anterior

rows: 18 to 80, single-level, one-sided radiculopathy from foraminal narrowing and/or disc herniation on MRI, needing surgery
Posterior: partial hemilaminectomy and/or foraminotomy, no implant
Anterior: discectomy plus cage (titanium or PEEK) or PMMA spacer, no plate
Odom success and VAS arm pain, margin 10%, over 2 years

slides.notes:
The framing matters. This is a noninferiority trial, so the question is not which operation is better. It asks whether foraminotomy loses no more than an agreed amount of benefit, in exchange for its supposed advantages: no fusion, motion kept, no implant and lower cost. The authors chose a 10% margin for that trade and admit it was set empirically, because no evidence-based margin existed.

Note how the anterior arm was done. The spacer was a titanium or PEEK cage or PMMA, and the paper says no additional instrumentation or braces were used in either technique. So this is stand-alone ACDF without a plate. Many surgeons plate, which may change fusion and reoperation rates. That last point is ours.

The paper does not say whether the foraminotomy was open, tubular or endoscopic. It says only that the patient was prone, with partial hemilaminectomy and/or foraminotomy, and removal of osteophytes and disc material when needed. Do not describe it as minimally invasive. The Discussion refers to minimally invasive results only when citing meta-analyses.

Excluded: patients without radicular pain, purely axial neck pain, and myelopathy with or without radiculopathy. CT was done only when MRI suggested pure spondylotic narrowing. The full eligibility criteria and the radiographic definition of foraminal narrowing are in the 2017 protocol, which was not reviewed.

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: 389 screened, 265 randomized, 243 analyzed; the primary outcome was available in 236 at 2 years.
points: Screened 389: 31 ineligible, 13 declined, 80 refused randomization
Web-based concealed block randomization 1:1, stratified by hospital
Patients and surgeons not blinded; interviewers for Odom and adverse events blinded
Questionnaires at baseline, 6, 26, 52, 78 and 104 weeks
Mean age 51.6 vs 51.0; women 55% vs 47%; soft disc 40% vs 31%
Planned 308; stopped at 265 (86%) after an interim analysis, partly due to COVID-19
slides.notes:
Check the flow arithmetic yourself. 389 minus 31, 13 and 80 is 265. Then 25 did not have the allocated operation, but the arms shrink by only 22 (132 to 119, 133 to 124). The other 3 were crossovers and stayed in the analysis. So 22 randomized patients, 13 posterior and 9 anterior by our subtraction, were dropped because they were never operated. The paper calls the 243 an intention-to-treat analysis. Strictly, that is a modified intention-to-treat analysis. That label is ours.

Why were they not operated? The abstract says 11 of the 25 improved and the rest had various reasons. The Results say mostly because of spontaneous improvement. 11 of 25 is 44%, so mostly is generous.

Also, 80 of 389 screened patients (21%) refused randomization. The authors themselves list surgeon preference for anterior surgery as a possible source of selection bias.

Sample size checks out. With 87% success in both arms, a 10-point margin, one-sided alpha 0.05 and 80% power, we get 140 per arm, 280 in all, and 280 x 1.1 = 308, the paper's figure. But observed success was 74 to 81%, not 87%, which increases variance, and enrollment stopped at 86%. The authors cite an interim analysis and post hoc power (appendix, not seen). Post hoc power adds little. The confidence interval is what tells you whether the trial was big enough.

Baseline table: we recomputed percentages and P values from the counts. Nothing reaches P < 0.05. The closest is neurological comorbidity, 3 vs 10 (chi-square P about 0.055). Two anterior patients are missing from the radiographic rows (38 + 14 + 70 = 122 of 124). The smoking and NSAID percentages imply small missing data. Note the table describes the 243 analyzed, not the 265 randomized.

slides.title: Primary outcomes
slides.lead: Both primary outcomes met the 10% margin; for Odom success the authors also claim superiority.
points: Differences are anterior minus posterior, the convention in Table II
Odom: noninferior, and the bound excludes 0, so the authors also call it superior
Arm pain: posterior had about 2.7 points more pain on a 0-100 scale; margin was 10 points
Complete-case sensitivity analysis: decrease in arm pain bound 10.6, beyond the margin
slides.see: Figure 2 (not seen) plots the estimates and bounds at each time point against the margin; the caption says noninferiority held at every time point.
slides.notes:
Read the signs carefully. In Table II, differences are anterior minus posterior; we checked this against the predicted means. For Odom, anterior minus posterior is -0.06, so the posterior arm did better. The one-sided 95% bound is -0.02, well inside the 0.10 margin and also below 0. That is why the authors add a superiority claim for this one measure. Treat it with caution. Our check: a simple 2-year comparison (0.81 of about 114 vs 0.74 of about 122) gives SE about 0.054 and a one-sided upper bound of about +0.02 to +0.03, which includes 0. The printed -0.02 needs an SE about half that, so superiority rests entirely on the longitudinal mixed model and would not survive a plain 2-year test. Also, a one-sided 95% bound is the same as a two-sided 90% interval, the methods mention a Bonferroni correction that the reported 95% bounds do not seem to show, Odom was not measured at baseline, and the abstract and conclusion claim only noninferiority. Our reading: posterior was not worse on Odom. Do not quote it as better.

Arm pain: 20.5 vs 17.8 at 2 years means the posterior arm had about 2.7 more points of pain, and -2.7 matches that. The noninferiority bound should then be on the negative side (about -7.4). The paper prints 7.4. Our check confirms a dropped sign: the 2-year arm CIs (16.6 to 24.4, 14.0 to 21.7) give a difference SE of about 2.8, and -2.7 - 1.645 x 2.8 = -7.3. The worst case is about 7.4 points, under the 10-point margin. The conclusion stands, but flag the sign.

Two more checks fail. If both models adjust for baseline as described, the follow-up difference and the change difference should mirror each other (2.7 vs 2.7). They are 2.7 and 1.5, so the models probably differ (the time interaction was optional); the bound half-widths also differ, about 4.7 vs 6.7 (ours). We cannot resolve this without the appendix. Second, the authors say sensitivity analyses showed robust results, but they also report that the complete-case analysis of the decrease in arm pain had a bound of 10.6, beyond the 10-point margin. That one analysis did not show noninferiority.

Absolute numbers: both arms improved by about 42 points of arm pain. On average, the two operations relieved arm pain about equally.

slides.title: Secondary outcomes and harms
slides.lead: Secondary outcomes were similar. Serious harms were similar, but the type of failure differed.
points: Neck pain, NDI, work ability, EQ-5D-5L and satisfaction: all 95% CIs include 0
Most improvement by 6 months, stable after
All 9 posterior reoperations were ACDF at the index level; 2 also included the adjacent level
Anterior reoperations: 3 index, 3 adjacent only, 1 non-adjacent
All serious AEs, any cause: 15 (13%) vs 24 (19%)
slides.notes:
Secondary outcomes were analyzed exploratively with two-sided CIs, as the paper says. Differences were small, and the neck pain difference was essentially zero (-0.09 points). The authors' earlier paper found more neck pain after posterior surgery in the first 4 weeks; this paper's first visit is at 6 weeks, so it cannot show that.

Reoperation is the clinically important harm. Table III shows that every failed foraminotomy was converted to ACDF: 9 of 119, or 8%, by 2 years, at 1 to 23 months. Table II reports differences as anterior minus posterior, so -0.02 means more reoperations after posterior surgery. The CI is wide (-0.09 to 0.05). The trial was not powered for this, and the authors say so. Recurrent radicular symptoms without reoperation were 8 vs 1. That CI barely excludes 0, from one of many adverse event categories, so treat it as a signal and not a proven difference. That reading is ours. The authors list possible causes: nerve root manipulation, indirect decompression when disc material is left, or compression type. They do not show which applies.

Anterior reoperations went to adjacent levels in 3 of 7. The authors suggest adjacent segment disease. Look at the timing: 2, 8 and 24 months. Our view: early adjacent-level operations could also mean the wrong level was treated first or new pathology developed. Two years is too short to judge adjacent segment disease.

The Discussion says all posterior reoperations were for persistent or reappearing radicular pain. Table III patient 6 was operated for new contralateral (right-sided) symptoms at the same level, and patients 3 and 4 had new symptoms too.

The MCID responder result (0.56 vs 0.58, difference 0.02, CI -0.05 to 0.05) cannot be right as printed. The point sits near one end, and with about 120 per arm the 95% CI should be about plus or minus 0.13.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: A well-run pragmatic trial whose noninferiority result is credible, with soft spots in the analysis set and reporting.
points: Strong: concealed central randomization, 9 centers, primary data at 2 years in 97% of the 243 analyzed (89% of 265 randomized)
Strong: registered, CONSORT-reported, prespecified margin and sample size
Weak: 22 randomized but unoperated patients dropped (modified ITT)
Weak: patients unblinded and both primary outcomes patient-reported
Weak: stopped at 86% of target; margin chosen empirically (authors)
Weak: superiority claim on Odom rests on a 1-sided 95% bound
Reporting: arm pain bound sign, responder CI, complete-case result vs robust claim
Scope: no myelopathy, single level, unplated ACDF, Dutch neurosurgeons acquainted with both
slides.notes:
What holds up. The allocation was concealed and centrally generated. Loss to follow-up was low, 5 vs 2 patients. The noninferiority margin and sample size were prespecified, and our recomputation reproduces the target of 308. The direction of the primary results is consistent: posterior did not look worse on Odom, and arm pain differed by a few points on a 100-point scale.

What is fragile. First, the analysis set. Excluding 22 randomized patients who were never operated can bias a comparison if the reasons differ between arms; 13 posterior and 9 anterior is not a large gap. In noninferiority trials, a modified ITT analysis is not automatically conservative. The per-protocol analysis is the usual companion, and it is in the appendix we did not see.

Second, blinding. The Odom interviewer was blinded, but the patient answering knew which operation was done. VAS arm pain is self-reported. Patient expectations, for example about a fusion, could move both outcomes.

Third, the margin. Ten percentage points of Odom success, and 10 points of VAS, is a lot to give up. The authors admit it was chosen empirically. Ask yourself whether you would accept 10 fewer successes per 100 patients for a motion-sparing, implant-free operation. The observed result was much better than that boundary, which reassures more than the margin itself does.

Fourth, the reporting problems we found: the arm pain bound printed as 7.4 next to a -2.7 estimate, arm pain models that do not mirror each other, a responder CI too narrow, a sensitivity analysis beyond the margin while the text calls the results robust, Figure 2 caption giving the VAS margin as 0.1, the satisfaction scale (1 to 7) not matching the 0.85 values, and the reoperation reasons in the Discussion not matching Table III. None reverses the main conclusion.

Generalizability (ours): Dutch neurosurgeons described as acquainted with both techniques, stand-alone ACDF, and foraminal radiculopathy only.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "In FACET, 265 patients with one-level, one-sided radiculopathy were randomized. At 2 years foraminotomy was noninferior to stand-alone ACDF: Odom success 81% vs 74%, arm pain about 3 points worse on average, worst plausible case about 7 points, inside the 10-point margin. Reoperation was 8% vs 6%, every failed foraminotomy went on to ACDF, and recurrent symptoms were more frequent after foraminotomy."
points: C08 and C09 figures come from their library records (abstract level), not from this paper
Expect: is foraminotomy better? Not established; noninferior is the claim
Expect: what about central discs or myelopathy? Myelopathy excluded; eligibility detail is in the protocol
Expect: does fusion cause adjacent-level surgery here? 3 of 7 anterior reoperations; authors suggest adjacent segment disease and want longer follow-up. Our view: 2 years is too short to judge
slides.notes:
Keep the spoken summary to the trial's claim: noninferior, not superior. If someone pushes the 81 vs 74 superiority line, explain that it rests on a one-sided 95% bound, a secondary claim the abstract does not make.

Likely follow-up questions:

Who is this for? Adults with one-level, one-sided radiculopathy from foraminal narrowing or disc herniation who needed surgery. Myelopathy and purely axial neck pain were excluded. The paper does not report how many herniations were central or foraminal, so do not claim it covers central discs. Soft disc alone was 40% posterior and 31% anterior.

Is the anterior arm what I do? It was discectomy plus a cage or PMMA spacer with no plate. If you plate, results may differ (our point).

What do I tell a patient? The authors say both should be discussed. Counseling should focus on complication types, patient factors and cost. From this trial: similar relief of arm pain and disability, no implant with foraminotomy, and a somewhat higher chance (8 vs 6 per 100) of a second operation, which in this trial was always an ACDF. The reoperation difference is uncertain (CI -0.09 to 0.05).

What about costs? Not in this paper; a cost-effectiveness study is promised.

Context from the library: C08 and C09 come from abstract-level records. C08 compares ACDF with physiotherapy over the long term, not with foraminotomy. C09 compares arthroplasty with ACDF in one- or two-level disease using a single device at selected sites. Neither changes FACET's result. C09 is the other motion-preserving option the authors mention in passing.

decks.not_reviewed: The earlier 2-year report (reference 9), the physiotherapy program description (reference 19), the subgroup paper (reference 8) and the nonparticipant comparison were not read. The PDF is the complete 9-page paper, not a critique. No supplement is cited. FACET figures come from its abstract-level library record.

slides.title: Engquist 2017: ACDF versus physiotherapy
slides.lead: 5- to 8-year follow-up of a small Swedish randomized trial in cervical radiculopathy.
points: Journal club · Cervical radiculopathy
Engquist M, et al. J Neurosurg Spine 2017;26:19-27
Bottom line: ACDF plus physiotherapy reduced NDI and neck pain more than the same physiotherapy alone. Arm pain and EQ-5D differences were not significant. Both groups improved a lot.
slides.notes: This is the long-term report of the trial whose 2-year results the authors published in Spine 2013. Both arms got the same structured physiotherapy, so the comparison is surgery added to physiotherapy, not surgery against nothing. Three Swedish spine centers, patients aged 18 to 65, study period June 2003 to February 2009, followed a mean of 70 months. Prepared from the full text of the paper. The earlier 2-year paper, the physiotherapy protocol paper and the subgroup paper were not reviewed. Keep one surprise in mind for the whole deck: the clearer win for surgery was neck pain and neck disability, not arm pain. The authors themselves say this may surprise readers, and they say the small sample should limit conclusions from it.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: Does ACDF add lasting benefit over a structured physiotherapy program in cervical radiculopathy?
points: Background, per the authors: earlier series report about 80% satisfaction and a 30 mm VAS drop after ACDF, but without a nonsurgical control or with an unstructured one.
The gap: no randomized study comparing surgery with nonsurgical care had followed patients beyond 2 years.
2-year result: outcomes favored surgery at 1 year, but over the 2 years only neck pain differed significantly on repeated-measures ANOVA.

rows: Radiculopathy, 1 or 2 levels, 8 weeks to 5 years, had chosen surgery
ACDF, then the physiotherapy program from 3 months
Change in NDI from baseline to 5-8 years

slides.notes: Set the context. The 2-year paper was largely negative on repeated-measures ANOVA, with neck pain the only significant difference. This follow-up asks whether the gap widens or closes with time. Note a selection feature that shapes everything: these were patients who had already elected surgery and then agreed to be randomized. The authors say this kind of randomization places high demands on patients, which helps explain the small sample. They also compared participants with 37 eligible nonparticipants (reported elsewhere): participants had longer neck symptom duration and lower pain levels. So this is not an acute radiculopathy population. Mean arm symptom duration at baseline was 13 to 16 months, and mean arm pain only 44 to 45 mm. The paper gives no minimal important difference for NDI or VAS, so the deck does not judge clinical importance against a threshold.

slides.title: Patients and methods
points: Included: arm pain with or without deficit, MRI-confirmed disc herniation or osteophytic stenosis, 1 or 2 levels, symptoms 8 weeks to 5 years
Excluded: myelopathy, whiplash, generalized pain such as fibromyalgia, need for corpectomy or foraminotomy, prior neck surgery, psychiatric or work-disabling disease
Randomization: centrally stored sealed envelopes; treatment began about 6 weeks after randomization in both arms
Surgery: 4 senior surgeons; BAK/C titanium cages, no graft; a plate added for 2 levels
Physiotherapy: neck stabilization and endurance exercise, pain coping, at least 3 months; adherence 94% nonsurgical vs 73% surgical (P = 0.09)
Baseline: NDI 37 vs 40%, neck pain 50 vs 47 mm, arm pain 44 vs 45 mm (surgical vs nonsurgical)
slides.see: Figure 1 is the flow chart: 68 randomized, 5 dropouts, crossovers at each follow-up.
slides.notes: Read the flow chart, not just the Methods. The Methods say 63 patients were included, but Figure 1 shows 68 randomized, with 5 dropping out before treatment, 4 of them assigned to surgery. Those 5 are excluded from every analysis, so the analysis the authors call intention to treat is really of 63, and at 5 to 8 years of 59 (2 declined, 2 unreachable). By our arithmetic 59 of 68 randomized is 87 percent. The 4 to 1 imbalance in early dropouts is our flag: the paper gives no reasons, and losing patients assigned to surgery before surgery may select. Crossover: 8 nonsurgical patients had surgery, 1 after 6 months, 4 after 12, 3 after 24. Seven of them are in this follow-up, 24 percent of the nonsurgical group, and they were analyzed in the nonsurgical group. No surgical patient had a second operation. Outcomes were self-reported questionnaires, followed by an observer not involved in treatment. The paper does not describe blinding of patients. No a priori power calculation was done; the authors say the data needed for one were lacking. Baseline: Table 2 shows no significant differences. Our check: age 48 vs 44 gives about P = 0.08 and EQ-VAS 54 vs 46 about P = 0.09, so these are near misses in a trial of 59. Table 2 percentages: 17 of 29 males is 59 percent, printed 57; 9 of 30 smokers is 30 percent, printed 33.

slides.title: Primary outcome: neck disability
slides.lead: NDI fell 21 points with surgery and 11 with physiotherapy alone. Difference 10 (95% CI 1 to 19), P = 0.03.
points: Both groups improved significantly from baseline.
NDI is scored as a percentage, 0 to 100; higher is worse.
No a priori sample size. The authors give post hoc power of 62% for NDI.
As-treated, moving the 7 crossovers to surgery: the NDI difference was no longer significant (P = 0.14), per the authors.
slides.see: Figure 2A shows NDI means with 95% CI bars at baseline, 12 and 24 months and 5-8 years; the curves separate after baseline.
slides.notes: How to read it: these are changes within each group, compared with a t-test, at a single time point. Our recomputation from the Table 3 intervals gives a difference near 10 with an interval of roughly 0 to 20 and P near 0.04, so the printed result is consistent but sits close to the edge. Three things make this primary result fragile. First, the lower bound of 1 point means the data allow almost no benefit. Second, the as-treated analysis lost significance (P = 0.14); the authors say the reason is unclear and that the more skewed group sizes may play a part. Third, the 2-year analysis of the same trial, by repeated-measures ANOVA with multiple imputation, did not show a significant NDI difference. The authors suggest one possible explanation is the change in statistical method; they do not rule out a real widening, and they note the surgical group's "somewhat unusual ongoing improvement" after 2 years. Hold both: there is a consistent direction favoring surgery on NDI, but the size is uncertain and the significance depends on the analysis. No multiplicity adjustment is described across the many outcomes. Ours: 5 dropouts after randomization, excluded, plus 4 lost later, means even the stated intention-to-treat analysis is not of everyone randomized.

slides.title: Secondary outcomes and harms
slides.lead: Neck pain and global rating favored surgery. Arm pain and EQ-5D did not differ significantly.
points: Better or much better: 28 of 30 (93%) vs 18 of 29 (62%); RR 1.5 (1.11 to 2.01), P = 0.005.
Much better: 23 vs 9.
Harms: no early complications, no reoperations, no second cervical surgery in the surgical group.
Fusion judged healed at 3 months on flexion-extension films; not assessed further.
Adjacent-level disease was planned but not analyzed; too few patients.
slides.see: Figure 2C shows arm pain: both curves drop steeply by 12 months, and their intervals overlap at every time point.
slides.notes: *The arm pain interval is printed as 5 to 32, which excludes zero and contradicts P = 0.1. Our recomputation from Table 3 gives about -5 to 33, so a minus sign is probably missing. Teach it as not significant. The global rating is the most robust result. Our recomputation gives 93 versus 62 percent, risk difference 31 percent, RR 1.50 with interval 1.11 to 2.03 (printed 2.01, a trivial difference). The printed P = 0.005 matches Fisher (0.005) or chi-square (0.004); a z-test on the log RR, the test the table names, gives about 0.008. The much better split (23 of 28 vs 9 of 18) reproduces P = 0.02 by chi-square, but Fisher gives about 0.05, and it is a comparison within responders. EQ-5D P is 0.12 in the Abstract and 0.1 in the text and Table 4; ours is about 0.14. At 5 to 8 years EQ-5D reached 0.80 vs 0.67, which the authors compare with Swedish population norms of 0.82 to 0.83. Between 2 and 5-8 years the surgical group kept improving on NDI, arm pain and EQ-VAS while the nonsurgical group did not, but no between-group change was significant, and the authors say to interpret it with caution. In Table 7 surgical arm pain is 11 (2 to 20) with P = 0.2, while the text calls it significant; our recompute gives about 0.02. The authors suggest the low baseline arm pain may explain the weak arm result. Harms are thin: no complication or reoperation in 30 to 31 operated patients cannot rule out uncommon events. The BAK/C cage without graft is an older technique, our note.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: An honest, small trial. Direction favors surgery; size and significance are fragile.
points: Holds up: randomized; same physiotherapy in both arms; independent observer; long follow-up with 59 of 63 treated patients answering
Holds up: global rating difference is large and recomputes cleanly
Weakens it: 59 patients, no a priori power; post hoc power 30-40% for arm pain and EQ-5D, per the authors
Weakens it: 5 randomized patients excluded before treatment, 4 from surgery
Weakens it: self-reported outcomes; patient blinding not described
Weakens it: primary NDI result loses significance as-treated
Weakens it: patients had chosen surgery; long symptoms, modest arm pain
Weakens it: no multiplicity correction; several table errors
slides.notes: The authors' own limitations are small sample size with possible type II error, no real power analysis, and the difference between participants and nonparticipants. They also say there was no untreated control, so natural history cannot be separated from treatment. The rest is our reading. Expectation bias matters here: patients had elected surgery before being randomized, and every outcome is patient-reported. A patient who wanted surgery and was assigned physiotherapy may rate the result lower, which would favor surgery on the global rating especially. That is our hypothesis, not tested in the paper. Neck pain responding more than arm pain is plausible but is unexpected, and with arm pain post hoc power of 30 to 40 percent the arm comparison is simply underpowered, not evidence of no effect. Flow: Methods say 63 included, Figure 1 says 68 randomized, and the Abstract says 59 were randomized (30 vs 29), which is the 5-8 year count, not the randomized number. Methods describe 26 one-level and 4 two-level fusions, 30 in all, while Figure 1 shows 31 operated; Table 1 also totals 30 for the surgical group, which may describe the follow-up cohort, but the paper does not say. Our checks on the tables: the arm pain interval missing a minus sign, the Table 7 arm pain P value, the EQ-5D P mismatch and two Table 2 percentages. None of these changes the direction of a conclusion, but they reduce confidence in the reporting. Funding: Medical Research Council of Southeast Sweden and Futurum; no conflicts section beyond that is printed.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "In a small Swedish trial in cervical radiculopathy (68 randomized, 59 followed to 5 to 8 years), adding ACDF to physiotherapy cut NDI by 10 more points at 5 to 8 years, P = 0.03, with less neck pain and 93 versus 62 percent rating themselves better. Arm pain did not differ significantly. Physiotherapy alone also helped, and 24 percent of that group crossed over."
points: The authors say it is reasonable to recommend a trial of structured physiotherapy early, and that ACDF is a good alternative for substantial residual symptoms.
Do not stretch it: no myelopathy, no posterior foraminotomy, and the NDI result is not robust to as-treated analysis.
FACET (C07, library record) compares posterior foraminotomy with ACDF, not surgery with physiotherapy.
slides.notes: Expect these follow-up questions. Does this prove ACDF beats physiotherapy for arm pain? No. The arm pain difference was 14 mm and not significant, with power the authors put at 30 to 40 percent. Should every patient try physiotherapy first? The authors say a trial of structured physiotherapy is reasonable before a surgical decision, and that timing of surgery remains undetermined. Only 8 of the 32 who started physiotherapy had surgery over the whole study, which the authors say may reflect good physiotherapy results and adaptation to living with the disease. Is the effect durable? The authors say outcomes at 5 to 8 years were consistent with or better than at 1 and 2 years, and no surgical patient had reoperation. Adjacent-level disease was not analyzed, so the trial cannot answer that. Why was NDI significant now when it was not at 2 years? The authors offer one possible explanation: the change from repeated-measures ANOVA with imputation to a simple t-test of change scores. Our reading: either way, it is not proof of a growing benefit. Who does it apply to? Patients aged 18 to 65 with 1 or 2 level disease, symptoms of 8 weeks to 5 years, who wanted surgery, without myelopathy. FACET, from its abstract-level library record, found posterior foraminotomy noninferior to ACDF at 2 years in 265 patients; it answers which operation, not whether to operate.

decks.not_reviewed: The full paper (11 pages, figures and tables) was read. Not reviewed: the earlier Mobi-C IDE reports the paper relies on for the protocol, inclusion and exclusion criteria and 7-year results (references 9-14), the IDE-wide baseline comparison the authors describe but do not tabulate, and the trial registration. No supplement is cited.

slides.title: Mobi-C CDA vs ACDF at 10 years
slides.lead: Ten-year follow-up of the randomized Mobi-C trial patients at 3 high-enrolling sites.
points: Journal club: cervical degeneration
Nunley PD, Hisey M, Smith M, Stone MB. Int J Spine Surg 2023;17(2):230-240

Bottom line: CDA had higher composite success (62.4% vs 22.2%) and fewer reoperations (Kaplan-Meier 7.2% vs 25.5%). Most patient-reported outcomes did not differ significantly. Only 27 of 50 ACDF patients were seen at 10 years.
slides.notes: This deck was prepared from the full published paper, including Figures 1-7 and Tables 1-4. It is the primary paper, not a critique. What it is: the Mobi-C cervical disc was approved by the FDA in 2013 for 1- or 2-level disease, with a required postapproval study to 7 years. After that ended, 3 high-enrolling centers kept following their own patients to 10 years. These 155 patients (105 CDA, 50 ACDF, randomized 2:1) are, per the authors, more than 25% of the original IDE cohort. So this is a randomized comparison, but a site-level subset with a 3-year extension that the 3 centers chose to carry out. Keep three facts in your head as you go: one device (Mobi-C, a mobile-bearing polyethylene core between cobalt-chromium endplates), one ACDF technique (allograft and anterior plate), and patients operated on between May 2006 and March 2008. Funding matters here. Zimmer Biomet funded the IDE trial and the postapproval study, helped design and run it, and helped with analysis and the manuscript. The acknowledgment says a ZimVie Spine employee did the data analysis and drafted the manuscript, tables and figures. The first author reports being a patent holder and consultant for Zimmer Biomet, and the second author reports patents for Zimmer Biomet. Not reviewed: the earlier IDE papers (references 9-14) that hold the full inclusion and exclusion criteria and the 7-year results.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: Does motion preservation keep its advantage over fusion at 10 years?
points: Rationale (authors): fusion changes adjacent-segment motion and stress, which may speed adjacent degeneration. CDA may reduce it.
Patients: 1- or 2-level DDD from C3 to C7 with radiculopathy or myeloradiculopathy, no prior cervical surgery
Intervention: Mobi-C arthroplasty at 1 or 2 contiguous levels
Comparison: ACDF with allograft and anterior cervical plate
Outcomes: composite success; subsequent surgery, index and adjacent; adjacent-segment pathology on X-ray; NDI, pain, SF-12; satisfaction; adverse events
slides.notes: Frame it this way: the short-term question (is CDA at least as good as fusion?) was answered by the IDE trials. The long-term question is whether the theoretical benefit, protecting the adjacent segment, shows up as fewer operations. Ten years is where that should become visible, because adjacent-segment disease after fusion accumulates over time. The authors cite an annual rate of 2.4% to 2.7% per year after ACDF from the literature. The library's Hilibrand record (C06) gives an annual incidence of 2.9% and an estimated 10-year cumulative incidence of 25.6% for symptomatic adjacent disease. Note the word symptomatic. Hilibrand counts disease, while this paper counts operations. The authors call the two numbers remarkably similar, but they measure different things. Notice the enrollment criteria too. Per the authors' limitations, patients had no substantial degeneration adjacent to the treated level. These were patients chosen as good arthroplasty candidates, and the fusion arm came from that same pool. That is fair for the randomized comparison, but it limits who the result applies to. The paper says details of the protocol and criteria were reported previously (reference 13), so we cannot list the exclusions here, for example facet arthrosis, instability, osteoporosis or a prior cervical operation beyond the one stated.

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: 155 randomized at 3 sites; 107 seen at 10 years.
points: Randomized 2:1 (CDA:ACDF), separately at each center. 1- and 2-level arms pooled because the 10-year numbers were small.
Baseline (Table 1): mean age 44, 50% men, NDI about 51, 54% 2-level. No significant differences.
Composite success needed all four: NDI gain (15 points, or 50% if baseline below 30); no index or adjacent reoperation; no serious treatment-related AE; neurologic function not worse.
Reoperation or treatment-related AE at any time carried forward as failure.
Tests: Farrington-Manning noninferiority, 10% margin, then superiority. Kaplan-Meier with log-rank for reoperation. Grade 3/4 Kellgren-Lawrence = significant RASP, read by an independent core lab.
slides.see: Figure 2, the flow diagram, shows why the ACDF arm thinned: between 7 and 10 years, 11 could not be contacted, 4 declined and 1 died.
slides.notes: Walk through Figure 2. CDA: 105 minus 7 lost and 3 withdrawn is 95 at 7 years. Then 10 could not be contacted and 7 declined, but 2 earlier dropouts re-enrolled, so 80 at 10 years. ACDF: 50 minus 6 lost and 1 withdrawn is 43. Then 11 could not be contacted, 4 declined and 1 died, leaving 27. The arithmetic adds up. The headline 78.1% is 107 of 137, meaning patients available after 7 years minus the death. That denominator flatters the follow-up rate. Against randomized patients it is 69%, and 76% versus 54% by arm. Our point: attrition was uneven, which the authors also say. Composite denominators are 85 CDA and 36 ACDF. These are the 80 and 27 seen, plus earlier failures carried forward. That leaves 20 CDA and 14 ACDF with unknown status, which match the sensitivity analysis. Five patients gave phone and record data only, so no 10-year X-rays. The paper says randomization was applied independently at each center. It does not describe allocation concealment or whether patients or clinical examiners were blinded, so neither can be stated. Radiographs were read by an independent lab (Medical Metrics). The authors say this subset matched the remaining IDE patients at baseline and at 7 years, but this paper shows no data for that comparison. Methods state that P values were adjusted for multiplicity by Monte Carlo simulation. Our check: the Table 2 P values match plain unadjusted Fisher exact tests on 53/85 vs 8/36 and 7/85 vs 12/36. So the adjustment, if applied, does not show in Table 2. Baseline balance holds on our recomputation: pooled t-tests give age P 0.83 (printed 0.79) and NDI 0.93 (printed 0.92). The tests do not match the footnote. Sex, obesity and Caucasian P values match uncorrected chi-square, not the Fisher test named (Fisher gives 1.0). BMI 0.66 matches Welch's t-test, not pooled t (0.68).

slides.title: Primary outcome: composite success
slides.lead: A 40-point gap, driven by reoperation and neurologic success, not by NDI.
points: Difference 40.1%, 23.9% to 56.4% (labeled 95% CI in Table 2; the text calls 23.9% a 1-sided 95% lower bound). Superiority required a lower bound above 0.
Worst case for missing data (all CDA dropouts fail, all ACDF dropouts succeed): 50.5% vs 44%, still noninferior.
slides.see: Figure 3 is the tipping-point grid: every combination of outcomes among the 20 CDA and 14 ACDF dropouts. Gray cells, where superiority is lost, sit only in the corner where most ACDF dropouts succeed.
slides.notes: How to read the table: these are proportions among patients with known 10-year status (Table 2, Fisher exact test). The 8.2% vs 33.3% subsequent surgery figures are crude proportions. They are not the Kaplan-Meier 7.2% vs 25.5% on the next slide. Don't mix the two. What drives the result: the authors say subsequent surgery and neurologic success. NDI success, the patient-reported part, was 84.8% vs 74.1%, P 0.25, noninferior but not superior. Neurologic success was defined as motor, sensory and reflex function not worse than baseline. The authors attribute the ACDF deficit mainly to diminished reflexes from 5 years on. Our point: a reflex change is a soft finding, and the paper does not say whether examiners knew the treatment. Also, reoperation counts twice. It is its own outcome and also a component that defines composite failure. Our recomputation: Clopper-Pearson intervals reproduce the group CIs in Table 2. The difference CIs do not reproduce. They are not all symmetric (serious AE 8.8%, -0.1% to 18.1%), and they are narrower than plain unadjusted Wald 95% intervals: composite 23.9-56.4 vs 23.1-57.2, neurologic 17.8-46.8 vs 12.1-52.5. Multiplicity-adjusted intervals should be wider, so the method is unclear. The label is also unclear: Methods and Results call 23.9% a 1-sided 95% lower bound, which makes a two-sided interval 90%, yet Table 2 labels it 95% CI. Neurologic success reproduces as 65/74 vs 15/27, which gives P 0.0015, but the Results text gives P 0.004 for the same comparison. Sensitivity analysis: 21 x 15 = 315 scenarios, as stated. We counted 21 gray cells in Figure 3, which matches the stated 6.7%. Two cautions, both ours. First, the authors call 6.7% the chance of a different conclusion. It is a share of scenarios, not a probability, because the scenarios are not equally likely. Second, the text's tipping point (at least 11 of 14 ACDF dropouts succeeding with at least 19 of 20 CDA dropouts failing) is only the first corner of the gray region; with all 14 ACDF dropouts succeeding, superiority is lost up to 8 CDA successes. Either way, losing superiority requires ACDF dropouts to succeed far more often than the 22% (8/36) in ACDF patients with known 10-year status. The result holds up against the missing data. The open question is what the composite measures.

slides.title: Secondary outcomes and harms
slides.lead: Fewer adjacent-level operations with CDA; pain and disability were similar.
points: Neck and arm pain, and SF-12 MCS, did not differ significantly. All PROs stayed better than baseline in both arms.
Very satisfied: 98.7% vs 88.9%, P 0.05.
All adjacent-level operations were for symptomatic adjacent disease. No CDA adjacent-level surgery after 7 years.
slides.see: Figures 5 and 6 show the Kaplan-Meier curves with patients at risk. The ACDF curves climb steadily through year 7, and only 20 ACDF patients remain at risk at 120 months.
slides.notes: The adjacent-level surgery gap is the clinically meaningful result: 3 versus 9 patients, Kaplan-Meier 3.1% vs 20.5%. Index-level reoperation did not differ significantly. Read the curves, not just the endpoint. Per the authors, CDA adjacent risk did not change after 6 years. The ACDF curve is built on small numbers late: Figure 5 shows 34 ACDF patients at risk at 72 months, 24 at 84 and 20 from 96 to 120. Each late ACDF event moves the estimate by about 3 to 4 points; the 84-month step goes from about 23% to 25.5%. Our checks found three problems. First, a Kaplan-Meier risk cannot be lower than the crude count over the starting group when all events fall inside the window. Yet 13 of 50 ACDF patients is 26%, above the 25.5% reported, and 7 of 50 index-level is 14%, above the 10.5% reported. Figure 5 shows an ACDF step after 120 months, and the text reports one ACDF patient with a nonadjacent fusion at 10.6 years, then an adjacent fusion at 11.7 years. Our inference: counting that patient could explain the any-surgery excess (12/50 = 24%), but not the index-level count. 10.5% of 50 allows at most 5 index events within 10 years, and no post-10-year index-level ACDF operation is reported. So post-10-year events explain the mismatch only in part. Second, Figure 6 reads 19.7% and P 0.0006 for ACDF adjacent surgery, while the text and Table 3 say 20.5% and P 0.0005. Third, the RASP denominators are not given. At most 27 ACDF patients had 10-year X-rays, and no whole-patient fraction of 27 or fewer rounds to 39.3%. The authors themselves say RASP is radiographic and may not track symptoms. Patient-reported outcomes: only the SF-12 PCS change differed. The authors say the other differences were below the MCID for NDI (15) and pain (10). Satisfaction is muddled. The text gives 89.9% [78/79] vs 85.2% [24/27] as satisfied, but 78/79 is 98.7% and 24/27 is 88.9%, the very-satisfied figures. Harms between 7 and 10 years: in CDA, 3 treatment-related AEs (subsidence in 2, radiculopathy in 1, which led to posterior fusion at 9.5 years). In ACDF, 4 AEs in 2 patients, none needing intervention. No device failures or explantations are described.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: A real randomized comparison, thinned and selected by the time it reached 10 years.
points: Holds up: randomized within each site; groups balanced at baseline (Table 1, recomputed)
Holds up: hard endpoint (reoperation) with Kaplan-Meier and log-rank; independent radiographic reads
Holds up: missing-data sensitivity analysis; worst case still noninferior
Weakens: 3 of the IDE sites, chosen because they enrolled most and agreed to continue
Weakens: 10-year follow-up 76% CDA vs 54% ACDF
Weakens: composite gain from reoperation and reflex-driven neurologic success; NDI not different
Weakens: blinding not reported; sponsor helped design, analyze and write
Weakens: internal number conflicts (see notes)
slides.notes: Be fair first. This is randomized evidence at 10 years, which is rare in spine surgery. The reoperation endpoint is objective and has a large effect, and the missing-data analysis is a good-faith attempt to stress it. The authors' own limitations: strict IDE criteria (no adjacent degeneration, no prior spine surgery), a subset that may not represent the whole IDE, attrition from 7 to 10 years that was higher in ACDF, and one ACDF technique chosen as the standard in 2004. Our additions: First, reoperation is a surgeon decision. The paper does not say whether patients or treating surgeons were blinded, and in an unblinded trial a surgeon's view of a fused neck could lower the threshold to operate at the next level. We cannot tell from this paper. Second, the claimed Level of Evidence 1 sits awkwardly with 31% of randomized patients missing at 10 years and uneven attrition. Third, multiplicity adjustment is stated, but Table 2 P values match unadjusted Fisher tests and the difference CIs are narrower than unadjusted ones. Fourth, industry involvement runs through analysis and writing. That does not make the result wrong, but it is a reason to check the numbers, which we did. Number conflicts found, also listed in the patch file: neurologic success P 0.0015 in Table 2 vs 0.004 in the text; the satisfaction fractions match the very-satisfied percentages, not the satisfied ones; Figure 6 shows 19.7% and P 0.0006 against 20.5% and P 0.0005 in the text; the Table 3 ACDF counts are too high for their Kaplan-Meier percentages if counted only through 10 years; the text describes only the first corner of the Figure 3 tipping region; the RASP 39.3% cannot be a fraction of 27 or fewer patients; and the Figure 7 axis reads '% change from baseline' though the bars are percentages of patients. None of these changes the direction of the main result. They tell you how carefully to quote the decimals.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: Fewer reoperations with Mobi-C at 10 years, in selected patients with half the fusion arm still followed.
points: "In the 3-site, 10-year Mobi-C follow-up, arthroplasty had fewer subsequent operations than ACDF, 7.2% vs 25.5% by Kaplan-Meier, with most of the difference at the adjacent level: 3.1% vs 20.5%. Neck disability and pain ended up similar. Only 54% of the fusion arm was seen at 10 years, and the sponsor helped analyze and write it."
Library records for context; designs and endpoints differ.
slides.notes: Spoken summary: randomized patients from 3 high-enrolling Mobi-C IDE sites, followed to 10 years. Composite success was 62% vs 22%, but that gap comes from reoperations and neurologic findings. NDI, pain and mental health did not differ significantly, and only physical SF-12 favored CDA. Kaplan-Meier subsequent surgery was 7.2% vs 25.5%, and adjacent-level surgery 3.1% vs 20.5%. Follow-up was 80 of 105 CDA and 27 of 50 ACDF. Expected follow-up questions. 1. Does this mean every 1- or 2-level patient should get a disc? No. These were IDE-selected patients without substantial adjacent degeneration and with no prior cervical surgery, and the protocol exclusions sit in an earlier paper. The trial says nothing about patients who were not arthroplasty candidates. 2. Is the adjacent-level advantage biology or behavior? The paper cannot separate those. RASP was also lower with CDA (12.9% vs 39.3%), which fits the motion-preservation story, but RASP denominators are missing, and surgeons deciding on reoperation would likely have known the treatment from imaging. That is our inference; the paper does not report blinding. 3. How does this square with Hilibrand? The authors compare their 20.5% ACDF adjacent-surgery rate with Hilibrand's 25.6% 10-year estimate. Hilibrand's figure, from the library record, is symptomatic adjacent disease, not surgery. 4. Would missing ACDF patients change it? The tipping-point analysis says superiority holds unless most ACDF dropouts did far better than ACDF patients who were followed. That is unlikely, but follow-up was 54%. 5. Does it apply to other discs? It is one device. The authors' conclusions speak of CDA as a class; only their Clinical Relevance line names the Mobi-C. Limiting it to Mobi-C is our caution, not theirs. FACET (C07, from the library record) tested a different alternative to ACDF for radiculopathy, posterior foraminotomy, on a different endpoint.

decks.not_reviewed: The four source articles themselves (Tetreault 2017, Al-Shawwa 2024, Badhiwala 2020, Ozaki 2025); the typeset journal version, including author affiliations, funding and conflict-of-interest statements, none of which appear in the reformatted PMC copy read here; any published images (the copy says images are omitted; Table 1 was available as text).

slides.title: AO Spine on mild DCM, 2026
slides.lead: Four mild-DCM papers, appraised with GRADE and turned into practice recommendations.
points: Journal club: degenerative cervical myelopathy
Neal CJ, et al. Global Spine J 2026. AO Spine Knowledge Forum Spinal Cord Injury
Design: literature review with critical appraisal and clinical recommendations. Not a systematic review and, in the authors' words, not a comprehensive clinical practice guideline.

Bottom line: grade severity by mJOA; no recommendation on using MRI parameters to predict deterioration or time surgery; surgery may be offered to selected mild patients with high baseline pain and NDI; warn that upper-limb sensory deficits frequently persist. All rest on low or very low evidence.
slides.notes: What this paper is: an expert group chose four articles on mild DCM, critically appraised each, rated the evidence with GRADE plus expert opinion, and wrote one recommendation per article. It is a structured journal club, not a search of the literature. The authors do not describe how the four were chosen beyond saying the topic, article selection and review were made by the Knowledge Forum. Why mild DCM: the 2017 AO Spine guideline (C01 in the library) gave strong recommendations for surgery in moderate and severe DCM on moderate evidence, but only a weak recommendation for mild DCM on very low to low evidence. This paper says that gap warranted further exploration. The four questions it maps onto: how do we define mild, who will get worse, who gains from surgery, and what should we promise them. What was reviewed for this deck: the full article text in a reformatted open-access copy, read end to end, including Table 1 as text. The copy says images are omitted. It does not carry author affiliations, funding or conflict statements, so those were not reviewed. The four source articles were not read; every number about them here is as this paper reports it.

slides.title: The four recommendations
slides.lead: One article, one recommendation. None is strong.

rows: Use mJOA: mild 15-17, moderate 12-14, severe 11 or less
No recommendation for routine use of these MRI parameters to predict deterioration or time surgery
Suggest offering surgery to carefully selected mild patients with high baseline pain and NDI
Warn that upper-limb sensory deficits often persist; treat angular-edged cord deformity on axial MRI as a risk factor

slides.notes: This is the slide to memorize. Listen for the word suggest: in this paper every recommendation that was made is conditional, and the MRI question ended with no recommendation at all. Two details hide in the wording. First, the counseling recommendation in the Article 4 recommendation section is aimed at mild patients being considered for surgery because of progressive symptoms; the abstract, the Discussion and Table 1 drop that qualifier. Second, the surgery recommendation changes verb. The body says surgery be offered to carefully selected patients; Table 1 says surgery be recommended. Offer is the safer reading, given low evidence and no control group. Table 1 also adds implementation advice: put the mJOA cutoffs into daily practice; consider incorporating the pain/NDI and counseling points; further study before using the MRI parameters. Our framing, not the authors': the recommendations describe a patient, not a scan. Severity is clinical, deterioration cannot yet be read off MRI, and selection and consent lean on what the composite mJOA score does not settle: pain, which the paper says the mJOA has limited ability to capture, and which upper-limb sensory deficits will persist.

slides.title: Defining mild: the mJOA cutoffs
slides.lead: Tetreault 2017: 740 patients from the AO Spine North America and International prospective studies, 2005 to 2011.
points: 18-point mJOA (Benzel modification). Mean 12.50 ± 2.74, range 3-17.
Cutoffs anchored to the Nurick score by ROC: AUC 0.81 mild vs moderate, 0.87 moderate vs severe.
Function, disability, quality of life and number of signs and symptoms tracked the severity groups.
Evidence low; conditional recommendation to use mild 15-17, moderate 12-14, severe 11 or less.
slides.notes: This article is here to give everyone the same vocabulary. The cutoffs were derived, not just agreed: the Nurick grade was the external anchor and ROC analysis picked the mJOA points that best separated the groups. Construct validity came from the other outcomes lining up with the groups. The appraisers name three weaknesses worth repeating. Nurick is weighted toward gait, so the thresholds may lean on walking and miss hand-predominant myelopathy. Very mild patients were underrepresented. And the mJOA itself has reduced sensitivity to subtle deficits, no patient-reported component and limited ability to capture pain. The authors therefore say severity should be read alongside examination, symptoms, function and imaging. Our points, not the paper's: the sample mean was 12.50 with a top score of 17, so the mild band sits at the thin end of the sample. And an AUC of 0.81 means that in about one in five pairs drawn from the Nurick-defined mild and moderate groups, the mJOA would rank the pair the wrong way, so a patient scoring 15 is close to the line. The library guideline (C01) already used these same cutoffs in 2017; this paper restates them with a GRADE rating rather than introducing them.

slides.title: Who gets worse? MRI did not answer it
slides.lead: Al-Shawwa 2024: nonoperated patients, predominantly mild DCM, in the Canadian Spine Outcomes Research Network, deterioration at 6 months.
points: 35 deteriorated and 45 did not. Manual MRI canal diameter and compression patterns, k-means clustering into five groups.
Focal compression alone did not reliably predict deterioration.
Pattern mattered less when the canal was very narrow (14.5 mm or less) or very wide (over 15.75 mm).
Severe compression at two disc levels, even with a normal canal, was associated with more deterioration.
Evidence very low (risk of bias, imprecision). No recommendation.
slides.notes: The question is the one we face every week: which mild patient will slip if we wait. The authors of the source paper used unsupervised machine learning on 80 patients (our sum of 35 and 45; the appraisal does not state the total). The appraisers downgraded from low to very low for risk of bias and imprecision, and their reasons are worth saying aloud. Clustering on a small sample can find patterns in noise; the clusters overlapped heavily; it is unclear whether image readers were blinded to outcome; there were more MRIs than patients and it is unclear which scan was used; confounders were not clearly handled; absolute canal diameter was used rather than a cord-canal ratio; and the mJOA may miss subtle worsening. The appraisers count the exclusion of operated patients as a strength, because it leaves the population in whom prognosis matters. Our reading, which cuts the other way: surgery in mild DCM is often triggered by deterioration, so removing operated patients may remove some of the very events being predicted. The paper is inconsistent here. The Discussion says no MRI findings were identified as prognostic factors, while the summary and Table 1 report that severe two-level compression was associated with deterioration. Teach it as: a hypothesis about compression pattern and canal size, not a rule for timing surgery.

slides.title: Who to operate on, and what to promise
slides.lead: Both articles studied operated patients only. Neither had a nonoperative control group.

rows: 185 mild (mJOA 15-17), AO Spine CSM NA and International
Cluster 1 (79) vs cluster 2 (106): more gain in NDI, SF-36 physical function, role physical and bodily pain; not mJOA
Of patients with UE sensory deficit before surgery (88.4%), 60.9% still had it at 2 years, more than any other JOA domain
Cluster 1 had more neck pain 32% vs 11%, gait difficulty 57% vs 40%, weakness 75% vs 60%
Angular-edged cord on axial MRI: OR 4.264 (1.312-13.854), P=0.016

slides.notes: Badhiwala, the same paper as C12 in our library, is a post hoc analysis of operated patients. K-means made two clusters. The more symptomatic cluster gained more on NDI and three SF-36 domains at 1 year, but not on the mJOA. Two cautions, both ours. First, more baseline symptoms leaves more room to improve, so greater gain in that cluster does not show that surgery helped them more than waiting would have. Second, the recommendation names baseline pain and NDI, but this paper reports baseline cluster differences only for neck pain, gait and weakness; baseline NDI values are not given. Our recheck of those baseline differences, counts rebuilt from 79 and 106: neck pain P<0.001, gait about 0.02, weakness about 0.04, about 0.06 with continuity correction, so weakness is borderline. The appraisers add: surgeon-chosen procedures, secondary analysis, and only 1 year of follow-up. Ozaki looked domain by domain because composite scores have a ceiling in mild DCM. 94.2% came to surgery for progressing symptoms, and despite mild scores the mean maximum canal compromise was 49.7% and cord compression 37.2%. Total JOA, finger motor and upper-limb sensory scores improved, with a mean recovery rate of 49.3%, and neck, arm and leg pain VAS improved. Upper-limb sensory loss was the most common symptom, 88.4% before surgery, and the most likely to stay. Angular-edged cord deformity was the only independent predictor. Our check: the printed interval is symmetric on the log scale around 4.264 and gives P about 0.016, so it is internally consistent, but it is wide. Percentages: 60.9% fits 56 of 92. 88.4% and 52.8% are 92 and 55 of 104 truncated (88.46%, 52.88%), while 92 of 104 is printed as 88.5% for posterior surgery: a rounding slip, not a wrong denominator. Intramedullary signal change was borderline, P=0.055. Persistence was binary, so partial recovery counted as failure. 88.5% had posterior surgery and 67.3% laminoplasty.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: Holds up: explicit GRADE rating for each article, limitations spelled out, the MRI question honestly left without a recommendation.
Four articles chosen by the authors; no search or selection criteria described.
All four are observational. None compares surgery with observation.
The pain/NDI and counseling advice comes from operated patients only.
Article 2: the Discussion says no MRI prognostic factor was found; the summary and Table 1 report one.
Article 3: 'offered' in the text, 'recommended' in Table 1.
Article 4: counseling qualifier for progressive symptoms dropped from abstract, Discussion and Table 1; 88.4% and 52.8% look truncated, while the same 92 of 104 is printed elsewhere as 88.5%.
No funding or conflict statements in the copy reviewed.
slides.notes: Be fair first. This paper does what it says: it takes four recent or foundational studies, grades them openly and resists overreaching on MRI. The authors call it not a comprehensive guideline, and it should be read that way. Now the weaknesses, which are ours unless stated. Selection: four articles chosen by the group, with no search, so other mild-DCM evidence, including the library's own Badhiwala 2019 surgical cohort (C03), is not weighed here. Design: every source is observational; two have no nonoperative patients, so no recommendation here can say surgery beats observation for any mild subgroup. Causal language creeps in: the Discussion says surgery is likely to improve NDI and pain at 1 year, from an uncontrolled cohort. Ozaki's appraisal ends by saying its findings support observation with structured follow-up for stable mild DCM; that study contains no observed patients, so that line is a consensus view the authors invoke, not a result of the study. Internal inconsistencies to flag: the Article 2 contradiction about MRI prognostic factors; offer versus recommend for Article 3; the progressive-symptoms qualifier lost from the abstract, Discussion and Table 1 for Article 4; Ozaki's 88.4% and 52.8% (92 and 55 of 104 are 88.46% and 52.88%, so they look truncated, while 92 of 104 is printed as 88.5% for posterior surgery; a 0.1-point rounding slip, not a denominator problem; 60.9% fits 56 of 92); and Article 3's clusters described as clustering of outcomes, which is unclear. Reference 24 (Badhiwala) is also numbered out of sequence. Arithmetic that checks: 104 of 679 is 15.3%; 156 of 185 is 84%; clusters 79 plus 106 make 185; Ozaki's OR interval and P agree.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "For mild DCM, AO Spine's 2026 review says: call it mild at mJOA 15 to 17; it makes no recommendation on using MRI parameters to predict deterioration or time surgery; consider surgery for selected patients with high pain and NDI; and warn that upper-limb sensory deficits frequently persist. Every recommendation made is conditional, on low or very low evidence."

rows: Guideline; mild evidence very low to low
Suggest surgery or supervised structured rehabilitation (weak)
Symptom phenotype predicts more improvement after surgery
mJOA severity; no MRI rule; pain/NDI selection; counsel on sensory loss

points: C01 and C12 entries are from the library records. C12 is this review's Article 3.
slides.notes: Expect four follow-up questions. Should a mild patient with severe two-level compression go to surgery? This paper made no recommendation on MRI parameters; the two-level signal is very low evidence from about 80 patients and the paper itself contradicts it in the Discussion. Decide on clinical course and symptoms. Does this replace the 2017 guideline? No. The authors say it is not a comprehensive guideline, and it does not revise the 2017 grades. The 2017 guideline, by its library record, still offers surgery or supervised rehabilitation for mild DCM as a weak suggestion and recommends surgery for deterioration. Which mild patient benefits most from surgery? The only data here are operated patients: more symptomatic patients, especially with pain and disability, improved more on NDI and three SF-36 components (physical functioning, role physical, bodily pain), not on mJOA or the other SF-36 components, at 1 year. That predicts improvement, not benefit over waiting; C12's library caveat says the same. What do I tell a patient about numbness? In Ozaki, upper-limb sensory loss was present in most operated mild patients and persisted at 2 years in 60.9% of those who had it; angular-edged cord shape on axial MRI raised the odds about fourfold, with a wide interval. This is one retrospective Japanese series, mostly laminoplasty, so use it for consent, not for choosing an operation. One sentence to close: mild DCM is defined clinically, decided clinically, and consented honestly, and the evidence for each step is still thin.

decks.not_reviewed: The four appraised articles themselves (Nouri 2017, Badhiwala 2019, Ghogawala 2021, Pedro 2024) and the systematic reviews and cost-utility study it cites were not read; their numbers here are as this review reports them. The copy read is a reformatted PMC text with images omitted and the knowledge-translation QR code not usable. No figures or tables are referred to in the text, but any published conflict-of-interest or funding declaration beyond the Acknowledgments was not seen.

slides.title: AO Spine DCM review, 2025
slides.lead: Four recent DCM papers, one per research gap, appraised by an AO Spine working group and turned into graded recommendations.
points: Journal club: degenerative cervical myelopathy
Fehlings MG, et al. Global Spine J 2025;15(5):2585-2593. AO Spine Knowledge Forum Spinal Cord Injury
Type: narrative literature review with critical appraisal. Not a systematic review and not a formal guideline update.

Bottom line: surgery is a valid option in mild DCM (conditional). Ventral and dorsal surgery give similar benefit when either can be used, with different complications (strong). Use cord MRI signal, pain, frailty and quality of life when counselling (conditional).
slides.notes: Frame this paper correctly before reading the content. It is not new data and not a guideline. A working group of the AO Spine Knowledge Forum Spinal Cord Injury chose four recent articles, one for each of four RECODE-DCM knowledge gaps, summarized each, appraised it, and attached a GRADE-style recommendation graded Strong or Conditional. The value is expert interpretation. The weakness is that four hand-picked studies stand in for whole bodies of evidence. What was reviewed: the full text of this review, end to end, from a reformatted open-access PMC copy whose header says images are omitted. The text refers to no figures or tables, so we do not think teaching material was lost, but we cannot confirm that. This PDF is the paper itself, not a critique of it and not a fragment. Not reviewed: the four source articles. Every number for Nouri, Badhiwala, Ghogawala and Pedro in this deck is as this review reports it, and where the library holds its own record (Badhiwala is C03, Ghogawala is C05) we compare against that record, not memory. The starting point the authors give: the 2017 AO Spine/CSRS guideline (library C01) strongly recommended surgery for moderate and severe DCM by mJOA. The review then says, in its own voice rather than citing the guideline, that mild DCM sits in relative equipoise between nonoperative management with careful observation and surgery. C01 itself weakly suggests surgery or a supervised trial of structured rehabilitation for mild DCM, not observation. This review is largely about moving that mild-DCM line and about how to counsel.

slides.title: The question and the four recommendations
slides.lead: One article per RECODE-DCM gap, chosen for relevance and quality.
points: Gaps: assessing heterogeneous presentations, MRI and recovery, surgery for mild DCM, anterior versus posterior when both work.
Method: reviewed by the working group, graded Strong or Conditional with GRADE. No search dates, databases or selection criteria beyond relevance and quality are given.

rows: Use cord MRI signal to counsel on expected recovery
Offer surgery as an option; structured follow-up still viable
Either approach when equipoise exists; discuss differing harms
Consider pain, frailty, quality of life when counselling

slides.notes: This is the slide to remember. Three of four recommendations are conditional. Only the approach question is strong, and it is the only one backed by a randomized trial. Notice what the grade column does not give you: the review rates quality of evidence for Badhiwala (moderate) and Ghogawala (high) but gives no GRADE quality rating for Nouri or Pedro, even though the Methods say GRADE was used. So the conditional grades on MRI and phenotypes rest on the group's judgment without a stated evidence level. Watch the wording of the MRI recommendation. The abstract says a conditional recommendation to use diffusion-weighted imaging signal changes to evaluate prognosis. The Nouri study it rests on looked at conventional T2 hyperintensity and T1 hypointensity, not diffusion. Quantitative MRI metrics appear only in two sentences citing references 8 and 9: fractional anisotropy and mean diffusivity, plus magnetization transfer and intracellular volume fraction, which are not diffusion measures. The Discussion adds a passing mention of advances in microstructural MRI. The body's actual recommendation is broader and softer: understanding how MRI findings correlate with outcome helps counsel patients on expected recovery. Quote the body, not the abstract. Similarly, the abstract's Pedro recommendation says pain, while the body says neck and arm pain; the Pedro summary only mentions neck pain. Selection: the Methods say articles were chosen for relevance and quality. Our observation from the author list: Nouri and Pedro, first authors of Articles 1 and 4, are co-authors of this review, and Articles 1, 2 and 4 draw on the AO Spine CSM-NA and CSM-I cohorts, whose primary reports (references 6 and 7) were led by Fehlings, this review's first author. The group is appraising largely its own program. That does not make it wrong, but it is not independent appraisal.

slides.title: Mild DCM: Badhiwala 2019
slides.lead: 193 surgical patients with mJOA 15-17 from AO Spine CSM-NA and CSM-I. No nonoperative control.
points: Mean age 52.4; 34.7% women. Approach and fusion at surgeon discretion.
Baseline SF-36v2 impaired in all domains versus Canadian norms, worst in social functioning, physical functioning and mental health.
Complications within 30 days 30% (Study Summary); the appraisal later gives 30.6% with no time window. Top three: worse myelopathy 6.74%, worse axial neck pain 6.22%, dysphagia 5.70%.
Follow-up 93.3% at 24 months.
slides.notes: Read this as before and after, not surgery versus observation. Every number is change from baseline in operated patients only. The review reports all changes as statistically significant but prints no confidence intervals and does not compare the mJOA gain of 0.87 with any threshold for a meaningful change.
