For comparison, the C01 library record (2017 guideline) reports a mild-group mJOA gain of 1.29 in the one severity-stratified study it used; we do not know whether those are overlapping patients. The 30-meter walk did not improve, and the review says the source paper explains why but does not give the explanation. Arithmetic checks, ours: 34.7% of 193 is 67 women; 93.3% is 180 followed; 6.74%, 6.22% and 5.70% are 13, 12 and 11 patients; 30% and 30.6% sit in different subsections: 30% in the Study Summary, labelled within 30 days, and 30.6% in the Methodological Review, with no time window. 58 of 193 is 30.1% and 59 of 193 is 30.6%, so they may be different counts or different windows; the review does not say, and we cannot settle it. The reviewers call 30.6% high for contemporary practice and say the cohort had predominantly anterior surgery, where mild transient dysphagia likely contributes to the rate. Note that dysphagia was only 5.70%, and worse myelopathy (6.74%) was the most common complication, so by our reading dysphagia is at most a modest contributor; the review also never gives the anterior/posterior split. Their stated limits: non-randomized, no nonoperative control, selection by recruiting surgeons, variable technique, and mJOA misclassification between mild and moderate in over 10% of patients. They grade the evidence moderate. The extra support they bring is a cost-utility study (reference 14, not read) reporting 1.26 more lifetime QALYs for surgery than observation. Their conclusion is careful: offer surgery as an option, no strong recommendation because there is no comparison with nonoperative care, and structured follow-up remains viable in the clinically stable patient. Compare C01: the 2017 guideline weakly suggested surgery or supervised structured rehabilitation for mild DCM, on very low to low evidence. This review keeps the same direction and strength, with one better cohort.

slides.title: Ventral versus dorsal: Ghogawala 2021
slides.lead: 163 patients needing decompression of at least 2 levels, with equipoise confirmed by a virtual surgeon panel.
points: Ventral: ACDF or corpectomy with plate. Dorsal: laminectomy and lateral-mass fusion, or open-door laminoplasty, surgeon's choice.
Primary: change in SF-36 PCS at 1 year. Secondary: mJOA, NDI, EQ-5D. No significant secondary differences.
Reoperations: 4 in each arm, which is 6.3% ventral and 4% dorsal (our arithmetic).
Dorsal-only harms: more wound healing problems or infection, systemic complications and new radiculopathy.
slides.notes: The headline is a null result on the primary outcome, 5.9 versus 6.2 points, P=.86, holding at 2 years. These match the C05 library record. Two reading cautions. First, the review turns no significant difference into equivalence and grades it strong: ventral and dorsal are equivalent in functional recovery, pain and quality of life. A non-significant superiority comparison does not by itself prove equivalence. The review prints no confidence interval for the difference and no equivalence margin, so from this paper you cannot say how large a difference was excluded. That is our critique, not the authors'. Also ours: the strong recommendation names pain, but the outcomes the review lists (SF-36 PCS, mJOA, NDI, EQ-5D) include no dedicated pain measure. Second, the arms are 63 and 100. By our calculation, 63 versus 100 is very unlikely under simple 1:1 allocation (exact binomial P = .005), so allocation was unequal by design or by some other mechanism. The review does not state the ratio, and neither does the C05 record. Harms: ventral complications were double, 48% versus 24%, driven by dysphagia at 41%, which by our arithmetic is about 26 of 63 patients, with about half still affected at 6 months. The reviewers suggest a very sensitive screening algorithm inflated dysphagia relative to earlier reports. They also say the number of major or minor events was equivalent between arms, which sits awkwardly beside 48% versus 24%; the review does not give the major/minor counts, so we cannot reconcile it. Their critique: SF-36 PCS is not myelopathy-specific, all outcomes were patient-reported, there were no objective hand or balance measures, and the panel's equipoise may not match an individual surgeon's. The laminoplasty result is the trap. The review reports laminoplasty beat both fusions at 2 years with fewer complications, less physical therapy and less opioid use, but this was a non-randomized secondary analysis and only 8 of 24 surgeons did laminoplasty. The reviewers themselves say it needs validation. Do not quote it as trial evidence.

slides.title: MRI signal and symptom phenotypes
slides.lead: Two conditional recommendations about counselling, not about who needs surgery.
points: Nouri: T1 plus T2 change had the worst baseline mJOA and Nurick and the least recovery. Hirabayashi recovery ratio r = -0.209, P < .001.
Nouri: T2 change alone was not significantly related to optimal outcome (mJOA over 16). Multilevel T2 change was.
Nouri: T1 hypointensity in only one-fifth, with only fair inter-rater agreement.
Pedro: 4 k-means clusters in 1047 surgical patients, outcome at 1 year: severe multimodal, minimal, motor dominant, pain dominant.
Pedro: the review names neck pain and frailty as important factors; mJOA measures neither. Whether frailty was a clustering input is unclear.
slides.notes: The MRI groups add to 100% and to 419 patients by our arithmetic, so the split is internally consistent. Read the correlation carefully: the review gives r = -0.209 for T2 plus T1 change against the other two groups pooled, on recovery ratio, but does not say what variable was correlated, and an r of about 0.2 explains roughly 4% of variance (our calculation). That is a prognostic association at group level, weak for an individual patient. The practical message the review gives: no signal change was the most likely to reach an optimal outcome (mJOA over 16), single-level T2 change is only weakly correlated with symptoms and prognosis, and T1 hypointensity and multilevel T2 change point to less recovery. Our caution: the review never says MRI signal should change the decision to operate, and the Nouri cohort was all surgical, so it cannot tell you about natural history without surgery. It is a counselling tool. The abstract's diffusion-weighted wording does not come from this study. Pedro is a description of clusters. The review gives no outcome numbers per cluster, only rankings: the severe multimodal group improved most on mJOA but had the worst quality of life; minimal impairment had the best physical but lowest mental quality of life; motor dominant improved modestly; pain dominant had the best mental quality of life. Note the review's methodological section only describes the methods. It names no limitations, such as the dependence of k-means on the variables and number of clusters chosen, or the absence of external validation. That critique is ours. The review is also unclear on inputs: the summary says clusters were based solely on symptoms but also that demographic, clinical and surgical data were combined, and the methods list NDI, Nurick, mJOA motor and sensory subscores and NDI neck pain as the clustering measures, with frailty only collected. Yet frailty is named as a discriminating factor. The recommendation drawn from it is modest and hard to argue with: when counselling, weigh neck and arm pain, frailty and quality of life, not mJOA alone.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: Holds up: clear questions, transparent grading words, appropriately cautious on mild DCM.
Holds up: flags the non-randomized laminoplasty comparison and mJOA misclassification.
Weak: one hand-picked study per question; no search strategy, and no selection criteria beyond relevance and quality.
Weak: authors appraising their own cohorts and papers.
Weak: GRADE quality given for 2 of 4 articles only.
Weak: Article 4 appraisal names no limitations.
Possible error: abstract recommends diffusion-weighted MRI; Article 1 studied T1/T2 signal.
Possible error: equivalence of approaches claimed from P=.86 with no CI or margin.
Possible error: complications 30% (within 30 days) in the summary, 30.6% (no window) in the appraisal.
Possible error: major/minor events called equivalent beside 48% vs 24%.
slides.notes: Be fair first. For a busy surgeon this is a useful, readable synthesis, and its conclusions on mild DCM are appropriately conditional. It does not oversell the cohort data. It names the lack of a nonoperative control, the selection bias, and the mJOA reliability problem. It also refuses to treat the laminoplasty subgroup as proof. Now the structural weakness. A review that selects one paper per question, by the authors' own judgment of relevance and quality, with no stated search, cannot tell you whether that paper represents the field. The Methods also say key findings extracted from systematic reviews were summarized. Several systematic reviews and meta-analyses are cited through the text, but only the two MRI ones (references 8 and 9) are presented as summarized findings, and no separate section delivers that promise. Our observation: two first authors of the appraised articles are co-authors here, and three articles come from the AO Spine cohorts led by this review's first author. The copy we read shows study support from AO Network Clinical Research in the Acknowledgments; we did not see a separate conflict-of-interest statement. Smaller issues: the Nouri citation omits the journal name; the Pedro citation reads Pedro KM, et.; the introduction says the purpose is to define this clinical entity, which we read as mild DCM from the sentence before, though it could mean DCM (references 1 and 4 are RECODE-DCM papers), while the abstract says it summarizes several key topics. The review calls Badhiwala both a post hoc analysis of prospective cohorts and a well-designed retrospective cohort study; both are fair, but know that the data were not collected to answer the mild-DCM question. Our overall grade of the paper: good expert commentary, weak as evidence synthesis. Use the source trials and the 2017 guideline for evidence, and this review for how AO Spine reads them.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "The 2025 AO Spine review appraised four papers. Surgery is a valid option in mild DCM, conditional, because there is still no nonoperative comparison. When either approach works, anterior and posterior give similar function, strong, but anterior had double the complications, mostly dysphagia. Counsel with MRI signal, pain, frailty and quality of life, not mJOA alone."
points: C01 and C03, C05 figures come from their library records. This review is not a formal update of C01.

rows: Mild DCM: very low to low
Mild: suggest surgery or supervised rehabilitation
Mild: conditional option; approach: strong equipoise

slides.notes: Expect four follow-up questions. Does this change the 2017 mild-DCM recommendation? Not in strength. Both are conditional or weak, and C01 rated the mild-DCM evidence very low to low. This review says its own recommendation is limited by the lack of comparative evidence against nonoperative care. This review adds one moderate-quality surgical cohort and a cost-utility estimate of 1.26 QALYs, which we did not read. Should T2 signal alone push you to operate? This paper does not say so. Its MRI recommendation is about counselling on recovery in surgical patients, and T2 change alone was not significantly related to optimal outcome. Are anterior and posterior really equivalent? The trial found no significant difference on SF-36 PCS, P=.86, and no difference on mJOA or NDI. The review calls it equivalence and grades it strong, but it reports no confidence interval or margin, so the honest phrase is no detectable difference in function, different harms. Anterior means dysphagia, 41%, half still present at 6 months. Dorsal means more wound problems, systemic complications and new radiculopathy. And what about laminoplasty? Promising, but non-randomized, 8 of 24 surgeons, so it is a hypothesis. A last point if asked about independence: the review's authors include first authors of two appraised papers, so treat it as the AO Spine group's own reading of its research program.

decks.not_reviewed: Supplemental Digital Content (Supplemental Methods with the k-means and kNN details, including any score scaling and how k was chosen) was not available and not reviewed. Parent AOSpine CSM-NA and CSM-I study reports were not reviewed. The PDF is the complete 9-page published article, not a critique.

slides.title: Mild DCM: who improves after surgery?
slides.lead: A post hoc machine-learning look at operated mild myelopathy.
points: Journal club: degenerative cervical myelopathy
Badhiwala JH, et al. Neurosurgery 2020;86(4):565-573

Bottom line: clustering on baseline SF-36 split 185 operated mild DCM patients into a more impaired group (79) and a less impaired group (106). The more impaired group had more neck pain, motor symptoms and women, and improved more in NDI and SF-36 physical scores at 1 year. Every patient had surgery, so this is prediction of change, not proof of who benefits from surgery.
slides.notes: Source checked: the full 9-page published article, including Tables 1-4 and Figures 1-3. This PDF is the paper itself, not a critique, and it is complete. Not reviewed: the Supplemental Digital Content, which holds the detailed k-means and kNN methods, and the parent AOSpine CSM-NA and CSM-I study reports. So we do not know from this paper how SF-36 scores were scaled before clustering or how the random splits were drawn. Frame the paper before the numbers. It comes from the Fehlings group using the AOSpine CSM-North America and CSM-International prospective cohorts, the same cohorts behind the library's C03 mild DCM record. All 193 eligible patients were operated on. The question the authors pose is whether mild DCM (mJOA 15-17) hides a subgroup that does better after surgery, and whether something other than the mJOA can find it. The answer they give is yes: a more impaired quality-of-life phenotype. The answer we will defend by the end: a group that started worse improved more, in an uncontrolled surgical series, which is interesting but is exactly what regression to the mean and more room to improve would also produce. The authors state they have no personal, financial or institutional interest in any drugs, materials or devices described; the PDF does not state funding.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: Mild DCM is a guideline toss-up, and the mJOA has a ceiling.
points: Guidelines recommend surgery for moderate (mJOA 12-14) and severe (11 or less) DCM; mild (15-17) remains controversial, and both surgery and nonoperative care are reasonable (authors, citing the 2017 guideline).
Authors' argument: the mJOA has a strong ceiling effect in mild disease, so it may hide real gains.
Hypothesis: mild DCM splits into at least 2 phenotypes by baseline SF-36, and the phenotype predicts outcome better than mJOA does.
What it cannot ask: no nonoperative arm, so it cannot say whether surgery beats observation for anyone.
slides.notes: The background is fair. The authors cite the 2017 AOSpine and CSRS guideline (library record C01), which recommends surgery for moderate and severe DCM and leaves mild DCM as a choice. They describe Kadanka's randomized study as the only one comparing surgery with conservative care in mild or moderate disease (mJOA 12 or more), limited by small size, heterogeneity and loss to follow-up. They also cite their own earlier work showing mild patients gain the least on mJOA after surgery. The core idea is reasonable: if mJOA 15-17 patients are near the top of the scale, mJOA change is a blunt tool, and patient-reported quality of life and disability may show who is actually suffering. Hold on to the distinction between prognostic and predictive. A prognostic factor tells you who changes more. A predictive factor, in the trial sense, tells you who gains more from one treatment than from another. With everyone operated on, this design can only be prognostic within surgery. The authors call their subgroups of 'both prognostic and therapeutic relevance' and speak of 'greater response to surgery'. That second claim needs a comparison group the study does not have. That reading is ours.

slides.title: Patients and methods
points: 193 mild DCM patients (mJOA 15-17) from the prospective multicenter AOSpine CSM-NA and CSM-I cohorts; all had decompression, with or without fusion.
8 lacked baseline SF-36, leaving 185. 156 (84%) had complete 1-year data.
Excluded: asymptomatic DCM, prior cervical surgery, infection, tumor, rheumatoid arthritis, trauma, ankylosing spondylitis, concomitant lumbar stenosis.
Step 1: k-means clustering (k fixed at 2) on 10 baseline SF-36 scores: 8 domains plus PCS and MCS.
Step 2: compare clusters on baseline traits and on 1-year change. Primary: change in SF-36. Secondary: mJOA, Nurick, NDI, SF-6D.
Step 3: kNN (k=5) predicts cluster from the traits that differed; 150 train, 35 test, repeated 10 times.
Fisher's exact and t-tests, alpha 0.05, no multiplicity adjustment reported; missing data assumed random and dropped.
slides.notes: Walk through the three steps slowly, because the logic is circular in a way that matters. Step 1 sorts patients by their baseline SF-36 alone. No clinical data enter the clustering. Step 2 then asks what else differs between the two groups and how each group changed. Step 3 asks whether the clinical traits found in step 2 can recover the cluster label. Three method points to notice. First, k was fixed at 2. The authors admit in their limitations that the number of clusters is chosen arbitrarily. No measure of cluster quality or stability appears in the main text. Second, the inputs include PCS and MCS, which are themselves built from the 8 domains. That gives the physical and mental summaries extra weight in the distance calculation. That point is ours; scaling details are in the supplement we did not see. Third, missing data were handled by dropping cases. 29 of 185 (16%) lack complete 1-year data: 13 of 79 in cluster 1 and 16 of 106 in cluster 2 (our arithmetic from Table 4), so loss was similar, but the paper does not compare those lost with those kept. The paper calls the primary outcome change in SF-36 but names no single SF-36 score as primary, so 10 SF-36 change scores plus 4 secondary measures are all tested. mJOA and Nurick are investigator-administered; NDI and SF-36 are patient-reported. The paper says nothing about whether assessors knew cluster membership, and the clusters did not exist when data were collected, so assessor bias by cluster is unlikely (our reading). The 3-group comparisons by mJOA level give one P value each; the paper names only Fisher and t-tests, so the 3-group test is not stated. Our one-way ANOVA from the printed summaries reproduces the mJOA change P of .015 and baseline Nurick P of .006, but not NDI (about .48 versus printed .542 at baseline and .533 for change), so ANOVA is confirmed for only 2 values.

slides.title: Who is in each cluster
slides.lead: Cluster 1 is the more impaired group on SF-36; mJOA did not separate them.
points: No differences in diagnosis, symptom duration, comorbidities, approach (about three quarters anterior in both) or levels.
By mJOA level (15, 16, 17), NDI and every SF-36 domain were similar; only Nurick differed (P=.006).
slides.see: Figure 1A shows the SF-36 scatter with mJOA colors fully mixed; Figure 1B shows the clusters separating, most clearly along the physical scores (our reading).
slides.notes: This is the most useful descriptive finding in the paper. Within mJOA 15-17, the mJOA level told you nothing about NDI or SF-36 at baseline (Table 3, all P above .07). That supports the authors' point that mild by mJOA does not mean mildly affected. Now read the cluster table critically. Table 1 runs 22 yes-or-no comparisons plus 2 continuous ones, with no correction. Four reach P<.05. By chance alone about 1 of 22 would (our arithmetic). Neck pain, at P=.001, is the robust one; female sex, gait difficulty and weakness, at .025 to .041, are fragile. We recomputed all 22 Fisher tests from the printed counts and every P value reproduced. That check exposed two count typos: diabetes and rheumatologic disease in cluster 2 are printed as 5 (5.7%), but 5 of 106 is 4.7%, and only a count of 6 gives the printed P of .735. Three percentages look rounded to 2 decimals and then to 1: neck pain 25 of 79 is 31.6% (printed 31.7%), cardiovascular in cluster 2 is 31 of 106, 29.2% (printed 29.3%), and Table 2 3+ levels in cluster 1 is 25 of 79, 31.6% (printed 31.7%). Trivial; no P value changes. Cluster SF-36 baseline means are not tabulated anywhere. The text says Table 3 presents baseline SF-36 and SF-6D by cluster, but Table 3 shows them only by mJOA level. So you cannot read how far apart the clusters were at the start, or whether cluster 1 ended up better than cluster 2 or simply caught up. Figure 2, the heat map, includes leg spasticity, which does not appear in Table 1. Note that the cluster 1 phenotype is defined after the fact by what differed; the authors did not prespecify neck pain, motor symptoms or sex.

slides.title: Outcomes at 1 year
slides.lead: The worse-off cluster gained more on disability and physical QOL; mJOA change did not differ.
points: Also favoring cluster 1: role emotional (.048), social functioning (.022), vitality (.025). Not different: general health, mental health.
By baseline mJOA: only mJOA change differed, +1.3 (mJOA 15), +0.7 (16), +0.09 (17), P=.015.
kNN on neck pain, gait difficulty, weakness and sex: mean accuracy 70.6% (95% CI 65.2-75.9%).
slides.see: Figure 3B shows cluster 2's physical-function and PCS changes sitting near zero while cluster 1's sit around 11 to 12; role physical, at +15.3 versus +2.5, shows the same contrast.
slides.notes: Read the table as change within operated patients, by cluster. The striking contrast is in the physical domains: cluster 2 gained almost nothing on physical functioning (+1.1) and PCS (+1.8), while cluster 1 gained about 11 to 12. MCS and mental health improved similarly in both. The neurological scales did not separate the clusters. So the clusters differ in how much patient-reported disability and physical QOL changed, not in myelopathy grade change. Our recomputation of the t-tests from the printed summaries agrees for the physical scores and SF-6D. NDI does not: with n of 66 and 90 we get P about .001 (pooled) or .002 (Welch), not .003, beyond rounding. Most likely some patients lacked NDI, so its n is lower than the headers and unreported (our reading), which adds to the complete-case concern. Role emotional does not reproduce cleanly: we get P about .051 (pooled) or .063 (Welch) versus the printed .048. That is within rounding range, so call it borderline rather than wrong. Our 95% CI for the PCS difference is about 7 to 13 points and for NDI about 4 to 15 points; the paper gives no CIs for these differences. Bodily pain is printed as 13.74, the only SF-36 value in Table 4 with two decimals. Now the kNN. 70.6% sounds decent until you compare it with always guessing the larger cluster: 106 of 185 is 57.3%. Our points: the four inputs are yes-or-no, so there are only 16 possible profiles and many ties. The inputs were chosen because they differed between clusters in the full dataset, then tested on random splits of that same dataset, which flatters accuracy. The CI reflects variation across 10 overlapping splits of 35, not sampling error. And kNN predicts cluster membership, not improvement. The paper never tests whether neck pain, motor symptoms or sex directly predict 1-year change. The abstract's line that mJOA correlated with neither baseline QOL nor outcomes overlooks the mJOA change result (P=.015). The Discussion's claim that baseline mJOA does not correlate with other baseline measures of functional status also conflicts with the baseline Nurick difference (P=.006).

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: Holds up: prospective multicenter data, standard validated outcome scales, 84% follow-up with similar loss by cluster, Fisher P values reproduce from counts.
Holds up: within mJOA 15-17, baseline mJOA level did not track NDI or SF-36.
Weakens it: no nonoperative group, so 'greater response to surgery' cannot be separated from natural course or regression to the mean.
Weakens it: cluster 1 was defined by worse baseline SF-36 and then gained more on SF-36, the same instrument (our reading).
Weakens it: k fixed at 2; phenotype traits found after the fact; dozens of baseline and outcome tests without correction.
Weakens it: kNN predicts cluster, not outcome, has no external validation, and beats a 57.3% guess by 13 points.
Errors: count typos in Table 1, missing cluster baseline SF-36 values, Table 4 column labeled 'Baseline QOL'.
slides.notes: Be fair first. The data are prospective and multicenter, the scales are standard, follow-up is 84%, and the descriptive statistics check out. The authors name two limitations: only 1-year follow-up, and the arbitrary number of clusters. Everything else on this slide is our reading. The central problem is regression to the mean plus room to improve. Cluster 1 was selected because its baseline SF-36 was worse. Any noisy score selected for being low will tend to rise on retest, surgery or not, and a group with lower physical scores has more room to rise. Then the main outcome is change in that same SF-36. A greater gain in cluster 1 is the expected result even if surgery had identical effects in both groups. NDI, a separate instrument, also favors cluster 1, which helps a little, but cluster 1 also started much worse on NDI (39.1 versus 24.9), so the same concern applies. Without baseline cluster SF-36 values in a table, and without any adjustment for baseline score, you cannot tell whether cluster 1 ended up better or just closed the gap. Second, the phrase 'therapeutic relevance' asks more than the design gives. No one was observed without surgery, so the study cannot show that cluster 1 patients benefit more from surgery than from waiting, or that cluster 2 patients would do as well without it. Third, the phenotype itself: neck pain is robust, while sex, gait and weakness sit at P .025 to .041 among about 22 baseline comparisons. Fourth, the classifier: modest gain over the base rate, inputs chosen on the full data, no external test set. Smaller issues for source problems: Table 1 diabetes and rheumatologic counts printed as 5 where 6 fits the percent and P; text calls Table 3 the home of baseline SF-36 by cluster, but it is not there; Table 4's column header reads 'Baseline QOL' over change scores; Figure 2 shows leg spasticity, which Table 1 omits; the 3-group test is not named; NDI change P does not reproduce from the printed n; three double-rounded percentages; an 'S3-36' typo; and Figure 3's caption claims 'nearly all' SF-36 domains when 3 of 10 did not differ.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "In operated mild DCM, patients in the worse-QOL cluster, which had more neck pain and motor symptoms, improved more on NDI and SF-36 physical scores at 1 year. It is an uncontrolled, post hoc cluster analysis, so it tells you who changes most after surgery, not who benefits most from surgery."

rows: Worse QOL cluster improved more at 1 yr
Values pain and NDI burden; low to very low evidence

points: C03, C04 and C10 figures come from the library records, which are abstract-level or partial reviews. Follow-up and endpoints differ.
slides.notes: Say the bottom line in one breath: worse quality of life at baseline went with bigger gains after surgery in mild DCM, and the mJOA level did not pick those patients out. Then add the boundary: no comparison group, so 'bigger gain after surgery' is not 'bigger benefit from surgery'. Our arithmetic, weighting the cluster means by their 1-year numbers, gives an overall mean change of about +0.88 mJOA, -10.1 NDI and +6.0 PCS at 1 year in this paper's 156 patients. That is broadly in line with C03's record from the same cohorts at 2 years, though endpoints and timing differ. Expect these follow-up questions. Should a mild DCM patient with neck pain and weakness be offered surgery on the strength of this? It supports listening to the patient's pain and disability rather than relying on the mJOA alone, consistent with the pain and NDI emphasis in the C10 record, but it does not show those patients do better with surgery than without. Should a mild patient with good SF-36 scores be steered away from surgery? Not from this paper: cluster 2 gained little in physical QOL, but nobody was followed without surgery, and the paper reports no neurological deterioration or complication data by cluster. Can I use the 4-item classifier in clinic? No. It predicts cluster membership with about 71% accuracy against a 57% base rate, was not externally validated, and was never linked directly to outcome. Is neck pain just axial pain that any fusion relieves? Possibly; the authors note most patients had anterior surgery and suggest neck pain and motor gains may be greater with that approach, but approach did not differ by cluster and the paper does not test approach by cluster. Why two clusters? The authors fixed k at 2 and acknowledge it was arbitrary.

decks.not_reviewed: The full 6-page paper was read, including Tables 1 and 2 and Figures 1 to 5 from the page images. No supplement is cited. The earlier 298-patient study by the same group (reference 14) and the other cited works were not reviewed. Values read off the bar charts in Figures 2 to 5 are our approximate readings; Figures 2 and 3 have no group sizes at all. For Figures 4 and 5, Table 2 gives the class sizes, but the paper prints no outcome-level n, group means, SDs, named test or exact P values.

slides.title: Glassman 2005: positive sagittal balance and health status
slides.lead: In adults with spinal deformity and a forward C7 plumb line, more forward offset went with worse pain, function and disability scores. The correlations were real but weak.
points: Glassman SD, Bridwell K, Dimar JR, Horton W, Berven S, Schwab F. Spine 2005;30:2024-2029
Retrospective review of a multicenter prospective adult deformity database, 2002 to 2003
752 enrolled; 352 with positive sagittal balance analyzed; baseline data only
Main result: Spearman rho about 0.2 to 0.3 between C7 plumb line offset and SF-12 PCS, SRS-29 and ODI; mental health score not related
Second result: relative lumbar kyphosis went with more disability, high thoracic kyphosis with less
Corporate or industry funds supported the work, per the paper's disclosure
slides.notes: This is the paper people mean when they say sagittal balance matters. It was built from the full text. Frame it correctly from the start: it is a cross-sectional correlation study of a single baseline visit, not an outcomes study, and nobody here was treated by protocol or followed. Every patient in the analysis already had a forward C7 plumb line, so the comparison is more forward against less forward, never balanced against unbalanced. The authors' abstract, Discussion and Key Points say severity of symptoms increases in a linear fashion with progressive imbalance. Keep that claim in mind; slide 4 shows it was not formally tested. The paper's own Key Points add that relative kyphosis is very poorly tolerated in the lumbar spine. The paper's funding disclosure states that corporate or industry funds were received, with benefits directed to a research fund or similar nonprofit. The paper does not name the company. The Acknowledgments thank a named analyst for assistance in preparing the data analysis, and the Spinal Deformity Study Group for its support.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: Among deformity patients who are already pitched forward, which sagittal features predict how bad they feel?
points: Background: the same group's earlier multicenter study of 298 adults found positive sagittal balance the radiographic parameter most correlated with poor health status (reference 14)
That earlier study was too small to sort out which features drive the effect, per the authors
Aim here: magnitude of the C7 offset, the region of the sagittal deformity, and possible confounders
Era: pelvic incidence, pelvic tilt and PI-LL were not measured. Sagittal balance meant the C7 plumb line only
slides.notes: Set the scene the way the authors do. Adult deformity ranges from stable painless curves to disabling deformity, and earlier studies had focused on curve progression and radiographic prognosis. The group's own earlier paper of 298 adults found that positive sagittal balance was more strongly associated with pain and disability than curve magnitude, curve location or coronal imbalance, and that unoperated deformities showed it as well as postoperative flatback. Those findings are as this paper reports them; reference 14 was not reviewed here. The authors list what they wanted to separate: magnitude, location, interaction with coronal deformity, and whether the imbalance was primary or postsurgical. Point out what is missing. There is no pelvic measurement anywhere in this paper. Later library papers built the pelvis in. In the master file, Schwab (D03) reports thresholds of PI-LL at least 11 degrees, PT at least 22 degrees and SVA at least 47 mm, and Lafage (D04) reports that alignment matching population-norm function loosens with age. Ours, not the authors': without pelvic tilt, a patient who compensates by retroverting the pelvis can show a modest plumb line offset with a large underlying deformity, and this study cannot see that.

slides.title: Selection and measurement
slides.lead: A broad, mixed deformity population, a simple plumb line, and three patient-reported scores.
points: Enrollment: age over 18, scoliosis over 30 degrees or other significant coronal or sagittal deformity; previously operated patients included if more than 18 months after the index surgery
Positive balance: C7 plumb line from the middle of the C7 body passing anterior to the posterosuperior corner of S1, on 36-inch standing films; any offset above zero counted
Regional sagittal Cobb: T2-T5, T5-T12, T12-L2 and T12-sacrum; each graded lordotic, normal or kyphotic at 1 SD from the regional mean
Outcomes: SF-12 PCS and MCS, SRS-29 pain, activity and total, ODI
Statistics: Spearman correlation, then 10 roughly equal groups by offset compared with ANOVA and Student-Newman-Keuls
slides.see: Figure 1 shows the plumb line measured from the center of C7 to the posterosuperior corner of S1.
slides.notes: Read the selection carefully. 352 of 752 is 46.8 percent, our arithmetic. The other 400, with neutral or negative balance, are dropped, so there is no reference group. The paper gives no baseline comparison of analyzed and excluded patients, but its sex counts allow one (our arithmetic): 63 of 352 analyzed are male (17.9 percent) against 44 of 400 excluded (11.0 percent), chi-square 7.3, P about 0.007. So the analyzed cohort differs from the excluded patients at least in sex mix. The cohort is heterogeneous: 30.4 percent adult idiopathic scoliosis, 9.4 percent de novo, 20.7 percent kyphotic deformities including fixed sagittal imbalance, 14 percent combined deformities such as junctional degeneration and iatrogenic imbalance, and 25.5 percent miscellaneous. Those five add to 100 percent, yet the paper then says diagnosis was unidentified in 11.1 percent. That cannot all be true; we flag it. More than half had prior spine surgery, so many have instrumented, fused segments. Measurement: the paper says radiographs followed a standardized positioning protocol and a standardized manual of measurement techniques. It does not say who measured, whether measurements were central, or give any reliability data. Missing data: SF-12 was available in 284 of 352 (81 percent, ours), SRS and ODI in 349 to 351. The SD of the offset is almost as large as its mean, with a range to 271 mm, so the distribution is skewed; Spearman, a rank method, is the right choice and the authors used it. The 10 offset groups are not given sizes in the paper; Figure 2 shows their bins, from 10 mm or less up to 130 mm or more. Confounders listed: prior surgery, coronal balance, smoking, age and BMI.

slides.title: Main result: C7 offset against health status
slides.lead: Every physical and pain measure worsened with offset. The rank correlations ran 0.21 to 0.29.
points: Signs match direction: higher SRS and PCS are better, higher ODI is worse
Our recomputation from rho and n is consistent with Table 1, reading its printed 0.000001 as a floor (the text writes P < 0.000001)
rho squared is 0.04 to 0.09: offset ranks account for under a tenth of score ranks (our arithmetic)
The authors call this a high degree of correlation and the trend linear
slides.see: Figure 2 shows mean PCS and ODI across the 10 offset groups with hand-drawn arrows; the ODI bars do not rise steadily.
slides.notes: This is the headline. The P values are tiny because n is about 350, not because the relationship is strong. We recomputed each from rho and n: PCS t about 5.1, P about 5 in 10 million; SRS pain P about 0.00009, matching the printed 0.0000917; MCS P 0.21, matching 0.206. ODI comes out near 1 in 10 million. So the three values Table 1 prints as 0.000001 are really below it; they fit only if 0.000001 is a floor, which the text supports by writing P < 0.000001. Our Fisher intervals: PCS rho -0.39 to -0.18, ODI 0.18 to 0.37. Either way the correlation is modest, and offset explains well under 10 percent of the ranking of scores. The authors' word is high; ours is weak to modest. The text gives SRS pain as P < 0.0009 while Table 1 prints 0.0000917, a loose bound rather than a contradiction. Now read Figure 2. Our approximate readings from the bars: PCS falls from about 39 in the 10 mm or less group to about 29 at 130 mm or more. ODI is about 34 in the 10 mm or less group, drops to about 23 at 11 to 18 mm and about 26 at 19 to 24 mm, then rises unevenly to about 44 in the top bins: about 38 at 25 to 32 mm, 30 at 33 to 42 mm and 34 at 43 to 54 mm. PCS also goes up and down: about 37 at 11 to 18 mm then 38.5 at 19 to 24 mm, and 35 at 25 to 32 mm then 37.5 at 33 to 42 mm. The arrows are drawn, not fitted, and exaggerate the change: each spans about 26 points (PCS about 35 to 9, ODI about 9 to 35) where the bars change by about 10. No regression line, slope or test of linearity is reported. So 'linear' is the authors' description of a monotone rank correlation, not a tested shape, and the first ODI group already argues against a straight line. The authors' conclusion that even mildly positive balance is somewhat detrimental also has no comparator, because patients with zero or negative offset were excluded. The abstract and text say all measures, naming SF-12, SRS-29 and ODI, worsened significantly with offset by ANOVA. Table 1 shows MCS was not significant on Spearman, and the ANOVA results are not tabulated. Say the mental component did not track.

slides.title: Where the kyphosis sits
slides.lead: Relative lumbar kyphosis went with more disability; high thoracic kyphosis with less. Thoracic and thoracolumbar Cobb showed nothing.
points: Counts and degree cutoffs from Table 2; negative is lordosis
Lumbar kyphotic group: more disability on SRS-29 and ODI, P < 0.05
High thoracic kyphotic group: less pain and disability, P < 0.05
More distal region of maximal kyphosis went with higher ODI, P < 0.05; no region related to PCS
Lumbar kyphosis was not significantly associated with C7 offset, per the authors
slides.see: Figure 4B shows mean ODI by lumbar group and Figure 5B by high thoracic group; Figure 3 shows ODI rising from high thoracic to lumbar maximal kyphosis.
slides.notes: Lumbar 'kyphosis' here is relative. The lumbar kyphotic group runs from -11 to +79 degrees, mean 11.6, so some of these 45 patients still have 11 degrees of lordosis. Call it hypolordosis to lordosis loss, which is what the abstract's phrase relative kyphosis means. Our readings from the bars: ODI about 30 lordotic, 35 normal and 41 kyphotic in the lumbar groups; about 34, 37 and 30 in the high thoracic groups; Figure 3 runs from about 32 to 38. Figures 4A and 5A plot SRS total with no axis values beyond zero, so they cannot be read. The paper gives only P < 0.05 for these comparisons, with no group means, SDs or exact tests, and it ran many of them across four regions and several scores with no correction. Treat the high thoracic finding as hypothesis level. The authors interpret it as upper thoracic kyphosis being better tolerated; the paper offers no mechanism. Check the cutoffs. The method says 1 SD either side of the regional mean. Applying that to the regional means the text prints (for example lumbar -29.5, SD 33) gives cutoffs of -62.5 and +3.5, which do not match Table 2. Pooling Table 2's own groups (our arithmetic) gives lumbar mean -37.8, SD 26.2, and cutoffs of -64.0 and -11.7, which match the table exactly; the same holds in all four regions. So the regional means and SDs printed in the text (12.7, 37.6, 11.6, -29.5) do not match Table 2 and cannot have produced its cutoffs. The paper does not say why; a different subset, a different calculation or a typo are all possible. The regional totals are 352, 345, 341 and 347, so some films could not be measured, unexplained. The authors argue that because lumbar kyphosis and C7 offset were not statistically associated, the two behave at least partly independently. Ours: the cohort is restricted to positive offset, which narrows the range and makes a null association easier to find; no numbers for that test are given.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: A landmark signal from a large cohort, carried by weak correlations and thinly reported subgroup tests.
points: Strength: large multicenter cohort, standardized 36-inch films, three validated patient-reported instruments
Strength: rank statistics suited to a skewed offset; recomputed P values are consistent with Table 1
Weakness: only positive-balance patients; no neutral or negative comparison group
Weakness: cross-sectional, so no causal or treatment inference
Weakness: no pelvic parameters; no measurement reliability reported
Weakness: confounders checked one at a time; no adjusted model shown
Weakness: regional results given only as P < 0.05, many tests, no correction
Errors: diagnosis percentages sum to 111.1%; text regional means do not match Table 2; MCS was not significant despite 'all measures'
slides.notes: Be fair first. For 2005 this was a large, standardized dataset with validated outcome measures, and the core correlation is internally consistent: P values recomputed from rho and n are consistent with Table 1, reading its printed 0.000001 as a floor. The authors themselves note that sagittal balance remains an inconsistent predictor of symptoms, that positive balance increases with normal aging in volunteers, and that compensation mechanisms may make some patients tolerate it. They suggest gait analysis may be needed. Now the limits, which are our reading unless stated. Confounding: ODI varied significantly with smoking and BMI, and the authors report no interaction of any confounder with sagittal balance. Testing interaction is not the same as adjusting, and no adjusted estimate is shown. The authors also found no variation of ODI with age, surgical history or coronal imbalance, and give no numbers for that. Selection: 55 percent had prior surgery; postoperative flatback and junctional failure are in the same pool as unoperated scoliosis, and results are not split by etiology even though the authors raised etiology as a question in the introduction. Diagnosis accounting does not add up: the categories reach 100 percent before the 11.1 percent unidentified. The text's regional means and SDs cannot be the source of Table 2's 1 SD cutoffs; Table 2's own data reproduce them. The abstract says all measures of health status worsened significantly with offset, while SF-12 MCS did not on Spearman. Figure 2's arrows are drawn, not fitted, and the ODI bars are not monotone. The Discussion moves from these associations to treatment: maintenance or restoration of lumbar lordosis appears critical in surgery, and improving standing balance might help nonoperatively. The authors hedge these with appears and might. This study did not treat anyone, so those are hypotheses, not findings.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: Glassman 2005 showed that, among deformity patients already pitched forward, more forward C7 offset and lumbar lordosis loss go with worse function. It did not set a target.
points: Spoken summary: In 352 adult deformity patients with a forward C7 plumb line, drawn from 752 in a multicenter database, larger offset correlated with worse SF-12 physical, SRS-29 and ODI scores, rho about 0.2 to 0.3, but not with mental health. Relative lumbar kyphosis went with more disability and high thoracic kyphosis with less. It is a single cross-section without pelvic measures or a balanced comparison group, so it shows association, not a correction goal.

Q: What SVA should I aim for? This paper gives no threshold. Schwab (D03, library record) later reported SVA 47 mm or more as a disability threshold, and Lafage (D04, library record) argued targets loosen with age
Q: Is the relationship really linear? Not tested. The arrows are drawn, and the lowest-offset ODI group sits above the next two
Q: Is lumbar lordosis loss the same thing as positive balance? The authors found no significant association in this cohort and say they act partly independently
Q: Does correcting SVA improve outcomes? Not addressed; nobody was treated or followed

rows: Weak correlation with worse PCS, SRS, ODI
Norm-function SVA -29 to +80 mm with age

slides.notes: Give the summary in under 30 seconds, then expect these questions. First, the target question. Do not quote a number from Glassman: the paper gives none. The D03 and D04 figures come from those papers' records in the master file, not from this paper, and both add pelvic parameters this study did not measure. Second, the word linear. The authors' abstract and Key Points say symptoms rise in a linear fashion; the evidence is a Spearman correlation and a bar chart with a drawn arrow. If someone presses, say the relationship was monotone on ranks and modest in size, and the shape was never fitted. Third, how strong it is. rho of 0.29 for PCS means offset accounts for under a tenth of the variation in score ranks, our arithmetic. Large populations make weak correlations highly significant. Many patients with a big offset will feel fine and many with a small one will not, which the authors themselves anticipate when they call sagittal balance an inconsistent predictor. Fourth, lumbar lordosis. The authors' clinical message is that maintaining or restoring lumbar lordosis appears critical in surgery, especially if balance is positive before surgery. Credit that to them, and note it is an inference from cross-sectional data. Fifth, applicability. Over half had prior surgery, there was no neutral comparison group, and the mental component score did not move, so do not claim that sagittal imbalance worsens mental health from this paper. Finally, mention the internal inconsistencies briefly: diagnosis percentages summing to 111.1 percent and regional means that do not fit Table 2. They do not overturn the main correlation, which is consistent on recomputation, but they lower confidence in the subgroup detail.

decks.not_reviewed: The PDF is the complete 6-page article (pages 1077-1082), not a critique; read in full. No supplement is cited. Not reviewed: the published comment on this paper (PubMed CommentIn 22976199), the SRS 2011 meeting abstract (reference 12) that Table 1 appears to come from, the 'ongoing study' that set the cutoffs, and the earlier Schwab classification papers (references 8-10).

slides.title: Schwab 2012: SRS-Schwab adult deformity classification, a reliability study
slides.lead: Bottom line: nine expert readers applied the new classification to 21 premarked cases with high agreement, but the study tests whether readers sort the same numbers the same way, not whether the grades predict anything.
points: Journal club · Adult deformity
Schwab F, Ungar B, Blondel B, et al. Spine 2012;37(12):1077-82
Full text read. The PDF is the complete article, not a critique.
Design: inter- and intra-rater reliability study, 21 cases, 9 readers, 2 readings about 1 week apart
Initiated by the SRS Adult Deformity Committee; no funds received, per the paper
slides.notes: This is the paper that introduced the SRS-Schwab classification most of us use when we talk about adult deformity: one coronal curve type plus three sagittal modifiers, PI-LL, PT and SVA. Say up front what kind of evidence it is. The title calls it a validation study, but what it measures is reliability: do the same readers give the same grade twice, and do different readers give the same grade. It does not test whether the grades relate to disability, guide treatment or predict outcome. The authors take the clinical relevance of the modifiers from earlier work (their Table 1, from reference 12, a 2011 SRS meeting presentation) and from 'an ongoing study'. That calling it reliability rather than validation is the fair label is our reading, not the authors'. The deck was built from the full article. The published comment on it, the meeting abstract behind Table 1, and the earlier Schwab classification papers were not reviewed here. Funding: the paper states no funds were received and no commercial benefits. Measurements were made in Surgimap Spine, which the paper says was provided by Nemaris Inc.

slides.title: The question and the classification
slides.lead: Earlier adult deformity systems were either hard to use or left out the pelvis; this version adds three spinopelvic modifiers tied to disability.
points: Authors' rationale: treatment of adult deformity is driven by pain and disability, so the grades should track HRQOL
Earlier Schwab system: 5 curve types and 2 modifiers (lordosis and subluxation), no pelvic parameters

Curve type, by the Cobb angle of the major curve: T (thoracic, more than 30°, apex T9 or higher), L (lumbar or thoracolumbar, more than 30°, apex T10 or lower), D (double major, each more than 30°), N (no coronal curve more than 30°)
Question: is the new system clear and reliable when applied by different readers and by the same reader twice?
slides.see: Figure 1 is the one-page guide to the grades; Figures 2 and 3 show two worked cases on full-length films.
slides.notes: Walk through the system once using the paper's definitions. PI is the angle between the perpendicular to the sacral endplate at its midpoint and the line to the midpoint of the bicoxofemoral axis. LL is the Cobb angle from the superior endplate of L1 to the superior endplate of S1. PT is the angle between the vertical and the line from the sacral endplate midpoint to the bicoxofemoral axis midpoint. SVA is the offset between the C7 plumb line and the posterosuperior corner of the sacrum. The authors argue PI-LL matters because osteotomy planning should account for how much lordosis the pelvis needs, and that PT matters because a retroverted pelvis can hide global malalignment; they cite a meeting presentation (reference 13) suggesting patients with similar SVA but higher PT need larger corrections. Worked examples from the paper: Figure 2 is a 41° lumbar curve, apex L2, PI 73° and LL 53° so PI-LL 20°, PT 27°, SVA 62 mm, graded L with PI-LL +, PT +, SVA +. Figure 3 is a double curve, thoracic 72° apex T9 and lumbar 59° apex L2-L3, PI-LL 15°, PT 24°, SVA 16 mm, graded D with PI-LL + and PT +. Our reading: Figure 3's caption leaves out the SVA grade, which by the text cutoffs is 0. Two definitional gaps worth noticing, both ours. First, the text defines PI-LL '0' as less than 10°, so a strongly negative value (lumbar lordosis exceeding PI) is graded 0, but Figure 1 says 'within 10°', which would exclude it. The study set included a case at minus 46°, and the paper does not say how it was graded. Second, values exactly at a cutoff (for example a 30° curve, or PI-LL of exactly 20° as in Figure 2) depend on whether 'between' is inclusive, which the text implies but Figure 1 does not settle. The Discussion also calls the N type a 'sagittal curve', while the Methods call it N for normal, meaning no major coronal deformity.

slides.title: Selection, measurement and analysis
slides.lead: Twenty-one premarked cases chosen to spread across the grades, read twice by nine people close to the system.
points: Cases: 21 premarked cases, selected to represent a distribution of classification grades; not consecutive patients
Readers: 9, made up of the authors and members of the SRS Adult Deformity Classification Committee
Second reading about 1 week later, cases in a different order
Measurements in Surgimap Spine; analysis by Fleiss' kappa in a MATLAB program, plus percent agreement
Scale (Landis and Koch): 0.61-0.80 substantial, 0.81-1.00 almost perfect
slides.notes: The case mix sums to 21 in every row, which we checked. The ranges are wide: PI 38° to 85° (median 61°), LL minus 9° to 85° (median 40°), PI-LL minus 46° to 70° (median 25°), PT 2° to 55° (median 25°), SVA minus 63 to 243 mm (median 34 mm). The medians fit the grade counts, for example 11 of 21 SVA grades are 0, so the median of 34 mm sits below 40. Three design choices shape every number on the next slide. First, premarked cases. The landmarks were placed before the readers saw the films, so readers did not have to find the femoral heads, the S1 endplate or C7 themselves. The authors say this was deliberate, 'to assess the agreement in classification and not the agreement in picking radiographical landmarks', concede the choice 'can be criticized', and plan a study with non-premarked cases. Our inference, not the paper's: landmark picking is likely a large source of disagreement in practice, so these kappas are probably higher than unmarked films would give. Second, selected cases. Choosing films to cover the grades, and including values far from the cutoffs such as PT 55° or SVA 243 mm, tends to make grading easier than in a run of consecutive clinic patients, where many sit near a threshold. That effect on kappa is our inference; the paper does not discuss it. Third, the readers were the developers and committee members, so this is expert agreement on their own system, not agreement among general spine surgeons. The paper gives no sample-size reasoning and no confidence intervals for any kappa; our intervals for the all-reader percentages are on the last slide and overlap heavily. Fleiss' kappa treats the grades as unordered categories, so a 0 versus ++ disagreement counts the same as 0 versus +; the paper does not report a weighted analysis.

slides.title: Results: agreement by component
slides.lead: Kappa was highest for PT and SVA, lower for curve type and PI-LL, and lowest for the whole grade.
points: Intra-rater kappa averaged 0.94 curve type, 0.88 PI-LL, 0.97 PT, 0.97 SVA, 0.87 for the entire grade
Same grade on both readings: 95.7% curve type, 93.6% PI-LL, 98.4% PT, 97.9% SVA, 87.8% entire grade
Inter-rater kappa rose from reading 1 to reading 2 for most components
All 9 readers agreed, on reading 2, in 66.7% of cases for curve type, 71.4% PI-LL, 95.2% PT, 90.5% SVA (abstract only)
slides.notes: We recomputed the Table 2 averages from the nine readers and they match: 0.94, 0.88, 0.97, 0.97 and 0.87. The printed ranges match the table too. Read the spread, not just the mean. Reader 7 had intra-rater kappas of 0.70 for curve type, 0.66 for PI-LL, 0.77 for SVA and 0.63 for the entire grade. Reader 8 had 0.75 for PI-LL, and reader 5 had 0.75 for the whole grade. So one reader's grading was only substantial on their own scale, while five readers were perfect on curve type. The inter-rater figures are the more useful ones for a surgeon reading someone else's report. PT and SVA were near-perfect from the start. The paper offers no reason; our reading is that with landmarks fixed, each is one measured number against a threshold. Curve type and PI-LL were substantial on reading 1 (0.80 and 0.75) and almost perfect on reading 2. The whole grade, which is what you actually write in the chart, was 0.70 then 0.79, substantial both times. The abstract gives a striking number that the body text does not repeat: even on the second reading, all nine readers agreed on curve type in only 66.7 percent of cases, which works out to 14 of 21, and on PI-LL in 71.4 percent, 15 of 21. Our arithmetic: that means 7 curve-type cases and 6 PI-LL cases had at least one reader who disagreed. High kappa and frequent incomplete agreement can coexist with nine readers; the paper does not say how many readers dissented in those cases. The authors read the rise from reading 1 to reading 2 as a learning curve. That is plausible, but with 21 cases and no confidence intervals, the paper does not show the rise is more than chance; that caution is ours. A small arithmetic point, also ours: with 189 paired readings (9 readers times 21 cases), 98.4, 97.9 and 87.8 percent match 186, 185 and 166 of 189, but 95.7 percent (curve type) and 93.6 percent (PI-LL) cannot be reproduced: 181 and 177 of 189 give 95.8 and 93.7. The paper does not explain this.

slides.title: Where the cutoffs come from, and what is not tested
slides.lead: The modifiers rest on disability thresholds from earlier work; this paper does not test them.
points: Table 1 lists thresholds predictive of an ODI of 40, attributed in the text to reference 12, an SRS 2011 meeting presentation
The modifier cutoffs are round numbers near, but not equal to, those thresholds
Neither the '+' nor the '++' cutoffs are derived in this paper; the body cites previous studies and 'an ongoing study', the abstract 'HRQOL analysis from a multicenter database'
No outcome, HRQOL or treatment data are analyzed in this paper
slides.notes: This is the slide that stops the classification being over-read. The authors state that the parameters were chosen for clinical relevance and that the cutoffs were set using outcome scores 'as reported in previous studies' (references 3 and 11) 'and determined in an ongoing study'; the abstract instead says 'HRQOL analysis from a multicenter database'. Table 1 gives r values of 0.38 to 0.47 but does not say what r is correlated with. If it is the correlation with ODI, which is our assumption, those are moderate. The paper does not explain why the '+' boundary sits at 10°, 20° and 40 mm rather than at the tabulated 11°, 22° and 46 mm. For the library comparison, the master record for the 2013 Schwab disability-threshold paper (D03, abstract-level record, 492 patients) lists PI-LL 11°, PT 22° and SVA 47 mm. That SVA figure is 1 mm different from this paper's Table 1 value of 46 mm. We cannot resolve the difference from this PDF; note that Table 1 here appears to come from the earlier meeting presentation. The authors themselves list the next steps: a reliability study with non-premarked cases, the incidence of each curve type in a consecutive database, and treatment success by category to build algorithms. In other words, by their own account, validity and treatment guidance were future work in 2012. The authors also say these spinopelvic parameters were used to set thresholds of correction for realignment surgery. Our caution: a threshold linked to an ODI of 40 at baseline is not the same thing as a proven postoperative target, and this paper contains no postoperative data at all. The Introduction's 'highly correlated with pain and disability' cites reference 11 (Lafage 2009), which we did not read, not Table 1.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: A clear, usable system with good expert agreement on premarked films; the conclusions run ahead of the data in places.
points: Holds up: a simple, explicit grading scheme with measured definitions and worked examples
Holds up: intra-rater reliability reported per reader and per component (Table 2), inter-rater per reading (Table 3); Table 2 averages recompute
Holds up: case mix reported and sums to 21 in every category
Holds up: authors name the premarked-case limitation and plan a non-premarked study
Weakens it: premarked landmarks mean landmark picking, a step real grading needs, was not tested; the authors concede the choice 'can be criticized'
Weakens it: 21 selected cases; experts and developers as readers; no confidence intervals
Weakens it: Discussion says intra-rater kappa was 'always greater than 0.81', but Table 2 shows several readers below that
Weakens it: Figure 1 and the text define PI-LL '0' differently for negative values
slides.notes: Be fair first: this is a short, clearly written methods paper and the system it introduced is easy to apply, which is why it spread. Table 2 recomputes. Table 3 has small slips: its title says 'for Each Reader' but it reports per reading, the PT average is printed 0.97 though (0.97+0.98)/2 rounds to 0.98, and PI-LL is printed '0.8'. Now the problems. The authors' Discussion says intra-rater reliability had Fleiss' coefficients 'always greater than 0.81' for curve type, each modifier and the entire grade. That is true of the averages but not of individual readers: Table 2 shows reader 7 at 0.70, 0.66, 0.77 and 0.63, reader 8 at 0.75 for PI-LL, and reader 5 at 0.75 for the entire grade. The same sentence says intra-rater agreement was 'always above 80%', but only average agreement is reported, so that claim cannot be checked per reader. The Conclusion calls inter-rater reliability 'excellent' for curve type and each modifier, yet by the paper's own scale the first-reading values for curve type (0.80) and PI-LL (0.75) are substantial. Key Points claims excellent reliability for the system as a whole, but the entire-grade inter-rater kappa never exceeded 0.79. 'Excellent' is not a Landis-Koch term; treating it as 'almost perfect' is our reading. The abstract reports neither the intra- nor the inter-rater kappa for the entire grade. The all-reader agreement percentages appear only in the abstract, not in Results or a table. The Conclusion that the system is 'easy and consistent', and the Key Points claim that it 'is clear', are stated as demonstrated; neither ease of use nor clarity was measured. On definitions: Figure 1 says PI-LL 0 is 'within 10°', while the text says less than 10°, and these disagree for lordosis exceeding PI, a situation present in the study set. Figure 1 also uses less than 30° for the N type and omits the apex rule for T versus L. Our reading on generalizability: on unmarked films, in community hands, with patients clustered near the cutoffs, agreement is likely lower than reported here; this paper cannot tell us by how much. Finally, the title says validation, but no validity was tested.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: SRS-Schwab is a reliable shared language among experts on premarked films; its link to outcome comes from other papers.
points: Spoken summary: 'Schwab 2012 tested the new SRS-Schwab classification with 9 expert readers grading 21 premarked cases twice. Agreement was high: inter-rater kappa on the second reading was 0.87 for curve type, 0.86 PI-LL, 0.98 PT and 0.96 SVA, and 0.79 for the full grade. It is a reliability study on premarked films, not proof that the grades predict outcome.'
Expect: does this validate PI-LL less than 10° as a surgical target? No. No outcomes were analyzed here; the cutoffs came from earlier disability work
Expect: will my residents agree this well? Not shown. Landmarks were premarked, readers were the developers, and cases were chosen to span the grades

Expect: why is PT more reliable than PI-LL? Our reading: with fixed landmarks PT is a single angle against a threshold, while PI-LL combines two measurements and lumbar lordosis may be harder to read consistently
Expect: what about hyperlordosis? The text grades any PI-LL below 10° as 0, including strongly negative values; Figure 1 says 'within 10°'

rows: PI-LL 11°, PT 22°, SVA 47 mm linked to ODI over 40
Places SRS-Schwab beside other alignment models

slides.notes: D03 and D13 entries come from their master-file records, which are abstract-level for D03 and abstract plus targeted full-text sections for D13; they were not re-read for this deck. Use the D03 row to make the key teaching point: the reliability comes from this paper, the link to disability comes from a different cohort, and neither paper establishes the right postoperative target for an individual patient. Follow-up questions to expect. First, is SRS-Schwab validated? Say it carefully: reliable among experts on premarked films in this paper; associated with disability in other work; not shown here to guide treatment. Second, does the grade tell me how much correction to do? Not from this paper. The authors mention correction thresholds from earlier work, but this study has no surgical data. Third, why was the whole grade only substantial between readers? Because every component must match: if each of four components disagrees occasionally, the full grade disagrees more often. That reasoning is ours. Fourth, is 21 cases enough? The paper gives no sample-size justification and no confidence intervals, so treat the decimals as approximate. Our recomputed Wilson 95% intervals for all-reader agreement on 21 cases: curve type 14 of 21, 45% to 83%; PI-LL 15 of 21, 50% to 86%; PT 20 of 21, 77% to 99%; SVA 19 of 21, 71% to 97%. They overlap heavily, so PT and SVA beating curve type and PI-LL on full agreement is not firmly shown. Kappa intervals cannot be rebuilt from the published data. Fifth, what would a stronger study look like? The authors themselves call for unmarked films and a consecutive database; we would add readers outside the development group and a weighted kappa for the ordered modifiers.

decks.not_reviewed: No supplement is cited in the PDF, so none was read. Figures 1 to 6 are schematics, two example radiographs and two bar charts. Only their captions and the text describing them were available as text. Bar heights in Figures 5 and 6 were not read beyond the percentages the text quotes. The earlier retrospective threshold paper (reference 12) and the normative sources reprinted in Table 1 were not reviewed.

slides.title: Schwab 2013: which alignment numbers go with disability?
slides.lead: In 492 adults with spinal deformity, the authors picked PT, SVA and PI-LL as the parameters most tied to disability and turned linear fits into the familiar 22 degree, 47 mm and 11 degree thresholds.
points: Schwab FJ, Blondel B, Bess S, et al., International Spine Study Group. Spine 2013;38:E803-E812
Baseline analysis of a prospective, consecutive, multicenter ASD database: 11 US sites, 15 physicians, October 2008 to December 2010
492 patients: 178 operative and 314 nonoperative, with treatment chosen by the surgeon
Thresholds the authors give for ODI over 40: PT 22 degrees or more, SVA 47 mm or more, PI-LL 11 degrees or more
Single parameters explain 14 to 22 percent of ODI variance (r squared 0.14 to 0.22). Combined model 24 percent
Deck built from the full text. No follow-up data: everything is baseline
slides.notes:
This is the paper behind the numbers most of us quote in clinic and in planning conferences: PT under 22, SVA under 47 mm, PI-LL under 11. Know what kind of evidence it is before you lean on it. It is a cross-sectional look at baseline radiographs and baseline questionnaires. Nobody was operated on as part of the analysis, and nobody was followed. The thresholds are numbers read off straight lines fitted through a cloud of patients. They are not cut points tested against an outcome.

The bottom line the authors draw is that the sagittal plane drives disability in adult spinal deformity, and that these three parameters can guide assessment and surgical planning. The first part is well supported here: the sagittal measures beat the coronal Cobb angles in Table 5. The second part, targets for surgery, goes further than baseline data can take you. The authors partly concede this when they say the study does not attempt to outline ideal treatment approaches.

Three things to carry through the deck. First, how weak the fits are: r squared of 0.14 to 0.22 means most of the variation in ODI is not explained by any one of these numbers. Second, the printed regressions run in a direction that matters for where the threshold lands. We show on slide 5 that flipping the regression moves the thresholds far upward. Third, the paper has a cluster of internal inconsistencies, including the nonoperative PT value in the abstract. Teach from the Results and tables, and say aloud which numbers do not reconcile.

Funding was a DePuy Synthes grant, and the authors list a range of financial relationships outside the submitted work.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: SVA alone may underestimate a sagittal deformity. Do pelvic and spinopelvic parameters track disability, and at what values?
points: Background (authors): sagittal alignment, not coronal Cobb, drives pain and disability in ASD
PI is fixed anatomy. PT and sacral slope share it: PI = PT + SS
PT measures pelvic retroversion, which the authors call a compensation to stay upright
PI-LL measures how flat the lumbar spine is for that pelvis
SVA: offset of the C7 plumb line from the posterosuperior corner of S1
Gap the authors name: earlier thresholds (their reference 12) came from retrospective data
slides.see: Figure 2 is the paper's schematic of the three key parameters: PI-LL, SVA and PT.
slides.notes:
Set the stakes the way the authors do. They cite a prevalence of adult spinal deformity as high as 60 percent in older people, and they argue that sagittal alignment, rather than the coronal curve, is the main driver of disability. Glassman's positive sagittal balance work is their landmark citation. Lafage and Schwab had already linked PT and SVA to HRQOL, and Schwab had proposed realignment goals from retrospective data: SVA under 50 mm, PT under 25 degrees and LL matched to PI.

What this paper adds, in the authors' framing, is a prospective, multicenter, consecutive cohort. Their aim was to correlate radiographic parameters with HRQOL and to set thresholds for severe disability, defined as ODI over 40.

A quick refresher on the geometry, because it matters for appraisal later. PI is a fixed morphological angle. PT plus sacral slope equals PI. PI-LL is PI minus lumbar lordosis. So PT and PI-LL both contain PI. Our inference, not the authors': part of the strong PT to PI-LL correlation reported later (r 0.844) may come from that shared term, plus the biology of compensation.

Table 1 reprints normative values from six volunteer studies, for example PT 15 plus or minus 7 degrees and SVA minus 20 plus or minus 30 mm in Schwab 2006. It is background only. It plays no part in the thresholds. One cell in it cannot be right: the Boulay sacral slope range is printed as 0.6 to 19.7 with a mean of 41.2. Two more, our checks: in the Schwab 2006 column PT 15 plus SS 30 is 45, not the PI of 52, while every other column reconciles within 1 degree. In the Berthonnaud 2005 column the ranges sit 5 to 8 SDs from the means (PT 12.1 plus or minus 3.2 with a range of minus 5.1 to 30.5; age 25.7 plus or minus 5.5 with a maximum of 70), so those SDs may be SEs or the ranges wrong.

Frame the question for the room. This is a measurement and association question: which radiographic numbers go with worse ODI, and where does a fitted line cross ODI 40? It is not a question about which operation, or which correction target, gives better results.

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: A consecutive baseline cohort, treatment chosen by the surgeon, radiographs measured with validated software.
points: Included: age over 18 and ASD by at least one of Cobb over 20 degrees, SVA over 5 cm, PT over 25 degrees, or TK over 60 degrees
Excluded: inflammatory arthritis, tumors, neuromuscular disease
492 patients, 70 men and 422 women, mean age 51.9 (range 18 to 85)
Entry deformity: 38% coronal only, 10% sagittal only, 52% combined
36-inch standing films measured in Spineview. HRQOL: ODI, SRS-22, SF-12
Pearson correlations, then a separate linear fit for each of the 3 parameters the authors selected, read at ODI 40
Missing data and blinding of measurers are not described
slides.see: *The abstract gives nonoperative PT as 11 degrees. Results give 19 plus or minus 11. Table 2 has the HRQOL baselines.
slides.notes:
Selection first. The cohort enters on radiographic criteria: any one of Cobb over 20, SVA over 5 cm, PT over 25 or TK over 60. Two of those entry gates are the same parameters later correlated with ODI. Our inference: selecting on the exposure shapes the spread of PT and SVA in the sample, which can change correlation sizes. And 38 percent entered for coronal deformity only, so many patients had little sagittal deformity at all.

Treatment was the surgeon's decision, made on his own clinical and radiographic criteria, without knowledge of study results. So operative versus nonoperative is a marker of severity and referral, not a randomized contrast.

The cohort is 86 percent female by our arithmetic (422 of 492) and relatively young, mean 51.9. Operative patients were older, more disabled (ODI 41.4 versus 23.9) and more malaligned. By the subgroup counts, 102 of 178 operative patients (57 percent, our arithmetic) had ODI of 40 or more, against 60 of 314 nonoperative patients (19 percent, ours). Small definitional slips: these counts use ODI 40 or more, while severe disability is defined as ODI over 40, and inclusion is age more than 18 years, yet the age range starts at 18.

Recompute the baseline P values. Age, 55.0 plus or minus 16.1 versus 50.1 plus or minus 16.9, gives P about 0.002 by our t test (0.0016 to 0.0018). That fits Table 2's 0.002, not the 0.02 printed in Results. PT is the problem row. Results give 22 plus or minus 12 versus 19 plus or minus 11, which by our t test gives P about 0.006, not the P under 0.001 printed. The abstract gives 22 versus 11. The overall mean PT implied by the paper's own regression line, about 20 degrees, fits 19, so 11 in the abstract looks like an error, possibly the SD. Treat the reported PT difference as real but smaller than the abstract implies.

Measurement: films were analyzed with validated software. The paper does not say who measured, whether measurers knew the HRQOL scores, or whether reliability was checked in this cohort. It also does not report how many patients had missing films or questionnaires. Table 8 suggests some did (slide 6).

Instruments: the abstract names SRS-22r and SF-12, and the tables report SF-12. Methods says SRS-22 and SF-36.

slides.title: Results: what correlated with disability
slides.lead: Sagittal parameters beat coronal ones. Correlations were moderate at best, and stronger in the operative group.
points: Coronal Cobb angles correlated weakly or not at all with ODI (maximal Cobb r -0.201)
ODI in the whole cohort by size of r: SVA 0.469, PI-LL 0.45, LL L1-S1 0.410, PT 0.381, T1 spinopelvic inclination 0.375 (all P < 0.001)
The authors chose PT, SVA and PI-LL as the most clinically relevant. By size alone, LL L1-S1 beats PT for ODI and PCS
PI-LL correlated with PT (r 0.844) and SVA (r 0.685)
Combined stepwise model kept SVA and PI-LL and dropped PT: r squared 0.24
Operative patients had worse scores in every ODI and SRS domain (Tables 3 and 4)
slides.see: Table 5 lists every coronal and sagittal parameter against ODI, SRS, PCS and MCS. *The sign for PI-LL flips between rows and tables. See notes.
slides.notes:
The clean message holds: in this cohort the sagittal parameters, not the coronal Cobb angles, carried the association with disability. Cobb angles barely registered.

Now size it. An r of 0.47 means about 22 percent of ODI variance explained. Even the combined model of SVA plus PI-LL reaches only 24 percent. Our arithmetic: with an ODI SD of 20.1, the scatter left around a single-parameter line is still about 18 to 19 ODI points. Two patients with the same PT can sit 30 or more ODI points apart. These numbers describe groups, not individuals.

Stronger in the operative group, weaker in the nonoperative group. The authors attribute this to wider ranges of deformity and disability among surgical patients, and they read the weak nonoperative correlations as showing that radiographs matter less when disability is low or moderate.

Which parameter is strongest? The Discussion says PI-LL had the strongest correlation with disability in both groups. For ODI, Table 6 does not support that: SVA is higher in the whole cohort (0.469 versus 0.45) and in the operative group (0.458 versus 0.425). PI-LL does lead for ODI in the nonoperative group, and for SRS and PCS in every row of Table 6. So the claim holds for SRS and PCS and fails only for ODI in the whole cohort and the operative group.

The PI-LL sign is a source problem. Table 5 and the whole-cohort row of Table 6 give PI-LL a negative correlation with ODI (minus 0.45), while the group rows give positive values. The regression slope is positive, and greater mismatch means more disability. So the negative signs are most likely a sign convention or printing error. Read the magnitude, not the sign. Table 5 and Table 6 also disagree on whole-cohort PCS values, for example SVA minus 0.426 versus minus 0.404.

The combined model's standardized coefficients were 0.298 for SVA and 0.246 for PI-LL, which the authors call equal importance. PT dropped out, which is unsurprising with r 0.844 between PT and PI-LL.

One odd HRQOL row: SF-12 MCS was 26.3 nonoperative and 34.3 operative. That would make operative patients mentally better off, which contradicts the statement that they were worse on all HRQOL measures. The levels look off too, our reading: PCS 50.1 is about a population-level score with mean ODI 30, and MCS 29.1 is very low, so the rows may be mislabeled or miscomputed. The MCS difference prints as minus 8.1; 26.3 minus 34.3 is minus 8.0. Treat the SF-12 values with caution.

slides.title: How the thresholds were made
slides.lead: Each parameter was fitted as a straight line against ODI, and the value at ODI 40 became the threshold. The direction of that fit moves the answer a lot.
points: Printed: ODI = 0.2106 x PT + 13.719 (r squared 0.1415), and similar for SVA and PI-LL
Table 7 and the thresholds only work if the equations are read the other way: PT = 0.2106 x ODI + 13.719
At ODI 40 that gives PT 22.1, SVA 45.9 mm, PI-LL 11.4. The text and abstract say SVA 47 mm
Ours: regressing ODI on each parameter instead puts ODI 40 at about PT 35, SVA 101 mm, PI-LL 28
No cut point was tested for sensitivity, specificity or later outcome
slides.see: Table 7 lists the parameter value the paper's lines give for each ODI from 0 to 100.
slides.notes:
This is the slide to slow down on.

The Results say the models were built to predict ODI, and print equations of the form ODI = slope x parameter + constant. Plug PT 22 into the printed PT equation and you get an ODI of about 18, not 40. Now read the same numbers as PT = 0.2106 x ODI + 13.719. At ODI 40 that gives PT 22.1, exactly Table 7. The same holds for SVA (45.9) and PI-LL (11.4). So, by our recomputation, the fits regressed each parameter on ODI, and the equations are mislabeled. Also note that the text and abstract round the SVA threshold to 47 mm, while the paper's own equation and Table 7 give 45.9.
