Why direction matters. With a weak correlation, the line of parameter on ODI and the line of ODI on parameter are very different lines. The paper's version answers: among patients with ODI 40, what is the average PT? The question a surgeon asks is the reverse: at what PT does the expected ODI reach 40? Our recomputation uses only the paper's numbers. The two slopes multiply to r squared, and both lines pass through the cohort means (mean ODI 30.2 from Table 2). That puts expected ODI 40 at about PT 35 degrees, SVA 101 mm and PI-LL 28 degrees. These are rough because they assume the same patients in every fit, but the direction is not in doubt. The published thresholds sit only slightly above the cohort averages, about 20 degrees, 31 mm and 7 degrees.

Neither version is a validated cut point. The paper reports no ROC analysis, no sensitivity or specificity for classifying ODI over 40, and no test in a separate cohort. The r values beside the thresholds in the abstract are just the correlations, not measures of threshold accuracy.

How to read it fairly: 22, 47 and 11 are the fitted average values for patients at exactly ODI 40, the boundary of severe disability. Patients above ODI 40 average higher: by the paper's own lines, a mean ODI of about 55 would give PT about 25, SVA about 70 mm and PI-LL about 18 (our arithmetic). They are reasonable flags that alignment may be contributing. They are not a level at which disability begins, and they are not proven targets for correction. Later library work moved away from single fixed numbers. Lafage 2016 (D04, from its library record) made the targets age-dependent, with PT from about 11 degrees under 35 to 29 degrees over 74.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: A large consecutive cohort with a clear sagittal signal, weakened by cross-sectional design, untested cut points and several numbers that do not reconcile.
points: Holds up: prospective, consecutive, 11 sites, nearly 500 patients, standardized software
Holds up: sagittal over coronal is consistent across ODI, SRS and PCS
Weak: baseline only. Association, not effect of correction
Weak: thresholds come from a reversed regression, with no accuracy testing and no validation
Weak: no age term in the models, for patients aged 18 to 85
Weak: missing data, measurer blinding and reliability are not reported
Numbers: abstract PT 11 vs Results 19; age P 0.02 vs 0.002; SVA 47 vs 45.9; PI-LL signs; Table 8 denominators
slides.notes:
Be fair first. This is a prospective, consecutive, multicenter look at radiographs against HRQOL in adult deformity, which the authors say had not been done before for these parameters. The main qualitative finding, that the sagittal plane matters more than the Cobb angle, holds for ODI, SRS and PCS in Table 5, but not MCS, where thoracolumbar Cobb has the largest r (0.239).

The design limits are the authors' own to some extent. They say treatment decisions depend on much more than radiographs, and they call for long-term follow-up to refine optimal treatment thresholds. Our reading goes further. Baseline correlations cannot show that correcting PI-LL lowers ODI. The Discussion's claim that restoring PI-LL should lead to concurrent correction of PT and SVA is reasoning from a cross-sectional correlation, not something this study measured.

Treatment distribution. The authors report lower surgical rates below each threshold, for example 29 versus 71 percent for SVA under 47 mm. Each pair sums to 100, so it reads as the operative versus nonoperative split below threshold, not a cross-threshold comparison. Denominators are not given. Table 8 counts parameters above threshold: none in 52.7 percent of nonoperative and 38.3 percent of operative patients, all three in 15.2 versus 31.1 percent. Our check: these percentages cannot come from 314 and 178 patients. They fit exactly with 296 and 167, a total of 463, which also reproduces the Total column. So about 29 patients appear to be missing from Table 8 without explanation.

The clinical relevance section reports that with PI-LL over 11 degrees, 80.6 percent had PT over 22 degrees and 64.4 percent had SVA over 47 mm. Relative risks were 4.2 for retroversion, 10.9 for SVA and 3.9 for severe disability. No counts or confidence intervals are given, so these cannot be checked.

Other items for the source-problem list. Age P is 0.02 in Results and 0.002 in Table 2; ours is about 0.002. The ODI over 40 definition cites Fairbank (references 15 and 16) in Results but references 5 and 7 in the Discussion, and those two are not ODI papers. The SF-12 MCS values run in the wrong direction. Tables 2 to 4 have last-digit slips, such as SRS 0.7 for 3.5 minus 2.9.

External validity, our inference: the cohort is mostly women, mean age 52, with many coronal-only curves, recruited at specialist deformity centers. Applying one set of numbers across ages 18 to 85 is the gap later age-adjusted work targeted.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "In 492 adults with deformity, the three parameters the authors chose, PT, SVA and PI-LL, tracked disability, but each explained about a fifth of ODI at most. The 22 degree, 47 mm and 11 degree numbers are fitted values at the ODI 40 boundary, not tested surgical targets."
points: Use them to flag a sagittal problem, not as a correction prescription
Do not apply one number to every age
Expect: are these postoperative targets? Not in this paper. It has no postoperative data
Expect: why is PI-LL emphasized? It is the parameter surgery corrects directly, in the authors' words, and it correlated with PT and SVA
Expect: is SVA 47 mm a cutoff? It is a point on a weak line (r squared 0.22). By our recomputation the expected ODI reaches 40 nearer 100 mm

rows: Fixed PT, SVA, PI-LL thresholds for ODI over 40
Untested cut points, no age term
Age-specific targets, PT about 11 to 29 degrees

slides.see: D04 and D05 entries come from their library records in the master file, not from this paper.
slides.notes:
Spoken summary, about 30 seconds. Schwab and the ISSG looked at baseline radiographs and questionnaires in 492 consecutive adults with spinal deformity at 11 US centers. Sagittal parameters, not coronal Cobb angles, tracked disability. The authors singled out SVA, PI-LL and PT, with correlations of about 0.38 to 0.47. Linear fits put severe disability, ODI over 40, at PT 22, SVA 47 mm and PI-LL 11, and operative patients were more often above those lines. It is cross-sectional, the fits are weak, and the thresholds were never tested as cut points or as surgical targets.

Likely follow-up questions.

Should I plan correction to PT under 22 and PI-LL under 11? This paper cannot tell you. It contains no surgery outcomes. The authors call the numbers radiographic objectives for surgical planning, but that is a claim beyond baseline data. Lafage 2016 (D04, library record) argues that targets should loosen with age, from PT about 11 degrees under 35 to 29 degrees over 74 and PI-LL from minus 11 to plus 14. AO Spine 2026 (D13, library record) makes a conditional recommendation, on low-quality evidence, to use SRS-Schwab to describe deformity, not to plan alignment. That record does not mention these thresholds; reading it as advice against planning to them is our inference.

Why do the numbers look so tidy? They are values read off a fitted line at ODI 40, not where outcomes change. The line runs from disability to parameter. Run it the other way and the values climb sharply, our recomputation. Either way the scatter is wide.

Which parameter matters most? The authors favor PI-LL because surgery can change it directly, and it correlated with PT (0.844) and SVA (0.685). For ODI, SVA had the slightly higher correlation in the whole cohort and in the operative group, and LL L1-S1 alone (0.410) beat PT.

Is the abstract trustworthy? Mostly, but its nonoperative PT of 11 degrees conflicts with 19 degrees in Results. Teach from Results.

decks.not_reviewed: Appendix 1 (supplemental digital content with the simplified clinical formulas, http://links.lww.com/BRS/B31) was not available and was not read. The published comment on this paper (PMID 27353551) was not reviewed. Figures 1 and 2 were read from the page images.

slides.title: Lafage 2016: should alignment targets account for age?
slides.lead: Modeled alignment targets for adult spinal deformity loosened steadily with age, so the authors argue younger patients need stricter correction goals.
points: Lafage R, Schwab F, Challier V, et al., International Spine Study Group. Spine 2016;41:62-68
Retrospective analysis of a prospective, multicenter ISSG database: 773 adult deformity patients at baseline
Method: regress alignment on age and disability, then plug in US population-norm SF-36 PCS (and an ODI converted from it) for each age band
Result: for norm-level disability, PT went from about 11 degrees under 35 to about 29 degrees over 74, PI-LL from -11 to +14 degrees, SVA from -29 to +80 mm (Table 3)
Level of evidence 3. DePuy Spine funds supported the work
Deck built from the full text. Appendix 1 with the simplified formulas was not read
slides.notes:
Read this paper as a modeling paper, not an outcomes paper. Nobody was randomized, nobody was followed to see whether hitting these numbers helped, and the analysis uses baseline data only. What it offers is a set of age-specific alignment numbers proposed as realignment targets. Knowing how those numbers were made shows you how far to trust them.

The logic runs in three steps. First, in 773 deformity patients, ODI and SF-36 PCS track each other closely, so the authors convert published US population PCS norms for each age band into an equivalent ODI. Second, they fit linear regressions with each radiographic parameter as the outcome and age plus HRQOL as predictors. Third, they enter each age band's norm HRQOL into those regressions and read off the alignment. That output is what the paper calls ideal or age-specific alignment.

The headline finding is not subtle. Under these models, the alignment that goes with population-average function in a 79-year-old is much worse than in a 26-year-old: about 18 degrees more PT, 25 degrees more PI-LL and 109 mm more SVA (Table 3, ODI-anchored). The authors conclude that younger patients need more rigorous realignment and that fixed SRS-Schwab modifiers are too strict for the elderly.

Two housekeeping points. The abstract quotes slightly different numbers from the tables, and one of them (SVA 4.1 mm under 35) appears in no table. Teach from the tables. Appendix 1, with the simplified bedside formulas, sits in online supplementary content that was not available here.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: Fixed SRS-Schwab sagittal modifiers apply the same cutoffs at 30 and at 80. Should they?
points: SRS-Schwab classification grades PI-LL, PT and SVA against single cutoffs at every age
Alignment and HRQOL both worsen with age in healthy people, so the authors ask whether ASD realignment goals should too
ODI has no published US age norms; SF-36 PCS does. The authors bridge the two with a regression
Aims: age-specific spino-pelvic values, age-specific ODI norms extrapolated from PCS, and age-specific realignment thresholds
slides.notes:
Set up the problem the way the authors do. The SRS-Schwab sagittal modifiers are fixed values. The authors grant that these work well in the bulk of ASD patients, those around 50 to 60 years old, but say they seem limited in the young and the elderly. Their background argument is that aging changes the whole system: loss of lordosis moves the spine forward, the pelvis retroverts and the knees flex to compensate, muscle atrophies, and visual, vestibular and somatosensory control decline. Population HRQOL also declines with age through comorbidity.

The practical obstacle is the outcome measure. Surgeons use ODI, but ODI has no US age-specific norms. SF-36 PCS has them. The authors cite one prior attempt at age-specific ODI norms, Tonosu, from a Japanese internet survey. So step one of this paper is to manufacture US ODI norms by age from PCS norms.

Keep the exact claim in mind. The aim is to describe the alignment that goes with population-average function at each age, and to propose that as a surgical target. It is not to test whether operating to that target gives better results than operating to a fixed target. Everything later in the deck hangs on that difference.

The fixed modifiers the authors argue against are those of the SRS-Schwab classification (their reference 5, Schwab 2012). The paper does not quote their cutoff values and does not cite the separate Schwab disability-threshold paper in our library (D03).

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: One baseline cross-section, mixed operative and nonoperative, modeled with linear regression.
points: ISSG database, 11 US sites, consecutive enrollment into operative or nonoperative arms by patient and surgeon choice
Inclusion: age over 18 and at least one of coronal Cobb 20 degrees or more, SVA 5 cm or more, PT 25 degrees or more, or TK 60 degrees or more
Excluded: neuromuscular, syndromic, autoimmune, infectious, tumor or post-traumatic deformity
Standing 36-inch films without walkers or bars, measured centrally with validated software
Models: each of PT, PI-LL, LL-TK, SVA and TPA regressed on age plus ODI (or PCS); all reported correlation coefficients above 0.5, P < 0.001
Age bands follow the SF-36 norm tables: under 35, 35-44, 45-54, 55-64, 65-74, over 74
slides.notes:
Cohort: 773 patients, mean age 53.7 (SD 16.4), 83% female, 54% in the operative arm. Baseline means: PI-LL 10.1 degrees, PT 21.5 degrees, SVA 41.1 mm, TPA 18.8 degrees, ODI 34.1, PCS 36.9 (Table 1). Our check: weighting the band mean ages by the band percentages gives 53.8 (dividing by the actual percentage total of 100.1), consistent with 53.7.

The paper does not give enrollment dates, the split by diagnosis, how many eligible patients were missing films or questionnaires, or the regression coefficients, standard errors or residual spread. Appendix 1 may hold the simplified formulas, but the main text gives only the outputs.

Notice the direction of the regression. Alignment is the outcome; age and HRQOL are the predictors. Entering a norm HRQOL gives the average alignment of ASD patients in this cohort who had that age and that level of function. It does not give the alignment that would produce that function after surgery. That is our framing, but it follows directly from the stated model.

Notice the entry criteria too (our point). A patient gets in by having abnormal sagittal alignment or a 20-degree coronal curve. Younger patients with good function and normal sagittal parameters can enter only through the coronal criterion, while older patients more often enter through sagittal ones. Who meets the criteria at each age is part of what the regression learns.

The authors name one limitation here: operative and nonoperative patients with any type of ASD were pooled, which they call selection bias. The over-74 band holds 6.2%, about 48 patients by our arithmetic. Treat the oldest row as the least stable.

slides.title: Results: age-specific ODI and alignment targets
slides.lead: ODI = 87.705 - 1.456 x PCS turned US PCS norms into ODI norms of 9.5 under 35 rising to 32.5 over 74. The resulting targets loosened with every decade.
points: ODI-PCS correlation r = 0.814 (printed without a sign; the slope is negative), r squared = 0.663
Alignment for norm ODI rose with age for every parameter; LL-TK fell from 29.2 to 0.2 degrees
TPA target: 4.4 degrees under 35 to 27.8 degrees over 74 (Table 3)
PCS-anchored targets (Table 4) are close under 35 but diverge in the oldest band: PI-LL 20.2 vs 13.7 degrees
slides.notes:
Table 3, the ODI-anchored targets. Angles are in degrees.

Start by checking the bridge. Our recomputation: 87.705 - 1.456 x PCS reproduces all six ODI norms in Table 2 exactly. From Table 1, a least-squares slope of r x SD(ODI)/SD(PCS) = 0.814 x 20/11 = 1.48, and an intercept of 34.07 + 1.456 x 36.9 = 87.8. Both agree with the printed equation, so the conversion is internally consistent. The r is printed as positive, but ODI and PCS run in opposite directions and the slope is negative, so it should read -0.814.

Our back-calculation: the six rows of Table 3 fit a straight line in age and ODI almost perfectly, so we can recover the implied model. At a fixed ODI, each extra decade of age adds about 2.9 degrees of PT, 2.8 degrees of PI-LL, 15.6 mm of SVA and 3.6 degrees of TPA. These slopes are ours; the paper does not print them.

Two reading points. First, the young targets are aggressive: an SVA of -29 mm and a PI-LL of -11 degrees, meaning lordosis exceeding PI, in patients under 35. Second, the anchor matters in the elderly. Anchored on PCS instead of ODI (Table 4), the over-74 PI-LL target is 20.2 degrees rather than 13.7. That 6.5-degree gap is model choice, not biology. The Figure 2 ideals for a 65-66-year-old (PI-LL 10.5, PT 25.0, SVA 54.5) equal the average of the Table 3 and Table 4 rows for 65-74, which suggests the clinical numbers average the two models. That inference is ours; the paper does not say so.

The Results text says PT ranged from 11 degrees to 39 degrees. Both tables top out near 29 degrees, so 39 is an error in the text.

slides.title: Disability-anchored thresholds: what moves the target
slides.lead: Using the same formulas at ODI 20 (moderate) and ODI 40 (severe), older patients reached a given disability level with more deformity (Table 5).
points: At fixed ODI, PT barely moves with disability: about 2 degrees from ODI 20 to 40 at every age
PI-LL rises 8.6 degrees and SVA about 22 mm from ODI 20 to 40, at every age
At 75 and over, PI-LL 8.3 and SVA 65.8 mm correspond only to moderate disability
Figure 2 shows two 65-66-year-olds 1 year after similar fusions, one corrected to the age-adjusted ideals and one overcorrected past them
slides.see: Figure 2: the overcorrected patient ends at PI-LL -3.9, PT 19.1 and SVA 9.1 mm against age-adjusted ideals of 10.5, 25.0 and 54.5. No outcome scores are shown for either patient.
slides.notes:
This table shows how the model divides the work between age and disability. Read across a row for disability and down a column for age.

PT: doubling ODI from 20 to 40 adds only about 2 degrees, while one decade of age adds roughly 2.6 degrees. In this model the PT target mostly tracks age, not function. PI-LL and SVA respond more to disability: 8.6 degrees and about 22 mm between ODI 20 and 40. These differences are our arithmetic from Table 5.

Our check found one problem. Table 5 says it uses the same formulas as Table 3. For PI-LL, LL-TK and TPA, Table 5 matches the Table 3 model within 0.1, and for SVA within about 0.2 mm. For PT it does not. Table 3 implies PT rises 0.29 degrees per year of age, while Table 5 implies 0.26. Table 5 PT values run 0.8 to 2.4 degrees below what the Table 3 model gives at ODI 20; for 75 and over, the Table 3 model gives about 27.6 degrees against 25.2 printed. So the PT column in Table 5 does not come from the Table 3 PT formula, and the paper does not explain the difference.

A cross-check against another library paper (ours, not the authors'): the D03 record (Schwab disability thresholds, a different Schwab paper that this one does not cite) lists PT 22, PI-LL 11 and SVA 47 mm. The 55-64 row at ODI 40 is close for PT (22.2) and PI-LL (11.5), but its SVA of 58.5 mm is about 12 mm higher. So for PT and PI-LL, those fixed cutoffs roughly match severe disability in a typical 60-year-old in this model; for SVA they sit lower.

Figure 2 is a picture, not data. It shows that a 65-year-old can be overcorrected relative to the age-adjusted targets. It does not report pain, ODI or mechanical complications for either patient, so it cannot show that the overcorrection caused harm. Note also the age-band labels: Tables 2 to 4 list 65-74 and 74 and over, so 74-year-olds fall in two bands. Table 5 uses 75 and over, and the abstract says over 75, which leaves 75-year-olds out of the top band only in the abstract.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: Internally consistent arithmetic, but the targets describe typical ASD patients with norm function. Nobody tested them as goals of surgery.
points: Strength: large multicenter cohort, central validated measurement, transparent age bands tied to published norms
Strength: the ODI conversion and Tables 3, 4 and most of 5 reproduce from a simple linear model
Weakness: cross-sectional baseline data only; targets never tested against postoperative outcomes, yet the Discussion says they correlated with satisfactory patient-reported outcomes
Weakness: regression direction gives the alignment typical of a given function, not the alignment that causes it
Weakness: ODI norms are extrapolated from an ASD-derived regression, not measured in healthy US adults
Errors: abstract values do not match the tables; PT 39 degrees in the text; Table 5 PT inconsistent; r sign missing
slides.notes:
What the authors themselves concede: the cohort pooled operative and nonoperative patients with any ASD type, which they call selection bias. Their extrapolated ODI norms differ from the published Japanese norms, which they attribute to method (regression versus direct survey) and cross-cultural differences. They do not know whether to target the patient's current age or an older one, and suggest age plus 5 years as an option. They say plainly that the study does not advocate operating to strict age thresholds for every patient, and that some patients with stenosis and radiculopathy may do better with decompression and stabilization than with long fusions and osteotomies.

What we add (ours):
1. Validity of the target. A regression of alignment on function, fitted in a cross-section of patients with deformity, cannot show that moving a patient to that alignment restores that function. No postoperative data enter the analysis. The authors overclaim here: the Discussion says the study provided age-adjusted, realistically achievable alignment objectives that correlated with satisfactory patient-reported outcomes. No postoperative outcomes were analyzed, so the only correlation shown is between baseline alignment and baseline function.
2. The anchor. US PCS norms fall with age partly through heart, lung and joint disease. Some of the loosening of targets with age may reflect nonspinal disability built into the norms rather than spinal tolerance.
3. Extrapolation. The cohort's mean ODI was 34, and the youngest band's norm ODI of 9.5 sits more than one SD (20) below it.
4. Precision. No confidence or prediction intervals are given, so each target is a point estimate with unknown spread. Table 1 shows wide variation (SVA SD 70 mm).
5. Model dependence. ODI and PCS anchors disagree by 6.5 degrees of PI-LL in the oldest band.

Source problems found on recomputation: the abstract gives PT 10.9, PI-LL -10.5 and SVA 4.1 mm under 35, and PT 28.5, PI-LL 16.7 and SVA 78.1 mm over 75. None of these match Table 3 or 4. PT and PI-LL are near the average of the two tables. An SVA of +4.1 mm under 35 matches neither table (-29.1 and -31.9) and may be an error, or may come from the simplified formulas we could not read. The Results text gives a PT range of 11 to 39 degrees, but the tables top out at 28.8. The Table 5 PT column is inconsistent with Table 3, as shown on the previous slide.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: Lafage 2016 modeled the alignment that goes with normal function at each age and found it loosens with age. It is a reasonable starting target, not a proven one.
points: Spoken summary: In 773 ISSG deformity patients, the authors regressed baseline alignment on age and disability, then entered US population-norm function for each age band. The alignment that matched norm function loosened with age: PT about 11 to 29 degrees, PI-LL -11 to +14 degrees, SVA -29 to +80 mm from under 35 to over 74. They conclude young patients need stricter correction and the elderly can accept more. The targets come from one cross-section and were never tested as surgical goals, and the abstract numbers do not match the tables.
Q: Does hitting the age-adjusted target improve outcomes? Not shown here. No postoperative analysis; Figure 2 is two illustrative cases with no outcome scores
Q: Why are the young targets so strict? The norm ODI under 35 is 9.5, and the model gives PI-LL -11 and SVA -29 mm for it
Q: Which table do I use? Table 3 (ODI-anchored) and Table 4 (PCS-anchored) differ most in the elderly; Figure 2 ideals look like their average (our inference)
Q: Should I operate an 80-year-old to these numbers? The authors say no single threshold should dictate surgery; decompression and stabilization may serve some patients better
slides.notes:
Keep the spoken version to the summary on the slide. Then be ready for these follow-ups.

What does a 10-year age difference buy? Our back-calculation from Table 3: at the same ODI, about 3 degrees of PT, about 3 degrees of PI-LL and about 16 mm of SVA.

Is PT a disability target? Barely, in this model. Going from ODI 20 to ODI 40 moves PT about 2 degrees at any age (Table 5).

Why might the elderly targets be too permissive? Our point: population PCS falls with age partly for nonspinal reasons, and the ASD-to-population ODI conversion is an extrapolation. A target built on those norms carries that bias.

How does this relate to other library papers? Our comparison, not the authors': the D03 record (a separate Schwab disability-threshold paper, abstract-level, not cited here) gives fixed thresholds of PI-LL 11 degrees, PT 22 degrees and SVA 47 mm. Here, the ODI 40 row for 55-64 is close for PT (22.2) and PI-LL (11.5), but SVA is about 12 mm higher (58.5 mm). Other approaches in the library, such as the PI-based GAP score (D05) and the T4-L1-hip axis (D14), scale targets to pelvic incidence and were assessed against complications or mechanical failure (per their abstract-level records). This paper scales only by age.

What would make it stronger? A prospective test: patients corrected to age-adjusted targets versus fixed or PI-based targets, with ODI, mechanical failure and revision as outcomes. That is our suggestion, not the authors'.

One line to end on: age-adjusted targets are a model of what normal function looks like in an aging deformity patient, built from a single baseline snapshot. Use them as a guide, check the tables rather than the abstract, and do not treat them as proven goals of surgery.

decks.not_reviewed: The full 12-page article was read, including Tables I-V and Figures 5, 6, 7 and 8. No supplement is cited. Not reviewed: the commentary by David W. Polly Jr. linked online; the online conflict-of-interest forms; the asymptomatic-volunteer papers that supplied the ideal-value formulas (references 16 and 17); the Excel calculator the authors mention; and later external validation studies, except the D06 master record, which is abstract level.

slides.title: Yilgor 2017: the GAP score
slides.lead: Bottom line: a 0-13 point score of postoperative sagittal alignment, scaled to pelvic incidence, separated patients who later had mechanical complications from those who did not. AUC was 0.92 in a 74-patient validation group split from the same database.
points: Journal club · Adult spinal deformity · Prediction score
Yilgor C, Sogunmez N, Boissiere L, et al, for the European Spine Study Group (ESSG). J Bone Joint Surg Am 2017;99:1661-72
Design: retrospective analysis of a prospective multicenter database at 6 European sites. 222 patients split at random 2 to 1 into derivation (148) and validation (74).
Validation group: mechanical complications in 6% (proportioned), 47% (moderately disproportioned) and 95% (severely disproportioned)
Prepared from the full text. External validity was not tested, as the authors say.
slides.notes: What this paper is: a prediction score built and tested inside one database. It is not a trial, and it does not show that aiming for a low GAP score prevents anything. Keep that line in mind for every slide. The authors' starting point is that Schwab targets are fixed numbers (PI-LL within 10 degrees, PT under 20, SVA under 4 cm), while normal pelvic tilt, sacral slope and lordosis all rise with pelvic incidence. A fixed target can therefore over- or under-correct at the ends of the PI range. GAP replaces fixed targets with ideal values calculated from each patient's PI and scores how far the patient sits from them. Two things to carry: AUC 0.92 in the validation group, and complication rates of 6%, 47% and 95% across the three GAP categories. The score was measured on 6-week postoperative radiographs, so it predicts the outcome of an alignment already achieved. Funding: the ESSG is funded by DePuy Synthes, which the authors say had no role and no approval rights. One or more authors declared a patent or copyright broadly relevant to this work. The deck was prepared from the full text. Our recomputation found that several cutoff statistics printed in the derivation section cannot come from the derivation cohort and largely match the validation cohort (slide 4). The master record says internal split-sample validation, which is correct. External performance is the subject of D06.

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: Consecutive operated deformity patients from the ESSG database, with 2-year follow-up and long posterior fusions.

rows: Age 18 or more plus one of: Cobb 20° or more, SVA 5 cm or more, PT 25° or more, thoracic kyphosis 60° or more
Posterior instrumented fusion of 4 or more levels and 2 or more years of follow-up
631 operated, 548 with 4+ levels, 251 eligible at 2 years, 29 lost (11.6%), 222 included
168 women, 54 men; mean age 52.2 (18-84); follow-up mean 28.8 months (24-62)
Degenerative 41%, idiopathic 40%, other 19% (our pooling of Table II)
Random 2:1, derivation 148 and validation 74; Table II shows no significant differences
Mechanical complications: PJK or PJF, DJK or DJF, rod breakage, other implant failure. Also mechanical revision

slides.notes: Read this as a selection funnel. 548 patients had long fusions, but only 251 were eligible at 2 years, and the paper does not say why the other 297 were not, our reading being that most had simply not reached 2 years yet. The text says 251 'had been followed for 2 years or more' and then that 29 were lost to follow-up, which reads as a contradiction. The likely meaning is 251 eligible for 2-year follow-up. The authors report no significant differences between included and excluded patients in demographics or levels fused. The population is broad. Mean age 52 with a range of 18 to 84, and 88 of 222 had idiopathic scoliosis (our sum of Table II). That case mix matters when you compare GAP with D06, which tested it in complex deformity patients, 76% with a three-column osteotomy. Definitions (Table I): PJK is a postoperative increase of 10 degrees or more in kyphosis between the UIV and two levels above. PJF is fracture of the UIV or UIV+1, pullout at the UIV, or sagittal subluxation. All types were pooled into one outcome, which the authors justify by overlapping biomechanics and list as a limitation. Blinding: in the validation group the examiner scoring the radiographs was blinded to outcome. The paper does not say who judged complications or whether that was blinded, and it says nothing about blinding in the derivation group. Statistics: chi-square tests across subgroups, univariate logistic regression for weights, ROC analysis, Cochran-Armitage trend tests, and one-way ANOVA for quality-of-life scores. Our checks of Table II: the sex, prior-surgery, prior-decompression and prior-fusion chi-squares and the age and follow-up t tests reproduce from the printed figures. The diagnosis chi-square gives 1.25 by our Pearson calculation against 1.366 printed. The printed P of 0.950 matches neither (our P: 0.928 for 1.366, 0.940 for 1.25), but the conclusion of no difference stands. Missing data: the t-test degrees of freedom show preoperative COMI for only 134 patients and ODI for 205.

slides.title: How the score is built
slides.lead: Each parameter is the measured value minus an ideal value set by pelvic incidence. Points add to 0-13.

rows: 0-2 proportioned; 3-6 moderately; 7 or more severely disproportioned

slides.see: Figure 6 is the score card with every cutoff and weight on one page; Figure 9 shows why the aligned band is off-center: retroversion, hypolordosis and positive malalignment are tolerated more than their opposites.
slides.notes: Where the ideals come from: simple linear regressions of SS, LL and global tilt on PI in a database of asymptomatic adult volunteers (references 16 and 17, not reviewed here). R-squared values were 0.65 for SS, 0.39 for LL and 0.41 for GT, so PI explains well under half of normal lordosis and global tilt. The ideal is a population average, not an individual's true ideal. Thoracic kyphosis was left out because it did not correlate with PI in the volunteers (R-squared 0.0078) and did not significantly affect complications (P = 0.667), which is not the same as showing no effect. How to read the signs: negative RPV means less sacral slope than ideal, which is retroversion. Negative RLL means hypolordosis. Positive RSA means more global tilt than ideal, which is forward malalignment. Note the asymmetry in points. Hyperlordosis scores 3, as much as severe hypolordosis, and hyperlordotic maldistribution (LDI over 80%) scores 3. Those are the overcorrection penalties. Our reading: the paper names the measured lordosis only as 'measured lumbar lordosis', but the inputs listed for the Excel tool are age, PI, SS, L1-S1 and L4-S1 lordosis and GT, so LL is L1-S1. A worked case from Figure 7, our arithmetic: PI 26, age 60, postoperative PT 17 and PI-LL 9, so SS 9 and LL 17. Ideal SS is 24.3, giving RPV −15.3, severe (3). Ideal LL is 45.1, giving RLL −28, severe (3). That matches the legend's 3 points each and a total of 13 with LDI, RSA and age. This patient was Schwab 0-0-0 after surgery and developed progressive PJK, which is the authors' point. Figure 8 does not reconcile as neatly. With PI 77 and postoperative PT 30, SS is 47 against an ideal of 54.4, giving RPV −7.4. By the printed cutoffs that is moderate retroversion, worth 2 points, yet the legend gives a total of 2 from RLL alone. It sits right on a boundary, so rounding may explain it; that interpretation is ours. Weights are rounded univariate logistic coefficients, shown on the next slide.

slides.title: Derivation: 148 patients, 68 complications
slides.lead: Every disproportioned subgroup had more complications than its aligned subgroup. The odds ratios are unadjusted.
slides.see: Figure 5 shows complication rates by single GAP score in the derivation group: 4.0% at 2 or less, 36-57% for scores 3 to 6, and 73-100% for 7 or more.
slides.notes: Derivation complication rate was 68 of 148, 46% (our sum of Table III; the text does not state it). Cutoffs were placed where the chi-square for complications was largest, in this same cohort. Weights were each subgroup's univariate logistic coefficient, rounded to an integer. We recomputed Table IV from the Table III counts: the coefficients and odds ratios reproduce, and the SEs and CIs reproduce to rounding, except the hyperlordotic LDI SE (0.651 by our calculation, 0.655 printed). That tells you each parameter was fitted alone, unadjusted for the others. Our concern, not the authors': RPV, RSA and RLL all depend on PI and on pelvic position, so adding unadjusted weights can count the same malalignment more than once. The paper reports no multivariable model and no check of correlation between parameters. Several subgroups are tiny: anteversion 8, hyperlordosis 6, negative malalignment 4, with wide intervals (hyperlordosis OR 15, 1.7 to 135.8). Those weights rest on 2 to 5 events each (3, 5 and 2). With 68 events and 13 subgroup terms, the data are thin for this many cutoffs and weights; that judgment is ours. Table III chi-squares reproduce for RLL (37.4), LDI (36.2), RSA (43.8) and age (9.6). RPV is printed as 39.1; we get 36.1 from its counts. Derivation AUC was 0.88 (SE 0.028, printed CI 0.83-0.94; our symmetric CI is 0.83-0.93, so the upper bound is slightly high). The 2-or-less cutoff was chosen at a printed maximal Youden index of 0.68, but that equals 0.938 + 0.738 - 1, so it comes from the same suspect figures below. Now the problem. The paper reports, in the derivation section, sensitivity 93.8%, specificity 73.8%, PPV 73.9%, NPV 93.9% and accuracy 82.4%. With 68 events, 93.8% sensitivity is impossible: 64 of 68 is 94.1% and 63 of 68 is 92.6%. These figures fit the validation cohort instead: 30 of 32 (93.8%), 31 of 42 (73.8%), 31 of 33 (93.9%) and 61 of 74 (82.4%). PPV there would be 30 of 41, 73.2%, not 73.9%. Figure 5's 4.0% in the derivation group's 2-or-less bar also cannot coexist with 73.8% specificity among 80 non-events. So quote the cutoff statistics as validation figures with a caveat, not as derivation figures. Irony worth one sentence: the authors cite Naggara (reference 21), titled 'categorizing or dichotomizing continuous variables is inadvisable', for how they chose their cutoffs.

slides.title: Validation: 74 patients, 32 complications
slides.lead: GAP category tracked both mechanical complications and mechanical revision in a stepwise way.
points: Trend test: complications chi-square 43.1, revisions 19.4, both P < 0.001
Complication types: rod breakage 14, PJF 11, PJK 8, other implant 6, DJK or DJF 3
Postoperative ODI 21.3, 35 and 36.3 across categories (P = 0.001); MCS not significant (P = 0.072)
slides.notes: The counts in brackets are ours, back-calculated from the printed percentages, and they add up: 2 + 9 + 21 = 32 complications and 1 + 4 + 12 = 17 revisions, matching the text. Our Cochran-Armitage calculation from those counts gives 43.1 and 19.4, as printed. How to read it: a proportioned patient had about a 1 in 17 chance of a mechanical complication over about 2 years; a severely disproportioned patient almost always had one, and more than half were revised. That is a striking gradient. Now the fragility. 74 patients and 32 events is a small test set, and the confidence interval for AUC runs from 0.85 to 0.98. Our arithmetic: 0.92 plus or minus 1.96 times 0.034 gives 0.85 to 0.99, so the printed upper bound is slightly low, a minor point. The validation AUC exceeded the derivation AUC (0.92 against 0.88). Usually a score loses performance when tested on new patients; a gain here most likely reflects chance in a small sample (our reading). The split was random within one database, so the validation patients came from the same centers, surgeons, era and measurement methods as the derivation patients. That tests overfitting to individual patients, not transportability. No calibration was reported. The complication types add to 42 among 32 patients, because some had more than one. Quality of life (Table V): the authors note that GAP was built on complications but quality-of-life scores also differed, and they say this is reasonable because complications affect quality of life. The moderate and severe groups are almost identical on ODI (35 and 36.3) and SRS-22 (3.2 and 3.3), so the step is between proportioned and the rest. The paper does not state the time point of these scores. The statistics column prints F(1,70) for a comparison of three groups; a one-way ANOVA of three groups has 2 numerator degrees of freedom. Our approximate F(2,71) from the summary data, assuming 33, 19 and 22 patients: ODI 6.8 (P = 0.002) and SRS-22 3.9 (P = 0.024) stay significant, but SF-36 PCS 2.9 (P = 0.064) does not, though the authors list it as significant (P = 0.020). MCS is 3.0 (P = 0.055). So the test reported is unclear and the PCS result is fragile.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: Holds up: multicenter prospective database, 6 sites; random split with balanced groups
Holds up: validation radiographs scored blind to outcome; dose-response gradient in complications and revisions
Holds up: Table IV coefficients and odds ratios reproduce from the Table III counts (our check)
Weakens it: cutoffs and weights chosen in the same data, from univariate fits, with small subgroups
Weakens it: internal split validation only, 32 events; no calibration; no external test (authors)
Weakens it: GAP measured after surgery, so it predicts; it does not show that planning to GAP prevents failure
Weakens it: no adjustment for bone quality, surgeon or technique (authors); reliability not studied (authors)
Source errors: derivation cutoff statistics match the validation cohort; RPV chi-square; Table V degrees of freedom
slides.notes: Credit where due. The authors' own limitations paragraph names: retrospective analysis of prospective data; external validity not yet evaluated; no comparison with other known causes of complications; osteoporosis, sarcopenia and neurodegeneration not considered directly; surgeon and technique not considered; standing radiographs only; complication types pooled; inter- and intraobserver reliability not studied, though they note the component measurements were shown to be reliable elsewhere. The rest is our reading. First, the leap from prediction to planning. The Abstract and Discussion say setting goals by GAP 'may decrease' complications. The study does not test that. It shows that patients left disproportioned at 6 weeks failed more often. Why they were left that way, whether because of stiffness, bone quality, surgical choice or the surgery's difficulty, is not analyzed, and any of those could cause failure on its own. Second, the score's circularity. Relative pelvic version and relative spinopelvic alignment both measure the same pelvic compensation, and global tilt includes pelvic position. Summing unadjusted weights may overcount. Third, optimism. Data-driven cutoffs plus rounded weights plus a small internal test set tend to overstate performance. The striking 95% rate in the severe group rests on 22 patients. Fourth, the population is mixed, with 40% idiopathic, which is not the typical older revision deformity patient. Fifth, reporting. The derivation cutoff statistics cannot come from the derivation cohort; the RPV chi-square in Table III does not reproduce (36.1 against 39.1 printed); and Table V reports F(1,70) for three groups. The flow sentence about 251 patients followed and 29 lost is contradictory as written. None of these overturns the gradient, but together they say the paper was not checked closely. Funding and interests: the ESSG is funded by DePuy Synthes; one or more authors declared a patent or copyright broadly relevant to the work. The paper does not say what it covers.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: “GAP scores sagittal alignment against ideals set by each patient's pelvic incidence. In the authors' internal validation it separated 6% from 95% mechanical-complication rates, but it did not hold up as well in an external complex cohort, and these papers do not show that planning to GAP prevents failure.”

rows: ESSG mixed ASD, mean age 52, 40% idiopathic

points: D06 comes from the library record, abstract level. Case mix differed.
Use GAP to describe and plan proportion, not as proof of risk reduction.
slides.notes: Spoken summary in 30 seconds: GAP replaces fixed Schwab targets with ideals scaled to pelvic incidence for sacral slope, lordosis and global tilt, adds lordosis distribution and age, and sums to 0 to 13. In a random two-thirds split of 222 ESSG patients, the validation third showed complication rates of 6, 47 and 95% and revision rates of 3, 21 and 55% across proportioned, moderate and severe categories, AUC 0.92. It is a score built and tested in one database, measured after surgery. Expect these questions. Does a low GAP target prevent PJK? Not shown. This paper is prognostic; nobody was randomized to a GAP-based plan here. Does it work in my older, osteotomy-heavy patients? D06, from the library record at abstract level, found AUC 0.60 for mechanical complications in Scoli-RISK-1, where 76% had a three-column osteotomy and only 159 of 272 trial patients could be analyzed. Case mix differed, but the record does not say why performance fell; case mix, the analyzable fraction and outcome definitions are all possible reasons (our reading). Is the 0.92 believable? It is honest internal validation but on 32 events, from the same centers, with cutoffs tuned on the same database, and several printed derivation statistics cannot come from the derivation cohort and largely match the validation figures. Treat 0.92 as a best case. Why penalize hyperlordosis and negative malalignment? The authors' point is that overcorrection is also a failure mode, which fixed Schwab targets ignore; in derivation, 5 of 6 hyperlordotic patients and 25 of 28 with LDI over 80% had complications. Small numbers, but the direction is consistent. Why is age in a radiographic score? Age 60 or older carried an unadjusted OR of 2.8, which the authors suggest may stand for osteoporosis, musculoskeletal and balance changes, or comorbidities. They did not measure those. Where does it sit in the AO Spine 2026 alignment reading list? D13 lists GAP alongside Roussouly, SRS-Schwab and the T4-L1-hip axis as complementary models, per the library record.

decks.not_reviewed: The PDF is a complete reformatted copy of the open-access PMC text of the primary paper (not a critique): abstract, full text, Tables 1-3 and references. Not reviewed: the images of Figure 1 (distribution across GAP categories) and Figure 2 (complication rates by GAP score), which the PDF omits; the article footnotes, which are empty in this copy, so table footnote letters (tests used, the Table 2 'd' footnote) and disclosures could not be read; the published comment on this paper (PMID 33332886); the full text of the original GAP paper by Yilgor et al and the Scoli-RISK-1 primary reports.

slides.title: GAP score: external validation
slides.lead: Does the Global Alignment and Proportion score predict mechanical failure outside the cohort it was built in?
points: Journal club: adult spinal deformity
Kwan KYH, Lenke LG, Shaffrey CI, et al, AO Spine Knowledge Forum Deformity. Clin Orthop Relat Res 2021;479(2):312-320

Bottom line: in 159 complex deformity patients from Scoli-RISK-1, GAP discriminated poorly. AUC was 0.60 for mechanical complications and 0.66 for mechanical revision. Rates still rose across categories: complications 13%, 24% and 31%.
slides.notes: Source check first. This deck was prepared from a complete reformatted copy of the open-access PMC text of the primary paper, not a critique. Text and Tables 1 to 3 were read in full. The images of Figures 1 and 2 are omitted from this copy, and the footnotes are empty, so the tests behind Table 2 and the disclosures could not be checked. The published comment on this paper was not reviewed. What it is: a retrospective secondary analysis of Scoli-RISK-1, a prospective multicenter international study of complex adult deformity surgery that the authors say was powered for neurologic complications. The authors took the GAP score, which Yilgor et al built to predict mechanical complications, and applied the original inclusion criteria and complication definitions to this independent cohort. The paper labels itself Level III, diagnostic study. Frame it for the room as a test of transportability: a score that looked excellent at home, tested in a harder population. Keep one distinction in mind throughout. The authors' headline is 'not associated'. The numbers show weak discrimination with a gradient in the expected direction. Those are not the same claim, and the deck returns to this on slides 4 and 6. Pairs with D05, the GAP derivation paper, whose numbers here come from its library record.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: GAP had a validation AUC of 0.92 at home. Does it hold in an independent cohort?
points: GAP sums 5 parts, 0 to 13 points: relative pelvic version, relative lumbar lordosis, lordosis distribution index, relative spinopelvic alignment, and an age factor.
Categories: 0-2 proportioned, 3-6 moderately disproportioned, 7 or more severely disproportioned.
Authors' gap: earlier external tests (Bari, 149 patients; Jacobs, 39) did not follow the original criteria or were small.
Questions: does a higher GAP score go with (1) mechanical complications, (2) revision for them, and (3) worse ODI, SRS-22 and SF-36?

rows: External, secondary analysis of prospective cohort
Posterior fusion of 4 or more levels

slides.notes: Why this matters. The authors say failure to restore sagittal alignment, over- or undercorrection, has been considered the main cause of mechanical complications and revision. They cite a series where patients fell within SRS-Schwab targets, yet 31.7% had implant-related complications and 52.6% of those were revised. The paper places that finding just before introducing GAP, which uses pelvic incidence-based proportional parameters. Our gloss, not the authors' wording: scaling to pelvic incidence means a patient's ideal lordosis and tilt depend on their own anatomy. GAP also includes age. The original validation group, as this paper reports it, had mechanical revision rates of 3%, 21% and 55% across the three categories, with a significant linear trend. Those are the numbers to beat. The D05 numbers in the table come from the library record, not this paper. Who is in Scoli-RISK-1: ages 18 to 80 having deformity surgery with any one of a major Cobb of 80 degrees or more, congenital or revision deformity needing osteotomy, preoperative myelopathy, OLF or OPLL with deformity, or a corrective or three-column osteotomy. In Limitations the authors acknowledge these patients had more complex deformities than the original GAP study and that correction was substantial. Our description: a more complex group than D05's population of posterior fusions of 4 or more levels. Their argument is that a score worth using should still predict in complex surgery. That is a fair argument, but our point is that it also means this is a test of transport to a different case mix, not a replication. Note that question 3 is worded two ways: the abstract asks whether a lower category goes with better scores, the Introduction whether a higher category goes with worse ones. Same question.

slides.title: Selection and measurement
slides.lead: 159 of 272 Scoli-RISK-1 patients met every criterion.

rows: Posterior fusion of 4 or more levels

points: Analyzed: mean age 58 (18 to 80), 72% female, 62% prior spine surgery, median 11 levels, 120 of 159 three-column osteotomy, median blood loss 2000 mL.
GAP from films at 3 to 12 weeks, measured by Nemaris software on centralized radiographs.
Complications sought on films from 12 weeks to final follow-up, identified by two authors, then reviewed by a clinical endpoint committee.
Analysis: ROC AUC for complications and revision; Wilcoxon rank-sum for outcome scores.
slides.notes: Read the flow carefully, because the paper does not give a diagram and the counts overlap. Table 1 lists each criterion separately. The 64 without 2-year films include the 55 who missed the 2-year visit, so the exclusions cannot be added. The abstract lists 39, 37 and 64, which would leave 132, not 159. The Methods text lists 2, 55, 64 and 37 and leaves out the 39 who failed the radiographic entry criterion. Neither sum gives 159. Our reading: overlap explains it, but the paper never shows it. The Methods also list further exclusions that Table 1 does not: neuromuscular disease, active infection, trauma or tumor, no full-length film at baseline, and a planned UIV within a previously fused segment. No count is given for any of them, which matters because 62% had prior surgery, and it is another reason the flow cannot be reconciled. Selection is the main threat. The authors say included and excluded patients were similar, and in Limitations that baseline characteristics did not differ. Table 2 says otherwise for sex: 72% female included against 60% excluded, P = 0.04. Our chi-square gives 0.035. GAP category was borderline, P = 0.07: 60% severely disproportioned included against 47% excluded. Our 3x2 chi-square reproduces it (0.068), and on its own it does not show a difference. Our ordinal trend test (Cochran-Armitage) across the three categories gives P = 0.024, which does support a shift toward more severe GAP in the analyzed group. That test is ours, not the paper's. Age, race and prior surgery were similar. The excluded group's GAP categories add to 76, the 113 minus the 37 with no score. Measurement strengths: centralized films and software measurement, and a committee check on complications. What is not stated: whether the two authors or the committee knew the GAP score. Table 1 refers to 6-week data, while the text says 3 to 12 weeks. Definitions follow the original: PJK is 10 degrees or more of increase between UIV and UIV+2; PJF is fracture of UIV or UIV+1, UIV pullout or subluxation; DJK or failure uses LIV to LIV-1 or LIV pullout. Rod fractures counted whether single or double, symptomatic or incidental.

slides.title: Primary outcome: mechanical complications
slides.lead: AUC 0.60 (0.50 to 0.70): weak discrimination, even though rates rose with category.
points: Mechanical complications: AUC 0.60, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.70.
Revision for a mechanical complication: AUC 0.66, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.78.
Types: PJK 17, other implant-related 31, DJK or failure 3. These add to 51 in 44 patients.
Mean postoperative GAP 7 (range 0 to 13). Only 8 patients were proportioned.
slides.see: Figure 2 plots complication rates by GAP score, but its image is not in this copy. The table here comes from the Results text.
slides.notes: How to read an AUC: the chance that a random patient with a complication has a higher GAP score than a random patient without one. 0.5 is a coin toss. 0.60 means GAP ranks them correctly 6 times in 10. The scale in the authors' Methods calls 0.5 to 0.7 no or low associative power, and they read both results as not associated. Be precise about what that means. For complications, the interval's lower bound is 0.50, so chance is not excluded. For revision, the interval 0.53 to 0.78 excludes 0.5. That is a weak but real ranking signal, not no association. This reading is ours; the paper does not make it. The rates also climb in the expected direction: 13, 24 and 31% for complications, 0, 11 and 20% for revision. Our Cochran-Armitage trend tests on those counts give P about 0.16 for complications and 0.06 for revision. So the direction matches the score, but this sample cannot separate it from chance. Compare with the original validation as this paper quotes it: revision 3, 21 and 55%. The steep separation did not reproduce, mainly because the severe group was revised far less often here. What limits the AUC estimate. The categories were unevenly filled: 5% proportioned, 35% moderate, 60% severe. The authors make this point themselves and tie it to lower power than a planned validation. The continuous score itself was not compressed: mean 7 +/- 3, range 0 to 13. The proportioned group had 8 patients and 1 event, so the low-risk end of the curve rests on almost nothing; the authors raise the 8-patient problem too. The CIs are plausible: our Hanley-McNeil estimate with 44 and 25 events reproduces both intervals. The subtypes add to 51, so some patients had more than one; rod fracture and PJF counts are not given separately.

slides.title: Secondary outcomes: 2-year scores
slides.lead: Moderately disproportioned patients scored better than severely disproportioned patients on all four measures.
points: Moderate vs severe, Table 3 P: PCS 0.047, MCS 0.01, SRS-22 0.02, ODI 0.001.
ODI P is printed 3 ways: 0.003 in the abstract, less than 0.001 in Results, 0.001 in Table 3.
Scores are 24-month values only. No baseline or change scores by category.
The proportioned group was not best on MCS, SRS-22 or ODI.
slides.notes: Read this slide as association, not proof that alignment produced better outcomes. The authors themselves say GAP was built for mechanical complications, not outcome scores, and that the proportioned group's scores could not be reliably compared. Two things to notice. First, the gradient is not clean. Results says the lower category was associated with better quality of life on all four measures. Table 3 shows the 8 proportioned patients were worse than the moderate group on SF-36 MCS, SRS-22 and ODI. The only clean comparison is moderate against severe. Second, the size. ODI differed by 10 points, SRS-22 by 0.3 and the mental component by 5 points. The paper makes no claim about clinical importance. Our reading, not the authors': a 10-point ODI gap is near commonly cited thresholds, but a 0.3 SRS-22 gap probably is not. A 5-point mental component gap is a reason for caution, because alignment is an odd explanation for mental health. These are postoperative scores only. Patients in the severe category may have started sicker, older or more disabled, and GAP contains an age factor. Without baseline scores by category, confounding cannot be excluded. Recomputation, moderate against severe: our t-tests from the printed means and SDs give PCS 0.024 (printed 0.047), MCS 0.021 (0.01), SRS-22 0.022 (0.02) and ODI 0.005. MCS and SRS-22 match. PCS and ODI do not match well: for ODI, the Table 3 value of 0.001 and the Results value of less than 0.001 are both several times smaller than our estimate, and the abstract's 0.003 is closest. Rank-based tests can differ from t-tests, so treat this as a flag, not proof of error. Which test? Table 3 gives one P value per row across three columns, and the Methods name a two-group Wilcoxon rank-sum test. Our three-group ANOVA from Table 3 gives PCS 0.017, MCS 0.063, SRS-22 0.066 and ODI 0.015, which does not match the printed values. So the printed P is not a three-group test, which supports the text's moderate-against-severe reading. The abstract prints PCS as 36 versus 40 and Results as 40 versus 36; both mean moderate 40, severe 36. Number completeness is not stated: the table shows all 159, so missing questionnaires were either absent or not reported. No harms are reported beyond the mechanical complications on slide 4.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: An honest external test, but small at the low-risk end and selected by missing films.
points: Holds up: independent prospective multicenter cohort, not the developers' data
Holds up: original inclusion criteria and complication definitions applied
Holds up: centralized software measurement; endpoint committee review of complications
Our view: enough events (44 complications, 25 revisions) for a rough AUC estimate, not a planned validation
Weakens: 42% excluded; included group had more women (P = 0.04) and more severe GAP (P = 0.07)
Weakens: 8 proportioned patients; not designed or powered for validation, by the authors' own account
Weakens: discrimination only; no calibration, no comparison model
Weakens: assessor blinding to GAP not stated; internal number conflicts
slides.notes: Be fair to the authors. They chose a harder test than earlier external attempts and stuck to the original definitions. Their Limitations name three problems: only 159 of 272 could be included because a 6-week film was not mandatory, so selection bias cannot be ruled out; the cohort was more complex than the original; and the categories were unevenly filled with lower power than a planned validation. They also concede in the Discussion that the study was not designed and powered to validate GAP. That sits uneasily with the title's 'external validation', and the reader should weigh the negative result with that in mind. The rest is our reading. Absence of evidence: a weak AUC with a gradient in the expected direction and a revision interval above 0.5 is not evidence that alignment does not matter. It is evidence that this score, in this population, does not sort patients well. A full external validation would also report calibration, meaning whether predicted and observed risks match, and would compare GAP with an alternative such as Schwab modifiers. Neither is reported. The case mix is the other big issue. With 75% three-column osteotomies, this is a test of transport to a harder case mix, and the categories were unevenly filled, with 60% severely disproportioned. The authors offer non-alignment factors as explanations, such as comorbidity, smoking, paraspinal muscle, and center variation in revision, citing other studies. Those are their hypotheses, not findings of this paper. Number conflicts to flag: the flow counts do not add without assuming overlap; included and excluded groups are called similar despite P = 0.04 for sex; the ODI P value is printed three ways; the abstract defines the severe category as higher than 7 while Methods says 7 or higher; three-column osteotomy is 76% in the abstract and 75% in the text for 120 of 159, which is 75.5%.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: GAP did not travel well to complex deformity surgery, but its direction held.
points: "In 159 complex deformity patients from Scoli-RISK-1, the GAP score discriminated poorly: AUC 0.60 for mechanical complications and 0.66 for revision, against 0.92 in its own validation set. Rates still rose from proportioned to severe, but only 8 patients were proportioned and 42% of the cohort was excluded. The authors conclude there is insufficient evidence to apply GAP in routine surgical planning. Our own take: at most one input, not a target that predicts failure on its own."
Expect: Is alignment irrelevant? Why did the derivation look so good? Is 0.66 'no association'? Does this apply to my 4-level degenerative fusions?
slides.notes: Spoken summary in one breath: a good score at home, a weak one away, in a sicker population with almost no proportioned patients. Likely questions and short answers. Is alignment irrelevant? No. This paper tested one score's ability to rank patients. The rates still climbed with category, and moderately disproportioned patients had better 2-year scores than severe ones. In the Discussion the authors say the outcome-score association highlights the importance of sagittal balance, and the abstract says factors beyond the GAP score need to be considered. Their closing conclusion is that there is insufficient evidence to apply GAP in routine surgical planning, and they call for powered prospective trials. Why did the derivation look so good? D05's library record describes a derivation with an internal split-sample validation, 148 and 74 patients, AUC 0.92. Internal validation from the same source population usually flatters a score; ours, not this paper's claim. Is 0.66 'no association'? Not strictly. Its interval, 0.53 to 0.78, excludes chance. It is weak discrimination, which is what the authors' 0.5 to 0.7 band labels it. Does this apply to routine 4-level fusions? Not directly. Scoli-RISK-1 enrolled complex deformity and 75% had three-column osteotomies, so the result speaks to that group. Conversely, D05 does not prove GAP works in complex cases. What would settle it? The authors call for prospective trials powered for GAP, strict inclusion and prospective documentation of all symptomatic and asymptomatic radiographic complications. Our addition: report calibration and test whether planning to GAP targets lowers failure, which no paper here has done. D05 numbers come from its abstract-level library record.

No supplementary appendix is cited in the PDF. Figures 1 and 2-A to 2-F were read from the page images.

slides.title: Kelly 2019: ASLS-1, operative versus nonoperative care at 2 years
slides.lead: Bottom line: analyzed as randomized, the groups did not differ significantly at 2 years; analyzed as treated, surgery was clearly better (randomized cohort, adjusted: ODI −16, SRS-22 subscore +0.7), with frequent serious adverse events and a 14% revision rate.
points: Journal club · Adult deformity
Kelly MP, Lurie JD, Yanik EL, et al. J Bone Joint Surg Am 2019;101(4):338-352
Full text read. The PDF is the complete article, not a critique.
slides.notes: This is the 2-year primary report of ASLS-1, the Adult Symptomatic Lumbar Scoliosis trial, funded by NIAMS (R01AR055176), run at 9 North American centers and registered as NCT00854828. It enrolled two concurrent cohorts: 63 patients who accepted randomization and 223 who declined it and chose their treatment. Say early what kind of evidence the headline is. The randomized comparison, analyzed as assigned, favored surgery at 1 year and was not significant at 2 years. By 2 years, 64 percent of those randomized to nonoperative care had had surgery. The authors therefore draw their conclusions mainly from as-treated and responder analyses, which are observational comparisons even inside the randomized cohort. They call the design pragmatic and label it Therapeutic Level II. Their recommendation: a patient satisfied with current spine-related health can stay nonoperative, understanding that improvement is unlikely; a patient who is dissatisfied and expects improvement is better served by surgery, accepting that complications, unplanned reoperation and neurological deficits are common. This deck was built from the full article. The 5-year report of the same trial is in the library as D08, and the ISSG complication cohort as D09.

slides.title: The question and the design
slides.lead: At first presentation, with no prior fusion, does surgery help adult symptomatic lumbar scoliosis more than nonoperative care?
points: Authors' rationale: adult symptomatic lumbar scoliosis is the most common adult deformity, carries disability similar to diabetes or rheumatoid arthritis, and has little comparative evidence.

Authors' critique of the ESSG, ISSG and SDSG registries: heterogeneity, nonconsecutive enrollment, and nonoperative loss to follow-up approaching 50%; the ISSG and ESSG studies also included revision deformity.
Two concurrent cohorts: randomized (permuted blocks of 4, 6 and 8, stratified by site, age group, sex and Cobb severity) and observational (patient choice). Enrollment April 2010 to July 2014.
Sample size: 82 planned for 80% power, assuming 20% crossover. An interim bootstrap on 1-year data from 26 patients cut it to 36. Enrollment stopped at 63.

rows: Age 40–80; lumbar Cobb ≥30°; ODI ≥20 or SRS-22 ≤4.0 in pain, function or self-image; judged surgical candidates; no prior fusion or multilevel decompression
Instrumented fusion for all, laminectomy for symptomatic stenosis; goal 30–50% coronal correction and normal sagittal alignment
Usual care directed by a designated physician at each site: physical therapy (not protocolized), injections, NSAIDs, gabapentin, intermittent opioids
Difference in mean change from baseline to 2 years in SRS-22 subscore and ODI; visits every 3 months

slides.notes: Read the eligibility as a surgical population. Every patient in both cohorts was judged a surgical candidate, and Figure 1 shows 101 screened patients excluded as not reasonable operative candidates. So the nonoperative group is people offered surgery who did not have it, not the average scoliosis patient. The SRS-22 subscore is the mean of the domains excluding satisfaction, scored 1 to 5 with higher better. ODI runs 0 to 100 with higher worse. So a positive SRS-22 difference and a negative ODI difference both favor surgery. Nonoperative care was deliberately usual care, tailored and not protocolized; the authors defend this as generalizable and list it as their first limitation. Look hard at the sample size. The original plan assumed 20 percent crossover. The interim recalculation used 1-year outcomes from 26 randomized patients and assumed an SRS-22 treatment effect of at least 0.714. That is well above the MCID the paper uses (0.43) and the minimum detectable difference (0.4). Our reading: recalculating power from early accruing data with a large assumed effect is fragile, and it gave no protection against crossover, which was the real problem. The paper also defines a noninferiority margin, the minimum detectable measurement difference (SRS-22 0.4, ODI 7.0), but reports no noninferiority analysis. The paper does not describe blinding or how allocation was concealed, so do not state either way.

slides.title: Patients and crossover
slides.lead: The authors report no significant baseline differences between randomized groups, although the nonoperative arm started with worse ODI (median 46 vs 34, P = 0.07); adherence then collapsed in the nonoperative arm.
points: 896 screened, 582 eligible, 306 consented, 286 enrolled: 63 randomized, 223 observational.
256 of 286 (90%) completed the 2-year visit; 12 withdrawals, including 1 death.

Randomized groups did not differ significantly at baseline. In the observational cohort, those choosing surgery had larger curves (median Cobb 57° vs 48°) and worse ODI (37 vs 32) and SRS-22 (3.1 vs 3.4).
Late crossovers (after 6 months) started worse and worsened before surgery: baseline ODI 48 vs 22, and 6-month ODI change +5 vs −7, compared with those who stayed nonoperative.
slides.see: Figure 1 shows the flow, with cumulative surgery counts at 3 months, 1 year and 2 years in each arm.
slides.notes: Do the arithmetic; it mostly holds. 896 less 314 excluded is 582 eligible; 276 declined, 306 consented, 20 withdrew or failed screening before treatment, leaving 286. The 2-year completers, 31, 27, 94 and 104, add to 256. Crossover: 21 of 33 is 64 percent, split in Table II into 7 of 33 early and 14 of 26 late. In the observational cohort it was 3 of 111 early and 11 of 104 late, 14 in all, and nobody who chose surgery switched. Two points shape everything that follows. First, patients who accepted randomization to nonoperative care were sicker than those who chose it: Table I gives median SRS-22 2.9 versus 3.4 (P = 0.01) and ODI 46 versus 32 (P = 0.002). Second, those who stayed nonoperative after 6 months were the least disabled: median ODI 22 and SRS-22 3.6 at enrollment, against 48 and 2.8 in the late crossovers. Our reading: in the as-treated analysis, the nonoperative group is enriched for milder patients, and patients who were worsening move into the surgical group. One discrepancy: the text says 45 randomized patients with 2-year follow-up had been treated operatively and 13 nonoperatively. Figure 1 shows 45 operated randomized patients in total (21 plus 24), and one operated patient in that cohort died, so at most 44 could have 2-year follow-up. Small, but the flow and the text do not reconcile. The authors say missing data did not differ between groups. In the observational cohort 93 percent of surgical and 85 percent of nonoperative patients attended at 2 years; our Fisher test gives P about 0.06, not significant but close. The early crossovers had baseline ODI 50 versus 44, P = 0.05, which the text calls no difference. The authors say randomization was successful in distributing baseline covariates. Our reading: with 63 patients, several randomized-cohort imbalances sit near significance in Table I: median ODI 34 versus 46 (P = 0.07), stenosis levels (P = 0.05), back-symptom duration 36 versus 96 months (P = 0.08) and coronal balance (P = 0.08). No significant difference is not the same as balanced. A printing error: Table III gives pelvic incidence-lumbar lordosis mismatch for patients still adherent after 6 months as 18 (22, 32), a median below its own interquartile range.

slides.title: Primary outcome: as assigned versus as treated
slides.lead: As randomized, the 2-year difference was not significant; as treated, surgery was clearly better in both cohorts.
points: Differences in mean change from baseline, operative minus nonoperative, with 95% CI. ITT values are unadjusted.
Authors' thresholds: MCID SRS-22 0.43, ODI 10.9; minimum detectable difference SRS-22 0.4, ODI 7.
As treated, nonoperative patients on average did not improve from baseline at 2 years in either cohort.
slides.see: Figures 2-A and 2-B show the randomized arms apart at 1 year and converging by 24 months; Figures 2-C to 2-F show flat nonoperative curves in the as-treated analyses.
slides.notes: Start with the ITT, the only comparison protected by randomization. At 1 year surgery led by 0.5 SRS-22 and 15 ODI points. By 2 years the gap was 0.1 and 4 points, not significant. In Figures 2-A and 2-B the nonoperative-arm curve improves through year 2; the figure tables give that arm a 2-year change of +0.5 SRS-22 and −9 ODI. Our reading: that improvement coincides with 64 percent of the arm having surgery, so the convergence most plausibly reflects crossover, not nonoperative care working. The authors attribute the ITT result to crossover and limited enrollment. Is the 2-year ITT a true null? It depends on the measure. The ODI interval, −13 to 4, includes both no effect and the 10.9 MCID, so it is inconclusive. The SRS-22 interval, −0.2 to 0.4, has an upper bound below the 0.43 MCID and equal to the 0.4 minimum detectable difference, so as assigned it excludes an MCID-sized SRS-22 difference between the arms. Our reading: that is a comparison of arms after heavy crossover, not evidence that surgery and nonoperative care are equivalent. Now the as-treated analysis. Treatment is a time-varying covariate, so a crossover's time before surgery counts as nonoperative and the time after as operative. Baseline for surgical patients could be updated within 4 months of surgery. Our reading: if that update captured patients who had deteriorated before crossing over, it enlarges the surgical change, and it leaves the milder patients in the nonoperative group. The authors adjusted for 12 baseline variables but state they could not control for unmeasured variables or resolve selection bias. Even so, the effect is large and consistent across both cohorts and both measures. One printing problem: in the as-treated figure tables the surgical baseline and 2-year levels do not subtract to the printed change. Figure 2-D gives ODI 41 at baseline and 19 at 2 years, a 22-point drop, beside a change of −18; Figure 2-C gives SRS-22 2.9 to 3.8 beside a change of 0.7. The caption says modeled and observed values differ. Quote the printed differences, not your own subtraction.

slides.title: Secondary outcomes and harms
slides.lead: Most surgical patients reached the MCID, but serious adverse events ran at about three times the nonoperative rate (2.7 times randomized, 3.8 times observational).
points: 171 operated: mean 386 minutes, 10.9 levels fused, blood loss 2,047 mL.
114 SAEs in operative patients. New neurological deficit in 17 (9.9%), 4 major (ASIA C); 1 patient with a major deficit died.
34 revisions in 24 patients (14%) by 2 years; leading causes pseudarthrosis (10) and proximal junctional failure (9).
Radiographs: reproducible lumbar Cobb improvement in 99% of operated patients; 25% of nonoperative patients had a reproducible Cobb difference, direction not stated.

rows: ODI change at 2 years, combined (Table VII)

slides.notes: The responder analysis is time to first reaching the MCID among patients adherent to their initial treatment, censored at crossover, withdrawal, death or last visit, with Cox regression for adjustment. The paper does not say how the printed percentages were derived. Our reading: a responder is anyone who reached the MCID at any visit, so these are not the share improved at 2 years, and censoring at crossover removes nonoperative patients exactly when they were doing badly. The Discussion says more than 80 percent reached the MCID in the combined population; the Results give 77.4 percent for ODI, so that holds only for SRS-22. Harms. SAE totals include events unrelated to the spine: 19 operative and 20 nonoperative SAEs were surgery unrelated to scoliosis. The spine-specific excess is clear: 31 spine SAEs and 17 neurological deficits in operative patients against 1 and 0 in nonoperative patients. Our arithmetic from the Table IV counts and rates: about 336 operative and 485 nonoperative person-years, roughly 34 versus 10 SAEs per 100 person-years overall. These are rates, not the chance that one patient has a complication. Table V revisions add to 34, 7 randomized and 27 observational, and they keep coming after 90 days, mostly pseudarthrosis and junctional failure, which is why the 5-year report (D08) matters. Four nonoperative patients (3 percent) had SAEs related to NSAIDs. Tables VI and VII ask whether an SAE erases the benefit. Operative patients with an SAE improved less than those without (ODI −10.51 versus −15.79) but more than nonoperative patients (−1.57); the difference against nonoperative care was −8.94 (−13.34 to −4.54), smaller than the 10.9 ODI MCID. Table VII prints its headings shifted: P Value sits over the confidence intervals and the P values have no heading. The master record notes that the online table is correct.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: Holds up: NIH-funded, registered, 9 centers, concurrent randomized and observational cohorts
Holds up: 90% follow-up at 2 years, which the authors contrast with registry nonoperative loss to follow-up approaching 50%
Holds up: the as-treated effect is large and consistent across both cohorts and both outcomes
Holds up: harms reported by type and time period, with person-time rates
Weakens: the only randomized comparison, the ITT, is not significant at 2 years
Weakens: 64% crossover from nonoperative care; 20% of the operative arm never had surgery
Weakens: as-treated comparisons carry selection bias, which the authors acknowledge
Weakens: interim sample size cut from 82 to 36 on early data, assuming an SRS-22 effect of 0.714
Weakens: nonoperative care not protocolized; outcomes patient-reported; blinding not described
Weakens: secondary analyses exploratory, no multiplicity correction
Weakens: text, table and flow discrepancies (see notes)
slides.notes: Be fair to the investigators: randomizing surgery against nonoperative care for deformity is hard, and in our view this is the best controlled evidence on the question. The authors name their limitations: nonprotocolized physical therapy; difficulty drawing ITT conclusions with limited enrollment and high crossover; selection, indication and expertise bias; and uncertain generalizability beyond 9 North American centers. They also contrast their 90 percent 2-year follow-up with registry nonoperative loss to follow-up approaching 50 percent. The rest is our reading. The central tension is that the trial randomized to escape selection bias, then had to fall back on analyses that reintroduce it. That does not make the as-treated result wrong: the effect is large, appears again in a separately recruited cohort, and the nonoperative trajectory is flat in every as-treated panel. Large consistent effects are hard to explain by confounding alone. But the size of the effect, more than its direction, is where bias lives. Now the discrepancies. The Discussion says crossover at 2 years exceeded 50 percent, mostly nonoperative to operative. Across the randomized cohort it was 27 of 63, 43 percent; only the nonoperative arm exceeded 50 percent. The Discussion says over 80 percent reached the MCID in the combined population, but ODI was 77.4 percent. Recomputed Table I P values mostly reproduce. Methods say Fisher exact was used for counts under 5, but three randomized-cohort P values with small cells match chi-square: female sex (0.89; Fisher gives 1.00), education (0.64) and smoking (0.59). Other small-count rows do match Fisher. Trivial, and no conclusion changes, but the stated method was not always the one applied.
