Baseline depression in the observational cohort, 31 versus 20 percent, P = 0.05, was adjusted for. Most Table VIII odds ratios differ from crude odds ratios from the printed counts: larger for 4 of 5 (lumbar lordosis 24.60 against our crude 15.4) and smaller for coronal balance (1.59 against our crude 2.1). Our inference: they are presumably adjusted, which the footnote does not say. The text says radiographic deterioration was uncommon with nonoperative care, but Table VIII counts a reproducible difference without direction.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "In ASLS-1, surgery for primary adult lumbar scoliosis improved ODI about 15 points more than nonoperative care at 2 years, but that is an as-treated result; analyzed as randomized, the 2-year difference was not significant, largely because of crossover (64% of the nonoperative arm had surgery) and small numbers. Nonoperative patients stayed about the same. Surgery carried a new neurological deficit in about 1 in 10 and revision in 14% by 2 years."
points: D08 and D09 entries come from the library records. Endpoints and follow-up differ between papers.
Do not stretch it: no prior fusion, surgical candidates only, ages 40–80, 9 expert North American centers.

rows: ITT not significant; as treated ODI −16, SRS-22 +0.7
As treated ODI −15.2, SRS-22 0.63; 74 revisions in 55 of 178

slides.notes: Expect five follow-up questions. First, is this randomized proof that surgery works? No. The ITT comparison was positive at 1 year and not significant at 2; the 2-year benefit comes from as-treated and observational analyses. Say it is strong, consistent observational evidence from a trial setting. Second, should every candidate have surgery? The authors say no: for a patient satisfied with current spine-related health, they advise nonoperative care, with the understanding that improvement is unlikely. In this paper nonoperative patients on average neither improved nor worsened over 2 years. Third, does waiting cost the patient? The authors say a patient who starts nonoperatively and becomes dissatisfied may then be considered for surgery with an expectation of benefit. The paper does not report outcomes for crossovers separately, so it does not show that delayed surgery is as good as early surgery; that inference would be ours and is untested here. Fourth, what risk numbers do I quote? From this paper: new neurological deficit 9.9 percent, 4 major; one death after a major deficit; 34 revisions in 24 of 171 patients (14 percent) by 2 years. The D08 record gives 74 revisions in 55 of 178 operated patients by 5 years, and the D09 record gives 28.2 percent reoperation at minimum 2 years in a broader ISSG population. Fifth, does the benefit last? The D08 record reports an as-treated ODI difference of −15.2 and SRS-22 0.63 at 5 years. The D08 and D09 figures are from the master file records, not from review here. Finally, keep the population in mind: adults 40 to 80 with lumbar curves of at least 30 degrees, no prior fusion, all judged surgical candidates by deformity surgeons at expert centers.

decks.not_reviewed: No supplement is cited in the PDF. The 2-year primary report (Kelly 2019, reference 10), the MDMD paper (reference 26) and the 5-year cost-effectiveness analysis (reference 27) were not reviewed. Figures were read from the page images.

slides.title: Smith 2021: ASLS-1 at 5 years, operative versus nonoperative care
slides.lead: Bottom line: in an as-treated analysis, the operative advantage in disability and SRS-22 seen at 2 years was still there at 5 years, alongside a heavy load of serious adverse events and revisions.
points: Journal club · Adult deformity
Smith JS, Kelly MP, Yanik EL, et al. J Neurosurg Spine 2021;35(1):67-79
Full text read. The PDF is the complete article, not a critique.
slides.notes: This is the 5-year report of ASLS-1, the NIH-funded Adult Symptomatic Lumbar Scoliosis trial at 9 North American centers. Say early and plainly what kind of evidence it is. ASLS-1 had a randomized cohort (63 patients) and an observational cohort (223). By 2 years, 64 percent of those randomized to nonoperative care had crossed over to surgery, so the authors abandoned intention-to-treat and pooled both cohorts into one as-treated comparison. Everything in this deck is therefore an adjusted observational comparison of people who chose or ended up with surgery against people who stayed nonoperative. The headline: ODI improved 15.2 points more with surgery at 5 years, and the SRS-22 subscore 0.63 more. Both exceed the minimum detectable measurement difference the authors used (ODI 7, SRS-22 0.4). The price: 127 treatment-related serious adverse events in the 179 operative patients and 74 revision operations in 55 patients. This deck was built from the full article. The earlier 2-year report and the cost-effectiveness paper it cites were not reviewed here.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: Surgery beat nonoperative care at 2 years in ASLS-1. Does that benefit last through the years when rods break and fusions fail?
points: Authors' rationale: most implant failures and nonunions present between 2 and 5 years after surgery.
Authors' rationale: surgery needs a large up-front investment in money and risk, which takes years of sustained benefit to recoup.
Authors' critique: earlier operative-versus-nonoperative ASD comparisons were short (1–2 years), mixed deformity types, and lost many nonoperative patients (follow-up as low as 45%).

rows: Age 40–80, adult symptomatic lumbar scoliosis, no prior fusion, surgical candidates
Operative care as received: instrumented fusion, with decompression for stenosis
ODI and SRS-22 subscore at 5 years; back and leg pain; serious adverse events

slides.notes: The authors frame three aims: durability of the treatment effect, the rates and types of serious adverse events, and whether treatment-related SAEs erode the benefit. The durability argument rests on their reference 19: implant failures and pseudarthrosis tend to declare themselves between years 2 and 5, so a 2-year result could overstate surgery. Keep that in mind when you reach the revision table, because the paper does show revisions continuing in years 2 to 5. The comparison papers they criticize are study group registry series with poor nonoperative follow-up: 55 percent lost before 2 years in one, a 55 percent nonoperative follow-up rate in another, and 49 to 59 percent follow-up at 1 year in the third. Note the selection built into eligibility: only patients judged to be surgical candidates could enroll in either cohort. So the nonoperative group is not the average scoliosis patient who never sees a surgeon. It is a group who were offered surgery and did not have it, at least during follow-up. The library has the 2-year report as D07 (abstract level): 286 patients, 63 randomized and 223 observational, and 64 percent crossover in the randomized nonoperative arm. This paper gives the same counts.

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: 286 patients, 9 centers, enrolled April 2010 to July 2014, analyzed by treatment actually received.
points: Inclusion: age 40–80, idiopathic or de novo lumbar scoliosis, Cobb ≥30°, ODI ≥20 or SRS-22 subscore ≤4.0 in Pain, Function or Self-Image.
Excluded: prior thoracolumbar fusion or multilevel decompression, high-grade spondylolisthesis, T-score below −3.0, heavy comorbidity, neuromuscular or congenital curves.
Nonoperative care was usual care directed by one nonoperative specialist per site: PT, NSAIDs or gabapentin, injections, judicious opioids.
Analysis: generalized linear mixed models, treatment as a time-varying covariate, adjusted for baseline scores and 12 baseline characteristics; missing data assumed missing at random.
At crossover, baseline was reset and the clock restarted, so '5 years' means 5 years in that treatment group, the latest visit at 60–72 months.
slides.see: Figure 1 shows the flow year by year, with crossovers, withdrawals and deaths in each arm.
slides.notes: The flow diagram adds up at every step; we checked each box. Overall follow-up was 90 percent (256 of 286) at 2 years and 74 percent (211 of 286) at 5 years. Split by group, our arithmetic from Figure 1 gives about 79 percent of operative patients (142 of 179) against about 64 percent of nonoperative patients (69 of 107) with a completed 5-year visit, so attrition was heavier in the nonoperative group. Withdrawals were 26 in each arm by 5 years, and the nonoperative withdrawals include 4 patients who had surgery outside the trial. The paper gives no outcomes for them; our speculation is that they may have been doing badly without surgery. Deaths: 5 operative, 2 nonoperative. The groups were not alike at baseline. The operated group had worse ODI (median 38 vs 30), worse SRS-22 subscore (3.1 vs 3.4), larger Cobb angle (54 vs 49 degrees), less lordosis, more sagittal imbalance, more stenotic levels and more depression, anxiety or other psychiatric disorder (32.4 vs 17.8 percent). The categorical P values recompute from Table 1. One reporting slip: tobacco use (P = 0.7703) matches a Fisher-type exact test, although no cell is below 5 and the stated rule calls for chi-square (our value 0.760); it changes nothing. The models adjust for these, but only for what was measured. The power calculation assumed a 0.30 SRS-22 difference, SD 0.60 and 40 percent loss, giving 86 percent power; the observed loss was smaller. Operations were large: on average 385 minutes, 10.9 levels fused, 2066 mL blood loss.

slides.title: Primary and secondary outcomes
slides.lead: Surgery was associated with more improvement on every measure at 5 years, and the gaps were at least as large as at 2 years.
points: Thresholds used (MDMD): ODI 7, SRS-22 subscore 0.4. Both primary effects exceed them at both time points.
All five SRS-22 domains favored surgery at 5 years, each P <0.001.
slides.see: Figure 2 shows the operative ODI curve falling to about 20 by 12–15 months and staying flat to 60 months, while the nonoperative curve stays near 33–35.
slides.notes: Read the table as adjusted model estimates, not raw change. Figure 2 does not show baseline because the curves are model-based and adjusted. Table 6 gives the model estimates of average change from baseline: the nonoperative group's average ODI change from baseline at 5 years was +0.13, essentially no change, while operated patients without a related SAE improved by 16.3 points. So this is mostly a story of surgery improving people and nonoperative care holding them steady, which is how the authors put it: some patients can be maintained at their presenting level, improvement is unlikely, deterioration is not inevitable. Durability: the 5-year estimates are numerically larger than the 2-year ones, but the paper reports no formal test of the 2-year against 5-year difference, and the patients contributing at each time point are not identical. Our reading is that 'maintained' is fair and 'improved further' is not shown. The MDMD is the smallest change the instruments can detect beyond measurement error. It is not a minimal clinically important difference, so do not call 15 ODI points 'clinically meaningful' on this paper's authority alone. The authors also label the MDMD a noninferiority margin, an odd term in a superiority comparison. Pain: back pain improved 2.4 points more, leg pain 1.2. The authors note that not every patient had back or leg pain (baseline median leg pain was 4 vs 2), and that modest average differences do not rule out larger, meaningful changes in individual patients. We checked CI symmetry and arithmetic in Table 2; the leg-pain P at 2 years (0.015) is a little higher than its CI implies (our estimate about 0.009), a minor point.

slides.title: Harms: serious adverse events and revisions
slides.lead: Surgery bought its benefit with frequent serious adverse events, and revisions kept coming after year 2.
points: Revisions: 34 in 28 patients by year 2, then 40 in 37 patients in years 2–5. Implant failure or pseudarthrosis and proximal junctional kyphosis dominate after year 1.
5-year effect by related SAEs (ODI vs nonop): none −16.4; one −12.2; two or more (n = 12) −8.34, P = 0.017.
SRS-22 with two or more SAEs: 0.32, P = 0.029, below the 0.4 MDMD.
slides.notes: SAE here is the NIH definition: death, life-threatening, significant or permanent disability, new or prolonged hospitalization, or unexpected but related. Sites graded relatedness and the classifications were centrally reviewed, and the authors say they erred toward calling events related, for example counting a new cancer as possibly related when rhBMP-2 was used. Rates are per 100 person-years because crossover gives each person different time in each group. Do not turn 127 related SAEs in 179 patients into a percentage of patients; the paper gives no count of patients with at least one SAE. Revisions are the one patient-level figure: 55 of the 178 patients who had surgery in the study had at least one revision by 5 years, about 31 percent by our arithmetic, and that is a floor because some patients left before 5 years. 42 had one revision, 7 had two and 6 had three. Unrelated events matter too. In Table 3, gastrointestinal SAEs were more frequent during nonoperative time (21 events) than operative time (16 events over more person-years), which the P of 0.042 reflects; the table does not show direction, so read the counts. The SAE subgroup analysis (Table 6) is the authors' attempt to answer 'what if I am the patient with complications'. Our caution: SAE count is something that happens after treatment, patients had to survive and stay in follow-up to be counted at 5 years, and the paper does not give the size of the no-SAE or one-SAE groups. Only the 12 with two or more SAEs are counted. Treat these as descriptive, not causal. The authors' own reading is that one related SAE had very limited impact on long-term outcome, with stronger impact as SAEs accumulated, while still raising cost and slowing recovery.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: Holds up: prospective, multicenter, NIH-funded, prespecified primary outcomes, 5-year follow-up far better than earlier ASD series.
Holds up: flow diagram and categorical baseline P values recompute; Table 6 differences and CIs are consistent with their SEs.
Weak: as-treated, not randomized; only 63 of 286 were randomized and crossover was 64%.
Weak: operated patients were sicker at baseline; adjustment covers only measured factors.
Weak: 26% missing at 5 years, heavier in the nonoperative group (our arithmetic), analyzed as missing at random.
Weak: MDMD is not an MCID; durability is judged by eye, not by a test.
Error: Table 4 prints P <0.001 for every row; by exact tests 8 of 11 category rows cannot be.
Outcomes are patient-reported, by patients who knew whether they had surgery; the paper does not discuss blinding.
slides.notes: The authors list their own limitations: selection, indication and expertise bias, uncertain generalizability beyond expert centers, no usable intention-to-treat analysis, loss to follow-up, and residual confounding despite GLMM adjustment. They also argue that randomizing surgery against nonoperative care in this condition may simply not be feasible, so these as-treated analyses may be the most rigorous evidence achievable. That is a fair point, but it does not make the estimate causal. Our additions follow. Direction of bias is not obvious. The operated group started worse, which leaves more room to improve and risks regression to the mean in their favor, but the adjustment for baseline scores helps. Resetting baseline and the clock at crossover means crossover patients enter the operative group at their worst, which also favors surgery. Patients who did badly without surgery and had it outside the trial were counted as withdrawals, which could flatter nonoperative results. Source problems we found: Table 4 shows P <0.001 in every row. Our exact Poisson tests using the paper's person-time (about 940 operative, 625 nonoperative) give about 1.0 for musculoskeletal (1 vs 0), gastrointestinal (5 vs 3) and genitourinary (3 vs 1), and also 0.52 for death (2 vs 0), 0.28 cardiovascular (3 vs 0), 0.16 circulatory (4 vs 0), 0.16 miscellaneous (5 vs 0), 0.025 cancer (8 vs 0) and 0.008 pulmonary (10 vs 0). Only spine (69 vs 1), neuro deficits (17 vs 0) and the total (127 vs 5) are truly below 0.001, so the column appears filled down in error. Table 1 tobacco use also uses an exact test where the stated rule calls for chi-square. The text says 149 patients were managed nonoperatively for part or all of the study, but 107 never operated plus 43 crossovers is 150. Table 5's total revision rate (7.50 per 100 person-years) implies about 987 person-years, more than the about 940 implied by Table 4, and its '4–5 years' interval implies about 287 person-years in what is labeled a single year, so that row probably runs to 72 months; this is our inference. These do not change the main result. Funding: NIH 2010 to 2017, then the Scoliosis Research Society. Many authors report industry relationships, mostly outside the submitted work.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "In ASLS-1, adults 40 to 80 with symptomatic lumbar scoliosis who had surgery improved about 15 ODI points more than those who stayed nonoperative, and that gap held from 2 to 5 years. It is an as-treated comparison, not a randomized one, and it came with frequent serious adverse events: 55 of 178 operated patients needed at least one revision."
points: D07 and D09 entries come from the library records (abstract level). D09 counts complications per patient, so its percentages are not comparable to D08's per-person-year rates.
slides.notes: Expect four follow-up questions. First, is this randomized evidence? No. The randomized cohort was 63 patients and crossover broke it, so this is an adjusted comparison of patients by treatment received. Second, does the benefit wear off as hardware fails? Not on average through 5 years: the adjusted ODI gap was 13.9 at 2 years and 15.2 at 5. But revisions continued, 40 of the 74 happening in years 2 to 5, mostly for implant failure, pseudarthrosis and proximal junctional kyphosis. Third, what do I tell the patient who is afraid of complications? The authors' answer: patients with one related SAE still did clearly better than nonoperative patients at 5 years, and the advantage shrank in the 12 with two or more. Add our caveat that this subgroup analysis is descriptive. Also say that the serious adverse event rate was 22.38 per 100 person-years in the first 2 years, which is a rate, not the chance that any one patient has a complication. Fourth, is nonoperative care reasonable? The authors say yes for patients satisfied with their current spine-related health: improvement is unlikely, but deterioration is not inevitable, and the nonoperative group's ODI was essentially unchanged over 5 years. For patients who want improvement, they say surgery should be considered. Do not stretch it to patients outside the entry criteria: under 40, prior fusion, high-grade spondylolisthesis, severe osteoporosis or non-surgical candidates. And do not call the effect clinically important on the MDMD alone.

decks.not_reviewed: No supplement is cited in the PDF. Figure 1 (SRS-Schwab distribution) was read only for the percentages quoted in the text. The two published comments on this paper (PMID 27911226 and 29856307), the unpublished data the authors cite (Gupta on multi-rod constructs, Soroceanu on antifibrinolytics) and later ISSG follow-up reports were not reviewed.

slides.title: Smith 2016 (ISSG): complications of adult deformity surgery
slides.lead: Bottom line: 69.8% of 291 patients had at least one complication by last follow-up (minimum 2 years, mean 2.1), but that count includes minor and radiographic events. 47.8% had at least one major complication and 28.2% had at least one reoperation.
points: Journal club · Adult spinal deformity · Complications
Smith JS, Klineberg E, Lafage V, et al, and the International Spine Study Group. J Neurosurg Spine 2016;25:1-14
Prospective multicenter database cohort, 11 US sites, enrolled August 2008 to August 2012
Prepared from the full text, including Tables 1-8 and Figures 2-4
slides.notes: This is a descriptive cohort, not a comparison of treatments. It answers one question: when 11 US sites of a deformity study group look hard for complications, how many do they find over a minimum of 2 years? The answer depends almost entirely on how a complication is defined and how long you look, so this deck spends a full slide on the definitions. Three numbers to carry: 69.8% any complication, 47.8% any major complication, and 28.2% at least one reoperation. The 47.8% is ours, read from Figure 2, where 52.2% of patients had zero major complications. The paper never states it as a headline, and it is the number most surgeons actually want. The study population is the 291 of 346 eligible patients (84%) who reached 2 years. The 55 others are reported separately in Table 3, and the 2 perioperative deaths are among them, not among the 291. The deck was prepared from the full text. No supplement is cited. The ISSG is funded through research grants from DePuy Synthes and individual donations, and most authors list industry relationships. That funding does not obviously push a complication paper in one direction, but say it.

slides.title: The cohort: who was counted
slides.lead: Consecutive operative ASD patients entered into the ISSG database, with procedures chosen by the operating surgeon.

rows: Age over 18 plus one of: scoliosis 20° or more, SVA 5 cm or more, PT 25° or more, thoracic kyphosis 60° or more
346 eligible; 291 (84%) with at least 2 years, mean 2.1 years
Mean age 56.2; 241 women, 48 men; 46% prior spine surgery, 34% prior fusion
Posterior 99%, mean 11.1 levels; anterior 25.4%; osteotomy 64.3% (PSO 16.2%, VCR 3.1%)
Mean OR time 7.1 h, EBL 1.9 L, stay 8.2 days

points: Data: standardized forms, on-site coordinators, central auditing of complications
Radiographs at baseline, 6 weeks, 1 year and 2 years, measured centrally
slides.notes: Read this as a selection slide. The patients were operative candidates at 11 US sites (the paper does not describe them further; the affiliations include both university and non-university centers), assigned to the operative group at enrollment based on the initial management plan. Procedure choice, instrumentation and extent of surgery were at the surgeon's discretion, so this is a picture of what these surgeons did, not of a standard operation. The authors call the patients consecutive. The paper does not report how many operative ASD patients at those sites were not entered in the database, so we cannot check that. Case mix matters for every rate that follows. These are big operations: a mean 11 posterior levels, two thirds had an osteotomy, and 19% had a 3-column osteotomy, per the abstract (Table 1 gives PSO 47 and VCR 9; reading that as 56 of 291 assumes no patient had both, which is ours). Nearly half had prior spine surgery: Table 1 prints 135 (46%), but its age groups sum to 132 (12 + 67 + 53), and 67 of 140 is 47.9%, not the printed 47.8%. Table 8's prior-surgery percentages (51.5%, 47.7%) fit 132, not 135. A rate from this cohort does not transfer to a short-segment fusion in a 50-year-old. Follow-up: 84% reached 2 years. The 55 who did not had a mean 0.57 years of follow-up. The paper says 7 had no follow-up after discharge, 19 none beyond 6 weeks and 29 none beyond 1 year. Those add to exactly 55, which reads as exclusive groups, but then no lost patient was followed past 1 year, 0.57 is about the ceiling for the mean, and it sits awkwardly with deaths recorded at about 1.6 and 1.9 years. Read cumulatively, the mean is barely reachable. The paper does not say which; our flag. The authors report no difference in age, sex, prior surgery, smoking, BMI, CCI, ASA or deformity type. We reproduce the sex and prior-surgery P values, but not smoking: 25 of 291 vs 9 of 55 gives Fisher P about 0.085, not the printed 0.19. The comparison of their complications comes later. One small inconsistency: inclusion says age older than 18, while the youngest age group is labeled 18-44. Also, Table 1 gives 241 women and 48 men, which is 289, not 291. The oldest group, 69 and 24, adds to 93, not 95, so sex is missing for 2 patients without comment.

slides.title: What counted as a complication
slides.lead: The authors chose to err on the side of inclusion. Every rate in the paper inherits these rules.

rows: Perioperative: within 6 weeks. Delayed: 6 weeks to last follow-up
Delayed rates grow with follow-up length
Major: substantially prolonged stay, invasive intervention, prolonged or permanent morbidity, or death
Any complication needing reoperation is major
Rod fracture always major, revised or not
Pushes events into the major column
EBL over 4 L is major; blood-loss anemia under 4 L is minor
Asymptomatic PJK and CSF leak in revision counted

points: Complications from the perioperative period of reoperations were included: 38 (16 minor, 22 major)
slides.notes: This is the slide that makes or breaks how you quote the paper. The definitions push the count up in some places and down in others. Up: rod fracture was classed as major even without revision, because in the authors' experience most need revision eventually and CT was not available to judge fusion. PJK without symptoms counted, and a CSF leak during revision counted. Complications from reoperations' own perioperative periods were added, 38 of them. Down: the authors list their own limits. Many sites did not get routine CT, so medial screw breach and pseudarthrosis were captured only when clinically significant. Reported pseudarthrosis was mostly instrumentation failure or frank nonunion on plain films. Painful implant depended on surgeon judgment. Without a common hematocrit cutoff, blood-loss anemia is likely an underestimate, in the authors' words. Two cautions of ours. First, the delayed window runs to last follow-up, so delayed rates are not a fixed 2-year rate. A patient seen at 2.5 years had more time to fail than one seen at 2.0. Second, a major event here is a category, not a measure of harm. The authors say plainly that not all complications are equally impactful and that many, if not most, likely have minimal or no effect on ultimate outcome. They did not measure impact on outcomes, which they say is beyond the scope of this study. So major does not mean disabling. It often means a trip back to the operating room or a broken rod.

slides.title: Headline rates and the common events
slides.lead: 469 complications in 291 patients: 1.61 per patient. Event counts and patient counts are different numbers.
points: Perioperative: 270 events (145 minor, 125 major); 152 patients (52.2%)
Delayed: 199 events (62 minor, 137 major); 124 patients (42.6%)
Any time: 469 events (207 minor, 262 major); 203 patients (69.8%)
Any major: 47.8% of patients (Figure 2); at least one reoperation: 82 (28.2%)
Deaths: none among the 291; 2 perioperative deaths among the 55 lost (PE, IVC injury)
slides.see: Figure 2 shows how many patients had 0, 1, 2 or more complications; 52.2% had no major complication.
slides.notes: The trap in this paper is the percentage column in Tables 2 and 4 to 7. Our arithmetic shows it is events divided by 291, not the share of patients affected. Implant complications, for example, are 81 events and 27.8, which is 81 over 291. The tables do not say so. So 13.7 for rod breakage is 40 events per 100 patients, and the text speaks of 39 patients with a rod fracture, which would fit one patient having two (our guess; the paper does not explain). Use per 100 patients when you quote these. Delayed events were more often major (137 of 199) than perioperative ones (125 of 270). Implant and radiographic events made up 137 of the 199 delayed events (69%). Rod fracture, PJK and pseudarthrosis alone were 82 (41%). Reoperation does not explain the major share: only 14 of 39 delayed rod breakages, 12 of 28 delayed PJK and 10 of 15 pseudarthroses had a reoperation (Table 4). Rod fracture counts as major by rule, revised or not. Our reading is that the definitions, not reoperation, drive much of the major share late on. The six largest categories, implant, radiographic, neurological, operative, cardiopulmonary and infection, held 88% of events, which we confirm (415 of 469). Postoperative ileus was 22 of 25 gastrointestinal events. Of note: dural tears were almost all minor, while blood loss was mostly major because of the 4 L rule. Venous thromboembolism: 6 PE and 6 DVT events in the 291. Mortality: the authors give 2 perioperative deaths among 339 patients with at least 6 weeks of follow-up, 0.6%, about 1 in 170. The 339 is 346 less the 7 with no follow-up after discharge. Our question: if the 2 who died were among those 7, they sit in the numerator but not the denominator. Either way the rate rounds to 0.6% (2 of 346 is 0.58%). Two more deaths in the lost group, MI at about 1.9 years and aplastic anemia at about 1.6 years, were judged unrelated to surgery.

slides.title: Who had more: age and risk factors
slides.lead: Older patients had more major complications. The share with a minor complication did not differ significantly by age.
points: Perioperative complications: higher BMI (P=0.015), CCI (P=0.002), prior fusion (P=0.029)
Delayed complications: higher BMI (P=0.031), CCI (P=0.007), ASA (P=0.006), 3-column osteotomy (P=0.036)
Not associated: sex, smoking, any prior spine surgery, combined anterior-posterior surgery (P≥0.095)
slides.see: Figure 3 gives these percentages by age group; Figure 4 gives mean complications per patient, with oldest versus youngest major complications 1.08 vs 0.57, P=0.024.
slides.notes: The age gradient is the finding the authors lean on: major complications rose from about a third of the youngest to more than half of the oldest. Our arithmetic from Figures 3 and 4 reproduces the totals of 203 patients and 469 events, and our chi-square on the any-major and any-complication counts gives P about 0.009, matching. How to read it: these are univariate comparisons. The Methods list t-tests, ANOVA, chi-square, Fisher and Kruskal-Wallis, and no multivariable model is reported. Table 1 shows the older groups also had higher BMI, CCI and ASA, more prior surgery, more decompression, longer operations and more blood loss. So age here is a marker for a bundle of risk, not an independent effect. That reading is ours. Note too that neither the share of patients with a perioperative complication nor the share with a delayed one differed significantly by age; only the combined shares did. Counts per patient tell a slightly different story: Figure 4 shows a significantly higher mean number of delayed complications at age 45 or older than under 45 (P=0.010). Risk factors in Table 8 come from many tests at P<0.05 with no correction. The prior-fusion row does not check out. From the printed percentages and the 99 prior-fusion patients in Table 1, our Fisher test gives P about 0.46 for perioperative complications, not 0.029, and about 0.53 for delayed, not 1.000. But the problem is the whole table, not one row. The same reading (row percentage times group size, Fisher test) also fails elsewhere: female perioperative about 1.0 vs printed 0.255, smoker perioperative 0.84 vs 0.680, prior spine surgery delayed 0.12 to 0.15 vs 0.095, and 3-column osteotomy perioperative 0.10 vs 0.075. Only some cells match, such as 3-column osteotomy delayed (0.036) and smoker delayed (1.000). So we cannot tell which test produced Table 8. Treat prior fusion as an unconfirmed risk factor even though the abstract lists it, and hold the other Table 8 P values loosely. Table 1 has a similar issue: its prior-fusion P of 0.046 comes out at about 0.09 on our chi-square. Smoking had no detectable association here, but only 25 patients smoked.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: A careful count from one research group in one era. Strong on capture, weak on generalizability and on risk factors.
points: Holds up: prospective capture, standardized forms, on-site coordinators, central audit
Holds up: 84% reached 2 years; the 55 lost had similar baseline and similar perioperative complications
Holds up: definitions stated, and lost patients reported separately rather than dropped silently
Weakens it: 11 study-group sites, 2008-2012, surgeon-chosen operations
Weakens it: inclusive definitions; asymptomatic radiographic events counted as complications
Weakens it: occult events missed without routine CT; no measure of impact on outcomes
Weakens it: univariate risk factors, no multiplicity correction
Source errors: text, tables and figures disagree in several places
slides.notes: Credit first. The authors built this to fix the usual faults of complication papers: retrospective, single-surgeon, short follow-up, loose recording. On-site coordinators and central auditing are real strengths. They also checked their own loss to follow-up. Perioperative complication counts per patient did not differ between those who did and did not reach 2 years (P=0.65), the share with any perioperative complication was not significantly different (63.6% vs 52.2%, P=0.14, which our Fisher test reproduces), and any complication overall was 70.9% vs 69.8%. Reasons for the 51 surviving patients being lost are unknown. The authors conclude that complications do not appear to be a primary reason for loss to follow-up. Our view: the 42.6% delayed rate is computed on the 291 only, so events missed in the 55 do not bias it. Their own delayed rate (23.6%) is low mainly because they were not followed. Following them would raise the delayed rate for all 346 only if their true delayed rate exceeded 42.6%, and their similar baseline gives no reason to assume that. The direction is unknown. The authors argue current rates are likely lower, citing multi-rod constructs, alignment targets for PJK, antifibrinolytics and vancomycin powder, partly from unpublished data. That is their expectation, not a finding of this study. Errors to know about, all ours to flag: the text gives delayed complications in 21.8% of lost vs 40.5% of retained patients, but Tables 3 and 2 give 23.6% (13 of 55) and 42.6% (124 of 291). The Discussion says infections were 9% of major complications; Table 2 gives 27 of 262, 10.3%. The other major-share figures (26%, 20%, 13%) check out. Figure 3's perioperative percentages by age imply 150 patients, not the 152 in Table 2. Table 5's three column headers all read perioperative; the values show they are perioperative, delayed and total. Several Table 8 P values, including prior fusion, do not reproduce. Table 1's prior-surgery count is 135 in total but 132 by age group. None of these change the headline numbers, which add up cleanly across Table 2, Figure 2 and Figure 4.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "In a prospective, audited ISSG cohort of 291 ASD patients followed at least 2 years, 69.8% had some complication, 47.8% had a major one, and 28.2% had a reoperation. Major complications rose with age, from 32% under 45 to 58% at 65 or older."

rows: As-treated favored surgery; 64% nonoperative-to-operative crossover in randomized cohort

points: D07 and D10 come from the library's abstract-level records, not full-text review here.
Do not quote 70% as the major-complication rate. Say which events, which patients, and how long.
slides.notes: Expect these follow-up questions. One: so is the major-complication rate 70%? No. 69.8% is any complication, including minor events and asymptomatic radiographic findings. About 48% had at least one major complication by Figure 2, and major includes a rod fracture that was never revised. Two: what do I tell a 70-year-old? This cohort gives about 58% with at least one major complication and about 79% with any complication by last follow-up (minimum 2 years) for ages 65 to 86. But those patients also had more comorbidity, BMI and prior surgery, and the analysis is univariate, so this is a crude benchmark, not a personal risk. The library's frailty paper, D10, from its abstract-level record, reports higher major-complication odds in frail and severely frail patients, adjusted ORs 2.8 and 4.1. Three: is surgery still worth it? This paper cannot answer that. It measures harm only, not benefit, and did not assess how complications affected outcomes. Pair it with ASLS (D07), whose library record notes that as-treated analyses favored surgery while crossover limited the randomized comparison. Four: are these rates current? The authors expect them to be lower now because of multi-rod constructs, alignment targets, antifibrinolytics and vancomycin powder, but this study does not show that. Five: what is the death rate? None among the 291. Two perioperative deaths among the 55 lost to follow-up, 0.6% by the authors' denominator of 339. Six: which risk factors are solid? Age, BMI and comorbidity show a consistent signal. Prior fusion as a risk factor rests on a P value we could not reproduce.

decks.not_reviewed: No supplement is cited; the Supplemental Information heading in the PDF is empty. The cited source papers were not reviewed: Searle et al. (frailty index method, ref 18), Glassman et al. (major complication definition, refs 8 and 9), the ASD invasiveness index (ref 14) and the NSQIP modified frailty index study (ref 1). The PDF is the complete 7-page article, not a critique.

slides.title: Miller 2017: Frailty as a tool for risk stratification in adult spinal deformity surgery
slides.lead: Bottom line: in 417 ISSG deformity patients, a 40-item frailty index went with higher adjusted odds of major complications, PJK and longer stay. The index was not tested as a predictor.
points: Journal club · Adult deformity risk
Miller EK, Neuman BJ, et al., International Spine Study Group. Neurosurg Focus 2017;43(6):E3
Design: retrospective analysis of a prospective multicenter database
slides.notes: This is the paper that introduced the ASD frailty index (ASD-FI). The authors built it from an existing ISSG database by counting health deficits, then asked whether frailty category tracked complications, reoperation and length of stay over at least 2 years. Frame it correctly from the start: this is an association study in one cohort. The same patients were used to build the index and to test it. No discrimination statistic (C-statistic or AUC), calibration or separate validation cohort is reported, so the paper shows that frailty is associated with risk, not how well the index predicts it for an individual. The authors go further than the method: they call the ASD-FI itself 'a validated tool for frailty assessment with a strong correlation to other frailty measures', and say their analysis was 'performed with a validated frailty assessment tool'. What they cite is Searle's procedure for building frailty indices, validated in geriatrics, and they show no correlation data for this index. Validating a method for building indices is not the same as validating this index for ASD outcomes; that distinction is ours. One correction to carry from the start: the abstract gives group sizes of 183, 158 and 109, which add to 450, the number with 2-year follow-up before exclusions. The Results text and Table 2 give 171, 162 and 84, which add to the analyzed 417 and match the printed 41, 39 and 20 percent. Use the full-text numbers. This deck was prepared from the full 7-page article. No supplement is cited, and the cited methods papers were not reviewed.

slides.title: The question and the tool
slides.lead: Deformity surgery has high complication rates. Does a count of health deficits flag the patients at highest risk, independent of how big the operation is?
points: Index = deficits present ÷ deficits scored; 10 of 40 gives 0.25. Items are unweighted.
40 binary items: 14 documented by a physician, 26 patient-reported (our count from Table 1)
Patients needed at least 30 of 40 items recorded to be scored
Mean ASD-FI 0.33, range 0.0–0.8
Cutoffs were borrowed from earlier frailty work based on mortality curves, not set for ASD
slides.notes: The method comes from Searle et al.: pick at least 30 deficits that rise with age, relate to health and do not saturate early, record each as present or absent, and divide. The authors stress that which deficits are chosen matters less than how many are present, and that this kind of index can be built from data already collected. The physician-documented items are mostly comorbidities: more than 3 medical problems, BMI under 18.5 or over 30, cancer, cardiac, lung, liver and peripheral vascular disease, diabetes, hypertension, depression, osteoporosis, prior clot or stroke, smoking, and being on disability. The patient-reported items come from the SF-36v2, ODI, SRS-22r and a lumbar stiffness index: stairs, walking 100 yards, dressing, bathing, lifting, travel, sleep, mood, fatigue, social life, incontinence, leg weakness and balance. Our count is 26 of 40 patient-reported, and many are the same questions used to measure deformity disability. Point this out: in deformity patients, a high ASD-FI partly reflects what the deformity is doing to them, and surgery aims to change some of those items. The authors acknowledge this in their own way: they say they cannot tell whether frailty leads to deformity or deformity leads to frailty. Note also that radiographic measures such as SVA were deliberately left out, and the authors suggest adding them in future. The cutoffs of 0.3 and 0.5 came from earlier frailty analyses built on mortality curves, not from ASD outcomes.

slides.title: Patients and methods
points: Source: ISSG multicenter prospective US ASD database; surgery 2010–2014; age 18 or older
Deformity entry: major curve ≥20°, thoracic kyphosis ≥60°, PT ≥20° or SVA >5 cm
450 had 2-year follow-up; 417 had enough data to score
Primary: major complications (potentially life-threatening, required reoperation or caused permanent injury, per Glassman)
Secondary: any complication, reoperation, PJK, pseudarthrosis, deep infection, dehiscence, LOS
Models: univariate screen at P < 0.3, then backward elimination; adjusted for invasiveness factors
slides.see: Table 2 gives the full baseline and procedure comparison. *Printed percentages; the printed counts give 25% (40 of 162) and 32% (27 of 84).
slides.notes: Selection first. The cohort is surgical ASD patients in a US multicenter database who reached 2-year follow-up. The paper does not say how many enrolled patients lacked 2-year follow-up, so we cannot judge loss to follow-up, and the frailest patients may be the ones most likely to drop out or die; that concern is ours. Of 450 with follow-up, 33 (7 percent, our arithmetic) were excluded for missing frailty data. The authors chose not to exclude by age, arguing frailty matters at any age. Measurement next. The groups differ on almost everything: frail patients were 12 to 14 years older, had higher ASA and Charlson scores, and had more decompressions, interbody fusions and 3-column osteotomies. The authors report no difference in frailty by sex or race (P > 0.05). Sex holds up: Table 2 counts give P of about 0.12 against the printed 0.15. Race does not: not frail versus frail alone (139 of 171 versus 146 of 162 Caucasian) gives P of about 0.02, and no possible severely frail count gives a 3-group P above about 0.07, so the printed 0.39 cannot come from these counts. Those checks are ours; treat the race claim as unsupported. The age row reads 49 (1.3); an SD of 1.3 years is not plausible for age in this cohort, so the bracket is probably a standard error. That reading is ours. Analysis. Each outcome had its own logistic model (Poisson for LOS). Variables with univariate P under 0.3 entered, and were trimmed until the model held the maximum supportable number. What stayed in were mostly invasiveness factors: osteotomy, levels fused, operative time, blood loss, BMP, allograft. The authors did not use their own invasiveness index in the models. Age, ASA and Charlson were not in any final model shown in Table 4, so the paper cannot say frailty adds information beyond age or comorbidity. Complication definitions for PJK and pseudarthrosis are not given, and the time window for complications is not stated beyond the 2-year minimum follow-up.

slides.title: Primary outcome: major complications and length of stay
points: Major complications in Table 2: NF 17%, frail 38%, SF 40%* (printed)
Adjusted for osteotomy, BMP, race, blood loss, levels fused and smoking
LOS: 6.8, 8.0 and 10.5 mean days; adjusted ratio 1.2 frail and 1.6 SF
slides.see: *Table 2 prints 44 SF patients with a major complication as 40%; 44 of 84 is 52%.
slides.notes: This is the headline. Adjusted odds of a major complication were 2.8 times higher for frail and 4.1 times higher for severely frail patients than not frail, P = 0.006 and 0.001. Adjustment barely moved the estimates, which the authors read as frailty being independent of surgical invasiveness. The intervals are wide: the lower bounds are 1.3 and 1.7, so the true effect could be modest. Our checks: the adjusted intervals are symmetric on the log scale and match their P values, so they hang together. Now read the raw counts. Table 2 gives major complications in 29 NF (17 percent), 63 frail (38) and 44 SF (40). 44 of 84 is 52 percent, not 40; 44 of 109, the abstract's SF count, is 40 percent. From the Table 2 counts we get a univariate OR of about 3.1 for frail and 5.4 for SF, not the printed 2.9 and 3.5. So at least one denominator or count in Table 2 is wrong, and we cannot tell which. The ORs in Table 3 and 4 are the paper's; quote those. Our overall rate from the printed counts is 136 of 417, 33 percent. Odds ratios exaggerate relative risk when an outcome is common. Our illustration: with a 17 percent baseline, an OR of 2.8 corresponds to about 36 percent risk, roughly double, not nearly triple. Length of stay: the abstract's 1.2 and 1.6 times longer are the adjusted Poisson estimates in Table 4. Raw means of 6.8, 8.0 and 10.5 days give ratios of 1.18 and 1.54 (our arithmetic), which match the univariate 1.2 and 1.5 in Table 3; the adjusted 1.6 for severely frail is a little higher. Table 4 labels them correlation coefficients, which they cannot be at 1.6; they read as rate ratios. That reading is ours. Our inference, not the paper's: an SD of 9.0 days against a severely frail mean of 10.5 suggests a few long stays pull the mean up.

slides.title: Secondary outcomes and harms
slides.lead: Most secondary signals come from the severely frail group, with very wide intervals.
points: Event counts for these outcomes are not reported by group.
PJK and pseudarthrosis definitions are not given.
slides.notes: PJK is the most robust secondary finding: both frail and severely frail had about 3 times the adjusted odds, P = 0.01 and 0.02, after adjusting for allograft, osteotomy and myelopathic symptoms. Reoperation was higher for severely frail (2.1, P = 0.02). For frail it sat at the boundary (1.7, lower limit 1.0, P = 0.05). Now the dramatic numbers. Pseudarthrosis 13.0, dehiscence 13.4 and deep infection 8.0 are severely frail only, and their intervals run from about 1.3 to 120. An upper limit 80 to 90 times the lower limit means very few events, probably single digits in the NF reference group; that inference is ours because the paper gives no event counts for any secondary outcome. With so few events, the deep infection model still carried six terms, including gait imbalance, levels fused and operative time, which risks overfitting. Read these as a signal, not a size. Do not quote 13-fold. Frail patients did not have significantly higher adjusted odds of pseudarthrosis, infection or dehiscence. That matters because the Conclusions say frail and severely frail patients had higher rates of reoperation and wound infection, and the Discussion says increasing frailty was associated with pseudarthrosis, dehiscence and deep infection. For the frail group, the tables do not support those statements for infection or pseudarthrosis. No mortality data are reported. Many outcomes were tested with no multiplicity correction, so a P of 0.03 to 0.05 on a secondary outcome is weak. Table 4 also prints unexplained P values of 0.906 and 0.369 against the deep infection and reoperation headings; the paper does not say what they test.

slides.title: Critical appraisal

rows: Index built and tested in one cohort; no C-statistic or validation
Established method for building a frailty index
26 of 40 items patient-reported; about 17 are function questions overlapping deformity symptoms
Age, ASA and Charlson not in final models
Major complication effect consistent across models
Secondary outcomes: no event counts, wide CIs, no multiplicity correction
Graded LOS effect (1.2 vs 1.6, CIs separate); major-complication ORs 2.8 vs 4.1 overlap, no trend test
Table 2 and abstract counts are internally inconsistent
Stepwise selection; database funded by DePuy Synthes

slides.notes: Be fair to it: this is an early, honest attempt to give ASD surgeons a frailty measure from data they already collect, and the major-complication association is consistent across models, and the LOS effect is graded. The major-complication ORs rise from 2.8 to 4.1, but their intervals overlap almost entirely and no trend test is reported, so the grading there is a point-estimate pattern only; that reading is ours. What the authors themselves concede: the 40-item unweighted tool is cumbersome; frailty and deformity may cause each other; radiographic measures were excluded. They propose patient-completed surveys and future weighting and trimming of items. The rest is our reading. First, the claim of risk stratification is not tested. An association with OR 2.8 does not tell you how well the score separates patients; no C-statistic, calibration or external validation is shown. Second, construct overlap: 26 of 40 items are patient-reported, from the ODI, SRS-22r, SF-36v2 and a lumbar stiffness index. By our count about 17 are function questions (stairs, walking, dressing, lifting, travel, work, social life, leg weakness, balance and similar), and the rest cover mood, fatigue, general health and incontinence; none is a pain question. So the index partly measures deformity disability. Third, confounding: age is the obvious one (49 versus 61 to 63 years), and it was never adjusted; the frailty index may be a better age, but the paper does not show that it beats age. Fourth, source errors. The abstract counts add to 450, not 417. In Table 2, Caucasian is printed as 93 of 84 SF patients, which is impossible; 3-column osteotomy percentages do not match their counts for frail and SF; and the SF major complication percentage matches the abstract's 109 rather than 84. The Discussion says frailer patients had more severe deformity, but no deformity measures by group are reported. Fifth, the Conclusions say frailty allows the surgeon to tailor invasiveness. Nothing in the study tests that. Disclosures: the database is funded by DePuy Synthes, and several authors report industry ties. Our recomputations: the adjusted frailty ORs and their CIs are consistent with their P values. Several Table 4 covariate rows are not (for example PJK osteotomy 0.5, 0.3–1.1, printed P 0.08, recomputes to about 0.04), though rounding may explain some. The female-sex P (0.15 printed) recomputes to about 0.12, close enough; the race P (0.39) cannot be reproduced from the Table 2 counts.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: “In the ISSG cohort, frail and severely frail deformity patients had about 3 and 4 times the adjusted odds of a major complication, more PJK and longer stays. It is a risk marker, not a validated predictor, and much of it measures disability.”

rows: Major complication OR 2.8 frail, 4.1 SF vs NF

points: D09 numbers come from the library record, abstract level only.
Do not stretch it: no evidence that changing the operation or prehabilitation lowers risk.
slides.notes: Spoken summary: in 417 adult deformity patients from the ISSG database with 2-year follow-up, a 40-item frailty index split patients into not frail (41 percent), frail (39) and severely frail (20). Adjusted for invasiveness factors, frail and severely frail patients had higher odds of major complications, 2.8 and 4.1, and of PJK, about 3, and stayed 1.2 and 1.6 times longer. Severely frail patients also had more reoperation and, with very wide intervals, more pseudarthrosis, deep infection and dehiscence. Expect four follow-up questions. Is frailty just age? Not shown either way: age was strongly linked to frailty and was not in the final models. Does this tell me to do a smaller operation? No. The authors suggest tailoring invasiveness, but the study did not test it. The paper reports no patient-reported outcomes or benefit by frailty group, so it cannot say whether frail patients gain more or less from surgery; that caveat is ours. How good is it at predicting an individual's complication? Unknown; no discrimination statistics are reported, and the cutoffs came from geriatric mortality work. Is a frail score modifiable? Some items are, such as smoking, BMI, depression and osteoporosis. The library's CNS osteoporosis guideline (O05) supports bone-health testing and considering teriparatide in osteoporosis before instrumentation, but this paper does not test any intervention. For context, the D09 record (Smith 2016, ISSG, abstract level) reports 69.8 percent with at least one complication and 28.2 percent with at least one revision, but that rate includes minor and radiographic events and is not a major-complication rate, so do not compare it directly with the 33 percent major rate we computed from this paper's Table 2 counts.

decks.not_reviewed: Nothing in the paper was skipped: the PDF is the complete 8-page article (Spine 2005;30:346-353), with Figures 1-6 and Tables 1-3. Not reviewed: the variability study the authors cite for measurement reliability (reference 19, a 2001 meeting presentation), the published comment on this paper (PMID 15990675), the 2026 AO Spine appraisal that selected it, and any later papers that build on these types.

slides.title: Roussouly 2005: four sagittal types
slides.lead: A descriptive classification of normal lumbar lordosis built on sacral slope.
points: Journal club: adult deformity, sagittal shape
Roussouly P, Gollogly S, Berthonnaud E, Dimnet J. Spine 2005;30(3):346-353
160 young asymptomatic volunteers, standing full-length lateral radiographs

Bottom line: lordosis shape follows sacral slope. Two types with sacral slope under 35 degrees, one at 35-45, one over 45. No outcomes, no reliability test of the types, and the main correlations are built into the geometry.
slides.notes: This deck was prepared from the full text of the paper. The PDF is complete, 8 journal pages, and it is the original article, not a critique. What it is: a cross-sectional radiographic study. The authors call it prospective; it measures each person once. It is the origin of the Roussouly types that later deformity planning papers build on, and the library records it as historical background. Set the frame for the room: this paper describes how normal spines vary. It does not test whether any shape causes pain or degeneration, and it does not test whether recreating a type after surgery helps anyone. The authors say so themselves: they present this as an initial cross-sectional data set and plan to follow the volunteers. Their clinical observations at the end, that disc herniations tend to be Types 1 or 2 and stenosis Type 4, come with no data in this paper. Treat them as hypotheses. Also note the disclosure: the paper states that one or more authors received benefits from a commercial party related to the subject, and that no funds supported the work. The paper does not say which party.

slides.title: The question and the geometry
slides.lead: Is there a common language for normal sagittal shape, as coronal classification systems such as Lenke's gave the coronal plane?
points: Thoracic and lumbar curves are split at the inflection point, not at T12-L1.
Each lumbar curve is two arcs of a circle, meeting at the apex.
By construction, the lower arc of lordosis equals the sacral slope.
Global lordosis is the upper arc plus the lower arc.

rows: Fixed shape angle; PI = SS + PT
Hip axis to S1 midpoint, from vertical; positional
S1 to inflection point; negative if the top of lordosis is behind S1
Lordosis above and below the apex

slides.see: Figure 2 shows the two lordosis arcs and why the lower arc equals the sacral slope.
slides.notes: The authors' argument: coronal alignment has a clear normal (straight), but sagittal normal is variable, and most degenerative disease happens in spines straight in the coronal plane. So they want a way to describe sagittal shape that includes the pelvis. The key teaching point is the geometry. The software fits tangent arcs to the anterior vertebral bodies. The lower arc ends tangent to a line perpendicular to the S1 endplate, and the apex arcs are tangent to vertical. That makes the lower arc of lordosis equal to sacral slope by definition. Table 1 shows it: lower arc and sacral slope have identical mean, SD, minimum and maximum (39.92, 8.17, 21.22, 65.90). Our arithmetic: mean upper arc 21.50 plus mean lower arc 39.92 gives 61.42, matching mean global lordosis 61.43. Why this matters: when the paper later reports that sacral slope correlates with global lordosis at r = 0.86, that value is what the construction alone predicts. Our recomputation from the Table 1 SDs and the near-zero upper arc to SS correlation (0.03) gives r = 0.856, so the whole printed 0.86 comes from the shared lower arc. That reading is ours; the authors do not discuss it. Similarly, pelvic incidence equals sacral slope plus pelvic tilt, and the same check reproduces the PI to SS correlation of 0.80, so it is built in too. Our check: 39.92 + 11.99 = 51.91, exactly the printed mean PI. The inflection point method is also worth saying aloud: kyphosis and lordosis are defined by shape, not by anatomic level, which is why a 'lumbar' lordosis can start at T10 or at L4.

slides.title: Selection and measurement
points: 160 volunteers: 86 women, 74 men, mean age 27 (range 18-48)
Mainly medical students, physical therapists, nurses and allied staff at the center
All of European heritage, from the Lyon area
Excluded: chronic back pain, deformity, significant orthopedic disease, spondylolysis, spondylolisthesis, scoliosis, Scheuermann
Standing, hands on supports, knees extended; 30 x 90 cm films, skull base to femora, 230 cm source distance
Films scanned at 75 dpi or more; a trained user marked landmarks in custom software; the number of readers is not stated
Unclear landmarks led to exclusion; how many were excluded is not reported
slides.notes: Selection: this is a convenience sample of young, healthy hospital workers and students. Mean age 27 and a maximum of 48 means the paper says nothing directly about the 65-year-old deformity patient. The authors themselves say the frequency of each type probably depends on age, because lordosis is lost with aging. The population is entirely European, so do not assume the type frequencies carry to other populations; that caution is ours. Asymptomatic was defined by history at enrollment. Measurement: the paper states that a trained user marked the points; it does not say how many readers there were, whether any film was read twice, or who assigned each type. Reliability is cited, not measured: the authors quote interobserver reliability of 0.92 to 0.99 and intraobserver 0.93 to 0.99 for locating points, from a separate study of 30 randomly selected radiographs presented at a meeting (reference 19). That is reliability of landmarks, not of assigning a type. Transitional vertebrae: the sacral slope was taken at the apparent fixed sacrum. Patients with significant landmark ambiguity were excluded, but the Results say 160 sequential examinations were analyzed and give no count of exclusions, so we cannot tell how many films were dropped or whether 160 is after exclusions. Our note: 75 dots per inch is a low scan resolution, which may matter for small angles such as the lordosis tilt angle. Correlation analysis used Pearson coefficients only; there are no confidence intervals and no comparisons between types. How apex and inflection level were turned into numbers for correlation is not described.

slides.title: The four types
slides.lead: The authors classify by apex, inflection point, vertebra counts, curve angles, tilt angle and sacral slope; in Table 3 the types are labeled by sacral slope band (our reading).
points: Pelvic incidence means rise by type: 41, 44, 51, 63 degrees, with wide overlap.
Upper arc stays about 20 degrees in every type (19 to 22).
slides.see: Figures 3 to 6 pair a radiograph of each type with a schematic of its lordosis.
slides.notes: How to read the types, in the authors' words. Type 1: low sacral slope, apex in the middle of L5, a short lordosis with a low, posterior inflection point and thoracolumbar kyphosis. Type 2: also low sacral slope but a flat lower arc, apex at the base of L4, a higher and more anterior inflection point that brings more vertebrae into the lordosis; the whole spine is hypolordotic and hypokyphotic. Type 3: sacral slope 35 to 45, apex mid L4, inflection at the thoracolumbar junction; the authors call it well balanced. Type 4: sacral slope over 45, high pelvic incidence, apex at the base of L3 or higher, a long curved lordosis with segmental hyperextension. Types 1 and 2 share the same sacral slope band. They differ by apex level and shape, and the paper gives no rule for splitting them, for example no threshold for the thoracolumbar kyphosis of Type 1; Table 3 does not report thoracolumbar kyphosis at all. Now check the text against Table 3; several definitions do not match the table. Type 3 is said to have a lordosis tilt angle near zero, but the table mean is minus 6.5, more negative than Type 2 at minus 5. Type 4 is said to have a tilt angle of zero or positive, but the mean is minus 2.5, range 6 to minus 12. Type 4 is said to have more than 5 lordotic vertebrae, but the mean is 5, range 3.5 to 6. Type 3 is said to average four lordotic vertebrae; the table gives 4.5. Treat the prose as an idealized picture and the table as what was measured. Our weighted means from Table 3 (SS 39.6, PI 51.7, lordosis 61.1) are close to Table 1 (39.9, 51.9, 61.4), so the table is internally consistent. Our note on Type 2: more vertebrae suggests a longer lordosis, and Table 3 gives a mean of 5 lordotic vertebrae, yet the Discussion calls lordosis with sacral slope under 35 'relatively flat, short'. The authors never call Type 2 long. The type boundaries at exactly 35 and 45 degrees are not stated clearly: the Type 1 range reaches 35 and the Type 4 range starts at 45.

slides.title: Correlations: read with care
slides.lead: Strong correlations, but the biggest ones are built into the definitions.

rows: Lower arc equals SS; fully reproduced
Shares the SS term; also built in
Upper arc does not follow SS

slides.notes: The authors read Table 2 as showing that lordosis is determined by the orientation of the sacrum. Our reading: correlation in one cross-section cannot show what determines what, and the top values are arithmetic. The lower arc is the sacral slope, and global lordosis is upper arc plus lower arc, so SS against lordosis is largely SS against itself. Our recomputation from Table 1 SDs and the Table 2 cross-terms reproduces r = 0.86 (we get 0.856), the 0.80 for PI to SS, and the 0.54 for upper arc to lordosis, so the whole of each printed value comes from the construction. The more useful finding is the one that is not built in: the upper arc, about 20 degrees, does not track sacral slope (r = 0.03), so the variation in lordosis between people sits in the lower arc. Pelvic incidence to lordosis, 0.64, is no less built in: PI is SS plus PT, and the same check reproduces 0.64 (we get 0.64). It is lower than 0.86 only because PI carries pelvic tilt, which barely correlates with lordosis. Recomputation problems, all in Table 2 or its text. First, the text gives sacral slope to apex as 0.52; the table prints 0.55, and 0.52 is the PI to apex value. Second, the text cites the correlations as Table 3; they are in Table 2. Third, column 9, the number of vertebrae in the lower arc, repeats the apex column value for value, and apex against column 9 is printed as exactly 1. So the two are the same measure, counted twice. Fourth, significance markers do not hold for the smaller values. With n = 160, our calculation gives P about 0.04 for r = 0.16, 0.03 for r = 0.17 and 0.01 for r = 0.20, yet these are marked P under 0.005; r = 0.22 is marked P under 0.001, and we get about 0.005. The large correlations are unaffected. Fifth, the abstract says the number of lordotic vertebrae was determined by sacral slope, but Table 2 has no column for number of lordotic vertebrae, so no correlation is reported for it. No multiplicity adjustment is reported across the 45 correlations.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: Holds up: standardized standing films with the pelvis included
Holds up: shape-based curve limits, not fixed anatomic levels
Holds up: full measurement table with SD and range; type counts add to 160
Weakens it: young, European, health-worker volunteers only
Weakens it: types designed by the senior author; no inter-rater test of assigning a type
Weakens it: key correlations built into the geometry
Weakens it: type descriptions do not match Table 3 for tilt angle and vertebra count
Weakens it: clinical claims about herniation and stenosis given without data
Weakens it: authors disclose a commercial benefit, party not named
slides.notes: Be fair to the paper: it gave the field a vocabulary that is still used, and it describes the whole lumbopelvic unit, not one Cobb angle. The measurement is laid out clearly enough that the geometry can be checked, which is how we found the built-in coupling. Validity as a classification. Content: the types capture lordosis shape and sacral orientation, but say little about thoracic kyphosis or global balance; sagittal vertical axis and the C7 plumb line are cited from earlier studies in the Discussion but not measured in this cohort. Reliability: not tested for type assignment. The authors acknowledge that a spectrum exists and that some people fall between two categories, but do not say how many. Construct: the authors state the types are meant to identify features that may affect back pain, deformity and surgical results. In this paper, that is a hypothesis. The only clinical evidence offered is the authors' preliminary observation, with no numbers, that disc herniations are mostly Types 1 or 2, stenosis mostly Type 4, and patients with significant complaints are rarely Type 3. Derivation: the paper does not say whether the 35 and 45 degree cut-offs were set before seeing these data. Our reading is that the scheme was proposed and applied in the same sample, so its fit here is not an independent test. Generalizability: maximum age 48. The authors expect type frequencies to shift with age; this cohort cannot show it. Prose against table: the Type 3 and Type 4 tilt angles and the Type 4 vertebra count in the text are not what Table 3 reports. When quoting a type, quote the table.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "In 160 young asymptomatic volunteers, Roussouly sorted lordosis into four shapes by sacral slope: two under 35 degrees, one at 35 to 45, one over 45. Lordosis rose from about 52 to 71 degrees across the types. It is a description of normal variation, not a surgical target proven to improve outcomes."
points: Lower arc equals sacral slope by construction; the upper arc stays about 20 degrees.
Type 3 was most common (60), Type 2 least (18).
Schwab 2013 (library record): 492 deformity patients; PI-LL, PT and SVA tied to disability.
Hills 2024 (library record): 247 patients; deviation from L1PA targets tied to mechanical failure.
Later papers are outcome-linked; this one describes shape only.
slides.notes: Expect these follow-up questions. Should I restore a patient's Roussouly type at surgery? This paper cannot answer that. It has no patients, no surgery and no outcomes. It shows what normal young spines look like. Why would I use it instead of PI minus LL? The answer: the same total lordosis can be distributed differently. The paper's point is that the variable part between people is the lower arc, which tracks sacral slope, while the upper arc stays near 20 degrees. That is shape information that a single lordosis number leaves out. How reliable is the typing? Not tested here. The cited reliability, 0.92 to 0.99, is for marking landmarks in a separate study of 30 randomly selected radiographs. Is the SS to lordosis correlation of 0.86 strong evidence? No. It is arithmetic: the lower arc is defined as the sacral slope, and our recomputation reproduces 0.86 from the construction. Pelvic incidence to lordosis at 0.64 is no better, because PI contains SS; it is lower only because PI also carries pelvic tilt. How do Types 1 and 2 differ if both have sacral slope under 35? By apex level and the shape of the lordosis, mid L5 and short in Type 1, base L4 with a flat lower arc and more vertebrae in the lordosis in Type 2 (calling it long is our inference); the paper gives no numeric rule. Does it apply to older adults? The oldest volunteer was 48. Comparison with the library: Schwab 2013 and Hills 2024 numbers come from the master file's abstract-level records, not from full-text review here. They link alignment to disability or mechanical failure; Roussouly 2005 only describes normal shape. When quoting the types, quote this paper's four as printed.

decks.not_reviewed: Nothing in the paper was skipped: the PDF is the complete 11-page original article (J Neurosurg Spine 2015;23:673-683), with Figures 1-7, and it is not a critique. No supplement is cited. Not reviewed: the color online versions of Figures 4 and 7, the earlier literature review that fed the classification (reference 37), the Delphi methods paper it cites (reference 6), the prospective multicenter cervical deformity study the authors mention, and any later validation or revision of this classification.

slides.title: Ames 2015: cervical deformity classification
slides.lead: An expert-built classification for adult cervical deformity, with a first test of whether surgeons apply it the same way.
points: Journal club: adult deformity, cervical alignment
Ames CP, Smith JS, Eastlack R, et al; International Spine Study Group. J Neurosurg Spine 2015;23:673-683
10 selected cases, each classified twice by 20 spinal deformity surgeons, with measured values supplied

Bottom line: 5 deformity types plus cervical, gaze, myelopathy and SRS-Schwab modifiers. Agreement between readers ranged from slight to substantial and fell on the second reading for 8 of 9 items. No outcome validation.
slides.notes: This deck was prepared from the full text of the paper. The PDF is complete, 11 journal pages, and it is the original article, not a critique. What it is: a classification proposal plus an agreement study. The classification came from a literature review and a modified Delphi approach with an expert panel. The paper does not report how many panelists took part, how many rounds were run, or what counted as consensus. The test is reliability only: do 20 surgeons put the same 10 cases in the same boxes, and does each surgeon repeat himself or herself a week or more later? It does not test whether the grades track symptoms, disability, or the result of surgery. The authors say so and name that as the next step, through a prospective multicenter cervical deformity study. The library holds this paper as historical background. The vocabulary matters more than the kappas. Set the frame: this is a common language, not a treatment algorithm. It gives no fusion levels, no approach and no correction targets. Disclosures: many authors report industry consulting, royalties or stock. Two authors (Schwab and Lafage) report stock in and employment by Nemaris Inc. The paper states that the International Spine Study Group is funded by research grants from DePuy-Synthes and individual donations. The paper does not say whether the 20 readers included the authors.

slides.title: The question and the classification
slides.lead: Thoracolumbar deformity has the SRS-Schwab classification; cervical deformity had no comprehensive system. The authors built one.
points: Descriptor, one of five: C (apex cervical), CT (apex cervicothoracic), T (apex thoracic), S (C2-7 coronal Cobb 15 degrees or more), CVJ (craniovertebral junction).
Four cervical modifiers plus the full SRS-Schwab thoracolumbar classification: curve type (T, L, D or N) and three sagittal modifiers, PI-LL, PT and C7-S1 SVA, each graded 0, + or ++.
Needs full-length standing films to the femoral heads, standing cervical films, a scored mJOA, and a photo or film showing the skull for CBVA.
slides.see: Figure 1 lays out the whole system on one page; Figure 2 shows a radiograph of each of the five descriptor types.
slides.notes: Teach where each cut-off came from, because the paper is candid about it. The 4 cm C2-7 SVA threshold comes from a regression in Tang and colleagues (113 patients after multilevel posterior cervical fusion), where 4 cm corresponded to moderate disability on the NDI. The 8 cm upper threshold is not derived from data. The authors say the doubling of modifier ranges was based on experience with the SRS-Schwab modifiers. The CBVA grades are expert opinion. The paper notes that normal CBVA has not been rigorously defined, cites 10 degrees as a described optimal target, and cites Suk's 7 patients with CBVA under -10 degrees who had worse gaze scores, especially going down stairs. The TS-CL grades are expert opinion, built on the analogy that T1 slope is to cervical lordosis what pelvic incidence is to lumbar lordosis. The mJOA bands follow expert opinion and earlier AOSpine myelopathy studies. The SRS-Schwab component is taken whole, because thoracolumbar malalignment can drive cervical compensation and the reverse. Points to notice, ours: the paper never states the sign convention for CBVA, which matters because the 1 grade spans both a chin-up range and a chin-down range. The gaze bands, written in whole degrees, leave 0 to 1 and 10 to 11 degrees unassigned if a reader measures to a decimal. The authors call these 5 modifiers, but the SRS-Schwab modifier is itself four graded items, so a full classification is a descriptor plus eight grades. Figure 1 heads the TS-CL box 'Cervical Lordosis Minus T1 Slope' while every grade inside it, and the text, is TS-CL; read it as TS minus CL, as the abstract, the section heading and the Figure 7 table state it (the Figure 5 legend says only 'the difference').

slides.title: Cases, readers and analysis
slides.lead: Ten hand-picked cases, twenty experienced readers, two readings, and the numbers handed to the readers.
points: Cases chosen to be representative of the descriptors and modifiers, not consecutive patients.
Images at least 300 dpi: a lateral cervical film and full-length standing PA and lateral films, occiput to femoral heads.
Readers: experienced spinal deformity surgeons, most from one multicenter deformity study group.
Second reading at least 1 week later, case order randomized; most returned within 7-14 days.
Fleiss kappa, computed in MATLAB, graded by Landis and Koch: 0.21-0.40 fair, 0.41-0.60 moderate, 0.61-0.80 substantial; as printed, the bands leave 0.40-0.41 and 0.60-0.61 unassigned.
slides.notes: The most important design fact sits in two places. Methods says CBVA and mJOA values were provided directly. The Discussion says readers were given values for all measured parameters, and Figure 7 shows the table each reader saw: mJOA, coronal Cobb, CBVA, C2-7 SVA, TS minus CL, PI minus LL, C7-S1 SVA and PT. So readers did not measure the graded cervical and sagittal values. The table gives no thoracolumbar coronal Cobb, so SRS-Schwab curve type, like the descriptor, had to be judged from the full-length PA film. The authors defend this as removing measurement error at a first step, and they say that if readers had measured, the values would likely have varied, perhaps resulting in greater inter- and intraobserver variation. What that means, ours: this study tests whether surgeons can look up a supplied number in a grading table, plus choose the descriptor and curve type from the images. It does not test the reliability of the classification as used in clinic, where the measuring is most of the work. Other things to notice. Ten cases is a small sample for kappa; the paper gives no confidence intervals and no per-case data, so the precision of each kappa is unknown. Kappa depends on how cases spread across categories, and these cases were picked to cover the categories, which is not how patients present. Fleiss kappa treats grades as unordered, so calling a 2 a 1 counts as fully as calling a 0 a 2; that is a choice the paper does not discuss. Fleiss kappa is a many-rater statistic; the paper does not explain how the mean intrarater value was computed from two readings by each surgeon. Nothing describes training before the first reading, and the authors later say more training would have prevented the C7-S1 SVA errors. The 20 readers were mostly from one study group; the paper does not say whether they were the authors or the Delphi panel, so readers may have known the system's intent better than an outside surgeon would.

slides.title: Results: agreement by item
slides.lead: Fleiss kappa between readers at round 1 and round 2, and within readers across rounds.
points: Our medians across the 9 items: 0.590 at round 1, 0.430 at round 2, 0.633 within readers.
Round 2 agreement was lower than round 1 for 8 of 9 items; only C2-7 SVA rose.
Worst item: C7-S1 SVA, slight between readers in both rounds.
slides.notes: Read the table by column first. Round 1: two items fall below moderate, C2-7 SVA at 0.338 (fair) and C7-S1 SVA at 0.071 (slight). Round 2: three fall below moderate, counting C2-7 SVA at 0.412 as moderate as the authors do (0.412 and mJOA round 1 at 0.602 sit in gaps between the printed bands), and the authors do not list two of them. The deformity descriptor dropped to 0.280 and PI-LL to 0.386, both fair on the paper's own scale. The Results text names only C2-7 SVA round 1 and C7-S1 SVA as the exceptions, and the Discussion says most parameters, including the descriptor, had moderate to substantial agreement for both inter- and intrarater reliability, which is misleading for the descriptor at round 2. The descriptor is the core of the system and, with curve type, one of the parts readers judged from images rather than from a supplied number, and between-reader agreement on it fell from 0.489 to 0.280 on the same ten cases. The fall across nearly every item at round 2 is our observation; the authors do not comment on it. We cannot say why from the paper. Possible reasons, ours: less care on the repeat, or the instability of kappa with ten cases. Now the grading table items. mJOA and CBVA values were handed to readers, so the only task was finding the band. Between-reader kappa was still 0.602 then 0.477 for myelopathy and 0.779 then 0.430 for gaze. The paper says only that agreement was not perfect and gives no reason.
