Our inference: the bands themselves were applied inconsistently, whether from clerical slips, the unassigned CBVA gaps or the round 2 decline, which is a point about the system, not about measurement. C7-S1 SVA: the authors queried readers and found several used absolute values, so a C7-S1 SVA of -9 cm, which should be 0, was scored ++. Figure 7 gives the example case's C7-S1 SVA as -102.4 with no unit, while the cut-offs are in centimeters; mixing units is another plausible source of error, ours. Within-reader agreement was higher than round 2 between-reader agreement for every item. PI-LL within readers was almost perfect at 0.826 while between readers it was fair at round 2: readers were consistent with themselves but not with each other.

slides.title: Reliability is not validity
slides.lead: The same SRS-Schwab grades agreed far less here than in the paper that introduced them.
points: Schwab 2012 numbers are from the library record (D02): 21 premarked cases, 9 readers.
No grade here is tested against HRQOL, myelopathy outcome or surgical result.
Authors' next step: correlate grades and grade changes with HRQOL in a prospective cohort.
slides.notes: This comparison is ours, and it is the most useful thing to bring to the room. The SRS-Schwab classification is a component of this system, and its own reliability paper is in the library (D02, Schwab 2012). That study, as recorded in the master file, had 21 premarked adult deformity cases graded twice by 9 readers, the authors and SRS committee members, and reported reading-2 inter-rater kappas of 0.87 for curve type, 0.86 for PI-LL, 0.98 for PT and 0.96 for SVA. In this paper, with most values typed out for the readers, the same four items reached 0.433, 0.386, 0.627 and 0.064 at round 2. Same grading rules, worse agreement. Reasons we can suggest, all ours: different readers, cervical cases in which the thoracolumbar spine may be near the cut-offs, ten cases, and the C7-S1 SVA sign error. The point for practice: a kappa belongs to the cases, readers and training of one study, not to the classification itself. Now validity. The authors argue that many of the parameters (C2-7 SVA, mJOA, TS-CL, CBVA and the SRS-Schwab type) have already been linked to clinical impact in other studies. That is a claim about each parameter, borrowed from the literature, not a test of this classification. Nothing here shows that a patient graded TS-CL 2 does worse than one graded 0, that the cut-offs are in the right place, or that a change in grade after surgery means a change in how the patient feels. The authors say these remain to be shown. The other paired library record (C05, the CSM-S trial) excluded kyphosis over 5 degrees, so its patients sit at the mild end of what this system describes; that link is ours.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: A useful vocabulary with a soft test; several statements in the paper do not match its own numbers or figures.
points: Strength: brings gaze, myelopathy and global alignment into one cervical description.
Strength: candid that cut-offs are largely expert opinion and that revision is expected.
Weakness: Delphi process not described; ten selected cases; no confidence intervals.
Weakness: readers did not measure; the authors say measured values would likely vary, perhaps lowering agreement.
Weakness: no validity testing of any grade.
slides.notes: Problems inside the paper, found on rereading. One: the Results list only round 1 C2-7 SVA and both rounds of C7-S1 SVA as falling below moderate between readers, but round 2 descriptor (0.280) and round 2 PI-LL (0.386) are also fair. The Discussion's hedged statement that most parameters, including the descriptor, had moderate to substantial agreement is misleading for the descriptor, fair at 0.280 in round 2. Two: the text says the SRS-Schwab classification has 5 coronal curve types and 3 sagittal modifiers; the Figure 6 legend says 4 curve types and 4 sagittal modifiers; Figure 6 itself shows 4 curve types (T, L, D, N) and 3 modifiers. The text is wrong on curve types and the legend on modifiers. Three: the Figure 1 legend defines L as lordosis; in the curve type key of Figure 6, L is a thoracolumbar or lumbar curve. Four: the Figure 1 TS-CL box is headed Cervical Lordosis Minus T1 Slope, the reverse of the TS-CL used everywhere else. Five: Methods says only CBVA and mJOA were supplied; the Discussion and Figure 7 show that all measured values were. Six: the Figure 7 value table gives no units, so C2-7 SVA 45.9 and C7-S1 SVA -102.4 must be read as millimeters against centimeter cut-offs. Our check of Figure 7: with those read as 4.59 cm and -10.2 cm, every numeric grade matches the rules (C2-7 SVA 1, CBVA 6 gives 0, TS-CL 80 gives 2, mJOA 15 gives 1, Cobb 13.4 is under 15 so not type S, PI-LL 9 gives 0, C7-S1 SVA 0, PT 31 gives ++). Curve type N and descriptor C cannot be checked from the table, which has no thoracolumbar Cobb or apex. The abstract's conclusion of moderate agreement is fair as a summary, but our medians show round 2 sat at the low end of moderate (0.430). What is fragile: every kappa rests on ten cases and the paper gives no precision. What is robust: the structure of the system and the reasoning for each modifier.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "Ames 2015 proposed the cervical deformity classification: five descriptor types, C, CT, T, S and CVJ, with modifiers for C2-7 SVA, gaze, TS-CL, mJOA and the SRS-Schwab grades. Twenty surgeons classifying ten selected cases, with the measurements supplied, agreed with each other slightly to substantially, mostly moderately, and the paper tests no link to outcome."
points: Cut-offs: C2-7 SVA 4 and 8 cm; TS-CL 15 and 20 degrees; CBVA 1-10 degrees is grade 0; mJOA 18, 15-17, 12-14, under 12.
Descriptor agreement between readers: 0.489, then 0.280; within readers 0.584.
Weakest item: C7-S1 SVA, from sign confusion over negative values.
Reliability study only; it does not set fusion length, approach or a TS-CL target.
slides.notes: Expect these follow-up questions. Is a TS-CL over 20 degrees a target to correct? Not from this paper. The 15 and 20 degree bands are expert opinion and are not tested against any outcome here. Where does the 4 cm C2-7 SVA come from? From Tang's regression, as cited, linking 4 cm to moderate NDI disability after posterior cervical fusion. The 8 cm band is a doubling borrowed from SRS-Schwab practice, not a data-derived threshold. How reliable is it? Only partly known. With the numbers supplied, agreement between readers ranged from slight to substantial, and fell on the second reading for 8 of 9 items. Real-world reliability, with surgeons measuring their own films, was not tested; the authors say measuring would likely add variance, perhaps lowering agreement. Why was C7-S1 SVA so poor? Readers scored negative values by absolute size, so a -9 cm SVA, which should be 0, was called ++. The authors think more training would have fixed it. Does a higher grade mean a worse patient? Not shown here. The authors planned that test in a prospective multicenter cohort. How does this compare with SRS-Schwab? Our comparison with the library record for Schwab 2012 (D02): on premarked films, that paper's own readers reached kappas of 0.86 to 0.98 for the SRS-Schwab items at reading 2. Here the same items ranged from 0.064 to 0.627. A kappa depends on who reads, what cases and how much training. What does it add to an exam answer? The habit it teaches: classify a cervical deformity by its apex, then always state gaze, myelopathy and whole-spine alignment, because the authors argue cervical deformity should not be assessed in isolation. Watch the figures if you cite them: the paper's text and Figure 6 legend disagree on how many SRS-Schwab curve types and modifiers there are; Figure 6 shows 4 and 3.

decks.not_reviewed: The four source articles themselves (Roussouly 2005, Schwab 2012, Yilgor 2017, Hills 2024) and the later validation studies the review mentions without citing; Figure 1 (the image is omitted in the reformatted PMC copy read here; only its legend, with the GAP formulas, is present); the GAP scoring table the text refers to as '(Table)', which is not in the copy; the typeset journal version, including author affiliations, funding and conflict-of-interest statements, none of which appear in the copy. The Table 1 'Grade' column is cut off at the page edge in this copy ('Mode', 'Low'), so evidence grades were taken from the body text.

slides.title: AO Spine on sagittal alignment planning, 2026
slides.lead: Four landmark alignment papers, each appraised with GRADE and given one recommendation.
points: Journal club: adult spinal deformity
Rienmueller A, et al. Global Spine J 2026;16(6):2490-2497 (volume, issue and pages from the library record; the copy read gives only 2026, PMID 42200259). AO Spine Knowledge Forum Deformity
Design: literature review with clinical recommendations. Four articles chosen by the Forum; consensus at a Forum meeting on July 30, 2025.

Bottom line: Roussouly to describe and anticipate shape; SRS-Schwab to describe deformity, not to plan; GAP for planning and postoperative risk assessment; T4-L1-hip targets for long fusions to the pelvis. All conditional. Evidence moderate, except low for SRS-Schwab.
Read end to end in a reformatted open-access copy. Figure 1 image omitted; Table 1 grade column cut off in this copy.
slides.notes: What this paper is: an expert group picked four papers that trace how we think about the sagittal plane, appraised each in a fixed format and wrote one recommendation per paper. It is a structured journal club, not a systematic review and not a guideline built from a search. The authors frame the four as a progression: descriptive types (Roussouly), categorical radiographic modifiers (SRS-Schwab), proportion to pelvic incidence (GAP), and finally continuous, intraoperatively measurable targets (T4-L1-hip axis). The stated aim is to help a clinician interpret and use this evidence, and the authors say the key takeaway is not to rank the models but to see how each built on the last. The framing problem they set: the question in deformity surgery is no longer whether alignment matters but how to define the right alignment for a given patient. They also say plainly that restoring normal alignment does not guarantee perfect outcomes, and that understanding individual alignment, physiologic tolerance and tissue properties is needed to minimize, not eliminate, the risk of PJK and implant failure. What was reviewed for this deck: the full article text in a reformatted PMC copy. The copy omits images, so Figure 1 (the evolution of alignment targets) was not seen, though its legend with the GAP formulas is present. Table 1 prints, but its last column (Grade) is cut off, so the grades here come from the body text; where readable, they agree. No funding or conflict statement appears in this copy. The source articles themselves were not read; anything said about them comes from this review or, where labeled, from the library records.

slides.title: How it was built, and the four recommendations
slides.lead: One article, one recommendation. All four are conditional; none is strong.

rows: Describe and anticipate sagittal shape; aim for the target shape
Describe and document deformity; not for alignment planning
Preop planning and postop assessment of mechanical risk; not intraop, not stand-alone
L1PA and T4-L1PA mismatch as preop and intraop targets in long fusions to the pelvis

slides.notes: Methods in full, because they are short. The Forum selected articles for relevance to surgical alignment planning in ASD. Each was appraised in a standard format: clinical rationale, study summary, methodological review, quality of evidence (high, moderate, low, very low) and strength of recommendation (strong or conditional). Evidence was graded by the 2013 GRADE Handbook, and each recommendation was built from strength of evidence and expert opinion. Consensus was reached at one Forum meeting on July 30, 2025. The authors say methodological limits and clinical gaps were explicitly considered. What is not described: how the articles were found or why these four, how many experts took part, how consensus was defined or voted, and funding or conflicts. The abstract allows strong recommendations; none was made. Listen for the verb in each: Roussouly and SRS-Schwab 'we suggest', GAP 'we conditionally recommend', T4-L1-hip 'we offer a conditional recommendation'. The SRS-Schwab recommendation is partly negative: it should not be used for alignment planning, because it was not designed for that and ignores compensation and patient variability. Our reading on the grades: three of the four are rated moderate although all are observational or descriptive (a volunteer radiographic series and two retrospective cohorts). GRADE usually starts observational evidence at low, and the paper does not explain what raised these. The SRS-Schwab reliability study is rated low. Treat the grades as the panel's judgment rather than a reproducible calculation. Table 1 also cites each model with reference numbers that do not match the reference list; see the appraisal slide.

slides.title: Describing the spine: Roussouly and SRS-Schwab
slides.lead: Both describe. Neither was built to give a surgical target.

rows: 4 morphotypes by sacral slope, each with its own lordotic and kyphotic arcs, apices and inflection points
Coronal curve type plus 3 sagittal modifiers (PT, PI-LL, SVA), each in 3 grades
Types strongly related to particular curve shapes
Inter- and intra-rater agreement averages excellent for all modifiers, kappa above 0.80
Young, all-European volunteers; no link to surgical outcome
Descriptive only; does not allow for how PI-LL and PT vary with PI; postural measures

slides.notes: Roussouly. The appraisers credit prospective enrollment, standardized positioning, defined inclusion criteria and digital measurement. The limits are a young, all-European volunteer cohort and no relationship to surgical outcome; the original authors themselves called for longitudinal follow-up. The most useful line for practice is the authors' own: the preoperative Roussouly type matters less than understanding the target shape, the postoperative type. In other words, ask what shape this pelvis should carry, not what shape the degenerate spine has now. Two cautions. The recommendation paragraph says the classification tends towards poor inter-rater reliability, complicating adoption. That point is given without a citation and does not appear in the methodological review or in Table 1, and the paper does not say why that did not lower the grade. Also, Table 1 lists 'no target parameters' as a limitation, while the text says recognizing the baseline type may help set alignment targets. The two fit if 'targets' means a shape to aim for, not a number. That reconciliation is ours. SRS-Schwab. The appraisers value its structure, reliability and immediate usefulness, and rate the evidence low. Their central criticism: the classification is descriptive, the original paper offered no alignment targets, and the modifiers were later adopted as targets anyway. It also does not account for the variable relationship between PI and the categories it uses, such as PI-LL and PT. Our reading: a reliability study on 21 cases tells you surgeons agree on the label, not that the label predicts anything. The Introduction adds that PT and SVA cannot be measured intraoperatively. Library check: D11 (160 volunteers) and D02 (21 cases, 9 readers) match these numbers; both library records are abstract level.

slides.title: GAP score: proportion to pelvic incidence
slides.lead: Yilgor 2017: 222 patients, 6 European centers, at least 4 posterior fused levels, minimum 2-year follow-up.
points: Four PI-specific parameters plus an age factor: relative pelvic version, relative lumbar lordosis, lordosis distribution index, relative spinopelvic alignment.
Scored on postoperative standing films. Several parameters cannot be measured prone, so not an intraoperative tool.
Internal validation only; later external studies performed slightly worse, in the authors' words.
slides.see: Figure 1 legend gives the PI-based formulas, e.g. relative lumbar lordosis = LL - (PI x 0.62 + 29).
slides.notes: Why GAP mattered: the appraisers say fixed targets like PI-LL, SVA and PT do not consistently track mechanical complications, are posture dependent, and force categories onto a continuum. GAP replaced fixed numbers with targets proportional to each patient's PI. Entry to the European database required at least one of coronal Cobb 20 degrees or more, SVA 5 cm or more, PT 25 degrees or more, or thoracic kyphosis 60 degrees or more. Health-related quality of life also differed across categories. How to read the table: the rates are within category, and the review gives no group sizes, so we cannot recompute them or judge how precise the 95% is. Library check: the D05 record (abstract level) gives 148 derivation and 74 validation patients, which add to the 222 here, and a validation AUC of 0.92. That is an internal split of the same cohort. A worked example, our arithmetic from the legend formulas: with PI 50, the ideal lumbar lordosis is 0.62 x 50 + 29 = 60 degrees, and the ideal sacral slope is 0.59 x 50 + 9 = 38.5 degrees. Limits named by the appraisers: retrospective, so selection bias; no external validation cohort; a classifier rather than a probability model; possible collinearity among the metrics; incorporation bias from relative spinopelvic alignment; and postural measures that cannot be used as intraoperative targets. They add that predictive power may be limited in elderly or osteoporotic patients, without data. Two inconsistencies to flag. The methodological review says the large multicenter European cohort enhances external validity, then says the lack of external validation raises questions about applicability, and Table 1 lists 'external validity challenged'. And the recommendation first says to use GAP in postoperative assessment, then says it is best used in preoperative planning and postoperative assessment; Table 1 covers both planning and postoperative risk. Also, the Figure 1 legend calls RSA 'Relative Sagittal Angle', while the text calls it relative spinopelvic alignment. The firm points are not intraoperative and not a stand-alone predictor.

slides.title: T4-L1-hip axis: continuous targets you can measure prone
slides.lead: Hills 2024: multicenter retrospective cohort of long constructs fused to the sacrum or pelvis.

rows: 247 ASD, fused from T1-T5 to sacrum or pelvis
PJK, rod fracture, or revision for either, within 2 years
0.5 x PI - 19 degrees, plus or minus 2

points: Risk rose with deviation in either direction: undercorrection and overcorrection, a nonlinear relationship.
Higher postoperative C2PA was linked to worse 1-year scores in all SRS domains and ODI.
Applies only to fusions from the upper thoracic spine to the sacrum or pelvis. External validation needed.
slides.notes: Why this model: vertebral-pelvic angles (L1PA, T4PA) are directly modifiable in surgery and, in the authors' account, more closely linked with PI and global alignment than Cobb measures. Earlier work defined normal T4-L1-hip alignment in adults without deformity or degeneration; this 247-patient surgical cohort tested whether realignment to normal lowered mechanical failure, and the lowest-risk ranges on this slide are the ones this cohort found. Worked examples, our arithmetic: PI 50 gives an L1PA target of 6 degrees (4 to 8); PI 70 gives 16 degrees (14 to 18). Our arithmetic again: 28% of 247 is about 69 patients with a mechanical complication. Strengths named: a homogeneous long-construct sample that limits confounding from UIV level, outcomes confirmed by 2 independent spine surgeons, and multivariable nonlinear regression on continuous variables without arbitrary thresholds. Limits named: observational design with possible unmeasured confounding, including preoperative cervicothoracic alignment and surgical technique; misclassification of failure; use only in long constructs; and later work showing the T4-L1PA relationship varies with PI, lower PI carrying a larger T4PA. The text prints 'T4PI' in that sentence, which we read as T4PA. Read the functional claim carefully. The recommendation says the targets were associated with lower mechanical risk and improved function. The function link shown here runs through C2PA: change in T4PA tracked change in C2PA, and higher C2PA tracked worse 1-year scores. That is indirect, and that reading is ours. The authors also say these are regional targets and do not define segment-specific alignment. Library check: the D14 record (abstract level) gives the same 247 and the same L1PA target.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: Holds up: one fixed appraisal format, GRADE language, limits stated for every model, and a clear statement that alignment alone does not prevent failure.
Four articles chosen by the group; selected for relevance to alignment planning, but no search, explicit inclusion criteria, panel size or voting method described.
All four sources are observational or descriptive. Three rated moderate without a stated reason.
GAP: external validity praised and doubted in the same section; recommendation names postoperative use first, then planning and postoperative use. RSA named two ways.
Discussion says planning systems ignore age, yet GAP includes an age factor.
Table 1 reference numbers do not match the reference list.
No funding or conflict statement in the copy; author list includes Yilgor C and Hills J, the lead-author names on the GAP and T4-L1-hip papers.
slides.notes: Be fair first. This is a teaching review, and it does that well: it explains why each model was built, what it measures and what it cannot do, and it refuses to crown a winner. The Discussion's point is sound and worth repeating: radiographic targets do not capture age, bone density, muscle quality, comorbidity or physiologic reserve, and 'perfect' alignment in a patient who cannot tolerate the operation may add morbidity. The weaknesses are ours unless stated. Selection: four papers, chosen by the group, with no search. Other alignment work is mentioned only in passing, for example subsequent external validation of GAP and later analyses of T4-L1PA by PI, without citations. Authorship: the author list in the library record includes Yilgor C and Hills J, the same names as the lead authors of the GAP and T4-L1-hip papers. If they are the same people, that is expertise, but the copy carries no conflict statement, and the two newest models get the firmest wording ('recommend' rather than 'suggest'), though Roussouly is rated moderate evidence too. Grading: moderate for a volunteer radiographic series and two retrospective cohorts is generous by usual GRADE rules, and no upgrade reason is given. Internal problems in the text: the Discussion says current planning systems fail to include age, but the GAP score as described includes an age factor. The GAP methodological review praises external validity and then says there was no external validation. The GAP recommendation's first sentence names postoperative assessment only; the next adds preoperative planning, which matches Table 1. The Figure 1 legend defines RSA as Relative Sagittal Angle; the text calls it relative spinopelvic alignment. Table 1 cites Roussouly as reference 8, SRS-Schwab as 3, GAP as 4 and T4-L1-hip as 5; the reference list has them as 10, 4, 5 and 6, and reference 8 is a different paper. The Discussion cites references 3 and 4 for norms in asymptomatic adults; reference 4 is the SRS-Schwab classification study, which the review describes as 21 deformity cases. The T4 section prints 'T4PI' for T4PA. The Roussouly reliability concern is uncited. Copy problems, not the authors': Table 1's grade column is cut off and Figure 1 is missing. None of this changes the four recommendations, but it does mean the details should be checked against the source papers before teaching numbers.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "AO Spine's 2026 review says: use Roussouly to understand shape, SRS-Schwab only to describe deformity, GAP to plan and to judge mechanical risk on standing films, and L1PA and T4-L1PA mismatch as intraoperative targets in long fusions to the pelvis. All are conditional, and none replaces patient factors such as bone quality and reserve."

rows: Four morphotypes linked to sacral orientation and lordosis distribution
High reliability of curve types and modifiers
Deviation from L1PA and T4-L1PA targets linked to more failure

points: Library entries come from the master records, all at abstract level.
Do not stretch it: no target is offered for short constructs, and no model here predicts failure on its own.
slides.notes: Expect five follow-up questions. Which of these can I use on the table? Only the T4-L1-hip measures. L1PA and T4-L1PA mismatch can be measured intraoperatively; the authors say GAP is not designed for intraoperative use because several parameters cannot be measured prone, and the Introduction says PT and SVA cannot be measured intraoperatively. If my patient is GAP proportioned, am I safe? No. Proportioned patients still had a 6% mechanical complication rate, and the authors say GAP is not a stand-alone prediction tool. The Introduction makes a related point: restoring normal alignment does not guarantee perfect outcomes, and even a full individual assessment only minimizes, and does not eliminate, PJK and implant failure risk. Do the T4-L1-hip targets apply to a fusion stopping at T10? No. The authors say the findings apply only to constructs from the upper thoracic spine to the sacrum or pelvis. The paper offers no target for shorter fusions. Is SRS-Schwab obsolete? Not for description and communication, which is what the recommendation keeps. It should not be used for alignment planning. What about the frail or osteoporotic patient? The Discussion says purely radiographic planning ignores biologic reserve, bone density and muscle quality, and that the aim is to normalize alignment within what the patient can tolerate. The paper gives no rule for how far to compromise; that remains judgment. One sentence to close: the field has moved from naming shapes, to proportions of pelvic incidence, to continuous angles you can measure prone, and every step is still observational, so these are targets to aim for, not guarantees.

decks.not_reviewed: The online Disclosure of Potential Conflicts of Interest forms (links.lww.com/JBJS/I191) were not reviewed. The paper cites no supplement. The source paper for the normal-alignment formula (Hills 2022, Spine, ref 19) was not reviewed, so the normal L1PA formula and the 4 degree normal T4-L1PA range are taken as this paper reports them. The PDF is the complete 10-page article (e48(1) to e48(10)), not a critique. Figure 4 counts were read from the bar chart; they sum to the reported 247 patients and 68 failures.

slides.title: Hills 2024: The T4-L1-Hip Axis, realignment targets in long-construct ASD surgery
slides.lead: Bottom line: in 247 ISSG patients fused from T1-T5 to the sacrum, 6-week alignment close to a PI-based L1PA target with T4 stacked over L1 went with fewer mechanical failures by 2 years. The targets were found and tested in the same patients.
points: Journal club · Adult deformity alignment
Hills J, Mundis GM, ... Kelly MP, International Spine Study Group. J Bone Joint Surg Am 2024;106(23):e48
Design: retrospective analysis of a prospective multicenter registry; authors grade it Therapeutic Level III
Target L1PA = 0.5 × PI − 19° ± 2°; target T4-L1PA mismatch −3° to +1°
slides.notes: This deck was prepared from the full 10-page article, not just the abstract and not a critique. The online conflict-of-interest forms and the 2022 normal-alignment paper that supplies the formula were not reviewed. Frame the paper from the start: it is an attempt to replace postural targets (PT, SVA) and PI-LL with two angles a surgeon controls directly on the table and that stay fixed once a T4-to-sacrum construct is in. The authors argue earlier schemes fail to validate because they use postural measures, cut continuous measures into categories, are built from asymptomatic rather than disease-free spines, and mix fusion lengths. This study answers the categorisation complaint by modelling continuously, the asymptomatic-versus-disease-free complaint by taking normal values from ref 19 (spines without degeneration or deformity), and the mixed-length complaint by restricting to long fusions to the sacrum. What it cannot do is show that aiming for these numbers lowers failure. The targets are the low point of a curve fitted to these 247 patients, and the comparison of at-target against off-target patients reuses those same patients. The authors say future studies will be needed to validate the findings. The abstract hedges: realignment to the targets 'may lead to fewer mechanical failures'. The body Conclusions go further: realignment based on these targets 'carried a lower risk of mechanical failure'. That stronger claim reuses the derivation sample; it is a hypothesis this cohort generated, not one it tested. Three aims: set L1PA and T4-L1PA targets that minimise mechanical failure; show how T4PA change drives C2PA change; and relate early C2PA to 1-year PROMs. The ISSG is funded by research grants from several implant companies and by individual donations, as the disclosure states.

slides.title: The question and the angles
slides.lead: Can PI-based targets for L1PA and T4PA, both set in surgery, predict who will fail mechanically after a long fusion to the sacrum?
points: Each vertebral-pelvic angle runs from a vertebral body centre to the femoral-head midpoint to the centre of the S1 endplate
L1PA reflects how much lordosis there is and where it sits
T4-L1PA mismatch = T4PA − L1PA. Positive means T4 is ventral to L1; at 0 the T4-to-hip line passes through L1
Normal spines, as reported from ref 19: L1PA = 0.5 × PI − 21°, T4PA within 4° of L1PA
C2PA = PT + C2 tilt and is the global measure. The authors treat it as an outcome, not a target
slides.notes: The table is our arithmetic from the two formulas: for PI 40, 0.5 x 40 - 21 = -1 for normal, and 0.5 x 40 - 19 = 1, plus or minus 2, for the target. Have the learner do one row aloud. The point to notice is that the risk-minimising L1PA sits 0 to 4 degrees above normal, which means slightly less lordosis than the normal spine formula, not more. The authors state this as 'a deviation from normal of between 0 and 4 degrees'. They do not explain why the optimum sits off normal. Our reading is that in older fused patients a little less than normal lordosis may suit the hips and the junction, but that is ours, not tested. Direction matters when you read the rest. A higher L1PA means less lordosis relative to PI. The paper calls L1PA above target 'undercorrection' and below target 'overcorrection'. For the mismatch, positive means T4 sits in front of L1, a kyphotic or forward thoracic segment relative to the lumbar spine; normal is a mismatch of 0, within 4 degrees either way; the target band, -3 to +1, lies inside that range but is centred at -1, slightly dorsal to 0. The authors' case for these angles: they are measurable on intraoperative prone films that show the femoral heads, T4 and L1; normal L1PA tracks PI more tightly than lumbar lordosis does; and once L1PA and T4PA are right, an appropriate lordosis follows, so a separate LL target is unnecessary. C2PA is geometrically PT plus C2 tilt, which Figure 2 bears out in both example patients (28 + 5 = 33; 16 - 2 = 14; 32 + 9 = 41; 30 + 0 = 30).

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: A registry cohort restricted to long fusions so that L1PA and T4PA are fixed inside the construct.
points: ISSG registry, 15 centres, 2008-2019. Registry entry: age 18 or over plus scoliosis >20°, SVA >5 cm, PT >25° or TK >60°
342 fused T1-T5 to sacrum or pelvis; excluded 68 without 2-year films, 23 prior upper-thoracic-to-lumbar fusion, 4 long cervical fusion; 247 analysed
Median age 64, 82% female, 92% White; 34% prior fusion, 25% 3-column osteotomy, 53% PJK prophylaxis; UIV T4 in 51%
Mechanical failure within 2 years: severe PJK (spondylolisthesis or >30° PJA increase), displaced rod fracture, or reoperation for junctional failure, pseudarthrosis or rod fracture
Predictors measured on 6-week films. Logistic regression with restricted cubic splines for L1PA deviation and T4-L1PA mismatch, adjusted for age only
PROMs (ODI, SRS-22r) at 1 year; missing values multiply imputed
slides.notes: The flow arithmetic checks: 342 - 68 - 23 - 4 = 247. Table I percentages all recompute from 247. Medians are shown; the paper gives IQRs. Notice what the table says about these patients. Their median preoperative L1PA was already only about 3 degrees from normal. The big preoperative abnormality was the T4-L1PA mismatch of about 12 degrees, T4 well in front of L1, which surgery brought to a median of 0.7. So in this cohort, the operation mostly fixed the thoracic-to-lumbar relationship. Median PI-LL went from 18.9 to -0.3 degrees. Things to say about the methods. 68 of 342 (20%, ours) were lost for lack of 2-year radiographs; the paper does not compare them with those kept. The failure window is 2 years although median follow-up was 3.1 years; the authors class later pseudarthrosis and slow, progressive PJK as biological failure rather than alignment failure. Two fellowship-trained spine surgeons independently reviewed every radiograph for failure; the paper does not say whether they knew the alignment values, and agreement between them is not reported. Films were measured centrally with validated software. Arm position changed over the study, from hands on clavicles to hands in front once biplanar imaging came in. The only adjustment was age. Prior fusion (34%), 3-column osteotomy, PJK prophylaxis, UIV level, BMI and bone density were not in the model. The authors say bone density, prophylaxis and sarcopenia were left out because they are 'unlikely to be associated with surgical alignment'. That is an assumption, not a finding. The number of spline knots, model degrees of freedom and any check on overfitting are not reported. With 68 events and two spline terms plus age, the model has limited room (our point). The number of patients with PROMs at 1 year, and how much was imputed, are not given.

slides.title: Primary result: the failure curve and the targets
slides.lead: 68 of 247 (28%) failed within 2 years. Risk rose with deviation in either direction from the low point of the fitted curve.
points: Risk lowest at L1PA 0.5 × PI − 19° ± 2° (0° to 4° above normal) and T4-L1PA mismatch −3° to +1°
L1PA deviation +14° vs +2°: aOR 7.0 (95% CI 2.3 to 21.6)
T4-L1PA mismatch +10° vs −1°: aOR 7.2 (2.9 to 17.9)
Age 65 vs 50: aOR 0.7 (0.4 to 1.2), from Figure 3-B
Failure types (Table I): pseudarthrosis or rod fracture 46, junctional or PJK 30; they overlap
slides.see: Figure 3-A shows the U-shaped failure curves for four mismatch values; Figure 4 shows these groups with failure type.
slides.notes: Counts were read from Figure 4 and sum to 247 and 68. The 50% and 7% rates match the caption. Under means L1PA above target (too little lordosis); over means below target. Ventral means mismatch above +1; dorsal means below -3. How to read it. Only 28 patients (11%, ours) reached both targets. The comparison is 2 of 28 against 23 of 46 in the worst group, with the target ranges chosen from these patients. The mismatch looks like the stronger axis (ours, from Figure 4): with T4 at target, 8 of 81 failed (10%); with T4 off target, 60 of 166 (36%). In the worst group most failures were pseudarthrosis or rod fracture, not PJK. That fits the authors' account of bending moments acting on the construct. The odds ratios compare far points on the curve: an L1PA 14 degrees above normal against one 2 above, and a mismatch of +10 against -1. These are big contrasts chosen by the authors. They are not the effect of a degree or two near target. The Figure 3-B caption calls them deviations 'versus normal alignment', but the reference points (+2 and -1) are the target centres, not normal (0 and 0). The abstract and Results also say deviation from normal 'in either direction' raised risk, yet a small positive L1PA deviation (0 to +4) was where risk was lowest; read it as deviation from the curve's low point, as the lead does. Both intervals are symmetric on the log scale (geometric midpoints 7.05 and 7.20), so the printing is consistent. In Figure 3-A the four curves have the same shape and are only shifted up or down. That suggests no L1PA-by-mismatch interaction was modelled, although the paper does not say. Figure 4 caption and Results say the worst group was T4 ventral with L1PA undercorrected. Two cautions. First, the minimum of a fitted curve is itself uncertain, and no confidence interval for the target bounds is reported; the plus or minus 2 is a range, not a CI. Second, Figure 4 sorts patients into one failure reason each (27 PJK and 41 pseudarthrosis or rod fracture by our bar reading), while Table I counts 46 and 30 with overlap. The paper does not explain the difference. Age was not significant, and the point estimate shows older patients at lower odds. The paper's figure caption describes the age contrast as 50 versus 65 while the plot shows 65 versus 50.

slides.title: Secondary aims: global alignment and PROMs
slides.lead: Change in T4PA tracked change in C2PA almost exactly; higher 6-week C2PA went with modestly worse 1-year scores.
points: Change in T4PA vs change in C2PA: r² = 0.96 (P < 0.001)
Change in L1PA vs change in C2PA: r² = 0.54 (P < 0.001)
Models for 1-year PROMs adjusted for the baseline score and age; coefficients are per degree of 6-week C2PA
slides.see: Figure 5 shows the tight T4PA-C2PA scatter against the looser L1PA one.
slides.notes: The r-squared of 0.96 needs care. T4PA and C2PA share the same pelvic arm (femoral heads to S1), and once T4 to the sacrum is fused solid, C2PA can only change by what happens above T4. A near-perfect correlation is close to what the geometry requires (our reading). It shows that the fused segment carries most of the change in global alignment. It does not show that T4PA causes a better outcome. The authors use it to say surgical plans that include T4PA 'can reliably predict postoperative standing sagittal alignment'. There is also a timing problem. Methods say the change in T4PA and L1PA was measured from preop to 6 weeks and the change in C2PA from preop to final follow-up. The Figure 5 caption says 'the change in T4PA at the time of final follow-up'. The Results sentence and the abstract can be read either way (the phrase may attach to the C2PA change, which fits Methods). The paper does not settle which. The Discussion points to Figure 6 for this result; it is Figure 5. PROMs: the ODI slope of 0.24 per degree recomputes (P about 0.006 from the CI). It is small per degree. Across the C2PA IQR at 6 weeks (11.5 to 24.9, about 13 degrees) it is about 3 ODI points (ours). For SRS Pain, -0.02 per degree is about -0.3 over the same span. These are associations after adjusting for baseline score and age only, at 1 year, in patients with complete or imputed data. The number who answered at 1 year is not given. Coefficients are printed to two decimals, so their P values are hard to check: Self-Image and Subscore both show an age coefficient of 0.01 (0.00 to 0.02), with P values of 0.20 and 0.003. Rounding probably explains this, but it cannot be verified from the print. The authors' wording 'more disability, more pain, and worse self-image' is right in direction. Say the size out loud.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: A coherent, surgeon-controllable framework, but the targets were derived and tested in the same 247 patients with only age adjusted.
points: Strengths: continuous modelling, homogeneous long-to-sacrum constructs, central measurement, two-surgeon failure review, prospective registry
Targets come from the same data used to show they work; no internal or external validation, no CI on the bounds
Confounding: only age adjusted; osteotomy, prophylaxis, prior fusion, UIV, bone density and surgeon not modelled
20% of eligible patients excluded for missing 2-year films
Failure outcome mixes PJK and pseudarthrosis or rod fracture and stops at 2 years
Applies only to T1-T5 to sacrum; no guidance on UIV or shorter constructs, as the authors state
slides.notes: The core issue is circularity. The model found where failure was lowest in these patients, and Figure 4 then shows that patients in that zone failed least. That is expected by construction. It is not independent evidence. Optimism from fitting splines to 68 events is not assessed: no bootstrap, no C-statistic, no calibration. The authors do say future studies will be needed to validate. What was done about bias. Two attending surgeons independently reviewed all follow-up films for failure, and severe PJK and displaced rod fracture count even without revision, which the authors use to limit misclassification. Their limitations section also names unmeasured confounding, surgeon-level factors and performance bias, and the small sample from retrospective design. What they do not address: how the 68 excluded patients differed; whether failure reviewers were blinded to alignment; why the optimum sits 0 to 4 degrees above normal L1PA rather than at normal; and the composite outcome. Rod fracture and pseudarthrosis dominate the failures, and these reflect construct strain, rod choice and biology as well as alignment. Our inference: whether a patient lands on target is partly a marker of the operation chosen. A 3-column osteotomy, a larger correction and PJK prophylaxis all change both alignment and failure risk. Leaving them out could make alignment look more powerful than it is, or less. The authors' claim that bone density and prophylaxis are unlikely to relate to alignment is untested here. Internal inconsistencies worth knowing: the Figure 2-A caption gives the normal L1PA range for PI 47 as -1.5 to 6.5 degrees, but the normal formula gives a single 2.5; the range is 2.5 plus or minus 4, a tolerance never defined for L1PA; Figure 3-B labelling deviations 'versus normal' when the reference points are the target centres; 'either direction' from normal when a small positive deviation carried the lowest risk; the Figure 5 versus Methods timing of T4PA change; the Discussion pointing to Figure 6 instead of 5; and Figure 4 failure-type counts differing from Table I. Library context: the SRS-Schwab thresholds in the D03 record (PI-LL 11 degrees or more, PT 22 or more, SVA 47 mm or more) were associations with disability (ODI above 40), and the age-specific values in D04 were derived from population SF-36 norms; neither used mechanical failure. This paper changes the endpoint and the measures, so the numbers do not convert directly.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: In ISSG patients fused from the upper thoracic spine to the sacrum, a 6-week L1PA of 0.5 × PI − 19° ± 2° with T4 stacked over L1 went with the fewest 2-year mechanical failures, 7% against 50% in the worst group. The targets have not been validated outside the cohort that produced them.
points: Expect: what is L1PA and why use it rather than LL? From the centre of L1 to the hip axis to S1; it captures size and distribution of lordosis and is fixed in surgery
Expect: what does a positive mismatch mean? T4 ventral to L1; above +1° with too little lordosis was the worst group
Expect: is the target normal alignment? Not exactly. It is centred about 2° above normal L1PA and about 1° dorsal on the mismatch, set where this cohort failed least
Expect: does hitting it prevent failure? Not shown. Same-sample derivation, age-only adjustment, no validation
Expect: what about PROMs? Higher 6-week C2PA, about 0.24 ODI points per degree worse at 1 year
Expect: shorter fusions? Not studied
slides.notes: A 30-second version: 'Hills and the ISSG took 247 patients fused from T1 to T5 down to the sacrum and modelled 2-year mechanical failure against two angles on the 6-week film. Failure was lowest when L1PA sat at half the PI minus 19 degrees, plus or minus 2, and when T4PA was within -3 to +1 degree of L1PA. Only 28 patients hit both, and 2 of them failed; in the worst group, T4 ahead of L1 with too little lordosis, half failed, mostly from rod fracture or pseudarthrosis. The targets came from this same cohort, only age was adjusted, and they still need external validation. T4PA change explained nearly all of C2PA change, which is largely geometry in a fused T4-to-sacrum spine.' Likely follow-ups and short answers. Why not PI-LL? The authors argue PI-LL ignores where the lordosis sits and that normal PI-LL varies with PI. Why 6-week films? Alignment is fixed inside the construct, and the 6-week film is the first standing measure after surgery. Was age protective? The point estimate was 0.7 for 65 versus 50 years, with a CI crossing 1; do not claim a protective effect. Was this a randomised test of planning? No, observational Level III. What would convince you? Our view: a separate cohort, ideally prospective, planned to these targets, with failure rates compared against usual planning and the analysis adjusted for osteotomy, prophylaxis and bone density. How does it sit in the library? D13, the AO Spine planning review, lists the T4-L1-hip axis alongside Roussouly, SRS-Schwab and GAP as complementary models, per its record.

decks.not_reviewed: The companion observational-cohort article, the design paper (reference 13), later SPORT disk follow-ups beyond 2 years, and the typeset JAMA version (the PDF read is the complete NIH author manuscript). The paper cites no supplement.

slides.title: Weinstein 2006: SPORT, surgery vs nonoperative care for lumbar disk herniation
slides.lead: Bottom line: both assigned groups improved a great deal over 2 years. Intent-to-treat differences on the primary outcomes were small and not significant, mostly favoring surgery (physical function at 2 years was 0), and crossover in both directions kept the trial from showing either superiority or equivalence.
points: Journal club · Disc herniation: surgery or not
Weinstein JN, et al. JAMA 2006;296:2441-50
Randomized cohort only: 501 patients, 13 US spine centers, 2 years
slides.notes: This is the randomized disk herniation arm of the Spine Patient Outcomes Research Trial. SPORT also enrolled an observational cohort of patients who chose their own treatment; that cohort is reported in a companion article and is not covered here. The comparison is assignment to open diskectomy against assignment to usual nonoperative care. Keep one fact in mind from the start: by 2 years 60% of the surgery arm and 45% of the nonoperative arm had been operated on, so the two arms were far less different in treatment than their names suggest. This deck was prepared from the full text of the NIH Public Access author manuscript, which is complete: Methods, Results, Comment, Figures 1 to 3 and Tables 1 to 5. It is not a critique. Page layout and minor wording may differ from the typeset JAMA version, which was not seen. The paper cites no supplement. The design paper (reference 13), the companion observational article and later SPORT disk follow-ups were not reviewed, so the deck says nothing beyond 2 years.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: Diskectomy was the most common US operation for back and leg symptoms, yet its benefit over nonoperative care was disputed. Does surgery do better?
points: Why it was open: herniations appear on imaging without symptoms and can regress without surgery.
Practice varied: up to 15-fold regional variation in US diskectomy rates, and lower rates abroad.
Earlier trials: the authors cite baseline differences, small samples or unvalidated outcome measures.

rows: Surgical candidates with imaging-confirmed herniation and radiculopathy for at least 6 weeks
Usual nonoperative care, individualized by the treating physician
Change in SF-36 bodily pain, SF-36 physical function and ODI to 2 years

slides.notes: Set the stakes. The authors frame this as an efficacy question: is surgery better than nonoperative care for a herniated disk? They point to up to 15-fold regional variation in diskectomy rates and the lower rates outside the US as reasons to doubt the appropriateness of some operations. SPORT was set up to compare surgical and nonoperative treatment for disk herniation, spinal stenosis and degenerative spondylolisthesis, and the trial included both a randomized and an observational cohort. This paper is the disk herniation randomized cohort, intent to treat, through 2 years. Enrollment ran from March 2000 to November 2004. Two design choices shape everything that follows. First, patients saw evidence-based videotapes on the expected benefits, risks and uncertainties of each option before consent, and then could choose the randomized trial or the observational cohort. Second, nonoperative care was deliberately left to the physician and patient. Ask the room before showing results: what happens when well-informed surgical candidates are randomized but stay free to change course? The answer drives the whole paper. The authors cite Weber's trial (reference 8) as the most comparable earlier study, with 26% crossover into surgery at 1 year and only 2% out of it. That figure is their account of Weber; Weber is not a library record. Note the question the design can answer cleanly is narrower than the efficacy question: intent to treat measures the effect of being assigned to a strategy.

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: Of 1991 eligible patients, 501 (25%) were randomized; 747 refused and 743 chose the observational cohort.
points: Included: age 18 or older; radicular pain below the knee (anterior thigh for upper levels); positive tension sign or matching deficit; MRI (97%) or CT herniation at the matching level and side.
Excluded: prior lumbar surgery, cauda equina syndrome, scoliosis over 15°, instability, fracture, infection, tumor, or unwilling to have surgery within 6 months.
Surgery: standard open diskectomy; loupes or microscope encouraged.
Nonoperative: usual care; protocol minimum of active physical therapy, education with home exercise, and NSAIDs if tolerated.
Randomized by computer in permuted blocks within site; analyzed 232 of 245 and 240 of 256 with any follow-up.
Power: 250 per group, 85% power for a 10-point SF-36 difference, allowing 20% missing data but no nonadherence.
slides.see: Figure 1, the flow diagram, gives cumulative surgery, missed visits and withdrawals for each arm at every follow-up.
slides.notes: Who got in: mean age 42, 59% male, 16% on compensation. Every patient had leg pain, 96 to 98% dermatomal. Any neurologic deficit 73% vs 74%, motor weakness 42% vs 39%. Herniations were mostly L5-S1 (59% vs 57%) and extrusions (67% vs 65%). Baseline SF-36 bodily pain about 27, physical function about 39, ODI 47.5 vs 46.3. 81% vs 76% were under 6 months from the start of the episode. Before enrollment, 67% had physical therapy, 42% epidural injections and 40% opioids. We recomputed the Table 1 P values: none reaches 0.05, matching the paper's footnote. The flow diagram adds up in every box. Now the crossover table. The percentages use the analyzed patients (232 and 240) as denominators, per the Figure 1 footnote. Over all randomized patients, 2-year surgery would be 57% and 42% (our arithmetic), and surgery among the 29 never followed is unknown. Read the 2-year gap: only 15 percentage points separate the arms. Table 4 shows who crossed. Those assigned surgery who did not have it were older, had better pain, function and ODI, and more often upper lumbar herniations. Those assigned nonoperative care who had surgery had worse pain, function and ODI and lower incomes. We recomputed Table 4 and its P values reproduce. Power: the paper gives no SD, so the 250 per group cannot be checked; our back-calculation implies an SD of change of about 33 to 37 points. The analysis excluded 13 and 16 patients with no follow-up, so strictly it is a modified intent-to-treat on 472 of 501 (our label). Data were available for 73% to 86% of an arm at each visit, and missing rates were similar between arms.

slides.title: Primary outcomes: pain, function, disability
slides.lead: Intent to treat: both arms improved by large amounts, and the between-group differences were small.
points: Surgery minus nonoperative change. Positive SF-36 and negative ODI favor surgery.
Global tests across all times: bodily pain P=.74, physical function P=.71, ODI P=.21.
1-year change, surgery vs nonoperative: bodily pain +39.7 vs +36.9; ODI −30.6 vs −27.4.
The ODI 3-month interval excludes zero, though the text says no time point was significant.
slides.see: Figure 2 shows the bodily pain and physical function curves almost on top of each other, both far above baseline and still below the age-sex SF-36 norms; the ODI curve for surgery sits visibly below the nonoperative curve from 6 weeks through 2 years.
slides.notes: How to read this. Each number is the difference in change from baseline, from a mixed model controlling for center. These estimate the effect of being assigned to surgery, with 60% vs 45% actually operated on by 2 years. Three things to notice. First, the size of the within-group change dwarfs the gap: both arms gained 37 to 40 points of bodily pain. The authors put the large nonoperative improvement partly down to the 43% of that arm who had surgery by 1 year. Second, the global tests ask whether there is any difference at any time point. They were clearly negative. Our reading: a global test across five time points is not built to detect a small difference, so a negative global test does not mean the curves are identical. Only 3 of the 5 time points are tabulated, and the gaps are not uniform: bodily pain about 3 points at each, physical function shrinking from 2.8 to 0, ODI from −4.7 to −2.7. Third, the ODI at 3 months. Its printed interval, −9.3 to −0.2, excludes zero; our estimate is P about 0.04. The text says the primary effects were not significant at any point. Treat that single time point as fragile: one of 15 comparisons, with no multiplicity correction reported. Now the useful reading of the intervals (ours). The protocol targeted a 10-point SF-36 difference. At 1 and 2 years the upper bounds were 7.8 and 8.4 for bodily pain and 6.5 and 5.5 for physical function. So for the strategy of assigning surgery, as delivered here with crossover, a 10-point SF-36 gain is unlikely. That says nothing direct about the effect of surgery itself in a patient who has it. Sensitivity analyses gave 1-year effects of 1.6 to 2.9 for bodily pain, 0.74 to 1.4 for physical function and −2.2 to −3.3 for ODI, so the result does not hinge on the missing-data method. Our check: every Table 5 interval matches the arm SEs treated as independent, and every difference matches the arm means within rounding.

slides.title: Secondary outcomes, as-treated analysis and harms
slides.lead: Sciatica bothersomeness and self-rated progress favored surgery on intent to treat; the as-treated analysis showed much larger effects.
points: As-treated, adjusted, 1 year: bodily pain 15.0 (10.9 to 19.2), physical function 17.5 (13.6 to 21.5), ODI −15.0 (−18.3 to −11.7), sciatica −3.2 (−4.3 to −2.1).
Harms (Table 3, detailed data on 243 of 247 operated): dural tear 10 (4%), superficial infection 4 (2%, apparently of 239 with postoperative data), transfusion 4 (2%), no perioperative deaths.
Reoperation 4% at 1 year and 5% at 2 years (Kaplan-Meier); 5 of the 9 at 1 year were recurrent herniation.
No patient in either group developed cauda equina syndrome.
slides.see: Figure 3 shows the sciatica bothersomeness gap opening by 3 months and holding through 2 years.
slides.notes: Sciatica is where surgery showed itself even through the crossover: −2.1 at 3 months, −1.6 at 1 year and −1.6 at 2 years, global P=.003. The authors call leg-pain relief the most striking and consistent improvement with surgery, matching clinical experience. Self-rated major improvement also favored surgery, global P=.04. Satisfaction with symptoms at 3 months was 11.3 points higher with surgery (1.6 to 20.9), which excludes zero; the text says none of the satisfaction or employment changes was significant, which fits the global P of .17 but not that time point. Work status favored nonoperative care at every time point, slightly. Now the as-treated analysis. It compares patients by the treatment they received, with surgery as a time-varying covariate, adjusted for time of surgery and for baseline factors that predicted crossover or missing data at 1 year. It produced effects several times the intent-to-treat ones. The authors accept the limit: it lacks the protection of randomization, and selective crossover may have biased it even after adjustment. Our reading of the direction: patients who chose surgery started worse, and worse baseline scores leave more room to improve, so residual confounding could push either way. The paper does not report which baseline variables entered the model. Harms were modest. Dural tear 4%, in line with the 2% to 7% the authors cite from earlier work. 95% had no intraoperative and 95% no postoperative complication. Table 3 has denominator problems: the footnote says data were missing for 7 surgical patients, while 243 of 247 means 4; length of stay and the postoperative rows (4 + 9 + 226) each sum to 239, not 243, and the printed percentages fit 239 (226 is 95% of 239), so the denominators are unstated rather than the percentages wrong. One death, from complications of childbirth at 11 months, was not perioperative; Figure 1 places a death in the nonoperative arm by 1 year (our match).

slides.title: Critical appraisal

rows: Computer randomization in blocks within site, concealed
Arms balanced at baseline; our recheck agrees
Standard outcome scales: SF-36 and ODI
Missing data similar by arm; sensitivity analyses agree
29 never followed were dropped from analysis
NIH funded; sponsors had no role
Nonoperative care not standardized or reported by arm
Most numbers recheck in Tables 1, 4 and 5
Text overstates consistency of the results

slides.notes: Be fair: the trial was large, multicenter and properly randomized, and the numbers mostly check, though some reporting is thin (see below). The authors' own limitations are three: nonadherence, which they call the major limitation and which makes the intent-to-treat analysis unlikely to estimate the true effect of surgery; no masking with sham procedures, so surgical gains may include some placebo effect; and nonoperative care left to physician and patient, so no conclusion is possible against any specific nonoperative treatment. They also name possible lack of representativeness and argue patients resembled other cohorts: mean ODI 46.9 vs 47.2 at Stanford, physical function 39 vs 37 in the Maine study. The authors also say crossover biases the intent-to-treat analysis toward the null, so it is unlikely to give a valid estimate of the true effect of surgery, and that baseline differences or selective crossover may have affected the as-treated results. The rest is ours. Table 2, the nonoperative treatment table, pools 323 patients from both arms who had nonoperative data, so you cannot see what the nonoperative arm received. Only 44% had physical therapy during the trial although the protocol minimum included active PT. Text versus tables: Results say every effect favored surgery at every point, and the Conclusion says all outcomes at all times. Work status favored nonoperative care at all three times, and physical function at 2 years was 0. Results also say no primary effect was significant at any point, yet the 3-month ODI interval excludes zero. Small items: three nonoperative distributions in Table 1 sum to 239, not 240; Table 3 denominators are inconsistent. Generalizability, by the authors: patients unwilling to wait 6 weeks, or without clear radiculopathy and matching imaging, were excluded, so no conclusion applies to them. Disclosures include consulting for or funding from Medtronic and St Francis Medical Technologies, and a Synthes gift to the University of Washington.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: “In SPORT, both groups with 6 or more weeks of radiculopathy improved a lot. Assignment to surgery gave small, nonsignificant differences in pain, function and disability, with a clear edge in sciatica. With 60% vs 45% operated on, the intent-to-treat analysis alone cannot say whether surgery is superior or equivalent.”

rows: Both improved; small ITT gaps; sciatica favored surgery
Faster leg-pain relief and recovery; 1-year outcomes similar
Leg pain 2.8 vs 5.2 on 0–10, favoring surgery

points: Peul and Bailey come from the library records. Endpoints, timing and follow-up differ between trials.
Do not stretch it: the ITT result does not show surgery fails, and the as-treated 15-point effect is not randomized evidence.
slides.notes: Expect four follow-up questions. First: does this show diskectomy does not work? No. The authors say conclusions on superiority or equivalence are not warranted from the intent-to-treat analysis. What it does show, in our reading, is that offering surgery to a well-informed patient who may decline, against usual care that allows later surgery, gives similar 2-year function, and that both paths improve a lot. Second: is the as-treated result the real effect? It is the larger signal, but it is observational within a trial; the authors say it lacks the protection of randomization. Quote it as supportive, not proof. Third: can I wait in a patient with weakness? About 40% had motor weakness at baseline, but the paper reports no neurologic recovery by group, and cauda equina syndrome was excluded. Do not use SPORT to justify waiting on a progressive deficit. Fourth: does it apply to my patient who cannot tolerate 6 weeks? The authors say patients demanding earlier surgery were not included and they draw no conclusions about them. Peul, from the library record, addresses the 6 to 12 week window and found faster relief with early surgery and similar 1-year outcomes, with 39% of its conservative arm operated on. Bailey, also from the library record, enrolled sciatica lasting 4 to 12 months and found lower leg pain at 6 months with microdiscectomy. Peul and Bailey numbers come from the master file records, not from full-text review here. A last point on durability: this paper stops at 2 years, and later SPORT follow-ups were not reviewed for this deck.

decks.not_reviewed: Reference 11 (the design paper) and any follow-up beyond 1 year. The PDF cites no supplement.

slides.title: Peul 2007: Surgery versus prolonged conservative treatment for sciatica
slides.lead: Bottom line: early surgery relieved leg pain and brought recovery faster. Disability over the year did not differ significantly, and perceived recovery at 1 year was 95% in both groups.
points: Journal club · Timing of disc surgery
Peul WC, et al. N Engl J Med 2007;356:2245-56
slides.notes: This is the Leiden–The Hague Spine Intervention Prognostic Study Group trial: 283 Dutch patients, nine hospitals by the Methods count, followed for one year. The comparison is timing, not surgery against no surgery. 39 percent of the conservative group had surgery, so read it as early surgery against wait and operate if needed. This deck was prepared from the full text of the paper. No supplement is cited in the PDF. The design paper (reference 11) was not reviewed, and neither was any later follow-up, so the deck says nothing about results beyond 1 year.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: Most sciatica improves on its own, yet some patients stay disabled. When should surgery be offered?
points: Natural history: favorable. Leg pain resolves within 8 weeks in the majority of patients.
The gap: surgery after failed conservative care was agreed. How long to wait was not.
Dutch practice: guidelines advised offering surgery if symptoms had not improved after 6 weeks.

rows: 6–12 weeks of severe sciatica with a confirmed disk herniation
6 more months of conservative care, with surgery if needed
Disability, leg pain and perceived recovery over 1 year

slides.notes: Set the stakes. The paper puts sciatica incidence at an estimated 5 cases per 1000 adults a year in Western countries and says rates of surgery vary widely with sociocultural preference, with relatively high rates in the US and the Netherlands. The authors state they knew of no earlier study of how timing affects outcome. SPORT came out the year before, and they contrast it directly: in their account of SPORT, surgery rates differed by only 14 percent at 6 weeks, only 59 percent of those assigned surgery had it, and at least 20 percent had symptoms for 6 months or more. The authors present their own 6 to 12 week window as a difference from SPORT and say the effects of crossover in their trial were mitigated by early surgery. They do not say the trial was designed in response, and enrollment began in November 2002, before SPORT was published in 2006. Those SPORT figures are as reported in this paper. Keep the question in mind: this asks when, not whether.

slides.title: Patients and methods
points: Mean age 42–43. Weakness in 66–70%. Baseline Roland about 16.
Included: age 18–65, confirmed herniation, incapacitating radicular syndrome for 6–12 weeks
Excluded: cauda equina, paralysis or strength below antigravity, prior spine surgery, bony stenosis, spondylolisthesis
Early surgery: unilateral transflaval microdiskectomy, no subtotal diskectomy; canceled if recovered first
Conservative: GP-led care; surgery at 6 months, or sooner for worsening pain or deficit
Primary: Roland, leg-pain VAS and Likert recovery, 7 visits to 52 weeks
Power: 140 per group, 90% power for 3 Roland points
slides.notes: Three details are worth saying aloud. First, this was a severe group with real deficits: about two thirds had weakness at baseline, but cauda equina, paralysis and strength below antigravity were excluded. Second, patients were checked one hour before randomization, and anyone who had recovered was excluded, so the trial enrolled people who were still sick at that moment. Before that, 31 had recovered by the MRI stage. Third, the conservative arm was active: patients got prognosis information, a trial website, medication adjustment and physiotherapy referral if fearful of moving. Randomization used permuted blocks stratified by center and numbered opaque envelopes. Patients could not be blinded, and research nurses saw their own patients and knew the assignment. Rehabilitation after surgery used a standardized home exercise protocol supervised by physiotherapists. The Methods count nine participating hospitals, while the Appendix lists 10.

slides.title: Primary outcomes: disability and leg pain
points: Roland gap was 3.1 at week 8, below the paper’s 4-point MCID.
Leg pain gap stayed under 20 mm and closed by 1 year.
*As printed; the printed means give −1.4
slides.see: Figure 2A: the mean Roland curve for early surgery starts higher, crosses below the conservative curve at about 4 weeks, and the curves meet by about 38 weeks. Figure 2B: the mean leg-pain curve for early surgery falls faster and stays lower until about 26 weeks, and the curves are equal at 52 weeks.
slides.notes: Figures are the paper's Figure 2, panels A and B. Red is conservative, blue is early surgery. Positive differences favor early surgery. Note the first 4 weeks: Roland favors conservative care at week 2, by 1.6 points as printed. The printed means, 14.4 and 13.0, give 1.4, while the printed interval centers on about 1.55, so we quote the printed value and flag it. Only 87 of the early group had been operated on by then. Our inference, not the paper's: many were fresh from surgery. The authors suggest standard microdiskectomy rather than modern methods may explain it, and they hedge that with 'may'. The curves cross at 4 weeks. Roland area under the curve differed by 42.5 (minus 12.4 to 97.4), P=0.13. Leg pain differed by 341.7 (163.8 to 519.6), P<0.001. Our arithmetic, not the paper's: divided over 52 weeks, those are average gaps of about 0.8 Roland points and 6.6 mm. So the leg-pain result is statistically clear but modest as a yearly average, and largest early: 15.7 mm at week 2 and 17.7 mm at week 8 in Table 2, against 6.1 mm at week 26. Back pain was not significant on AUC (P=0.14), although a Table 2 footnote says the scores differ in favor of early surgery, P=0.045. The paper does not state which analysis that is. At 52 weeks no outcome differed significantly, in the authors' words. Roland at week 8 has an upper bound of 4.3, so the 4-point MCID is not fully excluded at that single time point. That reading is ours.

slides.title: Perceived recovery and crossover
points: Median weeks to recovery: 4.0 vs 12.1
Hazard ratio 1.97, CI 1.72 to 2.22
At 1 year, about 95% had recovered in both groups.
16 of 141 recovered before early surgery.
Before crossover, the 55 had leg VAS 54 and Roland 15.0.
slides.see: Figure 3 (inverse Kaplan-Meier, cumulative recovery over 52 weeks): the early-surgery curve rises first and reaches about 0.88 by 12 weeks. The conservative curve rises in steps at visit times and joins it at about 0.95 by 52 weeks. Numbers without recovery are shown beneath the plot.
slides.notes: Figure 3 is the paper's own. Blue is early surgery, red conservative. Recovery means complete or nearly complete disappearance of symptoms on the 7-point Likert scale. At 1 year, the paper gives about 95 percent in both groups. The authors say relief was twice as fast, while medians are 4.0 and 12.1 weeks. Our reading, not the paper's: twice as fast appears to reflect the hazard ratio, a link the paper does not make. Also look at the steps. The curves jump at the visit weeks of 2, 4, 8, 12, 26 and 38, and the medians land almost exactly on the 4-week and 12-week visits. The authors admit recovery timing depends on the examination schedule. So treat the 8-week gap as approximate, and do not lean on the tight intervals around it. Back to the paper: it states that this underestimates the speed of recovery between visits, but that both treatment groups were affected in the same way. So our caution is about the precision of the gap, not a bias between groups. The next reading is also ours: crossover was not a late rescue. Median time to surgery in the conservative group was 14.6 weeks, interquartile range 6.4 to 26.0, and 42 of the 55 had surgery by week 26, ahead of or at the 6-month offer. Those who crossed over ended with similar 1-year scores, but that is a non-randomized subgroup. Reoperation was 4 of 125 (3.2 percent) versus 1 of 55 (1.8 percent). Complications were 2 dural tears and 1 wound hematoma, reported as 1.6 percent of surgical patients, and all resolved.

slides.title: Critical appraisal

rows: Randomized, stratified by center, at nine hospitals
Patients and research nurses knew assignment
Conservative arm had nurse support, not usual care
Recovery timing limited to visit dates
Funded by ZonMW and the Hoelen Foundation; no conflict reported
Neurologic exam planned, no group results reported
Table 1: ankle reflex 53% vs 75%, called balanced
Hazard ratio interval looks too narrow (our reading)

slides.notes: Be fair: this is a well-run trial. The authors' limitations paragraph names three limits, namely nurse support, no blinding, and recovery timed at visits. Elsewhere in the Discussion they also say crossover strongly influenced the primary outcomes, with its effect on group differences mitigated by early surgery. The rest are our reading. Blinding matters because every primary outcome is patient-reported. Nurse support is real but cuts both ways: it did not prevent surgery in 39 percent. Table 1 says no baseline difference was significant, yet ankle reflex difference was 53 versus 75 percent. Our own chi-square on those counts gives P about 0.0001. The same table's level counts for the conservative group add to 145, not 142, so a typo may be involved. On the hazard ratio: 1.72 to 2.22 is symmetric on the linear scale, and it is far narrower than the subgroup intervals in Figure 4 would suggest. Our rough estimate for about 270 recoveries is closer to 1.55 to 2.5. We quote the published value but cannot verify it. Figure 1 also does not add up: 141 less 1 and 3 lost is 137, not 140 assessed. Subgroups: 16 predefined, interaction cutoff 0.10, and only sitting-provoked sciatica reached it (P=0.07), which is what chance could produce. The absence of interaction with sequestration, pain intensity and patient preference was remarkable to the authors. The repeat neurologic examination has no group results; Results says only that none of the patients had neurologic signs after surgery. Methods says nine participating hospitals, while the Appendix lists 10. Leiden University Medical Center may be coordinating only, which is our guess. Table 2 has several CIs that look like printing errors, listed in the review file.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: “For 6 to 12 weeks of severe sciatica, early microdiskectomy got patients better sooner, median 4 versus 12 weeks. Disability over the year did not differ significantly, 1-year recovery was 95% in both groups, and 39% of the conservative group had surgery.”
points: SPORT and Bailey come from the library records. Endpoints and follow-up differ between trials.
Do not stretch it: no group data on motor recovery, and paralysis and strength below antigravity were excluded.

rows: Both improved; crossover blocked a conclusion
Leg pain 2.8 vs 5.2 on 0–10, favoring surgery

slides.notes: Expect three follow-up questions. Does this justify waiting in a patient with weakness? Not by itself. Two thirds of patients had weakness at baseline, but paralysis and strength below antigravity were excluded, and this paper reports no neurologic recovery results by group. Progressive deficit was a reason to offer surgery early. Is early surgery wrong, since 1-year outcomes were similar? No. The authors call it a valid option for well-informed patients. In their view, patients who cannot cope with leg pain or want the fastest recovery may choose surgery, and those with acceptable pain control may wait without reducing their chance of complete recovery at 12 months. Does it apply after 12 weeks? Peul stops at that window. Bailey, from the library record, enrolled sciatica lasting 4 to 12 months and found lower leg pain at 6 months with microdiscectomy, so the two trials answer different questions. SPORT and Bailey numbers come from the master file's abstract-level records, not from full-text review here. Also, Peul's conservative arm allowed surgery, so it never tests a no-surgery strategy.

decks.not_reviewed: The Supplementary Appendix (Tables S1 to S6 and Figure S1: the nonsurgical care protocol, extra baseline data including antidepressant use, crossover and noncompleter characteristics, secondary-outcome detail and the multiple-imputation sensitivity analyses), the trial protocol and the data sharing statement. The PDF is the complete 10-page article, not a critique.

slides.title: Bailey 2020: Surgery versus conservative care for persistent sciatica lasting 4 to 12 months
slides.lead: Bottom line: for sciatica that had already lasted 4 to 12 months, assignment to microdiskectomy gave lower leg pain at 6 months than 6 more months of standardized nonsurgical care, 2.8 versus 5.2 on a 0 to 10 scale.
points: Journal club · Timing of disc surgery
Bailey CS, et al. N Engl J Med 2020;382:1093-102
Single center, London, Ontario. 128 randomized, 64 per group.
Prepared from the full text of the paper. The Supplementary Appendix was not reviewed.
slides.notes: This is a single-center Canadian trial at London Health Sciences Centre. It picks up where Peul stops: Peul enrolled 6 to 12 weeks of sciatica, Bailey enrolled 4 to 12 months. The comparison is surgery within about 3 weeks against standardized nonsurgical care while the patient stayed on the surgeon's ordinary waiting list, which the authors say is typically more than 6 months at their center. So the control arm is, in effect, the usual Canadian wait with structured care. The primary endpoint is a single time point, leg pain at 6 months. Everything else, including the 1-year results, is a secondary outcome that the authors themselves say cannot support clinical inferences because there was no plan for multiple comparisons. The PDF is the complete published article. The Supplementary Appendix, which holds Tables S1 to S6, the injection protocol and the sensitivity analyses, was not reviewed, so anything the paper sends to the appendix is reported here only as the main text describes it. Funding was from the Physicians' Services Incorporated Foundation, with no industry involvement and no conflicts reported.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: Most acute sciatica settles within about 4 months. What should be offered when it has not?
points: Natural history: the authors cite improvement with conservative care in 90% within 4 months of onset.
The gap: earlier trials mostly enrolled symptoms under 3 months, and showed surgery's benefit fading by 6 to 12 months.
Controversy: longer symptom duration has been linked to worse discectomy outcomes in some studies.

rows: Age 18–60, unilateral sciatica for 4–12 months, posterolateral L4–L5 or L5–S1 herniation compressing the matching root
Standardized nonsurgical care for at least 6 months, surgery afterwards if needed
Leg-pain intensity, 0–10 visual analogue scale, at 6 months

slides.notes: Frame it as the authors do. Trials of acute sciatica, Peul among them, showed early surgery helps sooner, but outcomes converge by 6 to 12 months. Those trials enrolled mostly patients with symptoms under 3 months, so they do not answer what to do for the patient who is still in pain at 5 or 8 months. The authors set up the tension in the Discussion: some studies tie longer symptom duration to worse results after discectomy, including a post hoc SPORT analysis in which 6 months or more of symptoms predicted worse outcomes with either treatment, and a waiting-time study in which waiting 12 weeks or more for surgery predicted worse pain 6 months after surgery. Against that, patients may prefer to avoid surgery if nonsurgical care could still work. The authors describe Peul as showing the benefit of early surgery was no longer different by 6 months. That is their summary of Peul. Keep the question narrow: this asks whether to operate on persistent sciatica now or after another 6 months of structured care. It does not test never operating, because the control arm could have surgery after the wait.

slides.title: Patients and methods
points: Included: age 18–60, unilateral radiculopathy 4–12 months, MRI posterolateral herniation with root compression
Excluded: foraminal or far lateral disk, stenosis, deformity, prior surgery at the level, or an epidural injection or ongoing exercise physiotherapy for this episode
Randomized 1:1 by computer-generated permuted blocks, stratified by workers' compensation
Surgery: open or minimal-access microdiskectomy, loupes or microscope, day case or one night; no fusion
Nonsurgical: education, analgesics, active physiotherapy, optional epidural steroid (up to 3), reviewed every 6 weeks for at least 6 months
