Mean age 38, 41% female, 72–73% extruded, about 70% L5–S1, baseline leg pain 7.7 vs 8.0, ODI about 50
Sample size: 15 per group for leg pain; raised to 64 per group to power the ODI
slides.notes: Look hard at the funnel. Of 790 referrals, only 128 were randomized, 16 percent. Symptom reduction is the single biggest reason for exclusion: 174 at the telephone stage and 111 at the screening visit, 285 in all. Our reading: even at 4 to 12 months, many referred patients seem to improve while waiting to be seen, though the paper does not give the symptom duration of those excluded. Next, note who was excluded: anyone already treated with an epidural injection or ongoing exercise-based physiotherapy for this episode, and 75 who had already exhausted nonsurgical options. So the population is persistent sciatica that had not yet had structured nonsurgical care. That is a key boundary, and it is ours to stress, though the authors explain the reason: those treatments were part of the control arm. Patients came from referrals to four orthopedic surgeons and one neurosurgeon, and fellowship-trained spine surgeons operated. Sample size: our recomputation of 15 per group (SD 1.9, MCID 2, two-sided alpha 0.05, 80 percent power) and 64 per group for ODI (SD 20, MCID 10) both check out. The paper writes beta level of 0.80, which should read power of 0.80. Neither calculation allows for dropout (ours), and the authors say up to 20 percent of primary data were missing. Allocation concealment is not described, and the paper says nothing about blinding of patients or outcome assessors. Outcomes were patient-reported. The only baseline difference the authors call significant was more antidepressant use in the surgical group, a figure that sits in Table S2 and that we could not check. Our check of Table 1 found no other large imbalance: asymmetric reflex loss 56 versus 42 percent gives P about 0.11 by our chi-square. Means and proportions otherwise look balanced, but the spread does not: the age SD is 8.3 surgical versus 11.9 nonsurgical, a variance ratio of about 2.1 (F test P about 0.005, ours), alongside the BMI SD gap flagged under appraisal. Both are plausible with age capped at 18 to 60, but note them.

slides.title: Primary outcome: leg pain at 6 months
slides.lead: Adjusted leg pain 2.8 versus 5.2; difference 2.4 points (95% CI 1.4 to 3.4), P<0.001.
points: Mixed model for repeated measures, adjusted for baseline leg pain, intention to treat
Analyzed at 6 months: 51 of 64 surgical (80%) and 54 of 64 nonsurgical (84%)
Both groups improved; the nonsurgical group fell from 8.0 to 5.2
Lower CI bound 1.4 sits below the 2-point MCID used to size the trial (our reading)
slides.see: Figure 2A: the surgical curve drops by 6 weeks and stays low through 12 months, while the nonsurgical curve falls mostly in the first 3 months, from about 8.0 to 5.4, then is nearly flat to 4.7 at 12 months, staying above the surgical curve at every follow-up visit.
slides.notes: Read the table carefully. Baseline values are observed means with SD. Follow-up values are model-estimated means with SE, adjusted for baseline leg pain, so the plus-minus figures shrink from about 2 to 0.4 because they change from SD to SE, not because patients became uniform. The difference is printed as nonsurgical minus surgical, so positive favors surgery. Our check: 5.2 minus 2.8 is 2.4, and two SEs of 0.4 give a 95 percent interval of about plus or minus 1.1, close to the printed 1.0 once rounding is allowed for. The interval is plausible and symmetric. How big is it? The trial was sized on an MCID of 2 points. The point estimate, 2.4, clears it, but the lower bound, 1.4, does not, so an effect smaller than the MCID is not excluded. That reading is ours. Both groups got better: the nonsurgical arm improved by about 3 points without surgery, and 7 of the 64 assigned to surgery improved enough to cancel. This is intention to treat. In the surgical arm 56 of 64 had surgery, at a median of 3.1 weeks. In the nonsurgical arm 62 of 64 were still on nonsurgical care at 6 months, so crossover is far lower than in SPORT. The contrast is not free of nonadherence, though: 8 of 64 (12.5 percent) assigned to surgery never had it. Missing data: up to 20 percent were missing at 6 months. The patients who missed the 6-month visit were more often smokers, 61 versus 39 percent. The model assumes data are missing at random. Post hoc multiple imputation gave results similar in direction, per the main text; the numbers are in Tables S5 and S6, which we did not review. The 12-month row is secondary: by then crossovers were occurring, median 11 months, so the 12-month contrast is diluted to an unknown degree (our inference).

slides.title: Secondary outcomes and harms
slides.lead: Secondary outcomes all pointed the same way, but the authors say they cannot support clinical inferences: no multiplicity plan.
points: Back pain 6 mo: 3.0 vs 4.9, difference 1.9 (1.0 to 2.9)
Satisfaction 6 mo: 92.0% vs 71.4%; employed 80.0% vs 64.2%; neither interval excludes zero
Crossover: 22 of 64 (34%) nonsurgical patients had surgery, median 11 months (range 2 to 25); 2 before 6 months
Reoperation: 1 surgical patient, for recurrent herniation at 250 days
slides.notes: Signs: differences are nonsurgical minus surgical. For pain and ODI, positive favors surgery. For SF-36, satisfaction and employment, higher is better, so negative favors surgery. ODI was the outcome that set the sample size, and the 6-month difference, 10.9, sits right at the 10-point MCID used for that calculation, with a lower bound of 4.5. Our arithmetic from the printed SEs reproduces the ODI, SF-36 and pain intervals. The satisfaction and employment rows do not reconcile. From the group SEs, satisfaction at 6 months should have an interval of about minus 35 to minus 6, which would exclude zero, but the printed interval is minus 43.4 to 2.2. All four binary rows are about 1.6 times wider than the group SEs imply. The paper does not explain this. We quote the printed values. Harms: in the intention-to-treat analysis, 4 surgical-arm and 5 nonsurgical-arm patients had surgery-related events, nine in all. Superficial wound infection and new postoperative neuropathic pain were most common. The one dural tear and one nerve-root injury both occurred in crossover patients. Our observation, not the authors': as treated, 5 of 22 crossovers (23 percent) had an event against 4 of 56 (7 percent) after assigned surgery. The numbers are small and the comparison is not randomized, but it is not evidence that delay makes surgery safer. The authors call the rates similar, a statement that rests on the intention-to-treat figures. Who did not have assigned surgery? The 8 surgical-arm patients without surgery had shorter symptoms (5.8 versus 8.0 months), better PCS and less disability. The 22 crossovers were younger and less likely to have reflex loss than those who had assigned surgery.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: Holds up: randomized, intention to treat, prespecified single primary outcome
Holds up: 97% of the nonsurgical arm still nonsurgical at 6 months
Holds up: control care standardized by a separate trial physician
Holds up: arithmetic of the flow diagram, Table 1 and Table 3 checks out
Weakens: single center, referrals to 5 surgeons, 16% of referrals randomized
Weakens: up to 20% missing primary data; missing-at-random model
Weakens: blinding and allocation concealment not described; patient-reported outcomes
Weakens: no multiplicity plan; binary secondary intervals unexplained
Weakens: excluded patients already given injection or exercise therapy
slides.notes: Be fair: the primary result is robust in direction and the crossover problem that sank SPORT's intention-to-treat analysis is mostly absent at 6 months. The authors credit the Canadian waiting list for that, since only 2 nonsurgical patients had surgery before 6 months. The authors name three limitations: possible selection bias, single center, and up to 20 percent missing primary data, which they addressed with multiple imputation. They argue selection bias was limited because surgery outside the trial was not available at their center, which may explain why only 40 eligible patients declined. The rest is our reading. Neither blinding nor allocation concealment is described. A patient knows whether they had an operation and is reporting their own pain, so expectation effects can inflate the gap. With a lower bound of 1.4 against a 2-point MCID, modest bias would matter. The comparison was surgery at about 3 weeks against a 6-month wait with structured care, not surgery against a well-run conservative program after which surgery is easy to get. Source problems we found: Table 2 lists 54 nonsurgical patients for 12-month leg pain, while the flow diagram and every other 12-month row show 47. The statistics section says beta level of 0.80 for what is power. The flow diagram excludes 18 for symptoms over 13 months, while the criterion is 4 to 12 months. The Conclusions say more than 4 months, not 4 to 12. The abstract spells Owestry. Table 1 gives a nonsurgical BMI SD of 10.5, almost twice the surgical 5.6, which suggests an outlier or error (ours). Table 1 also shows a wider age spread in the nonsurgical arm, SD 11.9 versus 8.3 (ours). The Results text says 34 percent of screening-visit exclusions lacked an L4–L5 or L5–S1 posterolateral herniation on MRI, but the flow diagram labels those 70 as MRI not matching symptoms or bilateral radiculopathy. Table 3's footnote says 20 late crossovers were included in the primary analysis, though all 64 per group were analyzed by intention to treat. The interim analysis at 50 percent enrollment checked safety and protocol violations, not efficacy, so its lack of alpha adjustment is not a problem.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: “For unilateral sciatica that had lasted 4 to 12 months without injections or structured physiotherapy, microdiskectomy within about 3 weeks gave lower leg pain at 6 months than another 6 months of standardized care, 2.8 versus 5.2 out of 10. A third of the nonsurgical group eventually had surgery, mostly after 6 months.”
points: SPORT and Peul come from the library records. Endpoints, follow-up and symptom windows differ.
Do not stretch it: one center, age 60 or younger, L4–L5 and L5–S1 posterolateral only, 6-month primary endpoint.

rows: Faster relief; disability over the year not significantly different
Both improved; crossover blocked a clear conclusion
Leg pain 2.8 vs 5.2 on 0–10, favoring surgery

slides.notes: Expect four follow-up questions. First: does this mean every patient at 4 months should have surgery? No. Of 790 referrals, 285 were excluded because symptoms had eased, 7 surgical-arm patients improved enough to cancel, and the nonsurgical arm itself fell from 8.0 to 5.2. Two thirds of the nonsurgical arm had not had surgery by the time the paper reports. Our reading, not the authors': the trial supports offering surgery as a reasonable choice rather than insisting on more waiting. The authors conclude only that surgery was superior for leg pain at 6 months. Second: did the benefit last? At 12 months leg pain was 2.6 versus 4.7, but that is a secondary outcome with no multiplicity plan, and crossovers had begun. The paper reports nothing beyond 1 year. Third: how does this fit with Peul? Peul, from the library record, enrolled 6 to 12 weeks of symptoms and found faster recovery but similar results by 1 year. Bailey enrolls a later window and finds a 6-month advantage. The two are compatible: the advantage of surgery may persist longer when symptoms have already persisted, but no trial here compares windows directly, so that is a reading, not a result. Fourth: what about the patient who has already had an epidural and physiotherapy? They were excluded, so this trial does not speak directly to them. In our experience that is a common real-world case, so say it plainly (our opinion, not from the paper). SPORT and Peul figures come from the master file's records. The Supplementary Appendix was not reviewed.

decks.not_reviewed: The SPORT design paper (reference 13), the companion SPORT degenerative spondylolisthesis paper (reference 16), the typeset NEJM version (the PDF read is the complete 18-page NIH author manuscript, tables and figures read from page images), the two published comments listed in PubMed, and later SPORT stenosis follow-up. The paper cites no supplement.

slides.title: Weinstein 2008: SPORT, surgery vs nonsurgical care for lumbar spinal stenosis
slides.lead: Does decompression beat usual nonsurgical care for stenosis without spondylolisthesis?
points: Journal club: lumbar spinal stenosis
Weinstein JN, et al. N Engl J Med 2008;358:794-810
Randomized cohort (289) plus a concurrent observational cohort (365) at 13 US spine centers, followed 2 years

Bottom line: by intention to treat, surgery won only on bodily pain at 2 years. The adjusted as-treated analysis, combining both cohorts, favored surgery on all primary outcomes from 6 weeks to 2 years.
slides.notes: This is the stenosis arm of SPORT, the Spine Patient Outcomes Research Trial. Degenerative spondylolisthesis was studied in a separate SPORT paper (reference 16), and patients with instability were excluded here. The single most important thing to carry into the room: there are two analyses and they answer different questions. The intention-to-treat analysis of the randomized cohort is protected by randomization but is diluted by heavy crossover in both directions. The as-treated analysis is larger and cleaner in its contrast, but it is observational and depends on adjustment. The authors lead with the as-treated result in their conclusions. Our reading: the deck should keep both in view, because the honest summary is that randomized evidence here is weak and the strong signal is observational. What was reviewed: the complete NIH author manuscript from PMC, 18 pages, including Figure 1 (flow), Figure 2 (curves), and Tables 1 to 4, read from the page images. Not reviewed: the SPORT design paper (reference 13), the companion degenerative spondylolisthesis paper (reference 16), the typeset NEJM version, and the two published comments listed in PubMed. The paper cites no supplement. Funding was from NIH (NIAMS and others); several authors report industry consulting or equity, listed in the paper.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: Stenosis is the most common reason for lumbar surgery after 65, yet the authors knew of no randomized trial of stenosis without spondylolisthesis.
points: The authors cite a 2005 Cochrane review: evidence too sparse and heterogeneous to judge surgical efficacy
Earlier trials were small and mixed patients with and without degenerative spondylolisthesis
Procedure rates vary at least fivefold across US regions
Imaging stenosis is often asymptomatic, so clinical correlation is required

rows: Surgical candidates, claudication or radicular symptoms at least 12 weeks, imaging stenosis
Usual nonsurgical care: at least active PT, education and home exercise, NSAIDs if tolerated
SF-36 bodily pain and physical function, modified ODI, to 2 years

slides.notes: Frame the stakes the way the authors do. Stenosis surgery is common, rates vary widely by geography, and the 2005 Cochrane review could not draw firm conclusions. The prior comparative studies the authors name are the Maine Lumbar Spine Study (observational) and Malmivaara (a randomized trial of moderate stenosis), and both mixed in degenerative spondylolisthesis. The authors say they know of no randomized trial of isolated stenosis without spondylolisthesis, which is the gap this paper fills. Two features of the comparison matter. First, the nonsurgical arm was usual care, not a fixed protocol. It was recommended to include active physical therapy, education with home exercise and NSAIDs, but the authors state they did not test surgery against any specific nonsurgical treatment. Second, entry required that patients already be surgical candidates with at least 12 weeks of symptoms, and most had already had substantial care: physical therapy 68%, epidural injections 56%, NSAIDs 55%, chiropractic 28%, opioids 27%. So this is a population that had already been through a typical nonoperative course. Ask the room to hold one question through the deck: does this paper show what surgery does, or what happens when you offer surgery to a patient who can then decide?

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: 1696 screened, 1091 eligible, 654 enrolled: 289 randomized and 365 in the observational cohort.
points: Mean age 65; majority white men who attended college; 80% neurogenic claudication, 79% dermatomal radiation
91% stenosis at L4 or L5; 61% more than one level; most graded severe
Excluded: degenerative spondylolisthesis, and instability over 4 mm or 10 degrees on flexion-extension films
Randomization: permuted blocks of variable size, stratified by center
Planned 185 per group for 10 SF-36 points at 85% power, allowing 20% missing data but no nonadherence
slides.see: Figure 1 gives the flow chart with visits, withdrawals and cumulative surgery at each time point for all four groups.
slides.notes: Our arithmetic on Figure 1 checks out: 1696 minus 605 ineligible is 1091, minus 437 who declined is 654, and every follow-up box sums to its group total at every visit. The surgery percentages recompute correctly, and 92 + 65 + 211 + 32 gives the 400 patients who had surgery at some point, matching Table 2 (157 randomized plus 243 observational). Data were supplied by 83% to 89% of enrollees at each visit, and 634 patients with at least one follow-up were analyzed: 278 randomized (96%) and 356 observational (98%). Three things to notice. First, the randomized cohort is below its own target. The plan called for 185 per group, and 138 and 151 were enrolled. The paper does not comment on the shortfall. Our inference: the ITT analysis was underpowered even before crossover, and the sample-size calculation explicitly made no allowance for nonadherence. Second, the observational cohort is the preference cohort: 46% definitely wanted surgery versus 12% of the randomized cohort. Table 1 shows other significant cohort differences: nerve-root tension signs 15% vs 26% (P = 0.001), lateral recess stenosis 85% vs 75% (P = 0.003) and non-Hispanic 93% vs 97% (P = 0.03). Pain, function, ODI and most other measures were similar. Third, the paper does not say whether patients, clinicians or outcome assessors were blinded; the outcomes are patient-reported. Do not call it blinded or unblinded on this paper's text. The primary analysis used mixed-effects longitudinal models of change from baseline. In the as-treated analysis, treatment was a time-varying covariate: a crossover patient's pre-surgery visits count as nonsurgical, and follow-up restarts at the date of surgery. No adjustment was made for multiple comparisons.

slides.title: Primary outcomes: the randomized comparison
slides.lead: Intention to treat at 2 years: surgery better on bodily pain only.
points: Effect is surgery minus nonsurgical change from baseline; positive SF-36 and negative ODI favor surgery
Bodily pain effects before 2 years were smaller and not significant: 3.3, 2.4, 4.9 and 5.5
Physical function favored nonsurgical care at 6 weeks and 3 months (-4.2 at both), not significantly
The nonsurgical arm was 43% operated by 2 years; 33% of the surgical arm had not been operated
slides.see: Figure 2A overlays ITT (dashed) and as-treated (solid) curves for the randomized cohort: the ITT curves sit close together, between the widely separated as-treated curves.
slides.notes: Read this slide as the randomized evidence. The only significant ITT primary result is bodily pain at 2 years, 7.8 points, with a lower bound of 1.5. That is below the 10-point difference the study was powered to detect. Physical function at 2 years is essentially zero, and ODI favors surgery by 3.5 points with an interval that crosses zero. Our recomputation: the mean changes in Table 4 reproduce each printed effect (23.4 minus 15.6 is 7.8; 17.1 minus 17.1 is 0, printed 0.1 from rounding; -16.4 minus -12.9 is -3.5). The intervals are symmetric and match the standard errors. Note the 2-year bodily pain finding stands alone against earlier nonsignificant time points, and with five visits, three primary outcomes and no multiplicity adjustment, a single significant cell should be held lightly. The authors argue that crossover biases ITT toward the null and that ITT underestimates the true effect. That is a fair argument about dilution. But crossover was not random. Table 3 shows that nonsurgical-arm patients who crossed to surgery were worse at baseline: ODI 46.7 vs 39.4, more dissatisfied (77% vs 54%), more distressed, and more likely to prefer surgery. Surgical-arm patients who declined surgery were less often white (67% vs 90%), less bothered, less often worsening, and more likely to prefer nonsurgical care. Secondary ITT outcomes: stenosis bothersomeness and leg pain did not differ at 2 years. Satisfaction with care favored surgery at 6 months and 1 year but not at 2 years. The ITT secondary results are in Table 4; the text does not discuss them.

slides.title: As-treated results, secondary outcomes and harms
slides.lead: Combined, adjusted as-treated analysis: surgery better on every primary and secondary outcome at every visit.

rows: Very or somewhat satisfied with symptoms

points: Effects were significant at 6 weeks, peaked near 6 months (ODI -14.1) and persisted at 2 years
Separate as-treated estimates were similar by cohort: randomized ODI -8.7, observational -13.1; global P 0.60
Surgery: 89% decompression only, 11% fused (6% instrumented); dural tear 9%; wound infection 2%
Reoperation 8% by 2 years, under half for recurrent stenosis; 13 deaths in 2 years, 7 nonsurgical and 6 surgical
slides.see: Figure 2B shows the observational cohort: the as-treated nonsurgical curve barely moves after 6 weeks, while the surgical curve improves by 3 months and stays there.
slides.notes: This is the result most people quote, so read it carefully. Our recomputation: the Table 4 changes reproduce the printed effects within rounding, and the intervals are symmetric. But the as-treated intervals are about 5 to 15% narrower than independent arm standard errors would give (6-week bodily pain half-width 2.7 vs 3.05; 2-year ODI 2.9 vs 3.06). Our reading: that fits correlated arm estimates in a model where crossover patients contribute to both groups, so it is plausible, not an error, but these are not simple two-group intervals. The ITT intervals do match the independent standard errors. At 6 weeks the as-treated effects were already significant (bodily pain 10.0, physical function 9.1, ODI -10.3). The abstract says the advantage was significant by 3 months; the Discussion says as early as 6 weeks, which matches the table. The authors note the nonsurgical group improved only moderately, and that the stenosis effects were larger than in the SPORT disc observational study because the disc nonsurgical group improved much more. The as-treated N at baseline is 803, more than the 634 analyzed. The Table 4 footnote says only that the as-treated N reflects patients contributing to the estimate in each period under the longitudinal model and may not match Figure 1. Our reading of the Methods: crossovers contribute to both groups, since pre-surgery visits count as nonsurgical. The authors justify pooling because as-treated effects did not differ between cohorts (Wald P 0.93, 0.67, 0.60). Harms from Table 2, our pooling: dural tear 36 of 393, intraoperative transfusion 37 of 390, postoperative complications to 8 weeks 12%. Mean stay was 3.5 days in the randomized cohort and 3.0 in the observational cohort. One postoperative death within 3 months, attributed in a footnote to a myocardial infarction. Of 13 deaths, 12 were judged not treatment-related and one, 501 days after surgery, was of unknown cause. Figure 1 shows only 10 deaths summed across the four groups at 2 years; the paper does not reconcile this with the 13 in the text. The 1-year reoperation rate for recurrent stenosis, 1.3%, comes from a table category that also includes progressive spondylolisthesis. Fusion in 11% is worth saying aloud: the protocol operation was decompressive laminectomy, and the paper does not give the reasons for fusion.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: The randomized result is weak; the strong result is observational.
points: Crossover was heavy and selective, so ITT is diluted and as-treated groups are no longer randomized
Patients who had surgery started worse: ODI 46.0 vs 36.4, bodily pain 28.6 vs 36.6, and 48% vs 3% definitely wanted surgery
The listed adjustment covariates include baseline score but not treatment preference or imaging severity (our observation)
Randomized enrollment fell short of the planned 185 per group
Usual care was heterogeneous and unspecified; no blinding is described
No multiplicity adjustment across five visits and many outcomes

rows: Two cohorts gave similar as-treated effects
As-treated contrast is confounded by indication and preference
Only bodily pain significant by ITT, at 2 years only

slides.notes: Credit the authors with stating the main limitation themselves: the marked nonadherence, and that the as-treated analyses do not share the protection of randomization. They argue careful adjustment and agreement with earlier studies make the as-treated estimate credible. Our view: the baseline gap in Table 1 is large. Patients who ended up operated on had worse pain, function and bothersomeness, were more dissatisfied (78% vs 52%), more often worsening (67% vs 47%), and overwhelmingly preferred surgery. Adjusting for baseline score handles some of that. But the published covariate list does not include treatment preference, symptom bothersomeness or radiographic severity, and patient expectation can move patient-reported outcomes. The direction of that bias is not certain from this paper. Sicker patients have more room to improve, and preference could inflate or deflate reported benefit. So confounding could have moved the as-treated estimate in either direction; treat its size as an estimate, not a measured truth. The cohort-agreement argument helps less than it seems: both cohorts' as-treated estimates rest on the same kind of self-selection. Source problems to say aloud. The Discussion says the only baseline cohort differences besides preference were nerve-root tension and stenosis location; Table 1 also shows non-Hispanic ethnicity at 93% vs 97%, P = 0.03. Figure 1 totals 10 deaths, while the text reports 13. Some Table 1 categorical rows do not sum to their column N, with no missing-data footnote: self-assessed health trend sums to 273 of 278 randomized, 354 of 356 observational and 387 of 394 surgical; treatment preference to 277 of 278 randomized and 239 of 240 nonsurgical. Small, but unreconciled. Our recomputation of Table 1 P values: the proportions match a continuity-corrected (Yates) chi-square (non-Hispanic 0.027, printed 0.03; lateral recess 0.003), and age is close to the printed 0.10 within rounding of the means. The test is not named. External validity: mean age 65, mostly white, college-educated, already through PT and injections, at academic multidisciplinary centers. Spondylolisthesis and instability were excluded, so do not import these numbers into a slip patient, and this paper says nothing about whether to add fusion.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "In SPORT stenosis, offering surgery improved bodily pain at 2 years by intention to treat, but not function or ODI, with 43% of the nonsurgical arm operated on. Patients who actually had surgery did much better than those who did not, about 11 ODI points, but that comparison is observational."

rows: Surgery vs usual care, no slip
Surgery vs usual care, disc herniation

points: L01 and L07 numbers come from the library records; L01 values shown are at 1 year
Say: decompression for concordant, persistent symptomatic stenosis after failed care; no fusion indication from this paper
slides.notes: Expect four follow-up questions. First: is this proof that decompression works? Not from randomization alone. The randomized comparison gave a 7.8-point bodily pain advantage at 2 years, and no significant difference in physical function or ODI. The authors argue crossover biased this toward the null, which is reasonable, but the patients who crossed were systematically different. The strong evidence is the adjusted as-treated analysis, which is observational. Second: how big is the effect for the patient in front of me? As treated, operated patients improved by about 20 ODI points and nonoperated patients by about 9 at 2 years. Patients who had surgery were sicker and wanted surgery, so treat the 11-point difference as an estimate that confounding could have shifted. Third: what about waiting? The authors note nonsurgical patients did not, on average, get worse; they showed small improvements in all outcomes. The authors also found little evidence of harm from either treatment. Our inference, not analyzed in the paper: nonsurgical care looks like a reasonable option, and a patient who chooses it can later choose surgery. Fourth: should I fuse? This paper excluded spondylolisthesis and instability and was not designed to compare fusion. The library record for the Swedish Spinal Stenosis Study (L07) found that adding fusion did not improve 2-year ODI, including in the slip stratum. L01, the SPORT disc trial record, shows the same pattern of diluted ITT and large as-treated effects, which is a feature of the SPORT design. Durability: this paper reports 2 years only; later SPORT follow-up was not reviewed here. Harms to quote: dural tear 9%, reoperation 8% by 2 years, postoperative complications 12%.

decks.not_reviewed: Supplemental Table 1 (year-by-year ITT and as-treated results, not in the PDF). The final typeset journal version (the PDF is the author manuscript). Earlier SPORT reports and the design paper, cited for methods. Comment PMID 34618792, listed in the master record.

slides.title: SPORT degenerative spondylolisthesis at 8 years
slides.lead: Long-term results of surgery compared with nonoperative treatment for lumbar degenerative spondylolisthesis.
points: Journal club · Surgery or not for a degenerative slip
Abdu WA, et al. Spine 2018;43:1619-30
Source is the full author manuscript. Supplemental Table 1 is not in the PDF.
Bottom line: treated surgically, patients did better through 8 years on every primary outcome. As randomized, there was no surgical advantage, and ODI favored the group assigned nonoperative care.
slides.notes: This is the 8-year report of the degenerative spondylolisthesis arm of SPORT, a randomized trial with a concurrent observational cohort at 13 US centers. The deck was prepared from the full author manuscript. That manuscript is complete for text, tables and figures, but the year-by-year results sit in Supplemental Table 1, which we did not have. So several figures below are the ones the text chooses to quote. The whole paper turns on one tension. The headline comes from an as-treated analysis, which is observational in nature. The randomized comparison points the other way on one outcome. Keep those two apart all the way through. This paper asks whether to operate. It does not ask whether to fuse.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: Does the advantage of surgery for degenerative spondylolisthesis with stenosis last to 8 years, and does fusion technique matter?
points: Earlier SPORT result: surgery did significantly better through 4 years.
The worry: several studies found the early surgical advantage narrowed over time.
Earlier studies mixed patients with and without a slip, or were small and lacked validated measures.
Patients: surgical candidates with a degenerative slip, stenosis and at least 12 weeks of symptoms.
Comparison: decompressive laminectomy, with or without fusion, against nonoperative care.
Outcome: SF-36 bodily pain and physical function, and ODI, out to 8 years.
slides.notes: Two questions are stated by the authors: surgery against nonoperative care at 8 years, and comparison among fusion techniques. They are different kinds of question. The first has a randomized cohort behind it. The second does not, because fusion type was not randomly assigned. The intervention deserves care. The protocol operation was a standard posterior decompressive laminectomy with or without fusion using autogenous iliac crest graft. Pedicle screws and interbody fusion were at the surgeon's discretion. In practice nearly everyone was fused, as slide 5 shows. So surgery here means, for the most part, decompression plus fusion in patients enrolled from March 2000 to February 2005. Our comment: that is not the operative mix of a trial testing decompression alone, and no one should read this as a verdict on fusion. The nonoperative protocol was individualized by the treating physician and included, at a minimum, physical therapy, education and counseling on home exercise, and NSAIDs if tolerated.

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: 1,164 screened, 892 eligible, 607 enrolled: 304 randomized and 303 in the observational cohort.
points: Included: neurogenic claudication or radicular leg symptoms for at least 12 weeks, stenosis on cross-sectional imaging, slip on standing lateral film, physician-confirmed surgical candidate.
Excluded: spondylolysis and isthmic spondylolisthesis.
Slip level L4-L5 in about 90%. Mean age 64.6 surgery, 69 nonoperative.
ITT clock starts at enrollment. As-treated clock starts at surgery, or at enrollment for nonoperative patients.
Analyzed: 601 of 607 with at least one follow-up visit.
slides.see: Figure 1 shows crossover by visit: 36% vs 24% operated at 3 months in the randomized arms.
slides.notes: Read the table by columns. The randomized arms differ by only 18 points in surgery received at 8 years, 72% against 54% (our subtraction). At 3 months the gap was 12 points, 36% against 24%. All crossover in the nonoperative arm happened by year 4: 79 at 4 years and 79 at 8 years. In the combined cohort 412 of 607 (68%) had surgery by 8 years, 84% of them in the first year. As-treated baseline is not balanced and the paper says so. The surgery group was younger, more often on compensation and worse off: bodily pain 31.6 vs 36.9, physical function 32 vs 39.3, ODI 43.9 vs 36.5. Our recomputation of the Table 1 and Table 2 P values matched closely, so these are real differences. Models adjusted for age, sex, race, work status, BMI, depression, baseline scores, treatment preference and center, among others. Those lists do not name compensation, and Table 2 also shows lost patients differed on education, diabetes and heart problem, none of them named, though Methods say such variables were included. Tables 1 and 2 compare groups by treatment received and by retention. No table compares the arms as randomized, 159 vs 145, so their balance cannot be checked in this paper, which matters when weighing chance behind the ITT result on slide 4. Randomization method and any blinding are not described in this paper; it points to earlier reports. Outcomes are patient-reported. The as-treated rule needs saying aloud: every change before surgery counts as nonoperative and every change after counts as surgical. So a crossover patient contributes to both sides.

slides.title: Primary outcomes: ITT and as-treated
slides.lead: The analyses point opposite ways on ODI, and global ITT showed no significant difference on pain or function, so quote both.
points: ITT: nonoperative assignment did significantly better on ODI at years 6, 7 and 8, and on physical function at year 7.
Those gaps were about 5 ODI points and 7 physical function points, called relatively low by the authors.
As-treated: surgery better on all outcome measures at years 6, 7 and 8, in randomized, observational and combined groups.
Authors: little degradation in the surgical group from years 5 through 8.
slides.see: Figure 2 shows the dashed ITT curves running together between the solid as-treated curves.
slides.notes: Direction first. SF-36 higher is better and ODI lower is better, so all three as-treated effects favor surgery. The effect is a difference in mean change from baseline. It is not a difference between final scores. The 8-year effects are quoted just after a sentence on the combined analysis, so we read them as combined, but the paper does not label them. Our CI check: all three are symmetric and plausible. The abstract goes further than the Results. It says as-treated surgery won at all time points. The Results text states years 6, 7 and 8 plus the global test, and the rest is in Supplemental Table 1, which we could not check. Now the ITT result. The authors call it difficult to interpret because outcomes are inconsistent and crossover is high, and that is fair. Crossover dilutes an ITT contrast toward zero. But dilution alone does not flip the sign. Our rough arithmetic: if a 5-point ODI gap were carried only by an 18-point difference in surgery received, the implied harm per patient operated would be about 28 points. That is not believable, so chance, attrition or who chose to cross are likelier explanations. The ITT result is no proof that surgery harms. It is also no support for surgery: randomization does not show a benefit here. The abstract's conclusion does not report that ODI favored the nonoperative assignment. The body does. Figure 2's legend says combined cohort, but its panels show randomized and observational separately.

slides.title: Secondary outcomes and harms
slides.lead: Most patients were fused, and no fusion comparison here was randomized.
points: Of 406 with complete data: decompression alone 7%, PLF 21%, PPS 55%, 360-degree fusion 17%.
8-year reoperation 22% (91 of 406); recurrent stenosis or progressive listhesis was the most common reason.
Deaths: 33 surgery vs 53 expected; 17 nonoperative vs 37 expected. Age-adjusted HR 1.2 (0.63 to 2.1), P=0.64.
Two deaths judged probably treatment related: respiratory distress at 32 days, sepsis at 82 days.
Secondary outcomes were included in the as-treated finding, but their values are in the supplement.
slides.see: Figure 3, physical function panel: the 360 curve sits below the others from about 3 years on.
slides.notes: PLF is uninstrumented posterolateral fusion. PPS adds pedicle screws. 360 adds interbody fusion to instrumented posterolateral fusion. The groups are not comparable. 360 patients were younger, more often employed, with less severe and more localized stenosis. PLF patients had more baseline neurologic deficit and more multilevel central stenosis. PPS patients had more radiographic instability. Our reading: case mix may carry some of the operative numbers. 360 had the fewest levels decompressed, the most multilevel fusion and the longest operations. The dural tear difference (P=0.039) reproduces from the counts. Do not read it causally. The one technique signal is physical function, time-weighted over 8 years: PPS 24.5 vs 360 18, P=0.022; PLF 26.8 vs 360 18, P=0.062. Our check: treated as independent estimates, the printed intervals give about P=0.07 for PPS vs 360 and about P=0.04 for PLF vs 360, so the larger gap carries the larger reported P. The two values are hard to reconcile, but the covariance is unknown. P=0.022 may be correct: it needs a standard error 0.80 times the independent one, inside the 0.77 to 0.88 seen in Table 3 (slide 6). The real oddity is P=0.062, which needs 1.12 times, and positive covariance cannot widen an interval. Multiplicity: the authors first tested for any difference among the three groups and went to pairwise tests only at p<0.10. They called these planned comparisons, so made no adjustment. The overall results are not given, yet Figure 3 prints all 12 pairwise P values across four outcomes, 1 below 0.05. Mortality: both groups died less often than expected, which suggests a healthier sample (our reading). The HR comparison direction is not stated. Reoperation counts by fusion type sum to 80, so 11 of about 29 decompression-only patients is implied. That is our subtraction, about 38%, non-randomized and tiny. Do not quote it as a result.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: A long, honest follow-up, with the headline resting on the non-randomized analysis.
points: Holds up: multicenter, validated measures, 8-year horizon, and a randomized cohort beside an observational one.
Mostly holds: long covariate list, though compensation is not named in it; as-treated results agree in both cohorts.
Holds up: authors report the ITT reversal and state their limits, including the direction of attrition bias.
Weakens it: 54% and 28% nonadherence leaves little randomized contrast.
Weakens it: only 56 to 63% retained, depending on the count used.
Weakens it: surgery patients lost to follow-up had worse 2-year results.
Weakens it: unmeasured confounding remains, and outcomes are patient-reported.
Weakens it: fusion type not randomized; fusion comparisons unadjusted for multiplicity, which the authors justify as planned.
slides.notes: Credit first. Table 3 asks whether those who stayed differ from those who left, and the authors say plainly that this raises concern the surgical effect is overestimated. Its values are adjusted time-weighted averages over 2 years in the combined as-treated cohort, not estimates at the 2-year visit. Its differences and interaction P values reproduce on our recomputation. Its intervals are narrower than the printed SEs imply for independent estimates, in all 8 cases (for example SE 1.33 vs 1.56 for bodily pain, retained; ratios 0.77 to 0.88). Positive model covariance is a likely explanation (our reading). Those lost were older, less educated and sicker. Because surgical patients who left had worse early results while nonoperative patients who left did not, 8-year data over-represent surgical successes. Now the problems. Retention is printed two ways. Figure 1 gives 385 seen at 8 years, which matches the abstract's 69% and 57%, and pools to 63% of 607 (our arithmetic). The Results give 337 of 601 remaining, 56%, and Table 2 is built on that. The paper does not reconcile them. Deaths also differ: 50 in text, 46 in Figure 1. The observational surgery box at 8 years adds to 170, not 173. Table 1 has XX placeholders for leg pain in the fusion columns, which may be a manuscript artifact. As-treated limits, ours unless noted: surgery was chosen, so preference and expectation travel with it, and outcomes are patient-reported. The authors say unmeasured confounding cannot be controlled. Measured confounding is also not fully shown: the adjustment lists do not name compensation, 9% vs 3% by treatment received. Their statement that as-treated analysis may better reflect comparative effectiveness is a judgment, and they word it as may. Also, the clock differs by group: surgical follow-up starts at surgery, so anyone leaving before surgery counts only on the nonoperative side. Fusion technique did not affect outcomes is stronger than the data support. It is a non-randomized comparison with one nominally significant result, and absence of a difference here is not proof of none.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "In SPORT's slip cohort, patients who had surgery did better through 8 years than those who did not, ODI effect about 10 points. But that is as-treated. Crossover was heavy, attrition may flatter surgery, and the randomized comparison favored nonoperative assignment on ODI."
points: Reoperation was 22% at 8 years.
This does not test fusion against decompression alone: only 7% had decompression alone.
Fusion technique data are non-randomized, so they do not prove equivalence.
Library rows below come from the master records. Endpoints and follow-up differ.

rows: As-treated favors surgery; ITT ODI favors nonoperative

slides.notes: Expect four follow-up questions. Does surgery work for a degenerative slip? The honest answer has two parts. Comparing those treated, surgery is well ahead through 8 years in both cohorts. By randomized assignment, it is not. Our reading: the as-treated signal is probably largely real, given its size and consistency, but it is an adjusted observational estimate and attrition may inflate it. Does the ITT result mean surgery is harmful? No. The authors call it hard to interpret, the outcomes are inconsistent, and only 18 points separated the arms in surgery received at 8 years. It also cannot be waved away, so quote it. Does this tell me to fuse? No. Only 29 of 406 had decompression alone, and the authors say that group was too small for a robust comparison. The fusion question belongs to SLIP, the Swedish trial and NORDSTEN-DS, summarized here from master records and not reviewed against full text in this deck. The authors note that SLIP and the Swedish trial conflicted. Should I use a 360 or stick to a posterolateral fusion? The authors say technique had minimal effect, and that the studies they cite suggest no advantage to more complex fusion. The one significant gap favored PPS on physical function, but it is non-randomized. If the estimates are independent, the printed intervals do not reconcile it with P=0.062 for PLF vs 360, the larger gap; covariance is unknown. 360 also had the longest operations and stays, though case mix differed across groups. Two facts for a patient talk, from this paper: reoperation was 22% at 8 years, and most crossover into surgery happened early, with none in the randomized nonoperative arm after year 4.

decks.not_reviewed: Supplementary appendix

slides.title: SLIP
slides.lead: Laminectomy plus fusion versus laminectomy alone for lumbar spondylolisthesis
points: Journal club · Decompression versus fusion
Ghogawala Z, et al. N Engl J Med 2016;374:1424-34
Bottom line: fusion gave a small SF-36 gain and fewer reoperations in 66 patients, but the SF-36 gain lost significance after baseline adjustment.
slides.notes: SLIP is the Spinal Laminectomy versus Instrumented Pedicle Screw trial. It was published in the same NEJM issue as the Swedish Spinal Stenosis Study, which reached the opposite conclusion. This deck was prepared from the full text. The supplementary appendix was not reviewed.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: In 2016, fusion was common and costly, yet there was no class I evidence that it beat laminectomy alone for a stable grade I slip.
points: SPORT: Surgery beat nonoperative care, and most surgical patients were fused.
Herkowitz: Favored fusion, but the study was prospective and not randomized.
Decompression cohorts: Several reported excellent outcomes at 5 years or more without fusion.

rows: Stable grade I slip with stenosis

slides.notes: Set the stakes first. The paper opens with US hospital data from 2011: 465,000 fusions and 12.8 billion dollars in aggregate hospital costs, the highest of any procedure. The authors say there was no class I evidence that adding fusion was better. The hypothesis was superiority of fusion on a generic health measure, which matters later because the Swedish trial and NORDSTEN both used ODI.

slides.title: Patients and methods
points: 130 assessed at 5 centers
106 enrolled; 40 of them declined randomization
66 randomized: 35 laminectomy, 31 fusion
Mean age 67, 80% women
Included: age 50–80, 3–14 mm slip, stenosis, neurogenic claudication
Excluded: motion over 3 mm, surgeon-judged mechanical back pain, prior lumbar surgery, ASA IV or higher
Laminectomy: complete, with partial medial facet removal
Fusion: same decompression plus posterolateral pedicle screws and iliac crest graft; no interbody, BMP or MIS
Primary: change in SF-36 physical score at 2 years, MCID 5
Secondary: ODI, MCID 10
Power: 64 patients for 80% power to detect 7.5 points
slides.notes: Three details are worth saying aloud. First, these were stable patients: flexion-extension motion over 3 mm was excluded, and so was a history the surgeon read as mechanical back pain. Second, the decompression was a full laminectomy with partial medial facetectomy, so SLIP does not test midline-preserving surgery. Third, a panel of 10 spine surgeons reviewed a vignette and images for each patient before randomization. No patient crossed over, and each surgeon had done at least 100 of each operation. Of the 66 randomized, 51 came from one site.

slides.title: Primary outcome: SF-36 at 2 years
points: Change from baseline at 2 years: laminectomy 9.5, fusion 15.2.
Table below is Table 2, SF-36 rows. Decompression-alone is the laminectomy arm. Least-squares means, with no baseline or multiplicity adjustment.
Baseline-adjusted, 2 yr: 3.9 (−1.9 to 9.7), P = 0.19. Reported in the text only; no table or figure shows it.
The unadjusted 5.7 clears the MCID of 5, not the powered 7.5, and its interval reaches 0.1.
Modeled MCID responders: 91.9% fusion vs 76.1% laminectomy, P = 0.18.
slides.notes: This is the slide to remember. The boxed row of Table 2 is the headline result: a gain of 15.2 with fusion and 9.5 with laminectomy, a difference of 5.7 points with a lower confidence bound of 0.1. The table footnote says no adjustment for multiplicity was applied. The fusion group started 3.2 points lower on SF-36 (P=0.08), had the only ASA III patients, and had slightly smaller slips. The authors had no prespecified plan for adjustment, but when they ran it the 2-year difference fell to 3.9 and lost significance. That result appears only in the Results text, which is why it sits beside the table. It was also not significant at 3 years (5.8, P=0.07) or 4 years (4.6, P=0.10). The observed effect was also smaller than the 7.5 points the trial was powered for. The authors still conclude the gain was slightly greater but clinically meaningful, and they acknowledge baseline differences may explain part of it.

slides.title: Durability, reoperation and burden
points: Reoperation: laminectomy 34%, fusion 14% at 4 yr, P = 0.05.
Laminectomy reoperations were index-level for instability; fusion reoperations were adjacent-level.
slides.see: Figure 2A: unadjusted SF-36 physical-component score from 0 to 48 months. Fusion starts lower near 31, crosses above by 3 months and holds near 45 to 46. Decompression-alone starts near 35, meets fusion at 12 months near 45, then drifts down to about 42. Figure 2C: cumulative risk of reoperation over 48 months. Decompression-alone rises steadily from about month 4 to about 0.34. Fusion stays at zero until about month 36, then rises to about 0.14. Numbers at risk at 48 months: 17 and 23.
slides.notes: Panel A plots unadjusted scores, not change from baseline, so fusion starts lower and the curves meet at 12 months. The bars are standard errors. In Table 2, the change at 4 years was 14.1 with fusion and 7.4 with laminectomy. Our reading: the gap widens because the laminectomy curve falls after 12 months while the fusion curve stays flat. The unadjusted differences at 3 and 4 years were 7.4 and 6.7 points, both P=0.02, but follow-up had dropped to 68% by 4 years and the paper says those time points are weakened. ODI favored fusion by 8.5 points at 2 years, with an interval of −17.5 to 0.5, which is below the 10-point MCID and not significant. In panel C the at-risk counts at 48 months are 17 and 23, so the right end of the curves rests on few patients (an inference, not stated in the paper). On reoperation, P was reported as 0.05 and decisions were at surgeon discretion. The burden numbers come from Table 3, and the ODI column from Table 2. Fourteen patients were reoperated in total, and they were kept in the primary analysis in their randomized groups. The authors note outcome scores improved after revision fusion. All major complications were identified within 30 days, and minor ones were not recorded. No cost analysis was reported, though one was prespecified.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: What holds up: Randomized, with no crossovers
What holds up: No industry funding or involvement
What holds up: Central review of preoperative imaging
What holds up: Independent CT check of protocol adherence
What holds up: Experienced surgeons, 100 or more of each operation
What weakens it: Only 66 randomized, 51 of them from one site
What weakens it: Baseline imbalance, with no prespecified adjustment plan
What weakens it: ODI moved from primary to secondary in the 2006 protocol
What weakens it: Analysis plan written after the trial, before data review
What weakens it: No multiplicity adjustment across time points
What weakens it: Reoperation decided by the surgeon
What weakens it: Follow-up 68% at 4 years
What weakens it: Full laminectomy limits relevance to midline-preserving surgery
slides.notes: Be fair here. The registered primary outcome did change, but the final protocol was prepared in July 2006, before the trial was completed or data were analyzed, so this is a weakness and not evidence of misconduct. Analysis of the primary outcome covered patients with follow-up assessments, by their randomized group. Our reading, not a statement from the paper: the 34 percent reoperation rate is harder to explain than people suggest. These were stable patients, yet reoperation was far higher than in NORDSTEN, which allowed dynamic instability. The usual explanation is the wider decompression, but most Swedish decompressions were also central and showed no excess reoperation. Surgeon threshold for reoperation may matter as much as biology.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: “SLIP is the main trial favoring fusion: 66 stable patients, a 5.7-point SF-36 gain that lost significance after baseline adjustment, and reoperation of 34% with laminectomy versus 14% with fusion. At 5 years, fusion added no significant benefit in the Swedish trial, and decompression alone was noninferior in NORDSTEN.”
points: D, decompression alone. F, with fusion. SLIP reoperation is at 4 years. Swedish enrolled stenosis with or without a slip, and outcomes differ between trials.
slides.notes: Expect three follow-up questions. Why did SLIP and the Swedish trial disagree in the same NEJM issue? Different primary endpoint and a much smaller trial. Our reading: the wider decompression is the usual explanation, but most Swedish decompressions were also central, so it can’t be the whole answer. Does SLIP apply to a patient with motion on flexion-extension films? Only up to 3 mm; motion over 3 mm was excluded. Would you still fuse anyone? NORDSTEN’s results do not apply to multilevel slips, scoliosis over 20 degrees, severe foraminal stenosis or prior surgery at that level, and dynamic instability remains unresolved. Numbers in this table come from different endpoints and follow-up times, so compare them with care. The full debate brief in the Spine Library covers these trials together.

decks.not_reviewed: Supplementary Appendix (Tables S1 to S4, the reoperation figure, questionnaires, surgical approaches, health economic methods) and the trial protocol. The PDF is the complete 11-page paper, not a critique. Figures for the 2024 Swedish report, SLIP, NORDSTEN and AO Spine come from their master records, not from this PDF.

slides.title: Swedish Spinal Stenosis Study
slides.lead: A randomized, controlled trial of fusion surgery for lumbar spinal stenosis
points: Journal club · Decompression versus fusion
Försth P, et al. N Engl J Med 2016;374:1413-23
Bottom line: adding fusion to decompression gave no better ODI at 2 years, with or without a slip, and it cost more time, blood and money. Additional surgery was 22% vs 21% at a mean of 6.5 years.
slides.notes: This is the Swedish Spinal Stenosis Study, or SSSS: 247 patients from seven Swedish hospitals, published in the same NEJM issue as SLIP. Do not call it a spondylolisthesis trial. It enrolled stenosis at one or two adjacent levels, and 135 of 247 had a slip. Randomization was stratified on the slip, so our reading is that the slip result carries more weight than a post hoc subgroup. Read two things before quoting it. The primary analysis was per protocol, not intention to treat. And nobody measured dynamic instability. This deck was prepared from the full text. The Supplementary Appendix was not reviewed, so the surgical techniques, the modified intention-to-treat table and the 5-year table are known only from what the main paper says about them. The paper's 5-year numbers are partial, 138 of 144 eligible. The 2024 report in the library is the one to quote for 5 years.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: Fusion was being added to decompression to prevent instability and deformity, and the authors say the evidence for that was weak.
points: Trend: Surgery grew more complex over the decades. About half of US stenosis surgery included fusion.
With a slip: 96% of US patients had fusion added, and many surgeons saw a slip as a mandatory indication.
The gap: The authors call a randomized trial warranted, whether or not a slip is present.

rows: Age 50–80, stenosis at 1 or 2 adjacent levels, with or without a slip

slides.notes: Set the stakes first. The authors' claim is that decompression was increasingly supplemented with fusion to minimize a potential risk of future instability and deformity, on weak evidence. They name two studies, references 9 and 10, as the main foundation for the combined procedure and say their validity has been questioned. Reference 9 is Herkowitz, a prospective comparison of decompression with and without intertransverse arthrodesis. They also note that a slip was treated as so strong an indication for fusion that it was an exclusion criterion in a trial of nonsurgical treatment, reference 30. Note the framing of the question: this is superiority of fusion, not noninferiority of decompression. Everyone had decompression, so the trial asks only what the added fusion buys. It cannot tell you anything about surgery against no surgery.

slides.title: Patients and methods
points: 358 assessed; 111 excluded (59 ineligible, 52 declined); 247 randomized, October 2006 to June 2012
Included: pseudoclaudication and back pain (VAS over 30), symptoms over 6 months, dural sac 75 mm² or less at 1 or 2 adjacent segments between L2 and the sacrum
Excluded: spondylolysis, scoliosis over 20 degrees, prior surgery for stenosis or instability, herniated disk as the cause
Slip: at least 3 mm forward on conventional lateral radiographs; no flexion-extension films
Surgery: senior consultants; the method of decompression or fusion was chosen solely by the surgeon
Baseline: mean age 66–68, ODI 41–43, back pain 59–64, leg pain 61–65
Power: 40 in each of 4 strata, 80% power for a 12-point ODI difference; planned 320, stopped at 247
slides.notes: Three details to say aloud. First, the slip was not defined by motion. It was a forward slip of at least 3 mm on a conventional lateral film, with a mean of 7.4 mm and a range of 3.0 to 14.3. Second, fusion here is a category, not a technique. The paper says the method was determined solely by the surgeon and sends the reader to the appendix for details, so the main paper does not tell you the implants or how the decompression was done. Third, the outcome machinery is good. Most outcomes came from Swespine postal questionnaires completed without the surgeon or anyone involved in the trial, and the authors report under 2% missing outcome data. Trial design was open label. Patients and surgeons knew the assignment. The sample size was cut because slips were more common than the 25% expected, and randomization stopped once each stratum had more than 40 patients. All four per-protocol strata cleared 40: 44, 51, 67 and 66. Women were about two thirds of the treated patients and 79% of the slip stratum (our arithmetic from Table 2). The flow diagram adds up, but see the appraisal slide for a problem with the slip counts.

slides.title: Primary outcome: ODI at 2 years
slides.lead: ODI was 27 with fusion and 24 with decompression alone, P = 0.24. Both groups improved, and fusion added nothing measurable.
points: Change from baseline: 15 with fusion, 17 alone; difference −2 (95% CI −7 to 3), P = 0.36.
Slip by treatment interaction: P = 0.33 as printed; we could not reproduce it.
Modified intention to treat, adding 9 patients operated on later: the authors report similar results.
Scale: ODI 0–100, higher is worse.

rows: Slip 7.4 mm or more, post hoc

slides.notes: How to read the confidence interval. The difference in change is fusion minus decompression, so a negative number means fusion improved less. Our reading: the upper limit of 3 means the data allow fusion a benefit of about 3 ODI points at most, well short of the 12 points the trial was powered for. So although a nonsignificant superiority result does not itself prove equivalence, this interval does exclude the benefit the trial was looking for. It does not establish that the arms are equal, and the lower limit of −7 leaves room for fusion doing somewhat worse. The 15 points the authors cite from the FDA is a within-patient improvement after fusion, not a between-group target, and both arms improved by about that much (15 and 17). The whole-trial means reproduce from Table 3 (our weighted calculation gives 26.6 and 23.6, baseline 41.8 and 41.0, P about 0.24). In the slip stratum, the group most surgeons would have fused, point estimates lean toward decompression alone, not toward fusion. That is our observation, and the difference is not significant. The printed P of 0.11 does not fit the printed means: we get about 0.22, and 0.11 only at the extreme corner of rounding. The post hoc cut at 7.4 mm is simply the mean slip, with 35 and 34 patients. It shows ODI of 25 in both arms and back pain of 36 vs 32, P = 0.55. The authors call it exploratory and give no interval. Our estimate from an SD of about 19 is a standard error of about 4.6 and a 95% half-width of about 9, so a large effect is only weakly limited. Do not treat it as a separate finding. Our reading: interaction tests are low powered, so P = 0.33 is weak evidence that the slip does not matter. That P also does not reproduce: we get about 0.69 from the 2-year means, 0.43 at the rounding limit and also on change from baseline. The method is not stated.

slides.title: Secondary outcomes and harms
slides.lead: Fusion was not significantly better on any patient-reported measure or on walking, and it was clearly the bigger operation.
points: Patient-reported: no significant difference in EQ-5D, back or leg pain, ZCQ or satisfaction in either stratum (Table 3).
5 years, partial: ODI 27 vs 28 (P = 0.86) in 138 of the 144 eligible patients.
Authors: The trial was not powered for complications.
Cost: Indirect costs were similar, and 2-year resource use did not differ significantly. Operation costs came from one clinic.

rows: Operating time, min, no slip / slip

slides.see: Figure 1 lists every complication and 2-year reoperation by cause in each arm.
slides.notes: The walk result matters because stenosis is a walking disease. Among patients with a slip, distance rose by 73 m to 382 m with fusion and by 83 m to 396 m without (P = 0.60). The authors note this is well above their 18 m minimal clinically relevant difference and unrelated to type of surgery. Additional surgery matches at 22% and 21% at a mean of 6.5 years, but the main paper gives causes only for reoperations by 2 years, and those differ. In Figure 1, 11 of 17 fusion reoperations by 2 years were for adjacent-level stenosis and 6 were for infection. After decompression alone, 7 of 13 were at the index level (3 restenosis, 4 foraminal stenosis), 3 for infection, 2 for severe back pain and 1 adjacent level. Our calculation: 11 of 113 vs 1 of 120, Fisher P = 0.002, and 2-year reoperation of 15% vs 11%, P = 0.43. These are unplanned and unadjusted, so use them as a pattern, not a result. The authors argue that fusion's harm is real outside this trial, citing registry work in which fusion doubled severe adverse events, with a number needed to harm of 30. Those are their citations, not trial data. Wound infection of 10% vs 4% (our Fisher P = 0.12) counts only infections not requiring reoperation. Figure 1 lists infection reoperations separately, 6 vs 3. Added, assuming no overlap, which the definitions imply, that is 17 of 113 (15%) vs 8 of 120 (7%), our unadjusted Fisher P about 0.055. That fuller figure looks like a signal, but the trial cannot settle it.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: Our reading: the null result looks reasonably secure for the main endpoint, though we have not seen Table S4. The weak points are what was not measured and some reporting that does not reconcile.
points: Per protocol: 14 patients who did not get the assigned surgery were dropped, 10 from fusion and 4 from decompression, in an open-label trial.
Instability: never measured, so the result cannot separate stable from unstable slips.
Bundled techniques: Surgeons chose the method, so our reading is that this tests a strategy, not a specific fusion.
Imaging: Postoperative CT, MRI and radiographs were collected but not yet evaluated, so fusion status and slip progression are unknown.

rows: Pass: all 0.15 or higher in both strata
Plausible: symmetric, implied SD 17–21; P = 0.36 fits only near the rounding edge
Implausible: needs all 14 to have no slip
Table 3 P values vs printed means
Does not reproduce: about 0.69, 0.43 at the limit

slides.notes: Fairness first. Our reading: a per-protocol primary in a superiority trial may be less worrying here than it sounds, because the authors report only minor differences from the modified intention-to-treat analysis and call the 2-year outcomes robust, losses were only 5, and the question is whether fusion helps when actually delivered. Still, the exclusions were lopsided after randomization, and 3 of them were patients under 50 randomized in error, all in the fusion arm. The modified analysis added only the 9 patients who later had surgery, and we have not read Table S4. Table 2 problem: Figure 1 assigns 67 and 68 slip patients. Table 2 says it excludes the 14 who did not get assigned treatment, yet still shows 67 and 68. That works only if all 14 had no slip, which is unlikely by chance when 45% of patients had no slip (our estimate, about 1 in 100,000). That estimate assumes non-receipt is unrelated to slip, which is doubtful: the 3 under-50 patients would be unlikely to have a degenerative slip. The paper does not explain this. Table 3 problem: Methods describe Student's t-test, but some printed P values do not fit a t-test of the printed 2-year means, even allowing for rounding. No-slip walk test 417 vs 416 prints P = 0.38; we get about 0.97. Slip back pain 36 vs 26 prints 0.15; we get about 0.03. No-slip leg pain 35 vs 34 prints 0.46; we get about 0.88. Slip ODI 25 vs 21 prints 0.11; we get about 0.22. No-slip back pain 41 vs 45 prints 0.66; we get 0.54. Our guess is that some rows test change from baseline, but the table does not say, and it would not explain slip ODI: 16 vs 20 would need an SD of about 14, while the trial's interval implies about 19. Note that the back-pain discrepancy favors decompression, so it would not rescue fusion. Authors' overreach, our reading: they say results in slips of 7.4 mm or more strongly indicate that omitting flexion-extension films did not bias findings. Slip size is not motion, so that does not follow. Funding: Johnson & Johnson supported the health economic analysis, and the authors say no company had a role in analysis or writing. Disclosures: Mr. Ólafsson reports grant support from Medtronic, and Dr. Borgström is an employee of and holds stock in Quantify Research; both list Quantify Research as an affiliation.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: “The Swedish trial randomized 247 patients with stenosis, 135 with a slip. Adding fusion did not improve 2-year ODI, 27 vs 24. By our reading, the interval on change, −7 to 3, rules out the 12-point benefit it was built to find. Fusion meant longer surgery, more bleeding and a longer stay, and additional surgery was 22% vs 21% at a mean of 6.5 years. Instability was never measured.”
points: D, decompression alone. F, with fusion. Outcomes differ between trials, so compare with care.
Swedish 2-year analysis is per protocol, 228 of 247. The 5-year n is patients analyzed, 213 of 225 eligible. Comparator figures come from their library records.
slides.notes: Expect these follow-up questions. Why does this differ from SLIP? The authors say comparison is hampered: SLIP had more dropout and a much higher reoperation rate after decompression, 34% vs 14%, which could have hurt SF-36, and reoperation depends on surgeon choice as well as the patient. They also note SLIP found its benefit on SF-36 and not on ODI. Our addition: SLIP was far smaller, with 66 patients, and its record shows the SF-36 difference of 5.7 falling to 3.9 (−1.9 to 9.7, P = 0.19) after baseline adjustment. Does this apply to a slip with motion on dynamic films? Not directly. Those films were not obtained, so the trial cannot say. Our reading: NORDSTEN included such patients but did not answer the question. Its 2-year record says about 20% had dynamic instability and no subgroup conclusions can be drawn. Would you still fuse anyone? The trial does not address spondylolysis, scoliosis over 20 degrees, prior surgery for stenosis or instability, or stenosis beyond two adjacent levels. AO Spine's 2025 synthesis says both options can be considered, ideally reserving fusion for patients whose instability justifies it, and rates this trial Moderate. Does fusion prevent reoperation? Not here on total rates at 6.5 years. The causes differ by 2 years: adjacent-level stenosis after fusion, index-level problems after decompression. The 2024 record reports the same pattern. Is the 5-year result here final? No. It covers 138 patients, with ODI 27 vs 28. The 2024 report on 213 patients gives 28 vs 25, and 28 vs 23 with a slip. That is the same trial, not replication. What is the single best caveat? The trial tells you adding fusion for a slip seen on a static film did not help. It does not tell you what to do for proven instability.

decks.not_reviewed: Supplementary Appendix (including Tables S3 and S4, Figure S1 and Sections 2, 3 and 5), the protocol, the statistical analysis plan, and the disclosure forms. Later follow-up appears here only through the L09 library record.

slides.title: NORDSTEN-DS
slides.lead: Decompression with or without Fusion in Degenerative Lumbar Spondylolisthesis
points: Journal club · Decompression versus fusion
Austevoll IM, et al. N Engl J Med 2021;385:526-38
Bottom line: decompression alone was noninferior to adding instrumented fusion at 2 years. ODI responders were 71.4% vs 72.9%, and the lower confidence bound of −12.2 stayed inside the −15 margin.
Reoperation was 12.5% vs 9.1%. The trial was not powered for that comparison.
slides.notes: This is the Norwegian Degenerative Spondylolisthesis and Spinal Stenosis trial: 267 patients, 16 surgical departments, one country, two years. It asks a different question from the two 2016 NEJM trials. Those were superiority trials. This one asks whether leaving out the fusion loses an acceptable amount of benefit or less. So the result is a statement about a margin, and it stands or falls on whether you accept that margin. Hold on to one distinction through the deck: noninferior does not mean equal. The data still allow a loss of about 12 responders per 100. This deck was prepared from the full 13-page paper, and the PDF is complete. The Supplementary Appendix was not reviewed, and that matters here: the surgical and imaging details, including the fusion assessment, sit in Table S3, and only the summary figures appear in the main paper.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: Fusion is common for degenerative slip, yet the 2016 trials disagreed. Can decompression alone give up no more than an acceptable amount of benefit?
points: Practice: fusion accounts for more than 90% of these surgeries in some countries; in others about 50% of patients have decompression without fusion.
Cost: US lumbar instrumented fusion was estimated at $13 billion of hospital costs in 2011.
Evidence gap: two 2016 trials diverged, and later meta-analyses were equivocal.
Patients: stenosis with single-level degenerative slip of at least 3 mm
Intervention: midline-preserving decompression alone
Comparison: decompression plus instrumented fusion
Outcome: at least 30% ODI reduction at 2 years, margin −15 percentage points
slides.notes: The authors frame this as practice variation without settled evidence. Their introduction says an editorial on the 2016 trials suggested fusion adds no value, and that debate continued because entry criteria differed. Note the direction of the design. The burden is on decompression alone to show it is not worse by 15 points or more. The authors justify allowing that loss because decompression is less complex, less invasive, cheaper and possibly safer. The 2016 trial details here are as the authors describe them: one enrolled 133 patients with slips at one or two levels and no information on dynamic motion (the L07 library record gives 135 of 247 with a slip of at least 3 mm, a mismatch we did not resolve), and the other enrolled 66 single-level patients without dynamic instability. SLIP numbers later in the deck come from the L06 library record. A useful way to set up the room: if you already believe decompression is safer and cheaper, a margin makes sense. If you believe instability needs fusion, this trial deliberately did not screen those patients out. Flexion-extension films did not decide entry.

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: 738 assessed for eligibility, 267 randomized, 134 to decompression alone and 133 to fusion.
points: Included: age 18–80, 3 months of failed conservative care, MRI stenosis, slip of at least 3 mm on standing lateral films, solely at the stenotic level
Any slip grade above 3 mm, any flexion-extension result

Excluded: grade 3 foraminal stenosis, prior surgery at that level, thoracolumbar fracture or fusion. Figure 1 also lists multilevel slip, scoliosis over 20 degrees, isthmic defect and stenosis at more than three levels
Decompression alone: posterior, midline structures preserved; bilateral, ipsilateral, or ipsilateral with crossover
Fusion: any decompression technique, pedicle screws and rods with bone graft, cage optional
Baseline: mean age 66, about 69% women, ODI about 39, leg pain 6.7 of 10 in each arm, back pain 6.7 vs 6.6
Power: 232 patients for 80% power, 128 per group with 10% dropout
slides.notes: Randomization was strong: computer-generated, concealed, stratified by center, permuted blocks of four or six. Blinding was weak. The trial was open label, and the authors say only the data analyst, not the outcome assessors, was unaware of assignment. Patients were screened by surgeons involved in the operations, and 108 declined the trial while 86 opted for nonsurgical care. Exclusion reasons add to 549 because patients could have more than one, which the legend allows. Chronic symptoms were the norm: about 75% had leg pain and more than 80% had back pain for over a year. Table 1 gives no P values. On our recalculation no Table 1 row reaches P<0.05. The closest is ASA 3, 12.4% vs 20.2%: P=0.09 by chi-square, 0.12 by Fisher. Table 1 also hides a gap by rounding EQ-5D to 0.4 in both arms. Table 2 gives 0.44 (0.39 to 0.48) vs 0.38 (0.33 to 0.43), about P=0.08 from those intervals (ours). Both gaps run toward a sicker fusion arm, which matters when you read the EQ-5D change on slide 5. Notice the arms are not just fusion added to the same decompression. In the fusion arm the decompression technique was optional, and 70 of 128 did not have midline structures preserved. In the decompression arm 129 of 132 did. Table 3 is headed 133 and 129, but its surgical and complication rows use 132 and 128, and the paper does not explain the missing patient in each arm. So technique differs along with the fusion. Sample size: the paper does not state the responder rate it assumed. Our simple calculation says 116 per group implies about 79%. At the observed rate of about 72%, the same formula gives about 141 per group, against about 120 observed at 2 years. The trial still passed because the observed difference was close to zero. An interim analysis was run at 150 patients; the paper does not say whether alpha was adjusted.

slides.title: Primary outcome: ODI responders at 2 years
slides.lead: Noninferiority had to hold in both the modified intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses. It did.
points: Difference is decompression minus fusion. Negative favors fusion. Margin −15.
All lower bounds clear the margin. Post hoc ITT clears it by only 1 point.
slides.see: Figure 2 plots all five intervals against the −15 line.
slides.notes: Read the lower bound, not the point estimate. In the main analysis −12.2 means the data are compatible with fusion producing up to about 12 more responders per 100, a number needed to treat of about 8. That is our arithmetic. The authors set the margin at 15 points, which they equate to a number needed to treat of 7. We recomputed all five intervals with the paper's Newcombe method from the printed counts, and all reproduce to within 0.1. That includes the modified ITT row, although its counts are imputed. Now the fragile part. Modified ITT dropped patients who did not get the assigned surgery: 1 in the decompression arm and 3 in the fusion arm, plus 1 consent withdrawal. The post hoc ITT analysis adds back all but the withdrawal, and the estimate moves toward fusion, to −3.3, with a lower bound of −14.0. That shift is partly re-imputation, not only those patients' outcomes (ours): in Figure 2 decompression responders fall from 95 of 133 to 94 of 134 although a patient was added, while fusion goes from 94 of 129 to 97 of 132. Our reading: dropping them was not the conservative choice for a noninferiority trial, and the result passes with 1 point to spare. The paper does not say what those patients received in the main text. The per-protocol set is also unusual. It is defined by having no reoperation and available primary data, so it removes reoperated patients, 15 vs 11. Reoperation is plausibly a treatment failure, in our reading. The authors flag that this could favor decompression, and they say the conclusion holds because those patients stayed in the other analyses. So per protocol is a weak second check here. Mean ODI change agrees: −20.6 vs −21.3, difference 0.7 (−2.8 to 4.3). ODI was lower at 3 months and held. The 22 patients missing 2-year data, and 4 missing baseline, were imputed.

slides.title: Secondary outcomes and harms
slides.lead: Fusion added time, blood loss and dural tears. None of these intervals was adjusted for multiplicity, and the authors say no definite conclusions can be drawn.
points: Back pain did not favor fusion: responders were numerically higher with decompression alone.
Successful fusion was certain in 86 of 100 with imaging at 2 years.
slides.notes: Start with back pain, because surgeons expect fusion to win there. It did not: mean change −3.39 vs −2.94, difference −0.45 (−1.13 to 0.23). Among patient-reported results, EQ-5D comes closest to excluding zero: difference in change −0.08 (−0.15 to 0.00), favoring fusion. The fusion arm started lower, 0.44 vs 0.38, and ended higher, 0.70 vs 0.72, so the baseline gap may be part of this (ours). It is not the only lean to fusion.
