ODI mean change, ZCQ and leg pain responders, 2-year satisfaction (1.78 vs 1.73, lower is better) and patient-reported deterioration also lean that way numerically, by small amounts. Back pain is the only one leaning clearly to decompression. The authors describe the mean changes as similar small differences. Reoperation is the number to handle carefully. 15 of 120 vs 11 of 121 is 3.4 points, about 1 in 29 by our arithmetic, but the interval runs from −4.6 to 11.5. The authors say the trial was not powered for it and that they cannot rule out subsequent fusion after decompression. The paper gives no full breakdown of reasons for reoperation. Table 3 itemizes only hematoma during the hospital stay, 1 in each arm. Harms: 2 patients had wrong-side or wrong-level surgery, 1 in each arm, and a footnote calls this somewhat higher than the literature. Deep wound infection was 3 in the fusion arm and none in the decompression arm. Transfusion was 0 vs 4. Cardiovascular events went the other way: 3 vs 0 in hospital, including a stroke, and 1 stroke after discharge. Numbers are small. Patient-reported deterioration was similar at 5.9% vs 5.0%. Recomputed: all percentage-point intervals match to within 0.1 except one, venous thromboembolism after discharge, printed −3.9 where the method gives −3.0. Table 3 labels duration and stay as ±SD, but 104±4 and 174±6 fit the printed interval only if they are standard errors. Surgery difference is −70 (−84 to −55) in Table 3 and −69 (−83 to −56) in the text. Blood loss means differ by 288, printed −292. Quote the outcome, not the decimal.

slides.title: Critical appraisal

rows: Concealed, computer-generated randomization stratified by center
Margin chosen empirically, without an evidence base
Primary analysis is modified ITT, not ITT
Both required analyses pass; all three sensitivity lower bounds clear −15
Fusion arm decompression differed in technique
Funders not involved in design or analysis
Fusion assessed on CT, by majority of three readers

slides.notes: Be fair: this is a well-run trial, and its primary counts and intervals recompute. The limits the authors state themselves are the eligibility criteria, no subgroup conclusion for instability, open label, outcome assessors who knew assignment, an empirically chosen margin, and possible selection bias in the per-protocol set. The rest are our reading. The margin is the central judgment. The authors say an evidence-based margin does not exist. A surgeon who would not accept losing 15 responders per 100 cannot take the trial's conclusion as stated, but can still read the interval: −12.2 is the number. Open label matters for a patient-reported outcome, though the direction is hard to call. Patients may believe in hardware, or in the smaller operation. Instability needs saying plainly. About 20% had slippage of at least 3 mm or at least 10 degrees of angulation on dynamic films. Patients were included either way, which is a strength for applicability. But the authors state that no conclusions can be drawn from subgroups, including these patients. So the trial does not prove that unstable slips do not need fusion. The authors do observe that reoperation here was lower than in the trial that excluded instability, and they hypothesize that follow-up time and practice variation may explain it. The authors consider bias from fusion method low, because no fusion method has been shown superior and successful fusion on CT was frequent. Separately they report 38% cage use, against 17%, 6% and 0% in somewhat similar trials. That fusion rate rests on 100 patients with imaging out of 129. The paper also has internal inconsistencies, all small: enrollment start is February 12 in the Results and April 15 in the Figure 1 legend. One withdrawal is placed before randomization in the text and before the operation in Figure 2, and Figure 1 shows it after randomization. Imputed patients are 15 vs 11 in the text, while Figure 2 implies 16 vs 10. None changes the conclusion.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: “In single-level degenerative slip with stenosis, decompression alone was noninferior to adding instrumented fusion at 2 years: 71% vs 73% reached a 30% ODI drop, and the lower bound of −12 stayed inside a −15 margin. Surgery was about 70 minutes shorter. Reoperation was 12.5% vs 9.1%, a gap the trial was not powered to test.”

rows: SF-36 gain 9.5 vs 15.2; not significant after baseline adjustment

points: Pairs are decompression vs fusion. NORDSTEN 5-year and SLIP numbers come from the library records. Endpoints differ, and SLIP follow-up runs to 4 years.
Do not stretch it: no multilevel slip, scoliosis, severe foraminal stenosis or prior surgery at that level.
slides.notes: Expect four follow-up questions. Does this mean nobody needs fusion? No. It applies to the eligible population. The authors say that for excluded patients, such as degenerative scoliosis, radicular pain from extensive foraminal stenosis, prior surgery at that level, and multilevel slip, fusion is considered established practice. What about the unstable slip? About 20% had dynamic instability and were randomized, but the authors say no subgroup conclusions can be drawn, and they call for well-powered studies. You can say instability did not exclude patients. You cannot say instability does not matter. Will decompression patients come back for fusion? Possibly. Reoperation was numerically higher at 2 years with a wide interval, and the authors note that fusion patients also face hardware removal and adjacent-level surgery. The L09 record shows total subsequent surgery of 16% vs 18% at 5 years, with the timing of operations differing between arms. Note a small mismatch: this paper gives 11 fusion reoperations by 2 years, and the L09 record's table gives 12. We did not resolve it from this paper. Why does SLIP differ? From the L06 record, SLIP used complete laminectomy with partial medial facet removal, excluded motion over 3 mm, had 66 patients and a superiority design, and followed to 4 years. So technique, selection and follow-up all differ. The authors themselves point to follow-up time and practice variation for the reoperation gap. The practical line, ours: for a patient like these, offering decompression alone is supported, and the trade to discuss is a smaller operation against a reoperation risk that is not yet settled.

decks.not_reviewed: Source PDF is a reformatted PMC text, not the publisher version. It leaves out Figures 1 and 2, the footnotes to Tables 1 to 3 (so the thresholds for clinically important improvement on the Zurich and pain scales are unknown), and any funding, competing-interest or contributor statements. Also not read: the supplementary appendix (tables S2, S4, S6, imputation methods, patient involvement detail), the protocol and statistical analysis plan (references 17 and 19), and the treatment-effect-modifier paper (reference 41).

slides.title: Kgomotso 2024: Nordsten-DS at five years
slides.lead: Bottom line: decompression alone stayed noninferior to decompression with instrumented fusion at 5 years. 63% met the ODI goal in both groups, and 16% vs 18% had another operation.
points: Journal club · Decompression versus fusion
Kgomotso EL, et al. BMJ 2024;386:e079771
Source limit: our PDF is the full text reformatted from PMC. Figures 1 and 2, table footnotes, funding and conflict statements, and the appendix are missing.
slides.notes: This is the five-year report of the Norwegian trial whose two-year result is already in the library as L08. Same 267 patients, same comparison, same noninferiority margin. Keep the claim narrow. Noninferior means the data exclude a loss of more than 15 percentage points in ODI responders. It does not mean the operations are the same. Decompression here is midline preserving, in a group where a single level is slipped at least 3 mm. This deck comes from the whole article text. The PDF is not the publisher copy: it says images are omitted, and in practice it also drops the table footnotes and any funding or conflict statement. So we cannot say who funded the trial or whether authors had conflicts. Check the published version for those. The flow chart (Figure 1) and the primary outcome figure (Figure 2) are also missing, which limits our flow check and means we have only the authors' sentence on the sensitivity analyses. Differences throughout are decompression minus fusion, so a negative number favors fusion on responder rates.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: Trials and meta-analyses indicated decompression alone was sufficient for up to two years, one trial found fusion superior, and evidence past two years was sparse and contradictory. Does the answer hold at five years?
points: History: decompression came first; instrumented fusion became the preferred operation after studies from the early 1990s.
Recent: trials and meta-analyses suggested decompression is enough for up to two years.
Conflict: one trial (SLIP, reference 15) favored fusion.
Why five years matters: the fear with no fusion is late slip-related failure, which a two-year result cannot exclude (our framing).

rows: Age 18–80, stenosis, slip of 3 mm or more at that level
Decompression plus pedicle screws, rods and graft
30% or more ODI reduction at 5 years; margin −15 points

slides.notes: Set up the debate. The authors say decompression was the traditional goal, then instrumented fusion became preferred following studies from the early 1990s. Recent randomized trials and meta-analyses suggested decompression alone suffices to two years. One trial favored fusion. From the library records: SLIP randomized 66 patients with reoperation 34% after laminectomy vs 14% after fusion, and its laminectomy was complete with partial medial facet removal, so it does not test the midline-preserving operation used here. The Swedish trial enrolled stenosis with or without a slip and was a superiority design. Nordsten-DS differs in that it asks a noninferiority question directly and enrolled everyone with a slip of at least 3 mm whatever their instability signs. The obvious question for a surgeon is the slow failure: does the unfused segment slip, hurt and come back after two years? That framing is ours, and it is why the reoperation timing on slide 5 matters. Note what the trial does not test: it did not compare surgery with non-operative care. Patients had already chosen surgery through shared decision making before they were invited.

slides.title: Patients and methods
points: 738 screened, 267 randomized at 16 Norwegian public clinics, 134 decompression and 133 fusion
Analyzed: 133 and 129 modified intention to treat; 5-year questionnaires from 121 and 109
Mean age 66.2, 69% women, baseline ODI about 39, slip about 7 mm
Included regardless of instability signs: predominant back pain, higher slip, motion on flexion-extension, fluid in facets
Excluded: scoliosis over 20 degrees, deformed root in the foramen, prior surgery at that level, thoracolumbar fracture or fusion
Decompression: spinous process and supraspinous-interspinous ligaments preserved
Fusion: posterior decompression, midline optional, pedicle screws, rods, graft, optional interbody device
Margin −15 points, about NNT 7. Needed 116 per group, 128 with 10% dropout
Noninferiority had to hold in both modified ITT with imputation and per protocol
slides.see: Figure 1 (published version only; not in our PDF) gives the reasons 471 screened patients were not enrolled. Its legend says an ODI under 25 was an exclusion until 29 August 2015.
slides.notes: Four things to notice. First, inclusion ignored instability on purpose. On standing extension minus flexion films, 22% vs 17% had 3 mm or more of forward translation. Separately, 19% vs 20% had a facet fluid gap over 2 mm; Table 1 lists that apart from the films, and its reference is an MRI paper. This is what makes the trial relevant to the patient you were taught to fuse. Second, the sets are not the randomized sets. Modified intention to treat means received the assigned treatment and had data after randomization, so 5 of 267 are out: one withdrew and four did not receive the assigned treatment. The arms lost 1 and 4. Third, per protocol here does not mean followed the protocol. It removes everyone reoperated, 44 patients, plus those with missing primary data. Reoperation is an outcome, so this set is a post-randomization filter. Our reading: it is a weak check for a noninferiority claim, and the L08 record also notes it may favor decompression. Fourth, the trial was open label. Patients and surgeons knew the assignment, only the data analyst was masked, and the primary outcome is patient reported. Allocation looks sound: computer-generated, stratified by site with random blocks of 4 and 6, sent by email from a coordinating centre. Follow-up: 7 died (3 and 4) and 25 were lost (9 and 16), which leaves 121 and 109 and matches the text when counted from the modified sets. 230 of 267 is 86%; the printed 88% uses 262. Our baseline check, since the paper gives no P values: none of the Table 1 rows we tested reaches P<0.05. The largest gap is ASA 3, 12% vs 20%, P about 0.09, a little sicker in the fusion group. Table 1 prints EQ-5D SD as 3.0, which is impossible on that scale. The Fig 1 legend gives inclusion start as 15 April 2014, while the text says 12 February 2014.

slides.title: Primary outcome: ODI responders at 5 years
slides.lead: Both analyses cleared the −15 margin. Per protocol it cleared by half a point.
points: Authors' translation of the lower bounds: NNT 8.9 and 6.9 for fusion, so at least 7 to 9 fused to gain one responder.
Authors report the two sensitivity analyses went the same way and stayed inside the margin. Their figures are in Figure 2, which we lack.
Ours: one fewer per-protocol responder with decompression (64/100) moves the lower bound to about −15.5.
slides.see: Figure 2 (published version only; not in our PDF) gives counts and differences for each specified analysis, by its legend. Check it for the sensitivity results.
slides.notes: Read the lower bound, not the point estimate. A point estimate near zero with an interval of −11.2 to 11.9 says the data fit anything from a real fusion benefit of about 11 points to a real decompression benefit of about 12. Noninferiority looks only at the fusion side, and a loss that size is what it permits. We recomputed both intervals with the Newcombe hybrid score method the authors name, and the arithmetic reproduces the printed intervals exactly. For modified ITT that is less reassuring than it sounds. 84 and 81 are imputed counts, as the denominators show: 133 and 129 include about 32 patients with no 5-year data. So do not read them as observed responders. The interval comes straight from rounded imputed counts over the full denominators, so it appears to treat imputed patients as observed and may carry no between-imputation uncertainty. If so, −11.2 may be too narrow. That is our inference; the imputation method is in the appendix, which we did not read. Now the fragile part, which is ours. Per protocol has to pass, and it passes by 0.5 of a point. Change one decompression patient from responder to nonresponder and our recomputed lower bound is about −15.5, which fails. The authors themselves flag that the per-protocol sample was below the planned size: 100 and 89 against 116. They also say no evidence-based margin exists and that −15 was chosen empirically, justified because decompression is less extensive, cheaper and possibly safer. Would you accept losing 15 of 100 responders? That is the real question. Sample size: this paper does not state the expected responder rate. Our arithmetic: 116 per group implies a rate near 80%; at the observed 63% it would need about 163. Durability: from L08, two-year responders were 71.4% vs 72.9%, so about 8 to 10 points were lost in both arms by 5 years. That loss was shared. Reoperated patients stay in the modified ITT count, and they did about as well as others: 12/18 (67%) and 12/20 (60%) responders. So that analysis judges a strategy that includes later surgery, not a single operation. This reading is ours. The missing-data counts mostly reconcile, by our reading. 262 − 44 reoperated − 29 missing = 189, the printed per-protocol set, so the 29 are patients not reoperated (12 and 17 by arm) and the text's 7 are reoperated patients. That gives 31 missing at 5 years against 32 without 5-year data, and 7 against 6 reoperated missing (44 − 38). Figure 1 would be needed to settle those two.

slides.title: Secondary outcomes and harms
slides.lead: Long-term function showed similar small differences, with unadjusted intervals. Operative burden favored decompression. Differences are decompression minus fusion, with sign corrected where the paper flips it.
points: Total operations were 28 in each group; some patients had more than one.
Secondary results have unadjusted intervals. The authors say no definite conclusions can be drawn from them.
Wrong side or level: 1 in each group. Hematoma needing reoperation: 1 in each group.
slides.notes: Start with the back pain row, because it is the heart of the debate. The authors point out that the reduction in back pain was similar between groups, −2.84 vs −2.62 (difference −0.22, −0.95 to 0.52, unadjusted), even though many participants had radiological and clinical signs of instability. Leg pain leans to decompression at 5 years (3.12 vs 3.78 in Table 2), and all intervals cross zero. EQ-5D change leans to fusion only because fusion started lower: both groups are 0.68 at 5 years, from 0.44 vs 0.38 at baseline (0.43 vs 0.38 in Table 1; our z test on the Table 2 intervals, P about 0.10). Reoperation timing has more shape than early vs late. Fusion had more first reoperations before 3 months (2 vs 7). Decompression had more from 3 months to 2 years (13 vs 5). The authors say the first two years as a whole had slightly more reoperations with decompression, mainly a subsequent fusion at the index level; they give no reason by Table 3 window. Fusion had more from 2 to 5 years (6 vs 11), mainly at a new level. No window was significant as printed, though 3 months to 2 years is close: printed lower bound −0, our P about 0.05. By 2 years that makes 15 vs 12. The text says 11 and 15, which cannot be right: only the table adds to 21 and 23, and the Discussion agrees with the table. Those may be L08's 15 vs 11 reversed (our inference). The window denominators are not risk sets (decompression rises from 120 to 123), so the percentages are not cumulative rates. Explaining why the US trial's reoperation rate differs from this trial and the Swedish one, the authors offer a possibility: the threshold to offer fusion for persisting back pain could be low when none was done. Applying that to this trial's 3 month to 2 year window is our inference. They argue against routine fusion for that complaint. Harms. In Table 3 the difference column changes direction partway (dural tear to respiratory run fusion minus decompression); we show one direction. The authors name blood loss and dural tears as the differences. The printed blood loss difference is 292, but 429 minus 141 is 288. Duration and stay SDs (4.2, 6.15, 0.21, 0.23) look like standard errors, ours. Fusion rows carry more neurological deterioration: 32 vs 45, upper bound 0, our P about 0.05. The authors do not call it significant. The total equals the sum of four windows, so a patient reporting twice may count twice. This count is patient reported and unblinded. Reoperation here was not a powered endpoint.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: What holds up: Concealed computer allocation, stratified by site
What holds up: 16 public clinics, orthopaedic and neurosurgical surgeons
What holds up: Instability signs did not exclude patients
What holds up: Per-protocol interval reproduces from the counts (ours)
What holds up: Data closed to the research group until 23 March 2023
What weakens it: Open label with a patient-reported primary outcome
What weakens it: Margin chosen empirically; no evidence-based value exists
What weakens it: Per-protocol clears it by 0.5 point and is under-sized
What weakens it: Per protocol removes reoperated patients
What weakens it: Modified ITT interval may omit imputation uncertainty (ours; method in unread appendix)
What weakens it: 5 randomized patients excluded from analysis
What weakens it: 32 of 262 without 5-year data, more lost in fusion (16 vs 9)
What weakens it: 267 of 738 enrolled; patients chose surgery first
What weakens it: Funding and conflicts not in our PDF
slides.notes: Bias direction first. In a noninferiority trial, anything that blurs a real difference helps the new claim. Later fusion in the decompression arm, imputation and an imprecise patient-reported score all pull the groups together. Those readings are ours. The open-label design could push either way: patients were told the evidence for one over the other was scarce, so we cannot sign it. Selection: patients agreed to surgery, then to being randomized, with surgeons screening. Generalisation limits are the authors': not degenerative scoliosis, severe foraminal stenosis, prior surgery at that level, or multilevel slips. Spot the language that outruns the data. The abstract says reoperations were no different. A difference of −2 (−12 to 7) in a trial not powered for this cannot show no difference. The conclusion says a reoperation occurred in about one in five participants in both groups. Table 3 gives 16% and 18%, about one in six. The 22% figures count operations per participant. The conclusion that fusion is superfluous for most of these patients is the authors' opinion, and it goes beyond noninferiority within a 15-point margin. Their own Discussion says five-year data cannot exclude subgroups who benefit, and the secondary subgroup work (reference 41) was at two years and is exploratory. The Discussion also lists reference 15, SLIP, among results recommending decompression alone, although the same paper says SLIP favored fusion. The Discussion quotes Swedish reoperation as 22% and 21% over five years. Library records give 22% vs 21% at mean 6.5 years in the 2016 report, and 22% vs 24% in the 2024 five-year report. Neither matches that wording, and the 2024 report is not cited. Fusion quality is not reported here. L08 records 86 of 100 fusions confirmed at two years. Slip progression on imaging at five years is not in this text either, so the structural question stays open.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: “At 5 years, midline-preserving decompression alone was noninferior to instrumented fusion for a single-level degenerative slip: 63% ODI responders in each group, lower bound −11 against a −15 margin, and about 1 in 6 reoperated in each group. Fusion cost more time, blood and dural tears.”
points: D, decompression alone. F, with fusion. Rows come from library records; endpoints and follow-up differ between trials.
Do not stretch it: noninferior within 15 points is not equal, and per protocol cleared the margin by half a point.
slides.notes: Expect five follow-up questions. Does this apply to my patient with motion on flexion-extension? They were included: 22% vs 17% had 3 mm or more of translation. Reference 41 is exploratory and at two years, and found no benefit from fusion in such patients, by the authors' account. The five-year effect-modifier study is still to come, and the authors do not exclude subgroups. Our advice, not the authors': treat dynamic instability as not proven either way. Isn't reoperation higher without fusion? Not overall: 16% vs 18% of patients, 28 operations in each group. Timing differs. If the patient has decompression and persistent back pain, should you fuse? The authors argue against routine fusion for that, citing how common nonspecific back pain is and how little evidence ties it causally to the slip. That is their argument, not a trial result. Why not quote the mean ODI? −17.8 in both arms is a good number, but the primary outcome and the margin are on responders. What about SLIP? From the library: SLIP favored fusion on SF-36 in 66 patients, lost significance after baseline adjustment, and used complete laminectomy. The authors note its reoperation gap is unexplained, and suggest treatment traditions and radiological assessment may play a part. Table rows come from the master records except this paper's row, so SLIP and Swedish numbers are as stored there. The Swedish row is the 2024 five-year record, and that trial enrolled stenosis with or without a slip. Ten-year Nordsten-DS follow-up is planned according to the Methods. The L08 record gives 2-year reoperation as 12.5% vs 9.1%; the L08 deck gives the counts as 15 vs 11, and 15/120 and 11/121 give exactly those percentages. This paper's table gives 15/129 and 12/125, so the denominators differ and the fusion count rose from 11 to 12. Say the source limit if asked about funding: our PDF does not carry it.

decks.not_reviewed: No supplement is cited. The design and earlier papers (references 10 and 11) and the ClinicalTrials.gov record were not read. Figure values were read from the plots.

slides.title: Blumenthal 2013
slides.lead: Radiographic predictors of delayed instability following decompression without fusion for degenerative grade I lumbar spondylolisthesis
points: Journal club · Decompression versus fusion
Blumenthal C, et al. J Neurosurg Spine 2013;18:340-6
Bottom line: 15 of 40 had a fusion after laminectomy alone. Only motion at the slip reached significance, and the 75% versus 0% comparison did not (P=0.14).
slides.notes: This is a single-arm cohort from the SLIP group. Forty patients at one site, operated on by one surgeon, the senior author, between May 2002 and September 2009. Everyone had laminectomy without fusion, so the paper can describe who was reoperated. It cannot show that fusion would have helped any of them. Read the title with care: it says delayed instability, but the endpoint measured is reoperation. This deck was prepared from the complete 7-page paper, including its tables and figures. No supplement is cited. In the library it is historical context, and AO Spine selected it for appraisal (L13). The library record notes that AO rates it both very low and Low. The useful question for journal club: how much can 15 events and three cutoffs carry? Our answer is that they raise a hypothesis and do not set a fusion indication.

slides.title: The question and the patients
slides.lead: Can preoperative imaging show who will come back for a fusion after laminectomy alone?
points: Included: age 50-80, grade I degenerative slip (3-14 mm), neurogenic claudication with or without radiculopathy
Excluded: mechanical back pain, motion over 3 mm, prior lumbar surgery, ASA class III or higher
Mechanical back pain meant pain from standing over 5 minutes or lifting over 20 lb
Surgery: open facet-sparing laminectomy, no minimally invasive cases, one surgeon
Treatment was at the discretion of surgeon and patient
slides.notes: The authors start from a real dilemma: they had previously reported nearly 3 times as many reoperations with laminectomy alone as with fusion, yet laminectomy is associated with fewer complications and good function. Their aim is to separate good laminectomy candidates from those at risk. Now look at the selection. Motion over 3 mm and mechanical back pain were out. So every cutoff in this paper sits inside that screened group. The paper does not call these patients stable, and 37.5% were later reoperated for presumed instability. The paper says patients met criteria and were enrolled, but it does not say they were consecutive, and it gives no count of those screened. Forty patients in more than 7 years at one site is a small number. The paper does not explain how they came to have laminectomy alone beyond surgeon and patient discretion. The study is registered under the SLIP trial number and named as the Greenwich Lumbar Stenosis SLIP Study. The master record flags likely overlap with SLIP (L06), and the paper does not state it. Note the difference in exclusions: ASA III or higher here, ASA IV or higher in the SLIP record. Our reading: if some of these patients were randomized and others were not, the paper does not tell us. Baseline function did not separate the groups, and the table's overall means match the subgroup means when weighted. The largest non-radiographic gap is sex: 68.0% female without reoperation against 86.7% with it, 17 of 25 and 13 of 15. No P is printed and Results still call the groups similar. Our chi-square gives P about 0.19 and Fisher 0.27, so this is a gap to notice and not a finding. Our t tests for age, ODI and SF-36 PCS are all above 0.7. The authors name their own limits: small sample, possibly unrepresentative, BMI not measured, open technique only.

slides.title: Measurement and endpoint
slides.lead: Five radiographic variables were measured before surgery. The endpoint was a surgeon's recommendation accepted by a patient.
points: Flexion-extension films: motion and sagittal rotation. CT: disc height and facet angle
Read by 2 independent radiologists and the principal surgeon
No reliability statistic or blinding is reported
Endpoint: reoperation, always fusion at the index level
Indication: mechanical low-back pain, presumably from instability
No reoperation criteria are stated
slides.see: Figure 1 shows how each measurement was made. Panels A and B read 9.66 and 11.12 mm.
slides.notes: Start with the endpoint. The authors say it plainly: reoperation is subjective for surgeon and patient. All patients but one chose reoperation when the surgeon identified instability and recommended it, so by our arithmetic 16 were offered it and 15 accepted. The abstract says the pain was caused by instability. The Results say presumably caused. No postoperative imaging criterion is given, so instability here is an inference from pain plus a decision. Also note the odd loop: mechanical back pain was an exclusion at entry and became the reason for reoperation. Four of the 15 had surgery within 6 months, which we consider early for delayed instability. The paper says the other 11 were diagnosed and treated after 6 months. Now the measurement. The authors argue bias is unlikely because imaging review was independent and prospective. That protects the baseline readings. Our concern is different: the surgeon was also one of the readers, and the paper does not say he was blind to the measurements when recommending reoperation. If he knew a patient had more motion, that knowledge could steer the decision that defines the outcome. In our judgment 1.25 mm of motion is also a small distance, and no repeatability figure is given. In Figure 1 the legend says 1.46 degrees of motion, but the panels are in mm and 11.12 minus 9.66 is 1.46, so the unit is a printing error. Results call the groups similar except for motion. Our t test on the printed values gives about 0.01 for motion, in line with the printed 0.02, and about 0.06 for facet angle, so facet angle was close. Slip size and sagittal rotation did not differ, which is itself worth saying.

slides.title: Predictors of reoperation
slides.lead: One predictor reached significance, and two of the three cutoffs quoted in the text are not what the model tested.
points: Reoperation rate: motion over 1.25 mm 54%, disc height over 6.5 mm 45%, facet angle over 50 degrees 39%
Overall reoperation rate was 37.5%, so 39% is barely above it
By risk-factor count: 0 factors 0%, 1 factor 38%, 2 factors 35%, 3 factors 75%. 3 vs 0 factors, P=0.14
Group sizes are not printed. Our reconstruction: 3 of 4 versus 0 of 3
Motion over 1.25 mm is probably 7 of 13, about 30% below the cutoff (our reconstruction)
slides.see: Figure 2 shows the bars at 0%, 38%, 35% and 75%. Two factors did no worse than one.
slides.notes: Three things to notice. First, the odds ratio of 2.65 is not an odds ratio for motion over 1.25 mm. Table 2 enters motion in mm, so our reading is that it applies per mm. The 1.25 mm cutoff never appears in the model. Likewise, the P of 0.187 belongs to a three-band facet variable, not to the 50-degree cutoff. The paper does not say where any cutoff came from, or whether they were set in advance. Second, the threshold. A stepwise entry P of 0.35 is permissive, and the authors do not explain it. It lets disc height and facet angle stay in, yet their intervals cross 1 widely. The authors then call all three risk factors and conclude that such patients are more likely to develop instability. Their own P values support that for motion only. With 15 events and at least five candidate variables, there are about 3 events per variable, so this model is unstable. That is ours. No clinical variable such as age, sex or baseline ODI is reported in the model, so Table 2 is not adjusted for them (ours). The authors note only that BMI was not measured, and the paper does not say whether the others were candidates. No discrimination, calibration or validation is reported. Third, the headline. Denominators are not printed, so we rebuilt them. Only four whole-number splits of 40 patients and 15 events fit the printed 0%, 38%, 35% and 75%. Two of them have 0 of 3 and 3 of 4, which gives a Fisher exact P of 0.143, matching the printed 0.14. The other two give 0.007 and 0.4. Methods list chi-square rather than Fisher, so this is an inference. The four-group chi-square would be about 0.24 on this split. If it is right, the 75% versus 0% contrast rests on 7 patients, with exact 95% intervals of about 19 to 99% and 0 to 71%, and 12 of 15 reoperations occurred in patients with 1 or 2 factors. The 54% can be rebuilt the same way. Only 7 of 13, 13 of 24, 14 of 26 and 15 of 28 fit. Table 1 means and SDs fit 7 of 13 best: a normal approximation predicts about 9 of 15 and 6 of 25 above 1.25 mm. If so (ours), 8 of the 15 reoperations had motion at or below the cutoff, and the rate below it was about 30%, 8 of 27. That teaches more than the 54% alone. Table 2 passes our check: the odds ratios, SEs, z scores and intervals agree.

slides.title: Clinical outcomes and harms
slides.lead: Patients improved after laminectomy, and those who had a reoperation improved again. Neither result is controlled.
points: Complications within 30 days: 2 of 40 (5%), 1 wound infection and 1 new sensory deficit
Neither of those patients was reoperated; no CSF leaks
Reoperated patients: worse scores at 3 and 6 months did not reach significance
ODI P=0.094 at both times; SF-36 PCS P=0.211 and 0.191
The 5-year ODI may rest on about 6 patients, and the P is for the whole series (ours)
slides.see: Figures 3, 4 and 5 show these scores. Values marked about are read from the figures, and the paper does not define the error bars. Baseline bars match SE from Table 1 (ours).
slides.notes: The authors report significant improvement in ODI and SF-36 PCS that persisted through 5 years, P below 0.001. That P is one printed value for the whole series, from repeated-measures ANOVA per Methods, and not a 5-year comparison. Read Figure 3 carefully. Its caption says total population, and the paper does not say patients were dropped after fusion, so the later points probably include 15 people who had been fused. That is our reading. If so, Figure 3 does not show the durability of laminectomy alone. No patient numbers are printed at any time point. The baseline ODI bar of 2.4 equals 15.2 over the square root of 40, so the bars look like SE. If they are, and SD stays near 15, implied ODI numbers are about 40 at 1 year, 30 at 2, 21 at 3, 15 at 4 and 6 at 5 years (ours). So the 5-year value may rest on about 6 patients. ODI also rose to about 24 at 4 years. Figure 4 is the most interesting one. The groups start level, and the reoperated group stops improving early, about 25 against 16 on ODI at 6 months. The authors call this a trend, which is fair, because no P value reached 0.05. Our caution: 4 of the 15 had reoperation within 6 months, so some of those 3 and 6 month scores may be postoperative from a second operation. Figures 3 and 4 do agree. Weighting the two 6-month values gives about 20, matching Figure 3. Figure 5 is what the authors use as support: ODI P below 0.01 and SF-36 PCS P below 0.001 at 1 year after fusion. They say this gives some evidence that symptoms came from instability. Our reading is weaker. These patients were chosen at their worst, with no comparison group, so regression toward the mean and the response to any second operation are both possible. Our practical reading, not the authors', compares different clocks: reoperated patients reached ODI about 18 at 1 year after reoperation, and the non-reoperated group was about 16 at 6 months after the index operation. The paper makes no such comparison. It suggests delayed fusion can rescue some patients. It does not prove it was as good as a fusion up front.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: What holds up: Prospective enrollment and outcome collection
What holds up: Independent radiology review
What holds up: One surgeon, one technique
What holds up: Registered study with no conflict reported
What holds up: Table 1 and Table 2 pass arithmetic checks
What weakens it: 40 patients, 15 events, no fusion arm
What weakens it: Reoperation has no stated criteria
What weakens it: Surgeon was reader and decision maker
What weakens it: Entry threshold of P=0.35
What weakens it: Cutoffs unexplained and not validated
What weakens it: Logistic model ignores differing follow-up
What weakens it: Conclusion overstates two nonsignificant predictors
What weakens it: Follow-up completeness not reported
slides.notes: Be fair: this is a transparent small series, and the authors admit reoperation is subjective and that the sample may not represent practice. They call long-term follow-up the study's greatest strength, but the mean is 3.6 years and no minimum is stated. Our arithmetic: a patient enrolled in September 2009 could have had under 3 years by the May 2012 submission. Logistic regression treats a patient followed briefly as a permanent non-event, so a time-to-event analysis would have fit better. The paper does not report how many patients completed each visit. Generalization needs care too. One surgeon's threshold for offering fusion is built into the 37.5% rate. It was also a surgeon running a trial of that very question, which is our observation. The authors note that minimally invasive laminotomies preserving the interspinous ligaments might provide greater stability, and they did not test that. Internal inconsistencies are small, but they tell you how tightly the report was checked. The Figure 1 legend gives motion in degrees. The Abstract drops the word presumably. The Complications section says no CSF leaks in either group, in a single-arm paper, and Methods name neuroradiologists while another line says radiologists. Discussion says 3 risk factors gave a 75% chance of delayed instability, though the measure was reoperation. AO Spine (L13) repeats the 45%, 39% and 54% figures and calls all three significant risk factors, which goes beyond this paper's P values. That wording is from the L13 full text, not the library record, and we flag it. L13 also calls this a level 4 retrospective study, though this paper says prospective, and gives 39% to 54% as the rate with at least one parameter, though these are marginal rates and Figure 2 gives 38% for 1 factor. Citing the paper as three validated criteria is the error to avoid.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: “In 40 patients with grade I slips, motion up to 3 mm and no mechanical back pain, laminectomy alone was followed by fusion in 15. Only flexion-extension motion reached significance. The 75% versus 0% comparison did not, and it probably rests on seven patients. These cutoffs are hypotheses, not fusion indications.”
points: SLIP and NORDSTEN come from library records. The surgery, endpoint and follow-up differ, and both n values cover both arms.
Do not stretch it: there was no fusion arm, so this does not show who benefits from fusion.
slides.notes: Expect four follow-up questions. Should a patient with 1.5 mm of motion get a fusion? Not on this paper alone. Motion was the only significant variable, but the cutoff was not tested in the model and has not been validated here. In the library record, NORDSTEN enrolled patients regardless of signs of instability, and about 20% in the 2-year report had dynamic instability, with no subgroup conclusions possible. Is a patient with no risk factors safe with decompression alone? The authors call that chance minimal. We estimate 0 of 3, which allows a true rate as high as about 71%. Why is reoperation so much higher here than in NORDSTEN? This paper cannot answer that. Our reading: surgeon threshold, a wider open operation and differences in selection could all contribute, and the endpoints are not the same. SLIP's decompression arm had a similar rate, 34% in its record, also with reoperation decided by the surgeon, and it may share patients with this cohort, so the two are not independent evidence. Is it safe to wait and fuse later? Figure 5 suggests reoperated patients improved. But there are no controls, and those who declined or had milder symptoms are not described, apart from one patient who declined. Our advice, not the authors' or AO Spine's: treat motion on flexion-extension films as a reason to look harder and to counsel the patient about reoperation. Do not quote 75%. Say that motion was the only variable to reach 0.05, and that it is a hypothesis too. Its P came from a stepwise model with 15 events, and selection biases that P downward. Neither 0.02 nor 0.033 would pass 0.05/5 = 0.01 across the five radiographic variables, and no correction was made (ours). The rest is unproven.

decks.not_reviewed: Material on bmj.com (additional contributors and steering committee list), the rehabilitation programme description (reference 15), the separately reported economic analysis and recruitment report, and the later correction adding the trial registration number (ISRCTN88854663), which is not in this PDF. The PDF is the complete 7-page BMJ Online First article, not a critique.

slides.title: Fairbank 2005: MRC spine stabilisation trial
slides.lead: Bottom line: at 2 years, surgery beat intensive rehabilitation by 4.1 Oswestry points, a marginal result, and the co-primary shuttle walking test did not differ.
points: Journal club · Fusion for chronic low back pain
Fairbank J, Frost H, Wilson-MacDonald J, Yu LM, Barker K, Collins R. BMJ 2005;330:1233
349 patients, 15 UK centres, randomised June 1996 to February 2002
Prepared from the full text of the paper
slides.notes: This is the UK Medical Research Council trial: 349 patients aged 18 to 55 whom surgeons considered candidates for lumbar stabilisation, randomised to surgery or a 3-week intensive rehabilitation programme built on cognitive behaviour therapy principles, followed for 2 years. It is a pragmatic strategy trial. Surgeons chose the operation, and about 15 percent were planned for flexible stabilisation (Graf), not fusion, even though the abstract speaks of fusion (the title says stabilisation). The authors' own conclusion is guarded: the Oswestry difference was marginal and only just reached the predefined minimal clinical difference, and no clear evidence emerged that primary fusion was more beneficial than intensive rehabilitation. Keep that sentence in mind, because the result is often quoted as either 'surgery wins' or 'surgery fails', and it is neither. This deck was built from the complete 7-page BMJ Online First PDF. The rehabilitation programme paper, the economic analysis and the bmj.com extras were not reviewed. The trial registration number was added later by a correction and does not appear in this PDF.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: For surgical candidates with chronic back pain, is stabilisation better than a well-run rehabilitation programme?
points: Background: the authors cite a 1999 Cochrane review that found no randomised evidence for spinal fusion.
US fusions for degenerative changes rose from about 11 000 a year in 1996 to 37 000 in 2001, by the authors' figures.
Rehabilitation with physical, psychological, social and occupational focus had been advocated for chronic back pain.
The NHS standing group on health technology named surgery's weak evidence a priority in 1994.

rows: Age 18 to 55, back pain over 12 months, fusion candidates; surgeon and patient uncertain
Stabilisation of surgeon's choice: fusion, or Graf flexible stabilisation
Daily outpatient rehabilitation, 5 days a week for 3 weeks, CBT principles
Oswestry index and shuttle walking test at 24 months

slides.notes: The comparator is the story. This was not routine physiotherapy. Most centres gave about 75 hours (range 60 to 110), physiotherapist-led, with clinical psychologists in all but one centre and hydrotherapy in all but one. Exercises were individually paced, and cognitive behaviour principles were used to tackle fear and unhelpful beliefs. Follow-up sessions were offered at 1, 3, 6 or 12 months. The authors themselves stress that routine physiotherapy and intensive rehabilitation are not the same. They use that to explain why the Swedish trial found little effect of physiotherapy at 2 years. Note also the entry rule. Eligibility used the uncertainty principle: a patient entered only if surgeon and patient were both unsure which treatment was best. Surgeons may argue this excluded the best candidates, and the authors acknowledge that argument. They also note that certainty varied between surgeons, so the population is defined partly by surgeon attitude. Clinical classification at entry: about 81 percent chronic low back pain, 11 percent spondylolisthesis and 8 percent post-laminectomy. Prior decompression or discectomy was allowed, and referred pain was allowed. Prior stabilisation surgery, infection, inflammatory disease, tumour, fracture, psychiatric disease and pregnancy were exclusions. One arithmetic slip in the Introduction: 11 000 to 37 000 a year is a 236 percent increase (3.4-fold), not the 336 percent printed; we list it as a source problem.

slides.title: Patients and methods
points: Randomised centrally by computer, minimised for age, smoking, litigation, Oswestry, clinical class and planned Graf
Analysis by intention to treat; ANCOVA adjusted for baseline; multiple imputation as sensitivity analysis
Power: 133 per group for 80% power to detect 4 Oswestry points at alpha 0.05
Outcome assessors (trial research therapists) were not blinded after baseline
Received allocated treatment: surgery 139 of 176 (79%), rehabilitation 151 of 173 (87%)
slides.notes: The flow diagram adds up: 176 less 37 not operated is 139, and 173 less 22 is 151. The percentages recompute correctly, and 284 of 349 with a 24-month Oswestry is the 81 percent in the abstract. Two caveats on the flow. First, Table 4 gives shuttle denominators of 118 and 126, one fewer in each arm than the flow diagram's 119 and 127. Second, the shuttle walking test, a co-primary outcome, was missing in about 30 percent at 24 months, more than the 20 percent loss the authors quote. On power: the trial planned 133 per group and analysed 138 and 146 Oswestry scores, so it met the overall target. But the original plan was 133 in each of three clinical groups for subgroup analysis, and most patients fell in one group, so the subgroup aim failed. Our back-calculation, not the paper's: 133 per group for 4 points implies an assumed SD of about 11.6, which the paper does not state. The reported interval implies a residual SD near 17. That is why a 4.1-point estimate only just reached significance. Baseline balance, also our check, since the paper reports no baseline tests: the surgery group had more distressed-depressive DRAM patients (87 versus 69; the four-category DRAM distribution gives chi-square P about 0.03, distressed-depressive against the rest alone only about 0.09), a higher somatic perception score (9.0 versus 7.7; P about 0.05) and worse SF-36 physical functioning (33.6 versus 39.5; P about 0.008 if all patients contributed). The authors state that baseline-adjusted and per-protocol analyses did not change the interpretation, but they show no data.

slides.title: Primary outcomes
slides.lead: Oswestry favoured surgery by 4.1 points; the walking test did not differ.
points: Differences are adjusted for baseline; rehabilitation is the reference. Negative Oswestry favours surgery.
Both arms improved: Oswestry fell 12.5 points with surgery and 8.7 with rehabilitation.
slides.see: Table 6 gives Oswestry means by centre: at 24 months centre B favours surgery by about 12 points and centre D favours rehabilitation by about 6.
slides.notes: Read the interval, not the P value. The estimate is 4.1 points, and the interval runs from 8.1 to 0.1 in favour of surgery. The upper bound almost touches zero, and the interval is split roughly evenly around the 4-point difference the trial was powered for. The authors note that minimal important change in Oswestry has been put anywhere from 4 to 17. So a 4.1-point point estimate clears only the most generous threshold. The interval is symmetric, and our recomputation gives P about 0.044, so the printed numbers hang together. One thing does not: the Discussion says the intervals rule out more than 10 points favouring surgery and more than 2 points favouring rehabilitation. The interval printed in Table 4 rules out more than 8.1 points for surgery and any benefit for rehabilitation. We cannot tell which analysis gave 10 and 2, and we flag it as a source problem. The raw change scores (our arithmetic: 12.5 versus 8.7, a gap of 3.8) mix all randomised patients at baseline with completers at 24 months, so the ANCOVA figure is the one to quote. Our check suggests a further gap: getting from the raw 24-month gap (2.1) and baseline gap (1.7) to the adjusted 4.1 needs a baseline slope near 1.2, and the shuttle and SF-36 physical score need 1.1 to 1.3, which is implausible. So completers' baselines probably differ from Table 1, and the paper does not report them. The imputed estimate was similar (−4.5), but imputation assumes data are missing at random, so it cannot rule out bias from missing data. The authors say both groups improved, possibly through natural resolution or regression to the mean. The shuttle test, the other co-primary, favoured surgery by 34 metres with an interval crossing zero. With two co-primary outcomes and no stated multiplicity adjustment, one marginal hit out of two is weak. That reading is ours, and it matches the authors' caution.

slides.title: Secondary outcomes, crossover and harms

rows: Surgery by 2 years in rehab arm

points: No SF-36 summary score or domain differed significantly, including after imputation.
19 surgical patients had complications; the authors found no specific complications of rehabilitation.
Median time to treatment: 1.6 months for surgery, 0.9 months for rehabilitation.
slides.notes: Secondary outcomes: all eight SF-36 domain estimates were small with intervals crossing zero; pain favoured surgery by 4.1 on a 0 to 100 scale, P=0.16. Every interval we checked is consistent with its P value. Crossover is the biggest threat to the contrast. 48 of 173 rehabilitation patients (28 percent) had surgery by 2 years: 10 switched before any rehabilitation and 38 had surgery after it. 37 of 176 surgery patients never had surgery: 7 had rehabilitation instead, 3 physiotherapy, 11 medical treatment and 16 no recorded treatment. Intention-to-treat analysis with this much crossover pulls the groups together. The authors read the same number the other way: nearly three quarters of the rehabilitation group avoided surgery, and they call the 48 an additional outcome of the trial. Both readings are fair; say which one you mean. Further treatment after the allocated treatment was more common after surgery (97 versus 68: 55 versus 39 percent of all randomised, but 70 versus 45 percent of those who received their allocated treatment, our arithmetic; the paper's percentages use all randomised), mostly additional physiotherapy (47) and medical treatment (32). Harms: Table 3 lists 24 complications in 19 patients, including 5 dural tears, 5 implant problems, 2 vascular injuries (1 at the treatment site, 1 with the approach) and 1 lost swab, plus 11 further operations within 2 years. The text calls the 19 intraoperative, but the table also includes a systemic haemorrhage and the further surgery row, so treat 19 as patients with any surgical complication. Pseudarthrosis was recorded only when obvious and a problem to the patient, so it was not systematically sought. Work status was monitored but not reported here. Costs are mentioned in the conclusions, but the economic analysis is not in this paper.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: Holds up: central computer randomisation with minimisation
Holds up: intention to treat, ANCOVA, imputation sensitivity analysis agreeing
Holds up: active, defined comparator, 75 hours with psychology input
Holds up: pragmatic, 15 centres, experienced consultant surgeons only
Weakens it: outcome assessors not blinded after baseline
Weakens it: 28% of rehab arm had surgery; 21% of surgery arm did not
Weakens it: 19% missing Oswestry, about 30% missing shuttle at 24 months
Weakens it: mixed surgery, 15% planned Graf; technique not standardised
Weakens it: two co-primary outcomes, no multiplicity adjustment stated
Weakens it: baseline imbalance in distress and physical function (our tests)
Weakens it: slow recruitment; 39 more centres declined or could not run rehab
slides.notes: Be fair to the authors. They list recruitment difficulty, crossover and incomplete follow-up as limitations themselves, and they call outcome measures blunt instruments. Blinding: the paper says baseline outcomes were scored by research therapists, later ones were scored centrally, and the therapists could not be blinded after baseline. Patients obviously knew their treatment, and both primary outcomes depend on patient report or effort. Our reading: an unblinded walking test is effort dependent, which cuts toward whichever arm the patient believes in. Generalisability: 39 extra centres were approached but either the surgeon would not recruit or the rehabilitation programme could not be delivered. The authors say this kind of programme is not routinely available in the NHS. Our reading: the comparator is better than most patients will meet, which matters when you cite this trial to argue against fusion. Surgery was surgeon's choice, including Graf ligamentoplasty in about 15 percent; the authors cite the Swedish trial as showing no difference between three fusion techniques, but they cite it as reference 24 in that sentence, which is the European guideline. Reference 20 is the Swedish technique paper. Subgroups: Table 6 shows means only, and the authors report no significant heterogeneity. Centre B and the litigation group look strongly in favour of surgery, and centre D favours rehabilitation, but these are small, unadjusted means for groups that were predefined (and used in minimisation), with no significant heterogeneity; do not quote them. Competing interests: two surgeon authors received Synthes funding for a spinal fellow. Funding was the MRC, and the NHS or private insurance paid for treatment (326 and 23 patients).

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: “In fusion candidates with chronic back pain, surgery beat a 75-hour CBT-based rehab programme by 4 Oswestry points at 2 years, with an interval reaching almost zero, no difference in walking, and 28% of the rehab group still had surgery.”
points: Swedish figures come from the library record (abstract level), not this paper.
Do not stretch it: one marginal co-primary result, unblinded, heavy crossover.
Do not stretch the other way: it does not show fusion is useless, and the comparator is rarely available.
slides.notes: Spoken summary: a pragmatic UK trial of 349 surgical candidates with at least a year of back pain found that surgery, mostly fusion, gave a 4.1-point Oswestry advantage at 2 years over an intensive cognitive behavioural rehabilitation programme. The interval ran from 8.1 to 0.1. The shuttle walking test and SF-36 did not differ. Both groups improved. Expect these questions. One: does this mean fusion does not work? No. Surgery was slightly better on one primary outcome, and the trial can rule out large benefits but not small ones. The authors' claim is that rehabilitation may achieve similar benefit, not that surgery is useless. Two: why did the Swedish trial favour surgery? From the library record, the Swedish Lumbar Spine Study reported back pain reduced 33 percent with fusion against 7 percent with nonsurgical treatment; that record is abstract level. The MRC authors' explanation is the comparator: they say little effect of physiotherapy was seen in the Swedish trial, perhaps because of the type or intensity of treatment, and that routine physiotherapy is not intensive rehabilitation. Three: what about spondylolisthesis or post-laminectomy patients? They made up about a fifth of the trial, too few to analyse separately, and the planned subgroup analysis failed for lack of numbers. Four: what do I tell a patient? Our framing: a trial of a good rehabilitation programme is a reasonable first step, about three quarters avoided surgery for 2 years, and surgery remains an option if it fails. Five: what about cost? The authors say surgery's added risk and cost must be weighed, but the economic analysis is published separately and was not reviewed here.

decks.not_reviewed: The invited Point of View by Vert Mooney (journal pages 2532-2534) is truncated after its opening paragraphs in this PDF and was not reviewed. Separately reported material was not reviewed: the comparison of the three fusion techniques (reference 16), the comparison with the general population (reference 24), the diagnostic-procedure report, personality analyses and the planned 5-year results. The main article itself is complete in the PDF, not a critique.

slides.title: Fritzell 2001: Swedish Lumbar Spine Study
slides.lead: Bottom line: in highly selected patients with years of disabling back pain and sick leave, fusion reduced back pain and disability more than nonstandardized physical therapy at 2 years, but fused patients still averaged an Oswestry of 36.
points: Journal club · Fusion for chronic low back pain
Fritzell P, Hägg O, Wessberg P, Nordwall A, Swedish Lumbar Spine Study Group. Spine 2001;26:2521-2534. 2001 Volvo Award
294 patients, 19 Swedish orthopedic departments, randomized 1992 to 1998
Prepared from the full text of the paper. The invited Point of View by Vert Mooney is cut off after its opening paragraphs in this PDF and was not reviewed.
slides.notes: This is a large randomized trial of fusion against nonsurgical care for chronic low back pain; the authors say the evidence for fusion was weak in the absence of randomized controlled studies. Three fusion techniques were randomized as separate arms and then pooled as one surgical group of 222, against 72 patients given nonsurgical treatment, mainly physical therapy. The patients were a severe, long-suffering group: mean back pain duration about 8 years, mean sick leave about 3 years, and at least 1 year of sick leave or equivalent disability was required to enter. The authors conclude that fusion in a well-informed and selected group can reduce pain and disability more efficiently than commonly used nonsurgical treatment. Keep two words from that sentence in mind: selected, and commonly used. The comparator was not a defined program, and the selection was strict. Also hold the scale of benefit: back pain fell by a third, not to zero, and only 29 percent of the surgical group called themselves much better. This deck was built from the 12-page PDF. The main article is complete. The accompanying Point of View by Vert Mooney is truncated mid-sentence, so his critique is not summarized beyond his opening point, that surgery was compared with the same usual care these patients had already failed. Separately reported work, including the comparison of the three fusion techniques, the population comparison and the planned 5-year results, was not reviewed.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: For severe chronic back pain attributed to L4-L5 or L5-S1 degeneration, does fusion beat the nonsurgical care commonly offered?
points: The authors note fusion indications varied between and within countries, even among surgeons at one institution.
In their account, reported fusion results were mostly retrospective, in mixed groups, without controls.
They designed the trial to control for confounding, natural history and regression to the mean.
Patients were told that no treatment was known to be superior.

rows: Age 25 to 65, back pain at least 2 years, back worse than leg, no root compression, sick leave or equivalent major disability at least 1 year, nonsurgical treatment unsuccessful
Fusion at L4-L5 and/or L5-S1 by one of three techniques, in situ, no decompression
Physical therapy, with optional education, pain treatments, cognitive training and coping strategies
Pain, disability, patient global rating and return to work at 2 years

slides.notes: Set the stakes the way the authors do. Chronic back pain patients use health services heavily, and the return-to-work rate after 2 years off work is close to zero by the authors' cited figure. Fusion was being done more often without randomized proof. The entry rules matter more than usual here. The surgeon had to interpret the pain as coming from L4-L5 or L5-S1 from history, examination and imaging, and a second study surgeon had to agree on eligibility. Imaging needed degenerative change, spondylosis, on plain films, CT or MRI. A disc herniation was allowed if there were no clinical signs of root compression. Spondylolisthesis, fracture, infection, tumor, stenosis, painful hip arthritis and obvious psychiatric illness were excluded. Previous spine surgery was excluded except a successful discectomy more than 2 years earlier, which about 19 percent had. A Function and Working Disability score of at least 7 of 10 was required, and nobody scored under 3 on either scale. Neither compensation nor litigation excluded patients, and about 60 percent had a claim. Discography, facet blocks, external fixation and corset trials were used only after randomization in subgroups, so they were not selection tools here. Our point: this is the classic discogenic or degenerative back pain fusion candidate of the 1990s, chosen by surgeon judgment rather than by a test.

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: 310 randomized, 16 excluded afterwards for wrong diagnosis, 294 analyzed by allocation; 289 (98%) seen at 2 years.

rows: Posterolateral fusion, autograft, rigid brace 5 months
Posterolateral fusion plus VSP pedicle screws and plates, corset
As 1b plus ALIF or PLIF interbody graft, corset
Nonsurgical care by study guideline, local variation allowed

points: Computer list, sealed envelopes kept outside the departments
Crossover: 18 of 222 to nonsurgical, 7 of 72 to surgery
Fused 211: 122 single level, 89 two levels
Independent observer: a spine surgeon not engaged in the study
Power: 225 vs 75 for 18% vs 5% improved, 80%, two-sided Fisher
slides.notes: Read the flow first. 310 were randomized, and 16 were then excluded for erroneous diagnoses, spondylolisthesis or stenosis. The paper does not say which arms they came from. The abstract says 294 were randomized, which conflicts with the Results. The authors also say they cannot know how many patients declined before randomization; three were reported to have done so. So we cannot judge how representative the 294 are. Allocation was about 3 to 1 because the trial also planned to compare the three fusion techniques, reported separately. Twenty-six experienced spine surgeons operated, using iliac crest autograft in every case, fusing in situ with no decompression. Rehabilitation after surgery was early activity, not protocol-based. The nonsurgical program was a consensus guideline built around physical therapy, varying within broad but commonly used limits. Analysis used nonparametric tests, Mann-Whitney between groups on change from baseline, with intention to treat: group changers stayed in their randomized group. The 5 dropouts, 3 surgical and 2 nonsurgical, were excluded. Our recomputation of the power assumption: with 225 and 75 and true rates of 18 and 5 percent, power by simulation is about 84 percent, so the stated plan holds. But note what it assumed: only 5 percent improvement with nonsurgical care. The observed figure was 29 percent, so the planning assumption was far off, even though the result was still clear. Pain and complications were also recorded at 6 and 12 months. The paper describes no blinding of patients, and with fusion against physical therapy it could not have been done (our inference).

slides.title: Primary outcomes at 2 years
slides.lead: Every primary outcome favored fusion, but the improvement was partial: back pain fell by about 21 mm on a 100 mm scale.
slides.see: Figure 2A shows surgical back pain lowest at 6 months, near 30 mm, then rising to about 43 mm by 24 months, while the nonsurgical line falls from about 63 to about 56 at 6 months, holds near 55 at 12 months and rises to about 58 at 24 months. Pain rose in both groups between 1 and 2 years, significantly only in the surgical group.
slides.notes: How to read Table 3. The means shown exclude the 25 group changers and 5 dropouts, so they describe patients treated as allocated. The P values come from the intention-to-treat analysis with changers included. The authors make the underlying point themselves: because 6 of the 7 nonsurgical patients who were fused did far better than the nonsurgical average, intention to treat improved the nonsurgical results relative to surgery. Our corollary: excluding the changers makes the displayed means show a larger contrast than the intention-to-treat analysis, so quote the P values, not the means, as the trial result. The percentages are of group means, not individual change; we recomputed them and they match, except nonsurgical leg pain, printed as a 20.5 percent worsening and called 21 percent in the text, where the means give 19.7. Absolute size: Table 3 prints the changes, back pain 21.0 against 4.3 mm and Oswestry 11.6 against 2.8; the gaps, about 17 mm and 9 points, are our arithmetic. The authors computed post hoc power of only 61 percent for Oswestry. Leg pain here is nonradicular, since root compression was excluded; the authors believe it is referred from the back. Back pain in the surgical group rose significantly between 1 and 2 years, P<0.0001; the authors say this argues for longer follow-up. Global rating: in a worst-case analysis, counting the 14 surgical non-responders as worse and the 4 nonsurgical non-responders as improved, it was 56 against 38 percent, P=0.01. Work was analyzed only in those not on pension at baseline. The Results exclude full or supplementary disability pension, 47 surgical and 16 nonsurgical, because only 3 of them resumed part-time work; the Methods mention only full pension, and Table 2's 20.3 percent of 222 is 45, not 47, so the rule and count are inconsistent. Net back to work is back to work minus stopped working, 63 minus 6 against 11 minus 5. Our point: that is a difference of counts, not a yes-or-no outcome per patient. Plain back to work was 39 against 23 percent, P=0.049. The text calls the test chi-square; the Table 6 footnote says Fisher.

slides.title: Secondary outcomes and harms
points: Early complications 17% (Table 7: 37 of 211 patients)
New root pain in 9 of 140 screw patients; 3 deep infections
Unintended reoperation 16 of 211, printed as 7.8% (our arithmetic 7.6%)
Radiographic fusion 83% on plain films; no significant correlation with outcome
7 who crossed to surgery: back pain 67 to 26; 4 of 7 much better
slides.notes: The independent observer was a spine surgeon outside the study. The paper does not say he was unaware of the treatment, and a scar makes that unlikely (our inference). Excellent plus good plus fair was 78 against 58 percent. Would you go through it again is hard to read, as the authors admit: 22 percent of surgical patients who felt worse would repeat it, while 5 percent who felt better would not. Depression improved in both groups, and the between-group difference was not significant. The authors conclude depressive symptoms did not contraindicate fusion here. Harms. Early means within 2 weeks. Major early events included 6 new root pain without reoperation, 3 nerve roots hit by a screw with reoperation, 3 deep infections, 2 major bleeds during ALIF, thromboembolism, aspiration with ARDS, and 1 wrong-level operation. One long thoracic nerve injury, blamed on positioning, left persistent winged scapula. Nine had donor-site pain late. The abstract and text say 17 percent, the Table 7 footnote 18 percent; 37 of 211 is 17.5. The 16 reoperations are 7.6 percent of 211, not 7.8. Two surgical patients died within 2 years, one of myocardial infarction a year after surgery and one by suicide 2 years after surgery, for reasons the treating surgeon judged not back related. The nonsurgical group had no obvious complications, but three patients threatened suicide if not operated; those three were among the 7 who crossed to surgery. Fusion was judged by one blinded radiologist on plain films, which the authors call inexact; they do not claim 83 percent is the true rate. Group changers are a selected, non-randomized subgroup: 6 of the 7 who crossed to surgery, including the 3 who had threatened suicide, did far better than the average nonsurgical patient, while the 18 surgical-arm patients who were not fused did about as well as the nonsurgical average. Do not read either as a treatment effect.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: Holds up: concealed random allocation, 19 centers, 98% followed
Holds up: intention to treat, worst-case check, effects in one direction
Weak: comparator was the same kind of therapy patients had already failed
Weak: no patient blinding described; outcomes subjective
Weak: 16 excluded after randomization, arms not given; refusals unknown
Weak: shown means exclude group changers
Weak: comorbidity 39% vs 24% (P=0.020), our recomputation agrees
Funded partly by Acromed, maker of the pedicle screw system used
slides.notes: Be fair first. For its era this is a serious trial: concealed allocation, a large multicenter sample, 98 percent follow-up, intention to treat, an independent observer and a worst-case analysis that did not change significance. Every outcome pointed the same way. Now the problems. The comparator. The authors themselves raise the point Mooney makes in his Point of View: continuing the same therapy these patients already failed may behave like a waiting list. They reply that in 46 percent of nonsurgical records, special rehabilitation was started because of the study, and that the control group did improve significantly. On the back pain scale that was 4.3 mm. Our reading: this trial shows fusion beats more of the same, not that it beats a structured program, which is exactly the contrast the MRC trial tested. Blinding. The paper does not describe blinding, and every primary outcome is patient-reported or work-based. The authors accept that the placebo effect of surgery may explain part of the 6 and 12 month pain gap, but not the 2-year gap. Selection. Refusals were not counted, and 16 randomized patients were removed without arm labels. Baseline. Comorbidity was more common in the surgical group; the authors argue this would bias against surgery. From back-calculated counts, 84 of 215 against 16 of 68, Fisher's test gives P=0.020, matching the paper. Our recomputation of the other Table 2 rows also matches NS, for example smoking P=0.22 and work injury P=0.16. But some Table 2 percentages cannot come from the stated denominators: sick leave 58.8 percent of 222, nonsurgical litigation 64.5 percent of 72, and nonsurgical working 23.6 percent, which is 17 of 72 rather than of the 56 left after excluding pensioners as the footnote requires. Analysis. Many outcomes, no correction for multiplicity, and post hoc power, which is uninformative once results are known (our view). Litigation subgroup P values of 0.085 and 0.043 could not be reproduced from the printed counts; the test is not named. Pooling three fusion techniques hides any differences between them. Funding came partly from Acromed Corporation, and the VSP screws were made by DePuy Acromed; no conflict statement is given. Small slips: the fusion-definition paragraph names Groups 1, 2 and 3, but the surgical arms were 1a, 1b and 1c.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: “In carefully selected patients with years of back pain and sick leave, fusion beat commonly used, nonstandardized physical therapy at 2 years: back pain fell by a third against 7 percent, and 63 against 29 percent felt better. It rarely cured anyone, and 17 percent had an early complication.”

rows: Back pain -33% vs -7%; Oswestry 47 to 36 vs 48 to 46

points: MRC figures come from the library record, not this paper.
Do not stretch it: no standardized comparator, no blinding, 1990s techniques.
Do not stretch the other way: the effect was consistent across every primary outcome.
slides.notes: Spoken summary: in 294 Swedish patients with at least 2 years of back pain, at least a year off work or with equivalent disability, and degeneration at L4-L5 or L5-S1, fusion reduced back pain from 64 to 43 mm against 63 to 58 mm with nonsurgical care, improved all three disability scores, and more patients rated themselves better and returned to work. Pain relief peaked at 6 months and partly wore off, from about 30 to 43 mm in the surgical group, but was still well below nonsurgical at 2 years; disability and work were measured only at 2 years. Expect these questions. One: does this prove fusion works for discogenic pain? It shows fusion beat the nonsurgical care these patients had been getting, in strictly selected patients chosen by surgeon judgment, with no blinding. The MRC trial, against an intensive rehabilitation program with cognitive behavioral principles, found only a 4.1 point Oswestry advantage, with an interval nearly touching zero. The library record for this paper says the apparent conflict can partly reflect the control care, and we agree. Two: which fusion technique? This paper pools them; the comparison is a separate report not reviewed here. Three: does radiographic fusion matter? Here, plain-film fusion did not correlate with outcome, and the authors doubt the 83 percent figure. Four: what is the cost? Early complications 17 percent, new root pain in 6 percent of screw patients, unintended reoperation 16 of 211. Five: does compensation change outcome? Among surgical patients, 70 percent without a claim felt better against 58 percent with one, P=0.085 as printed. Treat that subgroup cautiously. Six: is it current? Techniques, implants and nonsurgical programs date from 1992 to 1998.

decks.not_reviewed: Images and anything shown only as an image: the PDF is a phone reformat of the PMC text that omits them, and no tables appear in it. Funding and conflict-of-interest statements are not in this PDF. The erratum (PMID 40900211) was not read. Gadjradj 2023 and Shukla 2023 are not in the library, so they are known here only through AO's summaries.

slides.title: AO Spine: decompress or fuse
slides.lead: AO Spine Clinical Practice Recommendations for the Surgical Management of Degenerative Spondylolisthesis: When to Decompress Alone and When to Fuse
points: Journal club · Decompression versus fusion
Martin CT, et al. Global Spine J 2025;15(7):3046-54
Source check: full article text, reformatted from PMC. Images are omitted. It is the paper itself, not a critique.

Bottom line: six hand-picked papers lead AO to say both decompression alone and decompression with fusion can be considered, with fusion ideally kept for instability that justifies it. It offers no validated way to find those patients, only advice to review pre-operative imaging closely for signs of instability.
slides.notes: This is a narrative appraisal by the AO Spine Knowledge Forum Degenerative, not a systematic guideline. The title promises when to decompress and when to fuse. The Conclusion concedes that precisely determining which patients need which operation is not clear, so hold the paper to that. This deck was prepared from the full text: abstract, methods, all six paper reviews, discussion, conclusion and references are present. The PDF omits images and shows no tables, so check the published version for anything printed that way. No funding or conflict statement appears in this PDF, and the erratum was not read. Comparisons with the source papers use the library records, not a fresh review of those papers. Gadjradj and Shukla are not in the library, so they are known here only through AO's summaries.

slides.title: The question and the method
slides.lead: Recent trials on fusion for degenerative spondylolisthesis disagree. AO set out to summarize them and give a consensus recommendation.
points: Selection: the steering committee chose 6 articles at its discretion, on quality, recency and relevance
Mix: 3 RCTs, 2 meta-analyses, 1 radiographic cohort
Appraisal: small groups of 3 summarized each paper; the first author merged the summaries
Consensus: reached after a virtual meeting; all 23 forum members reviewed the manuscript
Not stated: a search strategy, inclusion criteria, a single grading framework across the six papers, or a consensus threshold
slides.notes:
Read the Methods first, because they limit everything after them. The abstract calls this a literature review. Six articles were picked by a committee, so the result depends on what was picked. AMSTAR 2 is named for the two meta-analyses, and GRADE is mentioned only as Gadjradj's own method. AO ties its Low for Gadjradj and Shukla to AMSTAR 2, and its Low for Blumenthal to calling it a level 4 retrospective study. It never says how it reached High, Moderate, Conditional or strong, and it gives no single framework across the six papers.

The Methods also call both meta-analyses reviews of RCTs and prospective cohort studies. AO's later review of Shukla faults it for including level 4 retrospective cohorts, so the Methods description does not fit Shukla.

Our point: selection matters here because AO cites NORDSTEN at 5 years in a single sentence and leaves out the full Swedish 5-year report altogether. Neither is among the six. Both are in this library, and they are the fullest 5-year randomized data on the question.

slides.title: Recommendations, strength and evidence
slides.lead: Each paper gets a Conditional recommendation. The overall conclusion is called strong: both options can be considered.

rows: Midline-sparing decompression alone as first choice
Fusion may be considered in grade 1 slip for physical function
Midline-sparing decompression for predominant leg pain; with a slip, both are options
Decompression non-inferior in low-grade slip; consider fusion with pre-op instability
Consider both equally; consider fusion for greater baseline disability and back pain
Radiographic parameters may aid the decision to add fusion

points: All six recommendations are Conditional, including the one on High evidence.
slides.notes:
