Notice the pattern. Six Conditional statements become one strong statement, and AO does not explain the step. The word strong appears in the Conclusion and not in the abstract.

Our reading: this strong recommendation is a permission, not a direction. It says both options exist, which is hard to be wrong about, and it gives no validated way to choose. It should not be quoted as strong support for either operation.

The statements also pull apart. On AO's highest-rated evidence, decompression alone is the first choice. On Low-rated Shukla, surgeons should consider both equally. AO does not reconcile these, and the final line drops the first-choice wording. Our reading: if you weight by AO's own ratings, decompression alone comes first for a patient who fits NORDSTEN, and fusion needs a reason.

The Swedish recommendation also goes beyond that trial, by our reading. AO says its techniques were not standardized, yet it uses the trial to recommend midline-sparing decompression. The predominant leg pain wording is also unsupported, by our reading: AO describes inclusion as pseudoclaudication plus back pain VAS over 30, reports no leg-predominant subgroup, and says severe mechanical back pain was not described. The library note on that trial adds that most Swedish decompressions were central and showed no excess reoperation, so technique alone does not explain SLIP.

slides.title: Three trials, three populations
slides.lead: AO says the trials reached similar ODI results. Their patients and operations were different.

rows: SF-36 at 2 yr; 1 yr also primary at first
2 yr +5.7 fusion; adjusted 3.9, P=0.19. 4 yr +6.7, unadjusted

points: D, decompression alone. F, with fusion. Figures are from the library records.
slides.notes:
This is the core of the paper, and the table shows why no single statement fits. Read across the motion row. SLIP excluded motion over 3 mm. The Swedish trial never measured it. NORDSTEN included it in about 20% but did not analyze those patients separately. Our conclusion: no trial here tells you what fusion adds for the patient with dynamic instability, and that is the patient AO wants to fuse.

SLIP needs care. AO reports P = 0.046 at 2 years, and in its Methodological Review it says baseline differences might have affected outcomes, but it never gives the baseline-adjusted 2-year 3.9 points (95% CI -1.9 to 9.7, P = 0.19). AO does report that the unadjusted gain persisted at 3 and 4 years (6.7 points at 4 years, P = 0.02). Follow-up at 4 years was 68%, and the library record holds no adjusted 4-year result.

AO also says the 1-year and 2-year SF-36 changes were both primary outcomes initially, that the analysis strategy was developed after trial completion but before data examination, and that 1 year showed no significant difference. Our reading: that matters for a P = 0.046 result, and the library record notes no multiplicity adjustment. AO also calls the sample sufficient. By our arithmetic from AO's figures, the trial was sized for 7.5 points and found 5.7.

AO's Discussion says ODI showed no difference at final follow-up across any trial. Our reading: that smooths over a near-miss in a small trial, but it is not a contradiction. In the library record SLIP's 2-year ODI change was -26.3 vs -17.9, an 8.4-point gap by our arithmetic, and AO's own SLIP section gives P = 0.06 as not significant. The Swedish means ran the other way. SLIP and the Swedish trial were also not built to prove equivalence; the library record makes that point for the Swedish superiority design.

NORDSTEN is the only noninferiority trial. AO reports the 15-point margin but not that it was chosen empirically, and that margin accepts about NNT 7 for fusion. In AO's text only the per-protocol 75.5% in each arm appears.

slides.title: Meta-analyses and imaging markers
slides.lead: The two meta-analyses conflict, and the imaging cutoffs rest on 40 patients with no fusion arm.

rows: No difference in ODI, SF-36, VAS or walking at 2 yr. Less blood loss and stay with D. More slip progression with D, 2 studies
Similar final scores. Greater ODI change with F, SMD -0.38. Leg pain SMD -0.11
Retrospective studies, heterogeneity, RCT function data not pooled
Reoperation 15 of 40, 37.5% (AO prints 37%). Motion over 1.25 mm 54%, disc over 6.5 mm 45%, facet over 50 degrees 39%. All three 75%, none 0%
No control group, reoperation criteria missing

slides.notes:
The meta-analyses answer different questions. Gadjradj looked at outcomes at 2 years and, per AO, analyzed RCTs only. Shukla pooled retrospective cohorts with trials and based its conclusion on change from baseline. Its authors argue that fusion patients start worse and finish level, so they gained more. Our reading: worse-off patients tend to improve more under any treatment, and in nonrandomized studies surgeons chose who got fusion, so that gain cannot be credited to fusion. AO says the cause of the higher baseline disability is unclear and questions the veracity of the result, then still says consider fusion for greater baseline disability and back pain. Our reading: that is the weakest link in the recommendations.

AO calls decompression alone non-inferior on Gadjradj. Our reading: a nonsignificant pooled difference does not establish that without a margin, and AO gives none. AO then moves from slip progression after decompression to fusion for pre-op instability. Slip progression in 2 studies does not show that patients with pre-op instability do worse without fusion.

Blumenthal is the source of the imaging cutoffs. AO calls all three factors significant. The library record shows only motion was: P = 0.033, against 0.102 for disc height and 0.187 for facet angle. All three vs none was P = 0.14. Our reading: AO's phrase that at least one parameter gives 39% to 54% relabels rates for each single factor. With no fusion arm, it cannot show that fusing these patients helps. The library record notes likely patient overlap with SLIP, which AO does not mention. Our reading: AO treats them as separate lines of evidence.

slides.title: Errors and gaps
slides.lead: Our reading: the overall direction is reasonable, but several details are wrong or selective.

rows: 2-yr adjusted 3.9, P=0.19, not given. 4-yr 6.7, P=0.02, is unadjusted
SLIP, NORDSTEN: more index reoperation after D
Interval does not fit the estimate or P

points: Missing: the full Swedish 5-year report, with slip ODI 28 fusion vs 23 alone (P=0.152)

Missing: a recommended threshold for who needs fusion. Under 3 mm motion defines stable in SLIP, Blumenthal and Shukla's subgroup; Blumenthal's 1.25 mm is a risk factor inside that group, and SLIP also used surgeon judgment
Missing: a validated tool for sorting stable, unstable and potentially unstable patients
slides.notes:
Sort these by consequence. The two that matter most both lean toward fusion: SLIP is quoted without its 2-year baseline-adjusted result, and non-significant Blumenthal cutoffs are called significant. The abstract repeats both results without those limits.

The NORDSTEN per-protocol and midline points lean the other way, toward decompression. AO says the per-protocol analysis likely favors decompression because reoperated patients were excluded, yet that is the only primary figure AO prints. The other analysis in the library record also met noninferiority, so the conclusion holds. AO also uses a per-protocol primary analysis as a strength of the Swedish trial. Our reading: the two reviews apply different standards.

The reoperation row leans toward fusion. AO's own NORDSTEN text says the difference was not significant, and it does not say those were index-level operations. At 5 years the totals were 16% with decompression and 18% with fusion, with more early operations after decompression and more later ones after fusion. AO says 5-year outcomes were very similar and leaves this out. The Swedish 5-year totals were 22% alone and 24% fusion.

On the Shukla figure, the interval's midpoint on the log scale is about 0.60, not 0.53, and it implies a P near 0.10 or higher. Our guess is a misprint: an upper limit of 1.02 would fit both 0.53 and P close to 0.06. We have not seen the Shukla paper.

AO's abstract says Shukla found no difference in raw scores, which leaves out Shukla's main conclusion, though AO's Discussion relies on it. AO's '51 out of 106' at one SLIP site also differs from the library record, which ties 51 to the 66 randomized. AO's own 66 randomized and 40-patient registry sum to 106, and the L06 paper calls the 51 a majority, which 48% is not. Our guess is a denominator mix-up.

Smaller slips: AO prints 37% for 15 of 40, which is 37.5%. It calls Gadjradj's studies low or unclear risk of selection bias, then relatively high risk of bias. It cites high dropout after 4 years though SLIP follow-up stopped at 4 years. Blumenthal is one of the six papers but is not in the numbered references.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "AO Spine chose six papers and concluded that both decompression alone and fusion can be considered. Its best-rated evidence, NORDSTEN, supports midline-sparing decompression alone first in the patient who fits that trial. AO would keep fusion for instability and tells surgeons to look for it on pre-operative imaging, but it has no validated way to define that patient, and every paper-level recommendation is conditional."
points: Expect: Is this a strong recommendation for fusion? No. It only says both options can be considered.
Expect: Does SLIP prove fusion? No. The 2-year SF-36 gain lost significance after adjustment, in 66 patients. AO reports 6.7 points at 4 years (P=0.02), but that is unadjusted, with 68% follow-up.
Expect: Do 1.25 mm, 6.5 mm and 50 degrees mean fuse? No. Only motion was significant, and there was no fusion arm.
Expect: What about the patient with dynamic instability? NORDSTEN included about 20% but draws no subgroup conclusion.
Expect: Is reoperation higher without fusion? In SLIP, yes (P=0.05). Not at 5 years in NORDSTEN or the Swedish trial.
slides.notes:
Use the summary as written. It separates three things: what AO concluded, what its best-rated trial supports, and what it cannot yet define. Keep the middle statement tied to AO's own recommendation for NORDSTEN, and to the patients that trial enrolled.

On applying it, the library records say NORDSTEN does not apply to multilevel slips, scoliosis over 20 degrees, severe foraminal stenosis or prior surgery at that level. Those patients are outside this evidence, which does not mean they need fusion.

If asked why you would ever fuse, AO's position is selective fusion where instability justifies the added morbidity. It states that as an aim for future research, not a tested rule. Say that plainly. AO's stable, unstable and potentially unstable categories are a framework, and the paper offers no validated way to assign a patient to them.

If asked what AO adds, our reading is that it is a useful map of the debate and a fair statement of where the data stop. Read it alongside NORDSTEN at 5 years and the Swedish 5-year report, not in place of them. Quote the source papers' numbers instead of AO's where they differ.

decks.not_reviewed: The primary paper itself (Herkowitz and Kurz, J Bone Joint Surg Am 1991;73:802-8) was not available and was not read. The saved PDF is only a two-page critique of it: Vaccaro AR, Garfin SR. Spine 1997;22:368-369. Everything here is second hand. Also not read: the 1991 abstract, the published comment listed in the record (PMID 1624496), and the earlier fusion studies the critique mentions without citing. The critique has no tables, figures, baseline table or P values. It prints only three preoperative radiographic values by group, and nothing could be checked against the original.

slides.title: Herkowitz 1991
slides.lead: Degenerative spondylolisthesis with stenosis: decompression with or without intertransverse arthrodesis
points: Source warning: this deck reads a two-page 1997 critique, not the original paper.
Critique: Vaccaro AR, Garfin SR. Spine 1997;22:368-369
Paper critiqued: Herkowitz HN, Kurz LT. J Bone Joint Surg Am 1991;73:802-8
Bottom line: 24 of 25 good-to-excellent with noninstrumented fusion versus 11 of 25 without, in a small alternating-allocation study.
slides.notes: Say this first: nobody in this review has read Herkowitz and Kurz. The primary paper was not available. The saved PDF is a Journal Club critique by Vaccaro and Garfin, published in Spine in 1997, and it runs two pages. So every number here is the critics' summary of the paper. We cannot check their transcription, we have no baseline table, and we have no P values for the clinical result. When this deck says the authors did something, read it as: the critics say the authors did it. Two voices run through the deck. The critics are Vaccaro and Garfin. Anything marked as ours is our own reading of their text. Why read it at all? Because the critics state that this study changed practice: in their words it unquestionably altered the surgical treatment of degenerative spondylolisthesis, and most spine surgeons now recommend fusion for these patients when they have a laminectomy for associated leg pain. Our reading: it is the historical anchor that later fusion trials are read against. Quote its numbers as reported in the critique, not as checked figures.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: After decompressing stenosis over a degenerative slip, does adding a fusion improve the result?
points: The critics call this a pressing controversy at the time.
They say earlier articles suggested a trend toward better results with fusion after decompressive laminectomy in spondylolisthesis.
Those earlier articles are not cited in the critique.

rows: Degenerative slip, primary leg pain, stenosis at a single level
Single-level laminectomy plus intertransverse fusion, no instrumentation
Pain and activity graded excellent to poor; slip and motion on films

slides.notes: Set the frame. This asks whether to add a fusion, and it asks that only for noninstrumented intertransverse fusion. The critics note that no patient in the series was instrumented. Our reading: the study therefore cannot speak to pedicle screws. They propose a third arm with internal fixation for any repeat study, to measure whether a higher rate and degree of fusion improves function. Keep the population in mind too. These patients had primary complaints of leg pain related to stenosis at a single level. The critique gives no age range, no slip grade and no inclusion or exclusion list beyond that, so the population cannot be pinned down further from this source. It also does not say how many operations were at L4-L5 versus L3-L4, only that fusion was at one or the other. Our reading: because the question was framed around leg pain from stenosis, the result should not be stretched to patients whose main complaint is back pain, or to multilevel disease. The critics do raise the questions a small study cannot answer: is fusion most effective with more than 10 mm of slip, and is it most effective in younger, more active patients? Those remain open in this source.

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: 50 patients, 25 per group, followed an average of 3 years (range 2.4 to 4).
points: Allocation: admitted consecutively, then assigned alternately to one group or the other
Not randomized, per the critics: the surgeon knows the next assignment when enrolling
No significant difference in age or sex between groups
One surgeon (HNH) did all the surgery, with a similar technique, preserving the facet joints
Recorded: demographics, pain profiles, spine-specific neurologic exam, and radiographs
Radiographs: transitional L5, disc height, slip, slip on flexion-extension, angular motion
Fusion at L4-L5 or L3-L4, one level only
slides.notes: Three things to notice. First, allocation. Alternation is not randomization, and the critics say so plainly: the surgeon knows, when enrolling a patient, which treatment that patient will get. They then say this is unlikely to compromise the validity of the study, and give no reason. Our reading is less forgiving. The danger of a known next assignment is who gets enrolled, and balance on a few measured variables does not rule that out. The critics also note that alternation prevents stratified blocks for age, sex, radiographic variables, stenosis, claudication severity and pain profiles. Second, what balance was shown. The critique reports no significant difference in age or sex, then says the groups were well balanced on the fuller list. It shows no baseline table, so we cannot verify that. The preoperative values it does quote, fusion then no fusion: slip 4.8 and 5.3 mm, flexion-extension motion 2.8 and 3.4 mm, angle 9.3 and 9.6 degrees. No SD or test is given, so closeness cannot be judged. Ours: all three are higher in the no-fusion group, and the motion gap of 0.6 mm is 21% of the lower value. Third, one surgeon. The critics count this as a strength because surgical factors were well controlled. That is fair for technique. Our reading: it also limits how far the result travels, and the operator is the paper's first author. The critique does not say who graded outcomes or whether that person knew the treatment. Do not call the assessment blinded or unblinded; the source is silent. It also says nothing about losses to follow-up. Denominators of 25 in both groups imply complete follow-up, but that is our inference.

slides.title: Results as reported
slides.lead: Fusion patients did better clinically. With fusion slip rose little and motion fell; without it both rose.
points: Average follow-up 3 years; ranges are preoperative to postoperative values.
Ours: 96% versus 44% good to excellent, a 52-point gap, Newcombe score 95% CI about 28 to 70.
Ours: Fisher exact P about 0.0001 on the clinical counts.
slides.notes: The critics say fusion patients reported a consistently improved outcome for relief of back and lower limb pain. The headline is 24 of 25 versus 11 of 25. The 96% and 44% good-to-excellent figures, and everything labeled ours, are our arithmetic from those counts. The 28%, 36% and the 96% for slip are printed in the critique. Do not confuse the two 96% figures on this slide: slip increase without fusion, and good to excellent with fusion. The critique calls the clinical advantage statistically significant, but prints no P value for it. The only named test is the Fisher exact test, attached to the slip result. Our own Fisher test on 24 of 25 versus 11 of 25 gives P about 0.0001. Our Newcombe score 95% interval on the difference is about 28 to 70 percentage points, wide because there are only 50 patients. Is that chance? Almost certainly not. On our count, 6 of the 24 fusion successes would have to flip before P rose above 0.05. So the real question is bias, not chance: unconcealed allocation plus a soft ordinal outcome. Both can inflate a gap and could even produce one. The Fisher test speaks only to chance, so it cannot show the effect is real. Slip: the critique gives 28 percent (seven) versus 96 percent. It gives no count for 96 percent, which implies 24 of 25, our inference. The change is 0.5 mm with fusion and 2.6 mm without, our subtraction. The critique does not label the slip or dynamic figures as means, and the slip figures sit inside sentences about patients whose slip increased. Means are likely, since mean anterolisthesis is a listed variable, but that is our inference. The fused group's half millimeter is a small number, and the critique gives no measurement error. The critics say slip and angular motion correlated statistically with back and lower limb pain at follow-up, but give no coefficient. The critique does not report significance tests for the dynamic motion or angular results, so say they moved in opposite directions, not that the difference was proven.

slides.title: Pseudarthrosis and harms
slides.lead: 36% (nine) of fused patients had pseudarthrosis on plain films, yet almost all fused patients did well.
points: Definition: no continuity in the fusion mass at any point between transverse processes, on one or both sides
Critics: plain films are a poor indicator of pseudarthrosis if obvious trabeculation is absent
Critics would prefer dynamic films plus CT for clefts, or tomograms
Critics: a solid fusion is not necessary for an excellent or good result
Critics: a fibrous fusion may decrease translation and so relieve pain
Ours: at least 8 of the 9 plain-film pseudarthrosis patients must have had good-to-excellent results
Not reported in the critique: complications, reoperation, blood loss, operative time
slides.notes: This is the most useful slide for thinking. Nine of 25 fused patients had pseudarthrosis on plain radiographs, and that count is uncertain, because the critics say plain radiography is a poor indicator of pseudarthrosis if obvious trabeculation is absent. They do not say which way it errs here. Now do the arithmetic, which is ours. Only one fused patient missed good to excellent. So at least 8 of the 9 called pseudarthrosis on plain films had a good-to-excellent result. The critique gives no breakdown by fusion status, but the counts force that conclusion. The critics agree with the direction: the study shows, as others had, that a solid fusion is not necessary for a good result. Their explanation is that a fibrous fusion may reduce translation and so relieve back and leg pain. That is offered as a possibility, not shown. Our reading: dynamic motion in the fused group fell to 0.1 mm despite 9 pseudarthroses, which could fit that idea. It could also fit the rival reading that plain films overcalled nonunion and some of the 9 were solid. Our bound: if motion cannot be negative, the 9 averaged at most 0.28 mm (0.1 x 25 / 9). No subgroup data are given. Our reading: there is a tension here. The critics also write that the correlation of slip and motion with pain attests to the fact that successful fusion leads to a better outcome. But a group with 36 percent radiographic pseudarthrosis did well, so the benefit cannot rest on radiographic union alone. Because plain films are a poor indicator, this does not settle whether true bony union matters. A correlation of slip with pain also does not show that slip caused the pain. Harms: the critique reports none. That means no complications, no reoperations, no blood loss or operative time, and no donor site data. Do not read this as no harms; it is an absence in a two-page summary. It may well be in the original paper, which we have not seen. Any statement about the cost of adding fusion must come from another source.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: The critics praise the study, list four limits, and still call the data convincing.
points: Critique calls it not a true randomized study, then later a prospective, randomized analysis.
Balance claimed on many variables, but only age and sex have a stated comparison, and nothing is shown for stenosis, claudication or pain.
Funding and conflicts are not stated in the critique.
slides.notes: The critics are fair and specific, and their four limits are worth learning: small numbers, no true randomization, a weak definition of pseudarthrosis, and no functional outcome measure such as SF-36. On the outcome, they note good meant occasional discomfort and fair meant intermittent discomfort, and ask how often occasional is, and when it becomes intermittent. Excellent meant unrestricted activity and complete relief. Fair meant intermittent discomfort with restricted activity and occasional need for medication. So a patient with intermittent discomfort, unrestricted activity and no medications fits no category. The critics call the categories narrowly defined and also imprecise. Since 24 of 25 versus 11 of 25 is built on this scale, the headline rests on the study's weakest instrument. That reading is ours. Now the internal problems. Page 368 says the paper is not a true randomized, controlled study; page 369 calls it a prospective, randomized analysis. Page 369 is loose wording, and the alternating description is the one to trust, in our view. The critics call the study well conceived, list its limits, then call it well designed and the data convincing. They also write that it ideally should be redone with strict randomization, then that it appears the data are clear on the necessity for an adjunctive fusion. Our reading: chance is an unlikely explanation, but bias is not excluded, and the certainty stated reflects 1997 practice and leans on a study with no concealment and an imprecise grading scale. They say earlier articles plus this analysis make it extremely difficult to enroll multiple surgeons with a greater patient base in a repeat study. Historical point, ours: the library holds later randomized trials, but they are not that repeat. NORDSTEN-DS compared decompression with instrumented fusion, not noninstrumented intertransverse fusion, so it does not test their prediction. Credit where due: the critics commend Herkowitz and Kurz for following a prospective protocol when many colleagues had already settled on fusion, and for laying a foundation for later fusion studies. Keep the verdict proportionate. For its time this was a serious attempt to answer the question. It just should not carry today's decision alone.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "As reported in a 1997 critique, Herkowitz and Kurz alternated 50 patients and found 24 of 25 good-to-excellent results with noninstrumented fusion versus 11 of 25 without, despite 36% radiographic pseudarthrosis. The critics say it changed practice. It was not randomized and used an imprecise outcome scale."

rows: 24 of 25 vs 11 of 25 good to excellent

points: SLIP and NORDSTEN come from the library records. Endpoints differ, so do not compare effect sizes directly.
Do not stretch it: no instrumentation, one surgeon, and no harms data in this source.
slides.notes: Expect these follow-up questions. Was this a randomized trial? No. Patients were assigned alternately, the critics say it is not a true randomized study, and any description of it as randomized should be corrected. Does it justify fusing every degenerative slip today? Not by itself. It tested noninstrumented fusion, by one surgeon, in 50 patients, against an imprecise grading scale. The library's later randomized trials give a more mixed picture. SLIP favored fusion on SF-36 and reoperation, but the difference was not significant after baseline adjustment. NORDSTEN-DS found decompression alone noninferior to instrumented fusion at 5 years, with 63 percent ODI responders in both arms. Those are library-record numbers, with different endpoints and different operations, so the comparison is ours and is about direction, not size. Does the large gap prove later trials wrong? No. Different era, operations, patients and outcome measures. Our reading: an unconcealed study with a soft outcome is the kind likely to show a bigger effect than randomized trials, but the data here cannot prove that. Would these patients have qualified for SLIP? Unknown. SLIP excluded motion over 3 mm per its record; the reported motion here was 2.8 and 3.4 mm before surgery, so some probably would not have. That is ours. Does pseudarthrosis matter? In this source at least 8 of 9 did well, by our arithmetic, so radiographic union and clinical result were not the same thing. Which fusion did the study support? Intertransverse, noninstrumented, one level. Did instrumentation help? This study cannot say. Finally, where did your numbers come from? From the Vaccaro and Garfin critique, not the 1991 paper. Say that aloud. If the original is obtained, this deck and its card should be rechecked.

decks.not_reviewed: No supplement is cited. The cited method sources (including Hagg 2003, ref 11, and the reliability sources, refs 20 and 21) and the Lumbar Spine Study Group database itself were not reviewed. The 7-page article was read in full, tables checked against the rendered PDF.

slides.title: Copay 2008: choosing an MCID
slides.lead: Seven ways to compute a minimum clinically important difference (MCID), one lumbar surgery sample, very different answers.
points: Journal club: outcomes and optimization
Copay AG, Glassman SD, Subach BR, Berven S, Schuler TC, Carreon LY. Spine J 2008;8:968-74

Bottom line: thresholds varied about fivefold or more with the calculation method; the two anchors gave similar values. The authors picked the minimum detectable change (MDC): ODI 12.8, SF-36 PCS 4.9, back pain 1.2, leg pain 1.6.
Prepared from the full text of the paper.
slides.notes: This is the paper behind the ODI 12.8 figure. It is not a trial. It is a methods comparison: the authors took 1-year outcomes from one surgical database and ran the common MCID recipes side by side on the same patients. They state three aims: show the range of values the methods give, choose one value per instrument that is both statistically sound and clinically meaningful, and test whether a general health anchor behaves like a surgery-specific satisfaction anchor. Hold onto one idea for the whole deck: the headline number is not an anchor-based MCID at all. It is the MDC, a measurement-error threshold, which the authors adopted as the MCID because it sat above measurement error and near the change of patients who called themselves somewhat better, at least for ODI and PCS. Their own words at the end matter too: MCID is a minimum, not a desirable value, and it should not be the primary yardstick of treatment success. Disclosure: authors report research support from and consulting for Medtronic Sofamor Danek. The full article was read; no supplement is cited, and the cited method papers were not reviewed.

slides.title: The question and the methods
slides.lead: Anchor methods ask patients what mattered; distribution methods ask how noisy the score is.

rows: Mean change of 'Somewhat better' (HTI) or 'Satisfied' patients
That mean minus the mean of 'About the same' or 'Don't know'
Change score with equal sensitivity and specificity between those two groups
Half the SD of baseline scores
SD x square root of (1 - r)
1.96 x square root of 2 x SEM

points: r is test-retest reliability, taken from the literature: 0.90 ODI, 0.92 PCS, 0.95 for both pain scales.
The authors say no agreed method existed and no one had compared methods in one sample.
slides.notes: Set up the problem the way the authors do. Patient-reported scores have no built-in meaning, so MCID was proposed as the smallest change that is important to patients. A lower MCID makes any treatment look better, because more patients clear it; an artificially high one fails to credit a real benefit. Methods fall into two families. Anchor-based methods tie the score change to an outside judgment by the patient. Here the anchors were the SF-36 health transition item (HTI: health now compared with 1 year ago, five levels from much better to much worse) and a five-item satisfaction-with-results scale the authors built themselves; its psychometric properties are unknown, as they say. Distribution-based methods use only the spread of scores and ignore what patients thought. Note two details. First, the ROC cut-off used here is the point of equal sensitivity and specificity, not another rule, and no area under the curve is reported. Second, SEM and MDC depend on a reliability value r that was not measured in this sample; it was borrowed from other studies. Our arithmetic, not the paper's: MDC equals about 2.77 times SD times the square root of (1 - r), so it moves with both the sample spread and the borrowed r. Keep that formula in mind for the appraisal slide.

slides.title: Patients and measurement
slides.lead: A mostly fusion, mixed-diagnosis sample, retained because they answered the satisfaction questions.
points: Database of 948 patients; 460 retained because they answered the satisfaction questions.
11 surgeons at three centers; ODI v1, SF-36 v2 PCS, 0-10 back and leg pain scales.
Paired baseline and 1-year scores: 457 ODI, 460 PCS, 427 back pain, 430 leg pain. The abstract says 454.
Mean age 54.4, BMI 29.9, 59.1% female, 17.3% smokers.
Diagnoses: stenosis 28.5%, disc pathology or degeneration 15.8%, spondylolisthesis 14.7%.
88.5% fusion, 11.5% decompression; no significant differences between them, per the authors.
Change = 1-year score minus baseline, with ODI and pain sign-flipped so positive means better.
slides.notes: Read this as a cohort question: who is in it, and how was change measured. Selection: fewer than half the database (460 of 948, 48.5% by our arithmetic) entered, chosen by whether they answered the satisfaction items. The paper does not compare included with excluded patients, so we cannot tell whether responders differ. It gives no surgery dates. The sample is heavily fusion and diagnostically mixed by design; the authors wanted a general lumbar surgery value and acknowledge that MCID may differ by treatment, pathology and patient. Measurement: everything is a single 1-year change from a preoperative baseline. Group means improved on all four measures (P<.001 by paired t test). The mean ODI change was 14.90 points. Counts drift between sections: the abstract says 454 patients with 1-year ODI or PCS, while Methods says 460 retained, with 457 paired ODI and 460 paired PCS. 454 matches the HTI-by-PCS count in Table 2, so the abstract figure may be one analysis subset. We flag it rather than resolve it. Also note the HTI asks about health in general, not the spine. The authors name that drawback themselves: a patient can feel no better because of an unrelated illness.

slides.title: Results: the thresholds
slides.lead: Same patients, same scales, threshold set by the recipe. HTI anchor shown; Table 3 also gives satisfaction values.
points: *As printed; the row's own 0.5 SD and SEM imply about 0.38 (our arithmetic).
Satisfaction anchor MDC: ODI 11.67, PCS 4.57, back 1.19, leg 1.58.
Authors' range (HTI column): ODI 2.92-15.36, PCS 1.26-5.95, back 0.28-2.88, leg 0.53-2.85.
slides.see: Table 2 gives mean change in each HTI and satisfaction group; it shows why the anchor thresholds land where they do.
slides.notes: Read across a row and then down a column. Down the ODI column the candidates run from 2.9 to 15.4, which is why the authors say five- to tenfold. Average change was always largest and effect size always smallest. We recomputed what we could. The change-difference rows match Table 2 exactly (for ODI, 15.36 minus 7.40 is 7.96). The distribution rows hang together: in every column 0.5 SD is 2.5 times the effect size, SEM matches the stated reliabilities, and MDC is 2.77 times SEM. One cell breaks the pattern: back pain effect size, HTI column, 0.28. Its own 0.5 SD of 0.95 implies 0.38, and the satisfaction column gives 0.39. If 0.38 is right, the back pain range is about 7.6-fold, not 10-fold, so the abstract's 10-fold claim rests on what looks like a misprint (our inference). A second oddity: Methods says the distribution values use the SD of baseline scores, but the SDs they imply (ODI about 14.6 in the HTI column and 13.3 in the satisfaction column) differ from the whole-sample 14.06 in Table 1 and from each other. The paper does not say which subset was used. With the Table 1 SD the ODI MDC would be about 12.3 (ours). Now the clinical anchors. Patients who said 'About the same' still improved 7.40 ODI points on average, and 'Somewhat better' patients 15.36. The ROC cut-offs for pain fall on half points (2.50, 1.50); the paper gives no reason, but our inference is that this follows from whole-number change scores on 0-10 scales. Look at back pain: the anchor-based ROC value is 2.50, but the chosen MDC is 1.16, below the 1.50 mean change of patients reporting no change in health.

slides.title: Anchors and individual success
slides.lead: The two anchors gave similar thresholds even though they classified patients differently.
points: Spearman correlation with change: satisfaction ODI 0.46, PCS 0.40, back 0.42, leg 0.26; HTI 0.35, 0.29, 0.37, 0.26.
HTI and satisfaction correlated at 0.38.
Of 103 'Somewhat better' patients in the cross-tab, 37 were 'Satisfied' (Table 5).
Using average change as the bar would misclassify up to 61.7% of 'Somewhat better' patients, versus up to 46.7% with MDC, per the authors.
slides.notes: This slide is about validity. The authors' test of the HTI as an anchor was to compare it with the satisfaction scale, and since thresholds from the two were very similar, they say the satisfaction scale supports the HTI. Be careful with that logic. Neither anchor is validated, as the authors concede, and similar averages do not mean the anchors pick the same patients. Our count from Table 5: the two minimal-change groups, 'Somewhat better' and 'Satisfied', share only 37 patients, and only 199 of 434 (46%) fall in matching categories on both scales. Similar thresholds therefore come from groups that are only partly the same people. The table is the authors' main teaching point about group versus individual results. Every mean change is well above the MCID, so by group averages surgery looks highly successful. Yet only about half the patients cleared the MDC on each measure. With the smaller effect-size threshold, about 67 to 74 percent did. The share of successes depends on the threshold chosen. Mean changes in the table are as printed in the Discussion; Table 2 totals differ slightly (PCS 6.11, leg 2.44). We could not check the 61.7% and 46.7% figures, because individual change scores are not given. One more result: baseline and change scores were associated (r 0.11 ODI, printed as -13 for PCS, 0.37 back, 0.49 leg). The paper calls these small; 0.37 and 0.49 are moderate in our reading. The paragraph also argues in two directions about PCS (see appraisal).

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: A useful demonstration that MCID depends on method; a weak basis for one universal number.
points: Holds up: all methods applied to the same patients; prospective collection; four common instruments; two anchors.
Holds up: authors call MCID a minimum, not a measure of success, and say MDC depends on sample variability.
Weakens it: 460 of 948 selected by answering satisfaction items; no comparison with those left out.
Weakens it: both anchors unvalidated; HTI asks about general health, not the spine.
Weakens it: reliability values borrowed, not measured; MDC moves with them.
Weakens it: mixed, 88.5% fusion sample; one study group of 11 surgeons; 1-year change only.
Weakens it: back pain MDC (1.16) is below the change of 'About the same' patients (1.50).
Source problems: back pain effect size 0.28 (likely 0.38); 454 vs 460 patients; SD basis unclear; 'r = -13'.
slides.notes: Be fair first. The paper does what it set out to do: it shows clearly that the method drives the number, using one sample so nothing else varies. The authors name several limits themselves: MDC depends on sample variability and should be checked in other samples, MCID may differ by treatment, pathology and patient, the anchors are not validated, and the satisfaction scale has unknown psychometrics. The rest is our reading. Choosing MDC is a judgment, not a finding. MDC answers whether a change is bigger than noise, with 95% confidence for one patient. It says nothing directly about importance. The authors justify it by its closeness to the 'Somewhat better' mean, but for ODI that is 12.8 against 15.4 and for back pain the authors acknowledge the MDC is closer to the change of 'About the same' patients; by our comparison of Table 3 with Table 2 it is actually below it (1.16 vs 1.50). Sensitivity to r, by our arithmetic: with the HTI-column SD of about 1.9, back pain MDC is 1.2 at r = 0.95 but about 2.0 at r = 0.85. So a borrowed reliability alone can move the threshold by two thirds. The distribution values also differ between the HTI and satisfaction columns, which should not happen if they came from one baseline SD; the subset is not stated. Internal checks: the back pain effect-size cell, the 454 versus 460 count, the r printed as -13, and a Results paragraph that first says lower baseline health predicts greater improvement (consistent with the printed correlations, including -0.13 for PCS), then says the patients with greater ODI and back pain change had lower baseline disability and pain, and 'similarly' that those with the lowest baseline PCS improved less, citing Table 6. So for ODI, back pain and PCS the correlations conflict with the pattern across HTI groups. Mean changes in the Discussion differ slightly from Table 2. None of these alters the main message that methods disagree.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: Spoken summary for rounds.
points: "In about 450 lumbar surgery patients, mostly fusions, seven MCID methods gave ODI thresholds from about 3 to 15 points. The authors chose the minimum detectable change, 12.8 for ODI, 4.9 for PCS, 1.2 for back and 1.6 for leg pain, and they call it a minimum, not a measure of success."
Do not stretch it: 12.8 is a measurement-error threshold adopted as MCID in one sample, built on borrowed reliability values.
Do not stretch it: the back pain value is smaller than the change of patients who felt no different.

rows: No. It is one sample's MDC; anchor methods gave 8 to 18
Little here; thresholds were similar, though patients sorted differently
Can I use it for a trial's group difference?
This paper sets a within-patient threshold; it does not test group differences (our reading)
Group means improved; about half of patients reached the MDC

slides.notes: Expect four follow-up questions. First, is 12.8 the ODI MCID? Say it is the value these authors selected, the MDC, in a mostly fusion, mixed-diagnosis sample at 1 year. In the same patients anchor-based ODI values ran from 7.96 to 17.96 across both anchors, and the full range across all methods was 2.66 to 17.96. Second, why not take the anchor-based ROC value? The paper does not say. Our reading: the authors' general criterion is that an MCID must exceed measurement error and match patients' sense of importance, and the ODI ROC values (9.50 HTI, 11.75 satisfaction) are both below the adopted 12.8, though 11.75 is just above the satisfaction-anchor MDC of 11.67. Third, can a trial with a 5-point between-group ODI difference be dismissed because 5 is below 12.8? That is our reading, not the paper's: the paper derives a threshold for change within one patient and never addresses differences between group means, so applying it that way needs a separate argument. Fourth, does it transfer to decompression, cervical surgery or nonoperative care? The authors say MCID may differ by treatment, pathology and patient characteristics, and that MDC should be determined in several samples. Close with the authors' own conclusion: as a minimal change, MCID should not be regarded as the primary yardstick of treatment success, and a desirable amount of change might be a better estimate of success.

decks.not_reviewed: On-line Tables 1 to 3 (search strategies and the summary of the 33 included studies) are not in the PDF and were not read, and none of the 33 underlying studies was read. The 6-page article itself was read in full; it is the complete original paper, not a critique.

slides.title: Brinjikji 2015: asymptomatic degeneration
slides.lead: How often do pain-free people show degenerative findings on spine MRI or CT, by age?
points: Journal club: outcomes and optimization
Brinjikji W, et al. AJNR Am J Neuroradiol 2015;36:811-16
Bottom line: degenerative findings are common in people with no history of back pain and mostly rise with age. Modeled disk degeneration was 37% at age 20 and 96% at age 80.
slides.notes: This is a systematic review from Mayo Clinic, the University of Washington and collaborators, funded by an NIH grant. It pools studies that imaged people with no history of back pain and estimates, decade by decade, how often eight findings appear: disk degeneration, disk signal loss, disk height loss, disk bulge, disk protrusion, annular fissure, facet degeneration and spondylolisthesis. The authors say the results feed the LIRE trial (NCT02015455), which tests whether adding these prevalence figures to lumbar imaging reports reduces later imaging, injections and surgery. That tells you the intended use: putting a radiology report in context. Keep one idea in mind for the whole deck: this paper measures how common a finding is in people without pain. It does not compare people with and without pain, so it cannot tell you how well any finding separates a pain generator from a bystander. What was reviewed: the full 6-page article, including Figure 1 and Tables 1 and 2. Not reviewed: On-line Tables 1 to 3, which hold the search strategy and the list and details of the 33 included studies, and the studies themselves. So nothing in this deck checks individual study quality, imaging protocols or which spinal levels were read.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: Advanced imaging is used more and more for back pain, and degenerative findings are often read as the cause.
points: Authors' premise: findings such as degeneration, facet hypertrophy and protrusion trigger medical and surgical treatment that sometimes fails
Earlier studies had already shown such findings in many pain-free people
Aim: age-specific prevalence of 8 findings in asymptomatic individuals
Findings defined by the 2001 NASS, ASSR and ASNR combined task force nomenclature
Intended use: help clinicians and patients judge findings named in a radiology report
slides.notes: Set the stakes. The paper opens with back pain affecting up to two thirds of adults at some time and with rising use of MRI and CT. The authors' argument is that a report listing degeneration, bulge or protrusion invites a causal story, and that knowing the background rate in pain-free people of the same age should temper it. Our reading, not stated in the paper: the eight findings are not independent. Disk degeneration, disk signal loss and disk height loss overlap, and bulge and protrusion are adjacent categories of disk contour in the task force nomenclature. The paper gives the reference (Fardon and Milette 2001) but does not restate the definitions, and the authors later admit the included studies span more than 25 years and did not always use the standard terms. So 'disk degeneration' in one study may not mean the same thing in another. Our inference: that is a measurement problem, not a selection problem, and it likely matters more for the subtle findings such as annular fissure than for gross ones such as spondylolisthesis. Also our reading: for a surgeon the useful question is narrower than the paper's. You want to know how often a finding at the level you plan to treat is a bystander. This paper gives the base rate in pain-free people, which is one input to that judgment but not the answer.

slides.title: Methods: search, selection, model
points: Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid EMBASE and Web of Science through April 2014, plus reference lists
Included: English, MRI or CT, prevalence by age group, explicitly pain-free people
Asymptomatic: no history of back pain; studies with minor back pain, motor or sensory symptoms, tumor or trauma excluded
Each article evaluated by 2 reviewers
Pooling: mixed-effects binomial model, clustered on study, adjusted for age-interval midpoint
Predictions read off the model at ages 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70 and 80

rows: 21 no adults, wrong finding, or no symptom separation
25 no age strata, mild pain mixed in, or by level not by patient
32 MRI, 1 CT; 3110 people; study size 8 to 412

slides.see: Figure 1 is the flow diagram; its steps match the text (300 then 46 excluded).
slides.notes: The flow arithmetic holds: 379 less 300 is 79, less 21 is 58, less 25 is 33, and 21 plus 25 equals the 46 the text gives. Note two small wording slips. The text first says MEDLINE and EMBASE, then says 3 databases, adding Web of Science. It also once calls the work a meta-analysis. Now the model, because every number on the next slide comes out of it. Each study's age-range estimate is one record. A generalized linear mixed model with a binomial outcome and a random effect for study fits prevalence against the midpoint of each age range. The authors tested knots at ages 40 and 60 to let the slope change, found no significant evidence for it, and so used age as a single linear term. Our check: on the logit scale the Table 2 rows step up by an almost constant amount each decade, about 0.6 for disk degeneration and about 0.1 for protrusion. So each row is a fitted smooth curve, not observed decade rates. Two consequences, both our reading. First, the extremes, ages 20 and 80, are where the curve leans hardest on the straight-line assumption and where data are thinnest. Second, the knot test had little power with so few older people, so 'no significant interaction' does not show the curve is truly linear. Also, when a study gave only a mean and SD of age, the authors used a normal approximation to estimate how many people fell in each decade, so the counts in Table 1 are estimates. The paper reports no study quality appraisal, no heterogeneity statistic and no formal test for publication bias, though the authors list publication bias as a limitation.

slides.title: Results: modeled prevalence by age
slides.lead: Table 2, asymptomatic individuals.
points: Age 30: disk degeneration 52%, signal loss 33%, bulge 40%
Age 60: degeneration 88%, signal loss 86%, facet degeneration 50%, spondylolisthesis 23%
Protrusion and fissure were common at every age but rose little
slides.see: Table 2 gives all seven decades; Table 1 gives the people and studies behind each cell.
slides.notes: Read the table in two groups. The age-driven findings are disk degeneration, signal loss, height loss, bulge, facet degeneration and spondylolisthesis. They climb steeply, and the authors note height loss and bulge rose about 1% per year, which the table bears out (24% to 84% and 30% to 84% over 60 years). The always-there findings are protrusion and annular fissure. They are present in roughly a fifth to a third of pain-free people at age 20 and rise less steeply: protrusion 29% to 43% and fissure 19% to 29% from age 20 to 80. In the authors' words they were moderately prevalent across all age categories but did not substantially increase. For a surgeon that second group may be the more useful lesson: a protrusion on a 25-year-old's MRI is present in about 3 in 10 pain-free people that age, by this model. The facet and spondylolisthesis values at ages 20 and 30 are not observed data. Table 1 shows 0 people and 0 studies at those ages for both findings, so 4%, 9%, 3% and 5% are the model's extrapolation downward. The Results text says authors 'rarely reported' facet degeneration in younger people (4% to 9%), which overstates it; no included study reported it at those ages. No confidence interval is given for any cell. Our view: quote these as rough modeled rates, not as precise population prevalence. Also note what the table does not tell you: severity, level, number of levels, or whether the finding sat at a level matching symptoms. The authors say findings were not stratified by severity.

slides.title: How much data sits behind each number
slides.lead: Our sums from Table 1, which gives estimated people (studies) per decade.
points: Most data come from people in their 20s to 50s
The 96% at age 80 rests on an estimated 19 people in 2 studies
Spondylolisthesis: 148 people, 1 study per decade, none under 40
slides.notes: This slide is the fragile part, and the paper never puts it this way, so everything here is our arithmetic from Table 1. The row totals are estimated people contributing to each finding, summed across decades. Disk degeneration has the most data, 1722 people, but only 119 aged 60 or more, about 7%. The famous 96% at age 80 comes from an estimated 19 people in 2 studies plus the straight-line model reaching up from younger ages. For five findings the counts at ages 60, 70 and 80 are identical, 35, 15 and 14, each from 1 study at 70 and 80. Our guess is that a single study supplies most of the older data for those five, but the study list is in On-line Table 3, which we did not see. If so, the older estimates for signal loss, height loss, fissure, facet degeneration and spondylolisthesis share one study's readers, scanner and definitions. Spondylolisthesis is the thinnest: 148 people, 1 study per decade, and no data under 40, so 50% at age 80 is close to one small study plus a model. Facet degeneration has 596 of its 713 people in the 40s, from 3 studies. Why it matters for teaching: the high numbers in the elderly are the ones people quote, and they are the least supported. The direction is believable, since degeneration with age is consistent across the literature the authors cite, but the exact percentages after 60 are soft. With one study the random study effect cannot be estimated for that age band, so the model cannot separate age from that study's habits. That is our reading. To show how wide the uncertainty could be, our rough Wilson 95% intervals, treating each modeled rate as if observed in that cell's estimated people and ignoring study clustering, so the true intervals are wider: 96% at age 80 with 19 people gives about 77% to 99%; spondylolisthesis 50% at 80 with 14 gives about 27% to 73%; facet degeneration 83% at 80 with 14 gives about 57% to 95%. Compare annular fissure 19% at age 20 with 167 people, about 14% to 26%.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: Holds up: broad search of 3 databases plus reference lists
Holds up: strict definition of asymptomatic, mild pain excluded
Holds up: flow diagram arithmetic checks
Holds up: the same model form for each finding, age as a continuous term
Weakens it: no confidence intervals, heterogeneity or quality appraisal reported
Weakens it: thin data after 60; extrapolated cells at 20 and 30
Weakens it: volunteers, many single-reader studies, mixed nomenclature over 25 years (authors)
Weakens it: no severity grading, no symptomatic comparison group
Text conflicts with its own tables or itself in four places (see notes)
slides.notes: Be fair: the question is simple and the answer is robust in direction. The authors name their own limits: many participants were volunteers, so selection bias is possible; many studies used a single reader and interobserver agreement is moderate at best even with standard terms; the studies span more than 25 years without consistent nomenclature; findings were not graded by severity, and asymptomatic people may have milder changes; and publication bias may affect the data. They also state plainly that the study does not show these findings are always age-related rather than pathologic, and that it applies most to incidental findings or findings at a level that does not match the examination. The rest is our reading. Without confidence intervals you cannot tell a real 29% from a noisy one, and you cannot judge spread between studies. Defining asymptomatic as no history of back pain is strict, but the paper does not say whether leg pain without back pain was screened out, beyond excluding motor or sensory symptoms. Four places where the text conflicts with the tables or itself. Two are against Table 2: the Discussion says more than 50% of people aged 30 to 39 have disk degeneration, height loss or bulging, but at age 30 Table 2 gives 52%, 34% and 40%, so only degeneration passes 50%. The Discussion also says degenerative findings exceed 90% at 60 or older, while Table 2 gives 88% for degeneration and 86% for signal loss at 60. Third, a tension within the text: the Discussion lists protrusion as part of normal aging, though the Results say it did not substantially increase with age. Fourth, against Table 1 (Results slide): the Results say facet degeneration was 'rarely reported' at 20 and 30, but no included study reported it at those ages. One possible inconsistency we cannot settle: reference 34 (Feng 2000) is in Chinese and is a CT study, while inclusion required English; if it is among the included studies, which the uncited references 27 to 53 suggest, that breaks the stated criterion.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "In people with no back pain, degenerative MRI findings are common and rise with age: modeled disk degeneration is about 37% at 20 and 96% at 80, and protrusion is about 30 to 40% across ages. A finding on the scan is not, by itself, the pain generator."

rows: Disc-level degeneration 35% after discography vs 14% control
Fusion vs rehab ODI difference -4.1 (CI -8.1 to -0.1)

points: O08 and L11 figures come from their library records, which are abstract-level
Do not stretch it: no CIs, thin data after 60, no symptomatic comparison
slides.notes: Spoken summary: Brinjikji pooled 33 imaging studies of 3110 people with no history of back pain. Degeneration, signal loss, height loss, bulge, facet degeneration and spondylolisthesis rise steeply with age; protrusion and annular fissure sit at roughly 20 to 40% at all ages. The authors conclude these findings are often normal aging and must be read against the clinical picture. Expect these follow-up questions. Does this mean imaging findings never cause pain? No. The authors say so directly, and the paper has no symptomatic group, so it cannot give the odds that a finding is symptomatic. A concordant lesion with matching exam findings is a different situation; the authors say their conclusion applies most to incidental findings or levels that do not match the exam. Is 96% at 80 solid? No; it rests on about 19 people in 2 studies plus a linear model, by our sums from Table 1. What about a young patient with a protrusion? By this model about 29% of pain-free 20-year-olds have one, so it needs clinical concordance before it carries weight. How does this connect to fusion for back pain? Our link, not the paper's: if degeneration is near universal in pain-free older people, imaging alone cannot select fusion candidates. The MRC trial (L11) library record reports only a small ODI advantage for fusion over intensive rehabilitation. Carragee (O08) is a reminder that provocative discography to confirm a degenerate disc has its own cost: its library record reports more disc-level degeneration in punctured discs. Both comparisons come from abstract-level records in the master file, not from full-text review here.

decks.not_reviewed: Read end to end: the PDF is a reformatted copy of the open-access PMC full text (Introduction, Methods, Results, one Table, Discussion, Conclusions, references). It is the paper itself, not a critique, but it is incomplete: the structured abstract is cut to one sentence, the images of Figures 1-4 are omitted (captions only), and Supplement 1 (eTables 1-9, eFigures 1-6, eMethods) is not included. Not reviewed: the forest plots, the per-study table (eTable 5), the Newcastle-Ottawa scores (eTable 6), the metaregression table (eTable 8), the publication-bias funnel plot, the 44 primary studies, and the published version's author information, funding and conflict-of-interest statements.

slides.title: Javeed 2024: depression and lumbar surgery
slides.lead: Do patients with preoperative depression improve less after lumbar spine surgery?
points: Journal club: outcomes and optimization
Javeed S, Benedict B, Yakdan S, et al. JAMA Netw Open 2024;7(1):e2348565
Systematic review and meta-analysis: 44 studies, 21,452 patients
Bottom line: depressed patients started worse and finished worse, but improved by a similar amount (SMD 0.04, 95% CI -0.02 to 0.10)
Source note: our PDF is the reformatted PMC text. Figure images, the full abstract and Supplement 1 are missing.
slides.notes:
Frame first. This is a meta-analysis of studies that compared operated patients with and without depression, or correlated a depression score with outcome scores. Every patient had surgery. So it answers 'does depression blunt the change after surgery?' It does not answer 'does surgery beat no surgery in depressed patients?'

Source limits, said plainly. The PDF is a reformatted copy of the PMC full text, not the typeset article. The body text and the single Table are complete, but the four forest plots are captions only and Supplement 1 is absent. That supplement holds the search strategy, the study list, the quality scores, the PROM consolidation rules, the metaregression table and the funnel plot. So we cannot check how many studies or patients fed each pooled estimate, or the per-study effects. Funding and conflict statements are not in our copy.

Three messages to carry away. First, the primary outcome is change from baseline, and it did not differ. Second, absolute scores were worse in depressed patients both before and after surgery, by about half a standard deviation. Third, the evidence base is mostly retrospective, single-center, with depression defined many different ways, and heterogeneity was high. Hold all three at once: worse final state and similar improvement are both true.

slides.title: The question and the methods
slides.lead: Preoperative depression versus none, in adults having surgery for degenerative lumbar disease, with PROMs before and at least 6 months after.
points: Searched 7 databases from inception to September 14, 2023, with a librarian; PRISMA followed
Two reviewers screened, two extracted; conflicts settled by a third author
Depression: validated scale or recorded diagnosis, measured before surgery
Excluded: cervical, tumor, trauma, infection, administrative data sets, case reports, non-English
Primary: SMD of change in severity, baseline to latest follow-up
Secondary: absolute severity before and after surgery; correlation of depression score with severity
Random effects; I2; metaregression; Egger test; quality by Newcastle-Ottawa
slides.notes:
Walk through what was pooled. For comparative studies, the authors converted each study's means and SDs into standardized mean differences, so ODI, SF-PCS (Short Form physical component; the version is not named), and back and leg VAS can sit on one scale. Medians and IQRs were converted to means and SDs by Cochrane methods. All PROMs were flipped so lower means less severe. Related measures were consolidated, with rules in eTable 4, which we have not seen.

For correlation studies, Pearson r and regression betas were combined and turned into Fisher z. Mixing betas with correlations is an approximation; the authors cite a method for it (eMethods, not seen).

The depression definition is the soft spot. A recorded diagnosis and a questionnaire cutoff were both accepted. Requiring a preoperative measure was a good choice, and the authors say why: postoperative assessment could be confounded by recall bias.

What the text does not say, our reading: how studies with several PROMs were handled when 'all PROMs pooled' was calculated. If one study contributes ODI, back VAS and leg VAS as separate rows, the pooled estimate counts the same patients more than once and the interval is too narrow. The forest plots or eMethods may answer this; we could not check.

Sign convention, also ours: the text never defines which way the SMD runs. The Figure 1 and 2 captions read 'Patients Without vs With Preoperative Depression', and in Results the baseline SMD of -0.52 means depressed patients were worse while the change SMD of 0.04 means a larger, nonsignificant improvement in depressed patients. Both fit without minus with depression, change post minus pre. But the Discussion reads the metaregression the other way: it treats larger SMDs (older age) as possibly more severe depression and smaller SMDs (later studies) as a diminished role of depression. Under the Results reading, a larger change SMD means depressed patients did better. So the paper is internally inconsistent on direction, not just silent.

slides.title: What went in
slides.lead: 8459 records, 3813 after duplicates, 207 full texts, 44 studies.
points: 21,452 patients; 55% female; mean age 57 (SD 8)
Median follow-up 12 months, range 6-120
37% of patients in comparative studies had depression
Median Newcastle-Ottawa score 7 (IQR 5-9), called moderate
2 studies mixed lumbar and cervical patients and were dropped from all pooling
slides.notes:
This is the selection-and-measurement slide. Read the table as a quality profile. Two thirds retrospective, four fifths single center, a third adjusted for baseline severity, a sixth said how they handled missing data. The authors say nearly half of studies did not account for covariates such as age, comorbidities and baseline severity. Note the Table gives the counts that did adjust: 24, 20 and 16 of 44.

Depression measurement. Among the 37 comparative studies, 30 used a scale and 7 a chart diagnosis. The most common scale was the SF-MCS (Short Form mental component, version not named; 11 studies), which the authors note is not depression specific. Among studies using common depression scales, 20 used variable cutoffs. Only 4 used the PHQ-9.

Outcomes. ODI in 35 studies, back VAS in 22, leg VAS in 20.

Our arithmetic. The percentages do not follow one rounding rule. Some are rounded (29 of 44 is 65.9%, printed 66; 25 of 44 is 56.8%, printed 57). Others are truncated (age-adjusted 24 of 44 is 54.5%, printed 54; propensity matching and approach not reported, each 2 of 44 = 4.5%, printed 4; ODI 35 of 44 is 79.5%, printed 79; PHQ-9 4 of 37 is 10.8%, printed 10; SF-MCS 11 of 37 is 29.7%, printed 29). Two fit neither rule. Posterior approach 31 of 44 is 70.5%, printed 71. Publication years 3 + 8 + 34 sum to 45, not 44, and 34 of 44 is 77%, not the printed 75%; 33 would fit 75%. And of the four studies cited as PHQ-9 users, reference 7's title names the PHQ-2. That study may also have used the PHQ-9; we cannot tell without it.

Also ours: the mean age of 57 with SD 8 looks like the spread of study means, not of patients. And the 21,452 includes the 2 mixed studies that were not pooled, so the pooled analyses had fewer patients. The text does not say how many.

Scope, ours: the reference list includes adult spinal deformity and revision surgery series, and a quarter of studies used anteroposterior approaches. 'Degenerative lumbar' here is broad.

slides.title: Primary outcome: change after surgery
slides.lead: No significant difference in improvement between patients with and without depression.
points: Change: P = .21. Depressed patients improved slightly more, not significantly
Same result with chart diagnosis or scale, and with SF-MCS or a depression-specific scale
Negative severity SMDs mean worse in depressed patients, before and after
slides.see: Figures 1 and 2 show the per-PROM forest plots for ODI, SF-PCS and back and leg VAS. Our copy has captions only.
slides.notes:
How to read it. An SMD is a difference in standard deviation units. The change estimate is 0.04 with an interval of -0.02 to 0.10. Our reading: the mean effect is tightly estimated around zero; even the upper end is a tenth of a standard deviation, so a large average blunting of improvement is unlikely. But that interval covers the mean only. I2 is 75%, so studies truly differ. Our rough estimate, assuming about 35 studies: tau about 0.16, giving a 95% prediction interval of roughly -0.3 to +0.35. A single setting could still show a moderate effect either way. The paper reports no prediction interval.

Recomputation, ours. The interval is symmetric around 0.04. Back-calculating the standard error gives z about 1.3 and P about 0.19, against the printed 0.21. Close enough for rounding. The two severity intervals are near-symmetric too.

The severity gap. About half a standard deviation before surgery, and the same point estimate after. The postoperative interval is wider, and I2 is 98%. The text points to eFigure 2, which we do not have, and does not say how many studies fed each estimate. Our caution: the three rows probably come from different sets of studies, so do not do arithmetic across them.

Overstatement to flag. In Results the authors write 'despite experiencing greater improvement after surgery', and in the Discussion 'comparable or possibly even larger'. The difference was not significant. Similar is what the data support.

A text error. Results says depressed patients had worse preoperative status 'compared with patients with depression'. It must mean without.

Fragile, ours: change scores in people who start worse have more room to move and more regression toward the mean. The authors themselves say depressed patients may have greater room for recovery. So a similar change may partly reflect a worse start, not a resilient response.

slides.title: Correlations and heterogeneity
slides.lead: A higher depression score went with worse severity before and after surgery, but not with the size of the change.
points: Metaregression: older age and higher male-to-female ratio were associated with larger SMDs
More comorbidity, later study year and more attrition were associated with smaller SMDs
Model R2 75%; residual I2 48%
Egger z = -0.84, P = .40; funnel moderately asymmetric
slides.see: Figures 3 and 4 show the correlation forest plots by PROM; eFigure 6 is the funnel plot. Neither image is in our copy.
slides.notes:
Correlation results. Our conversion, not the paper's: a Fisher z of 0.36 is r of about 0.35, and 0.29 is r of about 0.28. These are moderate correlations. Depression explains a modest share of variation in spine severity. The change correlation is null, with a wide spread across studies (I2 93%). The authors offer two readings: depression severity truly does not track change, or the relation is nonlinear and a linear correlation missed it.

Heterogeneity. Overall I2 ran from 44% to 99%. The primary outcome range is given as 44% to 84%. Five variables explained heterogeneity on univariable metaregression: comorbidity percentage, first enrollment year, attrition, depression stratification method and number of levels. Age and sex were added a priori. The authors report R2 of 75% with age and sex in the model versus 38% without, and residual I2 48%.

How to read the metaregression, ours. These are study-level associations across at most 37 comparative studies (the number in the model is not reported), with seven covariates. That is ecological and easily overfit. 'Older age was associated with larger SMDs' is about studies with older average age, not older patients. Also, direction is contradictory. Under the Results reading, a larger change SMD means depressed patients improved more, yet the Discussion reads larger SMDs (older age) as possibly more severe depression and smaller SMDs (later years) as a diminished role of depression. So we cannot say whether 'larger' means depression mattered more or less. The authors read later study year as possibly reflecting better depression treatment. That is speculation; the paper had no treatment data.

Publication bias. Egger was not significant (our check: z of 0.84 gives P about 0.40, matching). The authors attribute the asymmetry to study quality and depression measures. With high heterogeneity, Egger has little power, which is our point, not theirs.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: Holds up: broad search, duplicate screening and extraction, preoperative depression required
Holds up: mean change effect tightly estimated near zero, stable in sensitivity analyses; but individual studies vary widely (I2 75%)
Weak: observational studies, two thirds retrospective; only a third adjusted for baseline severity
Weak: depression defined by chart, SF-MCS or scales with varying cutoffs
Weak: high heterogeneity, I2 up to 99%
Weak: no data on depression treatment, anxiety or kinesiophobia (authors)
Unclear: SMD direction (Results and Discussion read it oppositely), numbers per pooled analysis, handling of multiple PROMs per study
Errors: 'with' for 'without'; publication years sum to 45; posterior 71% for 31 of 44; mixed rounding and truncation
slides.notes:
Be fair. The authors list three limitations: heterogeneity across studies and depression screening methods; no data on co-occurring conditions such as anxiety or kinesiophobia; and no information on active or prior depression treatment, which may confound. They also claim a thorough search, robust synthesis and rigorous exploration of confounding.

Our additions.

Selection. Every study enrolled operated patients. Depressed patients who were not offered surgery, or declined, are invisible. If surgeons selected depressed patients with clearer indications, similar improvement could reflect that selection.

Confounding. Most studies did not adjust for baseline severity, and depressed patients started half a standard deviation worse. Change from a worse baseline is not the same contrast as change from an equal baseline.

Measurement. The outcome is self-reported, and so is depression in most studies. Mood can shape how patients rate pain and function at both time points.

Scope. Median follow-up was 12 months. The range reaches 120, but the text does not report results by follow-up length.

Causation. The authors themselves call for work on the causal link. This paper does not show depression causes worse spine status or that treating depression improves surgical outcome.

Reporting. The 'with' for 'without' slip in Results, the publication-year total of 45, the posterior 71%, and percentages that mix rounding with truncation are small, but they are on the slide so the group can see them. The SF-MCS count is attributed to eTable 2 in one place and eTable 3 in another.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "Across 44 mostly retrospective studies, depressed patients started and finished about half a standard deviation worse on disability and pain, but improved by a similar amount after lumbar surgery. As group averages, depression went with a worse start and a worse finish, not a significantly smaller improvement."

rows: Change SMD 0.04; absolute SMD -0.52 before and after
mJOA 16+ at 1 year, a final state
Psychiatric comorbidity did not hold up as a predictor
Thresholds varied with method and anchor

points: C04 and O01 come from the library records. Endpoints and populations differ.
Do not stretch it: this does not test surgery against no surgery in depressed patients
slides.notes:
Spoken summary: 'This is a meta-analysis of 44 studies, about 21,000 patients having degenerative lumbar surgery. Depressed patients had worse disability, pain and function before surgery and were still worse after, by about half a standard deviation. But the amount they improved was similar, with no significant difference: SMD 0.04, interval -0.02 to 0.10. Most studies were retrospective and single center, depression was defined many ways, and heterogeneity was high.'

Why the comparison table. Tetreault (C04, library record) predicts a final state, mJOA 16 or higher, in cervical myelopathy, a different disease and region. The record says psychiatric comorbidity did not hold up as a predictor in validation. Copay (O01, library record, abstract level) reminds you that a change threshold is not an acceptable final state. Javeed is the lumbar version of the same lesson: final state and change are different questions.

Expected questions.

Should I refuse surgery to a depressed patient? Not on this evidence. The authors say it supports appropriately indicated surgery in depressed patients and emphasizes mental health treatment.

What do I tell the patient? Ours: you can expect to improve by about as much as others, but you may end up with more pain and disability than someone who started without depression.

Should I screen and treat before surgery? The paper does not recommend screening surgical patients. The authors note that a depression screening initiative recommends the PHQ-9 in primary care, that only 4 of 37 studies used it, and call for standard methods in spine surgery research. Ours: screening seems reasonable, but that is our view, not the paper's. This paper had no data on treatment, so it cannot say whether treating depression first improves outcome.

Does it apply to cervical surgery or deformity? Cervical was excluded. Deformity and revision series appear in the references, but no subgroup results are given.

Is the SMD clinically meaningful? Ours: the paper does not convert SMDs back to ODI or VAS points, so do not quote point differences from it.

decks.not_reviewed: Supplemental Digital Content 1-6 (search strategies, inclusion criteria, level-of-evidence criteria, grade-linking table, PRISMA flowchart and the evidence tables), the full guideline on the CNS website, the audio abstract, and the 41 underlying studies. The 8-page journal article itself was read in full.

slides.title: CNS preoperative opioid guideline
slides.lead: Do preoperative opioid duration, dose or weaning change what happens after elective degenerative spine surgery?
points: Journal club: outcomes and optimization
Wang MC, et al. Neurosurgery 89:S1-S8, 2021 (Supplement to Number 5)

Bottom line: preoperative opioid use, and longer use, mark higher risk after surgery (Grade B). Whether a preoperative wean lowers that risk is not established: one observational study (Grade Insufficient).
slides.notes: This is one chapter of the Congress of Neurological Surgeons perioperative spine guideline series, endorsed by the AANS and CNS. It is a systematic review that turns graded evidence into graded statements. The population is adults having elective spine surgery for degenerative conditions. It asks three questions: does preoperative duration matter, does preoperative dose (morphine milligram equivalents, MME) matter, and does preoperative weaning help. Outcomes are postoperative opioid use, patient-reported outcomes and adverse events. Keep one idea in mind for the whole deck: two of the three answers are about prediction, and the third, the only one about an intervention, rests on a single observational study, which the authors judged insufficient. That is the trap the Anki card tests. What was reviewed: the full 8-page journal article. Not reviewed: Supplemental Digital Content 1 to 6, which hold the search strategies, inclusion criteria, grading rules, PRISMA flowchart and evidence tables, the full guideline on the CNS site, and the 41 studies themselves. So all study-level numbers here are as the guideline reports them, and we could not check the evidence tables.

slides.title: Questions and recommendations

rows: Longer use is associated with worse outcomes: chronic postoperative use, more complications, longer stay, higher costs and resource use
Use of any dose (yes/no) is associated with longer postoperative use and worse clinical and patient-reported outcomes
Insufficient evidence that weaning improves postoperative use, outcomes or adverse events

points: None of the 41 studies was Level I; the authors say most were Level II.
In this series a Grade B statement would normally 'suggest' an action. Here Grades B are association statements, with no action attached (our reading).
slides.notes: This is the slide to memorize. Read the wording closely. Question 2 asks about dose, but the answer is about any use versus none. The authors explain why: most studies compared any preoperative use with none, did not report MME, or used labels such as weak and strong opioids, and the dose association was inconsistent. So the dose question was in effect answered with a yes/no exposure. Our reading, not the authors': there is no Grade B dose threshold to quote from this guideline. Question 1 is about duration, and the cited studies used many cutoffs: more than 120 days, more than 180 days, more than 6 months, 250 days or more. The authors say definitions of chronic use varied and were not standardized.
