Question 3 rests on a single Level II study with no supporting studies, so it is Grade Insufficient, which in the guideline's own nomenclature means insufficient evidence to recommend for or against. That is not the same as evidence that weaning fails. The study counts per question are ours, from the references cited under each question. Refs 5 to 45 give exactly 41 unique studies, matching the stated total, with refs 11 and 17 used under two questions. Our second point: the methods define B as 'suggest' an intervention, but neither Grade B statement recommends doing anything. They grade a prognostic association.

slides.title: Methods: search, selection, grading

rows: Abstracts, all chapters of the series

points: PubMed and Embase, 1946 to September 20, 2019; librarian-run search
Double-blind abstract review; task-force articles held to the same criteria
Modified NASS levels: I (high-quality RCT) to IV (case series)
Level IV not reviewed when Level I to III evidence existed
slides.notes: The arithmetic holds: 78 full texts less 37 rejected gives 41. Note that the 6812 abstracts cover all chapters of the series, not just opioids, so the 845 is the relevant figure for this chapter. Inclusion criteria were set before the search, which reduces selection bias. The level of a study was assigned from its design and then downgraded for poor execution, so a randomized design was only a potential Level I. Grades are then linked to levels; the linking table is Supplemental Content 4, which we did not see. Three things to notice. First, these are prognostic questions, so Level II here largely means observational cohorts, many built on insurance claims (Humana, Optum, PearlDiver), state prescription monitoring data or workers' compensation records. Second, the decision to skip Level IV when better evidence existed is sensible, but it means the evidence base was filtered by design before it was graded. Third, the search ended September 2019 and the paper appeared in 2021, so any newer study, including any trial of preoperative tapering, is outside it. The methods heading reads 'Rating Quality of Diagnostic Evidence', although the questions are prognostic and therapeutic. The authors promise to confirm currency within 5 years of publication. The funding came only from the CNS and the AANS/CNS spine section, with no commercial funding; individual author industry disclosures are listed.

slides.title: Evidence: any use and duration
slides.lead: Odds of prolonged postoperative opioid use, as the guideline reports them.
points: Also linked with longer stay, complications, costs, ED visits, spinal injections, reoperation and lower return to work
Exception: Ahn (23) found no persistent difference at 4-6 or 8-12 wk. Kelly (22) found no effect of opioid strength, a dose question the authors already call inconsistent
slides.notes: The direction is consistent. In nearly every study, opioid users before surgery are more likely to be using opioids after it. But look at what each row measures. The exposure definitions differ (any use, a fill in the last 30 days, a prescription in the last 3 months, 250 days or more), and so do the outcome definitions (more than 90 days, 120 days or 10 fills, 365 days). These are not one effect estimated six times. Several are claims databases, which record fills, not pills taken. Our arithmetic check: on the log scale Harris, Reid, Kalakoti and the Deyo dose estimate are symmetric, as they should be. Deyo's 10.8 (8.2 to 13.2) is not: the upper arm is shorter than the lower, the reverse of a true odds ratio interval, so one number may be misprinted. Connolly's OR of 220 (149 to 326) is log-symmetric but implausibly large for an exposure that many patients share. Our guess, not verifiable without the source, is a decimal shift: either 22.0 (14.9 to 32.6) or 2.20 (1.49 to 3.26), both equally log-symmetric. Given Deyo 10.8 for long-term use and Harris 5.7 for any use, 22.0 is at least as plausible. Do not quote 220. Residual confounding is the central problem, and it is our point, not the authors': patients on opioids for months before surgery differ in pain severity, depression, disability and insurance. Several studies reported independent predictors, which implies multivariable adjustment, but adjustment in observational data cannot remove what was not measured, so the opioid effect may not be cleanly separated. Not every result points the same way. Ahn found no persistent difference in postoperative use, only higher inpatient use. Elsamadicy, in deformity surgery, found larger pain reduction to discharge and longer first walks in users, but users also had higher first postoperative pain scores. Mesfin found greater SRS pain improvement in users at 24 months, with similar ODI change, but users started with worse baseline ODI and SRS scores. In both, the larger improvement came from a worse starting point, which fits regression to the mean or ceiling effects (our reading), so these are weak evidence against the headline. The authors still call the literature consistent; on balance the association is real but the outcomes are heterogeneous.

slides.title: Dose and weaning: the thin part
points: Dose: Deyo (20), mean daily dose above 39 MME, OR 15.47 (8.53-28.06) for long-term use after lumbar fusion
Dose: Hills (38), above 30 MME linked with chronic postoperative use
Dose: Wick (39), odds of reaching MCID fell as dose rose; the printed range is garbled
The authors call the dose association inconsistent
Weaning: one claims study, Jain (17), in 1-2 level posterior lumbar fusion
Patients with a prescription-free 'drug holiday' before surgery had ED-visit, readmission and wound risks similar to opioid-naive patients and lower than those with more than 6 months of use
slides.notes: This is where the guideline is honest about its limits, and where people over-read it. Dose first. Three studies give thresholds (39 MME, 30 MME, and for Wick about 48 mg per day as we read it), but they used different outcomes and populations, and other studies used weak versus strong opioid labels. Weak meant codeine, propoxyphene and hydrocodone; strong meant oxycodone, morphine and meperidine. The authors note that for Anderson (21) the comparison group was presumably no opioid use, but this was not stated. The Wick sentence reads that odds of MCID fell as dose increased 'from 47.8 to 90 mg per day (95% CI 29.0-60.0 mg/day)'. A CI that excludes 90 cannot belong to that range. Our reading is that 47.8 mg was the threshold with CI 29 to 60, but the text does not say so. Now weaning. The single study is not a weaning trial. It is an observational claims study (Humana). The paper says patients were 'taken off opioids' for a prescription-free drug holiday, but does not say how the holiday came about, whether self-chosen or clinician-directed. Those patients were compared with naive patients and long-term users, and only adverse events (ED visits, readmissions, wound dehiscence and infection) were reported, not postoperative opioid use or patient-reported outcomes. The gap is printed as '3- to 489-mo', which is about 40 years at the top end, so the unit is probably wrong. The paper gives no event rates or effect sizes for this comparison. Our inference: the holiday was likely self-selected, and patients who stop on their own may have less pain or better coping, so this study cannot tell you whether a mandated taper helps. The authors list weaning and an opioid-free period as future research, with dose and tramadol (only 1 study). So the correct statement is not that weaning fails. It is that it has not been tested in a trial: one observational study, pointing in its favor, graded Insufficient.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: Holds: prespecified criteria, librarian search of two databases
Holds: double-blind abstract review, explicit levels and grades
Holds: limits stated plainly, dose and weaning not overcalled
Weakens: prognostic, observational data (many claims databases), so residual confounding is likely (our reading)
Weakens: no pooling; definitions of chronic use vary
Weakens: dose question answered with any versus none
Weakens: weaning rests on one observational study, likely self-selected (our inference)
Weakens: several numbers look misprinted
slides.notes: Be fair: within its method this is a careful chapter, and its conclusions are restrained. The authors themselves say definitions of pre- and postoperative use and outcome differed between studies, and that data for weaning are limited. The rest is our reading. No meta-analysis was done, so there is no pooled estimate to quote, and the 'consistent' conclusion is a vote count across varied definitions. A few reported results run against the headline, as the evidence slide showed, though the Elsamadicy and Mesfin findings started from worse baselines in users. The grading treats association as the recommendation, so a Grade B here tells you the association is reasonably established, not that any action is supported. Internal problems we found. The text says 'five other Level III studies', but names four (Armaghani 36, Dunn 37, Hills 38, Wick 39). Jain (12) defines chronic longer-term use as use '1 yr or less after surgery', which reads backwards. Rosenthal (18) compares patients with prescriptions at 3 and 6 months against patients with prescriptions at 3 months, which is garbled. Connolly's OR 220 and the drug-holiday range of 3 to 489 months look like unit or decimal errors. Hockley (14) compares minimally invasive with open TLIF, which is not a preoperative opioid exposure, yet it sits under question 1. Kanaan (40) is listed among studies agreeing on long-term opioid use but is described only as reporting leg pain at 2 weeks. Ref 28 is spelled Amraghani in the text and Armaghani in the reference list. Some cited studies have titles on other topics, such as diabetes (36) or donor-site pain (26). Opioid findings may have been secondary results; we could not check. Elsamadicy's walking distances (103.8 plus or minus 144.4 versus 46.4 plus or minus 84.0 feet) have SDs larger than the means, so the data are skewed. A mean comparison is fragile there. The disclosure table has no entry for coauthor Basma Mohamed.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "Patients on opioids before elective degenerative spine surgery, especially for months, are more likely to stay on them and do worse afterward. That is Grade B, from observational data. Whether a preoperative wean changes that has not been tested in a trial: one observational study, Grade Insufficient."

rows: Use and duration predict risk; weaning unproven
HbA1c above 7.5% associated with infection or reoperation; BMI evidence conflicting

points: O06 numbers come from its library record, not from full-text review here.
No Grade B dose cutoff exists; do not quote OR 220 unchecked.
slides.notes: Expect four follow-up questions. First: should I require a taper before I operate? This guideline cannot tell you to, and it cannot tell you not to. It found one observational study and graded the question Insufficient. A taper may be reasonable on other grounds, but this paper does not show it improves outcomes. Second: is there a safe MME threshold? No Grade B dose threshold exists here. Individual studies reported 30 and 39 MME, and the authors call the dose evidence inconsistent. Third: why does preoperative use predict worse outcomes? The paper does not test mechanism. Our view is that much of the signal may be confounding by pain severity, depression, disability and insurance status, which travel with long-term opioid use, so it is best used for counseling and planning, not as an exclusion rule. Fourth: does it still apply? The search ended in September 2019, and the authors planned a currency check within 5 years of publication. Newer studies are outside this review. Pair it with the diabetes, smoking and BMI chapter (O06), which, per its library record, covers 64 studies and cautions that the association is not a universal cancellation rule. Our parallel: in both chapters a risk association is not proof that changing the exposure changes the outcome. Close with the core distinction: predicting risk is not the same as reversing it.

decks.not_reviewed: Supplemental Digital Content 1-6 (search strategies, inclusion criteria, evidence grading criteria, grade-linking rules, PRISMA flowchart and the evidence table), the full online guideline at cns.org, and the 17 underlying studies. The deck relies on the guideline's own summaries of those studies.

slides.title: CNS guideline: preoperative osteoporosis
slides.lead: Should we test bone before instrumentation, and does treating it first help?
points: Journal club: bone health before spine surgery
Dimar J, et al. Neurosurgery 2021;89(Suppl):S19-S25

Bottom line: Grade B to assess suspected osteoporosis (DEXA, CT Hounsfield units or vitamin D3) and counsel about risk. Grade B to consider teriparatide. Insufficient evidence for bisphosphonates alone.
No Level I study supports any recommendation.
slides.notes: This is one chapter of the Congress of Neurological Surgeons perioperative spine guideline series, endorsed by the AANS and CNS. It asks two questions. First, which preoperative tests predict osteoporosis-related adverse events after spine surgery? Second, does preoperative treatment of low bone mineral density reduce those events? The authors frame the problem as undertreatment. Paraphrased: many spine surgeons poorly understand bone physiology and are reluctant to be the primary treating doctor or to consult an endocrinologist, and cost-effective interventions are limited. The abstract adds a lack of standardized treatment algorithms. They cite a vertebral fracture mortality of 22.4%, 32.7% and 49.4% at 1, 2 and 4 years to set the stakes. What was reviewed: the full 7-page published article, read end to end. The article has no figures or numbered tables. The evidence table and the PRISMA flowchart are in Supplemental Digital Content 5 and 6, which were not reviewed, so every study number in this deck is the guideline's own summary, not checked against the original studies. Set expectations early: a Grade B here rests on retrospective cohorts and small comparisons, none described as randomized. The literature search ended September 20, 2019.

slides.title: The recommendations
slides.lead: Two Grade B statements and one Insufficient.

rows: DEXA T-score < -2.5, CT HU < 97.9 or vitamin D3 < 20 ng/mL predicts higher adverse-event risk. Use one test in suspected osteoporosis and counsel confirmed cases.
Consider preoperative teriparatide in osteoporosis before instrumentation, to reduce screw loosening and delayed or lower fusion.

points: The paper's own wording rules: A is recommended, B suggests, C is an option.
The text says assessment should be performed. That is stronger than suggest.
slides.notes: This is the slide to memorize. Read the wording carefully. The Methods say a Grade B recommendation suggests a test or intervention. The first recommendation then says assessment should be performed, and the second says clinicians should consider teriparatide. Our reading: the second sentence ('should be performed') is phrased more strongly than its grade allows, so quote it as a suggestion. Who it applies to is also loose. Suspected osteoporosis is never defined, and the paper gives no age, sex or risk-factor trigger for testing. The three tests are offered as alternatives. The recommendation says 'or' and the abstract says 'and'. Notice also that vitamin D3 is listed as a marker that 'is associated with poor bone mineral density', yet the only vitamin D study summarized measured fusion, not bone density. The adverse events in view are nonunion and delayed fusion, screw loosening, cage subsidence, proximal junctional kyphosis (PJK) and proximal junctional failure (PJF). The teriparatide recommendation names screw loosening and delayed or lower fusion as the target. It does not claim fewer reoperations or better patient-reported outcomes, and the abstract Results say only that it may improve select patient outcomes, although the abstract Conclusion drops the hedge: optimization with select treatments 'improves certain patient outcomes'. The bisphosphonate statement is Insufficient for bisphosphonates alone. The Conclusions call that evidence conflicting. Denosumab appears only in the Future Research list and the keywords, where it is misspelled Denosamab.

slides.title: Selection and evidence base
slides.lead: 17 studies of 281 screened for this question.
points: PubMed and Embase, 1946 to September 20, 2019
6812 abstracts across the whole series, 5689 after duplicates
281 abstracts for this chapter, data collected on 78, 17 selected
Modified NASS method: levels I to IV, grades A, B, C, Insufficient
No Level I study for either question
slides.notes: The arithmetic holds: 11 plus 6 is 17, and the level counts add up within each question (4 plus 7 is 11; 3 plus 2 plus 1 is 6). Two task force members screened abstracts, and the whole task force graded the selected articles. The text calls the screening double-blind but does not say what that means. The 281 figure is called abstracts in one sentence and studies in another. There is no description here of why 61 of the 78 data-collected papers were dropped. That sits in the supplements we did not read. Levels were assigned by design and then downgraded for flaws in execution, per the Methods. Several studies called Level II are described as retrospective. The rules for that sit in Supplement 3 and 4, which we did not read, so do not call it an error. But keep it in mind when someone says Grade B: here it rests on Level II and III studies. The Methods heading calls the Q1 evidence diagnostic; we would class the question as prognostic (our classification). The Q2 question is therapeutic, but none of its six studies is described as randomized. One last point on currency. The task force committed to confirming within 5 years of publication that the content still reflects practice. Whether that has happened is outside this paper. Randomized teriparatide data published after the search date are in our library, and slide 7 covers them.

slides.title: Testing: what predicted trouble
slides.lead: Low bone density tracked with mechanical failure, but the thresholds vary by study.

rows: 147 vs 208 HU, osteoporotic vs not; more loosening
Osteoporosis in 20.4% with PJK vs 9.8% without, P = .016
No clear link to outcomes or sacral fracture

points: No study summarized in the text gives the 97.9 HU cutoff.
slides.notes: Notice the thresholds. The recommendation uses T < -2.5, but Yagi 2018 split at -1.5 and Oh found severe subsidence below -3.0. The 97.9 HU number is in the recommendation but in none of the study summaries. Sakai measured HU inside the screw path, not vertebral body HU, and reports means of 147 and 208. So 97.9 must come from a source we did not read, likely the evidence table. Treat it as unsourced. Read the effect sizes as associations. Cho 2018 compared only the 55 nonosteoporotic and 31 osteoporotic PLIF patients, which is the 86 PLIF patients out of the 268 described. The guideline text attributes subsidence and loosening to low body mass index, which looks like a slip for low bone mineral density. The 32.3% and 12.7% loosening figures fit 10 of 31 and 7 of 55. The subsidence figures (65.4% fits 17 of 26, 17.6% fits 3 of 17 or 6 of 34) fit neither 31 nor 55, and the reference title says one-level PLIF, so per-level counting would not explain them. Their denominators are unexplained. Fusion with vs without loosening (71.4% vs 93.9%) does not fit the 17 and 69 patients either. 10 of 31 vs 7 of 55 gives P = .029 exactly (our calculation), so 'P < .029' is probably P = .029. Clinical outcomes did not differ. Yagi 2018: OR 6.4 is printed with P < .01, but our back-calculation from its CI gives P about .03. Kim 2013 gives osteoporosis prevalence by PJK status, not PJK risk by bone status. Ravindra: unadjusted nonunion was 38% vs 20% (P = .063, not significant); only the adjusted model reached significance. Median time to fusion was 12, 8.6 and 6 months across deficient, insufficient and adequate groups. Contrary evidence counts too. Yagi 2011 found no link between T-score and fusion or complications. Salzmann found no link between bone density and sacral fracture. Kim 2012 and Oh found only weak associations, and Oh's subsidence did not worsen clinical outcomes.

slides.title: Treatment: the teriparatide evidence
slides.lead: Small comparisons, none described as randomized, mostly against a bisphosphonate.

rows: Fusion 82% at 8 mo vs 68% at 10 mo; clinical outcomes similar
Cyclic teriparatide plus bisphosphonate 23 vs bisphosphonate 24
Fusion 77.8% vs 53.6% at 6 mo; 92.6% vs 96.4% at 2 yr; loosening 11.1% vs 10.7%
Calcium, vitamin D, bisphosphonate 31 vs none
Better BMD, alignment, disc height, arm pain
Slower fusion at 6 mo, not at 2 yr; fusion > 80%

points: None of the teriparatide summaries says the drug started before surgery. Cho 2017 treated for 1 year after surgery. Kang's reference title calls its patients long-term bisphosphonate users, which implies use before surgery (our inference).
slides.notes: The first three rows are the Level II basis for Grade B. Ohtori 2012 was a prospective sequential cohort, not randomized: the first 28 women got risedronate, the next 29 teriparatide. Its headline compares 82% at 8 months with 68% at 10 months, two time points, so it mixes rate with speed. Ohtori 2013 is the only teriparatide study with an untreated control (Wang, Kang and Kim also had untreated arms). Its design is not stated. Its loosening rates (7%, 13%, 15%) cannot be counts out of 20 or 22, so they are probably per screw (our inference). Our reading: Cho 2017 cuts against the recommendation more than it supports it, though the guideline counts it as Level II support for higher 6-month fusion and faster union. Its authors concluded there was no significant benefit in fusion rate or clinical outcome, only faster union and better BMD recovery. Loosening and subsidence were equal. Fusion at 2 years was numerically higher with bisphosphonate alone. The teriparatide arm also got a bisphosphonate in alternating 3-month cycles. Its percentages fit 27 and 28 (for example 21 of 27 and 15 of 28), not 23 and 24 patients, so probably per level (our inference). On those counts the 6-month gap called significant gives P about .06 by chi-square or .09 by Fisher (our calculation). The CT P values (.374, .648, .626) do not fit 3 of 27 vs 3 of 28 or 4 of 27 vs 4 of 28, which give P near 1. The T-score gain (P = .013) gives about .04 to .06 on our recalculation. Bridging bone: 88.9% is exactly 24 of 27, the teriparatide denominator, but is assigned to the bisphosphonate group; 87.5% is 21 of 24 but is assigned to the teriparatide group. The arm labels may be swapped (our inference). The big gap: the question and recommendation say preoperative, but no teriparatide study is described as starting before surgery, and Cho's protocol ran 1 year postoperatively. The supplements may say more. Outcomes are radiographic surrogates. No study reports fewer reoperations. Clinical outcomes were similar in the teriparatide studies; Wang reported better arm pain with its bisphosphonate regimen. Wang combined three agents, and Kang's groups differed at baseline (T -2.7 vs -2.3, P < .001). The guideline calls Kang retrospective; its reference title says prospective.

slides.title: Gaps and possible errors
points: No Level I study; no Q2 study is described as randomized.
97.9 HU cutoff not traced to any study in the text.
Preoperative timing of teriparatide not shown in the studies described.
Grade B is defined as 'suggest', yet recommendation 1 says 'should be performed'.
Cho 2018 summary says low BMI where low BMD appears meant.
Yagi 2018: OR 6.4 (1.2-32.3) printed with P < .01; CI implies about .03 (our calculation).
Ravindra: 'nondeficient > 20' overlaps the 20-30 insufficient group.
Salzmann: 52.4% (11/21) is the whole cohort, not just obese patients.
Disclosure list includes a teriparatide maker, Eli Lilly; the nature of the tie is not stated.
slides.notes: Be fair first. The process is transparent: a librarian ran the search, criteria were set before searching, two members screened, the task force graded, and the reviewers were blinded to the authors. Funding came only from CNS and the Joint Section, with no outside commercial support. Then the problems. Most are reporting slips, but two matter for practice. First, the HU threshold. 97.9 is precise to one decimal but has no stated source, scanner protocol or outcome in the text. Do not use it as a universal cutoff. Second, timing. The title question is about preoperative treatment, yet the one study whose timing is described reports a 1-year postoperative protocol and does not say whether treatment also started before surgery. Our reading is that the evidence supports teriparatide around surgery, not specifically before it. The smaller errors: Ravindra's three groups are written as < 20, 20-30 and > 20, where > 30 is probably meant. Salzmann's 52.4% obese fracture rate is printed as 11/21, but 21 is the whole cohort. Kim 2014 reports endplate degeneration as 91.3% vs 52.4% in patients with and without nonunion. Those figures fit 21 of 23 and 11 of 21, the drug group sizes, while only 13 patients had nonunion by the fusion rates, so the comparison label may be wrong (our inference). Ohtori 2012's 82% does not fit 29 patients either. Cho 2018's loosening P is printed as P < .029. Puvanesarajah's 44.9% is called more than one-third. The PICO questions are cited to Supplement 5, which the list names as the PRISMA flowchart. The Q1 text says 10 studies used CT or DEXA, but Puvanesarajah is summarized only as an osteoporosis diagnosis. Yagi 2018 calls T > -1.5 'moderate osteoporosis', a contradiction. Misspellings: Denosamab, Puvansearajah, Eli Lily. Disclosures: the first author lists many companies, including Eli Lilly, which makes teriparatide. The paper does not say what each tie is, so state it as listed, not as a conflict.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "Check bone before instrumenting a patient you suspect has osteoporosis, using DEXA, CT Hounsfield units or vitamin D, and counsel them. Consider teriparatide. Both are Grade B, built on cohorts and small studies, none described as randomized. Bisphosphonates alone: insufficient evidence."

rows: Fewer reoperations and symptomatic pseudarthroses in treated osteoporotic vs matched osteopenic patients

points: O07 and Mohanty come from the library's abstract-level records, not this paper. Both postdate this guideline's search.
slides.notes: Expect four follow-up questions. Is 97.9 HU the cutoff to use? Not on this paper's evidence. The number appears in the recommendation, but no study summarized in the text reports it, and the one CT study with numbers measured the screw path, not the vertebral body. Say low HU is a risk marker, and the threshold depends on the source and protocol. Does teriparatide prevent complications? In the teriparatide studies this paper reports faster or earlier fusion, less screw loosening in one study, and similar clinical outcomes. It reports no reoperation outcome. Cho 2017 found equal loosening and similar fusion at 2 years. The later library evidence is stronger on one outcome: in the O07 randomized trial, per its abstract-level record, PJF was 3.4% with teriparatide vs 22.2% with denosumab, but the PJK difference was not significant, and denosumab was an active comparator. Keep PJF and PJK apart. The Mohanty cohort was matched, not randomized, and its comparators differed in bone-density category. Must treatment start before surgery? The guideline says preoperative, but the studies described do not establish that timing, and the one with stated timing describes a 1-year postoperative protocol. How long to treat before surgery is not addressed. Should I start a bisphosphonate? This guideline found insufficient evidence for bisphosphonates alone, with mixed results: delayed early fusion in one study, no effect in another, benefit in a third that gave calcium, vitamin D and a diphosphonate together, so no single agent was isolated. Two closing cautions. Suspected osteoporosis is never defined, so the testing trigger is the surgeon's judgment. And the vitamin D threshold predicted nonunion only in an adjusted model, from one study.

decks.not_reviewed: Supplemental Digital Content 1-6 (search strategy, inclusion criteria, evidence-level and grading criteria, PRISMA flowchart and the evidence table with per-study levels); the full online guideline at cns.org; the 64 source studies themselves. Every number about a source study is as this guideline reports it.

slides.title: CNS guideline: diabetes, BMI, smoking
slides.lead: A systematic review and evidence-based guideline on three preoperative risk factors before spine surgery.
points: Harrop JS, et al. Congress of Neurological Surgeons systematic review and evidence-based guidelines for perioperative spine: preoperative surgical risk assessment. Neurosurgery 2021;89(Suppl 1):S9-S18
Sponsored by the CNS and the Joint Section on Disorders of the Spine and Peripheral Nerves; endorsed by the AANS and CNS
Source read: the full 10-page article, end to end. It is the complete paper, not a critique. The supplements, including the evidence table, were not available.

Bottom line: check HbA1c in diabetics and counsel about infection and reoperation above 7.5% (Grade B). Counsel smokers having fusion about reoperation (Grade B). BMI evidence is conflicting (Insufficient). No study of stopping smoking met the inclusion criteria.
slides.notes: What this is: one chapter of the CNS perioperative spine guideline series. A task force asked three questions, searched the literature to September 20, 2019, graded each study with a modified North American Spine Society method, and linked evidence levels to grades of recommendation. Every recommendation here is about association and counseling. None says that fixing the risk factor lowers the risk, and the authors say so for smoking cessation in plain words. Units warning before you start: the paper prints HbA1c in mg/dL throughout, in the abstract, recommendations, discussion and conclusion. HbA1c is a percentage. Read 7.5 mg/dL as 7.5%. The one exception in the text is the Caputo threshold, printed as 8.0%. The master record blamed the PubMed abstract for the unit error; the full text carries it everywhere. What was reviewed for this deck: the full article PDF, including references, funding and disclosures. Not reviewed: the six supplements. That matters here because the per-study evidence levels live in Supplemental Digital Content 6, so we cannot check which studies were called Level II or III, or why. The disclosure table in the PDF is printed with names and disclosures out of alignment, and one author (Mohamed) has no row, so we could not attribute conflicts reliably. Funding was from the CNS and the Joint Section only, with no outside commercial funding, per the authors.

slides.title: Questions and methods
slides.lead: Three questions, NASS-style levels and grades, 64 studies kept.
points: Q1: in diabetics, which preoperative tests predict reoperation or infection?
Q2: is increased BMI associated with reoperation or infection?
Q3: is smoking associated with reoperation after fusion, and does stopping help?
Search: PubMed and Embase, 1946 to September 20, 2019 (the abstract says PubMed and the Cochrane Library)
Flow: 699 abstracts for this chapter, 192 full texts, 128 rejected, 64 included
Grades: A recommended, B suggest, C option, I insufficient. Level IV skipped when Level I-III existed.
slides.notes: How to read the methods. The initial search covered every chapter in the series: 6812 abstracts, 5689 after duplicates. A double-blind abstract review left 699 for this chapter. Note that the abstract says 699 articles met inclusion criteria, while Results says 699 abstracts were yielded and only 64 were finally included. The flow arithmetic holds: 192 minus 128 is 64. The per-question counts do not. Q2 is said to have 54 articles, but its two parts are 41 on SSI and 16 on reoperation, which is 57. Add Q1 and Q3 and the total is 67, not 64. Some studies are clearly counted under more than one question (Koutsoumbelis in Q1 and Q2; Hofler, Gerling and Puvanesarajah in Q2 and Q3), which may explain the gap, but the paper does not say so. That explanation is ours. There are no Level I studies anywhere in the chapter; everything is Level II or III, mostly retrospective or database work by our reading of the descriptions. The PDF does not say how levels map to grades; that is in Supplemental Digital Content 4, which we did not review. Our inference is that the lack of Level I evidence is why nothing rises above Grade B. Either way, the strongest statements here are Grade B, which the paper's own nomenclature words as suggest, not recommended. Also notice the source mismatch: Methods names PubMed and Embase, the abstract names PubMed and the Cochrane Library. The task force members also added articles from their own files, screened with the same criteria. The guideline promises a check of currency within 5 years of publication; this deck reports only the 2021 version.

slides.title: Recommendations, strength and evidence

rows: Test HbA1c before surgery; counsel about reoperation or infection risk if above 7.5%
Not enough evidence for other preoperative tests, such as preoperative glucose
Conflicting evidence; counsel patients with elevated BMI about possible SSI risk, given studies linking BMI over 30 to SSI, especially lumbar
Counsel active smokers having fusion about increased reoperation risk
No evidence that stopping lowers reoperation; still suggest abstaining before and after fusion

slides.notes: This is the slide to memorize. Two Grade B statements, four Insufficient. Every action word is counsel or test, never cancel, delay or require. Now check the language against the paper's own rules. Methods say Grade B should use the word suggest. Both Grade B statements use should instead: diabetic individuals should have an HbA1c test, and active smokers should be counseled. The BMI statement is Grade Insufficient, yet it says the task force recommends counseling. By the paper's own nomenclature, recommended is Grade A wording, and an opinion without reliable evidence should be framed as in the absence of reliable evidence, it is the task force's opinion. So read the BMI advice as task force opinion, not graded evidence. That reading is ours. The smoking cessation advice is in the same position: no study met criteria, and the counseling is suggested anyway. The Conclusion narrows the HbA1c statement to individuals with diabetes undergoing elective degenerative spine surgery; the recommendation itself says spine surgery. The Conclusion also says care should be directed toward reducing these variables, which goes past the graded statements. For smoking cessation the authors say no study met their criteria; the questions never asked about weight loss or HbA1c lowering, and the chapter reports no such result. One caution: the reference title of Jain et al (ref 12) says bariatric surgery before posterior lumbar fusion was associated with fewer complications and infections, but the chapter reports only its BMI-SSI association. We did not read Jain. The authors list exactly those optimization targets and their timing as future research.

slides.title: Diabetes: where 7.5% comes from
slides.lead: Five Level II studies, but only two derived the 7.5% cutoff, both by Cancienne and colleagues.

rows: Cutoff 7.5; sensitivity 53%, specificity 70%; deep SSI OR 2.9 (1.8-4.9)
No HbA1c link at 8.0%; perioperative glucose over 140 doubled SSI
No HbA1c result given; diabetes and postoperative glucose predicted SSI

slides.notes: The paper says all 5 articles demonstrate the HbA1c relationship. Read the descriptions and that is not quite true. Caputo found no HbA1c correlation, though at a higher 8.0% threshold. Koutsoumbelis, as described here, reports diabetes and postoperative glucose, not HbA1c. Hikata supports HbA1c as a risk factor but used 7.0. The 7.5% number comes from two Cancienne studies from one group. Our reading. How good is 7.5% as a test? Our arithmetic from the printed sensitivity and specificity: likelihood ratio positive about 1.4 for ACDF and 1.8 for lumbar decompression, likelihood ratio negative about 0.79 and 0.67. That is weak discrimination. About half of the infections occurred in patients below the cutoff. This is why 7.5% is a counseling threshold, not a go or no-go line. The adjusted lumbar result, deep SSI OR 2.9 (1.8 to 4.9), is internally consistent; its geometric midpoint is about 2.97. Hikata check, ours: 6 of 36 diabetics had SSI against 10 of 309 nondiabetics, 16.7% vs 3.2%. If all 6 were in the poorly controlled group, 35.3% fits 6 of 17. HbA1c was 7.6 in those with SSI and 6.9 in those without; the paper does not say whether these are means. Hikata's age is printed as a median of 64.3 years, an odd decimal for a median. The ACDF study is described as 3341 patients requiring reoperation, with HbA1c related to reoperation rate, while its reference title is about deep postoperative infection after ACDF. The description looks garbled; we quote it as printed. Preoperative glucose did not predict SSI in Hikata or Koutsoumbelis, but Caputo found perioperative glucose over 140 mg/dL doubled SSI risk (P = .0091). The paper gives no reason for the Insufficient statement on other tests; linking it to the glucose results is our reading.

slides.title: BMI and smoking: what the evidence shows
points: BMI and SSI: the authors say most lumbar studies found a link; negative studies tended to be smaller, anterior or minimally invasive
Largest positive series: NIS 244 170 (morbid obesity 70% more SSI), NSQIP 61 079 (Lieber, BMI over 30), Medicare 48 210, then NSQIP 36 440 (SSI 0.72%)
BMI and reoperation: 12 studies found no link, 4 did, all 4 lumbar
SPORT spondylolisthesis: 4-year reoperation 20% vs 11% with BMI 30 or more (the authors say twice; it is 1.8 times); 8-year data showed no link
Smoking: cervical studies consistent; Lee: smoking raised adjacent segment reoperation risk 1.75 times (1.15-2.67)
Smoking cessation: no study met criteria
slides.notes: BMI and SSI. The authors argue the negative studies were smaller and often anterior or minimally invasive, where infection is rare, so they were underpowered. That is a fair argument but it is the authors' explanation, not a tested one. Positive effect sizes range from OR 1.07 in a pooled international database to RR 9.3 for BMI over 30 in Chin's hospital and outpatient cohort; Ilyas (OR 6.99), Koutsoumbelis (OR 6.76) and Soroceanu (OR 4.88) sit in between. The Shamji National Inpatient Sample study covers 1988 to 2004, an old era. BMI cutoffs vary between studies: 30, 35 and 40. Reoperation. Most studies found no link. One pair is worth noting, ours: the same SPORT degenerative spondylolisthesis population gave a positive result at 4 years (Rihn) and no correlation at 8 years (Gerling). Bohl's 2-year reoperation risk after minimally invasive discectomy was 1.8% nonobese, 12.5% overweight, 9.1% obese, 25.0% morbidly obese, not a smooth gradient, from 23 events. Smoking. The question is about fusion, but the evidence mixes outcomes: pseudarthrosis (Hofler, state inpatient databases), adjacent segment reoperation (two Lee studies, same authors), reoperation for SSI (Macki, OR 5.75), and laminectomy without fusion (Bydon, OR 11.3 single level). Macki's rhBMP-2 study found the smoking effect also extended to the nonfusion population. Gerling found no link at 8 years, and De la Garza Ramos found a higher but not significant rate in deformity patients. Grade B for smoking rests on this mix. The counseling advice is reasonable; the precise size of the risk is not settled by this chapter. That last judgment is ours. Comparison within the library, from the master records: the sister CNS chapters on preoperative opioids (O04, 41 studies, none Level I, Grade B for association) and osteoporosis (O05, 17 studies, Grade B for assessment and teriparatide) also make Grade B statements. Whether either has anything graded higher, the records do not say.

slides.title: Gaps and errors
points: HbA1c printed in mg/dL throughout; it is a percentage
Search sources differ: Embase in Methods, Cochrane in the abstract
Question counts add to 67, not 64; BMI subcounts add to 57, not 54
Lumbar BMI and SSI: 42 articles stated, but 31 positive plus 10 negative is 41, and the levels for the 10 add to 11
BMI and SSI overall: Results gives 41 (30 Level II), but lumbar alone claims 42 (31 Level II) and cervical adds 5
Boston 2009 is cited both as positive (OR 2.81) and as negative
Smoking: 8 studies stated, 10 cited in the discussion, one of them laminectomy
Two implausible intervals (Klemencsics relative risk, Pahys odds ratio); Jalai printed backward
Recommendation wording breaks the paper's own grade language
slides.notes: The bottom line is usable, but the evidence narrative is not reliably counted. What fails our checks. Units: mg/dL for HbA1c everywhere except the Caputo threshold. Counts: per-question totals of 5, 54 and 8 sum to 67 against 64 included; Q2's parts are 41 plus 16, which is 57 against 54. Results gives 41 BMI-SSI articles (30 Level II, 11 Level III), yet the lumbar section alone announces 42, then 31 positive (25 Level II, 6 Level III) and 10 negative (6 Level II, 5 Level III): 31 plus 10 is 41, 6 plus 5 is 11, and 25 plus 6 Level II is already 31 before the 5 cervical Level II studies. Tallying the studies named region by region we found 27 positive and 11 negative, with Boston on both sides. Smoking: 8 studies stated, 6 positive, but 10 discussed, including Pahys with no smoking result. Intervals, our arithmetic: Klemencsics RR 6.216 (1.832 to 9.338) has a log midpoint near 4.1, and that interval implies P near .0006, not the printed .005, so something is misprinted. Pahys OR 4.1 (1.5 to 7.7) has a midpoint near 3.4. Jalai is printed backward; reordered, its midpoint is 1.162, as printed. Ilyas OR 6.99 (2.65 to 22.03) has a midpoint of 7.64, mildly off but plausible for a small-count interval. Koutsoumbelis, De la Garza-Ramos, Maragakis, Boston, Lee and Gaudelli are symmetric. Our Fisher P values match: Hikata 6/36 vs 10/309 about .003; Boston 32/47 vs 72/167 gives OR 2.81, P about .003. Lieber 1110 of 61 079 is 1.82%, printed 1.84%. Rihn's twice is 20% vs 11%, 1.8 times. Labels: Hofler measured pseudarthrosis but is used for reoperation; Leven, a subanalysis of surgically treated SPORT disc herniation patients, is loosely called a randomized discectomy trial (Gerling gets the same wording); Grade and Class are used where Level is meant. Wording: Grade B uses should; the Insufficient BMI statement uses recommends. None of this reverses a recommendation, but do not quote these counts as exact.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "In diabetics, check HbA1c and counsel that above 7.5% the risk of infection and reoperation is higher. Counsel smokers having fusion about reoperation. BMI evidence is conflicting. None of this shows that optimizing the factor lowers the risk."
points: Evidence: Level II and III only, literature to September 2019
Do not stretch it: 7.5% is a weak test, not a cancellation rule
slides.notes: Spoken summary, about 30 seconds: This 2021 CNS guideline reviewed 64 Level II and III studies on diabetes, BMI and smoking. It gives two Grade B statements: test HbA1c in diabetics and counsel about higher infection and reoperation risk above 7.5%, and counsel smokers having fusion about higher reoperation risk. BMI evidence is conflicting and graded Insufficient, though the task force recommends counseling patients with elevated BMI about the possible risk, as opinion rather than graded evidence. No study of smoking cessation met the criteria, and the chapter reports no test of weight loss or HbA1c lowering. Expect these follow-up questions. Should I cancel surgery for an HbA1c of 8%? The guideline does not say so. It says test and counsel. The cutoff came from two studies by one group, and our arithmetic gives likelihood ratios under 2, so it separates risk poorly. Where did 7.5 come from? An inflection point on ROC analysis in the Cancienne ACDF and lumbar decompression studies, sensitivity 46 to 53%, specificity 68 to 70%. Is the unit mg/dL? No; the paper misprints it, HbA1c is a percentage. Does BMI raise infection risk? Most lumbar studies say yes, especially above 30, but the evidence was judged conflicting, and the reoperation evidence mostly found no link. Does stopping smoking help? Unknown from this guideline: no qualifying study. Counseling to stop is suggested at Grade Insufficient. Is the smoking evidence specific to fusion? Partly. It mixes pseudarthrosis, adjacent segment disease, SSI reoperation and one laminectomy series. Why only Grade B? There are no Level I studies. The rules linking levels to grades are in a supplement we did not read, so tying the two is our inference.

decks.not_reviewed: Figures 1 to 4 (omitted from the reformatted PMC copy that was read: study design, flow diagram, PJK/PJF bar chart, PRO curves). ClinicalTrials.gov record NCT04241211. Funding and conflict statements, which were not in this copy. No supplement is cited.

slides.title: Park 2025: Perioperative teriparatide versus denosumab for PJK and PJF
slides.lead: Bottom line: in 56 analyzed osteoporotic women, teriparatide had fewer PJF revisions (1 of 29 versus 6 of 27). PJK was not significantly different, and the PJF result rests on 7 events.
points: Journal club: osteoporosis and adult deformity surgery
Park JH, Kwon O, Choi JH, Yeom JS, Park SM, Kim CH, Kim HJ. Osteoporos Int 2025;36(5):833-843
Source note: read in full from a reformatted PMC text with all four figures omitted. Tables were read; figures were not.
slides.notes: This is a single-center randomized superiority trial of an anabolic drug against an antiresorptive drug, not against no treatment. That framing matters: the authors chose denosumab as the active control on ethical grounds, so the trial asks whether teriparatide beats another good osteoporosis drug, not whether treating osteoporosis helps. 64 postmenopausal women were randomized, 32 per arm, and 56 were analyzed after 8 canceled their surgery. Follow-up was 1 year. What was reviewed: the full article text in a reformatted PMC copy whose header says images are omitted. So Figure 1 (study design), Figure 2 (flow diagram), Figure 3 (PJK and PJF bars with 95% CIs) and Figure 4 (PRO curves) were not seen. Arm-level dropouts and event counts in this deck are back-calculated by us from the printed percentages and Ns; the paper itself prints percentages, not counts. Also not reviewed: the ClinicalTrials.gov record NCT04241211, so we cannot check the registered primary outcome or sample size against the paper. No supplement is cited in the text. Listen for one theme throughout: the headline result is 1 PJF event against 6, and how significant that is depends on which test you use.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: Osteoporosis is a major risk factor for PJK. Does an anabolic agent around surgery protect the junction better than an antiresorptive?
points: Background from the authors: PJK incidence in the literature runs 17 to 39%, often within the first 2 to 3 months.
About one third of ASD surgery patients have osteoporosis, and two thirds of them go untreated (as cited by the authors).
Retrospective work suggested teriparatide reduces PJK, but high-level evidence was lacking.

rows: Postmenopausal women 50-85, T-score below -2.5, untreated, symptomatic degenerative thoracolumbar deformity
Teriparatide 20 mcg daily, 3 months before to 3 months after surgery
Denosumab 60 mg at 3 months before and 3 months after surgery, plus calcium and vitamin D
PJK or PJF within 1 year; PROs and hip BMD

slides.notes: Set up the biology the authors lean on. Teriparatide is PTH 1-34, an anabolic agent; denosumab is an antiresorptive. The authors' argument is that teriparatide improves fusion and reduces screw loosening and vertebral fracture in lumbar fusion, so it may also protect the proximal junction. The 6-month course was a compromise: they cite an anabolic window that peaks around 6 months, most PJK appearing within 3 months, and poor compliance with daily injections over a year. After the study drug, both arms switched to a bisphosphonate until final follow-up. The authors give two reasons: to mitigate the denosumab rebound, and in the teriparatide arm to minimize problems on stopping teriparatide. So the real comparison is teriparatide then bisphosphonate against denosumab then bisphosphonate. One point to notice, ours: denosumab is dosed every 6 months, so the injection at 3 months after surgery should carry its effect to about 9 months, while the paper describes both drugs as given for 6 months and then stopped. The paper does not say when the bisphosphonate started in the denosumab arm. Only the denosumab arm was told to take calcium 1000 mg and vitamin D 400 IU or more; the paper does not say whether the teriparatide arm took supplements. This is women only. The authors themselves say the results are hard to generalize, and osteopenic patients and men are untested. The library's CNS osteoporosis guideline (O05, abstract-level record) already supports considering teriparatide before instrumentation, Grade B, so this trial is asking a narrower question: which drug.

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: 207 screened, 64 randomized, 56 analyzed. One surgeon, UIV at T10 in every case, no cement or ligament augmentation.
points: Allocation: random number table, concealed, made by a research assistant not involved in the study.

Blinding: the paper calls it single-blind, but patients and investigators knew the drug. Only the radiographic assessor (also the analyst) and the PRO administrator were blinded: in effect open label with blinded assessment (ours).
Imaging: EOS for alignment, PJK and PJF; routine CT at 1 year for screw loosening and endplate fracture.
Power: 32 per group for PJK 39% versus 9.3%, alpha 0.05, power 0.80, 5% loss.
slides.notes: Flow arithmetic checks: 207 screened, 3 declined, 140 ineligible, 64 randomized. The paper says 8 were excluded from mITT for canceled surgery and gives Ns of 29 and 27, so 3 and 5 by arm. It says 2 more were excluded from per protocol for adverse events, and the per-protocol PJK of 18.5% and PJF of 3.7% only work with a denominator of 27 in the teriparatide arm (5 of 27, 1 of 27) while the denosumab rates stay at 27. So both per-protocol exclusions were in the teriparatide arm. That is our inference, consistent with Table 4, where the only drug adverse events were 1 vomiting and 1 diarrhea on teriparatide. The modified ITT excluded everyone whose surgery was canceled. The drug started 3 months before surgery, but the paper does not say when the 8 cancellations happened, whether those patients had started the drug, or the reasons by arm. The authors name this higher-than-anticipated dropout as their first limitation; our arithmetic: 8 of 64 (12.5%) against the 5% loss in the power calculation. Definitions. PJK: proximal junctional angle, UIV to UIV+2, of 10 degrees or more and at least 10 degrees above preoperative. PJF: need for revision surgery for UIV or UIV+1 fracture, UIV/UIV+1 subluxation, fixation failure, or neurological deficit. So PJF is a surgeon's decision to reoperate. The assessor was blinded, but the paper says investigators knew the drug and does not say who decided on revision. The blinded radiographic assessor and the blinded data analyst are the same person, a co-author. Baseline: Table 1 and 2 show similar groups, mean age about 71, SVA about 156 mm, PI-LL about 54 degrees, corrected to about 46 mm and 10 degrees. Our recomputed baseline P values mostly match, including hip BMD (0.367 vs 0.368). Two drift: SRS-22r mental health gives about 0.57 (printed 0.622), and DEXA T-score -3.0 vs -2.9, SD 0.4, gives about 0.35 (printed 0.190, reachable only near the rounding limits). Sample size checks: our calculation for 39% versus 9.3% gives about 31 to 33 per group. The trial was powered on PJK, not PJF.

slides.title: Primary outcome: PJK and PJF at 1 year
slides.lead: PJF was lower with teriparatide; PJK was not significantly different. Our counts are back-calculated from the printed percentages.
points: Our Fisher exact P: PJF mITT 0.048, PJF per protocol 0.10, PJK mITT 0.22.
Our risk difference for PJF: 18.8 points, Newcombe 95% CI about 0.8 to 37.5.
slides.see: Figure 3 plots PJK and PJF incidence with 95% CI error bars for mITT and per protocol. It was not seen in this copy.
slides.notes: Read the table in counts, not percentages. PJF is 1 event against 6, 7 events in total. The paper's Methods say the primary outcome was compared with the chi-squared test. We reproduce the printed P values exactly with an uncorrected Pearson chi-square: 0.034 and 0.043 for PJF, 0.165 and 0.214 for PJK. With 7 events, expected cell counts are about 3.5, below the usual threshold of 5 for chi-square. Fisher's exact test gives 0.048 for mITT PJF (barely significant) and 0.10 for per-protocol PJF (not significant). The Methods name Fisher's test for categorical variables, but the Table 1 category P values (0.700, 0.240, 0.310) also match only uncorrected chi-square, not Fisher (1.000, 0.279, 0.382), so uncorrected chi-square appears to have been used throughout (ours). The continuity-corrected chi-square gives 0.086. So the significance of the headline finding depends on the test. That reading is ours. Second, the paper names PJK or PJF as the primary outcome, analyzes them as two separate tests, and reports no multiplicity correction. The trial was powered on PJK, expecting 39% against 9.3%. The observed rates were 33.3% and 17.2%, a 16-point gap the trial had about 29% power to detect (our estimate). So 'teriparatide did not reduce PJK', as the Discussion puts it, overstates a null result in an underpowered trial. A halving of PJK is fully compatible with these data. Third, the PJF CI is wide: our Newcombe interval for the risk difference runs from roughly 1 to 37 points. The authors' mechanism: even if PJK occurs, teriparatide may prevent further collapse and metal failure. That is a hypothesis, not tested here; the paper does not report whether PJF cases were also PJK cases, or which PJF criterion each met. Notice also that the Discussion says no fractures occurred in either group, yet fracture at UIV or UIV+1 is one of the PJF criteria and the authors speak of preventing collapse. The paper never says which PJF criterion each revision met (6 denosumab revisions is our back-calculation). The no-fractures sentence sits in a paragraph on stopping the drugs, so it may mean osteoporotic fractures only.

slides.title: Secondary outcomes and harms
slides.lead: Back pain and EQ-5D change favored teriparatide. ODI, SRS-22r and hip BMD change did not differ.
points: Drug adverse events: teriparatide 1 vomiting, 1 diarrhea; denosumab none.
Surgical complications: teriparatide 3 of 29 (10.3%), denosumab 5 of 27 (18.5%). No major life-threatening events.
Complications included surgical site infection 0 versus 1, screw pull-out 1 versus 1, neurological deterioration 2 versus 3.
slides.see: Figure 4 plots VAS, ODI and EQ-5D at baseline, 3, 6 and 12 months with 95% CIs. It was not seen in this copy.
slides.notes: Methods say 1-year values were compared; Results and Table 3 compare change from baseline. We recomputed: VAS change P about 0.007 and EQ-5D change P about 0.02 to 0.024, close to the printed 0.008 and 0.026. ODI, SRS and VAS also match closely. But note EQ-5D at 1 year: 0.53 versus 0.33, our t-test P about 0.09. The teriparatide arm started lower (0.20 versus 0.29), so the significant change partly reflects baseline. Back pain is robust in both forms: 4.0 versus 5.9 at 1 year, our P about 0.007. On the same 1-year basis, SRS-22r pain (3.72 versus 2.77) gives P about 0.009, so 'SRS-22r did not differ' holds only for change scores. Count the tests. VAS, ODI, EQ-5D, four SRS domains plus total, hip BMD and hip DEXA T-score: about ten secondary outcomes, two significant, none corrected. The 1-year hip T-score is a declared outcome and the Discussion says it did not differ, but no T-score data are reported. ODI, the disability measure surgeons use most, did not differ. The authors' explanation for the back-pain benefit is teriparatide's known analgesic effect in osteoporosis, citing meta-analyses, with mechanism unclear in their own words. Hip BMD: the authors explain the null result by the short drug course and by the spine being instrumented, so spine BMD could not be measured. Hip BMD is not the junction, so it says little about the UIV. Table 3's hip BMD numbers are not usable anyway (see appraisal). Harms: the drug adverse events are small, but Table 4 prints 4.17% for 1 patient and 8.33% for 2, which is a denominator of 24, not 29. Surgical complications were small numbers and no test is reported. Whether any complication led to the PJF revisions is not stated.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: A real randomized trial with an honest active control, but the key result is fragile and several tables carry errors.
points: Holds up: randomized, concealed allocation, blinded radiographic assessment. PRO forms were handed out blind, but the patients filling them in knew their drug.
Holds up: one surgeon, fixed UIV at T10, no augmentation, so surgical technique is uniform.
Holds up: active control, so the comparison is drug against drug.
Weakens it: 7 PJF events; P=0.034 is uncorrected chi-square, Fisher 0.048, per-protocol Fisher 0.10 (ours).
Weakens it: PJF requires a revision decision, investigators knew the drug, and the paper does not say who decided (ours).
Weakens it: 12.5% excluded before analysis, against 5% planned; the decision not to add patients came after seeing the result.
Weakens it: two primary tests and about ten secondary outcomes, none corrected.
Weakens it: 1 year only; the authors say failures often appear in year 2 or 3.
slides.notes: Be fair: randomized trials in ASD are rare, and this one is clean on surgery. Same surgeon, same UIV, no cement, and the arms were balanced on alignment. The limits the authors themselves name: the higher-than-planned dropout from canceled surgeries, women only, the 6-month drug course shorter than standard, denosumab rebound risk (mitigated with bisphosphonates), and 1-year follow-up. Note one authors' statement carefully: after the planned sample finished follow-up, they analyzed the data, found the PJF difference, and decided not to recruit more. Our reading: a stopping decision made after seeing the result is a risk of bias, especially with dropouts above plan. Table errors we found: Table 2's postoperative TK row repeats the preoperative row exactly (12.4 plus or minus 14.2 versus 14.3 plus or minus 14.4) but carries a different P, 0.931 instead of 0.638. Our t-test on those numbers gives 0.62, so the postoperative values are a copy error. Hip BMD SDs are implausible: baseline teriparatide 0.651 plus or minus 0.462 against 0.569 plus or minus 0.080, and 1-year teriparatide 0.742 plus or minus 0.912, which would imply negative densities. Denosumab change SD 0.723 is impossible when its baseline and 1-year SDs are 0.080 and 0.044. Our test on the printed change values gives P about 0.59, not 0.496. SRS-22r pain baseline SD 2.64 is impossible: on a 1 to 5 scale the largest possible SD with n=29 is about 2.04. Denosumab SRS change scores do not equal 1-year minus baseline (function 0.27 computed versus 0.36 printed; total 0.59 versus 0.67); the teriparatide ones do. The denosumab change SDs also imply negative pre-post correlations (function about -0.55, total about -0.56), against 0.4 to 0.9 in every teriparatide domain, so that column may come from different data (ours). Table 4 percentages use a denominator of 24. The limitations list numbers two items as Third. Ours, lower confidence: baseline ODI of about 24 on a 0-100 scale is low for patients with VAS 7.7 and SVA 156 mm; we cannot tell if a raw score was reported. Funding and conflicts are not in this copy.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: “In 56 osteoporotic women having deformity surgery to T10, a 6-month perioperative course of teriparatide had fewer PJF revisions than denosumab at 1 year, 1 versus 6. PJK, 17% versus 33%, was not significantly different. It is one small single-center trial, and the PJF result is fragile.”

rows: Grade B for teriparatide before instrumentation

points: O05 and D09 numbers come from the library records; O05 is abstract-level.
Do not stretch it: no men, no osteopenia, no cement or tethers, no UIV other than T10, nothing beyond 1 year.
slides.notes: Expect these questions. Should every osteoporotic deformity patient get teriparatide? This trial supports it over denosumab for PJF in this narrow population, but on 7 events with a P value that depends on the test; and the CNS guideline already supports considering teriparatide, so the trial adds a drug-against-drug signal, not proof. Does it prevent PJK? Not shown. 17.2% versus 33.3% was not significant, but the trial was underpowered for a gap that size, so it is not evidence of no effect either (ours). Is denosumab bad? This trial cannot say; there was no untreated arm, and denosumab patients still had 22.2% PJF. Why is PJF lower if PJK is not? The authors suggest teriparatide stops a PJK from progressing to collapse or metal failure. That is their hypothesis; the paper does not report how the PJF cases arose. Does the back pain benefit matter? A 2.1-point larger VAS drop may be clinically meaningful (our judgment; the paper makes no MCID claim), but ODI did not differ, and unblinded patients reported their own pain. What about 2 years? The authors say late failures often appear in year 2 or 3 and long-term follow-up is needed. Context from D09, a library record: in a multicenter ASD cohort, 28.2% had at least one reoperation with minimum 2-year follow-up, so a PJF reduction matters if it holds up. Remember the deck was built without seeing the figures.

decks.not_reviewed: No supplement is cited. Earlier reports from this cohort (references 14-16, 19-21), the reliability studies for the MRI grading method (references 24-25), and the promised clinical follow-up were not reviewed. Figure 1 was read from the page image; the PDF is the complete 8-page article.

slides.title: Discography and disc degeneration
slides.lead: Does a modern, pressure-limited, small-needle discogram damage the discs it punctures?
points: Journal club: harms of disc puncture
Carragee EJ, Don AS, Hurwitz EL, et al. Spine 2009;34(21):2338-45. 2009 ISSLS Prize Winner

Bottom line: 7 to 10 years after 3-level discography (L3-S1), injected discs showed more grade progression (35% vs 14% of discs), more new herniations (55 vs 22) and more Modic change than the same levels in matched controls. Uninjected L1-L3 discs did not differ.
Imaging outcomes only. No symptom or clinical results are reported.
slides.notes: This is Carragee's Stanford volunteer cohort: people without serious low back pain illness who had experimental discography in 1997-98 for earlier studies of false-positive discograms, plus matched people who had the same baseline MRI and no injection. About ten years later, both groups had another MRI read blind to group. The comparison is the same disc levels, injected versus never injected. The design is a matched cohort, not a trial: nobody was randomized to discography. The only randomization was the side of needle entry in asymptomatic volunteers. Watch for one correction to our own record. The abstract says 50 discography and 52 control subjects. Figure 1, Table 1 and the Results say the reverse: 52 discography and 50 control. The full text is right, and our master record copied the abstract. This deck was prepared from the full 8-page paper, including Figure 1 and Tables 1 to 5. No supplement is cited. The earlier reports from this cohort (references 14-16, 19-21) were not reviewed, and the clinical follow-up the authors say is underway was not part of this paper. Frame it for the room: this is a paper about the cost of a diagnostic test, not about whether the test works. The authors' own primary hypothesis was the null, that modern discography would not be associated with more degeneration.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: Discography and intradiscal treatments puncture the anulus. Most practitioners estimated the risk of later degeneration as extremely remote.
points: Animal models use anular puncture to induce degeneration; small-gauge results in large animals were mixed
Earlier follow-up of discography patients used plain radiographs only; no MRI cohort had been followed
Earlier work in these volunteers found more back pain after discography that faded over 1 to 2 years, mainly in distressed subjects
Question: do discs injected 10 years earlier degenerate faster than the same levels in matched uninjected people?

rows: Same levels in matched subjects, no injection
Uninjected L1/2 and L2/3 in both groups

slides.notes: The authors set up the gap clearly. Needle puncture is a standard way to make discs degenerate in animals, usually with a large needle in a small disc. In large animals, small-gauge puncture has shown short-term change in some studies and not in others. In people, the only long-term follow-up they cite used plain radiographs. So when this was designed, nobody knew whether a clinical discogram leaves a structural mark. The technique is the point. The authors call it modern: small needles (25-gauge in 134 injections, 22-gauge in 21), a pressure relief valve capping injection at 100 psi (the paper calls this limited pressurization; its 'low pressure' means a positive injection under 22 psi, a different thing), antibiotics and nonirritating contrast, one experienced discographer. If harm shows up with this technique, the argument that harm comes only from older or rougher methods is weaker. The design has a useful internal control. The upper lumbar discs, L1/2 and L2/3, were never injected in anyone. If the discography group simply had worse discs or worse genes, the upper levels should also degenerate faster in that group. If the effect is local to the needle, the upper levels should look the same. Keep that logic in mind for the results. The authors also tested three within-group questions: needle size, whether the injection was painful, and whether new herniations fell on the side of the puncture. A side effect lined up with the needle is the closest thing to a mechanism this design can offer.

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: 150 volunteers recruited in matched pairs; 102 analyzed at about 9 years.
points: Recruitment pools, same in each arm: 40 cervical disc disease, 25 resolved lumbar herniation, 10 somatization history
Matched for age, sex, prior cervical or lumbar disc trouble and psychometric profile
Entry: not seeking or receiving care for LBP, no LBP medication or activity limits
Excluded at follow-up: interval lumbar surgery or intradiscal therapy, repeat discogram, fracture, infection, tumor, new rheumatic disease
Follow-up MRI: new study protocol scan, or a clinical scan in the last 3 years that met the protocol (13 discography, 8 control)
Readers: 4 experienced (2 radiologists, 2 spine surgeons), blind to group; Pfirrmann grade, herniation, Modic, HIZ; Videman method for height and signal
slides.see: Figure 1 is the flow chart: 14 discography and 19 control subjects were lost to follow-up after baseline.
slides.notes: Flow arithmetic checks: 75-4=71 and 75-2=73, 71-14=57 and 73-19=54, then 57-5=52 and 54-4=50. 155 of 156 expected discography discs and all 150 control discs were analyzed; the paper does not say why one discography disc is missing, and Table 3 lists 100 upper discs for discography where 52 subjects give 104. Selection matters here. These are volunteers, and most had prior cervical or lumbar disc disease, so they are a higher-risk group for degeneration than the general population. The authors name this limit and answer that patients offered disc injection are high risk too. The paper does not explain how people in the same pools ended up in the discography or control arm beyond 'would not have discography performed'. So the arms are matched, not randomized, and any unmeasured difference could matter. The internal control at L1-L3 is the main protection against that. Baseline: Table 1 shows close matching (age 40.2 vs 41.1, male 74% vs 75%, prior microdiscectomy 8 vs 7, starting smokers 21 vs 24, time to MRI 8.7 vs 8.9, printed without units or a statement of mean or median; we read it as mean years). No SDs or P values are printed, and the paper reports no confidence intervals for any estimate. The authors say the lost subjects did not appear to differ, but the lost column lumps 48 people from both arms, including the excluded. Exclusions are the fragile point, and this reading is ours: 5 discography subjects were removed for lumbar surgery before 7 years, against 1 control. Surgical discs are probably the most degenerated, so removing them likely biases toward no difference. It also hides a possible clinical harm. Measurement: two readers per scan, tie-breakers for disagreement; agreement in 95 of 102 subjects, and the method's published kappa is 0.81. Clinical scans came from several practices with variable technique, and more of them were in the discography group.

slides.title: Primary outcome: injected levels
slides.lead: At L3-S1, every measure moved further in the discography discs. Units are discs, not people.
points: *0.03 is the Table 2 P for the follow-up grade distribution; our chi-square on 54/155 vs 21/150 gives about 0.00002
**Text and abstract print 0.0003; Table 2 prints 0.00003, which our chi-square matches
Herniation subtypes alone were not significant (P 0.07 to 0.5)
slides.notes: Read this table at the disc level. Each person contributes 3 discs, and the chi-square and t tests treat discs as independent, which overstates precision. That point is ours; the paper does not discuss it. Even so, the main effect survives: with the full 3-fold design effect, grade progression still gives P about 0.015 (our check). Recomputed: 54/155 is 34.8% and 21/150 is 14.0%, about 21 more progressing discs per 100 injected (our arithmetic). The 0.03 printed beside it in the text belongs to the comparison of follow-up grade distributions, which we reproduce at 0.028. A test of the progression counts themselves would be far smaller. Baselines were balanced, supporting the Table 2 footnote (our checks): grade P about 0.6, Modic 10 vs 12 P 0.60, HIZ 13 vs 14 P 0.77, height 10.47 vs 10.56 P 0.52. Herniations reconcile: follow-up minus baseline by type gives 18+9+18+10=55 and 5+6+5+6=22. New herniation is significant either way; the abstract's 0.0003 is a typo for Table 2's 0.00003. Modic prevalence 29 vs 16 reproduces at 0.048. The HIZ P of 0.1 matches new HIZ (10 vs 4), not overall prevalence (17 vs 13). Disc height fell 1.54 versus 0.66 (our subtraction; the paper prints no units). The printed P of 0.05 is weaker than the table supports: our t test on the follow-up means and SDs gives P below 0.001, and about 0.002 even using subject counts. We cannot tell which test produced 0.05. The direction is not in doubt. Injected discs lost 13.3% of signal versus 8.5%; no SD is printed, so P=0.001 cannot be checked. Keep perspective, as the authors do: of 91 normal (grade I-II) discs injected, 50 were still normal 10 years later. The harm is a shift in rates, not universal damage. The abstract's 'in all graded or measured parameters' is true for direction only; HIZ and each herniation subtype were not significant on their own.

slides.title: Secondary analyses
slides.lead: Uninjected levels matched; herniations clustered on the needle side; needle size and pain did not separate.

rows: No difference: grade V 22 vs 25, new herniation 7 vs 6, signal -7.71% vs -7.52%
Control new herniation 6 does not match table counts (10)
Table 4 says 36; our test gives about 0.002 to 0.004
No significant difference; trend worse with 22 gauge
No difference by the authors; printed totals 18.8% vs 17.9%

slides.see: Table 4 lays out new herniations by side; check its row sums against its totals.
slides.notes: The upper-level comparison carries the causal argument. At L1/2 and L2/3, where nobody was punctured, grades, new herniations, Modic change and signal loss were similar (our chi-square on follow-up grades, P about 0.9; baseline P about 0.9). The 'similar' signal loss cannot be checked, since no SD is printed. Baseline upper-level height was 8.54 vs 8.29 (our P about 0.08): not significant, but the closest thing to imbalance, and unmentioned. Control discs at L3-S1 lost 8.5% of signal, close to the 7.5% to 7.7% lost at the uninjected upper levels, while injected discs lost 13.3%. That pattern points to a local effect rather than a sicker discography cohort. One oddity, our observation: about 17% to 19% of upper discs were grade V at baseline in both arms, more than at L3-S1 (10% to 8%), which is unusual for this age; the paper does not comment. Side of injection: the needle side was set by random number in volunteers, so side is the one randomized contrast in the study. The text gives 34 ipsilateral, 14 contralateral, 4 central and P=0.0006. Table 4 gives 36 and 14, but its ipsilateral rows add to 31, and the control right and left rows add to 7 and 10 against printed totals of 9 and 12 (the text says 10 and 11). None of these splits adds back to the 55 new herniations. Our goodness-of-fit test gives 0.004 for 34 vs 14 and 0.002 for 36 vs 14, so the side effect is real but less extreme than printed. Pain on injection: the text gives 32 painful and 273 negative injections, but only 155 discs were injected (134 + 21 by needle size). 305 is exactly 155 + 150, all L3-S1 discs in both groups, so the table may include control discs (our inference). Its percentages also sit one row low: the printed Total row reads 18.8% vs 17.9%, and the 37.5% (12/32) and 39.6% (108/273) on the HIZ row are new findings per disc, our reading after the shift. The authors' reading, no link with pain, is plausible, but the table cannot be checked. Needle size is underpowered and the authors say so.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: Strong design idea, credible direction, sloppy tables.

rows: Matched cohort with the same baseline MRI
Not randomized; allocation process not described
Readers blind to group, published grading method
Disc-level tests ignore clustering within people
Imaging only; no clinical outcomes reported

points: Only two time points: rate of change over time unknown (authors' limit)
Mostly high-risk volunteers; generalizability limited (authors' limit)
slides.notes: Be fair first. By the authors' account, no long-term controlled MRI follow-up of discography had been reported before this one. The readers were blind, and the internal control at uninjected levels is clever. Direction is consistent across every measure, the effects are large, and the side-of-needle clustering is hard to explain by confounding. The authors' own limits: a high-risk volunteer population, and only baseline and 10-year scans, so the kinetics of degeneration cannot be estimated. They add that by 7 years the discography group already had more clinical MRI for lumbar problems and more lumbar surgery (5 vs 1). The rest is our reading. Analysis: discs are clustered within people, and with 3 discs per subject the effective sample lies somewhere between 52 versus 50 people and 155 versus 150 discs; the paper gives no within-subject correlation, so the size of the penalty is unknown. With the full 3-fold penalty, grade progression still gives P about 0.015. Exclusions: removing interval surgery takes out the worst outcomes, which would mostly mute the difference, but it also means the paper cannot say whether discography raised the surgery rate. Ascertainment: more discography subjects had clinical scans from outside practices with variable protocols. If those scans were made because of new symptoms, the scan source is linked to outcome; images were de-identified, but readers may still have been able to tell a protocol scan from an outside scan (our inference). Reporting: no confidence intervals anywhere; the abstract reverses the group sizes; one herniation P value is printed two ways; Table 4 rows and totals disagree with each other and with the text; Table 5 has impossible denominators and shifted percentages; Table 3 control new herniations do not match its own counts; Table 1 percentages are not achievable from 52 and 50 (74% of 52 and 75% of 50). None of these reverses the main result, but they lower confidence in the secondary analyses. What it is not: a test of whether discography is accurate. The authors cite separate work questioning its validity (reference 30). The extension to adjacent-segment disease and to intradiscal therapies is the authors' hypothesis, not tested here.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "In volunteers followed 7 to 10 years, discs punctured by a modern, pressure-limited discogram degenerated faster than the same levels in matched controls: grade progression 35% versus 14% of discs, and 55 versus 22 new herniations, clustered on the needle side. Uninjected levels did not differ. Imaging only, no clinical outcomes."
points: Cite it as a harm signal for disc puncture, not as a verdict on discography's diagnostic value
Correct group sizes: 52 discography, 50 control (the abstract swaps them)
O02, from its library record: degenerative MRI findings are common in pain-free people and rise with age, so a degenerated disc on MRI does not mean a symptomatic one
slides.notes: Expect these follow-up questions. Did the injected discs cause pain or disability? This paper does not say. It reports imaging only, and the authors say a clinical evaluation is underway for a future publication. The one clinical hint is theirs: more lumbar MRI and more lumbar surgery (5 vs 1) in the discography group by 7 years, and those operated subjects were excluded. Does this apply to my patient with chronic low back pain? Partly. The subjects were volunteers without serious back pain, mostly with prior disc disease. The authors argue that patients offered discography are high risk too, but no clinical patients were studied. Should I stop using control discs? The authors note that injecting a probably normal control disc has never been shown to improve the test, and that these discs appear to degenerate faster. That is their argument; this study did not compare strategies. Does it explain adjacent segment disease? The authors raise it as a possibility, not a finding. Does a smaller needle make it safe? This study used mostly 25-gauge needles and still found harm; the 22-gauge comparison had only 21 injections. Was it painful injections that did harm? Table 5 suggests no difference, but its denominators do not add up, so do not lean on it. How big is the effect? About 21 extra progressing discs per 100 injected (our arithmetic), with most normal discs still normal at 10 years.
