The P values and some secondary counts in this paper have printing errors, but the main direction holds. Brinjikji numbers come from the master file's O02 record, not from this paper.

decks.not_reviewed: Nothing beyond the 8-page article was available. No supplement is cited. Figures 1 to 4 were read only through their captions and the Results text, because pdftotext gives no plotted values; the matched-cohort 2-year means are therefore not reported here. The ASLS trial comparison comes from the master-file record D07, not from a reading of that paper.

slides.title: Bridwell 2009: ASLS surgery vs nonoperative care
slides.lead: Does treatment improve 2-year quality of life in adult symptomatic lumbar scoliosis?
points: Journal club: adult deformity, operative versus nonoperative care
Bridwell KH, et al. Spine 2009;34:2171-8
Prospective observational cohort, Spinal Deformity Study Group, enrolled 2002-2005

Bottom line: at 2 years the 85 operated patients had improved on every measure and the 75 nonoperative patients had not. Only 45% of the nonoperative arm was followed, and treatment was chosen, not randomized.
slides.notes: This deck was prepared from the full article text. The PDF is the correct paper and is complete: 8 pages, abstract to references. Frame it first. This is a patient-choice cohort, not a trial. The patient and the medical team decided on surgery or nonoperative care individually, so every between-group comparison carries confounding by indication. The authors call it Level II. The authors say few studies had addressed the question and only 1 did so directly: Dickson, which used nonvalidated questionnaires and Harrington-era surgery. Our inference: it was among the first prospective studies with validated patient-reported outcomes on this question; the paper does not claim to be first. Funding came from Medtronic through the Spinal Deformity Study Group, and the last author lists a Medtronic affiliation. Read it as the hypothesis-generating study behind the later ASLS trial (record D07), which the authors foreshadow: they describe an NIH application for a randomized trial that had scored just inside the payline.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: Surgery for adult lumbar scoliosis is big. Does it beat common nonoperative care, and does nonoperative care help at all?
points: Population: age 40-80, lumbar Cobb at least 30 degrees, no prior deformity surgery
Symptomatic: ODI 20 or more and/or SRS pain, function or self-image domain 4.0 or less
Exposure: operative treatment versus nonoperative care, chosen by patient and surgeon
Primary outcome: SRS subscore (pain, function, self-image, mental health; satisfaction excluded)
Secondary: ODI, NRS back and leg pain, radiographs; age and complications as modifiers
slides.notes: The authors pose two questions. First, does each group improve with time and treatment? That is a within-group question, and it does not need the groups to be comparable. Second, if the groups are matched to look alike at baseline, do their outcomes differ? That is the causal question, and it rests entirely on the propensity match. Keep them apart when you present. The within-group finding, that nonoperative patients did not improve, is the more robust of the two, though it is weakened by 45% follow-up. The between-group finding is where selection bias lives. Inclusion wording differs slightly: the abstract says ODI of 20 or more or SRS domains of 4 or less in pain, function and self-image, while Methods says and/or, and pain, function or self-image. The thresholds came from deviation from normative values set by the authoring centers. Nonoperative care was observation 21%, medications 26%, medications plus physical therapy and/or injections 40%, and other treatment without medications 13%. Methods say only that basic treatment decision-making was agreed on by the centers at the start; the authors themselves say nonoperative care should have been described more fully.

slides.title: Selection and measurement
slides.lead: Who reached the 2-year analysis, and how comparable were they?
points: Nonoperative arm: 167 enrolled, 5 crossed over in the first 6 months, 75 followed at 2 years (45%)
Operative arm: 89 enrolled, 85 at 2 years including the 5 crossovers (reported as 95%)
Propensity match on Cobb, ODI, SRS subscore, back and leg pain: 41 per group
slides.notes: Rows come from Tables 1, 3 and 4 and the Results text; pain rows have smaller n (70 and 80 for back pain, 62 and 79 for leg pain). Our recomputation from the printed means and SDs reproduces the Cobb P (about 0.023) and the Table 3 and 4 baseline pain P values (about 0.006 and 0.67). The SRS P (about 0.016 from 3.3 vs 3.1) and ODI P (about 0.09) match the printed 0.047 and 0.17 only within rounding of the means. The text gives different values for two of them: back pain P=0.012 against 0.007 in Table 3, and leg pain P=0.561 against 0.68 in Table 4. The operated group was worse on curve, SRS and back pain, and much less satisfied. Satisfaction is not part of the SRS subscore and was not a matching variable. The authors make the point themselves: satisfaction is an important driver of treatment choice. Dissatisfied patients chose surgery. Now the flow. 167 less 5 crossovers is 162. With 75 followed, 87 were lost, yet the text says 86, and its sex counts add to 87 lost and 74 followed. The 5 crossovers were analyzed as operative, so this is an as-treated analysis. Our inference: removing early nonoperative failures could make the nonoperative arm look better, not worse. The operative figure of 95% is 85 of 89, but 85 includes the 5 crossovers, so the originally operative patients followed were 80 of 89 (90%), on our arithmetic. The abstract says 5 centers; Methods says 15 centers, 90% of patients from 5. The authors say lost and followed nonoperative patients were identical. Their figures are close for age 58 vs 60, ODI 31 vs 30 and SRS 3.21 vs 3.28, but less so for back pain 5.7 vs 5.3 and leg pain 3.1 vs 3.61, and no statistical test is given. Methods text also calls baseline ODI statistically different, against P=0.17 in Table 1 and 0.174 in Results. Matching did not include age or sex, although Methods says the intent was similar age and gender.

slides.title: Primary and secondary outcomes at 2 years
slides.lead: Unmatched cohorts: the operative group improved on every measure; the nonoperative group showed no significant change, with small nonsignificant declines on most.
points: Nonoperative SRS change not significant (P=0.494); operative change P<0.001
SRS satisfaction: nonop 3.3 to 3.5, operative 2.85 to 4.2
Propensity-matched cohorts (41 vs 41) showed the same pattern, per the authors
slides.see: Figures 1 and 2 show the SRS subscore lines for unmatched and matched groups; the matched 2-year values are given only there.
slides.notes: Positive SRS change is better; lower ODI and NRS are better. The operative SRS gain was 0.68 in Table 6. The paper gives no MCID. Do not compare it with the 0.4 MDMD in the D08 record: that is a between-group threshold from another study, not a within-group change, and D08 says it is not an MCID. The ODI drop was 14 points. In the nonoperative group nothing moved significantly: back pain drifted up (P=0.167), leg pain down slightly (P=0.565), SRS down. One check fails. Our arithmetic: Tables 1 and 2 print nonoperative SRS 3.3 then 3.1, a decline of at least 0.1 after rounding. With SDs near 0.52 at both times, n=75, and any non-negative pre-post correlation, a paired test should give P below about 0.25, not the 0.494 in Figure 1. The paper may have used a different n or analysis. We cannot resolve it without the data, so do not lean on the exact P. The matched-cohort findings are reported mostly as P values in the text and Figure 2; matched back pain P=0.639 nonoperative and leg pain P=0.841 nonoperative, operative both P<0.001. The operative SRS gain is P=0.001 in the text but P<0.001 in Figure 1, and the 2-year between-group SRS difference is P<0.001 in text and Table 2 but P<0.0001 in the Figure 1 caption. The text cites Table 4 for ODI, but Table 4 is leg pain; ODI is in Tables 1 and 2. Radiographs: kyphosis T5-T12 went from +28 to +34 and lordosis from -43 to -46 in the operative group. The paper gives no P values for Table 7, though the text calls the operative changes significant. In the authors' words, nonoperative satisfaction did not deteriorate, which they read as some potential benefit to nonoperative care. That reading is theirs. The paper does have an untreated comparison: 21% were observation only, and the authors report no changes or trends for any nonoperative subgroup and no trend toward different outcomes or satisfaction with observation versus active care. Our reading: if anything, that argues against an active-treatment benefit.

slides.title: Age and complications
slides.lead: Older patients gained as much as middle-aged ones; major complications showed a smaller, nonsignificant gain that was still significant within the group.
points: 31 of 85 operated patients (36%) had a complication: 15 major, 16 minor (Glassman definitions)
Complications were not collected for nonoperative patients
Age 40-59 vs 60-80: same incremental SRS improvement; older patients started lower
slides.see: Figures 3 and 4 show the age-group lines; they pool operative and nonoperative patients.
slides.notes: The percentages are our arithmetic: 31/85 is 36%, 15/85 is 18%. Each complication group improved significantly. Major complication patients started lower (P=0.031 in the Table 6 note) and finished lower (P=0.002). The authors read this as major complications reducing the likelihood of substantial benefit without precluding it, and they suggest, without data, that lower baseline scores reflect comorbidities. The P values disagree between text and table. The text gives P=0.031 for the major group change and 0.0002 for the minor group; the Table 6 note gives 0.027 and <0.0001, and uses 0.031 for the baseline difference. The text calls the 2-year difference between groups not significant (P=0.089), while the table note calls the 2-year scores different (P=0.002). The 0.089 most likely refers to the size of the change; the Discussion says P=0.09 for smaller improvement. The major row has 15 at baseline and 14 at 2 years, yet Table 6 still totals 85. Our weighted means reproduce the totals, 3.12 and 3.80. The minor-group change prints as 0.89, but its means give 0.91 (0.90 to 0.92 within rounding). The Table 6 note also says the change differs by complication group, then says the smaller major-group change did not reach significance. The age analysis is weaker than it sounds. Figures 3 and 4 pool both treatment groups, and after matching the older operative group had only 16 patients. Equal improvement with age here means no difference detected, not proof of equivalence. These are 2-year results only, and revision surgery was not reported.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: Holds up: prospective, consecutive, validated patient-reported outcomes
Holds up: operative follow-up high; large, consistent operative gains on every measure
Holds up: within-group stasis of nonoperative patients, seen in matched and unmatched sets
Weakens: treatment chosen, not assigned; operated patients less satisfied at baseline
Weakens: 45% nonoperative follow-up; the authors call it the major weakness
Weakens: crossovers analyzed as operative; nonoperative care described only by category
Weakens: no complication data for nonoperative care; 2-year horizon; industry funding
Weakens: several text, table and flow numbers disagree
slides.notes: Be fair. Our reading: in 2009 this was among the best prospective evidence on the question, and the operative gains were consistent across measures. The baseline differences alone are unlikely to explain them, but selection and regression to the mean, below, could add to them; the authors say only that baseline differences were often very small in clinical importance. The authors' own limitations are the 45% follow-up, the conclusion that nonoperative care does not help holding with certainty only if follow-up matched the operative arm, and the need to describe nonoperative care more fully. They also say patients lost to follow-up were unlikely to have improved substantially, but cannot state that with certainty. The rest is our reading. Propensity matching only balances what is measured; satisfaction, comorbidity, age and expectations were not matched. Matching kept 41 of 85 operative and 41 of 75 nonoperative patients. On our comparison of Table 5 with Tables 1, 3 and 4, the matched operative patients resemble the whole operative arm (SRS 3.0 vs 3.1, ODI 34 vs 34), while the matched nonoperative patients were sicker than the whole nonoperative arm (ODI 34 vs 30, SRS 3.0 vs 3.3, back pain 5.8 vs 5.34, leg pain 4.2 vs 3.68). The matched result applies to that overlap: nonoperative patients who looked like surgical candidates. Regression to the mean favors the group enrolled at its worst, likely those about to have surgery. Analysis was t-tests or repeated-measures ANOVA with many outcomes and no multiplicity correction. Operative follow-up visits were within 2 months, then at 1 and 2 years; actively treated nonoperative patients were asked back at 6 months, 1 and 2 years, untreated ones only at 2 years. The authors attribute the follow-up gap entirely to patient choice, despite identical efforts. Our reading: the visit asymmetry may contribute, but the 2-year-only schedule applied to the 21% under observation, so it cannot explain most of the loss. Number problems: 86 vs 87 lost, 5 vs 15 centers, 95% operative follow-up counting crossovers, baseline pain P values differing between text and table, Table 6 totals, the Table 4 reference for ODI, and a nonoperative SRS P value our arithmetic cannot reproduce. None of these reverses the main finding. They do argue for quoting the direction rather than exact P values.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: For adult symptomatic lumbar scoliosis, patients who chose surgery improved substantially at 2 years and those who chose nonoperative care did not, but this is a patient-choice cohort with 45% nonoperative follow-up.
points: Operative: SRS +0.68, ODI 34 to 20, back pain 6.3 to 2.4
Nonoperative: no significant change on any measure
36% of operated patients had a complication; with a major one the SRS gain was smaller (0.47 vs 0.67), not significantly
ASLS figures come from the D07 library record; its 64% crossover weakened the randomized comparison
slides.notes: Spoken summary: in 160 patients aged 40 to 80 with lumbar curves of at least 30 degrees, the 85 who had surgery improved on SRS, ODI, back and leg pain at 2 years, and the 75 followed on nonoperative care did not change. The pattern held after propensity matching. Expect these follow-up questions. Does this prove surgery is better? No. Treatment was chosen, the operated group was less satisfied at baseline, and more than half the nonoperative patients were never seen at 2 years. The later ASLS trial, from the D07 record, found an intention-to-treat difference that was not significant at 2 years, while as-treated analyses favored surgery. Does nonoperative care do nothing? The authors say it did not improve QOL, but they qualify this as certain only with matching follow-up. Satisfaction held steady. Should age alone deter surgery? In this cohort, older patients gained as much as middle-aged ones, though the matched older operative group was 16 patients. What does a major complication cost? The SRS gain fell from about 0.7 to about 0.5, a difference that was not significant (P=0.09), and the gain remained significant within the group. Watch for 2-year-only follow-up: durability and revision rates need D08, not this paper.

decks.not_reviewed: Nothing in the paper was skipped; there is no supplement. Figures 2 and 3 were read as counts from the rendered bar charts. Cited papers (Carreon 2003 definition, Fang 2005, Rhee 2003) were not read.

slides.title: Schwab 2012: risk factors for major complications in ASD surgery
slides.lead: A retrospective eight-center case-control study: no patient factor separated cases from controls, but combined anterior-posterior surgery did.
points: Schwab FJ, Hawkinson N, Lafage V, Smith JS, et al., International Spine Study Group. Eur Spine J 2012;21:2603-2610
953 consecutive ASD operations, 2002-2007, at eight centers; 80 (8.4%) had at least one major complication within 6 weeks
72 non-instrumentation cases compared with 78 randomly chosen controls without a major complication
Authors: no difference in age, sex, BMI, comorbidities, ASA or revision status; more staged and more combined anterior-posterior surgery in cases
Ours: the staging P value reproduces only as a test of the 1-, 2- and 3-stage mix, which Figure 2 shows is driven by three-stage surgery in controls; the analysis is univariate only
slides.notes: Deck prepared from the full 8-page article (pages 2603-2610), including Tables 1-4 and the Figure 1 case legend. Figures 2 and 3 are bar charts with readable counts; Figure 2 gives the stage distribution, which no table reports. There is no supplement. Framing for the room: this is an early ISSG paper, a retrospective chart review, and it asks a fair question with a small, unadjusted comparison. Its headline number, 8.4%, is a major-complication rate under a narrow, chart-based definition captured up to 6 weeks. Its headline risk factors are surgical approach and staging, and only approach holds up; on the paper's own Figure 2, the staging difference runs the other way. The take-home is less about what was found and more about what this design cannot show. Funding: a DePuy research grant to the International Spine Study Group; the conflict of interest statement says none.

slides.title: The question and the design
slides.lead: Which patient and surgical factors go with a major peri-operative complication after adult deformity surgery?
points: Design: multi-center retrospective review with a nested case-control comparison
Each center reviewed consecutive ASD operations until it reached 10 patients with a major complication
Controls: a randomization table picked a similar number from the 873 patients without one, same time span, same centers
Major complication: list modified from Carreon et al. (Table 1), intra-operative or up to 6 weeks after surgery
Primary instrumentation complications (for example rod fracture) excluded from the comparison: 8 of 80
Analysis: unpaired t tests and chi-square tests; no multivariable model

rows: Motor deficit, cauda equina, bowel or bladder deficit
Deep infection with return to OR, sepsis
Reintubation, respiratory failure, ICU over 72 h, unplanned return to OR

slides.notes: Name the design correctly. The 8.4% comes from the full consecutive series of 953. The risk-factor comparison is a case-control study: cases are those 72 patients, controls are a random sample of non-complication patients. So the comparison yields differences in exposure between groups, not risks, and the paper reports no odds ratios. The sampling rule matters. Each center stopped reviewing when it hit its 10th complication. That is inverse sampling: the series ends on an event, which pushes the crude rate up a little. Ours: a stopping-rule-corrected estimate would be nearer 7.6% (72 of 945 if each site's last case is set aside), and the Wilson 95% interval for 80 of 953 is about 6.8% to 10.3%. Per-center rates are not reported, so we cannot see how much they varied. Ascertainment was by chart review: medical records, operative summaries and office notes up to 6 weeks, abstracted by research assistants not involved in care. Ours: retrospective charts miss events, so 8.4% is likely an underestimate for this definition because of chart capture, partly offset by the stopping rule. The definition also builds outcomes into the complication: bleeding over 4 L, ICU stay over 72 hours and unplanned return to the OR are complications. That matters on the results slides. Inclusion was age 18 or over with at least one radiographic threshold: coronal Cobb over 30, sagittal or coronal imbalance over 5 cm, thoracic kyphosis over 60, thoracolumbar kyphosis over 20, or lumbar lordosis under 20 degrees, with untreated adolescent idiopathic or de novo degenerative scoliosis.

slides.title: Patients: who were the cases and controls
slides.lead: The groups looked alike on every patient factor the paper reports.
points: Two controls were dropped for missing data (80 chosen, 78 analyzed)
ASA missing in 2 cases and, by the paper's count, 9 controls
Smoking, pre-operative anemia (hematocrit 30% or less) and vitals reported as not different, with no data shown
slides.notes: Our recomputations from the reported summaries all agree that these are non-significant: sex P about 0.64, age about 0.46, BMI about 0.14, revision rate (38 of 72 against 32 of 78) about 0.15. Now the ASA problem, which is ours to flag. Cases: 7 ASA I, 28 ASA II, 35 ASA III, 2 missing, which adds to 72. The mean of those counts is 2.40, not the 2.33 in Table 2. Controls: 1 ASA I, 36 ASA II, 30 ASA III and 9 missing adds to 76, not 78, and the control percentages (1%, 46%, 38%) use 78 as the denominator while the case percentages use 70. The control mean of the 67 known grades is 2.43, which matches the table. On the counts given, a 3 by 2 chi-square gives P about 0.05 (exact about 0.05), but two expected counts are near 4, so the approximation is weak. The borderline result comes from ASA I (7 cases against 1 control): cases had more of the healthiest grade. ASA III against the rest (50% against 45% of known controls) gives P about 0.54. So there is no sign that sicker patients were overrepresented among cases, and the case mean of 2.33 in Table 2 is inconsistent with the counts; either could be the error. The authors explain the null patient findings by a ceiling effect: few elective ASD patients are ASA IV or V, or on a fourth or fifth operation. That is their interpretation. Ours: the simpler explanation is power. With about 75 per group, the study had about 80% power only for a 22-point difference in a binary factor near 50%, or about half a standard deviation in a continuous one, such as 3 BMI units. Read no difference here as no large difference, not no effect.

slides.title: Results: the complications and the hospital course
slides.lead: 72 cases had 99 major complications; hospital stay nearly doubled.
points: 80 of 953 (8.4%) had at least one major complication; 8 were primarily instrumentation-related
99 complications in 72 cases, 1.4 per patient
Most common: blood loss over 4 L (11), deep infection with return to OR (11), symptomatic PE (10)
Table 3 gives no SDs, and whether time and blood loss are per stage or total is not stated
slides.notes: The authors themselves flag EBL as confounded: bleeding over 4 L is a major complication, so cases must bleed more. Good, and say so. The same logic applies further, and this extension is ours. Hospital stay is an outcome of the complication, not a risk factor for it; it belongs in a consequences line, not alongside risk factors as the abstract places it. ICU stay is constrained by definition: an ICU stay over 72 hours makes a patient a case, so no control could exceed about 3 days. A control mean of 2.8 days and a case mean of 3.4 days with no significant difference is therefore hard to interpret and says nothing about whether ICU care was similar. The three most common complications cover 32 of the 99 events; the rest are not tabulated, so you cannot rebuild the mix of medical, neurological and wound events. Deaths are on the list of major complications, but the paper never says whether anyone died. Teaching point for the room: when a definition of the outcome contains a variable, comparing that variable between groups is circular.

slides.title: Results: approach and staging
slides.lead: Combined anterior-posterior surgery was more common in cases; on Figure 2, the staging difference is three-stage surgery in controls, not more staging in cases.
slides.see: Figure 2 shows the stage counts: no case had three stages while 6 controls did, and the control bars add to 72, not 78. Figure 3 gives the approach counts.
points: Counts are read from Figures 2 and 3; approach percentages fit 71 cases (one missing) and 78 controls
Ours: a chi-square on the approach counts gives P = 0.011, so the approach result reproduces
Ours: the 1-, 2- and 3-stage counts give P = 0.011 by 3 by 2 chi-square, so the staging P also reproduces
Ours: staged against single-stage (33 of 72 against 27 of 72) gives P about 0.31; the significant test is driven by 6 three-stage controls and no three-stage cases
slides.notes: This is the slide to slow down on. The approach result holds: the Figure 3 counts give the paper's P of 0.011, and combining anterior with posterior in a 2 by 2 against posterior-only also gives P under 0.01 (ours). The staging result reproduces but does not mean what the paper says. Figure 2 gives 39, 33 and 0 cases with one, two and three stages, against 45, 21 and 6 controls. A 3 by 2 chi-square on those counts gives P about 0.011 (ours), so 0.011 tests the whole stage distribution. But staged against single-stage, 46% against 37%, gives P about 0.31 (ours). The significant result comes from all six three-stage procedures being in controls, where about 3 per group would be expected: the opposite direction of the authors' claim that cases were more often staged. Treat 'more staging in cases' as not shown by this paper. Figure 2 also has its own problems: the control bars add to 72, not 78, and both groups average 1.46 stages, against 1.4 for controls in Table 4. Even the approach finding is fragile. It is univariate, with no adjustment for levels fused, osteotomies such as pedicle subtraction, deformity size or revision, which drive both the choice of a combined approach and complication risk: confounding by indication. Ours: staging and combined approaches probably overlap, but the paper gives no cross-tabulation of stage against approach, so we cannot tell whether they are separate signals. And the direction can run backwards (ours): an intra-operative complication such as bleeding over 4 L can make a surgeon stop and stage the case. The authors cite Fang 2005 for staging and infection, and note Rhee 2003 found staged posterior-only surgery did not raise complications. Their argument that approach and staging are controllable is reasonable, but this study does not show that changing them changes risk.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: A sensible question answered with a design too small and too unadjusted to rank risk factors.
points: Retrospective chart review to 6 weeks: complications are likely under-captured, so 8.4% is likely an underestimate, partly offset by the stopping rule (ours)
Inverse sampling, 10 events per site: crude rate slightly high, per-site rates hidden (ours)
Univariate tests only; correlation analyses are described in Methods but not reported
No sample-size calculation; about 75 per group misses moderate effects
Arithmetic: case mean ASA 2.33 against 2.40 from the counts; control ASA counts sum to 76 of 78; Figure 2 control bars sum to 72 of 78 and give a mean of 1.46 stages, not 1.4
Staging: the P of 0.011 tests the 1-, 2- and 3-stage mix and is driven by three-stage controls; staged against single-stage is not significant (ours)
Text against data: the Discussion says only EBL differed, but hospital stay did (P = 0.001); the Figure 1 case had a 3-stage procedure, yet Figure 2 shows no 3-stage cases
Outcome definition overlaps the compared variables: blood loss, ICU stay, return to OR
Conclusion speaks of multiple approaches in one setting, but staged cases are by definition not one setting
slides.notes: Strengths the authors claim: consecutive series, eight centers, and a randomly selected control group. The random selection of controls is real and protects against hand-picking. The comparison with the library's ISSG prospective cohort (record D09) is ours, and the numbers there come from that record: 69.8% had any complication and about 47.8% a major one over 2 years, with a broader definition that includes some radiographic events. The two figures are not comparable as rates, because definitions, follow-up and capture differ. The lesson is how much a prospective, audited design finds that a chart review does not. Other fragile points: Table 3 reports means without SDs; operative time and blood loss in staged cases are not said to be per stage or summed; deaths are not reported; the abstract lists hospital stay as though it were a risk factor. The Conclusion says multiple surgical approaches in one setting were linked to complications, but Table 4 does not separate same-day combined surgery from staged combined surgery, so that wording goes beyond the data (ours). What would fix it: prospective capture, a multivariable model with case complexity, and reporting odds ratios with confidence intervals.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: Say: in a retrospective eight-center review, 8.4% of 953 ASD patients had a major complication within 6 weeks; cases were more often treated with combined anterior-posterior surgery, but no patient factor stood out and nothing was adjusted.
points: Rate: 80 of 953, 8.4%, chart-based, 6 weeks, modified Carreon definition
Supported: combined anterior-posterior approach 56% of cases against 32% of controls
Not supported: more staging in cases; the P of 0.011 reflects three-stage surgery found only in controls, and staged against single-stage gives P about 0.31 (ours)
Not shown: that age, BMI, ASA or comorbidity are safe to ignore; the study was too small to see moderate effects
Consequence, not cause: hospital stay 14.4 against 7.9 days
slides.notes: Spoken summary, about 30 seconds: This ISSG chart review of 953 adult deformity operations at eight centers found an 8.4% major complication rate within 6 weeks. In a case-control comparison of 72 cases and 78 random controls, patient factors did not differ, while combined anterior-posterior surgery was more common among cases. The analysis is univariate and retrospective, and the paper's own Figure 2 does not support more staging in cases. Expect these questions. Is 8.4% a fair rate? The authors say it is consistent with previous reports. Ours: the narrow major-only definition, chart capture and 6-week window likely make it an underestimate, partly offset by the stopping rule. Is this an incidence or a risk factor study? Both: the rate comes from the full series, the factors from a nested case-control comparison with no odds ratios. Does staging cause complications? Not shown here; the significant test reflects three-stage surgery only in controls, staged against single-stage is not significant, and complications can cause staging. Does approach cause complications? Associated only, and confounded by case complexity. Why no patient factors? The authors suggest a ceiling effect on ASA and prior surgery; we think low power is the more direct reason. Were the ASA data clean? No: the case mean does not match its counts, and the control counts do not add up. Why exclude rod fractures? To focus on medical and surgical events; 8 of the 80 cases. Who funded it? A DePuy grant to the ISSG, with no conflicts declared.

decks.not_reviewed: No supplement is cited in the PDF. Not reviewed: the SRS-Schwab classification paper (reference 7), the threshold paper (reference 16) and the MCID source (reference 19, a 2005 meeting presentation). Values from Figures 6 to 8 are read off bar heights and are approximate.

slides.title: Smith 2013: does the SRS-Schwab grade track how patients feel?
slides.lead: Change in Classification Grade by the SRS-Schwab Adult Spinal Deformity Classification Predicts Impact on Health-Related Quality of Life Measures.
points: Journal club: adult spinal deformity classification
Smith JS, Klineberg E, Schwab F, Shaffrey CI, et al, International Spine Study Group. Spine 2013;38(19):1663-1671

Bottom line: in 341 adults with deformity followed 1 year, patients whose PT, SVA or PI-LL grade improved had larger gains in SRS-22 total score than patients whose grade worsened, and for PT and SVA also larger gains in disability (ODI); the ODI difference for PI-LL was not significant. In our reading, most of that grade improvement came from surgery.
Source: the full 9-page paper was read. No supplement is cited.
slides.notes: This is the clinical validation paper for the SRS-Schwab classification. The earlier work had set the grade cutoffs and shown the system is reliable between raters. This paper asks a different question: when the grade changes over time, does health-related quality of life change with it? That property is called responsiveness, and it is what makes a classification useful as a treatment target rather than just a label. The data come from the International Spine Study Group database, 10 US sites, with operative and nonoperative patients followed for 1 year. Keep three things in mind from the start. First, the title says the grade change predicts HRQOL change, but both were measured at the same 1-year visit, so what the paper shows is a concurrent association, not prediction in the forecasting sense (our reading). Second, only patients with complete data at both time points were included, and the paper does not say how many were enrolled, so the follow-up rate is unknown. Third, grade change and treatment are tangled together: surgery moves the grade and surgery moves HRQOL, and the analysis never separates the two. The study was funded through the ISSG Foundation, which receives research grants from DePuy Spine, and partly by an SRS research grant; the classification itself was developed by several of the authors. Level of evidence is listed as 3.

slides.title: The question and the classification
slides.lead: Is the SRS-Schwab classification responsive to changes in HRQOL after operative or nonoperative treatment?
points: The system has a coronal curve type (T, L, D or N) and 3 sagittal modifiers, each graded 0, + or ++.
The authors say the modifiers were selected for clinical relevance. An earlier 592-patient analysis found PI-LL, PT and SVA most correlated with HRQOL and was used to set the cutoffs.
Regression against ODI gave thresholds matching ODI 40 or more: PT above 22 degrees, SVA above 47 mm, PI-LL above 11 degrees.
Hypothesis: modifier grade change will track HRQOL change from baseline to 1 year.
slides.see: Figure 2 shows the full classification: curve types and the three modifier grades.
slides.notes: Make sure everyone has the grades in their head before the results, because every result is about moving between them. The grade cutoffs in the table come from Figure 2 of this paper. Note the step size. One grade on SVA spans 5.5 cm, so a patient can move several centimeters without changing grade, and another can cross a line by a few millimeters. That coarseness is the price of a simple system and it limits how responsive the grades can be. The paper also describes the thresholds that matched an ODI of 40 or more in the earlier work: PT above 22 degrees, SVA above 47 mm and PI-LL above 11 degrees. These are close to, but not the same as, the grade boundaries of 20 degrees, 4 cm and 10 degrees. The paper does not explain how the derived thresholds became the published cutoffs; our assumption is rounding, but it is not stated. Only the sagittal modifiers were tested here. The coronal curve type was not analyzed for responsiveness, so this paper says nothing about whether coronal type tracks outcome. The authors frame the need for an ASD classification against Aebi, the SRS system and the older Schwab system: Aebi is etiologic and gives little detail, the SRS system describes the radiograph richly but has unclear clinical use, and the old Schwab system was HRQOL-based but had no pelvic parameters.

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: A multicenter prospective database, analyzed as a consecutive series with complete data at baseline and 1 year.
points: Database entry: age over 18 with ASD and Cobb 20 degrees or more, SVA 5 cm or more, PT 25 degrees or more and/or thoracic kyphosis 60 degrees or more.
Study inclusion: complete SRS-Schwab parameters and complete ODI, SRS-22 and SF-36 at baseline and 1 year.
Treatment group assigned by the initial management approach, chosen by patient and surgeon.
All radiographs measured at one center (NYU) with Spineview software.
Grade change sorted into improved by 1 or 2 grades, unchanged, or deteriorated by 1 or 2 grades.
Paired t tests within groups; unpaired t tests or chi-square between groups; significance at 0.05.
slides.notes: This is a selection and measurement paper, so read the methods for what could bias the link between grade and outcome. Selection: patients entered only with complete data at both visits. The number enrolled in the database and the number excluded for missing data are not reported, so there is no flow diagram and no follow-up rate. The Discussion says full 1-year follow-up was obtained, but that is true by definition of the inclusion rule. If patients who did badly were less likely to return questionnaires, the association would be distorted in an unknown direction. Treatment allocation: not randomized; it reflects patient input and physician counseling. Measurement: a strength is that all radiographs were read centrally with validated software, which reduces site-to-site variation. Interobserver error for this cohort is not reported. The 1-year window is not defined further. HRQOL change was judged against MCID values from a 2005 meeting presentation (Table 1): ODI minus 15, PCS plus 5.2, SRS pain plus 0.587, appearance plus 0.8, activity plus 0.375, mental plus 0.42. Our checks: the overall counts add up (290 women plus 51 men is 341; 177 plus 164 is 341), the pooled mean age of 54.4 matches the group means, and the age, BMI, sex and prior-surgery P values reproduce (about 0.09, 0.008, 0.64 and below 0.001), as do the Table 3 chi-square P values. But many printed percentages are impossible with the stated group sizes. With 177 operative patients: female 83.9% (149 of 177 is 84.2%), prior surgery 36.9%, ODI MCID 53.6% and all three SVA grades in Table 3. With 164 nonoperative patients: PCS MCID 16.9% and all three SVA grades in Table 3. With 341 overall: PCS MCID 36.2%, SVA improved 22.5%, deteriorated 10.2% and SVA + at 1 year 20.6%. The SVA grade-change percentages fit about 325 or 334 patients, not 341 (our arithmetic). So some measures, SVA most clearly, appear to have been analyzed on fewer patients than the stated cohort, even though complete data was an inclusion rule. Every recompute that uses 177, 164 or 341 as a denominator inherits that doubt. No adjustment for treatment, age, prior surgery or baseline score is described for any analysis.

slides.title: Operative versus nonoperative at 1 year
slides.lead: Operative patients started worse and improved on every measure; nonoperative patients barely moved.
points: Baseline: operative patients were worse on every HRQOL score (P < 0.001) and had more malalignment: SVA 51 vs 19 mm, PT 22 vs 19 degrees, PI-LL 12 vs 5 degrees.
Reached ODI MCID: 53.6% operative vs 4.9% nonoperative.
Nonoperative SVA worsened slightly, 18.5 to 22.8 mm (P = 0.042).
slides.notes: This slide is context, not the main question, but it explains everything that follows. The two groups are different populations. Nonoperative patients had a mean ODI of 22.9, much milder than the operative group's 39.8 (the paper does not grade it), and only 7% had an SVA grade of ++ against 24.4% of operative patients. There is little room for them to improve, so their flat course is expected and says nothing about whether nonoperative care works (our reading). The authors read it as further support for surgery improving HRQOL and for nonoperative measures generally not doing so; given the baseline gap, that comparison is not like with like. Nonoperative patients did improve significantly in SF-36 MCS, SRS pain and SRS total, but the pain change of 0.2 is below the 0.587 MCID. Operative patients improved on all scores. Check the Discussion claim that operative patients reached at least MCID for all outcome scores against the means: ODI fell 14.8 points against an MCID of 15, so the claim fails for ODI even allowing for rounding (14.7 to 14.9). SRS mental rose from 3.5 to 3.9, but those are rounded to one decimal, so the true change could be anywhere from about 0.35 to 0.45 against an MCID of 0.42; it cannot be called short from the printed values (our arithmetic). More patients reached MCID after surgery on every measure (P < 0.001, Table 5). Note how small the operative PT change was: 22.2 to 20.2 degrees. Statistically significant, but small. A mean change does not tell you how many patients crossed a grade line: in the combined cohort 24.9% of PT grades changed, close to PI-LL (28.4%), and the paper gives no PT grade-change figures for the operative group alone. Recomputing Table 5: the operative and nonoperative MCID rates weighted by group size give 30.2% overall for ODI and 37.1% for PCS, against 29.6% and 36.2% printed. The other four columns reproduce. The paper does not explain the gap; given the denominator problems on the previous slide, the true group sizes for these columns may not be 177 and 164 (our reading).

slides.title: Main result: grade change and HRQOL change
slides.lead: Most grades did not move. When they did, improvement went with larger HRQOL gains than deterioration.
points: Unchanged grade at 1 year: PT 75.1%, SVA 67.4%, PI-LL 71.6%.
PT change tracked ODI and SRS total and appearance (P ≤ 0.034).
SVA change tracked ODI, SF-36 PCS and SRS total, activity and appearance (P ≤ 0.037).
PI-LL change tracked SF-36 PCS and SRS total, activity and appearance (P ≤ 0.03); not ODI.
Improved grade raised the chance of reaching MCID versus unchanged or worse: ODI, SRS activity and appearance for all three modifiers; plus PCS for SVA and PI-LL, and pain for PI-LL.

columns: Mean ODI change, worse vs improved
SRS total change, worse vs improved

slides.see: Figures 6 to 8 show the MCID rates by deteriorated, unchanged and improved grade; the deteriorated bars are often as tall as or taller than the unchanged bars.
slides.notes: Read the table carefully. Lower ODI is better, so a negative change is improvement. Even patients whose grade got worse improved on average: ODI fell 5.5 to 8 points and SRS total rose. So deterioration of a grade did not mean patients got worse, only that they improved less. Table 7 compares only improved against deteriorated, the two extremes, and leaves out the two thirds to three quarters whose grade did not change. That design maximizes the contrast. Figures 6 to 8 do include the unchanged group, and by our reading of the bars the deteriorated group often reached MCID as often as or more often than the unchanged group. For PT, for example, roughly 44% of deteriorated patients reached PCS MCID against about 33% unchanged, and 50% against about 36% for SRS activity. A truly responsive grade should give a stepwise pattern. What is consistent is that the improved group does best, which fits with surgery driving both the grade and the outcome. Group sizes are not given. Taking them from the percentages of 341 (our assumption: about 49 improved and 36 worse for PT, 77 and 35 for SVA, 71 and 26 for PI-LL), we recomputed the 12 significant Table 7 P values from the printed means and SDs. Only SVA PCS (0.008) and SVA appearance (below 0.001) reproduce cleanly. Almost all the rest come out about twice the printed value with a two-sided t test: for example PT appearance 0.005 vs 0.002, PT total 0.031 vs 0.017, SVA total 0.002 vs 0.001, PI-LL total 0.012 vs 0.006. Halving our values matches most printed ones (PI-LL total 0.006, PI-LL activity 0.029, PT ODI 0.031), which fits one-tailed testing; that is our inference, since the Methods say only independent t test. Under two-sided testing four results would lose significance: ODI for PT (about 0.06) and SVA (about 0.06), and SRS activity for SVA (about 0.07) and PI-LL (about 0.06). The denominators are themselves doubtful (previous slides), so treat this as a strong query rather than a proven error. The abstract and Key Points list MCID results for ODI, PCS, activity and pain but omit SRS appearance, which the Results say was significant for all three modifiers. There are 24 comparisons in Table 7 and 18 in Figures 6 to 8 with no correction for multiple testing.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: A large central-read cohort that supports face validity, but the analysis cannot separate the grade from the operation.
points: Strengths: prospective multicenter cohort, operative and nonoperative patients, central radiograph reads, standard HRQOL tools.
Confounding by treatment: no stratification or adjustment for surgery (ours).
Selection: complete-case only; enrolled and excluded numbers not reported.
Concurrent measures: grade and HRQOL measured at the same visit, so prediction is not tested (ours).
MCID values are from a meeting presentation; the authors note limited ASD-specific MCID data.
No standard nonoperative protocol (authors' limitation).
slides.notes: The core weakness, in our view, is confounding by treatment. Improved grades likely came mostly from surgery, since none of the modifiers improved significantly in the nonoperative group. Surgery may also improve HRQOL through decompression and other effects unrelated to the grade. So an improved-grade group is largely an operated group, and a worse or unchanged group is largely a nonoperated group with milder disease. The paper never repeats the analysis within the operative group alone, which is the analysis that would show whether the grade, rather than the treatment, carries the information (our suggestion). Our addition, not raised by the authors: patients with the worst baseline scores had the most room to improve, and regression to the mean (extreme baseline values drifting back on remeasurement) could add to the apparent gains. Second, the deteriorated groups are small, roughly 26 to 36 patients by our arithmetic, so their means are imprecise, and no confidence intervals are reported. Third, the claim that the classification is validated rests on P values below 0.05 for a subset of outcomes, without effect sizes, adjustment or a multiple-testing correction. Fourth, follow-up is 1 year. The authors cite earlier work that 1-year outcomes predict 2-year outcomes; durability of the link is not tested here. The authors list their own limitations: no standard nonoperative protocol, and limited ASD-specific MCID data that may be revised. They do not discuss confounding by treatment or missing-data selection. What holds up: the direction is consistent across three modifiers and several outcomes, the radiographs were measured centrally, and the result fits the earlier cross-sectional work linking these parameters to disability. Fair summary: good evidence that the modifiers move with HRQOL in a mixed operative cohort; weak evidence that changing the grade itself is what improves patients.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "In 341 ISSG patients followed 1 year, improvement in the SRS-Schwab PT, SVA or PI-LL grade went with bigger gains in SRS-22 total than a worsened grade, and in ODI for PT and SVA but not PI-LL, which supports the modifiers as clinically meaningful targets. Most grades did not change, grade improvement came mainly with surgery, and the analysis did not separate grade from treatment."
points: Grades: PT 20 and 30 degrees, SVA 4 and 9.5 cm, PI-LL 10 and 20 degrees.
Operative ODI 39.8 to 25.0; nonoperative 22.9 to 22.2.
Patients with a worse grade still improved on average.
Do not call it prediction in a separate cohort; it is association within one cohort.
slides.notes: Expect these follow-up questions. Does this prove that correcting the sagittal grade makes patients better? No. Grade improvement and HRQOL gain were measured together, and both were driven largely by surgery. It shows the grades move with outcomes, which is necessary for a useful classification but is not proof that the grade is the cause. Which modifier mattered most? SVA was associated with the most outcomes in Table 7: ODI, PCS and SRS total, activity and appearance. PI-LL was not significant for ODI on mean change, but improvement in PI-LL went with reaching ODI MCID in Figure 8 (P = 0.013). The paper does not rank the modifiers formally. Why did patients with a worsened grade still improve? Our guess is that many were operated or had mild disease, and a grade change is a coarse step. The paper does not break the deteriorated group down by treatment. Does it say anything about nonoperative care? Only that nonoperative patients started with milder disability (ODI 22.9) and changed little; the groups are not comparable. What about the coronal curve type? Not tested here. How strong are the MCID thresholds? They come from a 2005 meeting presentation, and the authors say they may be refined. Is it independent of the developers? No; the authors include the developers of the classification, and funding came partly through industry grants to the study group. If asked for the numbers to remember: 341 patients, 177 operative, 1 year, about 70% of grades unchanged, ODI MCID reached by 53.6% after surgery against 4.9% without.

decks.not_reviewed: The companion editorial in the same issue (Neurosurg Focus 36(5):E16), the Glassman 2007 complication classification it relies on, any longer follow-up of this cohort, and the two source databases themselves. Figures 1 and 2 are intraoperative photographs and an example radiograph and carry no data. The full 9-page paper was read.

slides.title: Uribe 2014: MIS, hybrid and open surgery for adult deformity
slides.lead: In 60 matched patients, 55 with complete complication data, MIS had no intraoperative complications against 25% in open surgery, but total and major complications did not differ significantly.
points: Uribe JS, Deukmedjian AR, Mummaneni PV, et al, International Spine Study Group. Neurosurg Focus 2014;36(5):E15
Retrospective comparison of two multicenter databases, 16 institutions, propensity matched
20 MIS, 20 hybrid (HYB), 20 open; complications analyzed in 55 with complete data
Any complication: MIS 30%, HYB 47.4%, open 62.5% (P = 0.147)
Intraoperative complication: 0%, 5.3%, 25% (P = 0.027)
Full text read end to end; no critique-only or partial PDF
slides.notes: This is a small matched comparison, not a trial. Two databases were joined: a retrospective MIS and hybrid database and a prospective open database, from 16 sites. 280 patients met the initial query and 60 were kept after matching, 20 per group. The headline the authors give is that MIS had significantly fewer intraoperative complications. Hold that against the numbers: the only complication category that reached significance across all three groups was intraoperative complications, plus deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in the hybrid group, both by chi-square on very small counts; an exact test (ours) keeps intraoperative significant but not DVT. And the authors say in the Discussion that 15% of the open group's intraoperative events were blood loss over 4 L, an event they themselves call of questionable impact. Total complications ran 30% to 62.5% in the expected direction but did not reach significance, and the authors attribute that to lack of power. We would teach this paper as hypothesis generating (ours). Its value in the library is historical: an early attempt to separate approach from patient factors in deformity complications. The paper is listed in the SRS Quality and Safety Resource Library. The companion editorial (E16) was not read. Disclosures: several authors consult for or hold royalties from implant makers, including NuVasive, and one author reports research support from RTI, NuVasive and Lanx for the study described.

slides.title: The question and the groups
slides.lead: Does approach, rather than patient profile, drive complications in adult spinal deformity surgery?
points: Hypothesis: minimally invasive surgery causes fewer complications than open surgery
MIS: stand-alone transpsoas lateral interbody fusion (LIF), LIF with percutaneous pedicle screws, or MIS TLIF with percutaneous screws
HYB: MIS LIF or TLIF plus open pedicle screws, laminectomy or osteotomy
OPEN: open pedicle screw fixation with or without interbody fusion
Outcomes: complications, VAS back and leg, ODI, radiographs, at 1 year
slides.notes: The authors frame MIS as having hypothetical advantages, less muscle injury, less infection, faster narcotic independence and lower cost, and a potential disadvantage, limited sagittal correction. Their question is whether the higher complication rates in open deformity surgery belong to the approach or to the patients who get it. Matching is meant to answer that. Note the comparison is three strategies, each a mixture of techniques. The MIS group mixes stand-alone lateral fusion with percutaneously instrumented constructs; the Discussion adds percutaneous presacral interbody fusion to the MIS definition, which the Methods do not list. Open includes patients with or without interbody work, and only 3 open patients had an osteotomy, so this is not a comparison against 3-column osteotomy surgery. Primary outcome is not named. Complications were the focus, classed as intraoperative or postoperative and minor or major using the Glassman 2007 list reproduced in Table 1. Under that list, excessive bleeding is a minor complication, and the authors define excessive blood loss as over 4 L. Keep that definition in mind for the main result.

slides.title: Selection and matching
slides.lead: 280 patients went in, 60 came out, and the two databases had overlapping but not identical entry rules, which the authors call similar.
points: Study entry: age over 45, coronal Cobb over 20 degrees, 3 or more fused levels, at least 1 year follow-up
Open patients with thoracic Cobb over 75 degrees excluded
Matched on age, preop SVA, posterior levels fused and preop lumbar Cobb
slides.notes: Read the database rules carefully. MIS and HYB patients came from a retrospective database whose entry needed age over 18 and any one of: Cobb over 20, 3 or more fused segments, SVA over 5 cm, pelvic tilt over 20, or at least 1 year of follow-up. Open patients came from a prospective database needing any one of: Cobb over 20, SVA over 5 cm, pelvic tilt over 25, or thoracic kyphosis over 60. The authors call the two sets of criteria similar; they share age over 18, Cobb over 20 and SVA over 5 cm, but differ on pelvic tilt (20 vs 25), fused segments and follow-up (MIS/HYB only) and thoracic kyphosis (open only). The study then applied its own filters. The matching method is thin: propensity scores 'by applying linear regression', four variables, three groups, no description of how triplets were chosen, no balance statistics. Only 60 of 280 (21%, ours) were used, so the matched sample may not represent either database. Check the matched variable itself: preop SVA was 28 mm in MIS against 61 and 65 mm in the other groups. Table 5 gives that open-versus-MIS gap as 36.6 mm, P = 0.100. Not significant in 20 per group, but a matched variable differing by more than 3 cm says the matching did not equalize sagittal deformity (ours). Thoracic Cobb was significantly larger in the open group (28 vs 16 and 15 degrees). BMI was lower in MIS than HYB (23.9 vs 28.1, P = 0.03). SDs are not given for Table 2, so most baseline P values cannot be recomputed; sex (3, 2 and 2 men) gives P = 0.85 (ours), consistent with no difference. The Results give the matched cohort mean age 63 and ASA 2.2, but Table 2 group means average 64.9 years and ASA 2.27 (ours); 63 is the 280-patient query cohort. 88% were women and 65% were primary cases, per the text. Interbody levels differed by design (MIS and HYB 4.5 and 4.1 vs open 1.6, P < 0.001).

slides.title: Complications
slides.lead: Denominators were 20, 19 and 16; five patients, four of them open, lacked complete complication data (our back-calculation).
points: Three-group P: any 0.147, intraoperative 0.027, postoperative 0.401, minor 0.065, needing surgery 0.952, DVT 0.049
Excessive blood loss over 4 L: 3 open patients, called 15% by the authors
Complications did not change ODI, per the authors; no data shown
slides.notes: We rebuilt the counts. The percentages only work with denominators of 20 MIS, 19 HYB and 16 OPEN: any complication 6, 9 and 10 patients, total 25 of 55 (45.5%). With those counts, an uncorrected chi-square reproduces every Table 7 P value (ours), so the table is internally consistent. But most expected cell counts are below 5, where chi-square is unreliable. Freeman-Halton exact tests (ours): intraoperative P = 0.019, DVT 0.058 (no longer significant), minor 0.044 (now significant), any 0.165. Which categories reach significance depends on the test. Intraoperative events were 0, 1 and 4. Pairwise (ours, Fisher exact): MIS vs open P = 0.031, matching the paper's 0.03; MIS vs HYB P = 0.49; HYB vs open P = 0.16. So the abstract's claim that MIS had significantly fewer intraoperative complications than both HYB and open is not supported for HYB. The Discussion itself says the only significant complication difference was MIS vs open intraoperative. Now the size of that signal: 4 open patients, of whom 3 had blood loss over 4 L. Blood loss is also an outcome (669 vs 2322 ml), so the intraoperative finding largely restates the blood loss finding (ours). The authors call 15% for those 3 patients, which uses 20 as the denominator; on the table's 16 it is 18.8% (ours). Odd pattern: major complications equal any complications in every group, yet HYB and open had minor complications of 21% and 25%. That is only possible if every patient with a minor event also had a major one (ours). Complications needing surgery were 15 to 19% in all groups, P = 0.952; for the patient that may be the most useful row. Missing complication data in 4 of 20 open patients (20%) is not explained.

slides.title: Operative, radiographic and clinical results
slides.lead: MIS bled less but left more PI-LL mismatch; all groups improved on ODI.
points: EBL MIS vs open P < 0.001; OR time HYB vs open P < 0.001; stay not different
PI-LL change open vs MIS: -14 vs -3 degrees, P = 0.04
VAS leg did not improve significantly in MIS (P = 0.564)
slides.notes: Blood loss and operative time behave as expected. HYB ran longest, and the authors attribute that to more interbody levels and repositioning between lateral and prone. Length of stay did not differ; the authors say further study is needed to explain why MIS stayed as long as open. Radiographs: the authors say they cannot judge sagittal correction because enrolled patients were, in general, already globally balanced. That fits MIS best, with preop SVA 28 mm; open and HYB started at 65 and 61 mm (ours). MIS was the only group whose postop PI-LL stayed above 10 degrees (17), and open corrected PI-LL more than MIS (change -14 vs -3, P = 0.04 in text, 0.035 in Table 5). Open ended with more residual lumbar Cobb (21 vs 11 and 10). Table 5 also shows postop pelvic tilt higher in HYB than both other groups (37 vs 26 MIS and 25 open; P = 0.003 and 0.001), which the text never mentions. Clinical results are thin: Table 6 gives only within-group change and P values, no baseline or 1-year values, no SDs, no between-group test. MIS improved ODI by 20.7 points but leg pain only 0.7 (P = 0.564). HYB leg pain change was also not significant (P = 0.057), although the Table 6 footnote says only MIS leg pain failed. The abstract says all ODI and VAS improvements were P < 0.001, but Table 6 gives 0.004 and 0.001 for HYB and open ODI and 0.001 to 0.057 for several VAS changes. With 20 per group, do not read the ODI ranking between groups as a finding (ours). Some Table 4 change values do not match post minus pre: MIS SVA 28 to 31 is given as -2, HYB PT 36 to 37 is given as -1, HYB PI-LL 26 to 11 is given as -12. Paired changes on incomplete data could explain small gaps, but not sign reversals (ours). The many Table 5 P values of 1.000 suggest adjusted pairwise tests, but the Methods name only ANOVA, chi-square and paired t tests (ours).

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: Small, retrospective, two-database, matched on four variables, with several text-table conflicts.
points: Confounding by database: retrospective MIS/HYB vs prospective open, different entry rules, 16 sites
Matching thin and possibly unsuccessful: SVA 28 vs 65 mm, thoracic Cobb 16 vs 28
1-year follow-up only; no fusion status
Power: authors say only large differences were detectable; no numbers given
Abstract overstates: MIS vs HYB intraoperative difference not significant
Internal errors: stay mean, levels fused, implant failure rate, matching variables
slides.notes: Authors' limitations: retrospective design, multicenter variability in data collection and complication reporting, 1-year follow-up as an interim analysis with no fusion or long-term conclusions, open group able to do 3-column osteotomy (only 3 did), difficulty matching such different procedures, and small sample. They add that the disparate databases may be a factor in the intraoperative difference, which is an honest admission that the main signal may be how each database recorded complications. The authors also say most of the open group's intraoperative complications were blood loss over 4 L. Our additions: the open group came from the prospective database, so if it recorded complications more completely, ascertainment alone could raise open rates (ours; not tested). And the signal is 4 patients versus 0 (ours). Source problems found: the overall mean stay is given as 8.5 days, but group means of 6.4, 4.5 and 7.4 in equal groups average 6.1. The Discussion says HYB fused 6.4 posterior levels versus 5.2 for MIS; Table 3 gives MIS 5.6 and open 5.2. The Discussion says MIS implant failure was 8%; Table 7 says 10.0%, and 8% is not possible in 20 patients. The Discussion says groups were matched on age, ODI and coronal and sagittal parameters; the Methods list age, SVA, posterior levels and lumbar Cobb. The Discussion says PI-LL correction did not differ between groups; Results and Table 5 say open corrected more than MIS. The Results say MIS vs open minor complications per patient was 0.4 vs 0 with P = 0.4 in a sentence about differences. Complications per patient (1.06, 0.84, 0.30, P = 0.04) are said to be in Table 7 but are not. The text says 46% of the 60 patients had a major complication; Table 7 is 45.5% of 55. Postop thoracic Cobb is given as P < 0.003 but Table 5 has P = 0.031 for open vs MIS. Table 6 footnote says every change was significant except MIS leg pain, but HYB leg pain has P = 0.057; the abstract's P < 0.001 for all ODI and VAS changes is contradicted by Table 6. The Discussion gives preop thoracic Cobb HYB 15 vs MIS 16 and open 28 with P = 0.008, but Table 5 has 0.008 for open vs MIS, 0.005 for open vs HYB and 1.000 for HYB vs MIS. Results give mean age 63 and ASA 2.2; Table 2 averages 64.9 and 2.27.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: An early matched comparison suggesting fewer intraoperative complications with MIS, driven by 4 open patients, 3 of them with blood loss over 4 L, with no significant difference in total or major complications.
points: Spoken summary: In 60 matched adult deformity patients from two databases, 55 with complete complication data, MIS had no intraoperative complications versus 25% in open surgery, mostly blood loss over 4 L. Total complications were 30%, 47% and 63% for MIS, hybrid and open, not significantly different. MIS bled less but left more PI-LL mismatch. It is hypothesis generating.
Q: Was the matching successful? Not fully: MIS preop SVA 28 vs 65 mm open; thoracic Cobb 16 vs 28.
Q: Is MIS safer overall? Not shown: any complication P = 0.147; needing surgery 15% to 19%, P = 0.952.
Q: What drove the intraoperative result? 4 open patients, 3 with blood loss over 4 L.
Q: Did MIS correct sagittal alignment? Not judged: the authors say the cohort was largely balanced; MIS started at SVA 28 mm and left PI-LL at 17 degrees.
Q: Denominators? 20, 19 and 16 for complications.
slides.notes: Lead with the design, because it decides how much the numbers can carry: two different databases, one retrospective and one prospective, matched down to 20 per group. Then give the result in the authors' words and the qualifier in yours: the authors conclude approach may affect complications and that less invasive techniques should be considered if deformity goals can be met. That conditional is the important part, since the MIS patients here had little sagittal deformity to correct (ours) and left with the largest PI-LL mismatch. Expect a question about whether hybrid is the worst of both worlds: it had the longest operations (665 min) and the only DVTs (3 of 19, 15.8%, chi-square P = 0.049, exact P = 0.058, ours), but intermediate overall complications; with 19 patients, treat the DVT result as a chance-level signal unless repeated (ours). Expect a question about selection: the MIS patients had lower BMI (23.9) and less sagittal imbalance, which suggests surgeons picked MIS for easier cases, and matching on four variables cannot remove that (ours). If asked whether this changes practice, our answer is that it supports considering MIS for well-balanced patients with lumbar coronal curves when goals can be met, and says nothing about patients needing major sagittal correction (ours).

decks.not_reviewed: Full text of the 14-page paper was read end to end, including Tables 1 to 8. Figures 2 to 5 were read only from their captions and the text; their plotted values were not extracted. No supplement is cited. The source studies for the MCID and SCB thresholds and the earlier Smith et al. back and leg pain papers (references 28 and 29) were not reviewed.

slides.title: Scheer 2015: back and leg pain after ASD surgery
slides.lead: Operated patients more often moved down a pain category at 2 years, but the comparison with nonoperated patients is unadjusted and the operated group started with far worse pain.
points: Scheer JK, Smith JS, Clark AJ, et al., International Spine Study Group. J Neurosurg Spine 2015;22:540-553
Retrospective review of a prospective 11-site US database; 421 patients with 2-year follow-up
235 operated, 186 nonoperated; pain measured on a 0-10 NRS and grouped as none, mild, moderate, severe
Reported odds ratios: 6.2 for back pain improvement and 3.0 for leg pain improvement with surgery
Among operated patients with preoperative pain, 24.3% were free of back pain and 37.8% free of leg pain at 2 years
Several tables contain internal errors; see the appraisal slide
slides.notes: This deck was prepared from the full text. The PDF is the correct paper and is complete. Frame it as a descriptive cohort, not a trial. The question is what happens to back and leg pain over 2 years, by treatment, surgery type, SRS-Schwab coronal curve type and baseline pain severity, and how pain change relates to ODI, PCS and satisfaction. The authors present it as a counseling reference. That is its real value: counts of how many patients improved, stayed the same or got worse. The headline 6.2 is an odds ratio, and the paper words it as 6 times more likely. Our arithmetic from Table 2: 68.2% versus 25.7% improved, a risk ratio of about 2.7. Say it that way at the podium. The study was run through the ISSG Foundation, funded by DePuy Spine research grants and donations, and many authors disclose industry consulting. There is no adjustment for baseline differences in any comparison, so every between-group result is crude.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: The authors say pain is the primary concern of ASD patients and often the reason they seek surgery, yet most research has tracked disability scores.
points: Earlier studies by Smith et al. showed surgery improved back and leg pain NRS more than nonoperative care
That work did not address baseline pain severity, curve type or osteotomy use
Aim: compare 2-year change in pain category by treatment, surgery type, SRS-Schwab curve type and baseline severity
Also asked: does back or leg pain drive ODI, PCS and satisfaction?
Pain categories: none 0, mild 1-4, moderate 5-6, severe 7-10
Improvement or worsening means a move of at least 1 category
slides.notes: Point out the outcome definition early, because it shapes everything after. A change of category is coarse. A patient at NRS 4 who drops to 1 has not improved by this rule, while a patient at 7 who drops to 6 has. Severe patients cannot worsen, so the worsening cell for severe is NA in Table 6. Mild patients can improve only by becoming pain free. This makes the category outcome favor whoever starts with more pain. The authors do note in the Discussion that patients with more severe pain have a greater likelihood of moving to a lower pain score because of the NRS design. The thresholds used for MCID and SCB were set by the authors from lumbar fusion literature: NRS MCID minus 2 and SCB minus 3, ODI MCID minus 15 and SCB minus 18.8, PCS MCID plus 5.2 and SCB plus 6.2. The Introduction quotes a pain MCID of 1.2 to 1.6 points and SCB of 2.5, so the chosen cutoffs are stricter than the ones cited in the Introduction. The authors concede these thresholds were not validated in deformity patients. Ask the room: is moving one pain category what a patient means by better?

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: Follow-up was 82.2% for operated patients and 46.2% for nonoperated patients.
points: Inclusion: age over 18 and Cobb 20 degrees or more, SVA 5 cm or more, PT 25 degrees or more, or TK 60 degrees or more
Excluded: neuromuscular deformity, active infection or cancer
Treatment chosen by surgeon and patient; progressive deficit, myelopathy or incontinence was generally advised surgery
Surgery groups: Other 40, osteotomy only 54, decompression only 41, both 100
No multivariable adjustment; chi-square and t-tests after omnibus tests
slides.notes: The two groups are not comparable, and the paper does not try to make them comparable. Operated patients had almost 3 points more back pain at baseline, two thirds were in the severe category against under a quarter, and they had worse ODI and PCS. Patients with neurologic deficit were steered to surgery. Then follow-up differed sharply: 235 of 286 operated (82.2%) against 186 of 403 nonoperated (46.2%). The authors name this loss in the nonoperated group as a limitation and suggest it may have exaggerated the benefit of surgery. Nonoperated patients who did well may simply have stopped coming back. The enrollment years, the content of nonoperative care, and the number of sites contributing each group are not given. Recompute check (ours): from the printed means and SDs, a t-test gives P about 0.14 for age, 0.002 for BMI and 0.0002 for CCI, against the printed 0.0934, 0.0001 and 0.0073. The paper may have used rank tests, which it mentions, so this is not proof of error, but the printed P values cannot be reproduced from the table. Sex split, 83.8% and 86.6% women, recomputes. Operated curve-type percentages use 234 classified patients, except D 25.5%, which is 60/235 (60/234 is 25.6%), a trivial mixed denominator; the nonoperated and overall percentages recompute, and our chi-square on curve type gives P about 0.56, consistent with the printed >0.05. Table 2 baseline P values also recompute by chi-square (ours), except back pain > leg pain, 124/225 vs 104/181: P about 0.64 against the printed 0.7007, still not significant. One operated patient could not be classified by curve type.

slides.title: Operated versus nonoperated at 2 years
slides.lead: Surgery was associated with more category improvement and less worsening, but leg pain NRS ended level.

rows: New leg pain, if none before

points: Mean back NRS at 2 years: 3.5 operated vs 4.5 nonoperated (P = 0.0004)
Mean leg NRS at 2 years: 2.5 vs 2.7 (P = 0.64)
Mean change: back -3.6 vs +0.1, leg -1.8 vs +0.4 (P < 0.0001)
ODI and PCS were similar at 1 and 2 years; operated patients started worse and ended level, so their change was larger
slides.see: Figure 2 shows the operated back pain curve starting well above the nonoperated curve and finishing below it; leg pain curves finish together.
slides.notes: We recomputed the odds ratios from Table 2 and they match: 6.21 for back improvement, 3.03 for leg, 10.98 for back worsening in nonoperated patients, 2.02 for leg worsening, 1.90 for staying in the same back category. As risk ratios, ours, these are about 2.7, 2.1 and 8.3. Read the end states, not only the changes. At 2 years operated patients still averaged 3.5 on back NRS, and their leg NRS ended level with nonoperated patients, as did ODI and PCS. Operated patients started worse and ended level, so their change was larger. Our reading: that fits real benefit, but it also fits regression to the mean in people who chose surgery at their worst, which this design cannot separate. The 37.0% at 6 weeks and 33.3% at 2 years figures quoted in the abstract are new leg pain among the operated patients who had no leg pain before surgery: 17 of 46 with 6-week data and 20 of 60. They are not rates for all operated patients. Of the 17 with new leg pain at 6 weeks, 10 still had it at 2 years and 7 had resolved. At 2 years only, 20 of 74 (27.0%) nonoperated patients without leg pain had new leg pain, P = 0.50 against 33.3% (Table 2); the 6-week figure has no nonoperated comparator. The authors draw no conclusion from this. Our inference from a crude comparison: new leg pain after surgery is not clearly due to surgery. Table 2 prints operated back no change as 60 (25.2%); 60 of 211 is 28.4%, and the reported OR of 1.9 only works with 28.4%. Table 2 also gives P = 0.0009 for back new onset, 1 of 1 against 7 of 14; a Fisher test on those counts gives P = 1.0 (ours). Table 2 prints only n (%); the denominators in our table are back-calculated by us. The no-change P values, 0.0026 and 0.7859, reproduce exactly with them, which supports them. But the rows do not add up: nonoperated back accounts for 172 of 179, operated leg 168 of 207 and nonoperated leg 115 of 169, although the footnote says worsening includes new onset. The leg pain rows are incompletely accounted for.

slides.title: Subgroups: surgery type, curve type, baseline severity
slides.lead: Every subgroup comparison is unadjusted, many cells are small, and several stated P values do not survive a recount.

rows: New leg pain: osteotomy only > decompression only
Leg improved: Type L > Type T
Leg improved: Type L > Type D
Leg worsened: Type D > Type T
Back pain-free: severe vs mild start
Back no change: mild > severe start

points: Decompression groups more often reached leg NRS and ODI MCID (authors)
Osteotomy only improved back pain more than Other, 74.0% vs 50.0% (Table 3)
Type N, sagittal only, improved least in back pain: 57.1% vs 80.6% for Type L
Severe preoperative pain: OR 3.6 for back and 4.5 for leg improvement vs mild
slides.notes: Our P values are Fisher exact tests on the table counts; the paper says it used chi-square, and its denominators may differ, so treat ours as a check, not a correction. The osteotomy and new leg pain message rests on 1 of 6 decompression-only patients who started without leg pain. The decompression plus osteotomy group had 7 of 16 (43.8%), the same as osteotomy alone. So the claim that osteotomy raises new leg pain is fragile. The abstract and Conclusions headline that decompression improved leg pain more than Other (p < 0.05) does not recompute from Table 3 either: 19 of 33 (D) and 50 of 88 (D+O) against 8 of 20, P 0.22 to 0.26 (ours). Type T had new leg pain in only 1 of 23, against 4 of 8 (N), 3 of 6 (L) and 12 of 22 (D) (Table 4), and that difference holds on recount: Fisher P 0.0002 vs D, 0.01 vs N, 0.02 vs L (ours, unadjusted, no multiplicity correction, cells of 6 and 8). For Type L the leg pain advantage holds against Type D but not against Type T. Surgery type was not randomized, and the authors say deformity severity by group was not evaluated. Decompression patients had the most severe leg pain at baseline, 57.9% in D only, which gives them most room to improve. For baseline severity the paper says severe patients were more often pain free than mild. Look at the arithmetic: 29, 10 and 12 pain-free patients are given as percentages of all 210, 13.8%, 4.8% and 5.7%. Within each group, ours, mild 12 of 29 (41.4%) were pain free, moderate 10 of 43 (23.3%) and severe 29 of 138 (21.0%). The direction reverses. The text also says mild patients more often had no change in back pain than severe, p < 0.05; Table 6 gives 13 of 29 vs 39 of 138, P about 0.12 (ours), not significant. Severe patients more often moved down a category, but mild patients more often ended pain free. For leg pain severe vs mild, the counts give an OR of 4.25 with the printed CI of 1.9 to 9.7, so the printed 4.5 looks like a typo. The other ORs recompute.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: Useful counts for counseling; weak evidence for causation; several printed errors.
points: Strength: large multicenter prospective database with standardized radiographs and pain NRS
Strength: reports category moves both ways, including worsening and new pain
Weak: treatment chosen by indication; baseline pain far worse in operated group; no adjustment
Weak: 46.2% follow-up in nonoperated patients (authors note this)
Weak: MCID and SCB cutoffs borrowed from lumbar fusion (authors note this)
Weak: dozens of comparisons; omnibus tests were run first to limit Type I error, but no formal multiplicity correction
Error: Table 5 ODI SCB exceeds ODI MCID in every curve type, which cannot happen
Error: Table 7 all-patient ODI change -8.2 conflicts with 41.3 to 25.8
slides.notes: Lead with what holds. The operated group did move down pain categories far more often, and worsening of back pain was rare after surgery, 3.3%. That is useful at the consent table. The limits the authors themselves list are the retrospective design, loss of nonoperated patients, no data on cause or duration of pain, no comparison of deformity severity across surgery groups, and unvalidated MCID values. The rest is our reading. The SCB threshold for ODI, minus 18.8, is stricter than the MCID, minus 15, so the SCB count must be at or below the MCID count. Table 5 prints ODI SCB above MCID for all four curve types, for example Type N 45 (78.9%) against 29 (50.9%), and the SCB row totals 153 against 95 in Table 8. The text's claims that Type N and Type L more often reached ODI SCB rest on that row. Table 7 gives all operated ODI 41.3 at baseline and 25.8 at 2 years, a fall of 15.5, but prints the change as minus 8.2, smaller than every subgroup change from minus 9.2 to minus 21.1. The PCS change, printed 4.1, has the same problem against 33.4 to 41.6. For satisfaction, the text uses 27 patients whose back but not leg pain improved, Table 2 gives 41, and the percentages in the same paragraph only work with 41. Several stated significant results recompute as not significant: ODI MCID for severe vs mild back pain, 73 of 145 vs 11 of 30, P about 0.2, and ODI SCB, 62 of 145 vs 8 of 30, P about 0.15 (ours); the PCS MCID and SCB differences do hold. The text says moderate leg pain patients more often reached PCS MCID than mild, but Table 8 shows the reverse, 41.2% vs 65.9%.

slides.title: How to say it
