slides.lead: "In a large ISSG cohort, about two thirds of operated ASD patients moved down a back pain category by 2 years, against a quarter of nonoperated patients, and back pain rarely got worse after surgery."
points: Counseling numbers: of operated patients with back pain, 24.3% were pain free at 2 years; with leg pain, 37.8%
About 1 in 3 operated patients without leg pain had leg pain at 2 years; 27% of nonoperated patients did too (crude comparison, ours)
Back pain improvement tracked ODI, PCS and satisfaction more than leg pain did (authors)
Do not quote 6 times more likely; it is an odds ratio from unadjusted, unequal groups
Do not lean on the surgery-type or curve-type subgroups or Table 5
slides.notes: A 60-second version: 421 ISSG patients, 235 operated and 186 not, followed 2 years. Operated patients started with much worse pain and more often moved down a pain category, 68% against 26% for back pain. Nonoperated patients more often got worse. By 2 years, leg pain scores, ODI and PCS had converged between the groups. Expect these questions. First, does this prove surgery works better than nonoperative care for pain? No. Treatment was chosen, the operated group started near 7 on the NRS against 4, and more than half the nonoperated patients were lost. The direction is consistent, the size is not reliable. Second, will my patient get leg pain from an osteotomy? About a third of operated patients without leg pain had it at 2 years, but so did 27% of nonoperated patients, and the osteotomy versus decompression contrast rests on 1 of 6 patients. Third, which patients do best? Severe pain moves down a category more often, but mild pain more often ends at zero; our recount of the paper's numbers, not the authors' reading. Fourth, does leg pain matter to ODI? In the authors' regressions back pain change explained more of ODI change, r2 0.22, than leg pain change, r2 0.17, and both together 0.32. Fifth, satisfaction: patients whose back pain alone improved were more satisfied than those whose leg pain alone improved, SRS-22 satisfaction 4.3 against 3.7, but the group sizes are small and inconsistently reported.

decks.not_reviewed: No supplement is cited in the PDF. The full paper was read, including Tables 1-6 and Figures 1-3. Cited studies (for example Glassman 2007 for the major and minor complication criteria, and the SPORT obesity subgroup analyses) were not reviewed. The database's total enrollment and the years of surgery are not given in the paper, so they could not be checked.

slides.title: Obesity and ASD surgery: Soroceanu 2015
slides.lead: Obese patients had more major complications and infections. The authors conclude they also improved less, but by our arithmetic on Table 6 their 2-year ODI gain matched nonobese patients.
points: Soroceanu A, Burton DC, Diebo BG, et al., International Spine Study Group. J Neurosurg Spine 2015;23:656-664
Retrospective review of a prospective multicenter ASD database, 11 US centers
241 patients with 2-year data: 175 nonobese, 66 obese (BMI 30 or more)
Bottom line: major complications 53% vs 33.7%, adjusted IRR 1.54. Both groups improved, but obese patients started worse and stayed worse
slides.notes: Frame it first. This is a cohort study, not a trial, so it can show association and nothing about what weight loss would change. The data come from the International Spine Study Group database. The paper describes it as multi-institutional and prospective, with consecutively enrolled patients at 11 US centers, each doing more than 100 ASD cases a year. This deck was prepared from the full text. No supplement is cited. The paper does not give the years of surgery or how many patients the database held in total. It starts its count at 286 patients eligible for 2-year follow-up. Funding: a DePuy Spine grant went to the ISSG Foundation, per the disclosure line. The paper has three messages: obesity raised major complications and infection, obesity did not change operative time, blood loss or length of stay, and obese patients gained less in health-related quality of life. Hold the third one loosely. Slide 5 shows that the net 2-year ODI change was the same in both groups. That reading is ours, from the paper's own Table 6.

slides.title: Selection: who got in
slides.lead: Only patients with complete baseline and 2-year data were analyzed, so this is a cohort of completers.
points: Database entry: age over 18 with Cobb 20 degrees or more, SVA 5 cm or more, pelvic tilt 25 degrees or more, and/or thoracic kyphosis 60 degrees or more
Excluded from database: neuromuscular deformity, active infection, malignancy
286 eligible for 2-year follow-up; 17 excluded for no baseline BMI, 28 for incomplete HRQL; 241 analyzed
Obese mean BMI 36.1 vs 24.2 nonobese
slides.notes: The flow arithmetic holds: 17 plus 28 is 45, 286 less 45 is 241, and 175 plus 66 is 241. Obese patients were 27 percent of the cohort, which matches 66 of 241. Three things to notice. First, the groups were not alike. Obese patients were 6 years older, had more comorbidity and more prior spine surgery, and were nearly twice as likely to have a 3-column osteotomy. Everything that follows depends on adjustment for these differences. Second, the analysis is limited to completers. Within the 286, 17 were dropped for no baseline BMI and 28 for incomplete HRQL data. The paper does not define eligible for 2-year follow-up or say who was lost before that count. The 45 excluded patients are not described, so we cannot tell whether they differed. Our inference: if the sickest obese patients were lost more often, complication and HRQL gaps could be understated, but the direction is not knowable from the paper. Third, Table 2 percentages do not all fit the group sizes. Our arithmetic: 83.1 percent, 55.4 percent and 3.1 percent fit 54, 36 and 2 of 65 obese patients, not 66. 86.7 percent and 38.1 percent fit 150 and 66 of 173 nonobese, and 11.7 percent fits 20 of 171. So some baseline data appear to be missing, which the paper does not report. Recomputed P values on those counts match the printed ones closely: prior surgery 0.017, smoking about 0.04, osteotomy 0.035, decompression 0.001. The one that does not reproduce is surgical approach. Posterior-only 61.1 versus 62.1 percent gives P about 0.89, not 0.34. The printed value may come from a test across all approach categories, which the table does not show. That explanation is our guess. Table 2 gives no standard deviations, so the age and CCI P values cannot be checked.

slides.title: Measurement: exposure, outcomes, models
slides.lead: Complications were collected on a standardized form; obesity was a single BMI cutoff.
points: Exposure: BMI 30 or more (CDC definition), measured at baseline; no class I, II, III split
Complications over 2 years: major and minor by a published checklist (Table 1), plus infection, implant, radiographic, neurologic, revision
Perioperative: EBL, operative time, LOS
HRQL: ODI, SF-36 physical, SRS-22 at baseline, 6 weeks, 1 year, 2 years
Complication models: Poisson or logistic, adjusted for age, smoking, comorbidity, prior surgery, osteotomy, decompression; radiographic, implant and revision models also rod size and material
HRQL models: repeated-measures mixed models adjusted for age, comorbidity, magnitude of surgery and major complications including revisions
slides.notes: The strength here is the complication capture. The authors stress that all sites prospectively collected complications on one standardized form, and they note that retrospective studies tend to undercount complications. Table 1 is worth a look: it is a long checklist split into major and minor. Note what it puts under infection. Major infection includes deep wound infection, pneumonia and sepsis. Minor infection includes superficial wound infection, urinary tract infection and Clostridium difficile. The text and abstract call the key result wound infection, but the outcome in Table 4 is labeled only Infection. The paper does not say which definition was used. Confounders were chosen by univariate analysis and expert opinion; the paper does not say whether they were prespecified. The HRQL models adjust for major complications and revisions. Our reading: if obesity worsens outcome partly by causing complications, adjusting for complications removes part of the effect being studied, so the HRQL gap shown is closer to a direct effect than a total effect. Obesity is one cutoff. The authors say sample size prevented a class III subgroup, so this paper cannot tell you whether risk climbs with BMI above 30. No minimal clinically important difference is stated for any HRQL score, and no sample size calculation is given.

slides.title: Complications and perioperative results
slides.lead: Major complications and infection were higher in obese patients; most other complication types were not significantly different.
points: Operative time, EBL and LOS: no significant difference (P 0.23, 0.98, 0.9)
No confidence intervals are reported for any complication or perioperative estimate
slides.notes: Read the counts behind the percentages. Our back-calculation: major complications 59 of 175 versus 35 of 66, infection 6 of 175 versus 7 of 66, revision 35 of 175 versus 15 of 66. Major adds up to the stated 94. The infection and revision totals of 13 and 50 are themselves our back-calculations from 5.4 and 20.7 percent of 241. Our unadjusted chi-square for major complications gives P about 0.006, so the adjusted IRR 1.54 is consistent with the crude gap. The infection result is the fragile one. It rests on about 13 events, the model has about seven terms, and the adjusted odds ratio of 4.88 is larger than our crude odds ratio of about 3.3. Our Fisher test on the crude counts gives P about 0.05. With so few events per variable, the adjusted estimate is unstable, and without a confidence interval you cannot see how wide it is. Our reading: quote it as roughly a three-fold infection rate, 10.6 versus 3.4 percent, not as a precise 4.9-fold odds. Table 4 has a reporting problem. Its column is labeled IRR or odds ratio, yet neurologic is 0.03 with P 0.881 and radiographic is negative, minus 0.139. A ratio cannot be negative, so these look like regression coefficients mixed with ratios. Implant risk: BMI P 0.804, while absolute weight gave an odds ratio of 1.16, P 0.064. The unit of weight is not stated. The authors suggest an absolute weight threshold may stress implants. That is a hypothesis, not a finding. Table 5 gives coefficients for LOS 0.05, EBL 5.99 and operative time 23.2, with units unstated and no group means. The authors say the study may be underpowered for these. Small print: 167 patients had any complication and 52 were obese, which leaves 115 of 175, or 65.7 percent, not 65 percent.

slides.title: Patient-reported outcomes
slides.lead: Obese patients scored worse at baseline and 2 years; the 1-year gap is within noise by our estimate. By our arithmetic their net 2-year ODI gain matched nonobese patients.
points: Group by time P: ODI 0.0001, SF-36 0.00001, SRS 0.0085
Model-adjusted means from Table 6; changes are our arithmetic
slides.see: Figure 2 shows the obese ODI curve rising between 1 and 2 years, from 29.7 to 33.2, while the nonobese curve keeps falling.
slides.notes: This is the slide to slow down on. The abstract says the overall magnitude of improvement was less for obese patients and cites ODI P 0.0035, SF-36 P 0.0012 and SRS P 0.022. In Table 6 those are the group P values. A group term tests whether the curves sit at different levels, and obese patients started worse: ODI 49.3 versus 40.3. It does not test improvement. Our arithmetic on Table 6: ODI fell 16.1 points in both groups from baseline to 2 years, and the ODI gap was 9.0 points at baseline and 9.0 at 2 years. On SF-36 physical the obese gain was 1.7 points smaller, and on SRS-22 it was 0.1 smaller. The group by time interaction, which the paper calls rate of improvement, is significant. Look at where the shape differs. At 6 weeks the nonobese group got worse, ODI 40.3 to 47.2 and SF-36 33.4 to 28.7, while the obese group was slightly better than baseline. Between 1 and 2 years the obese group lost ground on all three scores while the nonobese group held or improved. So the honest summary is: obese patients improved as much by ODI at 2 years, but lost some of their 1-year gain in the second year. Whether that late slide continues cannot be known from 2-year data, as the authors note. These are adjusted model means, adjusted among other things for major complications, so they are not raw scores. No MCID is given, so the paper does not say whether a 1.7-point SF-36 difference matters. Table 6 gives SEs, so our approximate 2-year gaps are: ODI 9.0 (about 4.2 to 13.9), SF-36 -6.2 (-8.9 to -3.6), SRS -0.31 (-0.49 to -0.13). At 1 year the gaps (ODI 3.1, SF-36 1.9, SRS 0.14) are within about 1.3 SE, so not clearly different. Change-score SEs cannot be derived. P values: Figures 1-3, the abstract and Results print time P 0.0001 for all three scores and SF-36 group by time P 0.0001; Table 6 gives 0.00001 for each. Trivial, but noted. Also note the authors' own point that obese patients started with worse HRQL, and that this added compromise did not prevent them from benefiting from surgery.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: Good complication capture, but completer-only selection, sparse infection events and loose reporting.
points: Holds up: multicenter prospective database with a standardized complication form
Holds up: complication models adjusted for the baseline and surgical differences; 2-year follow-up, repeated HRQL measures
Weakens: completers only; the 45 excluded are not described, and eligibility for the 286 is not defined
Weakens: no confidence intervals for complication estimates; infection OR from about 13 events (our back-calculation)
Weakens: Table 4 mixes coefficients and ratios; Infection not defined
Weakens: HRQL models adjust for complications, a likely mediator (our reading), but list no smoking or prior surgery
Weakens: improvement claim rests on group P values, not change scores
Weakens: single BMI cutoff; no class III analysis
Reporting: revision rate 20.7% in Results, 20.3% in Discussion
slides.notes: Be fair. For 2015 this is a useful paper: a prospective, multicenter ASD cohort with standardized complication capture and 2-year patient-reported outcomes, which most database studies of obesity lack. The authors name their own limitations. They name four: baseline differences with possible unmeasured confounding, a small sample that may be underpowered for EBL and operative time, no class III subgroup, and follow-up of only 2 years. The rest is our reading. Selection: only completers were analyzed, and the paper does not define eligibility for the 286 or say who was lost before that count. Precision: the complication and perioperative estimates have no confidence intervals. Table 6 does give SEs, from which we built rough HRQL intervals (slide 5). The infection model is overfit for 13 events. Mediation: adjusting HRQL for major complications and revisions may hide part of obesity's effect. Interpretation: the abstract's less improvement wording does not match Table 6 change scores for ODI. Internal consistency problems to list: the revision rate is 20.7 percent in Results but 20.3 percent in Discussion, which is the neurologic rate. The neurologic P value is 0.861 in the abstract and 0.88 or 0.881 in the text and table. Table 2 percentages imply denominators of 65, 171 and 173 that are not reported. Surgical approach P 0.34 does not reproduce for posterior-only, P about 0.89 by our test. Overall complications in nonobese patients compute to 65.7 percent, printed 65 percent. Table 5 coefficients have no units. The Results say baseline differences were accounted for in all analyses, but the HRQL models list only age, comorbidity, magnitude of surgery and major complications, not smoking or prior surgery. The paper also gives no years of surgery, and industry money went to the study group foundation.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "In ISSG patients with 2-year data, obesity was linked to more major complications, 53 versus 34 percent, and about three times the crude infection rate. Obese patients started and finished worse, but by our reading of the adjusted means gained a similar 16 ODI points."
points: Do not say obese patients improve less on ODI: net change was equal, by our arithmetic from Table 6
Do not quote OR 4.88 as precise: about 13 infections by our back-calculation, no interval
Do not stretch to BMI 40 or more: no class analysis
Do not read it as proof that weight loss lowers risk: observational association
slides.notes: Spoken summary: a retrospective review of 241 ISSG patients with complete 2-year data, 66 of them obese. After adjustment, obesity was associated with more major complications, IRR 1.54, and more infection, adjusted odds ratio 4.88, from crude rates of 10.6 versus 3.4 percent. Revision, neurologic, radiographic and implant complications were not significantly different, and neither were operative time, blood loss or length of stay. Both groups improved. Obese patients were worse at baseline and at 2 years, and by our arithmetic their ODI gain matched the nonobese group at 16 points, though they slipped between 1 and 2 years. Expected follow-up questions. Should I refuse ASD surgery for BMI over 30? The paper does not support that. The authors conclude obese patients do benefit from surgery and suggest using the findings in preoperative discussion. Does risk rise further with BMI over 40? Unknown here; the authors could not do a class III subgroup. Why no difference in length of stay or blood loss? The authors suggest ASD operations are so large and variable that obesity's effect is harder to detect, and that the study may be underpowered. Is the infection result wound infection? The text says wound infection, but the table label and the checklist's infection category also include pneumonia, sepsis, urinary infection and C difficile, so the paper is ambiguous. What about weight rather than BMI for implants? Weight gave OR 1.16, P 0.064, a trend only, per unit not stated. The library also holds Amin 2018 on BMI class and ASD outcomes, but its master record has no extracted results yet, so no numbers are compared here.

decks.not_reviewed: Nothing beyond the PDF. We read the full 11-page article end to end, including the two invited Comments (Park; Spitz and Refai). The paper cites no supplement. Earlier ISSG papers it relies on (the MCID sources, the SRS-Schwab classification papers) and the Bridwell 2009 matched study it compares itself with were not reread for this deck; figures for Bridwell are as this paper reports them.

slides.title: Smith 2016: operative vs nonoperative ASD at 2 years
slides.lead: Patients with adult spinal deformity chose surgery or nonoperative care. At 2 years, the surgical group had improved and the nonoperative group had not.
points: Journal club: adult spinal deformity
Smith JS, Lafage V, Shaffrey CI, et al, for the International Spine Study Group. Neurosurgery 2016;78(6):851-861
Prospective multicenter observational cohort, 11 US sites, with unmatched and propensity-matched comparisons
Bottom line: in 97 matched pairs, operative patients were better at 2 years on every quality-of-life measure except SF-36 MCS. 71.5% of operative patients had at least one complication.
slides.notes: This deck is based on the full article, read end to end, including the two invited Comments. The PDF is complete and the paper cites no supplement. Frame it before the numbers. This is not a trial. Patients picked their own treatment, so read it with the cohort questions: who was selected, how outcomes were measured, and whether matching made the groups comparable. The authors cite earlier reports (their refs 11 and 12) of surgery giving about 60% relief of back and leg pain and about 40% improvement in disability at 2 years, and they say additional high-quality studies comparing operative and nonoperative care are needed. Read the title with care: 'propensity-matched' applies to only 194 of the 469 patients analyzed. The rest of the paper is an unmatched comparison of groups that, by the authors' own Table 1, differed at baseline. Funding: the International Spine Study Group is funded by DePuy Synthes and individual donations, and most senior authors list industry relationships. The authors state this; we note it only as context. Neither Comment raises new data. Park calls the 71.5% complication rate a realistic risk and repeats the authors' limitations. Spitz and Refai summarize the paper. Their summary says nonoperative care neither improves nor worsens 'pain and deformity', but the paper's own Table 3 shows PI-LL and coronal alignment got worse in the matched nonoperative group.

slides.title: The question and the design
slides.lead: Does surgery give better 2-year quality of life than nonoperative care for ASD?
points: Inclusion: age over 18 plus at least one of scoliosis 20 degrees or more, SVA 5 cm or more, pelvic tilt 25 degrees or more, thoracic kyphosis 60 degrees or more
Treatment chosen through consent between patient and surgeon, 'ultimately guided by patient choice'; no randomization
Surgery at the surgeon's discretion. Nonoperative care was tailored and not standardized: physical therapy, epidural steroids, medications, orthoses
Outcomes: ODI, SF-36 PCS and MCS, SRS-22r total and domains, back and leg pain NRS, share reaching MCID. No single primary outcome is named.
Complications collected for operative patients only; nonoperative harms 'not consistently collected'
Matching on 5 baseline variables: ODI, SRS-22r total, maximum TL/L Cobb, PI-LL, leg pain NRS
slides.notes: Three design facts decide how far you can trust the result. First, the comparison is between people who chose surgery and people who did not. The authors state that patients could not be blinded, and that those who committed to surgery may have expected to get better. Second, the nonoperative arm is not a defined treatment. Nothing in it was protocolized, and the paper gives no data on what nonoperative patients actually received or how much. So 'nonoperative care' here means whatever these patients were given, not a tested program. Third, harms were counted on one side only, which makes any risk-benefit comparison one-sided. The matching set is sensible, and the authors explain it. ODI and SRS-22r capture how disabled patients were. Cobb and PI-LL capture deformity size and type. Leg pain partly stands in for stenosis, which they say is more common in degenerative curves. Age was deliberately left out. Statistics were unpaired t tests between groups and paired t tests within groups, with Fisher or chi-square for proportions. There was no correction for the many outcomes tested. What is missing from the methods (our observation): the enrollment dates, how the propensity score was built (model, caliper, with or without replacement), and whether the 97 pairs were analyzed as pairs. The MCID values in the table come from earlier reports the authors cite. Keep the ODI value of 12.8 in mind, because the mean operative gain only just clears it.

slides.title: Who was analyzed
slides.lead: 938 patients identified; 469 analyzed; 194 matched.
points: Unmatched baseline: operative patients had higher BMI (27.1 vs 25.5), more comorbidity (Charlson 1.4 vs 0.9), more depression (24.9% vs 15.7%), more previous spine surgery (42.6% vs 18.6%)
Operative patients were worse on every HRQOL measure (all P < .001) and had worse sagittal modifiers, pelvic tilt, PI-LL and SVA
Mean follow-up 24.7 months operative, 24.8 nonoperative
slides.see: Figure 1 is the flow diagram; every count in the table is from it.
slides.notes: The flow diagram arithmetic checks: 447 + 491 = 938; 447 - 135 - 26 = 286; 491 - 38 - 12 - 38 = 403; 286 - 40 = 246 (86.0%); 403 - 180 = 223 (55.3%). Three things to notice. First, 180 of 403 nonoperative patients were lost. The authors say some of them may have improved and so stopped coming back, which would bias against nonoperative care. The reverse is also possible, and the paper cannot tell which. Second, the 38 nonoperative patients who converted to surgery before 2 years were removed. They are presumably the nonoperative failures, so removing them may make the nonoperative arm look better than an intention-to-treat analysis would (our inference). Their outcomes are not reported. Third, the groups differed at baseline. The surgical group was sicker, more disabled and more deformed. The authors read this as a more advanced disease state, and they note that the patients who are worst off may stand to gain the most. The paper is inconsistent on age for the 689 eligible patients: the abstract says 53 operative and 55 nonoperative, while Results says 54 and 55. Table 1, which covers the 469 analyzed patients, gives 55.4 operative and 52.6 nonoperative (P = .06), so in the analyzed cohort the surgical group was the older one. Several Table 1 percentages are not whole-number fractions of 223 or 246, so some variables had missing data with no denominators shown. The paper does not say how 97 pairs were drawn from 223 nonoperative and 246 operative patients, or why only 97.

slides.title: Outcomes in the 97 matched pairs
slides.lead: Operative patients improved; matched nonoperative patients stayed about where they started.
points: Matched nonoperative patients improved significantly only on SRS-22r total (P = .02), pain (P = .03) and satisfaction (P = .001)
Radiographs: operative PI-LL 9.6 to 1.4 degrees and Cobb 28.1 to 13.0; nonoperative PI-LL worsened 7.7 to 10.2 (P < .001)
Unmatched cohorts gave the same picture, with nonoperative gains only in SRS pain (3.4 to 3.5) and satisfaction (3.3 to 3.6)
slides.see: Figure 4 shows the share reaching MCID in each matched arm. Figure 5 shows the diverging mean lines from baseline to 2 years.
slides.notes: Read the mean ODI change against the MCID: the operative mean improved by 13.0 points against an MCID of 12.8. That is a mean gain, not a patient gain. Only 53.6% of matched operative patients actually reached the ODI MCID (Figure 4), and 10.3% of matched nonoperative patients did too. The patient-level MCID shares are the numbers to quote when counseling. For the other measures, the matched operative shares reaching MCID were: SF-36 PCS 57.7%, SRS pain 70.1%, appearance 75.3%, activity 61.9%, mental 32%, back pain 73.2% and leg pain 38.1%. The nonoperative shares were 17.5%, 32%, 13.4%, 32%, 26.8%, 21.6% and 22.7%. SRS mental did not differ (P = .529). Leg pain was the weakest significant difference (P = .028). We recomputed the Figure 4 percentages as whole counts of 97, and they match. Recomputed chi-square P values match too. Now look at the baseline row the matching did not fix. Matched operative patients started with worse back pain (6.4 vs 5.1, P < .001), worse SRS appearance and satisfaction, and better SF-36 MCS and SRS mental scores. Back pain was the outcome with the largest operative gain, partly because there was more room to improve (our reading). The MCS difference at 2 years largely reflects baseline: both arms rose by less than 2 points. Two table claims do not hold up. Table 4 flags the operative leg-pain change as at least 1 MCID, but 3.1 to 1.8 is 1.3, below the stated MCID of 1.6. The text says every measure with a known MCID improved by at least 1 MCID, but SRS mental moved 0.2 against an MCID of 0.42. Also, the 2-year MCS P value of .06 is uncertain: an unpaired t test from the table's means and SDs with 97 per arm gives about .03 (our recomputation). Missing data could push it toward .06, since the paper gives no denominators, so this is not a definite error.

slides.title: Harms: complications after surgery
slides.lead: 407 complications in 246 operative patients over 2 years; 71.5% had at least one.
points: Major: substantially prolonged stay, invasive intervention, prolonged or permanent morbidity, or death; any reoperation counted as major
Largest categories over 2 years: radiographic 70 events, neurological 69, implant 64, operative 64, cardiopulmonary 53
Delayed problems were mostly mechanical: implant 56 and radiographic 58 of 167 delayed events
Surgery: 99% posterior fusion, mean 9.7 levels; ALIF 27.3%, lateral 7.3%, PSO 15.4%, VCR 4.5%; mean 7.4 h and 2.0 L blood loss
Nonoperative complications were not collected
slides.notes: Table 2 is internally consistent. The minor and major columns sum to 133/107, 57/110 and 190/217. The patient counts match the percentages: 132/246, 107/246 and 176/246. The mean of 1.65 complications per patient equals 407/246. Read the category percentage column correctly, though. It is events per 100 patients, not the percentage of patients with that complication. For example, implant total 26.0% = 64 events / 246. A patient with two implant events counts twice. In the reoperation column, the major events tied to reoperation add up to 95 (our count of events, not patients). The paper does not report how many patients were reoperated. That is a real gap, because reoperation is the number patients ask about. Notice the time profile. Perioperative events are mainly operative, cardiopulmonary and neurological. Delayed events are mainly implant and radiographic failures, and these dominate the reoperations: 23 implant and 27 radiographic. The authors say their rates are higher than in earlier reports because of the 2-year window and prospective audited collection. They also argue that many complications probably have little or no effect on final outcome, while acknowledging effects on length of stay, invasive procedures and recovery. That 'minimal effect' point is their judgment, not something the paper tests. Since nonoperative harms were not recorded, there is no comparative harm estimate. The benefit is shown head to head, but the risk is shown for one arm only.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: Good for its era of observational data, but matching cannot reproduce a randomized comparison.
points: Strengths: prospective multicenter enrollment, audited complication capture, central radiograph measurement with validated software, standard HRQOL tools, matched and unmatched analyses
Selection and expectation: treatment chosen by patients; no blinding; matching on 5 variables leaves age, back pain and unmeasured factors unbalanced
Attrition: 55% nonoperative follow-up; 38 crossovers to surgery excluded rather than analyzed
Nonoperative care undefined; its harms not collected
Reporting: no propensity model details, no enrollment dates, many unadjusted outcomes, and some table claims that do not reconcile
slides.notes: The authors name most of these limitations: lower nonoperative follow-up, older matched nonoperative patients, no standardized nonoperative protocol, no randomization or blinding, more previous surgery in the operative group, and no control over the type of treatment. Credit them for that. What we add is the following. One: regression to the mean works against the nonoperative arm. Patients who choose surgery often do so at a peak of symptoms, while nonoperative patients may enroll at a steadier point. Matching on baseline scores does not remove the difference in when people enroll (our inference). Two: even after matching, back pain was 1.3 points worse in the surgical group, and the nonoperative matches were 6.6 years older. The authors explain the age gap: matching on disability seems to have required older nonoperative patients. Three: excluding crossovers and losing 45% of the nonoperative arm makes the nonoperative estimate fragile in both directions. Four: the paper's conclusion calls this a 'case-control analysis'. It is a cohort, and the label is wrong. Five: in our internal checks, the flow diagram, the complication sums and the Figure 4 percentages reconcile. The leg pain and SRS mental MCID claims do not. Several Table 3 P values do not either: matched baseline pelvic tilt (21.0 vs 21.0, P = .78) recomputes to above .9, and 2-year coronal alignment (P = .61) to about .72. Missing data cannot lower a P value, so neither can be explained that way. Figure 3 percentages are not whole fractions of 246 or 223, so the unmatched MCID analyses also had unreported denominators. What survives all of this: the difference is large and consistent across measures, in both matched and unmatched analyses. The matched mean ODI gap at 2 years is 13.7 points. Unmeasured bias would have to be big to erase it. What does not survive: any claim that nonoperative care fails, because nonoperative care was never defined. And any precise estimate of the size of the surgical benefit.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: In matched ASD patients, surgery gave large 2-year gains in disability and pain. Matched patients on nonoperative care stayed about the same. Most operative patients had a complication.
points: Spoken summary: Smith and the ISSG followed 469 adults with deformity who chose surgery or nonoperative care. In 97 matched pairs, ODI fell from 30 to 17 with surgery and stayed at 30 to 31 without it. About half of surgical patients reached the ODI MCID versus 1 in 10. The cost: 71.5% had at least one complication by 2 years, 217 of 407 events major. It is observational, nonoperative follow-up was 55%, and nonoperative care was not defined.
Expect: was it randomized? No. Patients chose, and 97 pairs were propensity matched on ODI, SRS-22r, Cobb, PI-LL and leg pain.
Expect: does nonoperative care fail? No. It was not standardized, and 10% to 32% of matched nonoperative patients reached MCID on single measures.
Expect: how many needed reoperation? Not reported per patient; 95 major events were tied to reoperation by our count of Table 2.
Expect: is the 71.5% comparable to other series? The authors say it is higher because of 2-year prospective audited capture.
slides.notes: Keep the summary under a minute, and always state the limitations alongside the result. Two traps in questions. First, someone may say surgery doubled the chance of improvement. Be specific instead: the matched ODI MCID rate was 53.6% vs 10.3%, back pain 73.2% vs 21.6% and leg pain 38.1% vs 22.7%. The gap differs a lot by measure, and SRS mental did not differ. Second, someone may quote the mean ODI change as clinically important for the average patient. The mean gain of 13.0 only just clears the MCID of 12.8, and 46% of matched operative patients did not reach it. If asked about age: the matched nonoperative group was older (58.0 vs 51.4), a gap the authors describe and explain. If asked about Bridwell 2009: by this paper's account, Bridwell matched 41 per group, found surgical improvement with no nonoperative improvement, and also had low nonoperative follow-up (45%). If asked whether the complication rate argues against surgery: the paper does not weigh harms against benefit for individual patients. All it shows is that both are large at the group level. Use this paper when counseling an ASD patient who is deciding. The realistic picture is a better than even chance of a meaningful gain in disability, and a high chance of at least one complication. Most events were perioperative (240 of 407), but delayed implant and radiographic failures drove most reoperations.

decks.not_reviewed: No supplement is cited in the PDF. Not reviewed: the clinicaltrials.gov record NCT01305343, the prestudy power analysis (mentioned but not given in the paper), and the separate risk-factor manuscript the authors describe as in progress. Figure 1 is the blank ASIA examination form and carries no results.

slides.title: Scoli-RISK-1: neurologic outcomes after complex ASD surgery
slides.lead: About 1 in 5 patients lost lower-limb motor score by discharge; about 1 in 10 were still below baseline at 6 months.
points: Lenke LG, et al. Spine 2016;41:204-212
Prospective, multicenter, international observational cohort; Level of Evidence 3
273 enrolled at 15 sites, 272 analysed
Primary outcome: change in ASIA lower extremity motor score (LEMS) at discharge, 6 weeks and 6 months
Funded by SRS, AOSpine International and Norton Healthcare
slides.notes: This is the SRS and AOSpine Scoli-RISK-1 study, the prospective benchmark for motor decline after the most complex adult deformity operations. The design is a single-arm cohort, not a trial: there is no comparison treatment. The only comparison is between patients who were neurologically normal before surgery and those who already had a motor deficit. Enrollment ran from September 2011 to October 2012. Of more than 100 centers that applied, 15 were chosen: nine in North America, three in Europe and three in Asia. 43 surgeons enrolled consecutive patients. The headline the authors give is a 22.18% LEMS decline at discharge, falling to 17.91% at 6 weeks and 10.82% at 6 months, which they call by far the highest rates reported to date. Hold on to two things while reading: the cohort is deliberately the highest-risk end of deformity surgery, and the outcome counts any loss of even one motor point as a decline.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: How often does complex adult deformity surgery change lower-limb motor function, and does it recover?
points: Reported neurologic deficit rates after adult deformity surgery range from 0% to over 10%
The authors blame incomplete follow-up, mixed cohorts and nonstandard outcome measures
The five prior prospective-data studies they cite used no validated neurologic score; three were single-institution
Their answer: a prospective study with a certified ASIA exam at fixed time points
slides.notes: Set the stakes. Loss of neurologic function is, in the authors' words, one of the most significant complications of complex deformity surgery, and the published rates are all over the place. The SRS Morbidity and Mortality database, which the authors discuss, found new deficits in 1.0% of 108,419 procedures, but that was voluntary, nonconsecutive reporting with no standard exam. The authors argue that only a prospective design with a validated exam at set times can give a true rate and a baseline for judging new techniques. The paper aims to report motor function before and after complex ASD correction and how it changes over time. Note what it does not ask: it does not test any risk factor, technique or monitoring strategy. The authors say risk factors such as blood loss, approach, osteotomy problems and screw placement are in a separate manuscript.

slides.title: Selection and measurement
points: Age 18 to 80, deformity apex C7 to L2

Complex ASD: major Cobb 80 degrees or more, osteotomy for congenital or revision deformity, 3-column osteotomy C7 to L5, myelopathy from deformity, or OLF/OPLL needing decompression with reconstruction
Excluded: complete long-term paraplegia, active malignancy or infection, recent spinal trauma
ASIA exam by a certified examiner within 6 weeks before surgery, at discharge, 6 weeks and 6 months
LEMS: 5 muscle groups each side, 0 to 5, maximum 50; any change classed as decline, maintenance or improvement
slides.notes: The cohort is extreme by design. 79.04% had a 3-column osteotomy and 48.53% were revision deformity requiring osteotomy. Mean age was 57.42 years and 67.28% were women. Surgical approach, instrumentation and correction were left to the surgeon. Read the measurement carefully. LEMS is a 50-point scale and a decline means any drop from the preoperative score, so a one-point loss in one muscle on one side counts the same as a major deficit. The authors chose to report only the motor part of the ASIA exam because the sensory part would add subjective bias. Examiners were ASIA-certified but differed across sites. We recomputed the baseline tests from Table 2. Sex (Fisher 0.0525), prior surgery (0.0038), smoking (0.4796), approach (0.869) and age (t-test 0.256) all match. The stages P value of 0.7613 cannot be reproduced: 164 of 204 versus 55 of 68 single-stage gives Fisher 1.0 and chi-square 0.93. Note that a plain chi-square on sex gives 0.044, so the sex difference is borderline depending on the test. The groups differ in prior surgery (76% vs 56% in the deficit group) and possibly sex, and the paper never adjusts for either. Analysis used two-way repeated-measures ANOVA on preoperative, 6-week and 6-month scores, with Hochberg adjustment. Discharge is not one of the ANOVA levels.

slides.title: Primary outcome: LEMS change, all patients
slides.lead: Decline fell from 22.18% at discharge to 10.82% at 6 months.
points: Our 95% CIs (Wilson, not in paper): discharge 17.6 to 27.5%, 6 weeks 13.8 to 22.9%, 6 months 7.6 to 15.1%
At 6 months, 9 patients had declined 6 points or more: 5 by 6 to 10, 4 by more than 10
Most decline at every time point was 1 to 5 points (42 of 59 at discharge, 20 of 29 at 6 months)
slides.notes: All the counts in Table 5 add up to the percentages in the text and abstract. Read the size of the decline, not only its frequency. At 6 months only 9 of 268 patients (about 3.4%, our arithmetic) had lost 6 or more points, and 4 (1.49%) had lost more than 10. The 10.82% headline is mostly small losses of 1 to 5 points. That matters for consent: a 1 in 10 risk of measurable weakness at 6 months is a different conversation from a 1 in 10 risk of disabling weakness. The authors report the change from discharge to 6 weeks as significant (P = 0.0042), and 6 months as significantly different from both 6 weeks (P = 0.0011) and discharge (P below 0.0001). The paper gives no confidence intervals anywhere. The intervals above are ours. They show the 6-month rate could plausibly be anywhere from about 8% to 15% in a similar cohort. Missing data were imputed across time points, which affects exactly this time trend; see the appraisal slide. Two paraplegia cases are described. One patient with congenital kyphoscoliosis lost monitoring during a 3-column osteotomy, woke paraplegic, and recovered to LEMS 30 at discharge, 40 at 6 weeks and 50 at 6 months. Another became paraplegic at a revision for proximal junctional kyphosis 7 weeks after the index surgery and had not improved at 6 months. The authors' statement that no patient had sustained paraplegia refers to the index procedure only.

slides.title: By preoperative status
slides.lead: The deficit group mostly improved; the normal group could only stay the same or decline.
points: ABNML improved: 51.52% at discharge, 66.67% at 6 weeks, 83.33% at 6 months
Mean LEMS at 6 months: NML 49.35 (from 50.00), ABNML 47.02 (from 43.78)
Authors' Table 4 P below 0.0001 at every time point compares the whole distribution
slides.see: Table 5 splits each group's changes into 1 to 5, 6 to 10 and more than 10 points
slides.notes: This slide is where the paper is easiest to misread. Table 4 reports P below 0.0001 between groups at each time point. That difference is driven by improvement, which is impossible by definition in the normal group because 50 is the ceiling score. It is not evidence that decline differs. When we test decline alone, the groups do not differ at any time point (P 0.49, 1.0 and 0.18). Our 95% CIs for 6-month decline are 8.5 to 17.6% in NML and 2.4 to 14.6% in ABNML. So the Discussion's statement that a preoperative deficit carried a higher rate of postoperative deficit is not statistically supported by these data. That sentence also gives the NML rate as 22.17%; Table 4 gives 21.00% (42 of 200), and 22.17 to 22.18% is the overall rate. The text says decline in NML at discharge was transitory in about half. The counts go from 42 at discharge to 25 at 6 months, about 40% fewer, and these are not necessarily the same patients, because the paper does not track individuals across time points. The 83.33% improvement in the deficit group is described as significant improvement, but it counts any gain of 1 point or more; 38 of the 55 improved by 1 to 5 points. The deficit group was also more often revision surgery, which the analysis does not adjust for. The useful clinical message is still real: most patients with a preoperative deficit gained motor score by 6 months.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: Strengths: prospective, consecutive, certified ASIA exams at fixed times, high follow-up
6-week denominator does not add up: 272 minus 13 missed plus 8 imputed is 267, but 268 is reported
Missing 6-week values were filled from 6-month data and vice versa, which blurs the time trend
No confidence intervals reported; no adjustment for baseline group differences
67.6% of patients came from the 8 highest-enrolling surgeons
The stages P value (0.7613) cannot be reproduced
slides.notes: The strengths are genuine and are why this paper is cited: consecutive enrollment, a standard motor exam by certified examiners, and follow-up of 97.80% at discharge and 98.53% at 6 weeks and 6 months. The 6-month arithmetic works (272 minus 20 plus 16 is 268), but the 6-week arithmetic gives 267, not the 268 reported and summed in Table 4 (202 plus 66). The 97.80% for 266 of 272 is a rounding slip; it is 97.79%. The imputation is the more important problem. Eight missing 6-week values were carried back from 6 months, and 16 missing 6-month values were carried forward from 6 weeks. Because the main result is a change over time, borrowing values across time points pulls the two later rates toward each other. The authors list their own limitations: heterogeneous diagnoses and procedures, different examiners at different sites, motor score only, and results that should not be applied to all deformity patients. They add that 67.6% of patients came from eight surgeons and 18 surgeons enrolled only one patient. They report no difference in decline between single-case surgeons and the rest (P 0.285, 0.495 and 0.897), but with 18 patients in one group that test has little power (our inference). The Key Points say these rates should be considered the expected outcome for complex ASD. Given the authors' own limitations, that overstates how far the numbers travel: they describe high-volume academic centers doing the most complex cases. The paper says it was adequately powered but does not give the power calculation. Follow-up ends at 6 months, so nothing here speaks to late recovery or late deficits.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: In complex adult deformity surgery, about 22% lose some leg motor score by discharge and about 11% are still below baseline at 6 months, mostly by small amounts.
points: Scoli-RISK-1, 272 patients at 15 centers, ASIA motor score before surgery and at 3 time points
Decline 22.18% at discharge, 17.91% at 6 weeks, 10.82% at 6 months
Loss of more than 10 points at 6 months: 1.49%
83.33% of patients with a preoperative deficit had gained score by 6 months
Expect: is the deficit group riskier? Not shown; decline did not differ significantly
Expect: does this apply to my practice? Only to the most complex cases at high-volume centers
slides.notes: Spoken summary: Scoli-RISK-1 followed 272 consecutive patients having the most complex adult deformity operations at 15 international centers, with a certified ASIA motor exam before surgery, at discharge, 6 weeks and 6 months. 22.18% lost some motor score by discharge, and this fell to 10.82% at 6 months. Most losses were 1 to 5 points; only 1.49% had lost more than 10 points at 6 months. Of patients with a deficit before surgery, 83.33% had gained score by 6 months. Follow-up questions to expect. Why is this rate so much higher than the 1% in the SRS database? The authors point to a high-risk cohort, a sensitive exam, prospective design and complete follow-up; any one-point loss counts. Are patients with a preoperative deficit at higher risk? The Discussion says so, but in our test decline did not differ between groups at any time point, and the paper's P values are driven by improvement. Did the patients who declined at discharge recover? The paper reports group counts, not individual paths, so it cannot say how many of the same patients recovered. What about risk factors and monitoring? Not in this paper; the authors say a separate manuscript covers them. What should I quote for consent? Our suggestion: about 1 in 5 early, about 1 in 10 at 6 months, and severe persistent loss uncommon, for this class of surgery at these centers.

decks.not_reviewed: No supplement is cited in the PDF. The cited comparison series (Glassman, Schwab, Charosky, Blamoutier, Auerbach, Cho, Fischer) were not reviewed; their numbers are as reported in this paper. Figures 1 to 3 were viewed, but values were read by eye only and not digitized.

slides.title: Soroceanu 2016: Medical complications after adult spinal deformity surgery
slides.lead: Bottom line: 26.8% of 448 operative ASD patients had at least one medical complication within 6 weeks. Smoking, hypertension and longer symptom duration independently predicted them, and the authors found no difference in 2-year HRQL improvement between patients with and without one.
points: Journal club · Adult deformity: perioperative risk
Soroceanu A, et al, International Spine Study Group. Spine 2016;41(22):1718-1723
Full text read, including Tables 1 to 4 and Figures 1 to 3. Risk-factor cohort, level of evidence 3.
slides.notes: Frame it as a risk-factor study, not a comparison of treatments. Everyone had deformity surgery; the question is which baseline patient features predict a medical (not surgical) complication, and whether having one spoils the outcome. The authors' argument for separating medical from surgical complications is that the risk factors may differ, and most earlier series lumped them together. Their emphasis is on factors that might be modifiable through patient selection or medical optimization. The data come from the ISSG multicenter prospective database. The abstract calls the design a retrospective review of a prospective database, and the Methods call it a prospective study; both describe the same thing, prospective collection analyzed after the fact. The deck comes from the full six-page article. Expect several numerical inconsistencies between the abstract, text and tables, especially for the headline risk ratios. None of them reverses the main message, but they matter if you quote a number.

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: 448 operative ASD patients from 11 US centers, complications counted to 6 weeks.
points: Included: operative ASD with coronal Cobb >20°, SVA >5 cm, PT >25° or TK >60°, and at least 6 weeks of follow-up. No age limit or exclusions are stated.

Medical complications, intra- and perioperative (within 6 weeks): infectious (pneumonia, UTI, C difficile, sepsis, wound infection), neurologic (stroke, delirium), cardiopulmonary (DVT, PE, MI, arrhythmia, CHF, pneumothorax, atelectasis, ARDS, electrolyte imbalance), GI (obstruction, ileus, cholecystitis), renal failure.
Statistics: univariate screen at P < 0.2, then stepwise multivariate Poisson regression (removal at 0.1). Operative time compared by t test.
HRQL: ODI, SRS-22r, SF-36 at baseline, 6 weeks, 1 and 2 years; repeated-measures mixed models in the 2-year subgroup.
slides.notes: Cohort overall: mean age 56.8 (SD 15.45), 75% female, mean BMI 27.85, average 9.69 levels fused, mean SVA 65 mm. We recomputed the Overall column of Table 1 as the weighted mean of the two groups; all four rows check out. The authors present Table 1 only as a summary of baseline sagittal parameters and levels fused. Our reading: the complication group did not have bigger deformities or longer fusions, so the difference seems to lie in the patient, not the alignment. Table 1 gives no SDs, so its P values (0.91, 0.89, 0.97, 0.29) could not be recomputed; they look plausible if typical SDs are assumed (our check). Three things to notice. First, the list of medical complications is broad. It includes electrolyte imbalance and atelectasis, and wound infection, which many surgeons would call surgical (our view). The abstract list differs slightly from the Methods list (no electrolyte imbalance or cholecystitis). The authors say they evaluated major and minor complications, but no breakdown by severity is reported, so in the counts a low sodium weighs the same as a PE. Second, the paper never gives a baseline table of comorbidities, so we do not know how many patients smoked or were hypertensive. Third, the abstract says the model was multivariate logistic regression; the Methods, tables and abstract Methods say Poisson. The table footnotes define IRR as incidence risk ratio; in our reading these are incidence rate ratios, which fits Poisson. The paper does not say whether the outcome counted was complications per patient (185 events) or patients with any complication (120). Enrollment dates are not given.

slides.title: Result 1: how often, and what kind
slides.lead: 120 of 448 patients (26.8%) had 185 medical complications. Over half were cardiopulmonary.
points: Most patients with a complication had one (71.7%) or two (14.2%); 8 patients had 4 to 6.
Operative time: 422 minutes with a complication vs 372 without (P = 0.0004, t test, unadjusted).
slides.notes: We checked Table 2 arithmetic and it holds: 86 + 17 + 9 + 3 + 4 + 1 = 120 patients, and weighting each by its count of complications gives 86 + 34 + 27 + 12 + 20 + 6 = 185. The type counts also sum to 185, and every percentage recomputes. The 85.9% with one or two complications is 71.7 plus 14.2. The percentages are of complications, not of patients, so do not say 53% of patients had a cardiopulmonary event. Individual complications (how many DVTs, how many pneumonias) are not reported; the authors say each was too rare to analyze. The authors attribute their higher rate than earlier series to prospective collection and a long list that includes minor events. In their account, Glassman reported 24.9% (medical and surgical combined), Schwab 8.4% major complications, Charosky 40/306 (13.7%) medical and Blamoutier 16.1% medical. These figures are as reported in this paper. We recomputed them: Glassman 108/434 = 24.9%, Schwab 80/953 = 8.4% and Blamoutier 29/180 = 16.1% check out, but 40/306 is 13.1%, not 13.7%. Operative time: 50.7 minutes longer in the complication group (our subtraction). It was tested alone and was not entered into the multivariate model, which was restricted to baseline factors. The authors acknowledge surgical and anesthesia time may matter, but only surgical time is reported. Read it as a marker of bigger or harder cases, not a proven cause.

slides.title: Result 2: who is at risk
slides.lead: Three baseline factors survived the multivariate model, and the reported ratios differ across the paper.
points: Univariate (Table 3) also flagged heart disease 2.07, anemia 1.62, BMI >30 1.61, depression 1.6, female sex 1.54 and ASA 1.33. These dropped out of the final model.
Age was not significant (IRR 1.008, P = 0.1).
slides.notes: Trust Table 4. We recomputed each predictor row from its CI: the z values match (4.47, 5.60 and 2.16 against 4.47, 5.58 and 2.18 printed). The Constant row does not: IRR 0.1 (CI 0.04-0.25) is below 1, so z should be about -4.9, but it is printed as +5.01; the sign was lost. The Discussion also quotes 2.39, 2.43 and 1.24. The Results paragraph prints 2.38, 2.42 and 2.23 (P 0.02) for duration, which is almost certainly a typo for 1.23 or 1.24. The abstract has smoking at 2.49. The univariate text also has a typo (hypertension printed as P = 2.42) and gives anemia as 1.61 against 1.62 in the table. How to read an IRR of about 2.4: roughly 2.4 times the rate of medical complications, holding the other two factors constant. Because the paper does not report how many patients smoked or had hypertension, you cannot turn this into an absolute risk for your patient. Symptom duration is the fragile one. The abstract calls it number of years with spine problems, but the unit and coding are never given. If 1.24 were per year, ten years of symptoms would multiply the rate by about 8.6 (our arithmetic), which seems implausible to us; we suspect it is categorized, but the paper gives no coding and its wording (years with spine problems) points to a per-year unit. Stepwise selection with a P < 0.2 screen tends to pick one of several correlated factors: heart disease and hypertension overlap, as do BMI, ASA and comorbidity. Dropped does not mean harmless (our view). The abstract lists PVD and Charlson index among potential predictors, but neither appears in Table 3. The model was not validated in a separate sample.

slides.title: Result 3: does a medical complication spoil the outcome?
slides.lead: In the 2-year subgroup, both groups improved over time and the curves were not separable.
points: 286 patients eligible for 2 years; 256 completed HRQL (89.5%); 78 of them had a medical complication.
Time effect P < 0.0001 for ODI, SRS-22r and SF-36 PCS in Figures 1 to 3 (the abstract and Results text print P = 0.0001). Group and group-by-time effects not significant.
Adjusted for age, BMI, comorbidities and magnitude of surgery (figure legends also list baseline neurologic function).
slides.see: Figures 1 to 3 show the two curves overlapping at every time point, with ODI and SF-36 PCS slightly worse at 6 weeks than baseline before improving by 1 year.
slides.notes: Read by eye from Figure 2, ODI starts in the low to mid 40s in both groups, rises a little at 6 weeks, and falls to the high 20s by 1 and 2 years. SF-36 PCS goes from the low 30s to about 40. These are approximate readings, not published numbers. The authors frame this as reassurance: despite a medical complication, patients improved as much. That is fair as far as it goes, with three caveats. First, no difference found is not the same as no difference. There is no effect size for the group difference, no confidence interval around it, no power calculation and no equivalence margin. Second, the SRS-22r and ODI figures print identical P values for group (0.9857) and interaction (0.7364). Two different scores giving the same two P values to four decimals is very unlikely; one figure may carry the other's statistics. Third, the subgroup is selected: only those eligible for and completing 2-year follow-up. The authors name possible sampling bias. Deaths are not reported, and anyone too sick to complete follow-up would be missing. Note that 30.5% of the subgroup (78 of 256, our arithmetic) had a complication against 26.8% overall, so complicated patients were not obviously lost. The covariate list differs between the Results, Discussion and figure legends.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: Strengths (authors): largest prospective series of medical complications they know of, multicenter, extensive complication data. Ours: full regression output in Table 4.
Selection: 11 high-volume US centers; no age limit or exclusions stated; no baseline comorbidity table.
Measurement: broad list of major and minor complications with no breakdown by severity reported; smoking (history, current or former) and symptom duration undefined.
Validity: stepwise, unvalidated model; baseline factors only; reporting errors across abstract, text and figures.
slides.notes: The core finding is plausible and the model output is internally consistent. Smoking and hypertension each raise the rate about 2.4-fold, with CIs that sit well above 1. What is fragile is everything around it. The headline IRRs are printed three different ways (Table 4 and Discussion, abstract, Results text). The abstract says logistic and the paper says Poisson. The duration variable has no unit. Two figures share P values. The funding line reads Deputy Spine, presumably DePuy Spine. Each is minor alone, but together they suggest light editing. Generalizability: these are ISSG centers, mean age 57, mostly women, about 10 levels fused. The 6-week window catches early events only. Late medical problems are outside the study, and so are surgical complications such as PJK, pseudarthrosis and reoperation. Because no severity breakdown is reported, the 26.8% mixes trivial and serious events. You cannot read it as a major-complication rate. Confounding: smokers and hypertensive patients may differ in ways that were not measured. The authors acknowledge that surgical factors were left out by design, and that individual complications were too rare to model. Clinical use: the authors conclude that patients with these risk factors should be identified and informed of their increased risk at consent, optimized preoperatively and followed closely after surgery. Our caveat: the paper does not show that stopping smoking or controlling blood pressure lowers the rate, because nothing was intervened on.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: In 448 ISSG deformity patients, about one in four had a medical complication within 6 weeks, mostly cardiopulmonary. Smoking and hypertension each raised the rate about 2.4-fold, and longer symptom duration raised it modestly. In a 2-year subgroup the authors found no difference in HRQL improvement between patients with and without a complication.
points: Expect: is that 26.8% major? Not necessarily; no breakdown by severity is reported and the list includes minor events.
Expect: does stopping smoking fix it? Not tested; these are associations.
Expect: why was age not a predictor? IRR 1.008, P = 0.1, likely sharing variance with comorbidities in a stepwise model (our view).
Expect: which IRR do I quote? Table 4: 2.39, 2.43, 1.24.
slides.notes: The spoken version should take under 30 seconds. Lead with the rate and what it includes, then the two big modifiable-looking factors, then the reassurance about outcomes, with its caveat. Likely follow-ups and answers. How many smokers were there? Not reported, so no absolute risk per patient. What does duration of symptoms mean? The abstract says years with spine problems, but the unit is never defined, so quote it loosely. Did operative time matter? Unadjusted, 422 vs 372 minutes (P = 0.0004), and it was not in the model. Is the HRQL result proof that complications do not matter? No. It is a 2-year subgroup of 256 with no effect size, and two of the three figures share identical P values. How does this compare with other series? The authors say their rate is higher than earlier series because collection was prospective and the list included minor events. Glassman's 24.9% combined medical and surgical complications, as quoted here. One-line boundary for Anki: this paper covers early medical complications only. It does not address surgical complications, late events or the effect of preoperative optimization.

decks.not_reviewed: Nothing beyond the 8-page article (E1174-E1181) was available, and the PDF is the complete paper, abstract to references. No supplement is cited. Figures 1 and 2 are radiographs and were read only through their captions. None of the 26 cited studies was read, so every diagnostic accuracy figure in this deck is the authors' secondhand quotation, not a verified value. The Lenke 2022 comparison comes from master-file record PM35290626, not from a reading of that paper.

slides.title: Strike 2017: neuromonitoring in deformity surgery
slides.lead: A narrative review plus one institution's protocol, not a study with patient data.
points: Journal club: intraoperative neuromonitoring (IONM)
Strike SA, Sponseller PD, et al. Clin Spine Surg 2017;30:E1174-E1181
Johns Hopkins orthopaedics, anesthesiology and neurology; one author at University of Virginia orthopaedics
Design: PubMed review of 'neuromonitoring' plus experience of institutional experts
Bottom line: SSEP plus TcMEP is the working core, EMG covers roots, DNEP and NMEP are alternatives, and the wake-up test is still the confirmatory step after an unexplained signal loss.
slides.notes: Frame it first. This is a review of techniques and a description of how one high-volume center monitors, written by surgeons, an anesthesiologist and a neurologist. It reports no cohort, no counts, no outcomes and no accuracy data of its own. The methods are one sentence: a PubMed search for neuromonitoring, with no dates, search terms beyond that word, selection criteria or numbers screened, and expert opinion from the institution. So read it as Level V expert opinion with a literature summary attached. The master file lists it as historical context and background from the SRS Quality and Safety Resource Library, and that is the right role. Its value is as a structured primer: what each modality sees and misses, how anesthesia distorts each signal, what the authors monitor by spinal region, and the order of steps after a signal change. The PDF is the complete article. It was received February 2015 and accepted May 2016, so the literature is mostly 2010 or earlier. The authors declare no conflict of interest. Two illustrative cases appear only as radiograph figures with long captions, and they carry two of the most useful teaching points, covered on slide 6.

slides.title: What each modality sees
slides.lead: Each technique watches a different pathway, and each has a blind spot.

rows: Late, intermittent, no sensory or root data
Amplitude drop over 50% or latency rise over 10%
Signal averaging delay, misses anterior cord injury
Loss, 80% drop at 1 of 6 sites, threshold rise or waveform change
Not continuous; hard with motor deficit; needs no relaxant
Sensory, not motor; needs full relaxation
Spinous process version needs dissection, fluid pools

slides.notes: Teach this as pathways. SSEPs travel up the dorsal columns, so an anterior spinal artery injury can leave them intact; the authors cite reports of paraplegia with maintained SSEPs. Amplitude is the more specific SSEP sign, and the authors say isolated latency change often occurs without damage. TcMEPs test the corticospinal tract directly, but only when you stimulate, so they are snapshots, and they need muscle tone. The authors list four MEP alert rules in use, from all-or-nothing loss to an 80% drop at 1 of 6 sites, and do not say which their center uses. They list tongue laceration from jaw clench as common, so use a bite block, and they advise against TcMEP with seizure disorders or skull metal, and disabling pacemakers. D-waves are recorded from the epidural or subdural space; the authors, citing a review, call them particularly relevant in spinal cord surgery and say MEPs without D-waves often suffice when the cord is not operated on. H-reflexes are described but not used at their center. DNEPs need complete muscle relaxation, the opposite of MEP and EMG, which relaxants prevent; so, by our inference, they cannot be recorded at the same moment. Triggered EMG works because a cortical breach lowers the threshold to fire the root. One internal inconsistency to say aloud: the DNEP section says its alert is similar to SSEPs, then gives an 80% amplitude drop, while the SSEP section gives over 50%. These are different thresholds. The 1 missed deficit in 74 is quoted from Emerson (reference 21, a 2-page item), reviewing a 23-year study of 3436 children; the reference list shows that study is Thuet (reference 13), cited two lines earlier but not in that sentence. Treat the figure as unverified secondhand.

slides.title: Anesthesia and the signal
slides.lead: MEPs are the most fragile to anesthetic choices; EMG is the least.

rows: Under 50%, or avoid if baseline poor

slides.notes: This is Table 1 condensed. The rule in practice: run total intravenous anesthesia as a steady infusion, avoid boluses, keep volatile agent low and avoid relaxant after intubation if MEPs or EMG are in use. The authors, citing Deiner (reference 14), explain the greater anesthetic sensitivity of MEPs by the greater length of the motor tracts. Cortical SSEP recordings are the most anesthesia-sensitive, so a cortical drop can be checked against subcortical and peripheral sites to separate anesthesia from injury. That comparison is a useful thing to ask your neurophysiologist for. In children, the authors warn that TIVA can delay extubation and recovery. Three things in the table need care. First, the text says halogenated agents should be kept at 0.5 MAC or less for SSEPs, but Table 1 gives 0.5 to 1.0 MAC. Second, the table footnote has an asterisk that appears nowhere in the table. Third, the table cites single studies for 3 agents and gives no source for the rest, and the cited titles do not match the cells: the propofol row, which carries the TcMEP dose of 50-300 µg/kg/min, cites Liu 2005, a study of isoflurane and propofol on cortical SSEPs, and the remifentanil row cites a survey of anaesthetists' practices, not a monitoring study. So treat the cut-offs as this center's guidance, not established thresholds. Figure 2 shows the practical payoff: switching from gas to TIVA with remifentanil and propofol improved MEPs enough to monitor a child with myelodysplasia.

slides.title: What they monitor, by region
slides.lead: Table 3 plus the text: more cord at risk means more modalities.

rows: UE and LE SSEP, MEP, spontaneous EMG
1-2 level ACDF for radiculopathy often SSEP alone
SSEP and MEP in all cases; EMG uncommon
SSEP, spontaneous and triggered EMG; MEP for 3-column osteotomy only
At or above conus: full multimodal; no instrumentation: none

slides.notes: The authors' protocol: all adult deformity patients and all pediatric patients with idiopathic scoliosis or kyphosis, neuromuscular disease with residual motor function, or growing rod or VEPTR work are monitored. In severe myelopathy or instability, they take signals before any movement and again before manipulation, to capture the effect of intubation and positioning. Laminoplasty may get C5 EMG, which the authors tie to increased tension on the shorter C5 root after decompression. Below the conus they scale by what is done: no instrumentation needs no IONM, instrumentation needs EMG, and 3-column osteotomy needs MEPs. The paper is not consistent on this. The lumbar section says instrumentation with an osteotomy requires spontaneous EMG, with no mention of MEPs; the adult practice section and Table 3 say 3-column osteotomy requires MEPs. The adult section also says EMG alone is used without a 3-column osteotomy, citing Table 3, yet Table 3 adult lumbar lists SSEPs plus spontaneous and triggered EMG.Pediatric lumbar in Table 3 lists spontaneous cervical EMG, which looks like a copy error for lumbar (our inference), and lists no MEP, although the text says the center uses primarily SSEPs and TcMEPs for children. The authors also say there is little and often controversial evidence for cervical IONM, so the cervical column is practice, not proof. Neuromuscular patients are the hard group: the authors cite useful monitoring as impossible in at least 10%, especially cerebral palsy or severe atrophy. Spondylolisthesis is also hard, being single level and distal. The whole table is one center's practice, offered without outcome data.

slides.title: The evidence they cite
slides.lead: All numbers below are quoted from other studies and were not checked against those papers.

rows: SSEP sens 52%, spec 100%; MEP sens 100%, spec 96%, PPV 96%; EMG sens 46%, PPV 3%
Multimodal sens 100%, spec 84%; SSEP alone sens 33%

slides.notes: This is the evidence spine of the review, and it is all secondhand. Read it with a calculator. Kelleher as quoted: MEP specificity 96% and positive predictive value 96% at the same time. With a 3.2% deficit rate, a 4% false-positive rate would make false alarms outnumber true ones, and PPV would be under 50%. A 96% PPV with 96% specificity needs a prevalence near 50% (our recompute). So either the specificity or the PPV is misquoted, or the MEP figures come from a different denominator. Check the original before using them. The SSEP and EMG figures fit a low prevalence better but do not reconcile exactly at 3.2% (about 34 deficits in 1055): EMG sensitivity 46% and specificity 73% give a PPV near 5%, not 3%, and SSEP sensitivity 52% with specificity 100% gives an NPV near 98.4%, not 97% (our recompute). That suggests different denominators, such as an EMG-monitored subset. Quraishi is the one adult-deformity figure: multimodal monitoring caught every deficit, SSEP alone caught a third. That is the strongest argument in the paper for not relying on SSEP alone, and it agrees with the anterior-cord blind spot. The thoracic screw studies show triggered EMG has a high negative predictive value, meaning a high threshold is reassuring; they say less about a low threshold. Note the citation problem: the text says Rodriguez-Olaverri placed screws from T6 to T12, but reference 19's title says T3 to T6. The authors then say thoracic monitoring is not widely used, which sits oddly next to their own recommendation of SSEP and MEP in all thoracic cases; we read it as referring to thoracic EMG. The NMEP comparison, 147 spinous process versus 122 percutaneous cases, found no significant difference in reliability; no figures are given.

slides.title: After a signal change
slides.lead: Rule out the room first, then fix the cord's environment, then confirm with a wake-up test.
points: Technical: electrodes, stimulators, flooded recording boxes, unplugged wires, new equipment such as a microscope, warmer, lamp or Bovie
Anesthetic: recent gas change, agent switch, relaxant bolus
Then: stop inhaled agents, check arterial blood gas, raise MAP to 90 mm Hg, raise FiO2, reverse severe anemia
Then: reduce distraction, check anchors, translation and canal stenosis, irrigate with warm saline
Then: Stagnara wake-up test; if it is concerning for a deficit, consider modifying or removing instrumentation and giving steroids
slides.see: Figure 1 caption: MEPs lost and returned twice, yet the girl had weakness on the evening of day 0 that resolved with 2 days of dopamine pressure support. Figure 2 caption: MEPs lost at rod insertion and returned when the rod came out.
slides.notes: This sequence is the most usable part of the paper. Notice the order. The authors put technical and anesthetic causes first and blood pressure in the middle. The later consensus in the library, Lenke 2022 (PM35290626), makes elevating MAP the first step and gives no numeric MAP target, only an elevated MAP for 48 to 72 hours in ICU, and its draft steroid doses were removed. Strike gives a number, 90 mm Hg, without a source, and suggests steroids without a dose or evidence. So the 90 is this center's practice. The two cases teach more than the text. Figure 1: a 13-year-old with idiopathic scoliosis, 75 degree thoracic and 72 degree lumbar curves. SSEPs could not be obtained at baseline, MEPs were lost and returned twice, and despite MEP return she was found to have weakness and sensory changes on the evening of postoperative day 0. These resolved with dopamine-induced pressure elevation in the PICU for 2 days and so were thought to be cord ischemia. The caption reports no wake-up test or immediate postoperative examination, so it does not say when the deficit began. The lesson, ours: return of MEPs does not exclude an ischemic deficit, and blood pressure support may still matter after closure. It also shows the cost of having only one modality working. Figure 2: a 13-year-old ambulatory girl with myelodysplasia, a 75 degree curve, an asymmetric pedicle subtraction osteotomy and untethering. MEPs dropped at rod insertion and returned when the rod was removed; one concave screw was repositioned and one removed, and MEPs were intact at closure. The caption does not report her postoperative neurology. Neither case gives timing or the size of the change.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: A sensible primer and protocol, with no data of its own and several internal slips.
points: Spoken summary: a Hopkins narrative review. SSEPs miss motor and anterior cord injury, so MEPs are added; EMG covers roots; almost all anesthetics affect the signals, inhaled agents more than intravenous ones, and relaxant blocks MEP and EMG. After a change: exclude technical and anesthetic causes, raise MAP to 90, correct oxygen, anemia and distraction, then wake-up test.
Expect: what is the evidence level? Expert opinion; no patients counted, no outcomes
Expect: why not SSEP alone? Quoted Quraishi: SSEP sensitivity 33% versus 100% multimodal in 102 adults
Expect: can MEPs return and the patient still be weak? Yes, Figure 1: weakness found the evening of day 0, thought ischemic, resolved with pressure
Expect: what differs from Lenke 2022? MAP first there and no numeric target; Strike puts room checks first and names 90 mm Hg
slides.notes: Keep the claim modest. This paper tells you how one experienced center does it and summarizes older literature; it cannot tell you that monitoring changes outcomes, which modality combination is best, or what MAP target works. If asked about thresholds, say that the paper gives over 50% amplitude loss for SSEPs and 80% for DNEP and NMEP, lists four competing MEP criteria and does not choose one. If asked about anesthesia, say keep volatile agent at or below 0.3 MAC for MEPs by Table 1, use steady TIVA, and avoid relaxant after intubation; note the text and table disagree on the SSEP volatile limit. If asked about neuromuscular scoliosis, at least 10% cannot be usefully monitored, as cited. If someone quotes the Kelleher MEP figures, point out that 96% specificity and 96% PPV cannot both hold at a 3.2% event rate, by our arithmetic. Problems to own: no methods to speak of, quotations not verified, a clear citation error (T6-T12 for a T3-T6 paper) and a likely second (SSEPs 'developed in the late 1970s' cited to a 1973 wake-up test paper), a missing co-citation of Thuet for the 3436-child series, and an inconsistent lumbar osteotomy rule. A likely follow-up: should every deformity case be monitored? The authors monitor all adult deformity patients, and children with idiopathic scoliosis or kyphosis, neuromuscular disease with residual motor function, or growing rod or VEPTR work; that is their policy, not a finding of this paper.

decks.not_reviewed: No supplement is cited in the PDF. The comparison series cited by the authors (Kelly et al and Scoli-RISK-1, the SRS Morbidity and Mortality review by Hamilton, Cramer, Schoenfeld, Hassanzadeh) were not reviewed; their numbers are as reported in this paper. Figure 1 was read from the rendered page. The PDF is the complete published article, not a critique.

slides.title: Kim 2017: Neurologic complications in adult deformity surgery
slides.lead: Bottom line: 99 of 564 ISSG deformity patients (17.6%) had a neurologic complication, 13.7% a surgical one, most often radiculopathy. Prior spine surgery and interbody fusion were associated with more; osteotomies, including three-column, did not reach significance.
points: Journal club · Adult deformity: perioperative risk
Kim HJ, Iyer S, Zebala LP, et al, International Spine Study Group. Spine 2017;42(6):420-427
Full text read: Tables 1 to 6 and Figure 1. The PDF is the complete article, not a critique.
Retrospective review of a prospective 11-site US database, 2008 to 2014. Level of evidence 3.
slides.notes: Frame this as a consent-number paper. The authors say their purpose was to give the incidence, risk factors and outcomes of neurologic complications in the largest ASD series to date, and to provide benchmark numbers for informed consent. That is what it does best. It is weaker as a risk-factor paper, because every association is univariate. Two labels to fix before you start. The abstract calls the design 'prognostic study, case controlled', but Methods call it a retrospective cohort study from a prospective multicenter database. The cohort description is the accurate one: all 564 eligible patients were analyzed and then split by whether they had a complication.
