Second, the 17.6% is a patient count (99 of 564), while the abstract's 30% radiculopathy and 22% motor deficit are shares of the 116 complications, not of patients. Our arithmetic: 25 motor-deficit events in 564 patients is at most about 4.4% of patients, and 24 were graded major. Table 1 counts events, not patients, and 116 events fell in 99 patients, so 4.4% assumes one motor deficit per patient; the paper does not give the patient count. Keep the two denominators apart when you quote it. The library record was a bibliography entry only; this deck is the first full-text appraisal.

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: 564 operative ASD patients from 11 US sites with at least 6 weeks of data, split into 99 with and 465 without a neurologic complication.
points: Included: age 18 or older with Cobb 20° or more, SVA 5 cm or more, PT 25° or more, or TK 60° or more; at least 6 weeks of follow-up.
Excluded: neuromuscular deformity, active infection, malignancy, and patients not yet entered in the database.
Mean age 57, 78.7% women, mean follow-up 13 months. About 11 levels fused; 45% had prior spine surgery (ours, 255 of 564).

Surgical complications: motor, sensory, root injury, radiculopathy, myelopathy, bowel or bladder, epidural hematoma. Nonsurgical (Methods): meralgia paresthetica, mental status changes, peroneal nerve palsy, stroke. 'Other' (8 events) sits in the nonsurgical group only by our inference from the Table 1 sums.
Major: extra intervention lengthening stay, return to theatre, or unresolved. Minor: everything else.
Univariate t, chi-square or Fisher tests; significance P < 0.025, called a Bonferroni correction.

rows: Not enrolled (19 no surgeon follow-up, 7 data entry pending, 1 refused)
Analyzed: 99 with, 465 without a neurologic complication

slides.see: Figure 1 is the flow diagram; its numbers add up (635 - 27 = 608; 608 - 44 = 564).
slides.notes: What to notice. This is the ISSG prospective database, but the question was asked afterward, so complication classification is retrospective. The authors say the major-minor and surgical-nonsurgical labels were set by consensus of the senior authors and are necessarily subjective, which is why they printed every complication type in Table 1. There is no standard neurologic examination schedule, no ASIA or motor-grade scale, and no definition of the intraoperative, perioperative and postoperative windows. 'Other' (8 events) is never described. The flow arithmetic holds. 564 of 608 is 92.8% by our arithmetic; the paper prints 92.7%. 564 of the 635 who met inclusion criteria is 88.8% (ours). The 44 lost for inadequate follow-up could plausibly differ in complication rate, but no data are given on them. Follow-up is internally inconsistent: Methods require at least 6 weeks, while Results give a range of 6 months to 3 years. Mean age is also odd. The text says 57.02 years, range 18 to 68, but Table 2 gives 58.8 and 57.1 by group, which average to 58.5 (ours). A maximum of 68 is low for an adult deformity cohort with an SD near 14, so treat the age range as a probable printing error. The threshold: P < 0.025 corrects for 2 comparisons, not for the about 73 tests in Tables 2 to 6 plus 5 more in the surgical-complication subanalysis (our count). The abstract says a multivariate analysis was done; none is reported anywhere in the paper.

slides.title: Result 1: how often, and what kind
slides.lead: 116 neurologic complications in 99 patients (17.6%). Surgical: 88 in 77 patients (13.7%). Nonsurgical: 28 in 28 (5.0%). 6 patients had both.

rows: Myelopathy, bowel or bladder, epidural hematoma

points: About half of surgical complications were major (47 of 88); most nonsurgical ones were minor.
Timing: 28.6% intraoperative, 60.7% recognized perioperatively, 10.7% postoperatively.
Permanence: the authors 'are unable to make further conclusions about which deficits were temporary versus permanent'.
slides.notes: We rechecked Table 1. Event counts sum to 116, majors to 53 and minors to 63. The surgical rows named in Methods sum to 88, with 47 major. Patient counts reconcile: 77 + 28 - 6 = 99. Percentages are correct. Two problems. First, the Results text says 67 minor complications (54.3%); the table's 63 is the number that adds up and matches 54.3%. Second, the timing split 28.6%, 60.7% and 10.7% is exactly 8, 17 and 3 of 28 (our arithmetic). None of the three is a whole number of 116. So the timing appears to describe only 28 events, possibly the nonsurgical group, but the paper does not say which. Do not quote the timing as applying to all complications. How to read the table. Most of the 17.6% is radiculopathy, sensory change and mental status change, much of it minor. The events a surgeon fears most are rarer: 24 major motor deficits, 2 myelopathies, 1 epidural hematoma, 1 bowel or bladder event and 3 strokes. For consent, our reading is that 'up to about 4% get a new motor deficit' is the useful number, with two caveats: 25 is a count of events, not patients, so 4.4% is an upper bound, and the paper cannot say how many recovered. The authors state that they cannot distinguish temporary from permanent deficits and call this an important area for future research. The authors say their rate is consistent with Kelly et al (17.2% in a prospective study) and other prospective studies. They also cite the SRS Morbidity and Mortality review (1.0%) and say large retrospective database reports carry recall, reporting and sampling bias; those figures are as reported in this paper. That 17.6% is far above 1.0% is our contrast, not the authors' words. The authors take the match with prospective series as support for the accuracy of their audited data.

slides.title: Result 2: who is at risk
slides.lead: By printed P, only prior spine surgery and interbody fusion passed the P < 0.025 threshold; decompression recomputes to 0.024 (ours). All comparisons are univariate.
points: No difference in age, BMI, ASA grade, preoperative weakness or numbness.
Interbody approach (ALIF, PLIF, TLIF, lateral) made no difference within interbody patients.
SSEP or MEP changes were not associated (P 0.17 and 0.68), with only 20 patients each having a change.
slides.notes: The risk column is ours, from Table 2 and Table 5 counts, using 99 as the complication total. Read it first: about 1 in 5 with an interbody fusion versus 1 in 10 without. Now the labels. The paper calls these odds ratios, but they do not recompute as odds ratios. They do reproduce as risk ratios. Interbody: our risk ratio 2.15 (1.40 to 3.30) against the printed 2.1 (1.4 to 3.2); the odds ratio would be about 2.5 to 3.0. Prior surgery: our risk ratio 1.64 against printed 1.7; odds ratio 1.83. The Table 5 footnote reads them as 'times more likely', which is how a risk ratio reads. So the direction holds and the magnitude is roughly right, but the label is wrong. That is our inference. Interbody subtypes are a second trap. ALIF was 31.6% versus 21.1% of the whole groups, which alone gives P about 0.03, but the printed 1.1 (P 0.73) reproduces only when ALIF is compared within interbody patients. Our inference again; the paper does not say so. Several Table 2 rows do not reproduce from their own counts: deep infection (our ratio 2.7, printed 2.2), numbness (2.1 vs 1.7), weakness (1.6 vs 1.3), diabetes (P about 0.13 vs 0.3). SSEP changes print 1.2 (0.8 to 3.4); the counts give about 1.75. What is fragile: no adjustment at all. Revisions and interbody fusion likely travel with longer, more complex cases, so these are markers, not proven causes. The null for osteotomy, PSO and VCR is underpowered; VCR had a 28% rate on 25 patients. Decompression was called 'not increased' at printed P 0.04, but the Table 5 counts (70 of 99 vs 272 of 465) give P 0.024 by uncorrected chi-square or Fisher, under the paper's own 0.025 cutoff, and P 0.006 with the 95 denominator the percentages imply (ours). The decompression null does not hold up. Two more printed P values miss: prior surgery 0.002 in the text recomputes to about 0.007, and PSO 0.06 to 0.11-0.15 (ours). The authors suggest monitoring changes were unrelated because surgeons intervened when signals changed, but say the design cannot show what was done. That is their hypothesis, not a finding.

slides.title: Result 3: what follows a neurologic complication
slides.lead: Patients with a neurologic complication stayed longer, used the SICU more and were reoperated more.
points: No difference in operative time (395 vs 377 min), blood loss or levels fused.
Cardiopulmonary, implant, wound, GI and other complication rates did not differ.
The abstract says patients with a neurologic complication were not more likely to have other complications; Table 6 shows radiographic and infectious complications were.
slides.notes: Read the direction carefully. The authors themselves warn that the design cannot show cause, and give the example that proximal junctional kyphosis can produce myelopathy, so a radiographic complication may come first. The same applies to the SICU row: in our reading, ICU care may be a consequence of the complication, a marker of a sicker case, or both. It belongs with outcomes, not risk factors. Revision within 3 years is also an outcome, and follow-up averaged only 13 months, so the 27.4% depends on how long each patient was watched; no time-to-event analysis was done. Table 5 percentages for the complication group use 95, not 99, as the denominator (76 of 95 is 80.0%), so 4 patients are missing from that table without explanation (ours). The Table 6 ratios reproduce as risk ratios of having a neurologic complication given the other complication, not odds ratios: infectious 1.81 (1.12 to 2.93) and radiographic 1.88 (1.27 to 2.79) by our arithmetic, matching the printed values. The abstract contradicts the results. It says patients with neurologic complications were not more likely to sustain other complications, yet the Results report higher radiographic (P < 0.01) and infectious (P = 0.02) complication rates, both under the paper's own 0.025 threshold. Quote the table, not the abstract. Radiographs: SVA was not the only signal. Baseline SVA was 83.9 versus 62.2 mm (printed P 0.03), which the text calls 'similar'; from the Table 3 means and SDs we get P 0.010 (pooled t) or 0.022 (Welch), both under 0.025, so the Results claim of no baseline radiographic difference does not hold (ours). Baseline sacral slope also differed, 32.4 versus 29.7 (printed P 0.03; ours 0.024 Welch, 0.044 pooled). 6-week SVA was 40.3 versus 23.3 mm (P < 0.01), and 6-week upper thoracic Cobb (printed P 0.06) recomputes to P < 0.001 if all patients had radiographs. Baseline UT Cobb (printed 0.55) and thoracolumbar Cobb (0.25) recompute to about 0.22-0.29 and 0.09 (ours). The SVA modifier was P 0.032. The Table 3 footnote says there were no differences at follow-up, which contradicts the 6-week SVA row.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: Holds up: large multicenter audited prospective database; every complication type tabulated; flow diagram adds up; rate matches other prospective series (authors' point).
Selection: 11 US ISSG centers; 44 enrolled patients excluded for inadequate follow-up, not described.
Measurement: consensus classification, set retrospectively; no neurologic exam protocol or motor grading; timing windows undefined; permanence unknown.
Analysis: univariate only; multivariate analysis in the abstract never reported; 2-comparison correction for about 73 tests (our count).
Reporting: printed odds ratios behave as risk ratios (ours); several rows do not reproduce; abstract contradicts Table 6.
Underpowered nulls: VCR 25 patients, monitoring changes 20 each.
slides.notes: Be fair first. The incidence is the solid part. It comes from a prospective, audited database, the arithmetic in Table 1 and Figure 1 holds, and the authors make a reasonable point that prospective collection finds about twice the neurologic complications of retrospective review (they cite Kelly: 8.7% retrospective versus 17.2% prospective, as reported in this paper). The authors' own limitations are retrospective review, inability to infer causation, inability to know what was done after monitoring alerts, and no data on permanence. Our additions. One, no adjustment, so 'interbody fusion was required' in the conclusion reads as causal when it is an unadjusted association. Two, the labelled odds ratios reproduce as risk ratios, and interbody subtype ratios appear to be computed within interbody patients; neither is stated. Three, decompression, 1.5 (1.0 to 2.2) at printed P 0.04, is called 'did not increase the likelihood', but its own counts give P 0.024, under the 0.025 cutoff (ours), so that null is not supported. Four, the denominators drift: Table 5 uses 95 complication patients, monitoring percentages imply 558 patients, and sex data cover 545. Five, internal number errors: minor complications 67 in text versus 63 in Table 1; age range 18 to 68 against group means near 58; follow-up minimum 6 weeks versus 6 months; Kelly cited as 275 patients with 17% in the Introduction and 256 patients with 17.2% in the Discussion, and that reference's own title says retrospective. Six, the Discussion cites Table 3 for the SRS-Schwab result, which is in Table 4. None of these changes the headline rate. They do mean the risk-factor table should be quoted as direction, not precise magnitude.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "In the ISSG database, about 1 in 6 adult deformity patients had a neurologic complication around surgery and about 1 in 7 a surgical one, most often radiculopathy. New motor deficits were up to about 4%. Revision surgery and interbody fusion went with higher rates, unadjusted. The paper cannot say how many deficits were permanent."

rows: at most about 4.4% of patients (ours; assumes one event per patient)

points: Smith 2016 (library record D09), from the same ISSG group: 69.8% of 291 patients had any complication by 2 years, so neurologic events are one slice of a large total.
Do not stretch it: no permanence data, no adjusted risk factors, osteotomy nulls underpowered.
slides.notes: Expect four follow-up questions. Is a three-column osteotomy safe neurologically, since it was not a risk factor? Not proven. PSO and VCR numbers are small, 7 of the 25 VCR patients had a neurologic complication (28%, our arithmetic), and nothing was adjusted. Absence of significance is not evidence of safety. Does interbody fusion cause neurologic injury? The paper cannot say. It is an unadjusted association; interbody cases may be longer, revision or multi-approach cases, and the authors call for further research into interbody type. Approach did not matter within interbody patients. How many of these deficits were permanent? Unknown. The authors say so directly, and the paper reports no recovery data. That is the single most important gap for consent. Did neuromonitoring help? Not answerable here. Only 20 patients had an SSEP change and 20 an MEP change, and the interventions after alerts were not recorded. On the library comparison: Smith 2016 (D09) is another ISSG prospective cohort enrolled 2008 to 2012, so its patients likely overlap with this one (our inference). Its 69.8% counts all complications including minor and radiographic ones, so it is not comparable to Kim's neurologic rate; it only shows context. When you quote Kim, state that it is a neurologic complication rate to a minimum of 6 weeks, mixing major and minor events.

decks.not_reviewed: None known. The full 11-page article was read, including Tables 1-4 and Figures 1-4. The text cites Tables 2 and 3 'in online version', but both are printed in this PDF. The survey instrument beyond the table rows, and the cited Ames 2013 and Sethi 2014 studies, were not reviewed.

slides.title: The paper
slides.lead: Scheer JK, et al, for the SRS Adult Spinal Deformity Committee. Results of the 2015 SRS survey on single versus dual attending surgeon approach for adult spinal deformity surgery. Spine 2017;42:932-942.
points: Design: one electronic survey of SRS members and candidate members; the journal labels it Level of Evidence 5
199 of 1005 invited surgeons answered (19.8%), from 27 countries
Bottom line: most respondents believe a second attending surgeon makes deformity surgery safer, but most rarely operate with one
Reimbursement and surgeon availability were the barriers they named
It measures opinion, not patient outcomes. The authors say so themselves
slides.notes:
This deck was built from the full text of the paper, all 11 pages, including Tables 1 to 4 and Figures 1 to 4. The text cites Tables 2 and 3 'in online version', but both are printed in this PDF, so we know of no unread supplement. The survey instrument itself is not reproduced beyond the table rows.

Frame it before anything else. This is a health services survey, not a clinical study. No patient was measured. Every result is a percentage of surgeons choosing an answer. The paper's own last line says the results should be interpreted as a measurement of opinion and not as scientific fact or validation. Hold the room to that.

Why it is in the library: it sits next to the dual attending outcome studies it cites (Ames 2013, Sethi 2014). Neither is a library record, so their numbers appear here only as this paper reports them. Its role is background for why two-surgeon teams are uncommon: payment and access, as surgeons report it.

The paper reports that no funds supported the work. Authors list outside financial activities in general terms. Several authors come from centers that use or published on two-surgeon teams, including Sethi (Seattle) and Ames (UCSF). Our observation, not the paper's: the committee asking the question had an interest in the answer.

slides.title: The question and the survey
slides.lead: How often do deformity surgeons use a second attending, why, and what stops them?
points: Background as the authors give it: Ames et al and Sethi et al reported fewer complications with two attendings at select centers
Instrument: 27 questions on SurveyMonkey, sent by email by the SRS Adult Deformity Committee; no incentive
Domains: surgeon and practice details (Q1-9), assistant type and training (Q10-16), dual attending views and use (Q17-27)
Five reminder emails were sent
Comparisons: US vs international, academic vs private, under vs over 15 years in practice
Statistics: percentages, Pearson chi-square or Fisher exact test, P below 0.05
slides.notes:
The authors state there was no previous study of surgeon practice and views on this approach. Their stated uses for the answers: education, help with third-party payers, and groundwork for future research. Note the second aim. The paper was written partly to support a reimbursement argument, and the abstract conclusion calls for working with payers to improve dual surgeon payment in complex cases.

What the paper does not report: the dates the survey was open (the title says 2015), whether the questions were piloted or validated, whether answers were anonymous, and how missing answers were handled. Totals vary from 144 to 199 by question, so each percentage has its own denominator.

Read the questions carefully. Q15 asks what percent of cases have another attending as your only assistant. That is the use measure the paper reports. It is narrower than any case with a second attending present, and the paper does not ask how often a resident or fellow was also scrubbed. Q17 to Q20 are yes/no belief questions. Q26 is select-all-that-apply with an 'all of the above' option.

The group P values compare answer distributions between two groups. The overall P below 0.01 for Q17 to Q20 can only be a test of yes against no within one group. The paper does not name that test. Our reading: it shows only that more than half said yes.

slides.title: Who answered
slides.lead: An academic, orthopedic, experienced sample, two thirds from the US.

rows: At least 25 three-column osteotomies a year

points: Attendings were 98.0%; 1 resident and 3 fellows also answered
International surgeons and academics had more deformity and more pediatric work; US and private surgeons had more adult work
slides.notes:
We recomputed the percentages in this table and in the text from the table counts, and they match within rounding.

Three points about the sample. First, 1 in 5 answered. The authors call the response rate relatively low and say responders may favor the dual surgeon approach. They argue that 199 surgeons from 27 nations is still large, and point to other published surveys with 20 to 31 percent response. A large biased sample is still biased. Second, it is not a sample of adult deformity surgeons. 36.0 percent said at least half their deformity practice was pediatric, and 12.1 percent reported no adult deformity work. Third, neurosurgeons were 9.6 percent, so the views are mostly orthopedic.

Group sizes, our arithmetic: the international column never exceeds 57 (it is 57 for most questions, lower for Q10-12, Q14 and Q16), but 199 minus 133 US respondents is 66. The paper does not explain the other 9. Academic plus private is 185, because 13 chose 'other' and are left out of that comparison.

Within groups the paper reports that international surgeons had more of their practice in deformity than US surgeons (61.4 vs 34.8 percent at 51 percent or more), and academic more than private (53.0 vs 20.0 percent). Years in practice made no difference to practice mix. Three-column osteotomy volume did not differ significantly between any pair of groups.

slides.title: What surgeons believe
slides.lead: Belief was strongest for hard cases and weakest for outcomes in routine deformity.
points: Intl vs US was significant for Q17, Q19 and Q20, not Q18 (P=0.10)
Academic vs private and years in practice made no difference for Q17-20
Training concern: academic 59.0% vs private 36.0%; under 15 years 61.5% vs over 15 years 41.9%, P<0.01 for both
slides.see: Figure 2 shows the yes and no bars for Q17 to Q20 side by side.
slides.notes:
The headline of the paper is this slide. Read it closely. 'Safer' in Q17 and Q18 is one question: improves safety and decreases complications. It is a belief, not a measured complication rate.

The skepticism of US respondents is the most interesting finding. Only half of US respondents (50.8 percent) thought a second attending improves outcomes in all adult deformity cases. The gap closes for difficult cases: 82.0 versus 91.2 percent for safety, not significant. So the agreement that does exist is about three-column osteotomies and hard cases. Do not let anyone stretch it to routine deformity.

Our check: we reran uncorrected Pearson chi-square, the test the Methods name, on the printed counts. Q17 gives P 0.001, Q18 0.10, Q19 0.0001 and Q20 0.03, matching every printed value. The US vs international difference on Q20 is significant as printed, though not by a wide margin.

The training question split the room evenly, 52 to 48. Academic surgeons and younger surgeons worried more. The paper offers no explanation; our guess is that these are the people who teach residents or recently were one. The paper does not ask what share of cases a trainee would lose.

Authors' interpretation: a strong belief that the dual surgeon approach is very beneficial to patient care. Ours: a strong belief for difficult cases, a modest majority for routine cases, and a near coin toss in US surgeons on routine outcomes.

slides.title: How often, why, and what stops them
slides.lead: Watch the denominators. The headline percentages exclude surgeons who answered not applicable.

rows: Attending as only assistant in 0% of cases (Q15)
Limited by both payment and access (Q24)
Would use more often or always if paid (Q27)

points: 67.3% use an attending as only assistant in 25% of cases or fewer, and that figure includes the 33.2% who never do
Access meant surgeon availability given busy clinic schedules
Same-specialty second attending in at least 51% of co-surgeon cases: 48.2%, just under half; different specialty in at least 51%: 13.8%
slides.see: Figure 3 is the Q24 pie and Figure 4 the Q26 bars, both with their own denominators.
slides.notes:
We recomputed every row from Tables 3 and 4. All match. The 'of applicable' column is our arithmetic, but the paper's own headline numbers (51.1, 71.9, 72.3 and 67.5 percent) are the applicable versions. The abstract hints at this only for 51.1 percent ('that have a second attending'); the Results text gives the n each time. The 67.5 percent in particular is 104 of the 154 who did not answer not applicable. Of all 198 who answered Q27, it is 52.5 percent.

Q26 needs care. 'All of the above' bundled five reasons, including 'it's less work and stress for me.' The paper counts the single reasons only for people who did not also tick 'all of the above.' So '72.3 percent use one for all of these reasons' measures one tick box. It cannot tell you which reason drives the choice. Only 12 surgeons (6.1 percent) ticked improved outcomes without also ticking all of the above.

Q25 has a coincidence worth knowing so it does not confuse you. 82 answered not applicable and 82 reported some difficulty, both 41.8 percent of 196. The text's 41.8 percent refers to difficulty.

Of the 198 who answered Q27, 154 did not choose not applicable, more than the 114 who said Q25 applied. Our reading: many who do not use a co-surgeon still said they would if paid. That is a hypothetical answer, the weakest kind of survey evidence.

The experience of the second attending was under 15 years for 47.4 percent and over 15 years for 24.2 percent, from Q16. Most physician assistant or nurse practitioner assistants had 10 years of experience or less (81.9 percent of 144).

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: An honest opinion poll, reported with several text-table conflicts.
points: Holds up: large international sample and electronic collection (the authors' stated strengths), group comparisons planned, limits admitted by the authors
Authors' limits: low response, possible bias toward the dual approach, varied experience, no clinical scenarios, opinion not fact
Weakens it (ours): no instrument validation or survey dates reported, an applicable-only denominator in the headline numbers, and about 66 group tests with no correction
Text says no other group differences for Q10-16 and Q17-27, but the tables print P=0.02 for Q12 by years and P=0.01 for Q27 US vs international
Text gives P<0.01 for academic vs private on adult and pediatric share; Table 2 prints 0.02 for both
International column never exceeds 57, against 66 non-US respondents
Discussion repeats outcome figures from Ames and Sethi; this survey did not measure them
slides.notes:
Be fair first. The authors were open about what this is, and their limitations paragraph is better than many. They admit a low response rate, possible responder bias toward the dual approach, a varied population, and that the results are opinion.

Now the problems. The text contradicts its own tables. The results say there were no other significant differences for questions 10 to 16, yet Table 3 prints P=0.02 for Q12 (fellow as only assistant) by years in practice. They say no others for 17 to 27 and the discussion says the Q27 answer was similar between all groups, yet Table 4 prints P=0.01 for Q27 US vs international. Our chi-square on the printed counts gives 0.023 and 0.011, so the tables are right and the text is wrong. In Q27, 36.8 percent of international respondents answered not applicable against 16.7 percent of US respondents. The text also says P below 0.01 for academic vs private on adult and pediatric share. Table 2 prints 0.02, which our recalculation matches.

Multiplicity: 3 comparisons on each of 22 questions (Q6-27), about 66 group tests, plus 4 overall tests, with no correction. Some significant results will be chance. Our recalculation matches the tables except Q16: by years, printed 0.06, we get 0.03; US vs international, printed below 0.01, we get 0.013. Q26 is select-all, so its P values cannot be checked from the table.

The Q26 'all of the above' option and the applicable-only denominators both push the headline numbers up. That is our reading. It does not make the numbers wrong.

Last, the discussion. It quotes Ames (35 vs 109 percent blood loss, 5.0 vs 7.6 hours, 25 vs 45 percent major complications, 8 vs 19 percent unplanned surgery) and Sethi (16 vs 52 percent complications and more). Those come from other studies, which the paper calls select centers, reported here secondhand, and Sethi bundled the second surgeon with a screening conference and a coagulopathy protocol, as the paper itself notes. The authors write that this study 'adds to the evidence' that surgeons agree. It adds evidence of agreement, not of benefit.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "In a 2015 SRS survey, 199 of 1005 surgeons answered. Most believed a second attending makes difficult deformity cases safer, but most rarely used one, and cited payment and availability. It is opinion, not outcome data."
points: 84.4% believed two attendings improve safety in 3CO and difficult cases; 69.9% in all deformity
Only 24.1% had another attending as only assistant in at least half their cases; 33.2% never did
Of those it applied to, 71.9% had trouble getting the co-surgeon paid
Do not stretch it: no patient was studied, so it cannot show that two surgeons reduce complications
slides.notes:
Expect these follow-up questions.

Does this prove two surgeons are safer? No. It shows that surgeons believe so, and the authors say the results are opinion and not scientific fact. The outcome numbers in the discussion come from Ames and Sethi, which the paper calls select centers, and the Sethi program changed several things at once. Those papers are not in this library, so quote them only as this paper reports them.

Why do most not use one if they believe in it? The surgeons' answer is reimbursement and access. Of the 131 for whom Q24 applied, 51.1 percent named both. Of the 114 for whom Q25 applied, 71.9 percent had at least some difficulty getting paid. 67.5 percent of the 154 for whom Q27 applied would use one more often or always if payment were equal and assured, but that is a hypothetical.

Is the belief universal? No. US surgeons were split on routine cases: 50.8 percent thought it improves outcomes in all adult deformity cases. Agreement is strong only for three-column osteotomy and difficult cases.

What about training? 52 percent thought two attendings hurt resident and fellow training, more among academic and younger surgeons. Our inference: a two-attending model may have a cost in teaching, which the paper does not measure.

What would answer the real question? Our suggestion: a prospective comparison of single and dual attending deformity surgery, with cases matched for complexity, reporting complications, blood loss, operative time and cost. The authors call for larger prospective studies and clinical scenarios that define when a second surgeon is needed.

decks.not_reviewed: Nothing beyond the PDF. We read the full 6-page article (Spine 2018;43(10):693-698) end to end, including both tables, Key Points and references. The paper cites no supplement. Cited studies (Soroceanu 2015, Kalanithi 2012, Buerba 2014 and others) were not reread; figures for them are as this paper reports them.

slides.title: Amin 2018: BMI and inpatient outcomes after ASD surgery
slides.lead: In 244 single-surgeon ASD fusions, obese patients had more prolonged ICU stays, and BMI 35 or more was linked to longer stays and higher costs.
points: Journal club: adult spinal deformity, patient selection
Amin RM, Raad M, Jain A, Sandhu KP, Frank SM, Kebaish KM. Spine 2018;43(10):693-698. Johns Hopkins.
Retrospective single-centre, single-surgeon cohort, 2010 to 2014. Level of evidence 3.

Bottom line: adjusted against nonobese patients, class I obesity had higher odds of ICU stay over 2 days (OR 2.24). BMI 35 or more had higher odds of ICU stay over 2 days (2.35), total stay over 1 week (2.21) and episode cost over $80,000 (2.91). Inhospital complications did not differ.
slides.notes: This deck is based on the full article, read end to end. There is no supplement. Frame it before the numbers. This is a small retrospective cohort from one surgeon's registry. BMI was not assigned, so every result is an association, and the comparison is only as good as the adjustment. The outcomes are resource use, not clinical harm: ICU days, total hospital days and inpatient cost. Complications were also collected and did not differ between groups. The authors set it up as a gap filler. They say obesity class has been studied in non-deformity spine surgery, mostly in large national databases, but not in ASD with operative detail such as fusion length and osteotomy. Their stated hypothesis was that class II/III patients would have longer stays and higher costs than both class I and nonobese patients. Keep that in mind when you reach the comparator problem on slide 5. The headline is stronger than the data in two places (our reading). First, the abstract says BMI 35 or more is linked to 'significantly worse perioperative outcomes', but the only outcomes that differed were length of stay and cost. Second, the Conclusion says 'increasing class of obesity' is linked to longer total stay and higher cost. Class I did not reach significance on either, and no trend test was run. No funding was received, and the authors report no relevant financial activities.

slides.title: Question, selection and measurement
slides.lead: Is obesity class linked to transfusion, complications, ICU stay, total stay and cost after ASD fusion?
points: Source: surgical registry at one academic tertiary centre; all operations by the senior author
ASD defined as posterior arthrodesis of 5 or more levels, 2010 to 2014. No radiographic deformity criteria are given.
273 eligible; 16 excluded for missing BMI and 13 for missing outcome data; 244 analyzed (89%)
WHO groups: nonobese BMI under 30 (n = 155), class I 30 to 34.9 (n = 52), class II/III 35 or more (n = 37). Class II and III were pooled.
Outcomes: transfusion, inhospital complication, and three median splits: ICU stay over 2 days, total stay over 1 week, episode-of-care cost over $80,000 from billing records
Statistics: ANOVA and chi-square across groups; factors with P under 0.10 entered a multivariable logistic regression
slides.notes: Selection. 'ASD' here means a long posterior fusion, not a defined deformity. The paper gives no Cobb, SVA or pelvic parameter, so we cannot tell how many were degenerative scoliosis, sagittal imbalance or revision flatback. 56% were revisions. Fusion of 5 or more levels from one surgeon is a narrow, high-volume population, and this limits generalizing to other centres (our point). The 29 exclusions (11%) were for missing data, and the paper does not compare them with those included. Measurement. BMI was taken from the record, and the timing (preoperative or at admission) is not stated. Pooling class II and III means the 37-patient top group mixes BMI 35 with BMI 50. Outcome thresholds. ICU stay, total stay and cost were skewed, so the authors split each at its median: 2 days, 1 week and $80,000. These are statistical cut points, not clinical thresholds chosen in advance. Dichotomizing at the median throws away information, and 'prolonged' here just means the upper half (our point). Costs are inpatient billing costs, and the paper does not say whether they are hospital costs or charges, or whether professional fees are included. Adjustment. Covariates were picked by univariate P under 0.10. The paper never lists which entered each model, and gives no unadjusted ORs. Sex, hemoglobin and osteotomy differed at baseline, so they likely qualified, but that is our guess. With 58 prolonged-ICU events, the number of terms the model can support is limited. Complications were not modelled. They were 22 events in total, with one in the class II/III group.

slides.title: Who was studied
slides.lead: The groups were similar except for sex, hemoglobin and osteotomy.
points: Reported P values: female 0.002, hemoglobin 0.010, osteotomy type 0.018. Age 0.840, osteoporosis 0.248, CCI 0.921, platelets 0.552, levels 0.91, revision 0.263.
Overall: mean age 60, 175 women, mean CCI 1.1, mean 9 levels fused, 56% revision, 9% inhospital complication
slides.notes: We recomputed every baseline test from Table 1. Chi-square gives female P = 0.0018 (reported 0.002), osteoporosis 0.248, revision 0.263 and osteotomy 0.018, all matching. ANOVA from the reported means and SDs gives age about 0.86, platelets about 0.54 and CCI about 0.91, close to the reported values. Hemoglobin recomputes to 0.003 from the rounded means of 13, 13 and 14. The true means are not given, so the reported 0.010 is plausible. 273 minus 16 minus 13 is 244, which is 89.4% of 273, as stated. What to notice. The class I group carried the most three-column osteotomies (58% vs 37% in nonobese patients). A three-column osteotomy is a known driver of blood loss, ICU care and stay. If the model did not adjust for it well, part of the class I ICU signal could be osteotomy (our inference). The class I ICU OR fell from about 2.86 crude (our calculation from Table 1) to 2.24 adjusted, which fits partial confounding. Nonobese patients were more often women (79%). The class II/III group had more revisions (68%), although this did not reach significance. One text error: Results say 47% (n = 105) had a three-column osteotomy. Table 1 gives 58 + 30 + 17 = 105, and 105/244 is 43%.

slides.title: Unadjusted outcomes
slides.lead: ICU stay, total stay and cost differed across groups; transfusion and complications did not.
points: Reported P: ICU 0.003, total stay 0.016, cost 0.013, complication 0.218, transfusion 0.586
Means overall: ICU 2 days (SD 3), total stay 8 days (SD 5), cost $83,000 (SD $30,000)
slides.notes: How to read it. For ICU stay, the step is at BMI 30: class I and class II/III look the same (37% and 35%). For cost, the rate rises with each class (44%, 54%, 70%). For total stay, both obese groups sit above nonobese patients. So 'worse with each class' fits only cost. Recomputation. ICU chi-square is 11.50, P = 0.0032, matching the text and table. The abstract says P under 0.001, which is wrong. Total stay (0.016), cost (0.013) and complications (0.218) reproduce. Transfusion does not. Chi-square on 151/155, 51/52 and 34/37 gives 3.26, P = 0.196, not the reported 0.586. It is non-significant either way. Two of these tests are on thin data. Transfusion has an expected cell of about 1.2, and complications about 3.3, with one event in class II/III. An exact test would fit better than chi-square (our point). Complications are the most clinically relevant outcome here, and they did not differ. That makes the ICU result harder to explain as obese patients getting sicker. The authors suggest monitoring needs, pulmonary limits and opioid dosing, but they did not measure these. Almost everyone was transfused (97%), so transfusion cannot separate the groups. Obstructive sleep apnea appears only in the Discussion. The authors give rates of 1.3%, 3.6% and 8.1% (overall 2.9%). 3.6% of 52 is not a whole patient. 2 of 52 is 3.8%, and 7 of 244 (2.9%) fits 3.8%. OSA is not in the Methods data list or in any table.

slides.title: Adjusted odds ratios and the comparator problem
slides.lead: Both obese groups are compared with the 155 nonobese patients in the reading that fits the data.
points: Table 2 footnote, abstract, Discussion and Conclusion: versus nonobese patients
Results text and Key Points: class II/III versus class I patients. This is an error.
Table 2 header lists class II/III n = 122; Table 1 and text give 37
slides.notes: The comparator. The paper states the class II/III ORs two ways. The Table 2 footnote ('Versus 155 nonobese patients'), the abstract, the Discussion and the Conclusion say versus nonobese. The Results text and the third Key Point say 'compared with class-I obese patients'. Crude ORs from Table 1 settle it (our calculation). Class II/III vs nonobese gives ICU 2.69, stay 2.40 and cost 3.02, close to the adjusted 2.35, 2.21 and 2.91. Class II/III vs class I gives ICU 0.94, stay 1.20 and cost 2.03, which do not fit. Read every OR as against nonobese patients. The paper never directly tests class II/III against class I, so it has not shown that the top class is worse than class I. That matters because it was the authors' hypothesis. For ICU stay, the raw rates are 35% vs 37%. Interval checks. All seven ORs sit at the geometric midpoint of their CIs, so the intervals are internally plausible. The class I ICU lower bound is 1.06 in the abstract and Table 2 but 1.07 in the Results text, a transcription slip. The 122 in the Table 2 header matches no BMI group. The lower bounds sit close to 1 (1.02, 1.03, 1.06), with 37 and 52 patients. These are fragile, imprecise estimates. A doubling of odds is compatible with almost no effect. Odds ratios also overstate relative risk when outcomes are common. 41% to 70% of patients had the outcomes here, so an OR of 2.9 is a much smaller risk ratio (our point). The adjusted covariates are not reported, so we cannot judge what was controlled for.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: A plausible signal on resource use, from a small single-surgeon series with reporting errors.
points: Strength: one surgeon and one centre limit variation in technique and care pathway. The authors say this mitigates surgeon preference as a cost driver.
Strength: operative detail (levels, revision, osteotomy) was available for adjustment, unlike national databases
Weakness: retrospective, 37 patients in the top group, class II and III pooled, model covariates not reported
Weakness: median-split outcomes; inpatient outcomes only, no readmission, infection, implant failure or patient-reported outcomes
Reporting errors: comparator for class II/III ORs, Table 2 n, abstract P values, a CI bound, osteotomy %, OSA %, transfusion P
slides.notes: Validity. Selection: the cohort is defined by fusion length, not deformity, and comes from one surgeon at a tertiary referral centre. Obese patients who reached this operation were selected by that surgeon, so the series cannot tell us about obese patients who were turned down (our point). Measurement: BMI and outcomes come from records and billing, which is reasonable. But the median cut points mean the 'prolonged' labels describe this cohort and not a clinical standard. Confounding: the authors adjusted for univariate predictors but do not report them. Class I patients had more three-column osteotomies, and class II/III more revisions. Residual confounding by comorbidity is likely, because the CCI misses things like sleep apnea and pulmonary function. The authors' own limitations are retrospective design, fewer patients than database studies, and inpatient outcomes only. They say they accounted for operative confounders and had complete data for 89%. In the Discussion, the authors say comorbidities, transfusion and complications did not differ, so they did not drive cost. That is a fair point for complications. But 'no significant difference' in 37 patients is weak evidence of no difference. Context the authors give: Soroceanu 2015 found more complications and less 2-year improvement in obese ASD patients. Smaller ASD series (77 and 84 patients) found no difference. Non-deformity database studies tie class III obesity to stay. None of these are library records we have checked. What it does support: in a long-fusion ASD practice, expect obese patients, especially BMI 35 or more, to use more ICU time, stay longer and cost more. Do not expect this paper to show more complications.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: Obesity predicted more ICU time, longer stays and higher cost after long ASD fusions, but not more inpatient complications.
points: Spoken summary: 'In 244 single-surgeon ASD fusions of 5 or more levels, after adjustment against nonobese patients, class I obesity doubled the odds of an ICU stay over 2 days. BMI 35 or more roughly doubled the odds of ICU stay over 2 days and total stay over a week, and nearly tripled the odds of cost over $80,000. Inpatient complications did not differ. It is retrospective, with 37 patients at BMI 35 or more and wide intervals.'
Expect: is class II/III worse than class I? Not tested. The Results text says so, but the numbers are versus nonobese.
Expect: did obese patients have more complications? No: 9.0%, 13% and 2.7%, P = 0.218, with one event in class II/III
Expect: what does 'prolonged' mean? The cohort median: ICU over 2 days, total stay over 1 week, cost over $80,000
Expect: what was adjusted for? Not reported. Covariates with univariate P under 0.10 entered the model.
Expect: does it apply to class III or BMI over 40? Class II and III were pooled, so it cannot say
slides.notes: Keep the spoken version to resource use. The paper supports 'obese ASD patients use more ICU time and hospital days and cost more'. It does not support 'obese ASD patients have more complications'. Its own data show no difference, though with too few events to rule one out. Say 'versus nonobese' for every OR. If someone quotes the Key Points ('compared with class-I obesity'), point to the Table 2 footnote and the crude rates. The class II/III and class I ICU rates are 35% and 37%. Be ready to give the main limits in one breath: retrospective, single surgeon, 37 patients in the top group, median-split outcomes, unreported covariates, inpatient outcomes only. If asked how to use it in counselling or planning (our suggestion, not the authors'): it supports planning ICU beds and length of stay for patients with BMI 35 or more, and discussing cost. It does not give a BMI cut-off for declining surgery, and it says nothing about long-term outcomes, infection or instrumentation failure. The authors flag these as future work. Odds ratios with common outcomes overstate relative risk. In absolute terms, high cost went from 44% of nonobese patients to 70% of class II/III patients.

decks.not_reviewed: Read from papers/PM30202716.pdf, a reformatted copy of the open-access PMC text (PMC6125929), not the typeset journal PDF. It states that images are omitted. Its Footnotes section is empty, so funding, conflict-of-interest and any author-contribution statements were not seen. Any online supplement was not reviewed. Cited studies (Golinvaux, Browne, Cho, Shaffrey and others) were not read; their numbers appear only as this paper reports them.

slides.title: Diabetes and 30-day outcomes after elective ASD surgery
slides.lead: Di Capua J, et al. Global Spine J 2018. A national database cohort (ACS-NSQIP 2010-2014) comparing nondiabetic, non-insulin-dependent and insulin-dependent patients.
points: Bottom line: after adjustment, NIDDM went with longer stay, any complication and UTI; IDDM went with longer stay and cardiac complications
Absolute risks were small: cardiac events 2.8% IDDM vs 0.5% nondiabetic
30 days only, no glucose or HbA1c data, and deformity defined by billing codes
The patient counts do not agree between the text and the tables
slides.notes: This is a prognostic cohort, not a trial. Nobody was assigned anything, so every result is an association. The authors used the American College of Surgeons NSQIP database, which collects more than 150 variables through dedicated clinical abstractors at each institution at more than 500 hospitals, with outcomes to 30 days. They split patients into three groups by diabetes status: nondiabetic, non-insulin-dependent (NIDDM) and insulin-dependent (IDDM). Anyone on both insulin and oral agents was counted as IDDM. The authors say this is the first national study to separate NIDDM from IDDM after elective ASD surgery. Source note: this deck was built from a reformatted copy of the PMC open-access text. It says images are omitted, and its Footnotes section is empty, so funding and conflicts could not be checked. All three tables were present as text. Set expectations early. This paper can tell you which diabetic patients had more early events in a US registry. It cannot tell you that diabetes causes those events, or that better glucose control would prevent them, because glucose and HbA1c were never measured.

slides.title: The question and how patients were selected
slides.lead: Which 30-day complications are diabetic patients at risk for after elective ASD surgery, and does insulin dependence matter?
points: Adults 18 or older having fusion for deformity, found by CPT codes 22800-22819
Long-fusion codes 22843, 22844, 22846 and 22847 were also included
Codes 22842 and 22845 counted only with an ICD-9 deformity diagnosis (737.x)
Excluded: emergency or nonelective cases, wound class 2-4, open wound, sepsis, pneumonia, surgery in prior 30 days, preoperative CPR, cervical, trauma, tumor, missing preoperative data
Long fusion: 4 or more levels anterior, 7 or more posterior
slides.notes: Selection is the first thing to read in any database study, because the cohort is only as good as the codes that build it. Here ASD means a billing code, not a radiograph. There are no Cobb angles, no sagittal parameters and no SRS-Schwab type. The paper's wording also leaves one question open. Codes 22842 and 22845 needed a deformity diagnosis, but the long-fusion codes are described as 'also included' with no diagnosis requirement stated. Our reading: some long degenerative fusions may be in the cohort. The paper does not say either way. Candidate variables for the models came from NSQIP fields (the covariates each stepwise model kept are not reported): age bands, sex, race, obesity (BMI 30 or more), smoking, dyspnea, functional status, pulmonary, cardiac and renal comorbidity, steroids, weight loss, bleeding disorder, preoperative transfusion, ASA 3 or more, year, setting, fusion length, approach, pelvic fixation, osteotomy, operative time of 4 hours or more and relative value units. Note how broad 'cardiac comorbidity' is: it means use of hypertensive medication or a history of heart failure within 30 days, and it was present in 83.9% of NIDDM and 88.4% of IDDM patients against 49.5% of nondiabetic patients. Our reading: antihypertensive use probably drives most of that, but the paper does not break it down. There were 13 outcomes at 30 days, one of them length of stay of 5 days or more. Cardiac complication means cardiac arrest needing CPR or myocardial infarction. The paper does not define what goes into 'any complication'. Statistics: chi-square or Fisher tests, then multivariate logistic regression using stepwise entry and removal at P 0.05, run in SAS.

slides.title: Who was studied, and the counts that do not add up
slides.lead: The text says 5809 patients, but the three groups sum to 5406 and the tables use other totals.

rows: Table 1 year, setting and op-time rows

points: Group sizes in the text add to 5406, not 5809. The printed 84.2%, 10.7% and 5.1% are shares of 5406
Diabetics were older, more often obese, ASA 3 or more and more often had cardiac comorbidity (antihypertensive use or heart failure)
Nondiabetic patients more often had osteotomy (15.0% vs 11.3% and 10.4%) and surgery of 4 hours or more
slides.notes: This is our arithmetic, not the paper's. The Results say 5809 met inclusion, then give 4553, 578 and 275, which sum to 5406. The printed percentages fit 5406, and so does the Discussion figure of 15.8% with diabetes. Tables 1 and 2 are titled N = 5338, and their columns add to 4548, 540 and 250. The operation year, surgery setting and operative time rows in Table 1 add to 4965, 578 and 275, or 5818 in all, and the operative time percentages use those totals: 2427 of 4965 is 48.9%. Table 3, the regression, says N = 5809. So the bivariate tables and the regression may be run on different patients, and no flow diagram explains the gap of 400 to 470. We checked the tables themselves. Every percentage in Tables 1 and 2 matches its counts, and every bivariate P value we recomputed by chi-square matches the printed one. The internal arithmetic is sound; the denominators are not. Other small points. The text gives 'median age 61 ± 13.5', a median paired with what looks like a standard deviation. Methods give age bands of 71-80 and 80 or more, which overlap at 80, while the table prints more than 80. Baseline imbalance matters for what comes next. Diabetic patients carried more comorbidity: ASA 3 or more in 48.6% of nondiabetic patients, 78.9% NIDDM and 86.0% IDDM. Yet nondiabetic patients had more osteotomies and longer operations. Confounding therefore runs in both directions.

slides.title: Unadjusted 30-day outcomes
slides.lead: Table 2. Rates are shares of 4548, 540 and 250 patients.

rows: Length of stay 5 days or more (P .052)

points: Pulmonary complication was also significant: 2.4%, 3.7%, 4.4% (P .039)
VTE, renal, sepsis and transfusion did not differ significantly
The P values test all three groups at once, not each diabetic group against nondiabetic
slides.notes: Read the counts before the percentages. Cardiac complication in the IDDM group is 7 events, and mortality in that group is 2 deaths. Rates built on single digits move a lot with one or two patients. Notice also that the two outcomes that turn significant after adjustment, length of stay and any complication, were not significant here (P .052 and .158), while readmission, reoperation, wound complication and mortality were significant here but do not appear in the adjusted table. Wound complication is a good test of careful reading. The authors write that on univariate analysis diabetes, IDDM and NIDDM, is associated with wound complications. Table 2 shows that only NIDDM is higher, at 4.1%. IDDM is 2.0%, slightly below nondiabetic at 2.2%. The overall P value of .021 comes from the NIDDM group. Our arithmetic, not the paper's: the crude odds ratio for cardiac complication is about 5.7 for IDDM versus nondiabetic, and for 30-day death about 3.1 for NIDDM. The absolute difference in cardiac events between IDDM and nondiabetic patients is about 2.3 percentage points. 'Any complication' runs at about 30% in every group, close to the 27% transfusion rate. The paper does not define it, so our guess is that transfusion is counted, which would make it largely a transfusion measure. Treat that as unconfirmed.

slides.title: Adjusted results
slides.lead: Table 3. Odds ratios versus nondiabetic patients from stepwise multivariate logistic regression.

rows: Length of stay 5 days or more

points: Only these four outcomes are shown with adjusted estimates
NIDDM: longer stay, any complication, UTI. IDDM: longer stay, cardiac
Authors: diabetes was not an independent risk factor for wound complications or reoperation; no adjusted numbers are given
slides.notes: We checked the confidence intervals. All eight are symmetric on the log scale, as they should be, and P values recomputed from them match the printed ones to within rounding. So the table is internally consistent. Now read what it does and does not show. Three NIDDM estimates have lower bounds of 1.01 to 1.14, so they barely clear 1. The IDDM cardiac estimate of 4.05 is the largest effect, but it rests on 7 events in 250 patients, and the interval runs from 1.72 to 9.51. Our point: with only 37 cardiac events in the whole cohort, a model with many covariates is at risk of overfitting. Notice something odd, again our arithmetic. Adjustment usually shrinks an effect when the exposed group is sicker. Here the adjusted odds ratios for length of stay (1.27 and 1.55) are larger than the crude ones (about 1.13 and 1.35). One explanation is that nondiabetic patients had more osteotomies and longer operations, so adjusting for those raises the diabetic estimate. Another is that the regression used a different set of patients, since Table 3 says N = 5809 and Table 2 says 5338. We cannot tell which. The authors argue that NIDDM and IDDM behave differently, so a single diabetic label is inadequate. That may be true, but they never compare the two groups directly. The NIDDM and IDDM intervals overlap for every outcome, so the paper shows different significance patterns, not a proven difference between the groups. That reading is ours.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: A large, clean registry answers 'who has more early events', not 'why' or 'what to do about it'.
points: Holds up: national sample of more than 500 hospitals, abstractor-collected outcomes, NIDDM and IDDM separated
Holds up: table percentages and bivariate P values recompute exactly

Authors' limits: codes cannot capture osteotomy type or pelvic fixation detail; anticoagulation and Foley use not recorded; academic centers overrepresented; hospital anonymous; 30 days only; no glucose or HbA1c
Authors' distinction, which they say is not a limitation: patients were grouped as NIDDM or IDDM, not type 1 or type 2
Our concerns: patient totals inconsistent with no flow diagram; stepwise selection; covariates kept in each model not reported
Our concerns: about 13 outcomes times 2 comparisons with no multiplicity correction; adjusted results reported for only 4 outcomes
Our concerns: few cardiac events; no adjustment for clustering by hospital is described
slides.notes: Be fair to the paper. NSQIP data are collected by dedicated clinical abstractors rather than pulled from billing, and over 5000 patients gives real power for common outcomes such as length of stay. The authors list their own limitations clearly: CPT-based case finding cannot distinguish technique details such as osteotomy type or pelvic fixation; anticoagulation protocols and Foley catheter use are not captured, which matters for VTE and UTI; academic centers are overrepresented; hospitals are anonymous, so volume and surgeon experience cannot be adjusted for; follow-up stops at 30 days, which they say may underestimate risk; and there is no blood glucose or HbA1c. The rest are our reading. Stepwise selection at P 0.05 gives each outcome its own model, and the paper does not list which covariates stayed in, so you cannot judge what each odds ratio is adjusted for. With roughly 26 diabetic comparisons, one or two significant results near P 0.03 to 0.04 are what chance alone could produce. Only four outcomes are shown after adjustment, chosen because they were significant; the rest are reported only as words. The denominators in the text and tables differ by up to about 470 patients without explanation. One more inconsistency: the authors list type of osteotomy and pelvic fixation as things CPT codes cannot capture, yet osteotomy and fusion to pelvis are both variables in Table 1. Our guess is that they mean the detail within each, but the paper does not say. Finally, Discussion opens by saying patients with NIDDM or IDDM were at higher risk for longer stay, any complication, UTI and cardiac complications. Each finding belongs to one group only, except length of stay.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "In a US registry of about 5,400 elective ASD fusions, diabetes was linked to modestly higher 30-day risk. Non-insulin-dependent patients had more UTIs and longer stays. Insulin-dependent patients had longer stays and about 4 times the odds of cardiac arrest or MI, though that was 7 events and an absolute rate of 2.8%."
points: Adjusted OR for stay of 5 days or more: 1.27 NIDDM, 1.55 IDDM
IDDM cardiac complication: OR 4.05 (1.72-9.51); 2.8% vs 0.5% unadjusted
Wound complications: higher in NIDDM before adjustment (4.1% vs 2.2%), not independent after it, per the authors
Do not stretch it: no glucose or HbA1c data, 30 days only, ASD by billing code
slides.notes: Expect four follow-up questions. First, should I delay ASD surgery until HbA1c is lower? This paper cannot answer that. NSQIP has no glucose or HbA1c data, and the authors say so. They cite other work, which we did not read, linking perioperative glucose to infection even without diabetes, and they suggest that infection risk may relate to perioperative glucose level rather than to diabetes itself. That point is about infection only. Second, is insulin dependence really worse than oral therapy? The pattern points that way for cardiac events and length of stay, but the paper never tests IDDM against NIDDM, and the intervals overlap. Say 'suggested, not shown'. Third, does diabetes raise infection risk after deformity surgery? Before adjustment NIDDM had 4.1% wound complications against 2.2%, but the authors report it was not an independent risk factor, and they show no adjusted numbers to check. Late infection and pseudarthrosis are outside a 30-day window. Fourth, how does this fit the lumbar fusion literature? As reported in this paper, Golinvaux and colleagues found longer stay in both NIDDM and IDDM after elective lumbar fusion (OR 1.4 and 1.8), similar in direction to these results. Those numbers come from this paper's citation, not from our library. Close with the counts problem: if you quote a sample size, say 'about 5,400 patients, with group counts that differ between the text and tables', rather than quoting 5809 as fact.

decks.not_reviewed: The 32 included studies themselves; the images for Figures 1-3 (PRISMA flow, sample guides, printed kyphoscoliosis model), which were omitted from the reformatted PMC copy (Figure 1 counts are given in the text); any funding or conflict-of-interest declaration for the review authors, which was not in the copy reviewed; the Table 1 complications column, which is truncated in the copy reviewed. The PDF is the complete article text, not a critique.

slides.title: Lopez 2021: 3D printing in adult spinal deformity
slides.lead: Three-Dimensional Printing for Preoperative Planning and Pedicle Screw Placement in Adult Spinal Deformity: A Systematic Review.
points: Journal club: adult deformity, perioperative technology
Lopez CD, Boddapati V, Lee NJ, Dyrszka MD, Sardar ZM, Lehman RA, Lenke LG. Global Spine J 2021;11(6):936-949

Bottom line: across 32 small studies (703 patients), 3D-printed guides and models went with more accurate screws (96.9% vs 81.5% of screws) and about 14 minutes less surgery. Blood loss did not differ. Every comparison is between studies, not within them.
Source: the full open-access PMC text was read, including all four tables, though the Table 1 complications column is truncated in that copy. The figure images were not in the copy reviewed.
slides.notes: This is a systematic review, not a trial, and it is a descriptive one. The authors searched to November 2019, found 32 studies, sorted them into three overlapping uses (screw drill guides, presurgical planning, training and education) and then pooled numbers as weighted averages across studies. There is no meta-analysis, no forest plot, no heterogeneity statistic and no risk-of-bias table. Hold that from the start: the headline P values compare 3D-printing cohorts from some studies with non-3D-printing cohorts from other studies, plus the control arms of the comparative studies. What was reviewed: the full article text from the PMC open-access version, reformatted for phone reading, with Tables 1 to 4 and the reference list. Not reviewed: the images for Figure 1 (the PRISMA flow), Figure 2 (sample guides, courtesy of Medacta MySpine) and Figure 3 (a printed kyphoscoliosis model), and the 32 included studies themselves. The flow counts are in the text, so nothing numeric is lost with Figure 1. The reviewed copy has no funding or conflict-of-interest statement for the review authors, so we cannot comment on it. The master record was a bibliography entry only before this review. Why it matters for a deformity surgeon (ours): patient-specific guides are marketed for dysplastic and rotated pedicles, and this review offers an adult-deformity accuracy number. That number is real arithmetic, but read on before quoting it.

slides.title: Question and methods
slides.lead: What is 3D printing used for in adult spinal deformity, and do outcomes differ with and without it?
points: Search: EMBASE, Medline and PubMed to November 2019, PRISMA-guided; terms for 3D printing, rapid prototyping, additive manufacturing, scoliosis, kyphosis, spinal deformity.
Included: original clinical studies of 3D printing for planning or treatment of scoliosis or kyphosis in adults (>18 years), and 3D-printed implants in spine surgery.
Excluded: no 3D printing, non-deformity patients, animals, pediatric patients, non-English, inaccessible articles, reviews, editorials.
Title and abstract screening by 2 reviewers, then full-text screening; disagreements by consensus. Studies graded by Oxford CEBM level of evidence.
Analysis: weighted averages of cohorts across studies; Student t test or Fisher exact test; P < .05. Costs and times as simple averages.
slides.notes: Read the methods for what is missing as much as what is there. Two reviewers screened titles and abstracts; full texts were then screened against the criteria (the paper does not say by how many reviewers), and references of included papers were hand-searched. The paper does not say whether data extraction was done in duplicate, does not mention a registered protocol, and gives no risk-of-bias tool. The studies were graded by Oxford level of evidence, but no table or sentence reports those levels, and the levels are not used in the analysis. The analysis is the key weakness (ours). A weighted average of cohorts across studies, then a t test or Fisher test, treats patients or screws from different centers, surgeons, deformities and accuracy definitions as if they came from one population. It ignores clustering of screws within patients and patients within studies, so P values will look smaller than they should. The paper does not define screw accuracy (which CT grade, which breach threshold), and does not say how operative time or blood loss were measured in each study. The blood loss result is said to be after controlling for operating time and procedure type, but the methods describe no adjusted model, so we cannot tell how that control was done. Medline and PubMed overlap heavily, so the search is closer to two databases than three, English only (ours). No limit was set on level of evidence, and the authors say most studies were from the last 10 years.

slides.title: What went into the pool
slides.lead: 204 records, 32 studies, 703 patients, three overlapping uses.
points: Flow: 204 records, 92 duplicates removed, 112 screened, 39 full texts, 7 excluded, 32 included. The arithmetic adds up.
Screw drill guides 22/32 (68.8%); presurgical planning 20/32 (62.5%); training and education 7/32 (21.9%). Categories overlap.
Printing: stereolithography 18 (56%), laser sintering or melting 12 (37.5%), fused deposition 4 (12.5%).
Comparators in the 22 guide studies: freehand 6, navigation 3, fluoroscopy 2, none stated 10 in the text, 11 in Table 1.

rows: Trainee phantoms for CT-guided procedures and spinal injections

slides.notes: The flow diagram arithmetic checks: 204 minus 92 is 112; 39 minus 7 is 32. The category percentages check against 32. Table 1 has 22 rows, Table 2 has 20 and Table 3 has 7, and their union is 32 distinct studies, which also checks. The comparator split does not: Table 1 shows 6 freehand, 3 navigation, 2 fluoroscopy and 11 with no comparator, but the text says 10. Now the population. The title and the inclusion criteria say adults over 18, and pediatric patients were an exclusion. Yet the reference titles and the review's own tables describe pediatric, adolescent and congenital populations, and two studies are training phantoms with no patients treated. Yang 2015 alone, 126 adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis per the Discussion, is about 18% of the 703 patients (our arithmetic). We have not read those studies, so some may have enrolled adults; but on the review's own descriptions, the pool is not an adult spinal deformity pool. That matters because pedicle anatomy, bone quality and fixation in adolescents and congenital curves differ from degenerative adult deformity (ours). A second traceability problem: 10 studies named in the tables (Wang YT 2016, Mohar 2015, Zhang 2017, Zhang 2018, Otsuki 2016, Mokawen 2019, Marengo 2019, Kim 2016, Mobbs 2017, Wang H 2017) do not appear in the reference list, so a reader cannot check them from this paper. Wu 2011 and Chen 2016 are cited but do not appear in any table.

slides.title: Main results: guides and models
slides.lead: Higher accuracy and slightly shorter surgery with guides or planning models; no significant difference in blood loss; all pooled across studies.

rows: Fluoroscopy exposure (5 or 2 studies, see notes)

points: Non-3DP accuracy: freehand 81.6%, unspecified technique 81.3%. No accuracy data for navigation or fluoroscopy comparators.
Study counts: 9 of 11 found shorter surgery; 3 found less blood loss; 5 reported less fluoroscopy (30 vs 77 images in the 2 that measured it).
Harms: the text describes one CSF leak at the nerve root axilla, repaired with sutures, after 3DP planning (ref 21, Coote 2019); Table 1 gives its only complication to Luo 2019. The two do not agree.
slides.notes: How to read each row. Accuracy is counted per screw, and the denominators (number of screws) are not given, so we cannot recompute the P value. Screws cluster within patients and studies, so the true uncertainty is wider than P < .001 suggests (ours). The comparator is freehand or unspecified technique; the paper states accuracy was not reported for navigation or fluoroscopy comparators, so this review cannot say guides beat navigation. Accuracy definitions are not given. The Discussion quotes 96.5% for the same result; the Results and abstract say 96.9%. Operative time: 14 minutes, about 5% (our arithmetic). The authors say production time, which can take several hours, must also be considered; they also say clean bone preparation for template fixation is time-intensive and linked to more blood loss. A second figure, 236 vs 262 minutes, comes from 12 studies of planning models or drill guides, which overlap the guide studies, so it is not an independent confirmation (ours). Blood loss: the abstract gives 924.6 mL in 252 3DP patients vs 935.6 mL in 177 non-3DP patients; the Results text gives the same means with the patient counts swapped. Our recomputation: an 11 mL difference with 252 and 177 patients gives P = .058 only if the SD is about 59 mL; deformity blood loss SDs are usually hundreds of mL, so the P value is implausible, likely from treating studies or screws as independent or using the wrong test. Operative time (14 min, P < .05) implies an SD of 92 min or less, which is plausible. No screw denominators, so accuracy cannot be recomputed. Deformity correction of 72.5% has no comparator, so it shows only that correction was achieved. Of the 10 correction values in Table 1, the simple mean is 69.3% (our arithmetic); the gap from 72.5% may reflect weighting, studies outside Table 1, or both (ours). Fluoroscopy: the Results tie 61.2% to 5 studies, the Discussion to the 2 that measured exposure; 1 minus 30/77 is 61.0%, matching the 2-study figure (ours). Not significant either way. Harms: Table 1 has a complications column cut off in the reviewed copy; it appears to read none for every study except Luo 2019 (1), while the text places the one described complication, the CSF leak, in a planning study (Coote 2019). Complications were not pooled; the Discussion reports that some individual studies found fewer perioperative complications.

slides.title: Planning, education, cost and lead time
slides.lead: Mostly surgeon and patient impressions, with wide and partly inconsistent cost figures.
points: Planning: 19 of 20 studies reported a benefit, mostly surgeon understanding of anatomy. Results say Yang 2015 found no benefit and higher hospital cost ($22 342 vs $21 701, P = .03), but Table 1 and the Discussion credit Yang with shorter surgery and less blood loss.
Izatt 2007: surgeons reported a mean 22% shorter operation in deformity cases. Education studies report better patient understanding and trainee confidence; non-3DP operative times were not reported.
Materials: polymers in 24/32 (75%); titanium or stainless steel in 5/32. Takemoto 2016 reported 98.4% accuracy with titanium templates.
slides.notes: The planning and education evidence is largely surveys and author impressions: surgeons saw anatomy better on models than on imaging, patients understood their operation better, trainees felt more confident. These are reasonable and low-stakes, but they are not outcome evidence. The quoted rise in informed consent of up to 25% cites a cranio-maxillofacial biomodelling trial (reference 37), not a spine study. We recomputed Table 4: the 11 listed costs average $1058.25 and the 14 listed times average 149.54 hours, both matching the table. Four cost and time statements do not match it. First, the text says lead time ranged from 9 hours to 1 month; Table 4's shortest is 10.5 hours (Mao) and its longest is 840 hours, about 35 days (Cecchinato). Second, the Discussion says screw guide costs ranged from $175 to $290, but the Results give an average guide set cost of $415, which cannot sit above the top of its own range; the $415 is the mean of the 5 Table 1 costs (175, 250, 290, 361.50, 1000), so the range leaves out Takemoto's $1000 and Wang YT's $361.50 (our arithmetic). Fourth, the planning averages appear to include a non-planning phantom: the 7 planning studies with costs average $671.53 and the 8 with times 42.7 h (1.8 days); adding Li 2018 (a Table 3 trainee phantom, $5400, 720 h) gives exactly $1263 and 4.9 days (our recomputation). Third, polystyrene and resin are each said to be used in 5 studies, given as 17%; 5 of 32 is 16%, as the same paragraph says for metals. The Yang 2015 cost figure is printed as $22 342 + $1415.16; the plus sign is probably a lost plus-or-minus symbol (ours). The Discussion also cites one reference (Wang D 2016, a materials paper on laser-melted templates) for both a surgeon and patient survey and a steel versus resin accuracy comparison; we cannot tell from this paper which is correct. Conflicts: the authors note 4 included studies had industry ties (Medacta, Medtronic, DePuy). Practical point from the authors: costs vary likely because manufacturing is not standardized, and hospital setup and staff training add time and cost not captured here.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: A useful map of how 3D printing is used; a weak basis for an effect size.
points: Strengths: three-database search, PRISMA flow that adds up, two screeners, clear tables of what each study reported.
Design: between-study pooling with simple tests; no meta-analysis, risk of bias, heterogeneity or sensitivity analysis.
Population: several included studies describe pediatric, adolescent, congenital or phantom settings despite adult-only criteria.
Comparator: accuracy gain shown against freehand and unspecified technique only, not navigation or fluoroscopy.
Internal errors: swapped blood loss patient counts, 96.9% vs 96.5%, 10 vs 11 unspecified comparators, cost and lead time ranges, 10 tabulated studies missing from references.
slides.notes: Put the review in its proper place. As a catalogue of uses, materials and costs, it is helpful, and the authors are open that costs and lead times vary widely and that production time must be weighed against the operative time savings. As a source for an effect size, it is fragile. Every pooled comparison mixes cohorts across studies, so differences in surgeon experience, deformity severity, accuracy grading, imaging and era are folded into the 3DP effect (ours). The authors themselves point out that experienced freehand surgeons may gain less than general spine surgeons. Small single-center studies dominate, so publication bias is likely and was not assessed (ours). Several numbers in the paper disagree with each other, listed on the slide. None of them reverses a conclusion, but together they mean the exact figures should be quoted with care. The biggest generalizability issue is the population: the paper's own descriptions include adolescents, congenital scoliosis and pediatric cases, so the adult label is not fully earned. Adult degenerative deformity, with osteoporotic bone and revision anatomy, may behave differently (ours). What is not fragile: the direction across individual studies is fairly consistent, with 9 of 11 reporting shorter operations and most guide studies reporting accuracy above 90%. Bone preparation for template seating is noted by the authors as time-consuming and linked to more blood loss in some studies. Harms are barely reported.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "Across 32 small studies, 3D-printed guides and planning models went with more accurate screws, about 97% vs 82%, compared with freehand or unspecified technique, and about 14 minutes less surgery. Blood loss did not differ significantly. These are between-study comparisons, not a meta-analysis, and the pool includes adolescent and congenital cases."
points: Do not say guides beat navigation: no navigation accuracy data were pooled.
Do not quote 72.5% correction as a benefit: there was no comparator.
Do say cost and lead time vary widely: about $415 and 5.8 days for a guide set on average, not counting the 3D model.
slides.notes: Expect four follow-up questions. Does this justify patient-specific guides for my adult deformity cases? Not by itself. The accuracy gain is against freehand and unspecified technique, the pool includes adolescents and congenital curves, and the comparison is across studies. If you already use navigation, this paper has no head-to-head data for you. Is the time saving worth it? The pooled saving is about 14 minutes, and the authors say production time of several hours must also be weighed, and that clean bone preparation for template fixation is time-intensive. Which number should I quote for accuracy? The Results and abstract say 96.9% of screws vs 81.5%; the Discussion says 96.5%. Quote 96.9% vs 81.5% and say it is per screw, pooled across studies. Is there harm? Complications were barely reported; one CSF leak is described and the complications column suggests none in most guide studies, but small studies are not designed to find rare neurological events. The review also reports that Takemoto and colleagues, who used titanium templates for strength and durability, noted plastic guides are more likely to shed debris when drilled, a potential risk to nearby neurovascular structures. No other library paper on 3D printing is in the master file, so there is nothing to set beside it here. What would answer the question: a randomized trial in adults with deformity comparing guides against navigation, with CT-graded accuracy and total time including planning (ours). The reference list names one included study, Cecchinato 2019, as a prospective randomized trial against freehand; this review does not separate its result.

decks.not_reviewed: None of the 21 included primary studies were read, so every per-study number here is as tabulated by Zaed et al. No supplement is cited. The PRISMA flow diagram (Figure 1) is an image and was read from the rendered page. The comparison record (Sorour 2023) comes from the master file, not from this PDF.

slides.title: Zaed 2022: ERAS in spine surgery
slides.lead: A qualitative systematic review of 21 studies of ERAS pathways in spine surgery, 20 of them nonrandomized cohorts or case series.
points: Journal club: perioperative care and enhanced recovery
