Zaed I, Bossi B, Ganau M, Tinterri B, Giordano M, Chibbaro S. Current state of benefits of Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) in spinal surgeries: a systematic review of the literature. Neurochirurgie 2022;68(1):61-68

Bottom line: the included studies mostly report shorter length of stay with ERAS. Only 1 of 21 is a randomized trial, and all 6 deformity studies are pediatric posterior fusions, ages 8 to 21, for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis or other deformities.
Prepared from the full 8-page article. The included studies themselves were not read.
slides.notes: Why this paper is in the library: the SRS Quality and Safety Resource Library lists it, and the master record files it under adult deformity and perioperative evidence. Hold that filing against what the paper contains. The deformity section has 6 studies, all posterior spinal fusion in patients aged 8 to 21. The authors themselves say there is an important lack of studies on adult deformity reconstruction and degenerative scoliosis. So this review tells you almost nothing about ERAS after adult deformity surgery. That point is the most useful thing to take from it, and the conclusion is ours, built on the authors' own statements. Type of paper: the journal labels it a general review. The authors call it a systematic review following PRISMA. It is a narrative summary of study tables with counts of how many studies reported a benefit. There is no risk of bias assessment, no pooled estimate of its own, and no grading of evidence. The authors say a quantitative synthesis could not be performed because of heterogeneity. What was reviewed: the whole article, pages 61 to 68, including Tables 1 to 4 and the PRISMA diagram. Not reviewed: the 21 primary studies. Per-study numbers in this deck are as printed in the review's tables, and Table 4 has rows that do not add up (slide 6). Received June 2020, accepted April 2021, online April 2021. The authors declare no competing interest. No funding statement appears.

slides.title: The question and the search
slides.lead: What is the current evidence that ERAS pathways benefit adults having spine surgery?
points: Background (authors): ERAS combines pre- and postoperative care methods in a multimodal approach to reduce surgical stress. ERAS concepts were first applied to general surgery.
Search: three keywords, ERAS, Enhanced Recovery After Surgery and spine surgery. No search dates are given.
Databases: Methods lists PubMed, Cochrane Library, EMBASE and Google Scholar. The abstract lists PubMed/Medline, Web of Science, Cochrane Reviews, Embase and Medline.
Eligible: English, human, any design from case series to RCT, including systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Case reports, technical notes and editorials excluded.
Screening by three authors, disagreements settled by consensus. No risk of bias tool.
slides.see: Figure 1 is the PRISMA diagram; the drop from 861 to 827 has no box explaining it.
slides.notes: Read the methods with three questions: could the search find everything, could the selection be reproduced, and was study quality judged? On the first, three keywords is a narrow search. It would miss studies that say fast-track or enhanced recovery pathway without the exact phrase, although one fast-track study (Nazarenko) did get in. No search dates are given, so you cannot tell what period it covers. The two database lists in the abstract and Methods do not match, and Google Scholar is not a database you can rerun reproducibly. That judgment is ours. On selection, the eligibility paragraph contradicts itself. It first lists editorials among included designs and then says editorials were excluded. It says the study is about adult patients, yet all six deformity studies are pediatric. It lets systematic reviews and meta-analyses in as eligible, which mixes primary and secondary evidence. On the flow arithmetic, which we recomputed: 861 records after duplicates, but 827 screened. 34 records disappear with no reason given. From 827, the drop of 779 leaves 48, which checks, and 48 less 27 leaves 21, which checks. The abstract calls the 827 the studies found. On quality: none was assessed. The authors' limitations paragraph says the level of evidence was not homogeneous and some studies had no control group, but no study is rated. Without that, a count of studies reporting a benefit cannot separate a well-controlled study from a 10-patient series. The authors also note there is no agreed definition of ERAS in spine, so what counted as an ERAS study was itself a judgment call.

slides.title: What was included
slides.lead: 21 studies in four groups, though the abstract says three. Only one is randomized.
points: The authors grouped by surgery type, following an earlier review (Elsarrag 2019, their reference 9).
The commonest comparison is an ERAS cohort against historical controls: 10 of 21 by our count of the tables.
The one RCT is Liu 2020: 48 ERAS versus 46 traditional care, intradural spinal tumors.
Our sum of the tables: about 2776 patients in all. The paper gives no overall total.

rows: Cohorts; 3 single arm, 1 compares two ERAS variants

slides.notes: The four totals match the sums of the table rows, by our arithmetic: lumbar 1170, deformity 1158, cervical 257 and tumor 191. Each group total checks, so the row counts were added correctly even where the rows themselves are odd. The 2+11+6+2 studies also add to 21. But the abstract and the Results opening both say three main categories, lumbar, deformity and cervical, and the abstract says the benefits were seen across those three. The tumor group is a fourth category that appears only in the Results. Patients by arm in the tumor group: 89 of 191 had ERAS (41 in Grasu, 48 in Liu), which checks. In the cervical group 147 of 257 had ERAS (114 in Li plus all 33 in Soffin), which also checks. Design labels are inconsistent. The Li laminoplasty study is called a prospective comparative study in the text, a retrospective study in Table 1, and a retrospective case-cohort study in its own reference title. The cervical Soffin study is called a prospective cohort compared with an ACDF or CDA group in Table 1, but the text says it is a retrospective analysis without a control group, and the Note column says no comparison. When the same review gives two designs for one study, assume neither label was checked. That is our inference. Notice too what before-and-after designs with historical controls do: any secular change at the hospital, such as new surgeons, new implants, a minimally invasive switch or a discharge policy, lands in the ERAS column. Several lumbar ERAS arms were also minimally invasive or endoscopic. Wang 2018 compared endoscopic TLIF with ERAS against tubular MIS TLIF, so technique and pathway changed together.

slides.title: Results: lumbar, cervical, tumor
slides.lead: Length of stay is the outcome most often reported as shorter. Complications, readmission and cost are thin.
points: Lumbar (authors): significant LOS decrease in 5 studies; earlier ambulation, better pain scores, earlier analgesic stop and better disability scores in 1 or 2 each.
The authors say multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia was in all lumbar studies, but they cite 10 of 11, and Table 4 lists none for Hawasli. Early mobilization appeared in 9 of 11.
Cervical: Li found shorter LOS (5.75 vs 7.67 days), earlier Foley removal and ambulation, with no difference in complications or 30-day reoperation.
Tumor: Liu's RCT found shorter LOS (5 vs 12 days), earlier catheter removal and ambulation, and lower total cost.

Grasu: 30-day readmission 14.6% with ERAS vs 8.9% with controls, one extra event (6/41 vs 5/56, our Fisher P about 0.52); authors say pain improved but this was not significantly correlated with lower LOS, readmission or narcotic use.
slides.notes: These are per-study results as printed in the review's tables, not pooled numbers. The tables do not say which column is ERAS. We assumed the ERAS value is listed first, which fits the text in every case we could check. For Grasu it fits exactly: 6 of 41 is 14.6 percent and 5 of 56 is 8.9 percent, so readmission was higher in the ERAS arm by one event; our Fisher exact P is about 0.52, and the paper claims no trend. In the lumbar table, look at the size of the LOS gaps. Bradywood is 0.4 days and Smith is about 4 hours, while the endoscopic Wang 2018 comparison is 2.7 days and mixes a technique change with the pathway. No P values appear in the tables, but where a row gives mean, SD and arm sizes we recomputed approximate tests: Bradywood P about 0.004, Brusko about 0.02, Li below 0.001, Grasu about 0.24, Smith about 0.40. So Smith's 4-hour gap is compatible with no difference, and the authors do not cite Smith (ref 18) for LOS reduction. The text names refs 13 to 16 and 20 for significant LOS reduction. Complications: the lumbar text says decreased complication rates and cites reference 22, which is the Pennington 2020 meta-analysis, not one of the included lumbar studies. In the tables, complication rates (CR) appear for Wang 2018 (12 vs 21 percent) and Smith 2019 (7.9 vs 1.7 percent). If the ERAS-first ordering holds, Smith had more complications with ERAS, but by our arithmetic neither rate fits a whole-number count of 107 or 123, and Wang's 12 percent fits neither 38 nor 15. Treat both CR rows as unreliable. Cost: two lumbar studies (refs 13 and 16) and the Liu RCT reported lower cost, which the authors attribute mainly to shorter LOS. Elements: the lumbar text says early enteral feeding was in 5 studies but cites 6 references. Five studies are said to have a conventional care comparison (refs 14 to 18), but Table 4 shows comparison groups for at least 7 of 11. Liu's RCT is the strongest single piece of evidence here, and it is in intradural tumors, not degenerative or deformity surgery.

slides.title: Results: scoliosis and deformity
slides.lead: Six pediatric posterior fusion studies. Nothing on adult deformity.
points: All 6 studies: posterior spinal fusion for AIS or other deformity, ages 8 to 21 years, all retrospective.
Text: three had a comparison group. Table 3 shows ERAS versus traditional groups in at least four.
Pooled figures printed with no source: complications OR 0.37 (95% CI 0.20 to 0.68), P=0.001; pain on day 0 lower by 0.92 and on day 2 by 0.61.
No difference in reoperation or day 1 pain. Trend to more 30-day readmission with ERAS (P=0.06).
Authors: not enough data to define an economic advantage.
slides.notes: This is the slide to slow down on, because the record files the paper under adult deformity. All six studies are pediatric spinal fusion. The authors say so (ages 8 to 21, PSF for AIS or other deformities) and later say adult deformity reconstruction is understudied. So nothing here speaks to a 65-year-old having a long fusion with osteotomies. Rao 2019 is listed with time to sitting 27.2 versus 40.4 hours and time to discharge 84.3 versus 98.4, units not given. The pooled numbers: the review says a quantitative analysis showed an OR of 0.37 for complications and lower pain on days 0 and 2. Yet the limitations section says a quantitative synthesis could not be performed. The paper gives no citation, no method and no list of contributing studies for these figures. Our inference: they were taken from another meta-analysis, most likely one of the earlier reviews the authors cite, but the paper does not say so, and we cannot check which studies fed them. We recomputed the intervals. On the log scale 0.20 to 0.68 is symmetric about 0.37, and the implied standard error gives P near 0.0014, consistent with the printed 0.001. The pain intervals are symmetric and fit P<0.001. So the numbers are internally coherent; their source is what is missing. Pain is on an unstated scale. A 0.92 point drop on a 0 to 10 scale on the day of surgery is small, and that judgment is ours. The readmission trend runs against ERAS. Grasu's tumor cohort is also numerically higher with ERAS, but by one event (our Fisher P about 0.52), which is not a trend. Also note that the six deformity studies, Muhly, Gornitzky, Chan, Fletcher, Rao and Sanders, do not appear in the reference list at all. The list stops at 33 references, none of which is one of these studies. A reader cannot trace them from this paper.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: A useful map of what has been tried, with weak methods and a conclusion that outruns the data.
points: Holds up: covers four surgery groups, tabulates each protocol's elements, and admits the evidence is low level.
Narrow search, no search dates, and two different database lists.
34 records lost between deduplication and screening with no explanation.
No risk of bias assessment; benefit is counted by number of studies.
Abstract counts (LOS n=15, complications n=8, pain n=4) cannot be traced to the Results.
Pooled deformity numbers have no source, despite the statement that no quantitative synthesis was done.
Six deformity studies are missing from the references.
Table cross-references are wrong; Table 4 has rows that do not add up.
Discussion says no studies address intradural lesions, yet Liu's intradural tumor RCT is included.
slides.notes: Be fair first. As a 2020 snapshot, the tables are useful for seeing what ERAS meant in practice: education, carbohydrate loading, multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia, local anesthetic, early mobilization, early feeding and catheter avoidance. The authors do say the evidence is mostly retrospective without formal controls and call for RCTs. Now the problems. The conclusion says ERAS programs can shorten LOS, accelerate return of function, and minimize pain, complications and costs. The Results do not support all of that. Cervical complication rates did not differ in Li. Cost data come from three studies, and the deformity section says there are not enough data. Complication benefit in lumbar surgery is cited to an outside meta-analysis. The abstract says benefits were seen in all three categories. Our counts and checks of the tables, item by item: Section 3.2 calls the lumbar table Table 2, and Section 3.4 points the Liu RCT to Table 4; the tables are actually swapped against those labels (lumbar is Table 4, tumors Table 2). Row arithmetic: Bradywood 189 men plus 296 women is 485, against 458 patients. Feng 27 plus 49 is 76, against 74. Heo is described as 23 versus 23 but has 69 patients, and Wang 2018 is 38 ERAS versus 15 controls but has 38 patients. Smith's EBL is printed as 34.4 vs 19.5 percent, an odd unit. Several Results cells lack units or a comparator. The Results opening sentence, that ERAS programs are not widely used in the spinal surgery field in other surgical fields, is garbled. None of these are fatal on its own. Together they say the tables were not checked carefully, so do not quote any single per-study number from this review without going to the primary paper. That advice is ours.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "A 2022 systematic review of 21 ERAS studies in spine surgery found mostly before-and-after cohorts reporting shorter stays. Only one was randomized, and the deformity studies were all pediatric. It does not tell us whether ERAS helps adult deformity patients."
points: Strongest single study inside it: Liu 2020 RCT, intradural tumors, LOS 5 vs 12 days.

Readmission to watch: the deformity section reports a trend to more 30-day readmission with ERAS (P=0.06), in pooled figures with no stated source. Grasu's 14.6% vs 8.9% is one extra event (our Fisher P about 0.52), not a signal.
Library comparison, Sorour 2023 (master record): a narrative review offering an ERAS checklist for deformity surgery, with no ERAS bundle outcome data in deformity patients.
Do not stretch it: no pooled LOS estimate, no risk of bias rating, and no adult deformity data.
slides.notes: Expect three follow-up questions. Should we run ERAS for adult deformity? This paper cannot answer that. It has no adult deformity studies, and the authors say so. The library's other ERAS paper, Sorour 2023, is a narrative review whose master record says it presents no ERAS bundle outcome data in deformity patients. So for adult deformity both library papers offer elements and rationale, not outcome evidence. That synthesis is ours. Which elements matter? The review cannot tell you. It describes bundles, and in almost every study several elements changed at once, sometimes with a switch to minimally invasive or endoscopic technique. The authors suggest procedure-specific items and single-step changes analyzed by regression as a way forward. Is shorter stay safe? The review does not show worse complications overall, but the deformity section reports a trend toward more 30-day readmission with ERAS (P=0.06), from pooled figures with no stated source. Grasu's tumor cohort is numerically higher (14.6 versus 8.9 percent), but that is one extra event, our Fisher P about 0.52. Smith 2019's complication rates may favor controls, but they do not fit its arm sizes. Watch readmission if you shorten stay. That caution is ours. If asked for a single number, the most defensible ones are the per-study LOS differences, which range from about 4 hours (Smith, compatible with no difference by our recalculation) to about 7 days, with the largest in the tumor RCT and the endoscopic TLIF comparison. Do not quote the deformity OR of 0.37 as this review's finding. The paper prints it without a source and says it did no quantitative synthesis.

decks.not_reviewed: Nothing beyond the article itself. The paper cites no supplement or appendix. Figures 1 and 2 are schematic construct drawings; the PDF text was read in full but figure images were not inspected. The KEOPS database, the cited reference papers, and any data on patients lost before 2 years were not available.

slides.title: Marques 2021: pseudarthrosis after ASD fusion
slides.lead: A 6-center retrospective cohort of 524 long fusions asking what predicts rod-fracture pseudarthrosis and how it was revised.
points: Journal club: adult deformity, mechanical complications
Marques MF, Fiere V, Obeid I, et al., for the SFCR. Eur Spine J 2021;30(11):3225-3232

Bottom line: 65 of 524 (12.4%) had pseudarthrosis, defined by rod fracture at 6 months or later. Longer fusions, iliac fixation and osteotomy were linked to more of it, and staged anterior-plus-posterior surgery to less. The odds ratios as printed point the other way for three of four factors, and many P values do not recompute.
slides.notes: This deck was prepared from the full text of the paper; no supplement is cited. It is an observational risk-factor study, so read it for selection, measurement and validity, not as a test of any technique. What the paper is: a retrospective review of the KEOPS multicenter database, 6 spine centers, written on behalf of the French spine society (SFCR), patients operated from 1 January 2012 to 31 December 2016. What it adds: a sizeable European series with radiographic parameters, a list of correlates of rod fracture, and a short description of how 53 revisions were done. What to watch: the headline numbers in the abstract do not survive a careful read. The odds-ratio directions conflict with the text, the 30% reduction claim has no source in the results, the '88%' figure is undefined, and the 2-year outcome P values look wrong when recomputed. Our advice: learn the direction of the univariate associations and the definition of pseudarthrosis, and treat the multivariable numbers and the 'outcome not compromised' conclusion as unreliable.

slides.title: Question, patients and selection
slides.lead: Who was included decides what the 12.4% means.
points: Question: which demographic, surgical and radiographic factors predict pseudarthrosis after ASD fusion, and how was it treated?
Included: adults over 18 operated for ASD, fusion of 4 or more levels, minimum 2-year follow-up, full-body films before surgery, within 3 months and at 2 years or later.
Cohort: 524 patients, 76.5% women, median follow-up 2.9 years. Mean age is not reported.
Approach: 67.4% posterior only, 32.6% staged posterior plus anterior cages. No isolated anterior surgery.
Construct: 10 or more levels in 32.3% (n = 169), 5-9 levels in 41% (n = 215). Distal end S1 33.2%, iliac or S2 alar 46.6%.
Rods: titanium alloy 60.5%, CoCr 38.2%, other 1.4%. 5.5 mm 64.3%, 6.0 mm 28.2%, 6.35 mm 7.4%. Osteotomy in 51.9% (PSO 18.7%, Ponte/SPO 32.2%).
slides.notes: Selection first. Only patients with 2-year films and follow-up were included, and the paper does not say how many operated patients were excluded for missing follow-up. Patients lost early, including any who failed early and went elsewhere, are invisible. Our inference: the 12.4% is a rate among patients who completed follow-up, not among all operated patients. Second, the paper records age, smoking, comorbidities and BMI but reports only BMI and prior surgeries in the tables. Mean age, smoking rates and bone density are not given, so you cannot judge how comparable this cohort is to yours, and smoking and osteoporosis, which the authors themselves list as known risk factors in the introduction, do not appear in the model. Third, the 6 centers did not standardize technique (authors' limitation). 'Combined' here means a staged posterior instrumented fusion plus an anterior approach with cages; it is not lateral or TLIF interbody, which are tallied separately. A small arithmetic note: 169 plus 215 leaves 140 patients (26.7%) with fewer than 5 levels, which given the inclusion rule means 4-level fusions; the paper does not state this. The osteotomy breakdown adds to 50.9%, not the 51.9% stated. The study was approved by the institutions of all 6 centers (IRB GP-CE 2021-10) and the authors state all participants gave written consent.

slides.title: Measurement: how pseudarthrosis was counted
slides.lead: Pseudarthrosis here means a broken rod on plain film.
points: Definition: rod fracture on plain films 6 months or more after surgery. CT or SPECT-CT only in some cases and centers.
Levels: L5-S1 20 (30.8%), more than one level 18 (27.7%), L4-L5 13 (20%), L3-L4 7 (10.8%). These total 58 of 65.
Other mechanical complications: 87 of 524 (16.6%), most often PJK.
Comparison groups in Tables 1 and 2: 65 with pseudarthrosis versus 372 with no complications. The 87 with other complications are left out.
Model: variables with univariate P below 0.2 entered a multiple logistic regression. Table 3 lists 24 candidate variables against 65 events.
slides.notes: Three measurement issues shape everything downstream. First, the outcome is rod fracture, not fusion status. The authors say this underestimates true pseudarthrosis, because an intact rod does not prove fusion, and they note rod fracture can also happen over a solid fusion. So the study really describes risk factors for rod fracture. Second, the control group. Tables 1 and 2 compare the 65 pseudarthrosis patients with 372 who had no complications at all, dropping the 87 with PJK and other mechanical problems. Our inference: removing the other-complication patients makes the controls healthier and simpler than a true 'no pseudarthrosis' group, which can exaggerate differences. Some rows of Table 1 (osteotomy, rod diameter) actually use 459 controls, the full non-pseudarthrosis group, so the denominators change from row to row. The paper does not say which sample entered the regression. Third, the model. By our count Table 3 lists 24 variables against 65 events, under 3 events per candidate variable, and selection was by univariate P below 0.2. Our inference: that is a recipe for unstable, overfit estimates, which fits the very wide CI on approach (1.09 to 9.91). Several model variables (RPV, RLL, LDI) are not defined in the paper. Prior surgeries had univariate P = 0.04 but is not marked as a model input. BMI is printed P = 0.26, but recomputes to about 0.15 (ours, Welch), also under the 0.2 rule, and it is not an input either. Also note 7 of the 65 pseudarthrosis levels are not accounted for in the level list.

slides.title: Risk factors: what was found
slides.lead: The univariate rates are coherent. The printed odds ratios contradict them for three of four factors.

rows: 29 of 155 (19%) vs 36 of 282 (13%), printed P = 0.04; ours about 0.09

points: Not significant in the model: preoperative and postoperative alignment, operative time, blood loss, ALIF, TLIF, LLIF, any osteotomy (P = 0.583), distal fixation type, rod material, rod diameter.

Univariate only: pseudarthrosis patients had more blood loss (1634 vs 1095 ml), longer surgery (246 vs 205 min), lower preoperative L1-S1 lordosis (37.7 vs 44.7 degrees) and larger lordosis correction (14.3 vs 7.2 degrees).
slides.notes: How to read the odds ratios. An OR above 1 against the stated reference means more pseudarthrosis in the named group. As printed, combined approach (OR 3.29 versus posterior only) would raise risk, and iliac fixation (0.34) and 3-column osteotomy (0.28) would lower it. The authors' text says the opposite for all three, and their univariate rates agree with the text. Our inference: the reference categories were probably coded the other way round. Inverted, the ORs become about 3.3 for posterior only, 2.9 for iliac fixation and 3.6 for 3-column osteotomy, which fits the authors' sentence that each carries about 3 times the risk. The CIs are symmetric on the log scale and their P values recompute correctly (our check), so the arithmetic is fine; the labels are not. Fusion length has OR 1.17 with reference '?'; presumably per added level, but the paper does not say. The abstract calls the fourth factor 'osteotomy requirement', but the model found any osteotomy not significant (P = 0.583); only 3-column osteotomy was. The abstract also says '88% of pseudarthrosis cases are associated with' these factors; the results say 88.2% 'could be explained'. Neither is defined. Our guess is overall classification accuracy, which would be barely better than the 87.6% you get by predicting no pseudarthrosis for everyone (459 of 524). Table 1 counts (ours, chi-square): 3-column osteotomy printed P = 0.04 recomputes to about 0.09, so it was not univariately significant; the 'any osteotomy' rates are not the 3-column ones. The 155 with 3-column osteotomy exceed the roughly 98 PSOs (18.7% of 524) in the text, and 126 of 372 controls had 3-column but only 145 of 459 any osteotomy, leaving almost no SPOs. The approach rates in the text (7.6% vs 14.7%) use whole-cohort denominators; Table 1 counts give 9.3% vs 17.5%, same direction. Rods: the text says 18% of titanium versus 8.5% of CoCr patients had pseudarthrosis, but Table 1 counts give about 13% versus 17%, the other direction, and its printed P = 0.01 recomputes to about 0.25. By rod diameter the rate was highest with 6.35 mm (about 25%), lower with 5.5 mm (12.5%) and 6.0 mm (8.1%), so thicker was not simply safer, and rod diameter was not significant in the model.

slides.title: Revision and patient-reported outcomes
slides.lead: 53 of 65 were revised, at a median of 19 months.
points: Revision approach: combined 22 (41.5%), posterior only 23 (43.4%). The other 8 are not described.
Interbody fusion in 29: ALIF alone 2, TLIF 5, ALIF plus posterior 22. Rod exchange without interbody in 18.
Supplementary osteotomy in 7 (3 SPO, 4 PSO). Fusion extended in only 6; otherwise UIV and LIV unchanged.
Graft: iliac or autologous graft in 43 (81%); BMP in 4.
Authors' outcome claim: ODI at final follow-up 28% never revised versus 30% revised, reported as comparable.
slides.see: Table 2 gives the 2-year scores with SDs; our recomputed P values use those means, SDs and the full group sizes.
slides.notes: The revision description is the practical part of the paper: most revisions added interbody support, usually ALIF with posterior revision, used iliac autograft, and kept the original fusion levels. It is descriptive only. There is no comparison of revision techniques, and no healing or re-failure rates are reported after revision. Now the outcome claim. The abstract and conclusion say the final outcome is not compromised, because ODI was 28% in patients never revised and 30% in those revised. That comparison has no SD, no group sizes, no P value and no specific time point (only 'final' or 'last' follow-up), and 'no revision' appears to include patients who never had pseudarthrosis (our reading). Table 2 is more informative. At 2 years the pseudarthrosis group scored worse on ODI, SRS-22 and SF-36 PCS, and better on MCS, all reported as not significant. Our recomputation with a Welch t-test from the printed means and SDs, assuming all 372 and 65 patients contributed (inclusion required 2-year follow-up), gives P of about 0.048, 0.004, 0.002 and 0.013. The paper does not report how many completed 2-year questionnaires; if many were missing, the true P values would be larger. Either way, the data do not support 'patients revised do as well as those that never required a reoperation'. Also note the 2-year snapshot mixes patients before and after revision, since median time to revision was 19 months and follow-up was a median 2.9 years. The ODI gap of about 5.6 points is below the MCID values commonly used for ODI (our outside knowledge; the paper cites Carreon and Sherif but gives no value), so the safest statement is that pseudarthrosis patients were somewhat worse at 2 years, by a margin of uncertain clinical meaning.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: Useful direction, unreliable numbers.
points: Strengths: 6 centers, 524 patients, full-length films at fixed times, clear operational definition.
Outcome is rod fracture, which the authors say underestimates pseudarthrosis; CT use was not standardized.
Controls exclude the 87 with other complications; denominators change between rows.
About 3 events per candidate variable in the model (our count); reference categories appear reversed for three ORs.
Several preoperative P values in Table 2 do not recompute, and the 2-year PROM P values look too large.
The '30% lower rate' with anterior support and '88% explained' are not traceable to any reported analysis.
slides.notes: Recomputations (ours, Welch t-test from printed means and SDs, n = 372 and 65). Preoperative ODI 44.92 vs 46.11 is printed P = 0.01; we get about 0.55, and the text itself says preoperative PROMs did not differ. L4-S1 lordosis 30.90 vs 29.62, printed 0.01, ours about 0.42. Pelvic tilt 23.67 vs 26.34, printed 0.01, ours about 0.10. LLI 0.82 vs 0.63, printed 0.03, ours below 0.001. Cobb 27.51 vs 35.02, printed 0.039, ours about 0.005. Pelvic incidence 0.36, ours about 0.82; SVA 0.11, ours about 0.29; SRS-22 0.98, ours about 0.80. At 2 years: pelvic tilt 0.14, ours about 0.049; LLI 1.14 vs 0.80, printed 0.05, ours below 0.001; Cobb 0.24, ours about 0.74; L1-S1 lordosis 0.47, ours about 0.22. L1-S1 lordosis (0.003) and lordosis correction (0.003) do recompute. The pseudarthrosis L4-S1 lordosis is identical before surgery and at 2 years (29.62 plus or minus 11.56), which looks like a copy error. Rates that do not reproduce from Table 1 counts: iliac fixation 17.6% vs 7.9% in the text, but 51 of 218 (23%) vs 14 of 219 (6%) from the table; titanium 18% vs CoCr 8.5% in the text, but about 13% vs 17% from the table. Table 1 printed P values that fail on its own counts (ours): iliac fixation 0.01 (below 0.0001), operative time 0.01, text 0.006 (below 0.001), rod material 0.01 (about 0.25), 3-column osteotomy 0.04 (about 0.09). Osteotomy is 51.9% of patients in the text but 174 of 524 (33%) in Table 1. The '30% decrease' with anterior support is not in the results; the univariate rates 7.6% vs 14.7% are a 7.1-point absolute and about 48% relative difference (ours). On alignment, the authors conclude pseudarthrosis is not related to malalignment. What they showed is that alignment variables were not significant in an overfit model with 65 events, while preoperative lordosis, LLI and lordosis correction did differ univariately, and by our recomputation 2-year pelvic tilt and LLI also differed. Absence of significance is not evidence of no effect. Confounding by indication is the core problem, and the authors concede it: the pseudarthrosis group had more prior surgery, more osteotomies, more levels and longer operations, so the effect of any one factor cannot be isolated. Combined surgery may simply have been chosen for different patients. Minor: the IRB reference is GP-CE 2021-10 although the paper was received in July 2020.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: In an SFCR multicenter series of 524 adult deformity fusions, about 1 in 8 broke a rod during follow-up (median 2.9 years), most often at L5-S1, and more often with long fusions to the pelvis and osteotomies; staged anterior column support went with fewer.
points: Spoken summary: 12.4% rod-fracture pseudarthrosis; risk rose with fusion length, iliac fixation and 3-column osteotomy, and fell with staged anterior plus posterior surgery (7.6% vs 14.7% univariately). 53 of 65 were revised at a median 19 months, mostly with added interbody support and autograft.
Expect: is 12.4% the true nonunion rate? No. It counts rod fractures only, among patients with 2-year follow-up; the authors say it underestimates.
Expect: does an ALIF prevent pseudarthrosis? Association only, confounded by case selection, and the printed OR direction is mislabeled.
Expect: does alignment matter? The authors say not, but the model was underpowered and preoperative lordosis did differ.
Expect: do revised patients do as well? Not shown; 2-year ODI, SRS-22 and PCS were worse in the pseudarthrosis group, and our recomputed P values suggest real differences.
Expect: what about CoCr or thicker rods? Data are internally inconsistent and neither was significant in the model.
slides.notes: Say it in this order: definition, rate, direction of the four associations, revision pattern, then the warnings. The single most important caveat for an audience is the definition. This is a rod-fracture study, so it speaks to mechanical failure of long posterior constructs, which is why anterior column support, fewer levels and avoiding a stress riser at a PSO make biological and mechanical sense, as the authors argue with biomechanical references. The second caveat is that the paper's printed statistics are not trustworthy in detail: reversed odds-ratio labels, P values that do not recompute, and rates in the text that do not match the table. Quote the univariate rates rather than the odds ratios. The authors go further than the data in two places: they say they are persuaded to consider anterior fusion mandatory for Schwab grade 3 or 4 osteotomies with long constructs and pelvic fixation, and that the final outcome is not compromised by pseudarthrosis. Present both as the authors' opinion. If asked about multi-rod constructs: the authors cite other work favoring them, but report only that a 'double-rod construct' was used in 6.5% of cases, without analyzing it; our reading is that they meant supplementary rods, but the paper does not define it. A fair one-line verdict: a hypothesis-generating series that agrees with the broader literature on mechanical risk, not evidence that settles any technique choice.

decks.not_reviewed: The Supplemental Figure (http://links.lww.com/NEU/A962) and Supplemental Table (http://links.lww.com/NEU/A963), which hold the per-severity motor outcome counts, and the online analysis code at rpubs.com. Figure values were read from the printed figures; Figure 2B percentages are read off bar heights and are approximate.

slides.title: Thomé 2022: timing of surgery for disk-related weakness
slides.lead: Motor Recovery Depends on Timing of Surgery in Patients With Lumbar Disk Herniation.
points: Journal club: lumbar disk herniation with motor deficit
Thomé C, Kögl N, Grassner L, Vo AK, Kramer JLK, Petr O. Neurosurgery 2022;90(3):347-353

Bottom line: in 390 operated patients, weakness of MRC 2/5 or worse and paresis lasting more than 3 days before surgery went with worse recovery. Every patient had surgery; nobody was randomized to a time.
Source: the full 7-page paper was read. The supplement was not.
slides.notes: This is a single-center Innsbruck series of patients with a radicular motor deficit from a lumbar disk herniation, all of whom had nonelective microscopic disk surgery between January 2013 and December 2015. The question is not whether to operate. It is how fast. The authors used a data-driven tree method to find a time cutoff, and it returned 3 days. Hold two things in mind from the start. First, there is no conservative group, so the paper can only compare early surgery with late surgery. Second, the cutoff comes out of the same data it is then tested on. What was reviewed: the full article text, the Table, and both figures (read from the page images). Not reviewed: the Supplemental Figure and Supplemental Table, and the authors' online R analysis. The Supplemental Table is where the per-severity counts live, so some of the cross-checks in this deck use Figure 1B instead. The master record was abstract level before this review and called the study prospective. The Methods say patients were recruited retrospectively and follow-up examinations were done prospectively, so treat it as an ambispective cohort.

slides.title: Question, patients and methods
slides.lead: 390 adults with disk-related radicular weakness, all operated, split by time from onset of paresis to surgery.
points: Included: nonelective presentation, MRI or CT-confirmed herniation, radicular motor deficit, proceeding to surgery. Excluded: no motor deficit, extraforaminal herniation, unfit for anesthesia, declined surgery.
Surgery: microscopic fragmentectomy through an interlaminar speculum in most; microdiskectomy if a large annular defect.
Grading: MRC 0-5 before surgery, at discharge, 6 and 12 weeks, and 1 to 5 years. Mild = 4/5, moderate = 3/5, severe = 2/5 or worse.
Follow-up: 389/390 (99.7%) at last visit, mean 43.4 ± 19.7 months (range 12-73).
slides.notes: How was timing decided? The authors say patients with a motor deficit were sent acutely to anesthesia for unscheduled surgery as a department routine, so the duration of paresis mostly reflected how long the patient took to reach them, and to a lesser extent operating room availability. That is the exposure. Onset was taken from history and outpatient records, usually to the day, sometimes to the hour. Notice that the late group is older by about 4 years (52.9 vs 48.8) and has more mild deficits (34.8% vs 26.4%) and fewer moderate ones. The paper does not test these differences. Our recomputation from the Table's means and SDs: the age gap is significant (t = 2.77, P = .006); the severity mix is borderline (chi-square 5.36, 2 df, P = .07); sex, level and body mass index do not differ. Age could plausibly slow recovery. Age did not enter the tree, but that is not adjustment of the Figure 1B contrasts. The examiners were a resident or fellow followed by a board-certified neurosurgeon. The paper does not say whether they knew the timing, so do not call it blinded or unblinded. Patients were also treated with analgesics and re-examined to reduce pain-related weakness, which matters because pain-limited effort can mimic MRC 4/5. Recruitment: the Trial Design paragraph says patients were recruited retrospectively, with follow-up examinations done prospectively after consent. That fits the abstract's 'prospectively followed' and the Methods' 'consecutively enrolled'. The problem is the abstract's silence on retrospective recruitment, which led the master record to call the study prospective. Our inference: the ethics approval numbers (1004/2020, AN2021-1004) date from after the 2013-2015 operations, which fits a retrospectively assembled cohort. Covariates were sex, age, body mass index and level. In the Table, 2 of the >3-day percentages do not match their counts: L3/L4 25/178 is 14.0%, printed 14.5%, and L5/S1 49/178 is 27.5%, printed 28.3%. Small, but it tells you the Table was not cross-checked.

slides.title: Primary outcome: slope of recovery
slides.lead: A tree split first on severity, then on 3 days of paresis in both branches.
points: Outcome: each patient's slope of MRC recovery over time, from a linear mixed model. Higher slope means faster and fuller recovery, per the authors.
Method: unbiased recursive partitioning (conditional inference tree) chose the cutoff with the smallest Bonferroni-adjusted P value.
Mean slope: 0.328 (≤3 days) vs 0.272 (>3 days). The paper gives no units.
Age, sex, body mass index and level did not enter the tree.
slides.see: Figure 1A is the tree. Box plots show severe patients operated after 3 days sitting far below the other three groups, with slopes near 0.2.
slides.notes: Read the tree top down. The first split is preoperative strength at 2/5, which the authors call the most important predictor. Within each branch, duration of paresis then splits at 3 days. The method chose 3 days because it was the cutpoint with the smallest P value in this sample. That makes it a description of these 390 patients, not a validated threshold. No test or external sample checked it. The slope is a modeled quantity, not something you measure at the bedside. Look at the box plots: the MRC >2 and 3-day branch is packed against about 0.335, close to the maximum slope in the Table of 0.354. Our reading: the outcome has a ceiling. A patient who starts at 4/5 can gain only one grade, so a mixed-severity branch with more mild patients, like the late group, may show lower slopes partly because of where it started. The tree did not split mild from moderate within the >2 branch, so the paper cannot rule this out from this analysis alone. Two numbering checks fail. The abstract gives P = .017 for the severe split, while the Results and Figure 1A give P = .022. And the tree's MRC >2 nodes hold 176 and 133 patients, whereas the Table's moderate plus mild counts are 171 (115 + 56) and 138 (76 + 62). The total of 390 matches, so 5 patients sit in different timing groups in the tree and the Table. The paper does not explain this.

slides.title: Full recovery at last follow-up
slides.lead: Within 3 days, nearly everyone with a mild or moderate deficit regained full strength. After 3 days, no severe patient did.
points: Full recovery means MRC 5/5 at last follow-up (12-73 months; the authors say 1-5 years).
After >3 days, severe: 6 improved (15%), 34 unchanged (85%). Moderate: 26 improved (34.2%), 32 unchanged (42.1%).
At 3 months: recovered 168 (79.2%) vs 47 (26.4%), but missing 21 (9.9%) vs 39 (21.9%).
Authors: strength at 3 months correlates with final outcome, r = 0.96.
slides.see: Figure 1B shows the stacked bars by severity and timing. The contrast between the left and right panels is the paper's main picture.
slides.notes: The counts come from Figure 1B, and they agree with the Table totals of 192 and 64 recovered. Our recomputation of the NNTs: severe 1/(0.61 - 0) = 1.6; moderate 1/(0.974 - 0.237) = 1.4; mild 1/(0.982 - 0.754) = 4.4. All three match the authors. Note that the mild NNT of 4.4 matches this 3-day contrast, even though the Discussion places it in the paragraph about the 8-day window. The abstract says NNT <2 for both severe and moderate/mild deficits; that holds only for severe and moderate. How to read the effect: these are absolute differences of 61, 74 and 23 percentage points. They are very large for an observational timing comparison, which should make you ask what else separates the groups (next slides). The 3-month row has the most missing data in the late group, 21.9% against 9.9%, so do not lean on the 3-month split. There is also an internal conflict in the late column. Figure 1B shows 34 severe late patients unchanged, which should leave at least 34 with a severe deficit at last follow-up, yet the Table lists 17. Figure 1B also allows at most 38 late moderate deficits at last follow-up (32 unchanged moderate plus 6 improved severe), yet the Table lists 49. The late non-recovered total agrees (113 = 17 + 49 + 47), so our reading is that about 17 severe patients were counted as moderate in the Table. The early column's total agrees too (20 = 1 + 15 + 4). Three more Table percentages do not match counts: the early severe row 1/212 is 0.5%, printed 0.7%; the early mild row 4/212 is 1.9%, printed 1.8%; and overall missing 1/390 is 0.3%, printed 0.4%. Harms: the authors report no secondary deterioration in the mild group. Complications are not reported.

slides.title: Mild deficits: the 8-day sensitivity analysis
slides.lead: Can surgery wait for MRC 4/5? The tree put the cutoff at 8 days.
points: Purpose, per the authors: test whether surgery could be delayed in mild cases.
Figure 2: ≤8 days n = 65, >8 days n = 15. Slope split P = 0.002; outcome-category split P = 0.021.
Full recovery: >90% within 8 days per the text. From the bars, ours: about 96% vs about 60%.
No patient deteriorated after surgery, per the authors.
slides.see: Figure 2B shows the mild subgroup's outcomes on either side of 8 days. No patient fell in the deteriorated category.
slides.notes: This is the slide most likely to be quoted in clinic, and the most fragile. The 8-day analysis contains 80 patients (65 + 15), but the paper has 118 mild patients, of whom 117 have last follow-up in Figure 1B. About 38 mild patients are missing from the sensitivity analysis, and the paper does not say why. Our arithmetic shows how odd this is: 56 mild patients were operated within 3 days, so only about 9 fall between days 4 and 8, while Figure 1B has 61 mild patients after 3 days. Next, the methods say the dependent variable was last follow-up MRC, but Figure 2A shows a tree on slope (P = 0.002) and Figure 2B one on outcome category (P = 0.021). The text does not say which P it is quoting. The >8-day group is only 15 patients, so about 9 recovered and 6 did not (our reading of the bars). Any percentage on 15 patients is unstable. The Conclusion says disk surgery within 8 days ensures recovery. The paper's own text says more than 90%, so ensures overstates it. The authors also say that in their center mild weakness was operated only if functionally disabling, often knee extensor weakness limiting walking, and they note that MRC 4/5 spans trivial to disabling weakness and that onset is less certain in mild cases. So the mild group here is not every MRC 4/5 patient you will see.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: A large, well-followed surgical series with a striking signal, but no control arm, a data-picked cutoff, and counts that do not reconcile.
points: Strengths, per the authors: consecutive patients, near-complete follow-up (99.7%; the authors write 99%), and a data-driven cutoff search with no a priori assumption about timing.
Not randomized; authors say randomizing to delay would be unethical.
No conservative group, so the paper cannot say what happens without surgery.
Single tertiary center with referral of moderate to severe deficits, per the authors.

rows: Late severe and moderate at last visit

slides.notes: Selection is the core worry, and this part is our inference, not the authors'. Everyone in the cohort had surgery. A patient whose weakness recovered during the first days would probably never have been operated and so never entered the study. That removes spontaneous recoverers from the late group more than from the early group, and it would make late surgery look worse even if timing did nothing. The paper cannot test this without a conservative group. Second, time to surgery was driven by time to presentation. People who present late may differ in pain, herniation behavior or access to care. The tree tested only age, sex, body mass index and level. Third, the cutoffs are chosen by the smallest P value in this sample and never validated, so expect the true break, if any, to be less sharp. Fourth, the slope outcome has a ceiling for mild patients. Fifth, the paper does not say whether examiners knew the timing, and MRC grading is subjective at 4 versus 5. The authors' own limitations list covers nonrandomization, no conservative group, single center, the breadth of MRC 4/5, and uncertain onset in mild cases. Against that, the effect is very large and the follow-up nearly complete. Compare the library record for Peul 2007 (L02): that randomized trial of early surgery versus prolonged conservative care for 6 to 12 weeks of sciatica excluded paralysis and strength below antigravity, so it does not speak to this question, and this paper does not overturn it. The table lists internal inconsistencies; together they mean the exact counts should not be memorized as settled.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "In 390 operated patients with disk-related weakness, surgery within 3 days of onset went with full recovery in 61% of severe and about 97-98% of moderate and mild deficits, against 0%, 24% and 75% after 3 days. It is an observational series with a data-picked cutoff and no conservative arm, The authors conclude that immediate diagnosis, imaging and referral should aim for surgery within 3 days; the data support that urgency, but they do not prove 3 days is the line."
points: Severe weakness (≤2/5) was the strongest predictor of a poor result.
For mild weakness, the authors' window is 8 days, from an unexplained subset of 80 of 118 patients.
Do not call it prospective or randomized.
slides.notes: Expect these follow-up questions. Does this prove early surgery causes better recovery? No. Every patient was operated, timing was not assigned, and patients who recovered on their own would not appear. The direction and size of the effect still support treating disk-related weakness as urgent, which is what the authors recommend: immediate diagnosis, imaging and referral, with surgery within 3 days for moderate and severe weakness. Should a patient with 4/5 weakness be operated within a week? The authors suggest decompression within a week if the deficit is functionally disabling. That rests on 80 patients, 15 of them after 8 days, and the authors themselves say conservative care often gives acceptable recovery in mild cases. What about a patient seen on day 10 with 2/5 weakness? In this series none of the 40 severe patients operated after 3 days regained full strength, 15% improved and 85% were unchanged. The paper does not say what would have happened without surgery, so it can inform counseling about likely residual weakness but cannot say surgery is futile. How does this fit with Peul? Peul (L02, library record) excluded strength below antigravity and tested a strategy of waiting with surgery if needed, so the two papers address different patients. Which muscle was graded? The paper does not specify beyond the MRC grade of the deficit, with knee extensors mentioned as a common disabling deficit. Finally, if asked for the numbers to remember: 390 patients, 3-day cutoff, 61% vs 0% full recovery for severe deficits, NNT 1.4 to 1.6 for moderate and severe.

decks.not_reviewed: The paper has no supplement. Not read: the companion Iyer et al. 2022 article on high-risk determinants and prevention (reference 6), the 2014 Vitale stable-spine checklist this builds on (references 7 and 8), the Jarvis 2013 timing classification it adapts (reference 5), and the survey instruments, which are not published. Figures 1 to 4 are text charts and were read from the PDF text layer.

slides.title: Lenke 2022: responding to IONM alerts in high-risk deformity surgery
slides.lead: An expert Delphi consensus that turns the IONM alert response into stage-based checklists for the unstable spine.
points: Lenke LG, Fano AN, Iyer RR, et al. Spine Deform 2022;10:745-761. Consensus guideline, Level V.
Panel: 15 spinal deformity surgeons (10 orthopedic, 5 neurosurgical) from the US, Canada and Ghana. All 15 took part.
Output: 105 consensus items in four aids: Response Algorithm 53, Ongoing Consideration of Etiology 13, Real-Time Data Scenarios 31, Patterns of IONM Loss 8.
Bottom line: elevate MAP first. If signals do not return, gain the room's attention, optimize systemically, define the pattern and timing, then act by stage. Always consider calling a colleague.
Full text read end to end (17 pages). No supplement. Companion high-risk article not read.
slides.notes: What this is: a set of operating-room aids, not a study of patients. No patient outcomes were measured. The evidence level is expert opinion, Level V by the authors' own label. It is one of a pair. The companion paper (Iyer et al., reference 6) defines which patients and procedures are high risk and how to prevent events. This one covers what to do once an alert happens. Neither the companion paper nor the 2014 checklist was read for this deck. The starting point is the 2014 Vitale checklist for the stable spine, which the authors describe as covering the majority of deformity surgery. This paper extends it to the unstable spine, often created by a three-column osteotomy, where the authors argue the stakes and the options are different. Two definitions the panel agreed to before voting matter. An IONM alert is any MEP and/or SSEP change that meets the institution's own warning criteria and signals cord dysfunction, not nerve root dysfunction. So no numeric threshold is set, and what counts as an alert varies by hospital. A postoperative neurological deficit is any significant change from what was expected, or less than antigravity strength in one or both legs when full strength was expected. The panel is surgeons only. Neurophysiologists and anesthesiologists, who run much of the response, did not vote. Funding: none for the study. Many authors report industry relationships. Six (Matsumoto, Samdani, Smith, Gupta, Kelly, Vitale) state theirs are outside the submitted work; the others do not say either way. Read this deck as how a group of very experienced deformity surgeons say they would think through an alert, organized by when it happens.

slides.title: The question and how the consensus was built
slides.lead: What should the team consider, and in what order, when signals drop during high-risk deformity surgery?
points: Literature review: OVID Medline, 154 articles screened, 38 relevant, 49 responses to IONM change or postoperative deficit extracted.
Survey 1 (online): 13 completed, 2 partial. Survey 2: 14 completed, 1 partial.
Virtual face-to-face meeting: 14 of 15 attended. Live anonymous electronic voting, repeated until consensus or no further progress.
Thresholds on a 4-point scale: consensus at least 80% agree or strongly agree; near-consensus 60% to under 80%; equipoise 20% to under 60%; exclude under 20%.
Near-consensus items were reworded and revoted. Equipoise and exclude items were dropped.
slides.notes: Teach the Delphi method briefly: rounds of voting, feedback, rewording and revoting. Here the final round was a live meeting with anonymous audience-response voting, and the senior author facilitated. Live discussion led by a senior figure can pull a group toward agreement; that is our caution, not the authors'. Panel experience was high. Mean time in practice was 19 plus or minus 8.1 years (range 8 to 35). Mean deformity volume was 121.3 plus or minus 48.4 cases a year (range 50 to 200). Table 2 splits the practice mix: 4 were 100% pediatric, 1 was 75% pediatric, 2 were 50:50, 6 were 75% adult and 2 were 100% adult. The percentages in Table 2 check out against 15. So 5 of 15 do mainly or only pediatric work and 7 of 15 do at least half pediatric, which matters when you apply this to a 70 year old with a 3CO. Now the arithmetic. The per-round counts add up within each round, and the final per-section counts (53, 13, 31, 8) sum to 105. Every row of Tables 3 to 6 counts out to those numbers. But the rounds do not add to the final. Items meeting consensus across rounds sum to 124 (39 plus 43 plus 42). By section: Response Algorithm 29 in survey 1 plus 38 at the meeting is 67, against 53 final. The Methods say consensus items could still be reworded and sent back for another vote, which likely explains the overlap. The paper gives no item-by-item flow, so you cannot trace which items were revoted. Agreement percentages often do not sit on a denominator of 15, as the footnote says. Ours: with 15 or fewer voters, 92.9% and 85.7% fit only 13 and 12 of 14, and 92.3% and 84.6% fit only 12 and 11 of 13. So the weakest included items were backed by 11 or 12 surgeons. The 13 is a puzzle. Only survey 1 had 13 completers, and only 1 Real-Time Data Scenarios item passed there, yet 9 Table 5 items sit at 92.3% or 84.6%. Survey 2 had 14 completers plus 1 partial and the meeting had 14 attendees. So, by our arithmetic, some voters in survey 2 or the meeting must have skipped items, which the paper does not report. The search reports databases and terms but not dates.

slides.title: Response algorithm: what to do by stage
slides.lead: Elevate MAP first. Then the action depends on when the alert happens.
points: Stages 1a to 3: reduce or remove traction unless needed for stability, and wake-up test(s). Stages 1b to 3 add: if available, consider DSCM with DNEPs to assess the level of dysfunction. Stage 4 has no traction item; DSCM appears there only as part of re-exploration, and 4a has an end-of-case WUT.
Kyphoscoliosis: consider posterior column shortening (convex temporary rod or hook-rod construct); in Stages 2b and 3, ± anterior column lengthening to prevent or manage buckling.
Lordoscoliosis: consider dorsal decompression; in Stages 2b and 3, ± anterior column shortening.
Lowest agreement in the algorithm: reducing traction during or right after osteotomy, 85.7%.

Draft steroid doses (dexamethasone, methylprednisolone) were reworded to just IV steroids. No numeric MAP, hematocrit or steroid targets are given; the only time target is an elevated MAP goal for 48 to 72 h in the ICU.

rows: Adjust position; flip supine and recheck; WUT or abort and return later
Check screws (palpation, x-ray, CT), remove as indicated; look for dural compression or tension
Temporary rod(s); decompress as indicated; after 3CO check for subluxation and assess compression circumferentially
After osteotomy closure, during correction or during closure
Reverse the maneuver: reopen osteotomy, release distraction or compression
End-of-case WUT; raise MAP, reverse anemia; re-explore or image first; MAP goal 48 to 72 h in ICU

slides.see: Figure 1 is the one-page algorithm chart, laid out left to right by stage, made for use by the surgical team in the clinical setting.
slides.notes: The algorithm opens with one item at 100%: elevate MAP. If signals return, go back to the stable-spine checklist. If not, gain the room's attention, optimize systemically, determine the pattern and timing of change, then move to the stage. The stage scheme is adapted from Jarvis et al. 2013. How to read the stages. Stage 1a, before incision: think positioning, prone cord impingement and instability, and remember poor baseline signals from preexisting neurological disease. The authors suggest pre-positioning baselines in some high-risk patients, and baselines at halo placement before planned halo-gravity traction. Stage 1b, after incision but before destabilization: implants are the suspects. Look for breaches and pedicle fracture, with special attention to apical concave screws, which the cord may drape over. Stage 2: during PCOs the authors note the cord may stretch as the apex loosens, and they describe preemptive convex temporary rods. After a 3CO, check stability, subluxation and ventral decompression. Stage 3: undo the correction. The authors also say that, after a 3CO, the cord can often tolerate 2 to 3 cm of shortening, but overcorrection risks buckling, which a larger anterior graft or cage may reduce. Their suggestion to let MAP drift down before final closure, to check that supraphysiologic perfusion is not required, is worth teaching. Stage 4a: they strongly favor a neurological check in the OR. Stage 4b, ICU: if loss is progressive, ascending or complete, return to the OR emergently. If incomplete, stable or resolving, consider imaging first. They warn that metal artifact and delay can make imaging the wrong first move. Delayed deficit typically appears 8 to 48 hours after surgery, by their account. Not every item says consider. Many are direct, such as elevate MAP, reduce or remove traction, and return to the OR emergently if loss is progressive. In Figure 1 the stage lists sit under the header consider each of the following, but the opening elevate MAP step does not. The authors say an absolute algorithm is nearly impossible and decisions stay with the surgeon.

slides.title: Etiology and patterns of IONM loss
slides.lead: Keep asking why. The pattern of loss points to a cause, but loss is often multifactorial.

rows: MAP, Hgb or Hct, pH, pCO2, temperature
Raise MAP, reverse anemia, normalize pH, pCO2 and temperature; check equipment
Look at the dura; x-ray, fluoroscopy, CT, ultrasound
Reduce and stabilize; restore column length and alignment
High DAR, high-risk cord shape, taut dura; mixed MEP and SSEP loss, unilateral (often concave side) or bilateral
Release traction or correction, apical pediculectomy, 3CO, steroids
Possible MEP loss alone if ventral, SSEP loss alone if dorsal; or mixed
Decompress (laminectomy, facetectomy, pediculectomy, VCR), then allow time
Diagnosis of exclusion; may contribute to other causes; bilateral MEP/SSEP loss, or isolated bilateral MEP loss with SSEPs spared (may be evolving ischemia)
Raise MAP, reverse anemia, decompress, steroids

points: Unknown cause: image, map the cord, get upper-extremity and EEG data to rule out a brain cause, consider occult intradural pathology; then WUT, abort or brain imaging.
Isolated MEP loss: unilateral suggests stretch or cord trauma; bilateral, strongly consider ischemia or compression.
Isolated SSEP loss: rare; consider dorsal compression.
Combined MEP and SSEP loss: consider stretch, circumferential compression or major ischemia.
Excluded at 0%: crossed motor and sensory signs as a sign of stretch.
slides.see: Figures 2 and 4 are the etiology and pattern charts as printed for OR use.
slides.notes: This is the diagnostic half of the guideline. Teach it as a loop that runs alongside the algorithm, not a one-time step. The disclaimer at the top of both charts reached 100%: loss may be multifactorial and patterns will vary. Read the patterns as hints, not rules. Points worth noticing. Ischemia is a diagnosis of exclusion; rule out the mechanical causes first. The draft ischemia item said it was not expected to change SSEPs. That wording was replaced by: isolated bilateral MEP loss with SSEP sparing may reflect evolving ischemia. The bilateral MEP item first named ventral compression and was broadened to compression. Watch the cord-shape detail. Table 4 lists Type 2 SCS as high risk for stretch, Figure 2 lists Type 3 SCS, and the Discussion describes the type 3 cord, deformed at the apex, as the risky one. Table 4 looks like the error, but the paper does not say which is right. The cord-shape scheme itself is the Sielatycki 2020 MRI classification (reference 16), not read here. On DSCM the authors make three practical points: DNEPs largely reflect sensory pathways, interpretation needs an experienced team, and it depends heavily on TIVA. They argue it helps because the lesion may not sit at the main correction site. TcMEP changes are sensitive but not specific for the level. For the unknown cause, the upper-extremity and EEG step is easy to forget. It looks for a central cause, such as a stroke or intracranial hematoma, as the paper lists.

slides.title: Real-time data scenarios
slides.lead: Six signal trajectories, each starting with systemic optimization and defining the pattern and timing, then a menu of options. A seventh section covers aborting in the setting of a 3CO.

rows: Poor or absent baseline before positioning
Proceed if it matches baseline function; WUT; abort and investigate
Poor, absent or worse after positioning
Release traction, check bolsters, flip supine, WUT, abort
Proceed as planned, or modify; or abort to let the cord recover
Out of warning zone, not baseline
Check distal muscle MEPs; WUT; modify or abort
Reverse last maneuver; stabilize, decompress; WUT; modify or abort; image after
Reverse; decompress; WUT; DSCM to localize; abort; image after

points: Modifications to proceed: gradual correction, accept less correction, temporary rods across the apex while placing the contralateral rod, earlier apical pediculectomy during VCR.
If aborting after a 3CO: temporary rods, cover the laminar defect with bone, mesh or connector, consider a subfascial drain.
Excluded at 0%: intraoperative myelogram for persistent loss.
slides.see: Figure 3 lays out the six scenarios and the 3CO abort steps as a single chart.
slides.notes: This section takes on a practical question: the signals came back, now what? The panel gave three options when signals return to baseline: carry on as planned, carry on with modifications, or stop and come back. Note where agreement thinned. Aborting after full recovery got 84.6%, ours about 11 of 13. Proceeding with modifications after signals improve and then degrade again also got 84.6%, as did aborting in that scenario. These are the true judgment calls, and the paper offers no data to choose between them. The distal muscle MEP point is a useful pearl. The panel agreed that return of distal muscle group MEPs to baseline may be a good prognostic sign for overall leg function. It is offered as an opinion, without a cited outcome study in that item. Two scenarios list postoperative advanced imaging with MRI, myelography or spinal angiography. Abort means place temporary rods as indicated and make sure screw placement is acceptable. The aim is to let the neural elements recover and return another day. Three items cover aborting after a 3CO, all at 100%: temporary rods, cover the exposed cord, consider a drain. The scenarios do not say how long to wait before declaring a change persistent, and they do not rank the options. Read each list as a menu, in no fixed order. The intraoperative myelogram was voted out at 0%.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: A clear, usable checklist. It is expert opinion from 15 surgeons and has not been tested on patients.
points: Strengths: formal Delphi with preset thresholds; all 15 invited surgeons agreed to take part (with partial survey completions and 14 of 15 at the meeting); agreement reported for every final item and the 2 excluded items; organized by the stage of surgery; printable OR aids.
Panel: surgeons only, no neurophysiologists or anesthesiologists, yet much of the response is anesthetic or neurophysiological. 5 of 15 work mainly or only in pediatrics.
Nearly everything passed: every included item is at least 84.6%, most at 100%. Consensus does not mean the action works.

No numbers where you most want them: alert criteria are left to each institution; no numeric MAP, hematocrit or steroid targets. The only time target is an elevated MAP goal for 48 to 72 h in the ICU (92.9%).
No validation: no test of whether teams using these aids have fewer or milder deficits.
Reporting gaps: no item-level flow across rounds; per-round counts do not add to the final 105.
Source errors: Table 4 says Type 2 cord shape, Figure 2 says Type 3; the companion paper is cited as reference 8, which is Vitale 2014 (it is reference 6), and references 7 and 8 duplicate.
slides.notes: Put it in its place. This is the best structured statement of expert practice for unstable-spine alerts, from people who do this often. It is not evidence that any one action changes neurological outcome, since no outcomes were measured; that reading is ours. The authors make a narrower point: they note a lack of evidence guiding specific blood pressure goals, hematocrit levels and steroid type and dosing, and call these high-interest areas for study. They also say prior evidence suggests blood pressure escalation alone can reverse IONM decrements (reference 9). Steroids are a good teaching case. The draft items carried specific dexamethasone and methylprednisolone regimens. The panel reworded them to just IV steroids, and the final guideline gives no dose. Do not quote doses from this paper. On MAP, the authors cite a study (reference 9) whose title states that raising MAP alone restores 20% of IONM losses. We did not read it. The panel and its makeup. All voters were surgeons, by the paper's own list. Several authors share institutions, notably Columbia, where the senior author and the IRB sit. 5 of 15 do mainly or only pediatric deformity, so adult issues such as vascular disease, osteoporosis and revision anatomy may be underweighted; that is our inference. Most items passed at 100%, which tells you the items were reasonable, not that they were tested against alternatives. Selection of the 49 starting items came from a literature review whose dates are not given. The round counts are internally consistent within each round, but they do not trace to the final 105 (see slide 2). This is a gap in reporting, not proof of an error. Wording drift: Figure 1 sometimes drops consider from items, for example proceed with advanced imaging in Stage 4b, where the voted Table 3 item says consider proceeding. The column header in Figure 1 says consider each of the following, so the meaning holds.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "Lenke 2022 is a 15-surgeon Delphi consensus that gives 105 agreed items in four OR aids for IONM alerts in high-risk deformity surgery. Raise MAP first. If signals do not return, get the room's attention, optimize, define pattern and timing, and act by stage: release traction, stabilize, decompress, reverse correction, wake-up test, abort if needed, and call a colleague. It is Level V and untested on outcomes, with no numeric MAP or steroid targets."
points: What is the first step? Elevate MAP. If signals return, use the stable-spine checklist.
Why does stage matter? The likely cause changes: positioning before incision, implants after incision, instability and subluxation after osteotomy, the maneuver during correction.
Bilateral MEP loss with SSEPs spared? Strongly consider ischemia or compression.
Signals back to baseline: must you stop? No. Proceed, proceed with modifications, or abort were all agreed options.
Postoperative deficit in the ICU? Progressive, ascending or complete: back to the OR emergently. Incomplete, stable or resolving: consider imaging first.
What steroid dose? The paper gives none; the draft doses were removed.
How strong is this? Expert opinion, surgeons only, no outcome data.
slides.notes: Say the summary in under a minute. Then expect these follow-ups. Is this a guideline? It is consensus-based best practice guidance. The authors call it a set of aids to use at the surgeon's discretion, case by case. What defines an alert? Each institution's own warning criteria; the paper sets no threshold. Which patients count as high risk? That is in the companion Iyer paper, not this one, and we did not read it. What is DSCM? Dynamic spinal cord mapping: stimulating the cord at various levels and recording DNEPs from a peripheral sensory nerve to localize the problem to one or two levels. It needs an experienced team and largely depends on TIVA. When do delayed deficits show? Typically 8 to 48 hours after surgery, by the authors' account, so repeat neurological exams. What should you not claim from it? Do not say it lowers paralysis rates; that was never tested. Do not quote a MAP number or a steroid dose from it. Do not cite Table 4's Type 2 cord shape; the chart in Figure 2 says Type 3 and matches the Discussion. If asked how it differs from the 2014 checklist: the authors say the earlier checklist addressed the stable spine, and this one targets the unstable spine, organized by stage of surgery. We did not read the 2014 checklist, so we cannot say which specific steps are new.

decks.not_reviewed: Supplemental Digital Content 1 (Supplemental Figure 1, the age analysis) was not available and was not read. The full main paper was read, including figure images. No later or companion papers were read except library records D14 and PM40980941, used only for comparison.

slides.title: Hills 2022: the T4-L1-hip axis in normal spines
slides.lead: Normal values from 320 healthy volunteers: lumbar lordosis follows PI plus the L1 pelvic angle, and the T4 pelvic angle tracks the L1 pelvic angle.
points: Hills J, Lenke LG, ... Kelly MP. Spine 2022;47:1399-1406
Cross-sectional radiographic study, 5 countries on 4 continents, EOS standing films
No surgery, no outcomes, no follow-up: this is a normative anatomy paper
Bottom line: PI alone explained 30% of the variance in L1-S1 lordosis; PI plus L1PA explained 74%. T4PA correlated with L1PA at r = 0.9
slides.notes: Frame this correctly before anything else. It is not a surgical study. The authors measured standing EOS films in healthy adult volunteers and fitted regressions to describe what a normal sagittal profile looks like. The surgical claim, that these are good targets, is a hypothesis this paper sets up but does not test. The authors say so in their limitations: the data do not show these targets to be superior to any other scheme. The library pairs this with D14 (Hills 2024), which derived and tested its own L1PA and T4-L1PA targets in 247 ASD fusions, and PM40980941 (2026), which used L1PA within 5 degrees of 0.5 x PI - 21 as its ideal. Read this paper as the source of the formulas. The deck was built from the full main text and figures. The supplement, which holds the age analysis, was not read. EOS Imaging provided direct research support, and the authors report no conflicts of interest.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: Can normal spines give alignment targets that surgeons can actually set at surgery?
points: Authors' critique: SRS-Schwab and age-adjusted targets came from correlating films with HRQOL in deformity patients, not from normal spines
Pelvic tilt, sacral slope and SVA are postural and cannot be set directly in surgery
No existing scheme defines thoracic alignment relative to the lumbar spine
Aims: define normal balance by vertebral tilt; normal lordosis and pelvic angles relative to PI; lumbar and thoracic targets from fixed or modifiable measures

rows: Femoral head axis to vertebral centroid, against vertical; positive when anterior
Pelvic tilt + vertebral tilt (e.g. L1PA, T4PA, C2PA)
Cobb from each vertebra's upper endplate to S1

slides.see: Figure 1A shows how the tilt and pelvic-angle lines meet at the femoral heads.
slides.notes: The argument rests on geometry. Any vertebral pelvic angle equals pelvic tilt plus that vertebra's tilt. Tilt is the posture part, and the pelvic angle is the shape part, which a fusion fixes. So if normal people keep C2 tilt within a narrow band, the pelvic angles set how much pelvic tilt they need to stay balanced. Watch the sign conventions, because they trip people up: in the paper's Figure 1 caption, pelvic tilt is positive when posterior to the femoral heads, while vertebral tilt is positive when anterior to them. Normal C2, T4 and L1 tilts are all negative, so the vertebrae sit slightly behind the hips. The authors' criticism of earlier targets is that they came from deformity patients or from asymptomatic but degenerated volunteers. This study deliberately excludes degeneration. That makes the reference cleaner, but also younger and less like a typical ASD patient. Keep that tradeoff in mind for the appraisal.

slides.title: Selection and measurement
slides.lead: 485 community volunteers enrolled; 320 kept after strict radiographic exclusions.
points: Included: over 18, no spine disease or surgery, recruited from the community, not from spine clinics
Excluded: disc degeneration (osteophytes, endplate sclerosis, disc narrowing), spondylolisthesis, coronal Cobb over 10 degrees, ODI over 20%
Imaging: standing full-body or full-spine EOS, measured in sterEOS 2D/3D software
Analysis: median and IQR; Spearman for tilt vs PI; linear regression on PI; multivariable LL model; Pearson for T4PA vs L1PA; 80% prediction intervals
slides.notes: Check the flow: 129 + 35 + 1 = 165, and 485 - 165 = 320, so it adds up. The exclusions sum exactly, which suggests each person was counted under one reason, but the order of exclusion is not stated. Country counts also check: 77 France, 78 Japan, 59 Singapore, 52 Tunisia and 54 USA make 320, and the printed percentages are correct. Female 194 of 320 is 60.6%. Notice that 129 of 485, about 27%, were excluded for a coronal curve over 10 degrees (our arithmetic). The paper gives only the Cobb threshold as the reason and does not interpret it. In our reading, that is a high share for self-described healthy volunteers, and it shows how filtered the final sample is. Things the paper does not report: who did the measurements, whether they were blinded to anything, and any intra- or inter-observer reliability. It also gives no upper age limit or age range, and no sex-specific analysis. Statistics were run in R 3.5.3 with the rms package. The prediction intervals are 80%, not 95%. That matters when the paper calls something a normal range, because 1 in 5 normal people fall outside an 80% band by construction.

slides.title: Normal values
slides.lead: A young, low-disability sample with a balanced, slightly posterior C2.
points: Median age 37 (IQR 27-46); 61% female; BMI 23.2; ODI 0 (IQR 0-2.2)
C2 tilt was narrow and did not correlate with PI (P 0.44)
PT correlated moderately with PI (adjusted rho squared 0.38)
By the geometry, PT explained most of the variance in C2PA (r2 0.86), T4PA (0.82) and L1PA (0.64)
slides.see: Figure 2A shows vertebral tilt narrowing toward C2; Figure 2B gives the P value at each level.
slides.notes: Recompute the geometry from the medians: PT 11.5 plus T4 tilt -8.2 is 3.3, matching the T4PA median. PT 11.5 plus L1 tilt -7.5 is 4.0, against a printed L1PA of 3.9. Medians need not add exactly, so this is consistent. The strong PT to pelvic-angle r2 values come mainly from that identity, as the Figure 1 caption admits, so they are not an independent finding. One error needs flagging. The text says vertebral tilt from C2 to L4 was independent of PI, and the Figure 2 caption says only L5 correlated. But Figure 2B prints P = 0.02 at L1 and P = 0.04 at L2. The plotted correlations are close to zero, so the practical point probably stands. Still, it is not what the text says. C2 tilt itself had P = 0.44. The abstract prints median age as 37%; it means 37 years. The abstract also says 60% were female, while Table 1 gives 194 (60.6%) and Results give 61%; 194 of 320 is 60.6%, so 61% is the correct rounding. The authors say there was no meaningful association between age and any sagittal measure. That analysis is in the supplement, which we did not read. With a median age of 37 and an upper quartile of 46, the sample may simply not have had enough older people to show an age effect. That is our inference.

slides.title: The formulas
slides.lead: PI alone predicts lordosis poorly; PI plus L1PA predicts it well, and T4PA should match L1PA.
points: L1-S1 lordosis on PI alone: r2 0.30, wide prediction intervals
L4-S1 lordosis on PI: r2 0.02 (independent)
PI predicted the pelvic angles best caudally (L1PA r2 0.58)
T4PA vs L1PA: r = 0.9; 80% prediction interval about plus or minus 4 degrees
slides.see: Figure 5 prints the lordosis equation and shows, for each PI, the normal L1PA range and the lordosis it implies. Figure 6 shows the T4PA on L1PA scatter.
slides.notes: Only the L1PA formula appears in the text (Results and the Figure 4 caption).
