The T4PA and C2PA formulas (Figure 4B) and the lordosis equation (Figure 5) are printed only in figure panels, with no confidence intervals. Check the lordosis model at the medians: 1.4 x 51.8 - 1.7 x 3.9 - 2 is about 64, against a median of 61.5. Part of that gap is rounding. The regression lines plotted in Figure 5 sit about 1.5 to 3 degrees below the printed equation, and the gap grows with PI: at PI 70 and L1PA 7 the equation gives 84 against about 81 plotted. A PI coefficient of about 1.36 reproduces the plot and gives about 62 at the medians (our arithmetic). So the printed 1.4 is rounded, and plugging it in at high PI overestimates lordosis by about 3 degrees. Read the sign this way: for a fixed PI, each degree of extra L1PA predicts 1.7 degrees less lordosis. If you substitute the normal L1PA, our algebra gives lordosis of about 0.55 x PI + 34 with the printed coefficient, or about 0.51 x PI + 34 with 1.36, so about 60 to 62 degrees at a PI of 50. Treat that as our derivation, not the paper's. What is fragile here is that the fit is partly built in. L1PA contains pelvic tilt, and lordosis relates to sacral slope, which is PI minus PT. So a high R2 is expected from geometry alone (our inference). In our reading, shared pelvic tilt likely also inflates the T4PA to L1PA correlation; the paper does not discuss this. An r of 0.9 means r2 of about 0.81. The authors call this nearly perfect. With 80% bands of about plus or minus 4 degrees, about 1 in 5 normal people differ by more than 4 degrees. The Key Points say often within 4 degrees, which is the honest wording. The text says T4PA and L1PA differ by less than 1 degree for each Figure 8 volunteer; the figure prints whole degrees (-6 and -6, then 9 and 10), so this cannot be checked, but it is not contradicted.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: Clear purpose and explicit geometry; weak on measurement reporting, generalizability and validation.
points: Strengths: multinational community sample, low-dose standing full-body or full-spine EOS, no missing data, explicit geometry
Selection: strict exclusions make a young, non-degenerated reference that differs from ASD patients
Measurement: no reliability data and no measurer details
Validity: one sample, 80% intervals, no validation set, no clinical outcomes
Funding: EOS Imaging provided direct research support

rows: Strong; shared PT may inflate it (ours)

slides.see: Figure 7 is a simulation, not patient data: it plots model spines at PI 50 to show the compensation needed when L1PA and lordosis are mismatched.
slides.notes: The authors list their own limitations: a relatively small sample; young, non-degenerated spines that may differ from elderly patients; an L1 choice for the upper end of the arc that is somewhat arbitrary because the inflection moves with PI; unknown effects of lost cervical lordosis; and no evidence that these targets beat others. Two claims in the Discussion are not backed by data in the paper. First, it gives a normal L4-S1 range of 25 to 55 degrees and says the mean L4-S1 lordosis was nearly identical to earlier work, but no L4-S1 mean or range appears in the table or text. Second, the limitations say the sample included ample elderly people, but no age range or count of older volunteers is reported. With a median age of 37 and IQR 27 to 46, we cannot check that. The illustrative high-PI volunteer in Figure 8 (PI 80) has an L1PA of 10, while the formula predicts 19 (our arithmetic). The paper's 80% normal L1PA band is about plus or minus 5 to 5.5 degrees (the Figure 5 x-axes run -2 to 9 at PI 50 and 7 to 18 at PI 70). Extrapolated to PI 80, that is roughly 13.5 to 24.5 (ours). So by the paper's own definition, its exemplar normal volunteer has an abnormal L1PA, about 9 degrees off, and the paper does not comment on it. For the surgical question, go to D14. In that library record, failure risk was lowest at L1PA 0.5 x PI - 19, plus or minus 2, with a T4-L1PA mismatch of -3 to +1. The targets there were derived and tested in the same 247 patients.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: Spoken summary and the questions to expect.
points: Say: In 320 healthy, non-degenerated volunteers, C2 tilt sat near -3 degrees whatever the PI. PI alone explained only 30% of the variance in lordosis. Adding the L1 pelvic angle raised that to 74%, and normal L1PA was about half the PI minus 21. The T4 pelvic angle tracked L1PA, usually within 4 degrees. These are normal values, not proven surgical targets.

Expect: Why L1PA and not PI-LL? The authors say PI explains only a fraction of lordosis, and L1PA captures both lordosis magnitude and shape as a continuous measure that can be set directly in surgery.
Expect: Is r 0.9 real? In our reading it is likely inflated, because both angles contain pelvic tilt; the paper does not address this.
Expect: Does this apply to a 70-year-old? It is not clear: the median age was 37 and degenerated spines were excluded.
Expect: Did hitting the targets reduce failures? Not tested here; see D14 and PM40980941
slides.notes: Keep the summary to the numbers you can defend: C2 tilt median -2.7, L1-S1 lordosis on PI r2 0.30, PI plus L1PA R2 0.74, L1PA = 0.5 x PI - 21, and T4PA against L1PA r = 0.9 with 80% bands of about 4 degrees. If asked how to use it in the OR, the paper's own conclusion gives four measures. PI is fixed. Lordosis comes from PI and L1PA. T4PA should roughly equal L1PA. Say plainly that these come from normal people, and that the authors concede years of follow-up are needed. If someone quotes 0.5 x PI - 19, that is the D14 surgical cohort, where the lowest-risk point sat slightly above this paper's normal. Do not mix the two. PM40980941 used 0.5 x PI - 21 plus or minus 5 as its ideal in an MIS and open ISSG cohort. Points to watch in discussion: the sign conventions, the 80% (not 95%) intervals, the geometric coupling, and the age skew. If pressed on error checking, mention these inconsistencies in the paper: Figure 2B shows significant P values at L1 and L2 despite the text, the abstract prints the age as a percentage, and the abstract says 60% female where Table 1 gives 60.6% and Results 61%. Also, the Figure 8 high-PI volunteer has an L1PA of 10, outside the paper's own normal band at PI 80.

decks.not_reviewed: All eight figures, including the PRISMA flow diagram (Fig. 1) and every forest plot (Figs. 2-8), because the reformatted PMC copy omits images. The right-hand columns of Table 1 (follow-up and beyond) are cut off in the copy. The PROSPERO protocol, the 50 included studies themselves, and any supplementary material were not reviewed.

slides.title: Rod material and size in ASD
slides.lead: A systematic review and meta-analysis asking whether rod material or diameter changes alignment or complications after adult deformity surgery.
points: Journal club: adult deformity instrumentation
Bowden D, Michielli A, Merrill M, Will S. Spine Deform 2022;10(6):1265-1278
Funded by Johnson & Johnson; all four authors are Johnson & Johnson employees
Copy reviewed is incomplete: figures are omitted and Table 1 is cut off on the right

Bottom line: almost no head-to-head data exist. The alignment comparisons by material rest on one study per arm, and the paper's own numbers do not support its no-difference conclusion for pelvic tilt.
slides.notes: Frame this as an evidence map, not an answer. The authors set out to compare rod materials (titanium, cobalt-chromium, stainless steel) and diameters across adult spinal deformity surgery. They found 50 eligible studies, and only 17 said anything about rod material or size. The meta-analyses that follow pool one to four studies at a time. What was reviewed: the full article text, in a reformatted PMC copy whose header says images are omitted. So the PRISMA flow diagram and all forest plots (Figures 1-8) were not seen, and every number in this deck comes from the text. The copy also cuts off the right side of Table 1, so per-study follow-up was not readable. Disclose the conflict at the start: the study was funded by Johnson & Johnson and all four authors are its employees. That does not make the numbers wrong, but the closing message, that rods with improved fatigue performance are needed, is a product-shaped conclusion, and the data in the paper do not test any rod technology. Level of evidence as stated by the authors: III.

slides.title: Question and methods
slides.lead: Does rod material or diameter change postoperative alignment, pseudarthrosis or rod breakage?
points: Search 20 Nov 2020: MEDLINE, Embase, KOSMET, APA PsycInfo, BIOSIS; English, 2010 onward
Terms: (spine* OR vertebra*) AND (fusion AND stabilization) AND (rods) AND (adults)
Included adults over 18 with any spinal deformity treated with rods or pedicle screws
Outcomes: Cobb angle, SVA, pelvic tilt, pseudarthrosis, rod breakage. PJK not analyzed: no eligible study reported it by rod type
Random-effects pooling in RevMan 5.4 when at least 2 studies reported an outcome
Quality graded with the Johns Hopkins Nursing evidence guide; no ratings reported
slides.notes: Read the methods with three questions in mind. First, the search. The databases are unusual for a surgical question: KOSMET is a cosmetic-science index and PsycInfo is psychology, while Cochrane and Web of Science are not listed. The string requires both fusion AND stabilization AND rods, which is narrow. Second, the flow. Our arithmetic: 537 full texts minus the six listed exclusion reasons (336 in total) leaves 201, but 50 studies were included. 151 studies are unaccounted for in the text. Figure 1 may explain it, but it was not available in this copy. Third, the analysis plan. The statistics paragraph describes mean differences for length of stay and operating time, standardized mean differences for pain, risk ratios, and surgical versus non-surgical groups. None of those outcomes appear anywhere in the results. Our reading: this paragraph appears to be carried over from a different analysis, and the paper does not say which methods were actually applied to the single-arm pooled means and proportions. A planned subgroup by follow-up duration is also never reported. PROSPERO registration is stated but no registration number is given. The authors graded quality with a nursing evidence tool, yet no study-level quality or risk-of-bias ratings appear in the paper.

slides.title: What got into the 50
slides.lead: Inclusion was broad, and several included studies are not adult deformity studies of rods.
points: Table 1 includes a meta-analysis (Kim 2018, 973 patients) and a systematic review (Echt 2020, listed as a cohort)
Also included: an RCT of laminectomy with or without fusion for spondylolisthesis (Ghogawala 2016) and a bone-graft granule study (Hao 2018)
Akazawa 2013, one of three titanium rod-breakage studies, lists mean age at surgery 19.0 ± 12.8 years
Descriptive counts of which studies used which material do not match their citations
slides.notes: This slide is about selection and measurement, the core of any review. The eligibility rule was adults over 18 with any deformity and any rod. Table 1 shows how wide that net was. It includes another meta-analysis and a systematic review as if they were primary studies, which risks counting patients twice. It includes Ghogawala 2016, a degenerative spondylolisthesis trial of laminectomy with or without fusion, which is not adult spinal deformity or a rod study, and studies on bone graft volume and facet violation. Akazawa 2013 lists a mean age at surgery of 19.0 with SD 12.8. If that is accurate, many of its patients were younger than 18. Akazawa feeds the titanium rod-breakage pool. Iida 2015 is a 20-year follow-up of scoliosis fusion, which suggests adolescent surgery, though the table gives no age. Now the internal counts, all our arithmetic. The text says 17 studies described rod material but cites references 23-35, which is 13 papers. It says 14 used titanium, but lists 12 references. References 26, 28 and 36 appear both as titanium-with-other-materials or titanium-alone and as cobalt-chromium-alone. The cobalt-chromium pseudarthrosis pool cites reference 46 (Lewis 2018), which is not among the studies said to describe rod material. Stainless steel is never mentioned in the descriptive section, yet it gets its own pooled estimate. The table on this slide shows sex counts that do not add to the stated sample size; for Smith 2017 the reference title says 82 patients, matching 20 + 62, so the 106 looks wrong. Prost 2020 is listed with 43 patients but its title says 77 cases, Uddin 2015 prints identical ages for its two groups, and Wang 2017 lists a mean age of 37.8 with SD 12.8. None of these alone overturns a result, but together they say the data extraction was not tightly checked.

slides.title: Rod material: alignment
slides.lead: Each material is one study. This is a comparison between two different cohorts, not a pooled head-to-head.
points: CoCr: Buell 2020, 19 patients, kickstand rods for coronal correction
Ti: Banno 2019, 106 patients, one study with two subgroups (the paper does not name them; from the reference title, probably multi-rod vs 2-rod, our inference)
SVA is printed in degrees; SVA is a distance, so the unit is wrong
Authors: no statistically significant differences between CoCr and Ti. No test for these comparisons is reported
slides.see: Figures 2 and 3 show these two estimates; they were not available in this copy.
slides.notes: This is the slide where the paper's headline fails. The abstract says postoperative outcomes did not statistically differ between cobalt-chromium and titanium, with n = 2 studies. But it is one study per material. The CoCr number is Buell 2020, 19 patients treated with kickstand rods. The Ti number is Banno 2019, one study with two unnamed subgroups; its title is about multi-rod constructs and iliac screw loosening. Any difference between them reflects two different patient groups, surgeons, constructs and deformities, not the rod material. Now recompute. All CIs are symmetric around their means, so the standard errors can be backed out as width divided by 3.92. For pelvic tilt, CoCr 26.20 and Ti 20.15 have non-overlapping 95% intervals. Our z test on the difference gives z about 3.0 and P about 0.003. So by the paper's own numbers pelvic tilt did differ, by about 6 degrees, worse with CoCr. For SVA our test gives P about 0.67, so no difference there. We checked the method against the paper's one reported subgroup test (pseudarthrosis): our arithmetic gives chi-square 0.08 and P 0.78, matching the printed 0.07 and 0.79. Two cautions about our own result. It is a between-study contrast and is confounded, so it does not show that CoCr worsens pelvic tilt. And preoperative values are not reported, so a postoperative pelvic tilt alone cannot separate correction from baseline severity. The correct reading is that these data cannot answer the material question either way. Also note the unit error: the paper calls SVA an angle and prints it in degrees throughout.

slides.title: Complications and diameter
slides.lead: Pooled proportions from one to three studies each, and pooled alignment for 6.0-6.35 mm rods only.
points: Pseudarthrosis CoCr vs SS: Chi2 0.07, P = 0.79 (our recomputation agrees)
Rod breakage: no subgroup test, too few studies
No study reported complications by rod diameter, and no other diameter was pooled
slides.notes: Start with how studies entered these pools. The text says the pseudarthrosis studies 'reported at least one case' and the rod-breakage studies 'reported the presence of broken rods'. Our inference: if studies with zero events were left out, the pooled rates are biased upward. The paper does not say whether zero-event studies existed. Definitions of pseudarthrosis and rod breakage, and follow-up length, are not given for any pool. The stainless-steel interval runs from minus 8 percent, which is impossible for a proportion. The paper never says how proportions were pooled; our inference is that they were pooled on the raw scale with a normal approximation and no transformation. Either way, with two studies the interval is nearly meaningless. Multi-rod construct papers sit inside these pools, for example Gupta 2018, a 4-rod technique paper and the only CoCr rod-breakage study. Construct type is mixed up with material. The authors compare their 12 percent titanium rod-breakage rate with another meta-analysis (Noh 2021) that found 12 percent overall. That paper is not in the library, so we quote the authors' citation only. Diameter: the only analyses pool 6.0-6.35 mm rods. Rods of 5.0 and 5.5 mm are mentioned but never pooled, so nothing compares diameters. These are single-arm benchmarks, not comparisons. The pelvic tilt pool has I2 80% (P = 0.002), so the single pooled number hides wide spread between studies. Our recomputation: all pooled intervals here are close to symmetric around their point estimates, so no printing errors were found in these numbers.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: Holds up: two independent screeners, PRISMA reporting, prespecified extraction fields
Holds up: the authors clearly state how few studies compare rods directly
Weak: one study per arm for material alignment, so between-cohort confounding
Weak: conclusion of no difference by diameter, but no diameter comparison was done
Weak: pelvic tilt CIs do not overlap, yet called not different
Weak: methods paragraph describes outcomes never reported (LOS, OR time, pain)
Weak: 151 full texts unaccounted for in the selection text
Weak: non-ASD studies and a likely adolescent cohort included
Weak: no study-level quality or risk-of-bias results reported
Weak: industry funding and employee authors
slides.notes: Be fair first. The authors are candid in their Discussion: they call the data sparse, say it is unfortunate how few studies directly compared rod materials or diameters, and say the absence of evidence on rod diameter is a finding. Their stated limitation is heterogeneity of patients, techniques and outcome definitions, and they call for high-volume multicenter studies with shared definitions. That is the honest core of the paper. The problems are in how the abstract and conclusion turn sparse data into a no-difference claim. Absence of a significant difference with one study per arm is not evidence of equivalence. For diameter, the abstract conclusion says no significant differences in outcomes or complications among rods of varying diameter, while the results contain no diameter comparison and no complication data by diameter. For pelvic tilt, our recomputation finds P about 0.003. The heterogeneity paragraph is also odd: it says the random-effects model was chosen because Q was significant and I2 exceeded 50%, and that I2 ranged from 0% to 98%. Only one I2 (80%) is reported, and the material comparisons with one study per arm cannot have an I2 at all. Choosing a model after seeing heterogeneity is a weak practice, in our view. The search used unusual databases and a narrow string. Data extraction shows several mismatches (slide 3). On the conflict: Johnson & Johnson funded the work and employed all authors. The final sentence promotes rods with improved fatigue performance, which nothing in the data tests.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "This review found 50 deformity studies but only 17 that described the rods, and almost none that compared them. The material comparisons are one study per arm, so they cannot show equivalence, and the paper's own pelvic tilt numbers actually differ. Use the pooled rates only as rough benchmarks: about 12-15% pseudarthrosis and 10-12% rod breakage in small, selected pools."
points: Do not quote it as showing CoCr and Ti perform the same
Do not quote it as showing rod diameter does not matter; diameter was never compared
Industry-funded, employee-authored; conclusion goes beyond the data
slides.notes: Expect these follow-up questions. Does this tell me to use cobalt-chromium or titanium? No. Each material's alignment number comes from a single different study, and the complication pools are one to three studies, and the pseudarthrosis studies are described as reporting at least one case; whether zero-event studies were left out is not stated. The paper gives no basis for choosing a material. Does it show that 6.0-6.35 mm rods are as good as 5.5 mm? No. Only the 6.0-6.35 mm group was pooled. Smaller rods are mentioned and never analyzed. What is the rod breakage rate? The authors pool 12% with titanium (three studies, CI 1-22%) and 10% with CoCr (one study). They say this matches another meta-analysis's 12% overall, but that paper is not in our library. Does it address multi-rod constructs? Not directly. Multi-rod studies are mixed into the material pools, which confounds material with construct. What about PJK? Not analyzed: the authors found no eligible study that reported PJK by rod type. Why is this paper in the curriculum? It is a listed SRS Quality and Safety resource, and it is a good teaching example of how a small, heterogeneous evidence base can be turned into a no-difference headline. The skill is reading the n per arm before reading the P value.

decks.not_reviewed: Supplemental Digital Content 1 (Supplementary Table 1, round-by-round Delphi results with per-item agreement) and Appendix 1 (panelists' qualitative comments on specific AC/AP drugs) were not available and were not read, so no per-item agreement percentage could be checked. The literature review and best-practices update given to panelists was not published in the paper. Cited studies were not reviewed. The PDF is the complete 9-page article (pages 301 to 309), not a critique.

slides.title: Zuckerman 2023: AC/AP and VTE prophylaxis consensus
slides.lead: Bottom line: 20 spine surgeons agreed on stop times (DOAC 2 days, warfarin 5 days, aspirin and all other AC/AP 7 days), point scores for when to restart (POD7/5/2) and when to start enoxaparin (POD5 or none / POD3-4 / POD1-2). This is expert opinion with no patient data.
points: Zuckerman SL, Berven S, Streiff MB, et al. Spine 2023;48(5):301-9.
Modified Delphi, three online rounds, January 26 to June 21, 2021. Consensus defined as at least 70% agreement.
Elective adult spine surgery only. Supported by OMeGA and AO Spine North America.
Prepared from the full article. The supplement with per-item agreement was not read.
slides.notes: Frame this as what it is: a structured agreement among surgeons, not a guideline built from a systematic review and not a study of patients. The authors say this twice. In the Results they write that the recommendations are not supported by evidence and simply represent the group's consensus, and in the limitations that no actual patient data were used. So the right question for the room is not whether the numbers are proven, but whether they are a sensible, safe default when you have no medical consultant's instructions. The paper also makes that hierarchy explicit: when an internist, hematologist or cardiologist gives patient-specific instructions, those supersede the consensus. The paper is filed under Diagnostics in the journal, which fits poorly; treat it as a consensus statement. The master record listed it as a bibliography entry only; this deck was prepared from the full text, but the supplement holding the round-by-round results and agreement percentages was not available, so we could not see how close any item came to the 70% line. Our checks found several internal inconsistencies, mostly in the scoring tables and the reference numbering; they are on the appraisal slide.

slides.title: The question and the panel
slides.lead: Three questions: when to stop AC/AP before surgery, when to restart it, and when, how and in whom to start VTE chemoprophylaxis in patients not on long-term AC/AP.
points: Background cited by the authors: VTE after spine surgery 0.2% to 13.6%, PE 0.03% to 2.4%.
Panel: 20 board-certified or eligible spine surgeons (14 orthopedic, 6 neurosurgery) from 18 institutions; 65% academic.
21 invited. One completed all meetings and surveys, then asked to be removed after disagreeing with grouping drugs into 2/5/7-day stop times.
Internal medicine and hematology experts helped plan and review, but did not vote.
A priori assumptions: adults over 18, elective surgery, routine mechanical prophylaxis, ambulation from POD1. Arterial and venous thrombosis treated as one risk.
slides.notes: Panel arithmetic checks: Table 1 sums to 20 for age, years in practice, specialty, region (7/7/4/2, matching the 35/35/20/10% in the text) and practice type (13 academic, 7 private). Question counts in each round sum correctly. Two design choices matter more than the numbers. First, the dissenter. The abstract says 21 were invited and 20 completed all rounds, which reads like one dropout. The Methods say otherwise: the 21st surgeon completed everything and then withdrew because they thought each drug should have its own stop time based on its half-life. The paper does not say whether that surgeon's votes were kept in the reported percentages. If they were dropped, agreement could shift either way: up on items where he dissented, down on items where he sided with the majority. The paper does not say he was the only dissenter; the authors call the grouping 'a point of controversy among the group'. Second, the grouping. The panel first proposed lumping all AC/AP drugs together; the authors report that many surgeons called that inaccurate, unsafe and dangerous, so DOACs and warfarin were split out, leaving four groups: DOACs, warfarin, all other non-DOAC AC/AP drugs, and aspirin. Arterial and venous thrombosis were merged by a priori agreement so the result would be simpler to adopt. That means a recent coronary stent and a recent DVT feed the same score, even though they call for different drugs. Tranexamic acid was set aside by citing a meta-analysis that found no association with thromboembolic events. Expert selection was not systematic; the authors say they used a network of surgeons from earlier studies and guideline work.

slides.title: Stopping before surgery, and how to give enoxaparin
slides.lead: Consensus was reached on every stop-time item. Patient-specific instructions from the internist or specialist override these.
points: Aspirin: 81 mg and 325 mg both stopped 7 days before surgery.
Warfarin bridging with enoxaparin may be needed and should be discussed with a specialist (authors' Discussion).
Reversal agents for emergent settings are listed in the Discussion: vitamin K, FFP and 4-factor PCC for warfarin; protamine for heparin; idarucizumab and andexanet for certain DOACs.
Chemoprophylaxis delivery: POD1 is the morning after surgery whatever the finishing time; enoxaparin, standard dose (40 mg) once daily.
slides.notes: This is the most usable slide and also the bluntest. One number per drug class is easy to remember, which was the authors' goal: they write that knowing every half-life is not the reality of practice. The cost is that a single 2-day DOAC rule takes no account of renal function or of bleeding risk of the procedure, and the paper does not discuss either; that is our observation, not the authors'. The 7-day 'all other' bin covers the classes the paper lists (ADP receptor and reuptake inhibitors, GP IIb/IIIa, phosphodiesterase and thromboxane inhibitors); in our view these differ in how fast their effect wears off, which the paper does not address. The aspirin rule is where to slow down. The panel says stop aspirin 7 days before surgery, but the authors' own Discussion cites one narrative review finding increased risk with both continuing aspirin and stopping it 3 to 7 days before, while stopping 7 to 10 days before was not associated with more complications (this half supports the 7-day rule), and a 200-patient study of patients with cardiac stents having spine surgery that found no increase in complications when aspirin was continued. The paper also says the decision in practice depends heavily on stent history. So the honest reading is: 7 days is the default when no one has told you otherwise, and a patient with a coronary stent needs the cardiologist's instruction, which the paper says supersedes. Table 6 items: POD1 means the morning after surgery, enoxaparin is preferred, dosing is standard rather than weight based, and dosing is once daily; the text gives 40 mg as the example dose. The paper does not report what proportion agreed on each of these; that sits in the supplement we did not read. Note a slip in the Discussion: it says DOACs were decided to be stopped 'POD2', which would mean postoperative day 2; the Results and Table 3 say 2 days before surgery.

slides.title: Restarting AC/AP after surgery: the 5-factor score
slides.lead: Each factor scores 0, 1 or 2; the total (0 to 10) sets restart day: 0-2 POD7, 3-6 POD5, 7-10 POD2. Surgeons did not want to restart on POD1.
points: History of VTE: none 0; more than 2 years ago 1; within 2 years 2.
Prior cardiac intervention: more than 5 years 0; 2 to 5 years 1; under 1 year 2. One to 2 years is not assigned.
Ambulation: normal 0; cane, walker or assistance 1; wheelchair or bed 2.
Anterior abdominal approach: none 0; ALIF of 2 levels or fewer, or any prepsoas or antepsoas 1; ALIF of 3 or more levels 2.
Procedure: anterior cervical or fusion of 2 levels or fewer with no decompression 0; 3-4 fusion levels or 1-3 decompression levels 1; 5 or more fusion or 4 or more decompression levels 2.
slides.notes: Read Table 4 carefully, because its layout misleads. The Timing row sits under each column, so it looks as if any single high-risk factor means restart on POD2. The footnote and the scoring paragraph say points are summed across all five factors and the total sets the group. But the Discussion says recent VTE within 2 years, cardiac intervention within 1 year and being nonambulatory 'placed patients in the high-risk category', which reads as if one such factor is enough. The paper contradicts itself here and does not resolve it. 'Risk' here means risk of thrombosis, so higher risk means earlier restart. The cut points were not voted from data. The authors describe assigning 0, 1 and 2 points, putting mostly-low patients with one or two medium or high factors in the low group, and splitting the rest evenly into medium and high (3-6 and 7-10 are four values each). The stated rule does not fit Table 4: two high-risk factors score 4, which is medium, not low. It does fit Table 5, where low is 0-4. Every factor has the same 0/1/2 scale, so a stent placed under 1 year ago scores 2, the same as being in a wheelchair or bedbound, and a recent VTE within 2 years also scores 2. Our worked example, not the authors': a patient with a drug-eluting stent placed 6 months ago, normal walking, no anterior approach and a 1-level fusion without decompression scores 2, which is low risk, so the summed score says restart on POD7. Read by the Discussion's sentence, the same patient would be high risk and restart on POD2. The summed score lets the absence of other factors outvote the one factor driving the question. This is why the authors' caveat about cardiologist instructions matters more than the table. Gaps in the table: prior cardiac intervention 1 to 2 years ago has no category (low is over 5, medium 2 to 5, high under 1), while the matching row in Table 5 uses 1 to 5; and there is no cell for never having had a cardiac intervention (VTE history has 'No prior history'), so scoring that as 0 is only implied. The scores apply to restarting a patient's own long-term medication, not to starting prophylaxis.

slides.title: Starting VTE chemoprophylaxis: the 12-factor score
slides.lead: For patients not on long-term AC/AP. 12 factors gained consensus; staged same-day surgery did not. Total 0-4 POD5 or none, 5-13 POD3-4, 14-22 POD1-2.
points: Scored 0/1/2: age (65-80 is 1, over 80 is 2), BMI (30-40, over 40), VTE history, ambulation, prior cardiac intervention (1-5 years, under 1), cancer (remission, active), surgery, anterior approach, operative time (2-5 h, over 5 h), transfusion (1-2 units, 3 or more).
Scored 0/1 only: oral contraceptives or hormone therapy; staging on separate days.
Maximum is 22 (10 factors x 2 plus 2 factors x 1), which matches the table.
The low group includes 'none' because many panelists do not routinely give chemoprophylaxis.
slides.notes: The score arithmetic holds: 10 two-level factors and 2 one-level factors give a maximum of 22, and medium and high each span 9 values, the even split the authors describe. Ranges rather than single days were a compromise; the authors say ranges were needed to meet the needs of all panelists. The 'none' option exists because many panelists strongly preferred no routine chemoprophylaxis, even though the authors cite a meta-analysis of cranial and spine surgery finding chemoprophylaxis prevented VTE without a significant increase in bleeding. Our worked example, not the authors': a 70-year-old with BMI 32 having a 2-level posterior lumbar fusion with decompression in 3 hours, no transfusion, no other factors, scores 4 (age 1, BMI 1, decompression 1, time 1). That is low risk: POD5 or no chemoprophylaxis at all. Our inference, not the paper's: the paper has no patient data on how cases spread across the score, but from this example a fair number of elective degenerative cases may land in the low group. Table problems to point out: age low is printed as '<40-65', which as printed leaves ages under 40 undefined, and 65 sits in both low and 65-80; there is no cell for never having had a cardiac intervention; surgery medium says 3-5 fusion levels while high says 5 or more, so 5 levels scores twice, and decompression medium is 1-3 with high over 4, so 4 levels is unassigned; and the row labeled 'staged on separate days' gives its medium-risk option as combined anterior and posterior surgery on the same day, the scenario the next row says reached no consensus. The abstract's list of the 13 factors omits ambulation. Table 5's surgery row adds posterior cervical surgery to medium, which Table 4 does not.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: Useful as a uniform default; not evidence of benefit or safety, and the scoring tables need a careful read.
points: Strength: transparent process, timeline and round structure; hematology and medicine input; a clear deferral to patient-specific specialist advice.
No patient data. Point weights and cut-offs are unvalidated; the authors call for prospective testing.
Selection: non-systematic expert choice; one surgeon who disagreed with the grouped stop times completed all rounds, then asked to be removed.
Per-item agreement and the literature review given to panelists are not in the main paper.
Arterial and venous risk merged by design; simplified scenario that the authors say generalizes to only a small subset.

rows: Maxima consistent (10 and 22); Table 4 low cut-off conflicts with the stated rule
Abstract says over 70%, Methods at least 70%
Cannot be reconstructed from the tables
Citations from about ref 18 on are unreliable

slides.notes: Grade this as expert opinion. Delphi methods reduce the loudest-voice problem but cannot create evidence; agreement among 20 surgeons tells you what they would do, not what works. The authors say the 70% threshold follows prior Delphi recommendations; in our view it is a low bar. Its wording differs between abstract (over 70%) and Methods (at least 70%); without the supplement we cannot see which items passed narrowly. The 27 items do not map onto the tables: Table 3 has 8 questions, Table 4 has 5 factors, Table 5 has 13, Table 6 has 4, and no grouping we tried gives 27 with only one failure. The Methods say 'clinical equipoise was obtained in all areas except one', which misuses the term; they mean consensus. Reference problems we checked against the list: the tranexamic acid meta-analysis (216 trials, 125,550 patients) is cited as 38, a mental-health Delphi, while it is ref 37; the 200-patient stent and aspirin study is cited as 45, an anterior exposure review, while it is ref 44; the 200-patient ALIF study with 0% VTE is cited as 48, which is the 367-patient enoxaparin study; the cranial and spine meta-analysis is cited as 49, a thoracic fusion study, while it is ref 47; reversal agents are cited as 46, an ALIF VTE study. The 2009 guideline statement is cited as 18, a 2022 trauma protocol. More: 'in-depth reviews' and the half-lives remark are cited as 44 (the stent aspirin cohort), where 43 (Epstein, when to stop anticoagulation) fits; the aspirin narrative review is cited as 43, where 42 (Epstein, low-dose aspirin) fits better; 'hematology-specific studies 35-37' and 'consensus statements 35,37' include 37, the tranexamic acid meta-analysis, while the Douketis papers are 34-36; the 70% threshold citations 32,39-41 include 32 (skin-lesion imaging) and 41 (an OTA thromboprophylaxis update) and leave out 38, a Delphi; protocol refs 19-25 include 25, a Delphi methods textbook; and 'other specialties' Delphi refs 32-34 include 34, the NEJM bridging trial. Many look like an off-by-one shift. Treat the citations from about ref 18 onward as unreliable; a reader following them may land in the wrong paper. The 3.8% VTE and 0.0% hemorrhage figures belong to that 367-patient study (ref 48), which is correctly cited. Conflicts: one author reports royalties from Globus, Stryker and Wolters Kluwer. A prospective multicenter evaluation is planned by the authors; until then, the scores are a framework for discussion, not a validated tool.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: A 20-surgeon Delphi gives a simple default: stop DOACs 2 days, warfarin 5, aspirin and everything else 7; restart and start enoxaparin by point score; specialist instructions override it all.
points: Spoken summary: 'Zuckerman 2023 is a modified Delphi of 20 spine surgeons for elective adult surgery. Stop DOACs 2 days, warfarin 5 days, aspirin and other AC/AP 7 days before. Restart AC/AP POD7, 5 or 2 by a 5-factor score; start once-daily standard-dose enoxaparin POD5 or none, POD3-4 or POD1-2 by a 12-factor score. It is opinion, not data, and the patient's own cardiologist or hematologist overrides it.'
Expect: Is this evidence? No. The authors say it is consensus without patient data.
Expect: Would you stop aspirin in a patient with a recent coronary stent? The paper defers to the cardiologist.
Expect: Why 2 days for every DOAC? Simplicity; renal function is not addressed.
Expect: What about staged same-day anterior-posterior surgery? No consensus.
slides.notes: Lead with the three stop numbers, because that is what people will use. Then say the two scores exist and what they decide: the restart score applies to patients already on AC/AP, the chemoprophylaxis score to patients who are not. Keep the direction straight: higher thrombotic risk means earlier restart and earlier prophylaxis. Likely follow-ups and short answers. Was it validated? No; the authors propose prospective multicenter testing and plan to report it. Who voted? Surgeons only; hematologists and internists advised and reviewed. Was anyone excluded? One surgeon who disagreed with grouped stop times withdrew after completing all rounds. Does a single high-risk factor change timing? The paper is inconsistent: the summed score says no, and our worked examples (a recent stent alone, or a 2-level fusion in a 70-year-old) both score as low risk; but the Discussion says a recent stent, recent VTE or being nonambulatory places a patient in the high-risk category. Ask the cardiologist. Is the 'none' option safe? The authors cite a meta-analysis favoring chemoprophylaxis without significant extra bleeding, yet kept 'none' to satisfy panelists. What about trauma, tumor or children? Out of scope by design. Mechanical prophylaxis and POD1 ambulation were assumed for everyone, so the timings presume both. Anything to distrust in the tables? Yes: boundary overlaps (age 65, 5 fusion levels), unassigned bands (cardiac intervention 1-2 years and never in both scores, ages under 40 as printed, 4 decompression levels in the VTE score), a low cut-off in the restart score that conflicts with the stated rule, and a mislabeled staging row. Use the scores as a checklist of risk factors to discuss, not as a calculator.

decks.not_reviewed: The PDF is the complete 11-page article (pages 677-687), not a critique; read in full, including Table 1, Figure 1 and the Clinics Care Points. No supplement is cited. None of the 87 cited references were read, so every study result in this deck is as the review reports it, not checked against the original. The Handbook of Spine Surgery chapter that Table 1 was adapted from (reference 25) was not reviewed.

slides.title: Sorour 2023: ERAS protocols and spinal deformity, a narrative review
slides.lead: Bottom line: a readable checklist of perioperative steps, but it reports no ERAS outcome data in deformity patients, and most of its evidence comes from lumbar degenerative, adolescent or non-spine surgery.
points: Journal club · Adult deformity / perioperative care
Sorour O, Macki M, Tan L. Neurosurg Clin N Am 2023;34(4):677-87
Full text read. The PDF is the complete article, not a critique.
Design: narrative review, organized preop, intraop, postop; no search method or evidence grading stated
UCSF Department of Neurosurgery; authors report no relevant conflict of interest
slides.notes: Say first what kind of paper this is. It is a Clinics review, not a trial, a cohort or a systematic review. The paper gives no search strategy, no inclusion rules and no grading of evidence, so the recommendations are the authors' synthesis. Judge each claim by the study behind it, not by the confidence of the sentence. The authors trace ERAS to Kehlet in 1997 and give three pillars: optimize the patient before surgery, best practice and safety during surgery, and the highest standard of postoperative care and rehabilitation. The review then walks through 11 topics: imaging, HbA1c, osteoporosis, prehabilitation, antibiotics, liposomal bupivacaine, Foley catheters, analgesia, nausea and vomiting, thromboprophylaxis and early mobilization. Notice what the title promises and what the text delivers. Our reading: no study of an ERAS bundle in adult deformity is presented, with length of stay, complications or readmissions as the outcome. The one ERAS-in-complex-spine reference (Angus 2019) is cited only for the definition, and the ERAS Society lumbar fusion consensus (Debono 2021) is cited only for the harms of immobility. Many studies cited are single-level lumbar fusion, adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, awake minimally invasive TLIF, a distal radius fracture study and laparoscopic surgery. That does not make the advice wrong. It means the deformity-specific evidence base is thin, and the paper does not say so. Use it as a checklist and a reference map, not as proof that ERAS improves deformity outcomes.

slides.title: Preoperative optimization
slides.lead: The strongest part of the review, but the cutoffs come from lumbar and mixed spine cohorts, not deformity series.

rows: Designs not given: >7.5% (lumbar interbody, CNS guideline), >7% (thoracolumbar), >8% (MSSIC lumbar)
Teriparatide improves BMD, quality and fusion
Pedicle screw torque, posterolateral fusion vs risedronate, PJK in one ASD study
23% deficient in one fusion cohort; <20 ng/mL flagged in CNS guideline
Shorter recovery and stay, less pain
Gometz systematic review; Nielsen 2010 prehab RCT

points: Imaging: full-length films, flexion-extension films, MRI and CT or CT myelogram; EOS for 3D planning
Diabetic thoracolumbar instrumentation: no SSI below HbA1c 7% vs 35.3% above, as reported (no denominators given)
Rolving CBT RCT: lower ODI at 3 months, higher QALYs at 1 year; education RCT (Louw): less health-care use at 1 year
slides.notes: HbA1c. The 7 percent target is stated as a recommendation and cited to a systematic review (Suresh 2022). The review does not give the designs of the supporting studies (our guess is that most are observational): above 7.5 percent, cited to a CNS systematic review and guideline, in single-level lumbar interbody fusion, the Hikata figure of no SSI below 7 percent against 35.3 percent above it in diabetic thoracolumbar instrumentation, and above 8 percent with longer stay, more readmission and more complications in Michigan lumbar data. The review gives no denominators for the 35.3 percent, so we cannot judge how many infections that is. The sentence that diabetes increases the proportion of SSIs upward of 53 percent is ambiguous: relative or absolute is not stated. Osteoporosis. The evidence ladder is mixed. Faster fusion against risedronate comes from postmenopausal women in instrumented lumbar posterolateral fusion (Ohtori). Higher pedicle screw insertional torque comes from postmenopausal osteoporotic patients during fusion surgery (Inoue); the fusion type and level are not given. One adult deformity study (Yagi 2016) found less fracture-type PJK with prophylactic teriparatide. A systematic review is quoted as finding teriparatide better than multi-rod constructs, cement augmentation and tethers for PJK and PJF. Our reading: that is an indirect comparison across different studies, not a head-to-head trial. The functional benefit sentence rests on a distal radius fracture study, and that reference is printed with 'undefined' as its journal. Table 1 says randomized trials showed superior fusion efficacy for teriparatide, but the fusion study the text cites is titled a prospective study. Prehab. The Rolving trial was cognitive behavioral therapy around lumbar fusion, not deformity surgery. The shorter recovery, stay and pain claim is cited to the Gometz systematic review and the Nielsen 2010 prehabilitation RCT; Rolving supports ODI and QALYs, and the Louw education RCT supports health-care use. The care point folds these different interventions into one claim.

slides.title: Intraoperative steps
slides.lead: Antibiotic advice is the best supported here; the liposomal bupivacaine claim rests on a manufacturer webpage and a technical note.

rows: Cited to a pediatric sedation guideline (mismatch)
'Guidelines' cited to a StatPearls chapter; 24 vs 72 h no difference (ref title says 48 vs 72); Macki: short and long both cut deep SSI
Exparel website and an awake MIS TLIF technical note
Retention 5.6-27.1%; one AIS PSF series; one TL fusion protocol

points: Cefazolin 1 g about 2 hours before surgery beat placebo for wound or urinary infection, per the cited RCT
SSI organisms in adults: gram-negative 30.5%, methicillin-resistant 34.3%; 61.6% of gram-negatives cefazolin-resistant
Protocol example: catheter out day 1-2, straight cath if scan >300 mL after 4-hour void trial, Foley and tamsulosin after 3 failures
slides.notes: Antibiotics. The review cites NASS 2013 for a single preoperative dose in uncomplicated laminectomy and discectomy, and a NASS Grade C statement that prolonged regimens can be considered with comorbidities such as spinal cord injury or diabetes. Neither NASS statement has a reference number. The spine-specific timing of 30 to 60 minutes before incision is cited to SIGN Guideline 58, which is on sedation of children. Treat that as a citation error. On duration, the review says current guidelines advise stopping within 24 hours, but the citation is a StatPearls chapter (reference 33), not a guideline. Macki and colleagues found that short (under 24 hours) and long (over 24 hours) postoperative antibiotics both lowered deep SSI against none, with no effect on superficial SSI. The authors infer that superficial infection depends more on closure technique. That is their inference. The 24 versus 72 hour study is titled a comparison of 48 and 72 hour protocols, so check the original before quoting it. Recompute: 61.6 percent of 30.5 percent is 18.8 percent, which matches the review's statement that cefazolin-resistant gram-negatives were 18.8 percent of all SSIs. The authors themselves say more work is needed in complex deformity. Liposomal bupivacaine. The review says it 'has recently been shown to improve outcomes' but the citations are the product website and a technical note, and the use described is the authors' institution in awake minimally invasive decompression and TLIF, not open deformity correction. Figure 1 is an operating-room photo of the navigated injection; it adds no data. Foley. The AIS numbers are adolescents after PSF. The review reads them as reflecting long fusions and advises a lower threshold to keep the Foley in complex cases. That is the authors' inference from a pediatric series.

slides.title: Postoperative care
slides.lead: Sensible defaults, with causal language that runs ahead of the observational evidence on mobilization and heparin choice.

rows: Epidural PCA beats IV PCA; weigh respiratory risk
General meta-analysis; AIS comparative study; no basal infusion
Spine meta-analysis favors ramosetron; one trial equal
Mechanical for all; LMWH and UFH both safe
Up to 2-4% with prolonged immobilization; PLUSS: choice did not predict VTE or hematoma
MSSIC registry: day 0 ambulation linked to shorter stay, fewer complications

points: Epidural PCA was better than IV PCA at rest and with activity on days 1, 2 and 3, per the cited meta-analysis
Hydrophilic-only epidural opioid regimens had higher VAS than lipophilic ones; the authors advise avoiding them
Ondansetron 4 mg IV or 8 mg orally disintegrating tablet; the 'guidelines' cited are the IMPACT trial protocol (reference 70)
slides.notes: Analgesia. The epidural versus IV PCA meta-analysis (Wu 2005) is not spine-specific. Milbrandt is adolescent scoliosis: a single intrathecal opioid dose plus IV PCA lowered pain scores and adverse events, as reported. The review recommends against a background infusion because respiratory depression risk rises while the analgesic gain is inconclusive. The review does cover local anesthetic adjuncts: lidocaine in morphine PCA, epidural ropivacaine with sufentanil, and a care point favoring local anesthetic combinations. Our reading: it does not discuss systemic non-opioids such as acetaminophen, NSAIDs, gabapentinoids or ketamine, which most spine ERAS pathways lean on. PONV. The review says prophylaxis is recommended with one or two risk factors and lists age without saying which direction. The care point then upgrades this to 'strongly recommended' in deformity patients. On ramosetron, the authors set conflicting results aside because ondansetron is everywhere. That is a practical point, not evidence. Our reading: the review says an oral dose 1 hour before surgery may give long-lasting relief because the half-life is 3 to 4 hours, and a 3 to 4 hour half-life argues against long-lasting relief. That source is a laparoscopic surgery study. VTE. The review says VTE incidence with prolonged immobilization after spine surgery may reach as high as 2 to 4 percent. That is an upper range under prolonged immobilization, not a general incidence. It says LMWH versus UFH 'failed to predict' VTE or epidural hematoma in PLUSS. The body text already infers that both drugs are safe, and the care point drops the hedge and states it flatly. Failure to find a difference is not proof of equal safety, especially for rare hematomas. The Sanofi black box statement has no reference. Mobilization. The review says early ambulation decreases stay and 90-day complications, but the cited source is titled 'associated with'. A randomized trial is mentioned with no reference. The 30-foot threshold is cited to a Spine Journal supplement page, which looks like a meeting abstract (our reading). The fear-avoidance point is reasonable, but the sentence that disability and pain worsen in patients who fear ambulation is cited to reference 83, a Macki study titled 'The Effect of Physical Therapy on Time to Discharge After Lumbar Interbody Fusion'. By its title (our reading), it does not address fear avoidance. The same reference supports the distance-walked claim.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: Useful as a map; weak as evidence, with several citation and reasoning errors to know before you quote it.
points: Strength: covers the full pathway and gives concrete, usable defaults
Strength: points to Michigan (MSSIC) and PLUSS data on ambulation and heparin choice
Weakness: no methods, search or evidence grading; selection of studies unexplained
Weakness: no ERAS bundle outcome data in deformity patients
Weakness: evidence drawn from lumbar degenerative, AIS, awake MIS, fracture and laparoscopic studies
Weakness: several authors' own studies cited (Macki, MSSIC, PLUSS); disclosure states no conflict
Citation errors: antibiotic timing, hematoma reports, a broken fracture reference, a 48 vs 72 h study quoted as 24 vs 72 h; 'guidelines' cited to StatPearls and a trial protocol
Causal wording for associations: MSSIC ambulation data, PLUSS heparin choice
Missing topics (our reading): blood management and tranexamic acid, nutrition, smoking, anemia, systemic non-opioid analgesics
slides.notes: Be fair first. This is a short review, and its practical defaults are mostly mainstream: optimize glucose and bone, give cefazolin before incision and stop within 24 hours, avoid background PCA infusions, use mechanical prophylaxis, get patients up early, and prepare them for walking. The problems are in how strongly it states them. Citation errors you can check from the reference list alone. Spine antibiotic timing is cited to a pediatric sedation guideline (reference 32). The anesthesia reports of spinal hematoma with LMWH and epidural catheters are cited to references 79 to 81, which are the PLUSS study, a heparin meta-analysis and a training-program survey, all first-authored by Macki, the second author. The teriparatide functional outcome reference lists its journal as 'undefined'. Reference 34 is titled 48 versus 72 hours while the text says 24 versus 72 hours. The PONV guideline is listed under the author 'Ashp'. Two 'guidelines' are not guidelines: the 24-hour antibiotic stop is cited to a StatPearls chapter (reference 33), and the ondansetron dose to the IMPACT trial protocol (reference 70). Reasoning gaps are ours to point out. 'Failed to predict' becomes 'safe'. 'Associated with' becomes 'decreases'. A 3 to 4 hour half-life is offered as a reason for long-lasting relief. A pediatric AIS urinary retention series is used to argue for adult deformity practice. The AIS catheter numbers hang together if 53 is the retention group: 33 percent (n=53) had retention, 49 percent of them needed straight catheterization beyond 24 hours, and 16 of the 53 needed one catheterization with the rest needing more. The cohort size is not given; our estimate is about 160. The number of authors' own studies cited is not a conflict of interest, but know it when you read the PLUSS and MSSIC sentences. The care points sometimes say more than the text, for example 'strongly recommended' PONV prophylaxis.

slides.title: Teriparatide claim against the library
slides.lead: In our judgment, the review's strongest adult deformity claim is teriparatide for junctional failure; a later library trial helps frame it.

rows: Less fracture-type PJK, higher BMD and bone quality, as reported
Teriparatide better than multi-rod, cement, tethers for PJK/PJF
PJF 3.4% vs 22.2% vs denosumab; PJK 17.2% vs 33.3%, P=.165

points: Park 2025 comes from the library record at abstract level and was published after this review
It compares teriparatide with an active drug, not with no treatment
slides.notes: This slide is here because teriparatide is the one recommendation where the review cites adult deformity data (its other deformity data are adolescent AIS series on urinary retention and pain), and residents will be asked about it. The review cites Yagi 2016 for less PJK of the vertebral fracture type with prophylactic teriparatide, along with higher bone mineral density and better bone quality. It also cites a systematic review (Echt 2021) for teriparatide being more effective against PJK and PJF than multi-rod constructs, cement augmentation and sublaminar tethers or banding. Our reading: comparing a drug with construct techniques across separate studies is indirect and should not be quoted as a head-to-head result. From the library record, not from this paper: Park 2025, a randomized trial of 64 osteoporotic adults having thoracolumbar deformity surgery, found PJF of 3.4 percent with perioperative teriparatide against 22.2 percent with denosumab in a modified intention-to-treat analysis. The PJK difference, 17.2 against 33.3 percent, was not significant (P=.165). The library caveat flags the small sample, modified ITT and active comparator, and warns that PJF and PJK are different outcomes. So the current position is that teriparatide has some randomized support against PJF, and not yet clear support against PJK. Our reading again: the Sorour care point, 'useful in improving bone mineral density, bone quality, and fusion' in deformity patients, is broader than the deformity data it cites. Most of that claim comes from lumbar fusion studies in postmenopausal women. Note that Table 1 is adapted from the authors' own handbook chapter, which we did not review.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "Sorour 2023 is a narrative ERAS checklist for deformity surgery: HbA1c below 7%, bone health with teriparatide, cefazolin before incision and stopped by 24 hours, protocol-driven bladder care, cautious PCA, PONV prophylaxis, mechanical VTE prophylaxis, with LMWH or UFH if chemoprophylaxis is used, and walking on day 0 or 1. It reports no ERAS outcome data in deformity patients, and much of its evidence is borrowed from other spine and non-spine surgery."
points: Quote the defaults, not the strength: most claims rest on observational or non-deformity studies
Do not quote it as showing ERAS shortens stay in adult deformity
Check the original for antibiotic timing, the 24 vs 72 h study and the hematoma reports before citing them
LMWH vs UFH: no difference found in PLUSS, which is not the same as proven equally safe
slides.notes: Expect these questions. Does ERAS improve outcomes in adult deformity? This paper cannot answer that. It presents no study of a bundle in deformity patients. The library has a 2022 systematic review of ERAS in spinal surgery (Zaed, PM33901525) that is not yet appraised, so do not quote numbers from it. What HbA1c should I require? The review says below 7 percent and cites a systematic review, with observational cutoffs of 7, 7.5 and 8 percent from lumbar and thoracolumbar cohorts. Say it is a target, not a proven threshold for deformity. Should every osteoporotic deformity patient get teriparatide? The review leans yes. The direct deformity evidence is one cohort it cites and, from our library, a later 64-patient randomized trial showing less PJF than denosumab but no significant PJK difference. Is liposomal bupivacaine worth it? This review gives no comparative data; its sources are a manufacturer page and a technical note in awake MIS TLIF. LMWH or heparin? The review reports that choice did not predict VTE or epidural hematoma in PLUSS. Hematoma is rare, so a null result is weak reassurance. Keep the Foley? The review supports a protocol with void trials and bladder scans, and a lower threshold to keep the catheter in long fusions, based partly on an adolescent series. What is missing? By our reading: blood management and tranexamic acid, nutrition, smoking, anemia, systemic non-opioid analgesics, and any measure of protocol compliance. These are topics this review does not cover, not evidence against them.

decks.not_reviewed: The online appendix (Supplemental Tables 1 to 7: implant-failure definitions, missing-PRO analyses, mean alignment, MCID proportions and PRO change scores) was not available and was not read; values the text cites from it could not be checked. The linked commentary by Kang was not reviewed. Cited studies (Seki, Yagi, Ohtori, Cho, Jespersen and others) were not reviewed.

slides.title: Mohanty 2024: teriparatide in long fusion, by bone density
slides.lead: Bottom line: in one surgeon's 540 long ASD fusions, osteoporotic patients prescribed teriparatide had half the 2-year reoperation rate of matched osteopenic patients (11.5% vs 23.1%) and fewer symptomatic pseudarthroses (6.4% vs 21.8%). Against matched normal-BMD patients, no clinical outcome differed significantly; only NRS pain favored OP-T.
points: Mohanty S, Sardar ZM, Hassan FM, Lombardi JM, Lehman RA, Lenke LG. J Bone Joint Surg Am 2024;106(3):206-17.
Retrospective single-surgeon cohort, Columbia, 2014 to 2021, with two separate 1:2 propensity-matched comparisons. Therapeutic Level III.

Not randomized. Teriparatide and osteoporosis travel together: every treated patient was osteoporotic. Untreated osteoporotic patients existed (82 in Figure 1) but were excluded by design, not used as a comparator.
Prepared from the full 12-page article. The online appendix was not read.
slides.notes: Frame this before anyone reads a number. The study asks a narrow question: once an osteoporotic patient has been put on teriparatide, do they do as well after a long deformity fusion as patients with better bone? The authors say so directly in the Discussion: of three lines of evidence (teriparatide versus placebo, versus bisphosphonates, and equivalence with normal BMD), this study addresses the third. It does not compare teriparatide with no teriparatide in the same kind of bone. The headline comparison is osteoporotic patients on teriparatide against osteopenic patients on vitamin D and calcium. That makes the OPE result a comparison of two packages (worse bone plus the drug, against better bone without it), and the authors' own conclusion is phrased as a difference between groups, not a drug effect. The normal-BMD comparison found no significant difference in reoperation, pseudarthrosis or PJK, which the authors read as osteoporotic patients on teriparatide being brought up to normal. Keep that reading at arm's length until the appraisal slide: no significant difference is not the same as equivalence, and the confidence intervals are wide. This deck was prepared from the full text. The appendix, which holds the missing-data analyses and change scores, was not available, so some text values could not be checked. Our checks found several internal inconsistencies; they are listed on the appraisal slide and do not overturn the main OPE result, but they lower confidence in the precision of the reporting.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: Osteoporosis roughly doubles reoperation after long fusion. Does an osteoanabolic agent close that gap?
points: Background cited by the authors: pseudarthrosis after ASD surgery 5% to 24%, and more than 40% of reoperations.
Pedicle screw pullout in osteoporotic lumbar spine is 61.1% to 78.9% of normal, per the authors' citations.
Prior teriparatide spine data were mostly short degenerative fusions or small, single-sex Japanese ASD cohorts.
Gap stated by the authors: few long-term reoperation, pseudarthrosis and PRO data for teriparatide in ASD.

rows: ASD, posterior fusion of more than 7 levels, minimum 2-year follow-up
Osteopenia on vitamin D and calcium (OPE); normal BMD

slides.notes: The authors open with the burden: an estimated more than 28 million people over 65 affected by ASD, pseudarthrosis as a common failure mode, and a cited analysis of 2,293 ASD patients (Puvanesarajah) with twofold higher odds of reoperation in osteoporosis. Those figures are as reported in this paper's introduction; the source studies were not reviewed. The prior teriparatide work they cite is mostly short fusions for degenerative disease: Ohtori on screw loosening, Cho on earlier fusion with PLIF, Jespersen finding no benefit in noninstrumented fusion, and Ebata showing early bone formation. For deformity they cite Seki (58 osteoporotic patients with ASD, fewer postoperative fractures and better facet fusion, but no long-term pseudarthrosis or reoperation data) and Yagi (43 patients). So the clinical question is real: surgeons already prescribe teriparatide before long fusions, and the outcome that matters, reoperation, had not been studied well. Note the shape of the question. The exposure is not the drug alone. It is a patient category (osteoporosis), restricted to those who were treated. The two comparator groups answer different questions. Versus osteopenia: are treated osteoporotic patients better off than a group with milder bone loss that got no anabolic? Versus normal: are they as good as patients with normal bone? Neither is the randomized question of teriparatide versus none in osteoporosis. Ask the room which comparison they would have wanted, and why it is missing: Figure 1 lists 82 osteoporotic patients not on teriparatide among those ineligible for the study aims. An untreated osteoporotic group existed; the authors chose not to use it as a comparator.

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: 540 of 1,295 screened patients; one surgeon, one implant system, two 1:2 matched comparisons.
points: Inclusion: ASD, posterior instrumented fusion of more than 7 levels with cobalt-chromium rods, at least 2 years of follow-up. 22 (4.07%) also had anterior fusion for VCR.
BMD: hip and femoral neck T-scores for the 488 patients aged 45 or more; under 45, osteoporosis ruled out by CT at an HU threshold of 160.
Teriparatide 20 µg/day for 24 months: at least 6 months before surgery and at least 1 year after; the commonest regimen ran 18 months after surgery.
Primary outcome: 2-year reoperation. Secondary: symptomatic pseudarthrosis with or without implant failure, PJK (10 degrees or more, UIV to UIV+2), PROs (NRS, SRS-22r, ODI).
Matching variables: age, indication, levels, 3CO, revision, osteotomies, pelvic fixation, BMP, TLIF, BMP volume, supplemental rods, baseline and correction of Cobb and T1PA. Sex was not matched.
Power: 217 patients needed to detect an OR of at least 2 with 80% power and alpha 0.05.
slides.see: Figure 1 is the flow diagram: 1,295 assessed, 755 ineligible (including 82 osteoporotic patients not on teriparatide), 540 included, the two separate 1:2 matches, and 2-year PRO completion per group.
slides.notes: Read the groups carefully. 284 + 178 + 78 = 540, and 1,295 minus 755 = 540, so the totals hold. Ours: the listed reasons for ineligibility (276 + 212 + 82 + 303 + 9) add to 882, not 755; overlap between reasons is not stated. The treated group is sicker on paper: unmatched, OP-T patients were 68.5 years against 55.9 for normal BMD, had 15.7 instrumented levels against 11.8, and all had supplemental rods (normal BMD 71.8%). Against unmatched OPE they were similar in age but still had longer fusions (15.7 vs 13.1 levels, p = 0.0002), although the text calls the OPE group similar at baseline. After matching, OPE (156) and normal BMD (156) were each compared with the same 78 OP-T patients. The OPE match took 156 of only 178 available osteopenic patients, so it could do little selecting. Matching with or without replacement is not stated. Matched normal-BMD patients were imbalanced in sex (74.4% vs 88.5% female, p = 0.0163), significant at 0.05 but not at Table VI's adjusted alpha of 0.0025; sex was not a matching variable. Outcome definitions: pseudarthrosis was symptomatic and confirmed by CT or dynamic films, by radiologist and surgeon consensus. The authors note only symptomatic patients had CT, so silent nonunion was not counted. PJK used a 10 degree threshold; PJF was not reported separately. Dose and regimen: 20 µg/day for 24 months, at least 6 months before and at least 1 year after surgery; the commonest regimen ran 18 months after, so 6 + 18 = 24. The authors state they cannot confirm patients took the drug, only that it was prescribed.

slides.title: Primary outcome: 2-year reoperation
slides.lead: Lower than osteopenia, similar to normal BMD.
points: Odds ratios are OP-T relative to the comparator, from conditional logistic regression.
Absolute difference versus matched OPE: 11.5 percentage points (ours).
Reasons for reoperation are not reported.
Ours: both OPE reoperation P values look too small for their intervals (Wald about 0.04 matched, 0.04 unmatched).
slides.notes: The percentages recompute from the counts. The crude odds ratio for the matched OPE comparison is about 0.43 (ours: 9/69 against 36/120), close to the adjusted 0.45, so adjustment changed little. Same direction matched and unmatched. Now the fragile part. The matched OPE interval, 0.203 to 0.906, is asymmetric on the log scale around 0.449, but so are the unmatched intervals in Tables V and VII (probably profile-likelihood), so asymmetry alone is not an error. The problem is that P and interval disagree. Ours: a Wald test from that interval gives P about 0.036, and a crude Fisher test on 9/78 vs 36/156 also gives 0.036, not 0.0188. The unmatched result has the same problem: OR 0.4536 (0.196 to 0.905) implies a Wald P of about 0.043, and crude Fisher on 9/78 vs 39/178 gives 0.056, against a printed 0.0181; the abstract cites this unmatched result as significant. The upper limit sits just below 1. Read the primary result as real in direction but less secure than the printed P value suggests. Nine events in the treated group drive everything; a few reoperations either way would move the result across 1. The normal-BMD comparison is the one the authors lean on for 'not different'. The OR is 0.85 but the interval runs from 0.37 to 1.98, which includes a near doubling of reoperation risk. The study was powered to detect an OR of 2, not to show equivalence, and no equivalence margin was set. So 'no significant difference' is the honest phrase. Notice also that matched normal-BMD patients had a higher reoperation rate (13.5%) than the unmatched normal pool (10.2%): matching picked longer, harder normal-BMD cases. What counts as a reoperation is not broken down: we do not know how many were for pseudarthrosis, PJK, infection or other causes. The authors raise one more bias themselves: the surgeon may have been reluctant to reoperate on patients with advanced osteoporosis, which would lower the OP-T reoperation rate for reasons unrelated to bone healing.

slides.title: Secondary outcomes and harms
slides.lead: Fewer symptomatic pseudarthroses than osteopenia; no PJK signal; PRO gains mostly against osteopenia.

rows: 2.74 vs 1.51, p 0.0184 (fails adjusted alpha); change from baseline p 0.0025

points: Matched OPE vs OP-T at 2 years, adjusted alpha 0.017: SRS Function 3.46 vs 4.07 (p 0.0022) and SRS Total 3.67 vs 4.14 (p 0.0058) survive; SRS Pain (p 0.0302) and Satisfaction (p 0.0226) do not.
OP-T improved ODI by 21.4 points from a baseline of 43.0; matched OPE by 16.5.
No teriparatide adverse events, adherence or drug harms are reported.
slides.notes: Pseudarthrosis is the strongest signal: 5 of 78 against 34 of 156, a crude OR of 0.25 that matches the adjusted value, with a symmetric interval that recomputes to the printed P value. That is the most robust number in the paper, with the caveat that it counts only symptomatic, CT-confirmed nonunion. PJK did not differ in either comparison, and the authors note this agrees with Yagi. Remember that PJK here is the radiographic 10 degree definition, and the matched interval (0.41 to 3.39) is too wide to rule out benefit or harm. PROs: baseline scores were similar across groups. At 2 years the OP-T group was better than matched OPE on pain and SRS measures. Table IV's footnote sets the adjusted alpha at 0.017 and flags SRS Pain and Satisfaction as failing it, yet the Results text lists them alongside the others as worse in OPE. Against normal BMD, the text calls OP-T pain better on two numbers: the 2-year value (p 0.0184, failing the adjusted alpha) and the change from baseline (p 0.0025, Supplemental Table 7), which would pass it. That claim is defensible. The 2-year ODI value did not differ in either comparison. The ODI change from baseline favored OP-T against OPE by the authors' report (matched p 0.0411, unmatched p 0.0387, appendix values), which would fail alpha 0.017. Figure 1 gives 2-year PRO completion: OP-T 61 of 78 (78.2%), matched OPE 125 of 156, matched normal 128 of 156. Ours: the OP-T 2-year ODI standard error is 3.97 against 2.18 at baseline; losing 17 of 78 would widen it only about 1.13 times, not 1.82, so missing data do not explain the spread. The authors modeled missing PROs as missing at random; their missing-data analyses are in the appendix. Harms: there are none reported for the drug. Cost and access are raised by the authors as a selection issue, not measured.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: A useful single-surgeon signal with a confounded comparator, a fragile primary P value, and several reporting errors.
points: Confounded exposure: drug and bone category are inseparable. The OPE comparison is two packages, not a drug effect.
Unmeasured confounding remains after matching, as the authors state; sex was not matched against normal BMD (74.4% vs 88.5% female, p 0.0163, not significant at the adjusted alpha).
Adherence unknown: prescribed, not confirmed taken (authors).
Pseudarthrosis was counted only when symptomatic (authors); PJF not reported.
Possible reluctance to reoperate on severe osteoporosis lowers OP-T reoperation (authors).
Single surgeon, single implant system, mostly white women: limited generalizability (authors).
Our checks: several tables and text disagree; matched OPE cannot be a subset of the unmatched OPE pool without replacement.
slides.notes: Strengths first: one surgeon and one implant system reduce technical variation; two comparator groups; matching on 15 surgical and alignment variables; a minimum 2-year follow-up for everyone; an a priori power estimate. Our recomputation found these problems. 1. Results text gives pelvic fixation 444 (82.2%) and TLIF 424 (78.5%) for the whole cohort; Table I gives 452 (83.70%) and 436 (80.74%), and Table I's group counts add to 452 and 436. 2. Table I overall ASA (2.22) and levels (12.42) do not equal the weighted means of the three groups (about 2.40 and 12.80); age and T-score do. 3. Table I's composite indications do not reconcile with its Schwab components: Type N should equal regional plus isolated sagittal (320 overall) but is 296, and SVA under 4 cm should equal regional plus isolated coronal (124) but is 182. 4. Matched OPE (156 of 178) has 140 TLIFs against 165 in the full pool, so 25 TLIF patients would have to be among only 22 excluded; and its mean of 14.86 levels would require the 22 excluded to average about half a level; likewise matched baseline T1PA 28.56 against 25.13 for the pool implies the excluded averaged about 0.8 degrees, and matched T1PA correction -14.65 against -10.11 implies they worsened by about 22 degrees (ours). Either matching was with replacement, which is not stated, or the tables are wrong. 5. Both OPE reoperation P values (0.0188 matched, 0.0181 unmatched) look too small for their intervals and counts, as discussed. 6. The same OP-T ODI change is given as -21.36 (SE 2.97) and -21.4 (SE 1.97). 7. The abstract says 1:2:2, Table IV says 2:2:1, Methods says two separate 1:2 matches. 8. The Discussion calls Seki's patients osteopenic though the Introduction and the reference title say osteoporotic, cites rod breakage 4.8% and adjacent fracture 0% for this study that are not in the main text (the appendix was not read), gives this study's fusion length as 14 levels against an OP-T mean of 15.73, and counts Cho among 7 RCTs though its reference title says prospective cohort. 9. Table I significance claims for pelvic fixation (p 0.016) and BMP (p 0.0102) do not meet Table I's adjusted alpha of 0.00625. 10. Table I isolated regional deformity, 17/284 vs 4/78, prints p 0.2625; chi-square gives 0.77, Fisher 1.00. 11. Figure 1's ineligibility reasons add to 882, not 755. None of these reverses the OPE pseudarthrosis result. Together they argue for treating exact values as approximate.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: In one surgeon's long ASD fusions, osteoporotic patients prescribed teriparatide had about half the 2-year reoperation rate of matched osteopenic patients (11.5% vs 23.1%) and far fewer symptomatic pseudarthroses (6.4% vs 21.8%), with no PJK difference. Versus matched normal bone, no clinical outcome differed significantly (only NRS pain favored OP-T), but the intervals were wide. Observational, drug confounded with bone category.
points: Does teriparatide cause fewer reoperations? Not shown. Untreated osteoporotic patients were excluded, not compared; drug and bone category are inseparable.
Are treated osteoporotic patients equivalent to normal bone? Not proven: reoperation OR 0.85 (0.37 to 1.98), and no equivalence margin.
Does it prevent PJK? No signal here: 7.7% vs 6.4% (OPE) and 7.7% vs 10.3% (normal), both nonsignificant.
How solid is the primary result? Direction consistent, but the interval nearly touches 1 and the printed P value looks too small (ours).
What about the dose and duration? 20 µg/day for 24 months, starting at least 6 months before surgery; the commonest regimen ran 18 months after.
slides.notes: Say the summary in about 30 seconds. Then expect these. Is this randomized? No. Retrospective, single surgeon, propensity matched; Level III. Do not describe it as a trial. Why compare with osteopenia rather than untreated osteoporosis? Untreated osteoporotic patients existed (82 in Figure 1) but were excluded by design; the authors chose not to use them. The OPE group is the comparator they chose, and it has better bone, which biases against teriparatide; that the treated group still did better is the authors' strongest point. Ours: that argument holds only if the groups are otherwise comparable, and the matched OPE table has numbers that do not reconcile with the pool. What does the normal-BMD comparison add? The authors read it as treated osteoporotic patients reaching normal outcomes. The honest phrase is no significant difference, with intervals that allow a doubling of risk. Is pseudarthrosis really lower? It is the cleanest number, 5 of 78 against 34 of 156, but only symptomatic nonunions were imaged. What about PROs? Better pain and SRS function and total than OPE at 2 years; the 2-year ODI value did not differ in either comparison. Several PRO differences in the text fail the paper's own adjusted alpha. Could surgeon behavior explain it? The authors concede reluctance to reoperate on severe osteoporosis could lower OP-T reoperation. Did patients take it? Unknown; prescriptions only. How does this fit with this week's trial evidence? Treat this as supportive and hypothesis-generating for anabolic optimization before long fusion, not as proof of a drug effect. Be ready to name the reporting errors: overall-cohort counts, the Schwab cross-tabulation, the matched OPE arithmetic and primary P values that disagree with their intervals.

decks.not_reviewed: The PDF is a reformatted copy of the open-access PMC text, and it is incomplete. It omits Tables 1 to 3 (baseline characteristics, multivariable regression, model performance), Figures 1 to 3 (workflow, ROC curves, calculator screenshot), and the age-adjusted ideal PI-LL formulas, which appear as a blank after 'were as follows'. Every table value here comes from the Results text only; confidence intervals for the odds ratios, the full univariable comparison and the per-model metrics for LDA, CART and KNN could not be read or checked. No supplement is cited. The online calculator was not tested. GAP comparisons come from master-file records D05 and D06, not from this paper.
