slides.title: Lee 2023: an online PJK risk calculator
slides.lead: Can machine learning give an individual probability of PJK after adult deformity surgery, instead of a 3-tier risk class?
points: Journal club: adult deformity, prediction model
Lee CH, et al. Neurospine 2023;20(4):1272-80
Retrospective multicenter cohort, Korean spinal deformity database, 16 centers, 2011-2020
Source warning: this PDF lacks Tables 1-3, Figures 1-3 and the ideal PI-LL formulas. Numbers come from the text only.
Bottom line: PJK in 49 of 201 (24.4%). A random forest reached accuracy 0.83 and AUROC 0.76 on a small internal test split. No external validation and no calibration were reported.
slides.notes: Say the source limit first. The PDF is a phone reformat of the PMC article. It states that images are omitted, and the tables did not survive either. So we have the text but not Table 1 (baseline), Table 2 (multivariable model) or Table 3 (model performance), and the formula for age-adjusted ideal PI-LL is missing where the Methods say 'were as follows'. Anything below that would normally be checked against a table is checked only against the text. Frame the paper. This is a prediction-model study, not a trial and not a causal study. It does two things: a conventional logistic regression to find independent predictors, then 5 machine learning models trained on a 70:30 random split of the same cohort. The best model, a random forest, was put online as a Shiny calculator. The title says development and validation. Our reading: validation here means a held-out internal test split from the same database, not testing in a new population. The paper is on the SRS Quality and Safety Resource Library list, which is a listing, not an endorsement of every claim.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: Existing alignment scores sort patients into 3 groups. The authors argue surgeons need a personal number.
points: PJK occurs in 17-39% of ASD cases, per the authors' introduction
The authors say SRS-Schwab, SAAS and GAP share similar key variables: age, PI, LL, PT or sacral slope, and global tilt or TPA (SRS-Schwab itself has no age term)
Their complaint: 3-tier outputs (undercorrected, matched, overcorrected; or proportioned to severely disproportioned) do not guide individual decisions
Aim: an accurate ML model for PJK risk, deployed as a free web calculator
slides.notes: The authors' case is practical: GAP and SAAS give a category, and they say a category does not tell you how to counsel or whether to revise. They also argue that existing scores are sums of first-order (linear) terms chosen for simplicity, and that ML can capture higher-order interactions. They cite a review that 7 of 10 papers found GAP AUROCs of 0.5 to 0.68. Note the cited reference 11 is a McCarthy paper on lumbar lordosis targets, which does not obviously match that description; we flag it as a possible citation error. For context from our library, not this paper: the GAP derivation record (D05) reports a validation AUC of 0.92, and the external validation record (D06) found 0.60. The authors also misquote GAP: they say the 70% not proportioned after surgery carried 'a risk of 47% or 95% for revision surgery', but in the D05 record 47% and 95% are mechanical complication rates; the revision rates are 21% and 55%. So the bar the authors set is real. Prior scores did not travel well. The trap is that a new model built and tested inside one database may look good for the same reason GAP did in its own validation set. Also be clear on what is predicted. GAP predicts mechanical complications broadly; this model predicts radiographic PJK only, and the authors excluded clinical outcomes because of missing data.

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: 201 Korean adults with sagittal deformity, fused 3 or more levels, followed at least 1 year.
points: ASD: age 18 or older with SVA 50 mm or more, PT 25 degrees or more, PI-LL over 10 degrees, or TK 60 degrees or more
Excluded: coronal deformity only, fusion under 3 levels, missing key spinopelvic parameters
PJK: PJA 20 degrees or more at final follow-up, OR PJA increase of 10 degrees or more from preoperative
PJA: UIV lower endplate to UIV+2 upper endplate
Regression: univariable P 0.20 or less, then backward stepwise, keep P 0.05 or less
ML: 70:30 random split, 5-fold cross-validation for tuning, complete cases only; SVM, RF, LDA, CART, KNN
slides.notes: Read the PJK definition closely. The paper uses 'either' and 'or': PJA of 20 degrees or more at final follow-up, or an increase of 10 degrees or more. Our inference: with 'or', a patient whose PJA was already 20 degrees before surgery counts as PJK without any change, and the outcome becomes partly a baseline measure. Final follow-up varies by patient, with a 1-year minimum, and mean follow-up is not reported. Someone followed 8 years has more time to develop PJK than someone followed 1 year, and a yes or no model ignores that. There is no flow diagram: we do not know how many were screened or excluded, or how many dropped out of the ML set for missing values, which the authors say were excluded, not imputed. The BMD row is a mean of -1.04 with an SD of 3.12; units are not stated, and an SD that large is unusual for a T-score. Only 119 patients have a PI-LL match category (50 + 53 + 16), and the remaining 82 are not explained. Percentages recompute: 49/201 = 24.4%, 50/119 = 42.0%, 53/119 = 44.5%, 16/119 = 13.4%, and 78.6% female equals 158 of 201. Continuous data are shown as mean and SD but tested with Mann-Whitney. Fine, but mildly inconsistent.

slides.title: Regression: three predictors, weak model
slides.lead: Postoperative PJA, BMI and deformity type stayed in the model. The paper reports an 'adjusted R2' of 18.8%, of unstated type.
points: Univariable P 0.20 or less: postop PJA 0.007, BMI 0.029, SRS global balance 0.090, SRS PI-LL 0.097, curve pattern 0.105, hypertension 0.132, TL alignment 0.176, deformity type 0.184, PI 0.196
Age and BMD were not significant in this cohort
Authors: explanatory power was low
slides.notes: Look at the direction of the odds ratios before accepting the story. As printed, both continuous ORs are below 1. If PJA and BMI were entered per degree and per kg/m2, which the text does not state, then a larger immediate postoperative PJA and a higher BMI each go with lower odds of PJK. For PJA in particular that runs against intuition, and the authors never discuss the direction. It may be a coding or sign issue in Table 2, which we could not see. Deformity type is categorical, and the reference category is not given in the text, so 1.655 cannot be interpreted. No confidence intervals are in the text. All three P values sit just under 0.05 (0.034, 0.046, 0.049) after stepwise selection from 9 candidates, which is a fragile pattern: stepwise selection in 201 patients with 49 events tends to overfit and to give optimistic P values. The paper says 'adjusted R2 of 18.8%' for a logistic model; this is presumably a pseudo R2, but the type is not given. The authors describe the univariable results as a significant association for all 9 factors, including P = 0.184; those met their 0.20 screening threshold, not significance. Age and BMD, both established PJK risk factors elsewhere, were not significant. The authors attribute this to their Korean-only population, which they describe as 'a smaller yet racially homogeneous patient cohort', so they raise both homogeneity and size. Our addition: the paper offers no data to tell the two apart, and with 49 events the small size alone could hide real effects.

slides.title: Machine learning and the calculator
slides.lead: Random forest was best of 5 models on the held-out 30%.
points: Inputs: deformity type, BMI, SRS curve pattern, SRS PI-LL modifier, SRS global balance modifier, baseline PI, postop PJA, age
Thoracolumbar alignment dropped for missing data; hypertension not used and not explained
Calculator example: age 70, degenerative deformity, BMI 27, PI 60, PI-LL 15, SVA 50 mm, postop PJA 5 gives 13.81%
slides.see: Figure 2 shows the ROC curves and Table 3 the full metrics; neither is in this PDF.
slides.notes: Do the arithmetic the paper does not. Accuracy of 0.83 sounds good, but most patients had no PJK, so a model that always says no scores well too. Test-set composition is not reported. Our approximation: if the test set matched the cohort (75.6% no PJK), always-no would score about 0.76. The reported metrics do not quite fit that, though. From F1 0.67 and sensitivity 0.57, our back-calculation gives a positive predictive value of about 0.81, and with those values accuracy 0.83 implies a test-set PJK rate near 30%, where always-no would score about 0.70. At the cohort's 24.4%, the same sensitivity and PPV would give accuracy about 0.86. Either way the gain over always-no is modest. Sensitivity 0.57 means it missed about 4 in 10 PJK cases in the test set. Test-set size is not reported. If it was 30% of 201, about 60 patients with about 15 PJK cases, our Hanley-McNeil approximation puts the 95% CI for AUROC 0.76 at roughly 0.61 to 0.91. The true CI is unknown, but this one is wide. Other points the paper leaves open. The 8 inputs were picked from univariable tests on the whole cohort, test set included, before the split; our concern is that this leaks test information and inflates performance. No calibration is reported, yet the calculator outputs a percentage to two decimals. A model can rank patients well and still give wrong probabilities. The calculator example gives raw PI-LL and SVA. Our reading: in the SRS-Schwab classification the PI-LL modifier is graded from PI-LL and the global balance modifier from SVA, so these are likely how the two SRS modifier inputs are derived; the paper does not say so. The example does leave out a listed input, the SRS curve pattern, and the paper does not say what value was assumed. The abstract calls the input variables 'hyperparameters'; they are features, not hyperparameters. The 'sigmoid basis function kernel' with a sigma parameter reads like a radial basis kernel. Earlier AI models in the authors' own citations reached 0.8 to 0.9, so by the authors' own citations their model performs below those.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: A reasonable idea built on a small, internally tested model with untested probabilities.
points: Strength: multicenter national database, PJK definition taken from a cited prior study, freely usable tool
Small: 49 events across 8 inputs and 5 model types
Internal split only; no external or temporal validation
No calibration, no CIs for AUROC or ORs in the text
Outcome is radiographic PJK, not PJF, revision or patient-reported outcome
Inconsistencies: OR directions, missing PI-LL denominators, baseline-only claim despite postop PJA input, GAP risks misquoted, citation 11
slides.notes: The authors list three limitations: retrospective multicenter data over a long period with changing technique and alignment targets; the 0.20 screening threshold; and radiographic outcomes only, since clinical outcomes had too much missing data. They note that radiographic PJK may overstate clinically bad outcomes. Add ours. First, events per variable. With 49 PJK cases total and roughly 15 in the test set, any performance number has wide uncertainty, and model ranking among the 5 could flip on a different random split. Second, there is no external validation. GAP is the warning from our library: strong in its own validation set (D05) and weak externally (D06). Third, calibration. A tool that prints 13.81% invites patients and surgeons to treat the number as accurate. Nothing in the paper shows that predicted percentages match observed rates. Fourth, timing. Postoperative PJA is an input, so this is a postoperative tool, not a planning tool. The authors' conclusion fits this: they frame it for patients who did not reach target alignment after surgery. But the paper contradicts itself here. The Limitations say the analysis 'relied solely on baseline patient characteristics and their radiologic parameters', and the abstract aims to 'enhance treatment planning precision', yet postoperative PJA is both a multivariable predictor and a model input. Fifth, the PJK definition with 'or' and variable follow-up. Sixth, internal inconsistencies we flagged. The authors claim 'diagnostic value' in the Discussion and say in the Conclusion that the model 'exhibited good capabilities in predicting PJK risk'. Our view is that AUROC 0.76 from a small internal split is moderate discrimination, short of what the authors cite for prior models. The racial-homogeneity explanation for absent age and BMD effects is the authors' hypothesis, not a finding.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: In 201 Korean ASD patients, 24% developed radiographic PJK. A random forest from postoperative PJA, BMI, deformity type, SRS modifiers, PI and age gave AUROC 0.76 on an internal test split, and it is online as a calculator.
points: Independent predictors: postop PJA (OR 0.942), BMI (OR 0.883), deformity type (OR 1.655)
RF accuracy 0.83; always-no would score roughly 0.70 to 0.76 (our approximation; test-set makeup not reported); sensitivity 0.57
Not externally validated or calibrated; treat its percentage as rough
PDF lacked tables and figures; text-only review
slides.notes: Spoken summary: This is a 16-center Korean registry study of 201 adult deformity patients fused 3 or more levels and followed at least a year. PJK, defined as a junctional angle of 20 degrees or a 10 degree increase, occurred in 49, or 24.4%. Logistic regression kept immediate postoperative PJA, BMI and deformity type, but its fit was weak, with a reported adjusted R2 of 18.8%, likely a pseudo R2 of unstated type. Five ML models were trained on 70% and tested on 30%. Random forest did best with accuracy 0.83 and AUROC 0.76, and it was released as a free web calculator. Expect these questions. Is it better than GAP? It was not compared head to head. GAP figures in our library run from 0.92 internally (D05) to 0.60 externally (D06), and this model has no external test yet. Is 83% accuracy good? Only modestly. Our approximation is that always predicting no PJK would score about 70 to 76%, depending on the test-set PJK rate, which is not reported. Can I use it before surgery? Not as described: it needs postoperative PJA. Why are the ORs below 1? The paper does not explain. As printed, a higher PJA and higher BMI go with lower odds, which is odd for PJA; treat it as unresolved. Why did age and bone density drop out? The authors point to their smaller, racially homogeneous Korean cohort; we add that the paper cannot separate the two. Would I quote its percentage to a patient? Our view: as a rough discussion aid at most, until it is calibrated and validated elsewhere.

decks.not_reviewed: Supplementary material 1 (the final GRADE Evidence-to-Decision frameworks), the separate methods paper, and the 15 underlying systematic reviews in the AOGO focus issue. Our copy is a reformatted PMC text with images omitted; it has no funding or conflict-of-interest statement, so those were not reviewed. Every number in this deck comes from the guideline's own summaries of evidence, not from the primary studies.

slides.title: AOGO guideline: osteobiologics in ACDF
slides.lead: Which graft or osteobiologic to use in ACDF for degenerative disease.
points: Journal club: cervical degeneration
Meisel HJ, et al. Global Spine J 2024;14(2 Suppl):6S-13S
AO Spine Knowledge Forum Degenerative; 73 panelists from 22 countries; 15 systematic reviews

Bottom line: five conditional suggestions, all on low or very low certainty evidence. Autograft, allograft and cage plus osteobiologic give similar results; avoid BMP-2 in common cases; no recommendation for revision ACDF.
slides.notes: Frame it first: this is a guideline, so the questions are what it recommends, how strong each suggestion is, what evidence sits under it, and what is missing. Every recommendation is conditional. The authors call it the first guideline on osteobiologics in ACDF. The motivation in their introduction: little high-quality evidence, regulations that vary by country, and graft choice that is often driven by surgeon familiarity, education, consulting or hospital inventory. They cite an AO Spine member survey in which 74% used non-structural graft material for single-level ACDF and 72.8% for multi-level. What we reviewed: the full guideline text in a reformatted PMC copy whose header says images are omitted. The text has one table, the list of review topics. Not reviewed: Supplementary material 1, which holds the final Evidence-to-Decision frameworks where the panel's judgments are recorded; the separate methods paper; and the 15 systematic reviews themselves. Our copy has no funding or conflict-of-interest statement, so we cannot comment on either. So every number in this deck is the guideline's own summary of the reviews, one step away from the primary studies.

slides.title: How the guideline was built
points: Process: AO policies plus the GIN-McMaster Guideline Development Checklist
Panel set topics and outcomes: benefits (fusion, function), harms (pain, medical and surgical complications), plus resources, feasibility, acceptability and equity
15 review topics (1, 2, 3, 4a-4d, 5-12); searches to October 2020 stated for Topics 1, 2, 4b and 4c; Topic 7 ran 2000-2021; no dates given for the rest
Methodologist built GRADE Evidence-to-Decision frameworks in GRADEpro; panel commented through Panel Voice and meetings
Final recommendations by consensus; reviewed by panel, review teams and external reviewers

rows: Benefits clearly outweigh harms; most surgeons should follow
Benefits probably outweigh harms; different choices fit different patients

slides.notes: The process is standard and well described for a GRADE guideline: a defined checklist, systematic reviews per question, a methodologist assembling the evidence, and a panel judging it in Evidence-to-Decision frameworks. Note what the outcomes list includes beyond fusion: cost, feasibility, acceptability and equity. That matters, because once the panel judged benefits and harms similar, cost and availability became the deciding factors in most recommendations. Notice also how consensus was reached: the paper says only that final recommendations were by consensus. It does not describe a voting threshold, and the methods paper that may do so was not reviewed. Every recommendation here is in the 'we suggest' form. The paper's own definition: surgeons should likely follow the action but recognize that different choices will suit different individuals. The abstract says surgeons 'are recommended' to choose graft by clinical situation, cost and availability; that is looser than the GRADE wording in the body, which is all conditional. The evidence summaries cite by number only Topics 1, 2, 4b, 4c, 5, 6, 7 and 10. Seven topics are never cited: 3 (plated vs unplated), 4a (autograft network meta-analysis), 4d (multilevel complications), 8 (dosing), 9 (fusion assessment), 11 (comorbidities) and 12 (revision). The text does say no comorbidity data and no revision evidence were found, which fits Topics 11 and 12, but it never cites either topic, and plating, the autograft network meta-analysis, dosing strategy and fusion imaging do not shape any recommendation that we can see. That last point is our reading of the text.

slides.title: The five recommendations
slides.lead: All conditional. None is strong.

rows: Autograft vs cage plus osteobiologic, primary ACDF
Structural iliac crest autograft or cage plus osteobiologic (TCP, DBM, HA or allograft); similar outcomes
Allograft vs cage plus osteobiologic, primary ACDF
Either, by availability, cost and resources
Use osteobiologics other than BMP in common situations
An osteobiologic can be used at single or multiple levels
Structural iliac crest autograft, allograft or cage plus osteobiologic (DBM, bovine bone or BMP-2); similar outcomes

points: Revision ACDF: no recommendation, because no evidence was identified
Comorbidities: no data to guide graft choice
slides.notes: This is the slide to memorize. Two rows are low certainty and three are very low. Four of the five say, in effect, choose by availability and cost because the outcomes look similar. Only the BMP-2 row steers away from an option, and it steers on harm and cost, not on fusion. Read the remarks, because they narrow the rows. The autograft row means structural iliac crest graft only; the remarks say it does not address morselized local autograft (bone dust) packed in a cage, which is what many surgeons actually use. It applies to PEEK or titanium cages. It tells you to discuss donor-site morbidity. The BMP row allows that BMP-2 may be reasonable in some situations, but asks for close monitoring for anterior soft tissue complications such as dysphagia. Two wording tensions to notice. First, the autograft row lists DBM as an example osteobiologic, yet its own evidence summary says DBM was not assessed in those studies. Second, the BMP row suggests avoiding BMP with a cage, while the hybrid row lists BMP-2 as an acceptable fusion-level option. The paper does not reconcile these; our guess is that the hybrid row simply lists what its few studies used. Also note that allograft is an osteobiologic in row 1 and the comparator in row 2; row 2's review is of structural allograft, by its topic title.

slides.title: Evidence: autograft and allograft
slides.lead: Small, mostly non-randomized, and summarized as ranges.

rows: Fusion difference 0-12%, favoring autograft; reoperation difference 3-4%
Allograft vs ceramic glass or DBM
3 comparative; 2 at lower risk of bias (n = 110)
Fusion difference 0-14% at 1 year, 3% at 2 years

points: Pain (one study, n = 71): VAS fell 2 points with allograft, 1.2 with osteobiologic
Non-comparative complications (18 studies): dysphagia or dysphonia 0.4-22%, wound 0-7%, new deficit 0-1.9%, radiculopathy 0-2%
slides.notes: Recomputed: 14/172 is 8.1% and 24/107 is 22.4%, so the printed 8% and 22% hold. The 2 RCTs in the autograft comparison both used titanium devices, with cancellous allograft or a hydroxyapatite coating; neither tested PEEK, and none tested DBM. The fusion difference is printed as 'from 12 to 0% in favour of autograft'. Read that honestly: up to 12 points, always in autograft's direction, called 'little to no difference'. With 375 randomized patients across two trials, a modest real difference could not be excluded; that is our judgment, and the paper gives no confidence intervals to test it. Donor-site morbidity is the one consistent harm of autograft, and it nearly triples outside the RCTs. In the allograft row, the paper lists 3 reviews and then 3 comparative studies. Its phrase '1 included study' most likely means the first of the 3 reviews, not a count of studies; the wording is ambiguous, not a clear contradiction. The 'trivial difference' comes from the 2 lower-bias studies. The third, by its title in the reference list, reports more than 6-fold higher pseudarthrosis with PEEK than structural allograft in multilevel ACDF. That result is not discussed in the text, and it is the one finding here pointing clearly toward a graft. The rest of the allograft evidence is a comparison of ranges across separate case series, which is weak: a range of 68.5 to 100% will contain almost anything. Costs were judged variable and locally dependent, with cell-based allografts likely costlier.

slides.title: Evidence: BMP-2, levels, hybrids

rows: Fusion about 98% and 87%; dysphagia 26% vs 21%; other soft tissue 27% vs 20%
8 comparative; very little at 3 or more levels
No difference in fusion, pain or function reported
Dysphagia 0-14% allograft vs 1-22% osteobiologic; wound 0-2% allograft (one study 23%, 43/188) vs 0-7%
7 publications, no direct comparison; fusion data n = 99

points: 3-level ACDF with osteobiologics: very few to no complications in 3 studies (n = 96)
Hybrid C2-C7 motion: fell 6.8 and 11.1 degrees with osteobiologics; fell 2.7 with iliac and rose 1.28 with allograft
Revision ACDF: no evidence found
slides.notes: BMP-2 first. The paper writes: there may be no difference in fusion with BMP at doses above or below 0.75 mg per level or with autograft, allograft or other osteobiologics, about 98% and 87%, respectively. The sentence does not say which group is 98%. If it is BMP versus comparators, an 11-point gap is being called possibly no difference. Flag it as unclear. The harm signal is small in absolute terms, 5 to 7 points more soft tissue complications, regardless of dose, and the effect of dose was inconsistent. The recommendation against BMP-2 rests on that signal plus cost, at very low certainty. Excluding large retrospective databases was a deliberate choice, for reporting bias. Single versus multi-level: the reassurance at 3 levels is 96 patients in 3 studies. Calling complications similar while one allograft study reported 23% wound complications is generous; the paper does not explain that outlier. Hybrids: no study compared graft choices within hybrid surgery; studies compared hybrid surgery with ACDF or TDR alone. So the hybrid recommendation is extrapolated from single arms. The authors count 7 studies and note themselves that the South Korean cohort was reported in 2 publications, so 6 cohorts. Pain fell 3.4 to 6.5 points and NDI 18% to 47% across arms. The hybrid search ran 2000 to 2021, later than the October 2020 cutoff stated for Topics 1, 2, 4b and 4c.

slides.title: Critical appraisal: gaps and errors
points: Strengths: GIN-McMaster checklist, a review per question, GRADE EtD frameworks, external review, honest certainty ratings
Evidence base: few, small, mostly non-randomized studies and case series; the authors say so
Similar outcomes is inferred from no detected difference, without confidence intervals
Many comparisons set ranges from separate case series side by side
No data on comorbidities; no evidence for revision ACDF
Internal inconsistencies: DBM named but not studied; BMP-2 discouraged yet listed for hybrids; 98% vs 87% unassigned
Undisclosed in our copy: funding and conflicts; the EtD judgments sit in a supplement we did not read
slides.notes: Credit the method: this is a properly built GRADE guideline, and it rates its own evidence low or very low without spin. The weakness is the evidence, and how 'similar' is used. Most summaries report no detected difference and then conclude equivalence. With small studies and no intervals, absence of evidence is being read as evidence of absence; that is our critique. The paper itself ties the conditional strength to low or very low certainty evidence from few, small, non-randomized studies. Second, ranges. Fusion of 68.5 to 100% with allograft versus 73% and 100% with osteobiologics is called similar, but ranges that wide cannot distinguish much. Third, inconsistencies inside the paper: DBM is offered as an example in the autograft row although none of those studies assessed it; the BMP sentence gives 98% and 87% 'respectively' without saying which is which; a third allograft study whose title reports more than 6-fold higher pseudarthrosis with PEEK is not discussed. Minor: the survey order lists ceramic 9% after cancellous allograft 8%, and the text has the typo 'ADCF'. Fourth, applicability: the autograft row covers structural iliac crest only, not local bone in a cage; the evidence for 3 or more levels is tiny; and cost was judged locally dependent, so the guideline hands that judgment back to you. Finally, the Evidence-to-Decision frameworks, which show how the panel weighed each criterion, are in Supplement 1, which we did not read, and our copy has no conflict-of-interest statement. Osteobiologics are a commercial field, so a reader should check those disclosures in the published version.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: Spoken summary, about 30 seconds.
points: The 2024 AO Spine osteobiologics guideline for degenerative ACDF used 15 systematic reviews and GRADE. It made five suggestions, all conditional, on low or very low certainty evidence.

Structural iliac crest autograft, allograft and a cage with an osteobiologic gave similar fusion and complications, so choose by availability, cost and setting. Autograft adds donor-site morbidity: 8% in RCTs, 22% in non-randomized studies.
Avoid BMP-2 in common cases: soft tissue complications and dysphagia ran 5 to 7 points higher, and it costs more.
Osteobiologics are acceptable at one or several levels and at the fusion level of a hybrid. There is no recommendation for revision ACDF.

Expect: Does this cover local bone in a cage? No. Is the cage as good as autograft? No difference was detected, up to 12 points favoring autograft, at low certainty. Why not BMP-2? Harm and cost. Is BMP-2 ever acceptable? The authors allow it in some situations, with monitoring. What about revision or high-risk patients? No evidence.
slides.notes: Practice the summary aloud with the certainty level attached to every claim. The guideline earns its place by stating clearly how thin the comparative evidence is. If asked what the guideline actually changes, our view is very little, apart from the BMP-2 row: it confirms that common graft choices are reasonable and moves the decision to cost and availability. Likely follow-ups and answers. Does it apply to PEEK? Yes, the first row covers PEEK or titanium cages, but the two RCTs used titanium. Is DBM supported? It is named in the first recommendation, but those studies did not assess it, and in the allograft comparison the comparators were ceramic glass or DBM. Is allograft as good as a cage? The 2 lower-bias studies, n = 110, found fusion differences of 0 to 14% at 1 year; the evidence is very low certainty, and one multilevel PEEK study reported much higher pseudarthrosis, by its title. Multilevel? 8 comparative studies, very little at 3 or more levels, and 96 patients in the 3-level complication data. Hybrid? No direct comparisons of graft choices; fusion data on 99 patients. Comorbidities such as smoking or diabetes? No data found, so no guidance. Revision? No evidence and no recommendation. Who funded it, and were there conflicts? Not in our copy; check the published version. Our inference: the most useful practical lesson is the donor-site figure, which is the one harm consistently attributed to one option.

decks.not_reviewed: Not read: the Evaniew systematic review, the focus-issue introduction and methods articles, the companion decompression guideline, the appendix of external reviewers and societies, the conflict disclosures, and the primary studies in Tables 1-5. The library PDF is a reformatted PMC text with figures omitted; the paper appears to have no figures.

slides.title: SCI hemodynamics guideline
slides.lead: How high to push MAP after acute traumatic spinal cord injury, for how long, and with which drug.
points: Journal club: acute spinal cord injury
Kwon BK, et al. Global Spine J 2024;14(3 Suppl):187S-211S. AO Spine/Praxis guideline.

Bottom line: suggest MAP at least 75-80 mmHg, with no active augmentation above 90-95 mmHg, for 3-7 days. Both are weak recommendations on very low quality evidence. No specific vasopressor and no SCPP target is recommended.
slides.notes:
What this is: the AO Spine and Praxis Spinal Cord Institute update of the 2013 AANS/CNS hemodynamic recommendation, which said keep MAP between 85 and 90 mmHg for 7 days. It is one chapter of a focus issue; the companion decompression timing guideline, the methods paper and the systematic review by Evaniew et al are separate articles and were not read here.

The frame to carry through the deck: these are numbers chosen by vote from associations in observational data. No included study compared one MAP target or one duration against another. The authors say so directly. Read every number on the next slides as a consensus range, not a dose-response threshold.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: The 2013 target of 85-90 mmHg for 7 days was narrow, hard to hold, and loosely followed.
points: 2013 AANS/CNS: cardiac, hemodynamic and respiratory monitoring, correct SBP below 90 mmHg, keep MAP 85-90 mmHg for 7 days. Literature reviewed to 2011.
Authors' reasons to revise: new MAP and SCPP studies since 2011; a 5 mmHg window cannot be held with vasopressors; centers read it as 85 or above, or 85-95.
Key questions: lower and upper MAP limit, duration, choice of vasopressor or inotrope, and SCPP targets.
Population: adults with acute traumatic SCI.

rows: Correct SBP below 90 mmHg as soon as possible

slides.notes:
The authors make three arguments for revisiting the MAP target. First, MAP augmentation is one of the few treatments for acute SCI and the literature grew after the 2011 cutoff of the old review. Second, the cord is sensitive to small pressure changes: they point to raising MAP when neuromonitoring signals drop, to CSF drainage in thoracoabdominal aneurysm repair, and to one report that average MAP differed by only 2-3 mmHg over the first 3 days between patients who improved by an AIS grade and those who did not. Third, the 2013 wording, between 85 and 90 mmHg, may have been unintentional, since the cited studies did not test such a narrow band, and it cannot be maintained in practice.

Note the endorsement of the first two 2013 statements. The 2013 monitoring statement does not name the ICU; ICU care comes from the authors' discussion, which also allows step-down care for mild central cord syndrome. The authors state this step was expert opinion only and did not follow GRADE. Ninety percent agreed to address the three statements separately rather than adopt 2013 as is.

The authors also say the 2013 target came largely from Levi and Vale. Vale's own patients were weaned before 7 days if they held MAP above 85 mmHg off pressors and were stable. So the 7-day number was never firm even in its source. That is worth saying aloud, because the 7-day rule is often treated as fixed.

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: A systematic review fed a one-day GRADE panel that voted anonymously.
points: Panel at the meeting: 20. Eleven spine surgeons, 3 critical or neurocritical care, 2 neurologists, 1 physiatrist, 1 first responder, 2 people living with SCI.
Evidence: Evaniew et al systematic review, PRISMA, PROSPERO registered, GRADE certainty.
Meeting: Zoom, November 5, 2022, GRADE Guideline Development Tool, anonymous votes.
Consensus threshold: 80%.
Critical outcomes: AIS grade or ASIA motor score change, and adverse events such as arrhythmia, MI, hypertensive hemorrhage, stroke and skin necrosis.
Funding: AO Foundation, AO Spine, Praxis. Methodology support from Aggregate Analytics.
slides.notes:
This is a guideline, so read it for selection of evidence, how the panel turned it into numbers, and validity.

Selection: the evidence comes from one updated systematic review cited as in review. Its search dates, inclusion criteria and study count are not given in this paper. For MAP limits the panel used 14 studies on a lower limit, 3 on an upper limit and 5 on adverse events. For duration, 14 studies. Tables 1 (lower limit) and 4 (duration) list the same 14 studies. Table 2 (upper limit) is Ehsanian, Hawryluk and Hogg, all also in Table 1. Tables 3 and 5 (harms, vasopressors) are mostly a separate set: Inoue and two Readdy series from UCSF, plus Vale and Weinberg in Table 3.

Measurement: outcomes in those studies were AIS grade conversion or ASIA motor score change, measured anywhere from within the first week to 1 year after injury. Some measured MAP every minute, some intermittently, one only during surgery, one only the first 24 hours. Several were single-severity groups, such as AIS A only (Cohn) or AIS C only (Hogg).

Process: twenty members took part. Our observation: many reported percentages fit 17, 18 or 19 voters rather than 20. For example 63%, 32% and 5% fit 12, 6 and 1 of 19. The upper-limit split of 70%, 18% and 12% cannot be produced exactly by any panel of 20 or fewer; 17 voters (71, 18, 12) comes closest. The paper never states the denominators, so a 2-person swing can move a result by more than 10 points.

The authors state members disclosed conflicts and were editorially independent of funders. The detailed disclosures are in the methods paper and appendix, not reviewed here. The authors report an AGREE II internal appraisal and external review by stakeholders and societies; the AANS/CNS joint committee and NASS reviewed the focus issue without endorsing it.

slides.title: The recommendations
slides.lead: Two weak suggestions and one deliberate non-recommendation.

rows: Suggest at least 75-80 mmHg, not augmented above 90-95 mmHg

points: Lower limit vote: 75 mmHg 32%, 80 mmHg 63%, 85 mmHg 5%. Nobody chose 60, 65, 70 or 90.
Upper limit vote: 90 mmHg 12%, 95 mmHg 70%, no upper limit 18%.
Duration vote: 5 days 50%, 3 days 30%, 7 days 10%, 1-2 days 5%, no duration 5%. 82% agreed to the 3-7 day range.
Vasopressor: 89% voted to leave the choice to the treating physician.
The upper limit applies only to active augmentation. A patient who sits above 95 mmHg on their own is not treated down.
slides.notes:
Read the upper limit carefully, because it is the most misquoted part. The authors give the example of a patient at 125/80, MAP 95, with no vasopressors: no treatment is needed. The ceiling means do not use fluids or pressors to push MAP above 90-95. It is not a trigger for antihypertensives.

Why ranges at each end? The authors anticipated the question: if a 5 mmHg window was the problem, why use 75-80 and 90-95? Their answer is that aiming at or above 75-80 should mean fewer dips below 75, and approaching 90-95 cautiously should mean fewer excursions above 95. In effect the hard floor is 75 and the hard ceiling is 95, with a buffer at each end. That is the authors' reasoning, not a tested result.

On the target, only 78% agreed the balance of effects probably favors the intervention, below the 80% consensus threshold (95% for duration); the process went on anyway. 89% judged that desirable consequences outweighed undesirable ones; 84% chose suggest and 16% recommend. The final wording passed with more than 85%. Some members still worried that 75-80 is too low.

On duration, the same split was reported, 89% and 84 versus 16, and the final wording passed with more than 90%. Members worried the 3-day end would be abused to stop management early in patients who might benefit. Acceptability was only 61%, with 39% uncertain.

Feasibility had no consensus for either: for the target, 28% uncertain, 50% probably yes, 6% yes, 17% varies. The authors tie that to low and middle income settings without ICU capacity.

Timeline: they plan review at 3 to 5 years after publication.

slides.title: What the evidence shows
slides.lead: Associations from small observational cohorts, read in both directions.
points: Lower limit: 14 studies. Nine tie worse recovery to MAP below 65 to 85 mmHg; five found no association.
Upper limit: 3 studies. Ehsanian, Hawryluk and Hogg saw no further gain at or above 95 mmHg.

Harms: 3 UCSF series reported complications in 74%, 91% and 94% of patients on vasopressors, mostly heart-rate changes. The text says all three targeted MAP 85 or above, but Table 3 lists no MAP goal for Inoue.
Weinberg: complications 28.3% with vasopressors vs 10.0% without, OR 3.6 (95% CI 1.0-12.6), a lower bound at 1.0, so borderline. Elevated MAP itself was not linked to complications.
Dopamine vs phenylephrine complications: 69.2% vs 46.5% (Inoue), 68% vs 45%, nonsignificant (Readdy, central cord), 76% vs 40% (Readdy, penetrating).
Duration: no study compared durations. Hawryluk, Haldrup and Squair point to the first 1-3 days mattering most.

rows: AIS improved 11% if MAP fell below 85 for over 2 h vs 57% if not
Admission MAP below 75 vs 85 or above; 1-week mean MAP not related
Proportion of MAPs 85 or above, per 10%
Lowest MAP separating no change from 1 grade gain

slides.notes:
How to read this slide: every effect is an association between recorded MAP and recovery. Sicker patients are harder to keep at target, so low MAP may mark severity rather than cause poor recovery. The authors note this themselves through Martin: patients with more hypotensive episodes had worse admission motor scores. Martin, Chen, Park, Saadoun and Sewell found no link between MAP and recovery, and Sewell's checklist reduced hypotensive episodes without changing AIS conversion.

The Dakson interval runs from 1.6 to 75.6. The paper does not give Dakson's sample size; our inference is that the width reflects few events. Our recomputation from 11% vs 57% gives an unadjusted OR of about 10.7, close to the printed 11.1. Only 20% of its patients avoided a 2-hour dip below 85, which supports the authors' point that 85 or above is hard to hold.

SCPP: the Papadopoulos group measured pressure at the injury site and the Kwon group used a lumbar intrathecal catheter. Both report recovery tracks SCPP better than MAP, and the optimal SCPP may differ between patients. The panel still chose a MAP target because SCPP monitoring is rare and injury-site and lumbar pressures can differ when the subarachnoid space is closed. The CASPER trial (NCT03911492) is the one to watch.

Vasopressor choice: no included study tested norepinephrine. The authors describe a clinical crossover study (Altaf, Kwon group) in acute SCI patients in which dopamine raised intrathecal pressure independent of MAP, lowering SCPP. From that they remark that, if the clinician is otherwise indifferent, norepinephrine may have an SCPP advantage over dopamine. Separately, in pigs, Streijger found norepinephrine better than phenylephrine at restoring cord perfusion, and Williams found dobutamine better than norepinephrine at restoring cardiac output and cord oxygenation, which the authors use to argue for a cardio-centric approach in some patients. None of this is a recommendation.

Duration: Haldrup reported a significant MAP-outcome relation only in days 1-2, but the authors point out that the paper's own figure shows nearly identical median MAPs across outcome groups.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: A transparent process sitting on weak evidence, with several internal inconsistencies.
points: Holds up: GRADE process, an 80% consensus threshold, anonymous votes, people living with SCI on the panel.
Holds up: evidence labeled very low and recommendations labeled weak; authors say no study compared targets or durations.
Fragile: the cutoffs come from a vote. Nobody chose 70 mmHg, although Cohn, Squair and Ehsanian point to 70.
Fragile: GRADE was applied to the whole body of evidence, not separately to lower and upper limit studies. The authors disclose this as a limitation.
Fragile: only 78% agreed the balance of effects favors the MAP target, below the 80% threshold.
Fragile: vote denominators are not reported. Our arithmetic suggests 17-19 voters on many items, not 20.
Fragile: upper limit evidence is 3 studies, and Ehsanian's 95-104 mmHg effect had P = .764.
Errors: Squair motor-score OR printed as .16 with CI .36 to .69, which cannot contain its own estimate.
Errors: Tables 1 and 4 disagree for Dakson, Hogg, Weinberg and Ehsanian follow-up, and text and tables disagree on Chen's target and Squair's monitoring.
slides.notes:
Recomputation. Vote totals add up: lower limit 32+63+5, upper 12+70+18, duration 50+30+10+5+5, all 100. Feasibility sums to 101 for target and duration, which is rounding. Resource votes for the target sum to 95% (78 moderate, 6 large, 11 do not know). Weinberg's OR 3.6 recomputes from 28.3% vs 10.0% as about 3.55; its interval (1.0-12.6) is symmetric but the lower bound sits at 1.0, so the vasopressor-complication link is borderline. Dakson, Park and Squair's "more likely to improve" ORs look symmetric on the log scale. Squair's hypotension-episode AIS OR 1 (0.98-1.1) does not: the upper arm is nearly 5 times the lower, consistent only with an OR near 1.04 printed as 1. Weinberg's HR 1.17 (1.03-1.42) is also asymmetric; we cannot check it from this paper.

Flat errors to flag:
1. Squair, Table 1: motor score OR .16, 95% CI .36 to .69. An estimate cannot lie outside its interval; likely a typo.
2. Squair monitoring: subdural probe at the injury site (Table 1) vs lumbar intrathecal drain (text).
3. Chen: target 85-95 (tables) vs 85-90 (text); outcome AIS grade at 2 weeks (tables) vs motor recovery (text); Table 1 suggests benefit, text lists it as null.
4. Dakson outcome: rehab discharge, about 252 days (Table 1) vs acute admission, about 22 days (Table 4, Cohn's wording).
5. Timing: Hogg, Weinberg, Ehsanian follow-up differ between Tables 1 and 4; Squair low SCPP 36 h (text) vs 48 h (Table 4).
6. Ehsanian lowest band: 50-64 (Lower Limit column), 50-69 (Table 1 Results and Conclusions), 50-65 (body text).
7. Cohn outcome: motor score in tables, AIS grade in duration text.
8. Both recommendations are numbered Recommendation 1.
9. "Similar to part 1" in part 2: inequity 89% vs 95%, outcome values 89% vs 88%.
10. Text says all 3 UCSF series targeted MAP 85 or above; Table 3 lists no goal for Inoue.
11. Text says one of the largest studies found no vasopressor-adverse event link; no study in Tables 3 or 5 matches, and Weinberg found the opposite.

None of these changes the recommendations, but the tables were not cross-checked. Our view: the voted cutoffs are reasonable compromises, not thresholds the evidence identified.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "After acute traumatic SCI, the 2024 AO Spine/Praxis guideline suggests MAP at least 75-80 mmHg, and do not use pressors to push it above 90-95, for 3 to 7 days. Both are weak suggestions on very low quality, observational evidence. Choice of pressor is left to the physician, and there is no SCPP target yet."
points: Expect: why lower than 85? Answer: several studies tied worse recovery to MAP below 70-80, and others found no link at all. The panel voted, 63% for 80 and 32% for 75.
Expect: should I lower a MAP of 100? Answer: not if it is the patient's own pressure. If pressors or fluids are driving it, wean them: support should not exceed 90-95 mmHg.
Expect: 3 or 7 days? Answer: no study compared durations. The first days seem to matter most; the authors leave the choice to the clinician.
Expect: which pressor? Answer: no recommendation. Dopamine had more complications than phenylephrine in UCSF series. No included study tested norepinephrine's safety or effectiveness.
Expect: what about SCPP? Answer: promising but not widely used. No target was set; CASPER is ongoing.
slides.notes:
Spoken summary in under a minute: this guideline replaces 85-90 for 7 days with a floor of 75-80, a ceiling of 90-95 for augmentation only, and 3 to 7 days. The change widens the window, lowers the floor, and raises and clarifies the ceiling (2013 said between 85 and 90, but some centers read it as having no upper limit), because the evidence for 85 was mixed, the narrow band was impossible to hold, and vasopressors carry frequent if usually minor cardiac complications. Everything rests on observational associations and a panel vote. The panel itself was not unanimous: 18% wanted no upper limit and some feared 75-80 was too low.

Harder questions to prepare for:

Is a low MAP causing worse recovery, or marking a worse injury? The authors say no study showed causation. Martin found more hypotensive episodes in patients with worse admission motor scores, which fits confounding by severity.

Why not run a trial? The authors think a randomized trial of MAP targets is almost impossible given the history of acute SCI trials, and call instead for high-quality prospective studies with creative designs. They suggest machine learning on large databases specifically for the vasopressor adverse-event question, and name injury-site monitoring as a knowledge gap.

Does this apply to central cord syndrome or mild injury? The authors say the literature does not address severity and that mild central cord patients may be managed in a step-down unit for monitoring. The recommendation itself does not separate by severity.

What is the cost? The panel judged costs moderate (78% for the target, 83% for duration) and could not judge cost-effectiveness. Feasibility had no consensus.

Tell the room about the numbering error and the Squair interval if anyone quotes the tables directly.

decks.not_reviewed: The 2016 two-year report (reference 8) and its supplementary appendix, which this paper cites for the sample size reasoning, procedural settings, health economy, surgical details and complications; the two-year MRI report (reference 16); and the Swedish protocol (reference 38). The 8-page PDF is the complete article and cites no supplement of its own.

slides.title: Karlsson 2024: Decompression alone or with fusion for lumbar stenosis, five-year results
slides.lead: Bottom line: adding fusion did not improve ODI at 5 years, with or without a slip, and subsequent surgery was similar at 24% with fusion and 22% without.
points: Journal club · Lumbar stenosis and degenerative slip
Karlsson T, et al. Bone Joint J 2024;106-B(7):705-12
Swedish Spinal Stenosis Study, ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01994512
slides.notes: This is the five-year clinical follow-up of the Swedish Spinal Stenosis Study, the same trial as the 2016 two-year report. It is not a new trial and not a replication. Same patients, longer look. The deck comes from the complete 8-page article. The two-year report and its appendix hold the sample size reasoning, surgical details and complications, and they were not reviewed here, so this deck says nothing about operative burden beyond what this paper states. Three things to hold onto. First, the primary result is a neutral ODI, in the same direction and about the same size as at two years: the library record gives 27 fusion vs 24 alone at 2 years, and here it is 28 vs 25. Second, the authors go further than neutral: they conclude that their results support decompression alone as the preferred method. That rests partly on three secondary results, which we will take apart. Third, patients with a slip were found on supine films, with no dynamic views, so this trial cannot speak to measured instability.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: Does fusion added to decompression give better five-year outcomes in central lumbar stenosis, with or without a slip?
points: Why fusion was added: to prevent instability and recurrent stenosis at the decompressed segment, particularly with a slip.
The cost, per the authors: longer surgery, more bleeding, longer stay, higher cost, more severe complications in older patients, and possibly more cranial adjacent degeneration.
The gap: a recent meta-analysis found no functional difference at two years in stenosis with a slip, and called for longer-term studies.
P: age 50-80, 1 or 2 adjacent stenotic segments, with or without a slip of 3 mm or more
I: decompression plus fusion
C: decompression alone
O: ODI at 5 years
slides.notes: Set the stakes with the authors' own framing. Fusion was added by tradition, to protect the segment. They cite US data: among stenosis patients without spondylolisthesis, the proportion fused rose from 17.8 percent in 2004 to 26.2 percent in 2009. The two-year report from this trial showed no advantage of fusion, regardless of slip, and the two-year MRI work showed less new stenosis after decompression alone. So the honest question at five years is the late one: does fusion pay off with time, as the instability argument would predict? If decompressed segments were going to slip, fail and need rescue, five years is when you might expect the curves to turn. That reading is ours, not the authors'. The authors say simply that further long-term studies were needed. Note the population is broader than SLIP and NORDSTEN-DS, which both took single-level slips. This trial took one or two levels, with or without a slip. Also note what was stratified: only the presence of a slip of 3 mm or more on supine lateral films. Keep in mind that a subset of 91 patients had a single-level slip, the population closest to those two trials.

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: Open-label superiority trial at seven Swedish sites, recruiting September 2006 to February 2012.
points: 358 assessed, 111 excluded, 247 randomized 1:1, stratified by slip.
Included: pseudoclaudication with back pain over 30 of 100, dural sac 75 mm2 or less, symptoms over 6 months.
Excluded: spondylolysis, Cobb over 20 degrees, prior surgery for stenosis or instability, stenosis from a herniated disc.
Fusion method was the surgeon's choice: 102 instrumented posterolateral, 6 uninstrumented, 5 PLIF. All had central decompression.
Decompression alone: 97 central, 23 bilateral laminotomies.
Mean slip 7.3 mm. Baseline ODI 41 to 43. Mean age 67.
Powered for ODI 12 or more and VAS 20 or more.
slides.notes: Read the flow diagram before believing 95 percent. It is 213 of 225, and the 225 excludes the 14 who never had surgery, the 6 who died and the 2 too ill to answer. Against the 247 randomized it is 213, or 86 percent. By arm that is 101 of 123 (82 percent) and 112 of 124 (90 percent). These percentages are ours; a simple test gives P about 0.06. The flow arithmetic adds up: 113 less 12 is 101, and 120 less 8 is 112. The gap in who got surgery matters: 10 of 123 fusion patients did not, against 4 of 124. Three of those 10 were randomized in error. The whole report runs on the 233 who had the assigned surgery, including Table II, which means there is no intention-to-treat analysis in this paper. The library record for the 2016 report calls that primary analysis per protocol. This paper does not use the term. The paper states that patients, surgeons, radiologists, research nurses and statisticians were all unblinded. Questionnaires came from Swespine at 1, 2 and 5 years. Our count from Table II: 13 of 232 patients with MRI measured over 75 mm2, 8 fusion and 5 alone. The recruiting surgeon decided entry, and a spine surgeon took these measures after the study ended. Baseline is described as not different, with no P values printed. We recomputed age, ODI, EQ-5D, VAS, dural area, smoking and ASA by stratum and pooled, and nothing fails: every P is 0.15 or more. The two lowest are women without a slip, 41 vs 56 percent, and women overall, 62 vs 71 percent. Fusion had fewer women in both strata, and a stratified Mantel-Haenszel test gives P about 0.10, stronger than either figure. Table II covers the 233 treated, not everyone randomized. No baseline table exists for the 213 analyzed, the set the primary result rests on, and attrition differed by arm.

slides.title: Primary outcome: ODI at 5 years
slides.lead: ODI did not differ, and both the paper's interval for change and our interval for the 5-year means exclude the 12-point effect the trial was powered for.
points: ODI fell 14 with fusion (95% CI 10 to 17) and 16 alone (95% CI 13 to 19).
95% CI for the difference in change: -2 to 8. The Discussion calls change in ODI a secondary outcome.
Primary 5-year mean difference: 3 points, no CI printed. Ours from the means and SDs: about -2.4 to 8.4.
1-level slip: fell 11 vs 18, 95% CI for the difference -1 to 16.
Both arms ended in the paper's moderate band, ODI 21 to 40.
slides.notes: The number that matters is the interval, not the P value, so be clear which one. The paper prints no CI for the primary 5-year mean difference. Ours is about -2.4 to 8.4. The printed -2 to 8 is for change from baseline. Both lead to the same conclusion. The paper does not state the sign convention. By our reading a positive difference favors decompression alone, because the fall was larger in that arm. On that reading, -2 to 8 means fusion is unlikely to be more than about 2 ODI points better over the whole group, and the study's 12-point target is excluded in either direction. That is a stronger statement than not significant. It is ours, and it needs a caution. This is a superiority trial, so the authors' phrase that decompression alone confers no inferior outcome is an interval reading and not a tested noninferiority claim. The library record for the 2016 report makes the same point. Subgroups are a different story. The 1-level slip interval of -1 to 16 still argues against a useful fusion benefit, but its upper end passes 12, so a large advantage for decompression alone is not excluded either. With a slip overall, our approximate interval from the printed means and SDs for the mean difference is -2 to 12. We recomputed P values and intervals from the printed figures. ODI gives 0.28 against 0.226, and the slip subset 0.17 against 0.152. The largest gap is VAS back, 0.47 against 0.366. That needs a true difference of about 3.8, which only just fits rounding of 38 vs 35. The -2 to 8 has midpoint 3 against 16 minus 14, which is 2: rounding, and its width fits the arm CIs. EQ-5D gain 0.01 to 0.21, 1-level -1 to 16 and -0.10 to 0.23 fit their arm CIs too. No interval fails. Subset means reweight correctly to the overall means, 27.6 and 24.8. The 5-year analysis was an unadjusted independent-samples t-test on patients who answered, and the paper describes no imputation. Baseline ODI was 41 to 43 by subset, so both arms show a large fall at 5 years. There is no surgery-free control, so that fall cannot be credited wholly to surgery.

slides.title: Secondary outcomes and harms
slides.lead: EQ-5D favored decompression alone. VAS back and leg pain and reoperation did not differ.
points: Subsequent surgery after decompression: 26 patients, 19 for index-level restenosis or foraminal stenosis, 14 fused at the decompressed level.
After fusion: 27 patients, 23 for adjacent stenosis, 9 extensions. None at the distal adjacent level.
Wound infection revisions 6 fusion, 3 alone. These are not counted as reoperations.
slides.see: Figure 2 shows reoperation curves where decompression alone drops earlier, then the two meet by about year 3 and stay together to year 5, near 0.77.
slides.notes: The authors list three secondary outcomes favoring decompression alone. Count them with care. Two of the three are EQ-5D, the level and its change, so they are one finding measured twice. The third is a patient-reported global question in one subset. That leg-pain subset result has no matching signal on the leg VAS, 34 vs 32 in that same no-slip group (P=0.751), as the authors themselves say. The authors state no adjustment for multiple testing was made. Our count: 8 outcomes across 3 strata is 24 comparisons in Table III, before reoperation and the 1-level subgroup, so about one false positive is expected by chance. A Bonferroni line across the 7 secondary outcomes in the Methods would be about 0.007, or about 0.006 for 9 if the Discussion's change in ODI and EQ-5D gain count, before subsets. 0.027 clears neither. For the leg-pain split, our rough interaction test comparing RR 0.71 with RR 0.95 gives P about 0.14, and the paper reports no interaction test. So treat all of this as signals. Our recomputation of EQ-5D gave P about 0.02 from rounded data, and the relative risks reproduce. The paper gives no minimal important difference for EQ-5D. In our judgment reoperation is the most useful clinical result. The rates were similar and did not differ significantly, but RR 1.1 (0.69 to 1.8) is compatible with about 31 percent fewer to 80 percent more reoperations with fusion, so equality is not shown. The failure mode differs. Decompression alone mostly failed at the index level, 19 of 26, and 14 of those 26 went on to fusion there: 12 percent of 120, our arithmetic. Fusion mostly failed at the adjacent level, 23 of 27, cranially by the paper's account, since none was distal. Causes of the other 7 and 4 are not given. It says 23 had adjacent stenosis but only 9 had extension, and it does not say what the rest had. Indications were not standardized, and surgeons knew the allocation. Figure 2 is the paper's, and no time-specific test is reported. The pattern looks like NORDSTEN-DS, where the library record, using that paper's table, notes earlier operations after decompression and later ones after fusion, though its text and table conflict. Revisions for wound infection, 8 of 9 within 3 months, sit outside these rates. Deaths were 4 vs 2. This paper does not report other complications, blood loss or operating time.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: Holds up: randomized by computer with stratification by slip; seven sites; high retention among survivors; ODI intervals exclude the target effect (printed for change, ours for the 5-year means); reoperations from a registry plus medical records.

Weakens it: open label with patient-reported outcomes; analysis of treated patients only; 82% vs 90% of randomized patients analyzed; no multiplicity adjustment; reoperation indications not standardized.
Cannot answer: instability, sagittal alignment and developmental stenosis were not assessed. Newer fusion and minimally invasive techniques were not evaluated.
Source errors: the Discussion puts the leg-pain finding in the slip subset, but the Results, abstract and Table III put it in patients without a slip. Other errors are in the notes.
slides.notes: Be fair: this is a real multicentre randomized trial, and the authors name their main limit themselves. No standing or flexion-extension films, so they may have underestimated slips and included patients with instability who would have been excluded from other studies. Their defenses: instability is ill defined, in NORDSTEN 21 percent had instability and fusion was not better in that subgroup, and in their two-year report slips over 7.4 mm did about the same. They also concede that unidentified subgroups who benefit may exist, and that spinopelvic malalignment and developmental stenosis were not addressed. Our note: fusion lost more patients between randomization and analysis, 22 vs 12, and the paper reports no sensitivity analysis. In our judgment that is unlikely to flip a 3-point gap, but it is untested. Source problems. One, Discussion says the leg-pain result was in the DS subset; Abstract, Results and Table III say no-DS. We use the table. Two, the abstract attaches 155 female (67 percent) to the 213 followed, but those figures fit the 233 treated: 155 of 213 would be 73 percent. Three, Figure 1 gives 67 and 68 with a slip among those assigned, and Table II gives the same 67 and 68 among those treated. Taken literally, all 14 untreated patients had no slip, which is very unlikely by chance, or else the Figure 1 counts are of treated patients. We cannot tell which. Four, global-question denominators are not printed. Ours from n, percent and RR: fusion 99, 94, 95, 98 and alone 110, 108, 102, 109 (satisfaction, back, leg, walking), below the 101 and 112 headers. All 12 RRs and CIs reproduce. Five, Figure 2 at-risk rows have no year 0 column; the first counts sit at year 1. The Results cite Figure 2 for stratification, but it shows the whole population. Six, Figure 1 says did not meet exclusion criteria, which must mean inclusion, and its randomization in error asterisk has no footnote. Seven, the Discussion lists four RCTs then says three, and gives SSSS as n = 233. Eight, change in ODI and in EQ-5D are secondary outcomes in the Discussion but not in the Methods list. Nine, Methods say reoperations are by allocated group, but the denominators are the treated 113 and 120. Ten, the statements that stratification and slip did not affect the results rest on no reported interaction test. Eleven, the 2016 record gives subsequent surgery 22 vs 21 percent at mean 6.5 years, lower than 24 vs 22 percent here at 5 years. We cannot resolve that.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: “In this Swedish trial, adding fusion to decompression did not improve ODI at 5 years, 28 vs 25, with or without a slip. Reoperation was similar at 24% vs 22%, but for different reasons: adjacent stenosis after fusion, index restenosis or foraminal stenosis after decompression. It was open label and did not assess instability.”

rows: ODI 28 fusion vs 25 alone; reop 24% vs 22%
SF-36 favored fusion, not after baseline adjustment; reop 14% fusion vs 34% alone
ODI response 63% each; noninferior; reop 18% fusion vs 16% alone

points: SLIP and NORDSTEN-DS come from the library records. Endpoints differ. The 135 for SSSS may be treated patients only; see Critical appraisal, problem three.
Do not stretch it: this says nothing about measured instability, deformity over 20 degrees, purely foraminal stenosis or newer techniques.
slides.notes: Expect these questions. Does this settle the unstable slip? No. Nobody had dynamic films. The paper's reassurance comes from NORDSTEN's subgroup and its own two-year post hoc look at slips over 7.4 mm, and neither is a randomized test of instability. Note SLIP excluded motion over 3 mm, per its library record, so it did not test it either. Is decompression alone better? The authors say their findings support decompression alone as the primary operative method for stenosis, even for patients with a slip, at lower risk and cost. They also state that 5-year ODI did not differ and that secondary outcomes were not adjusted for multiple testing. Our addition is that the risk and cost claim leans on outside sources such as reference 5, an older-adult study, not on data in this paper. The defensible statement is no added benefit from fusion here, with a clear operative cost per the authors. What should I tell a patient about reoperation? Similar either way, a little under 1 in 4 at 5 years, but the interval is wide, so equality is not shown. With decompression alone the next operation may well be a fusion at that level; with fusion it may be an extension or surgery at the level above. Those are the authors' reported patterns; the patient counseling framing is ours. Does the slip subset change the answer? ODI was 28 vs 23, nonsignificant and pointing away from fusion. The authors found no trend suggesting patients with a slip benefit more from fusion, and they say their conclusion holds even for patients with a slip. Why does SLIP disagree? It was small, single-level, with a full laminectomy and partial medial facet removal, and its SF-36 result did not survive baseline adjustment, per its library record. The authors add that an associated editorial read SLIP as no difference. How does the NORDSTEN comparison hold? Better, but the design differs: single-level slips on standing films, noninferiority, and a responder endpoint. This report is a later look at the same trial as the 2016 paper, so count the Swedish trial once when weighing the evidence.

decks.not_reviewed: The Supplementary Appendix (Tables S1 to S13, including full eligibility criteria, grip strength results, the per-protocol and as-treated tables, the full adverse event list in Table S11, and the descriptions of the surgical and nonsurgical treatments and of blinding), the trial protocol and statistical analysis plan, and the companion publications on the nonsurgical intervention (reference 20) and expected outcomes (reference 31).

slides.title: Taso 2025: ACDF versus rehabilitation
slides.lead: Two Norwegian randomized trials, one for disc herniation and one for spondylosis, each comparing ACDF with a brief nonsurgical program.
points: Journal club: cervical radiculopathy
Taso M, Sommernes JH, et al. Surgical versus Nonsurgical Treatment for Cervical Radiculopathy. NEJM Evid 2025;4(4):EVIDoa2400404

Bottom line: at 12 months, ACDF lowered NDI by 7.4 points more than nonsurgical care in disc herniation (P=0.01). In spondylosis the difference was 2.3 points (P=0.52), with 11 of 46 nonsurgical patients crossing over to surgery.
Prepared from the full article. The Supplementary Appendix and protocol were not reviewed.
slides.notes: This is one paper reporting two separate randomized trials run side by side at Oslo University Hospital, registered together as NCT03674619 and funded by the Southern and Eastern Norway Regional Health Authority. Patients were first classified by imaging as disc herniation or spondylosis, then randomized within that trial. Keep the two trials apart in your head: they share a protocol, surgeons and rehabilitation team, but they are not one trial with a subgroup analysis, and the paper does not test whether the treatment effect differs between them. That last point is ours, and it matters later when someone says surgery works for soft disc but not for spondylosis. The comparison is ACDF against a six-session functional and cognitive program, not ACDF against no treatment. What was reviewed: the full 12-page article, including Tables 1 to 3 and Figures 1 and 2. Not reviewed: the Supplementary Appendix, which holds the grip strength numbers, the per-protocol and as-treated tables, the full adverse event table, and the description of blinding. Anything on those points in this deck is limited to what the main text says. The master record was built from the abstract only; this deck replaces that with a full-text reading.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: Does surgery beat structured nonsurgical care, and does the answer depend on whether the root is compressed by soft disc or by bone?
points: Background (authors): cervical radiculopathy often settles without specific treatment, yet ACDF rates are high and forecast to rise.
Gap (authors): only two small earlier RCTs compared surgery with nonsurgical care, and neither separated disc herniation from spondylosis. Two systematic reviews found no clear benefit to surgery.
Patients: ages 20 to 65, disabling arm pain for at least 3 months, C5/C6 and/or C6/C7 pathology
Intervention: ACDF with a stand-alone titanium cage
Comparison: three physiatrist and three physiotherapist sessions over 12 weeks
Outcome: Neck Disability Index (0 to 100) at 12 months
slides.notes: Set the stakes with the authors' framing. They cite an incidence of 83.2 per 100,000 and more than 1 million primary ACDFs in the United States between 2006 and 2013. The two earlier trials they mean are Persson 1997 and Engquist 2013 (references 3 and 4). Both were small, and neither split patients by pathology. The hypothesis behind the split is clinical: disc herniation tends to start suddenly, and spondylosis builds up over time. The authors also question the pathoanatomical idea that the root must be decompressed to get lasting relief. Notice what the question is not. It is not early versus delayed surgery: the median arm pain duration was 20 to 49 weeks depending on group, so these were chronic patients, all of whom the authors say would have been offered surgery outside the trial. It is also not about myelopathy, which was excluded, or levels other than C5/C6 and C6/C7. The NDI scale runs 0 to 100, higher is worse, and the paper cites a minimal important difference of 15 (Carreon 2010, reference 17). That MID was derived from change after cervical fusion in individual patients. Keep that in mind when the 7.4-point group difference appears on slide 4.

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: 1361 referrals screened, 180 randomized between October 2018 and January 2023.
points: Eligibility: NDI above 30 and arm pain NRS 4 or more; myelopathy excluded. Both MRI and CT were obtained.

Spondylosis meant bony narrowing and osteophytes causing lateral recess or foraminal stenosis; disc herniation meant an intraspinal or foraminal disc herniation without bony narrowing causing root impingement.
Randomization: computer-generated, 1:1, random block sizes, separately in each trial.
Surgery: seven neurosurgeons, always two operating together. Usually one level for disc herniation, one or two for spondylosis.
Nonsurgical: physiatrist visits at weeks 1, 5 and 12; physiotherapy at weeks 2, 3 and 8. No added analgesics or epidural steroid injections.
Power: 36 per group for 80% power to detect 12 NDI points (SD 18). Target was 100 per trial; recruitment stopped early during Covid-19.
slides.notes: Read the denominators. Both trials stopped short of the 100-patient target, but both stayed above the 72 needed by the power calculation. Our check: 2 x (1.96 + 0.84) squared x (18/12) squared gives about 35.3, so 36 per group is right. The 20% allowance in the target was meant to cover crossover and dropout together. In the spondylosis trial, nonsurgical crossover alone was 23.9%. That is our observation. Follow-up was high: 98% and 97% had 12-month data, and our recalculation of those percentages and of the Figure 1 arm counts agrees. Two things the paper calls intention to treat deserve a closer look. First, the primary analysis included only patients with 12-month data, analyzed as randomized. Strictly, that is a complete-case analysis. The mixed-model sensitivity analysis included everyone and gave similar results. Second, five patients assigned to surgery never had it because their symptoms resolved, and they stayed in the surgical arm, as they should. Baseline: the authors call the four groups similar, and Table 1 gives no P values. Our rough tests found no clear imbalance. Age in the disc trial (46 vs 43) gives P about 0.08, motor deficit (28.9% vs 43.2%) P about 0.16, and baseline NDI was 3 to 3.5 points higher in both surgical arms (P about 0.2 to 0.3). The one row that did reach nominal significance: hip or knee osteoarthritis in the spondylosis trial, 1 of 45 (2.2%) surgery vs 7 of 46 (15.2%) nonsurgical, chi-square P about 0.03 (Fisher about 0.06). It sits in the comparator arm and is unlikely to drive NDI, but name it. The ANCOVA adjusts for baseline NDI. Spondylosis patients had longer arm pain, and the spondylosis surgery arm had a longer median duration than its comparator. Note the Table 1 footnote: the levels listed for nonsurgical patients are the crossovers' operated levels. Blinding: patients reported outcomes knowing their treatment. Follow-up examiners were not blinded, per the paper. The paper says the statistician and primary investigator were blinded to the PROMs and analyzed data while blinded to assignment; the exact arrangement is in the appendix we did not read.

slides.title: Primary outcome: NDI at 12 months
slides.lead: Surgery won in disc herniation by 7.4 points; spondylosis showed 2.3 points with a confidence interval crossing zero.
points: Mean NDI fell in every arm. Our arithmetic from the printed means: disc 30.3 vs 21.4 points, spondylosis 23.7 vs 18.8.
Authors: the disc trial's upper bound (13) barely exceeds the planned 12-point difference and is below the 15-point MID.
slides.see: Figure 2 plots mean NDI at baseline, 3, 6 and 12 months for each trial; compare the early gap with the 12-month gap.
slides.notes: Direction first: the tables print the difference as nonsurgical minus surgery, so a positive number favors surgery. Our recomputation: the 7.4 interval is symmetric (midpoint 7.45) and implies P about 0.013, matching P=0.01. The 2.3 interval implies P about 0.53, matching 0.52. The unadjusted 12-month gaps are 5.9 and 1.4. Adjustment raises them because both surgical arms started worse. How to read the disc result. It is statistically clear and robust across ITT, mixed model and per-protocol. But the whole interval sits below 15, the MID the paper quotes, and the lower end is 1.6. The authors themselves say the upper bound is only marginally above the 12 points the trial was built to find. Caution: the MID of 15 comes from individual change after fusion. Comparing a between-group mean difference to it is not like for like, and a 7-point mean gap can hide many patients who individually crossed a threshold. That reading is ours. How to read the spondylosis result. The authors say no difference. Our reading: the ITT upper bound of 9.6 sits below the planned 12, so a 12-point average benefit at 1 year looks unlikely in this population. The per-protocol upper bound is 11.8. But 11 of 46 nonsurgical patients had surgery, which pulls an ITT comparison toward zero. Per-protocol and as-treated analyses were reported as similar; their tables are in the appendix we did not read. Do not call this proof of equivalence: it was not designed as an equivalence or noninferiority trial. The paper also notes a protocol change: the original analysis plan named two primary outcomes, NDI and arm pain NRS, with no multiplicity control. This report keeps NDI as the sole primary because the sample size used NDI. That is a reasonable choice but a departure from the original analysis plan; the paper does not say when it was made. Nonsurgical improvement exceeded 13.5 points in both trials, which the authors note is a proposed success threshold after surgery.

slides.title: Secondary outcomes and harms
slides.lead: Surgery's NDI advantage at 3 months was about 8 points in both trials; by 12 months it persisted in disc herniation (8.0 by mixed model) but faded in spondylosis.
points: No serious adverse events, per the authors. No adverse events in nonsurgical patients.
Spondylosis surgery: one permanent recurrent laryngeal nerve injury with dysphonia and dysphagia; one antibiotic rash.
Disc surgery: one temporary dysphonia. One disc crossover needed reoperation for pseudarthrosis.
Grip strength favored nonsurgical care in spondylosis; the numbers are in the appendix.
slides.notes: Continuous secondary outcomes come from a mixed model; categorical ones (sick leave, analgesic use, global rating of change) from chi-square tests reported as odds ratios. The authors say plainly that the intervals are not adjusted for multiplicity and should not be used to infer definitive effects. Take them as supporting color. The 3-month row is the most useful teaching point: both trials favored surgery early by about 8 points. In spondylosis that early benefit faded by 12 months (8.5 at 3 months, 2.8 by mixed model at 12); in disc herniation it held (8.0 at both 3 and 12 months), so in the disc trial the gap was not larger early. That is the Figure 2 picture. Pain: in disc herniation, arm pain was 1.0 vs 2.4 at 12 months and neck pain 1.9 vs 2.9. The adjusted differences of 1.4 and 1.0 are below the 2.5-point NRS MID the paper cites; that comparison is ours. Global rating of change (better or much better): 40 of 43 vs 25 of 39 for arm pain in the disc trial, odds ratio 7.47 (1.95 to 28.61). Our recomputation reproduces that odds ratio. In spondylosis, neck pain improvement favored nonsurgical care numerically, 65.1% vs 74.4%. Emotional distress favored surgery in both trials, by a similar small amount. Absence from work and analgesic use did not differ. Note: the analgesic odds ratios in Tables 2 and 3 run in the opposite direction to the other odds ratios in the same tables (our recomputation), so read them only as near 1. Harms. The paper reports no serious adverse events, yet it describes a permanent recurrent laryngeal nerve injury with dysphonia and dysphagia and a reoperation for pseudarthrosis. Our reading: many trial definitions would count a permanent deficit or a reoperation as serious. The authors' definition is not given in the main text, so we flag this tension rather than call it an error. With about 90 surgical patients in total plus crossovers, the trials cannot estimate rare complication rates. Most surgical patients got perioperative glucocorticoids, while nonsurgical patients got none, by the authors' design choice.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: Holds up: randomized within each pathology, computer-generated schedule with random block sizes
Holds up: 97 to 98% follow-up; prespecified analysis plan published before database lock
Holds up: consistent results across ITT, mixed model and per-protocol analyses
Holds up: sponsor had no role; trial populations compared with a national registry
