Weakens: single center; patients and follow-up examiners knew assignment; no sham
Weakens: patient-reported primary outcome in an unblinded surgical trial
Weakens: 23.9% crossover in the spondylosis nonsurgical arm
Weakens: two primary outcomes in the plan became one in the report
Weakens: pathology classification not externally validated
Weakens: 12-month follow-up only; no reoperation or adjacent-level horizon
Source problems: flow diagram exclusions, a sign error and odds-ratio direction (see notes)
slides.notes: Be fair first. This is a well-built pair of trials on a question surgeons rarely test, with very little missing data and an analysis plan published before unblinding. The authors list single center, no sham, patient awareness of treatment, spondylosis crossover, patients improving before inclusion, and an unvalidated imaging split as their own limitations. They also suggest that surgery's advantage may partly reflect higher expectations and a larger placebo effect. Our additions. Bias from unblinded self-report most likely runs toward surgery, which fits the authors' placebo point; the paper gives no estimate of its size, so we cannot say how much of the 7.4 points it explains. The nonsurgical arm got no steroids or injections, so it tests a minimal, education-based program, not everything nonsurgical care can offer. Eligibility required at least 3 months of arm pain, NDI above 30 and arm pain 4 or more, so results do not reach acute radiculopathy or myelopathy. Our recomputation found these problems in the paper. Figure 1 says 1181 were excluded, but the listed reasons add to 1161 (111 + 1004 + 2 + 44); 1361 minus 1181 does give 180. In Table 3, FABQ work is printed as 1.0 (-5.5 to 3.5); that interval centers on -1.0, and the raw means (16.1 surgery vs 15.1 nonsurgical) also point the other way, so the sign is probably wrong. The analgesic odds ratios in both tables (1.07 and 0.91) are calculated as nonsurgical against surgery, while the sick-leave and global-change odds ratios are surgery against nonsurgical. Baseline sick leave in Tables 2 and 3 (26 vs 20, 18 vs 24) differs from sickness absence in Table 1 (22 vs 19, 15 vs 19); Table 1 uses at least 50% absence, so the definitions likely differ, but the paper does not explain it. The Results text calls the second trial the disc spondylosis trial. None of these touch the primary result.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "In Taso's two Oslo trials, ACDF beat a six-session rehabilitation program at 1 year for disc herniation, by 7.4 NDI points, below the 15-point MID the paper quotes. For spondylosis the difference was 2.3 points and not significant, though a quarter of the nonsurgical group had surgery. Mean scores improved in every arm; in spondylosis, surgery's edge was seen only at 3 months."

rows: NDI reduction 21 vs 11 points, ACDF plus physiotherapy vs physiotherapy

points: Engquist C08 is the library record of the 2017 5-to-8-year follow-up, abstract level; Taso compared against the earlier 2-year Engquist report. Populations, comparators and follow-up differ.
Do not stretch it: 12 months only, ages 20 to 65, C5 to C7, no myelopathy, at least 3 months of arm pain.
slides.notes: Expect four follow-up questions. First: so is surgery better for a soft disc? On average yes, at 1 year, by about 7 NDI points, with arm pain about 1.4 points lower and 93% vs 64% reporting arm pain better. Whether that is worth an operation is a judgment. The authors say the relatively small differences should be weighed against the risks and costs of surgery. Second: does this mean spondylotic radiculopathy should not be operated on? Not quite. The ITT result was null and the upper bound (9.6) argues against a large average benefit at 1 year. But crossover was 23.9%, follow-up was 1 year, and the trial was not built to prove equivalence. The authors say the result may question the decompression paradigm; they do not say surgery is useless. Also, the paper never tests whether the effect differs between the two trials, so 'works for disc, not for spondylosis' is an informal comparison of two separate results. That point is ours. Third: is 7.4 points clinically meaningful when the MID is 15? Explain that the MID is an individual-change threshold, while 7.4 is a difference in group means. The paper does not report the proportion of patients reaching the MID in each arm in the main text. Fourth: how does it fit with earlier evidence? The authors say their spondylosis result agrees with the two smaller earlier trials, and that their nonsurgical patients improved about three times as much as in the Swedish trial (Engquist, their reference 4, the 2-year report). The C08 numbers in the table are from a later report, the 5-to-8-year follow-up in the library record, built from the abstract; against C08's 11 points the ratio is nearer 2, so do not pair the authors' 'three times' with the C08 numbers. Approach choice is a separate question: the week 6 curriculum pairs this paper with FACET (C07), which compares posterior foraminotomy with ACDF. Also mention: these patients averaged NDI around 40 with months of arm pain, all considered surgical candidates, and nonsurgical patients improved by roughly 19 to 21 points on average without surgery.

decks.not_reviewed: Nothing beyond the 8-page article was available: no supplement is cited. The parent CSM-NA and CSM-I study reports and the cited MCID papers were not read. Figures were read from the PDF image, so curve values from them are approximate.

slides.title: Mild DCM recovery trajectories
slides.lead: Who does well after surgery for mild degenerative cervical myelopathy?
points: Journal club: mild DCM, prognosis after surgery
Bak AB, Alvi MA, Moghaddamjou A, Fehlings MG. Spine 2025;50(16):1102-1109
Retrospective analysis of prospectively collected AO Spine CSM-NA and CSM-I data, 198 operated patients with mJOA 15-17
Bottom line: about 70% followed a good mJOA path and about 60% a good SF36-PCS path over 2 years. Older age, smoking and lower baseline SF36-PCS predicted the poorer path on both scales.
Every patient had surgery. This is prognosis after surgery, not surgery versus observation.
slides.notes: This deck was prepared from the full 8-page article. It is the original paper, not a critique, and it is complete. The authors grade it Level 3 evidence. Two things to hold in mind from the start. First, the title promises to identify optimal candidates for operative management, but there is no nonoperative group. The data can say who recovers after surgery. They cannot say who gains from surgery compared with waiting. That point is ours. The authors' conclusion calls for comparative studies of conservative management versus surgery, but in the same paragraph still describes a group that does not respond positively to surgical management. Second, the abstract has a number error: it puts the SF36-PCS good-recovery group at 166 patients (59.5%). The Results text and Table 1 give 116, and 116 of 195 is the 59.5%. 166 is a typo. The master record withheld these numbers pending full text, and they can now be filled in. Funding: the authors received no support for this analysis; AO Spine North America funded the original studies. No conflicts reported. The senior author led the parent studies, which is ordinary for a secondary analysis but worth knowing.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: Guidelines give only a weak recommendation for surgery in mild DCM. The authors asked whether recovery paths can sort good candidates from poor ones.
points: Mild DCM: mJOA 15-17. Moderate 12-14, severe 0-11, as defined in the paper
The guideline the paper cites offers surgery or supervised structured rehabilitation for mild DCM
Aim 1: describe 2-year recovery after surgery for mild DCM, by clinician score and by patient report
Aim 2: find preoperative factors linked to the better recovery path
Design: retrospective cohort built from two prospective multicenter surgical studies

rows: mJOA and SF36-PCS paths to 2 years

slides.notes: Frame the clinical problem the way the authors do. A patient with mJOA 16 has little function to regain on the clinician scale, so surgery risks look large against small gains. Yet DCM can progress, and the patient may feel much worse than the score suggests. The authors cite estimates that 20 to 62 percent of nonoperated DCM patients decline over 3 to 6 years and 4 to 40 percent eventually need surgery. Those figures come from their references, not from this study. Note what the design can and cannot answer. The comparison is between kinds of operated patients, so every finding is a prognostic association. It is not an effect of surgery. When the paper says patients may respond poorly to surgery, read it as recovered poorly after surgery. Without an untreated comparison the paper cannot show that the same patient would have done better or worse without the operation. That reading is ours, and it matches the authors' own call for comparative studies.

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: Selection, measurement and modeling decide what the classes mean.
points: Sources: CSM-NA, 12 sites in the US and Canada, Dec 2005 to Sep 2007; CSM-I, 16 sites across Europe, Latin America, North America and Asia, Oct 2007 to Jan 2011
Included: age 18 or older, symptomatic DCM with at least one myelopathic sign, cord compression on imaging, no prior cervical surgery
Excluded: active infection, rheumatoid arthritis, trauma, ankylosing spondylitis, concomitant lumbar stenosis, neoplasm
Visits: baseline, 6 months, 1 year, 2 years
Latent class trajectory modeling sorted patients into the path they most probably followed
A class was called good if its mean 2-year gain reached the MCID: 1 point for mJOA, 4 points for SF36-PCS
Multivariable logistic regression for predictors of the good class, with surgical approach and levels controlled
slides.notes: Selection. The paper gives no flow diagram and no count of mild patients who were screened, excluded or lost before 2 years. The SF36-PCS model holds 195 patients, three fewer than the 198 in the mJOA model, and the paper does not say why. Badhiwala's earlier mild-DCM analysis of the same AO Spine studies (library record C03) had 193 patients. Ours: the difference of 5 is not explained here. Measurement. mJOA is clinician-administered, 0 to 18. SF36-PCS is patient-reported and includes bodily pain. Starting at 15 to 17, mJOA has at most 1 to 3 points of headroom, a ceiling effect the authors list as a limitation. The modeling step matters most. Latent class trajectory modeling finds groups whose mean curves differ. Each patient goes to the class with the highest posterior probability. The authors then labeled the whole class good if its mean change reached the MCID. So good means belonged to the class whose average improved by an MCID. It does not mean that each of the 138 patients improved by 1 mJOA point, though the abstract words it that way. That reading is ours. Model choice used five criteria from the literature: lowest BIC, each class at least 5 percent, posterior probability above 0.70, odds of correct classification above 5, and agreement between estimated and assigned proportions. The authors added a sixth: curves should not cross on visual inspection. The paper does not report the values for the posterior probability, classification odds or proportion criteria. Pain was taken from the Neck Disability Index pain item. The parent studies were observational surgical cohorts. The paper calls them trials, but no treatment was randomized.

slides.title: Two recovery paths per scale
slides.lead: Both scales split into a good class and a marginal class.

rows: Flat to 6 months, then modest fall

points: Whole cohort mJOA: 15.8 at baseline, 16.6 at 1 and 2 years
Whole cohort SF36-PCS: 39.9 at baseline, 45.9 at 1 year, 45.5 at 2 years
Agreement between the two classifications: kappa 0.436, McNemar P<0.001
slides.see: Figures 1 and 2: the marginal mJOA curve falls from about 15.3 to a low of about 14.3 near 1 year and ends near 14.5, below its starting point, while the good curve rises to about 17.4.
slides.notes: Read the figures, not just the labels. The marginal mJOA class did not improve slightly. In Figure 1 its mean falls about a point, to about 14.3 near 1 year, and ends near 14.5. That is still above the moderate band of 12 to 14. Those figure values are our approximate readings. The text calls it a gradual and slight decline. So for about 30 percent, the average course after surgery was mild worsening. Without a control group we cannot tell whether that is less decline than they would have had without surgery. The good class starts slightly higher and climbs toward the ceiling. By our arithmetic the class means check out: 69.7 percent of 17.4 plus 30.3 percent of 14.5 gives about 16.5, close to the reported 2-year mean of 16.6. The SF36-PCS good class starts near 41 and rises to about 50. The marginal class sits near 38 and drifts down. The two scales disagree. 69.7 percent were good on mJOA and 59.5 percent on SF36-PCS. Kappa 0.436 is moderate agreement. The authors read the McNemar result as a systematic difference, and suggest it arises because SF36-PCS contains pain and mJOA does not. Our check on the McNemar P: the cross-table is not published. From the reported margins and kappa we reconstructed about 51 discordant pairs split roughly 35 to 15. That gives P of about 0.002 to 0.01, not below 0.001. The direction holds, but the printed P looks too small. The model choice is fragile, so treat the two-class split as a simplification. Details are on the appraisal slide.

slides.title: Who followed the good path
slides.lead: Adjusted odds ratios for belonging to the good class. Below 1 means less likely.
points: Preoperative pain did not predict either class
Worse pain at 6 months, OR 0.29, and 1 year, OR 0.06, and worsening pain by 2 years, OR 0.27, went with the marginal SF36-PCS class
Pain at any time did not relate to the mJOA class
slides.notes: Three factors are significant in both models: age, smoking and baseline SF36-PCS (OR 1.07 per point, P=0.029 for mJOA and 0.018 for SF36-PCS). The authors name all three in their conclusion. Age and smoking follow the wider DCM literature, as the authors note. In the SF36-PCS model the baseline PCS result needs care: the trajectory model includes the baseline score, and the good SF36-PCS class started higher, 41.5 versus 37.5 in Table 1, so some of that association is built into how the classes were formed. That caveat is ours and does not apply to the mJOA model. Higher baseline mJOA predicted the good mJOA class, OR 2.20 per point, though baseline mJOA spans only 15 to 17. Ours: less headroom might be expected to mean less gain, but the authors cite studies (refs 17-20) in which a higher baseline predicts better outcomes. The single-scale findings look unstable to us. Hyperreflexia was 69.6 versus 71.6 percent in the raw SF36 groups, yet the adjusted OR is 3.92. Congenital stenosis points opposite ways on the two scales. The Black and Other race intervals run as wide as 0.24 to 56. Our count: Table 2 lists about 38 terms, plus approach and levels, fit with 60 marginal-class patients for mJOA, under 2 events per term. That is far below usual guidance, so expect overfitting. The authors offer two explanations. Male sex: female patients do worse after lumbar surgery in a review. Asian race: possibly more laminoplasty at the Japanese centers. Both explanations are untested here. The pain rows are not preoperative predictors. Pain at 6 and 12 months is measured alongside the outcome, and PCS contains bodily pain, so these associations are partly the same thing measured twice. The authors' key point calls postoperative pain a driver of PCS; association is all the data show. Text errors to flag: the male-sex P is 0.016 in the text but 0.009 in Table 2, and the table value recomputes from its CI. The text CI for baseline PCS on the SF36 model is 1.01-1.23, but Table 2 gives 1.01-1.13. All other Table 2 P values match their CIs.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: Large prospective multicenter data, but class selection and the regression are fragile.
points: Strength: prospective multicenter data with standard outcomes at fixed visits to 2 years
Strength: clinician score and patient report analyzed side by side
Weakness: no nonoperative group, so it cannot identify who benefits from surgery
Weakness: two-class mJOA model chosen although the four-class model had lower BIC, 2045.39 vs 2090.30
Weakness: SF36-PCS BIC paragraph lists four values for five models and contradicts itself
Weakness: under 2 events per regression term (our count); several wide or flipped estimates
Weakness: surgery not standardized; approach differed by class
Weakness: no complication data, no flow diagram, 3 patients missing from the SF36 model
Number errors: abstract 166 for 116, a text P and a text CI that disagree with Table 2
slides.notes: Model selection is the main problem. The authors list least BIC as their first a priori criterion. For mJOA, the cubic BICs for 2 to 6 classes were 2090.30, 2116.75, 2045.39, 2169.63 and 2074.01. The four-class model is lowest, not the two-class. The authors chose two classes because curves crossed in the larger models, then state the two-class model met the a priori criteria. By their own first criterion it did not. For SF36-PCS the cubic two-class model (4755.94) was lowest among cubic models. The text says a quadratic four-class model was lower still, at 4737.10. It then lists four increasing quadratic BICs for five models, which cannot all be right. It also says only models with more than three classes had crossing curves. That leaves a three-class model that passed the crossing rule, and the paper does not say why it was rejected. Methods are internally inconsistent on shape: one sentence says quadratic or cubic growth terms were introduced, a later one says shape was tested by trialing linear or quadratic functions, and cubic models were chosen. None of the posterior probability or classification values are reported. So the good-versus-marginal split is one defensible simplification, not a discovered natural law. Confounding by indication: posterior laminectomy and fusion was 28.8 percent of marginal mJOA patients versus 10.9 percent of good ones. By our chi-square, P is about 0.002. Approach was adjusted, but sicker spines may have got bigger operations. Table 1 has no P values, although Methods says baseline groups were compared. Our tests show many imbalances. mJOA classes: age (P about 0.001), hypertension (0.005), spondylosis (0.002), baseline mJOA (0.01), Nurick (0.02), baseline PCS (0.02), smoking (0.03), ACDF (0.03). SF36 classes: age (0.002), baseline PCS (0.002), Asian race (0.0001), weakness (0.002), more than 2 levels (0.003), spondylosis (0.014), posterior approach (0.018). Small table issues: procedure-type counts sum to 59 of 60 and 137 of 138 in the mJOA columns, and 77 of 79 in the SF36 marginal column. The authors list as limitations the mJOA ceiling, unstandardized surgery and no complication data.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: Prognosis after surgery for mild DCM, not proof of benefit.
points: "In 198 operated mild DCM patients from the AO Spine studies, about 70% followed a path of meaningful mJOA gain by 6 months and about 60% a path of meaningful SF36-PCS gain by 1 year. The rest drifted slightly down. Older age, smoking and lower baseline SF36-PCS predicted the poorer path on both scales. With no nonoperative group, it tells us who recovers after surgery, not who should have it."

rows: 69.7% good mJOA path; 59.5% good PCS path
Phenotype with more pain improved more

slides.notes: C03 and C12 figures come from the library records, which are abstract-level, not from this paper. Badhiwala gives the average gain; Bak splits the same kind of patients into who gained and who did not. Expect these follow-up questions. Should a smoker with mild DCM avoid surgery? The paper cannot say. Smokers were less likely to be in the good class after surgery, but nobody was observed without surgery, so their natural history may be worse too. Say smoking predicts a poorer course after surgery and supports counseling and cessation. What does marginal recovery mean? On mJOA the marginal class averaged about a point below baseline from Figure 1, by our reading. It is a modest decline, not a small gain. Why do the scales disagree? The authors point to pain: SF36-PCS includes bodily pain and mJOA does not. Patients with more pain after surgery were less likely to be in the good SF36 class. Are there really two kinds of patients? Only by modeling choice. A four-class mJOA model fit better by BIC and was set aside because curves crossed. Does preoperative pain predict outcome? Not here: OR 1.66 for mJOA, P=0.071, and 1.20 for SF36-PCS, P=0.499. What about complications? Not reported in this analysis.

decks.not_reviewed: The six appraised source studies themselves (all their numbers here are as the AO authors report them). The published layout: this is a reformatted PMC text with images omitted; the only table, Table 1, came through as text. The reformatted copy has no funding, conflict-of-interest or author-contribution sections, so those were not reviewed. No supplement is cited.

slides.title: AO Spine: osteoporosis in ASD
slides.lead: A consensus review of six hand-picked studies on finding, weighing and treating poor bone before deformity surgery.
points: Journal club: bone health in adult spinal deformity
Kato S, et al. AO Spine Knowledge Forum Deformity. Global Spine J 2026;16(2):854-861 (online July 2025)

Bottom line: test bone before ASD surgery, add forearm DEXA and CT Hounsfield units, and consider teriparatide in osteoporotic patients. All six studies are observational or nonrandomized; none is graded high.
slides.notes: Source check first. This deck comes from the full text of the paper itself, in a reformatted open-access PMC copy. It is not a critique and it is not truncated: abstract, introduction, all six article appraisals, discussion, conclusion and references are present. The header says images are omitted; the only table, Table 1, came through as text. The copy has no funding or conflict-of-interest section, so we cannot comment on either. What kind of paper this is: an AO Spine Knowledge Forum clinical practice recommendation. Members picked six articles, wrote a structured appraisal of each (clinical rationale, study summary, methodological review, quality of evidence, recommendation), then made consensus recommendations. It is not a systematic review. There is no search strategy, no date range and no stated selection criteria; the abstract says only that the articles were selected by practicing spinal deformity surgeons. Hold that thought, because it decides how much weight the conclusions can carry. Every number in this deck about the six source studies is as the AO authors report it. We did not read the source papers. Several of the source cohorts are not ASD cohorts: one is lumbar fusion, one mixes deformity with degenerative disease, one includes progressive adolescent idiopathic scoliosis. The authors say so in places and then generalize to ASD, a point we return to in the appraisal.

slides.title: How the recommendations were built
slides.lead: Six articles in four themes: assessment, risk, management, and osteoporotic fracture.
points: Methods: articles selected by deformity surgeons, each appraised, then graded strong or conditional by consensus
Grading was meant to combine evidence quality with expert opinion on risks, burdens, costs and patient values
Table 1 lists the recommendations but gives no evidence grade or strength
slides.notes: Read the tally: four low, two moderate, none high. No randomized trial appears among the six. The abstract says recommendations were graded dichotomously into strong and conditional. In the body, only Article 1 is labeled outright as a conditional recommendation. The others use wording: we recommend HU analysis (Article 2), we suggest blood management (Article 3), we suggest teriparatide (Articles 4 and 5), and clinicians should not use these guidelines (Article 6). Table 1 drops the grade and strength entirely. Our reading, following usual GRADE convention rather than anything this paper states: recommend signals strong and suggest signals conditional. If that holds, the HU recommendation is strong on low-quality evidence. The authors justify it by low risk and cost, which GRADE allows, but they do not say so in those terms. Also compare the grading of two similar studies. Both are single-center retrospective reviews, but Mugge drew on a prospectively maintained database (2006 to 2017, 3 surgeons), while St Jeor is a plain retrospective review (2 surgeons). St Jeor is graded low for single center, residual confounding and modest sample. Mugge is graded moderate, and the paper never says why. Its methodological review praises clear procedures, well-described outcomes, a relatively large sample and appropriate statistics; our inference is that these drove the grade. That is a defensible call, but it is a judgment, not a rule. The scope statement is wide: identification, treatment and surgical implications of osteoporosis in ASD. Ask how six studies, chosen without a search, can cover that. The introduction also gives screening guidance it attributes to current guidelines: everyone 65 and older, and ages 50 to 64 with one or more risk factors, including glucocorticoids, low-energy fracture, chronic kidney disease, prior failed spine surgery, vitamin D deficiency and diabetes.

slides.title: Assessment: DEXA misleads, HU helps
points: Gupta: lumbar DEXA reads falsely high in curves; arthritic hips can too
St Jeor: lower HU predicted osteoporosis-related complications; DEXA did not hold up in the multivariable model
Authors: add the forearm (conditional) and read HU on the preoperative CT (we recommend)

rows: St Jeor: complications by bone class

slides.notes: Gupta reviewed 286 patients coded with scoliosis and osteoporosis, but only 85 had forearm DEXA, about 30 percent, which the authors flag. Over 90 percent were women. Diagnosis rested on ICD-10 codes, with no severity of osteoporosis or deformity. Our recomputation fits the site percentages to 85 patients exactly. One number does not fit: 46.4 percent former or current smokers cannot be a proportion of 85 (the nearest values are 45.9 and 47.1), so that figure is wrong or uses another denominator. Also note a puzzle we cannot resolve from the review: all patients already carried an osteoporosis diagnosis, so it is not clear what 17 percent missed means. St Jeor checks out arithmetically. 10 percent of 140 is 14 osteoporotic, 58.6 percent is 82 osteopenic, which leaves 44 normal. The complication percentages give 7, 33 and 5, adding to the reported 45. Notice two things the authors pass over. First, complication rates did not rise steadily by bone class. Normal bone against osteopenia, 7 of 44 against 33 of 82, is a real gap (our recomputation, P about 0.005). Osteopenia against osteoporosis, 40.2 against 35.7 percent, shows no clear difference, with only 14 osteoporotic patients (our recomputation, P about 0.75). Second, teriparatide in the 6 months before surgery was an independent predictor of more complications. The obvious explanation, ours, is confounding by indication: sicker bone got the drug. But it sits awkwardly next to a review that recommends the drug, and the paper does not discuss it. Population: St Jeor is lumbar spine fusion, not ASD. The Conclusion says HU has shown better correlation with mechanical complications in ASD patients. That generalizes past the cohort reviewed. Practical point from the Discussion: low HU alone may not confirm osteoporosis under WHO criteria, so in some jurisdictions DEXA is still needed before treatment can be started.

slides.title: Risk: what osteoporosis costs in surgery
points: Mugge: 144 of 532 (27%) had osteoporosis by DEXA T-score of -2.5 or below
Associated with more blood loss, instrumentation failure and revision after adjustment
Alpantaki: osteoporotic fracture kyphosis treated mostly with short fusion; authors advise against using its rules
slides.notes: Mugge is the risk anchor. A prospective single-institution database from 2006 to 2017, reviewed retrospectively, three surgeons, any thoracolumbar fusion for scoliosis, including progressive adolescent idiopathic scoliosis as well as ASD. So the cohort is not purely adult deformity. Our check: 33 and 16 percent of 144 and 388 fit 48 plus 63, which equals the reported 111 revisions. With confounders controlled, osteoporosis stayed associated with instrumentation failure (P=0.022) and revision (P<0.001). One oddity: the review lists more levels fused as an adjusted association, which reads as a difference in the operations rather than an outcome, and prints it as P<0.002. The authors' practice advice adds venous thromboembolism and early transfusion planning. VTE does not appear anywhere in their own study summary, so that part of the recommendation cannot be checked against the numbers given. Alpantaki is a different question: deformity caused by osteoporotic vertebral fracture with pain or neurologic deficit. 51 registered, 31 followed for at least 2 years; 28 had positioning reduction, kyphoplasty-type augmentation and short posterior fusion, and 3 had multilevel fixation. Cement complications in 4 of 28 and screw pullout in 4 of 28, both 14.3 percent. The authors describe a 77 percent success rate defined as pain improvement without a denominator; 24 of 31 would fit, which is our guess. The AO appraisal lists rules adapted from Hu, such as not ending fixation in the kyphotic segment and avoiding hooks alone, then concludes clinicians should not use them until more evidence exists. Teach that as an honest negative: the panel declined to recommend.

slides.title: Management: anabolic treatment
points: Mohanty: teriparatide-treated osteoporosis did better than untreated osteopenia, and did not differ from matched normal bone
Sawakami: bone formation peaked 3 to 4 months into teriparatide; complications fell against untreated controls
Authors suggest teriparatide when available, affordable and not contraindicated
slides.notes: Mohanty: 542 patients, more than 7 levels, single surgeon and center. Osteoporotic patients got teriparatide at least 6 months before and 1 year after surgery. PJK did not differ. The trap, which the AO authors themselves name: there is no untreated osteoporosis group. The comparison is treated osteoporosis against untreated osteopenia, so it cannot isolate a drug effect. The library record for Mohanty (PM37973052) makes the same point. Arithmetic, ours: the group percentages of 52.6, 32.9 and 14.4 imply 285, 178 and 78, which add to 541, not 542. The reported odds ratios are identical for the unmatched and matched analyses, 0.45 and 0.25, although the osteopenia rates differ. Our crude recomputation gives 0.47 and 0.43 for reoperation and 0.26 and 0.25 for pseudarthrosis. They may be adjusted values; the review does not say. Significance, ours: the unmatched reoperation rates imply 9 of 78 against 39 of 178, which gives P=0.050 uncorrected chi-square and 0.056 Fisher, borderline at best, though the review calls it significantly lower without saying whether that was adjusted. Matched reoperation (9 of 78 against 36 of 156, P about 0.035) and both pseudarthrosis comparisons (P about 0.003 to 0.004) hold up. No difference against normal bone, in 78 patients, is not proof of equivalence. Sawakami: hip T-score below -1.5, deformity or lumbar degenerative surgery, so not ASD-only. Patients chose their group, open label. Preoperative teriparatide ran 1, 2, 3, 4 or 6 months (9, 8, 9, 7, 9, which add to 42). Our check: an uncorrected chi-square on 15 of 42 against 12 of 15 gives P=0.0032, matching; Fisher exact gives about 0.006. Six treated patients had prior bisphosphonate, and they loosened screws at control rates. The review frames this as the exception to no significant baseline differences, but 6 of 42 against 0 of 15 is not significant on our recomputation (Fisher P about 0.32). Note what supports the 3-month rule: the bone formation peak, not complications by duration. Cancellous bone structure did not differ, yet the Discussion says anabolics improve trabecular structure. The abstract says at least 3 months, while Mohanty used at least 6. The Discussion lists harms: transient hypercalcemia, orthostatic hypotension, an osteosarcoma risk seen in animals but not confirmed in humans, and contraindications including hypercalcemia, Paget disease, skeletal malignancy, prior skeletal radiation and severe renal impairment.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: Strength: practical, low-cost steps; harms and contraindications of teriparatide are listed
Strength: authors say the evidence is not robust enough to mandate these steps globally
Weakness: six studies chosen without a search; no high-quality evidence
Weakness: strength of each recommendation is mostly implied by wording, not stated
Weakness: abstract and Conclusion claim more than the graded studies support
Weakness: lumbar fusion and mixed cohorts generalized to ASD
Not discussed: teriparatide predicted more complications in St Jeor
slides.notes: Be fair first. The assessment advice is cheap and safe: a forearm DEXA and reading HU on a CT you already have. The authors state their own limit plainly: strong associations exist, but they do not feel the evidence is robust enough to mandate the recommendations globally, and they note that urgency, cost and health systems will limit uptake. The main problem is the gap between that hedge and the headline. The abstract says there is clinical benefit in anabolic agents for at least 3 months to improve bone stock and prevent mechanical complications. The Conclusion says anabolic agents have demonstrated excellent results in restoring bone health before surgery and have been shown to reduce mechanical complications in spinal deformity surgery. The supporting studies are one low-quality retrospective comparison against a different bone class and one moderate nonrandomized trial of 57 patients with mixed indications. The 3-month figure comes from bone markers, not from complication rates by duration. Our reading: the honest statement is associated with fewer complications in nonrandomized cohorts. The Discussion also leans on degenerative-fusion teriparatide studies (Ebata, a randomized study per its reference title, and Pan, a meta-analysis) and says it seems reasonable to extrapolate to deformity constructs. That is an extrapolation, and the authors frame it as one. Selection bias of the review itself: no search, no stated criteria, so we cannot know what was left out. Romosozumab, abaloparatide and denosumab are not appraised. Smaller errors are listed in the patch file: the 46.4 percent smoker figure, Mohanty group counts adding to 541, identical odds ratios across analyses, VTE advice without VTE data, the trabecular structure claim, and a citation year mismatch for Sawakami (2021 in the heading, 2022 in the references).

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "AO Spine says check bone before every ASD operation, with forearm DEXA and CT Hounsfield units, and suggests teriparatide for osteoporosis when available. The six studies behind it are observational or nonrandomized, and none is high quality."

rows: Grade B for testing and teriparatide

points: Dimar, Park and Mohanty numbers come from abstract-level library records
Do not say teriparatide is proven to prevent PJK: Mohanty found no PJK difference
slides.see: Table 1 in the paper is the one-page summary of all six recommendations
slides.notes: Spoken summary: bone quality predicts mechanical failure in deformity surgery, DEXA is unreliable in a curved, arthritic spine, so add the forearm and read Hounsfield units off the CT. Osteoporotic patients should be considered for anabolic treatment, teriparatide here, for at least 3 months, when it is available and not contraindicated. The evidence is observational, and the authors stop short of mandating it. Expect these follow-up questions. Is there randomized evidence? Not in this paper. The library has Park 2025, a small randomized trial of teriparatide against denosumab in osteoporotic deformity patients, with PJF 3.4 against 22.2 percent but no significant PJK difference (P=.165). That record is abstract-level, this review does not cite it, and its comparator is active, so it tests teriparatide against denosumab, not against nothing. Does this say what HU cutoff to use? No. This paper gives HU means and a risk gradient of 1.7-fold per 25 units in a lumbar fusion cohort, not a threshold. How long before surgery? The authors say at least 3 months; that rests on bone-formation markers in Sawakami, and Mohanty used 6. Bisphosphonate pretreatment may blunt the effect. What about PJK specifically? Mohanty found no PJK difference; St Jeor counted PJK inside a composite. How does this fit the CNS guideline? Dimar 2021, from the library record, also supports bone testing and considering teriparatide, at Grade B, so the two societies point the same way. This review contains no randomized trial; the Dimar record is abstract-level and does not describe the designs of its 17 studies.

decks.not_reviewed: No supplement is cited in the PDF. Cited sources were not reviewed, including the ASLS papers used to justify the ODI 40 threshold (references 12 and 13), Fried's definitions (reference 10) and the PhenoAge method (reference 5). Figure r2 values were checked against the text (Figure 6A prints 0.166, given as 0.16 in the text); individual scatterplot points were not digitized.

slides.title: Kelly 2026: Conflating disability, frailty and multimorbidity in adult spinal deformity
slides.lead: Bottom line: in 861 surgical ASD patients, frailty (Edmonton Frail Scale 8 or more) was rare at 6% and never occurred without disability or multimorbidity. Disability and frailty scores overlapped and spread along a continuum.
points: Journal club · Adult deformity: who is vulnerable
Kelly MP, et al, on behalf of the International Spine Study Group. Spine 2026;51:343-353
Full text read. Baseline data only: no surgical outcomes or complications were analyzed.
slides.notes: Frame this before anyone gets excited. It is a retrospective look at baseline (preoperative) data from a multicenter ISSG registry of operative thoracolumbar deformity. Nobody is followed. The paper says nothing about who does badly after surgery, and the authors say so: they did not investigate negative outcomes, saying the paucity of frail patients and few complication categories prevent strong conclusions, and they deliberately avoided a composite adverse event outcome because composite outcomes are rarely externally valid. What it does is descriptive and conceptual. It asks how often three labels that get used loosely (disabled, multimorbid, frail) actually apply, how much they overlap, and whether each one behaves like a category or a continuous scale. The deck comes from the full text of the paper, including the Venn diagram, Table 1, Table 2 and the scatterplots in Figures 2 to 6. No supplement is cited. The references the authors lean on, especially the ASLS work behind the ODI 40 threshold, were not reviewed here. Expect to find several reporting errors in Table 1 and in the Results arithmetic. None of them overturns the main message, but they matter for how much you trust the detail.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: An ASD patient who walks slowly and needs help looks frail. Is that frailty, disability from the deformity, comorbidity, or all three, and are these real categories at all?
points: Fried, as quoted by the authors: multimorbidity is the aggregation of clinically manifest diseases; frailty is the aggregate of subclinical losses of reserve across multiple physiological systems.
Authors' aim: the prevalence and relationships of the three conditions in complex ASD patients.
The relationships of the three conditions with chronological age and with biological age (DNA methylation PhenoAge) were explored; no secondary aim or a priori comparison is stated.
slides.notes: The clinical stakes are the authors' own framing in the Discussion. The patient disabled by a severe deformity or a failed long fusion stands much to gain from reconstruction. The multimorbid patient needs preoperative optimization. The truly frail patient may not recover from the physiological burden of surgery regardless of comorbidity. If those three present alike in clinic and we call them all frail, we counsel badly. That framing is argued, not tested here. Look at the thresholds. ODI 40 was chosen because, by the authors' account, it was roughly where patients in the ASLS trial chose to cross from nonoperative to operative care. Our reading: that makes it a treatment-preference threshold rather than a disability construct. The authors concede the threshold can be argued against. Edmonton 8 or more is a frailty cutoff from the cited literature; the authors say 7 or more would double frailty to 12%. Multimorbidity is defined as two or more chronic conditions collected on the Charlson form; the paper does not say which conditions counted or whether the Charlson score itself had a cutoff. PhenoAge is an epigenetic estimate of physiological age, and here it was available only where the needed lab data happened to be collected.

slides.title: Patients and methods
points: Multicenter ASD registry (NCT04194138), patients enrolled 2018 to 2024, age 18 or older, planned thoracolumbar deformity surgery.

Complex cases only: radiographic (PI-LL 25° or more, T1 pelvic angle 30° or more, SVA 15 cm or more, thoracic curve 70° or more, thoracolumbar or lumbar curve 50° or more, coronal malalignment 7 cm or more), procedural (fusion of 12 or more levels, three-column osteotomy or ACR) or geriatric (65 or older with 7 or more instrumented levels).
Excluded: infection, tumor, acute trauma, neuromuscular or syndromic deformity, inflammatory or autoimmune disease, prisoners, pregnancy.

Analysis: one-way ANOVA and chi-square across 7 overlap groups; linear regression r2 against age, PhenoAge and physical function tests; scatterplots inspected for clusters; exploratory factor analysis (principal axis, oblique rotation, loadings 0.4 or more meaningful). No sample size calculation.
slides.notes: The cohort: median age 66 (IQR 55.1 to 71.6), 68% female. The authors add that most were white; their figure is inconsistent (see appraisal). The abstract says most were undergoing primary surgery, but no revision count appears in the body or in Table 1. Three things to notice. First, this is a surgical, complex, elective cohort. Patients judged too frail for surgery were never enrolled, so frailty prevalence here is the prevalence among those a surgeon already offered a big operation. The authors themselves expect a lower prevalence in elective surgery than in hospitalized or nonelective populations. Second, 27% of the enrolled were dropped for missing data. The authors flag the risk that the frailest were the ones omitted. We are not told how the 312 differed. Third, PhenoAge rests on 208 patients chosen by whether lab data happened to be collected, which was not standardized across the registry. The 18% in the Results is 208 of the 1173 enrolled, not of the 861 analyzed (our arithmetic: 24% of 861). The cluster question is answered by eye: if the conditions were true categories, the authors expected clumps in the scatterplots. No formal cluster or mixture model was fit. The factor analysis used complete cases, but its sample size and the variance explained by each factor, which the Methods name as the measure of distinction, are not reported.

slides.title: Result 1: how the labels overlap
slides.lead: Disability was common and frailty rare. No patient was frail alone.
points: Our totals: disabled 535 (62%), multimorbid 238 (28%), frail 53 (6.2%). The 8 groups sum to 861.
Our count: 52 of the 53 frail patients were also disabled (ODI 40 or more).
Table 1 means: the None group was youngest (age 53.0, PhenoAge 39.0, versus age 62.0 to 69.1 in the multi-patient groups).
slides.see: Figure 1 is a Venn diagram: the Frail circle has nothing outside the overlaps.
slides.notes: This is the headline. Frailty by the Edmonton definition affected 53 patients, and every one also met another label; 52 of 53 were also disabled. So in this cohort, almost every frail patient is a disabled patient, while most disabled patients (483 of 535 by our count) are not frail. That asymmetry is what the authors mean by conflation risk: a slow, dependent ASD patient is much more likely to be disabled than frail. Read Table 1 for the sagittal story, our inference. The None group had the largest mean coronal Cobb (46.1°) but the smallest sagittal mismatch (PI-LL 9.8°, L1 pelvic angle mismatch 3.1°). Every disabled group carried more sagittal mismatch. That fits the idea that disability here is partly driven by sagittal deformity rather than physiology, but the table is unadjusted and the None group is also the youngest. The all-three group had the highest mean BMI (32.3). The authors also say it had significantly worse sagittal deformity; the P values are omnibus ANOVA across all groups, and the single frail plus multimorbid patient had a larger PI-LL (48.6°), so that statement is not shown by the table. Be careful with the Table 1 columns: the Frail column is empty (0 patients, all dashes), and the Frail + multimorbid column is a single patient with no SD, yet that patient is mixed into the omnibus ANOVA. The paper's 38.5% for disabled only should be 38.9%, and Figure 1's percentages sum to 99.5%.

slides.title: Result 2: continuous measures and factor analysis
slides.lead: Age, biological age and grip strength explained little of either score; the timed 3 m walk tracked EFS moderately (r2 0.27). The two scores shared a functional core.
points: Factor analysis: one dominant factor carried the ODI items and the Edmonton functional performance (0.599), functional independence (0.591) and medication use (0.498) items, plus the timed walk (0.564).

Multimorbidity loaded weakly, the authors say, reading it as relatively independent. Table 2 cannot confirm this: it lists no CCI item, and its Multimorbidity factor shows only the timed walk at -0.339.
Grip strength showed essentially no association with EFS (0.02), ODI (0.03), age (0.06) or PhenoAge (0.05).
slides.see: Figures 2 and 3 plot ODI and EFS against age and PhenoAge: a broad cloud, no clumps. Figure 6D shows the tight ODI versus PROMIS-PF line.
slides.notes: Translate r2 into plain words. An r2 of 0.10 means age explains about a tenth of the variation in ODI. As correlations (our conversion), 0.22 is r about 0.47, 0.13 is r about 0.36 and 0.6 is r about 0.77. The authors call PhenoAge stronger than birthday age for both scores, but the comparison is not like for like (ours): the chronological-age plots use the full analyzed cohort, the PhenoAge plots only the 208 with lab data. It still explains a minority of variance; the authors call it an imperfect biomarker. Also look at Figures 2B and 3B (ours): PhenoAge values run from about 5 to 115 in an adult cohort, and Table 1 mean PhenoAge sits 14 years below age in the None group (39.0 vs 53.0). Those values are hard to take at face value. The strongest relation, ODI with PROMIS Physical Function, is close to expected (ours): both are patient-reported scales of physical function. The useful finding is the weak one: the timed 3 m walk related moderately to EFS (0.27) and, per the Results, weakly to ODI (0.16), though the Discussion calls both walk associations moderate; grip strength related to nothing. The authors conclude grip strength may be a poor frailty screen in ASD and the timed walk a better one, at more effort. Caution (ours): EFS contains a functional performance item, and the paper does not explain how it relates to the separately recorded timed walk. If they overlap, part of that 0.27 is built in. Table 2 has its own problems: no CCI item appears, sub-threshold loadings (-0.339, -0.326) are printed despite the 0.4 footnote, and the timed walk is not among the EFA inputs the Methods name. The factor analysis is the formal version of the overlap argument: EFS functional items load on the same factor as ODI, so a high EFS can be partly a disability score. Note the inconsistent labels: PhenoAge with PROMIS-PF (0.25) is called small, EFS with PROMIS-PF (0.26) moderate. Other values from the text: age with 3 m walk 0.08, grip 0.06, PROMIS-PF 0.16; PhenoAge with 3 m walk 0.1.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: Strengths: large multicenter surgical cohort; three established instruments; the authors analyze scores without thresholds as well as with them.
Selection: complex elective surgical patients only, and 27% of enrolled were excluded for missing data. Both likely push frailty prevalence down.
One frailty instrument and one cutoff. EFS 7 or more would make frailty 12%, by the authors' statement.
No clusters was judged by eye from the scatterplots in Figures 2 to 6 (against age, PhenoAge, EFS and ODI); no cluster or mixture model was fit (ours).
No outcomes. The paper cannot say whether frailty, disability or multimorbidity predicts complications or recovery.
Table 1 and Results contain duplicated cells and arithmetic errors.
slides.notes: The core message survives the errors, but list them. In Table 1, VR-12 MCS values in the disabled + frail, frail + multimorbid and all-three columns repeat the VR-12 PCS values; the PROMIS Social Roles values in four columns also repeat PCS. The race rows look shifted by one label, and the Disabled and All-three race columns sum to 334 and 19 against Ns of 335 and 20. One P value is garbled (the VR-12 MCS row) and one mean is printed as 48/6. The Methods promise multimorbidity regressions against age and PhenoAge and the variance explained by each factor; neither is reported. A further point the authors get wrong: they say categorizing continuous measures loses power and so raises the risk of type 1 error. Lost power raises the risk of missing a real effect (type 2). The better argument against cutoffs is misclassification at the boundary, which they also make. Think about the no-clusters claim (ours). A scatter of one score against another variable (Figures 2 to 6) tests association, not whether a score has natural groups; a histogram or latent class model would. And in a cohort selected for surgery, most patients are disabled, which narrows the range. There is also a tension in the conclusions: the summary calls the three distinct composite conditions with some overlap, while the abstract says they do not form discrete categories. Both can be true: distinct concepts, each continuous. Finally, frailty and disability were measured before surgery in patients with severe deformity, and the authors note ASD can itself cause both. Some frailty points may be deformity, and could reverse with surgery; this paper cannot test that.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: In 861 ISSG surgical deformity patients, Edmonton frailty was rare at 6% and never seen alone, while 62% met ODI 40. Disability and frailty scores overlapped and ran on a continuum, so a slow, dependent ASD patient is more often disabled than frail. Baseline data only, no outcomes.
points: Is frailty unimportant in ASD? No. The paper studied prevalence and overlap, not outcomes, and the frailest may never have been enrolled.
Which simple screen? The timed 3 m walk tracked EFS moderately (r2 0.27); grip strength did not (0.02).
Is PhenoAge ready for clinic? No: 208 patients, r2 0.13 with EFS and 0.22 with ODI.
Would a lower cutoff change things? EFS 7 or more doubles frailty to 12%, still uncommon by the authors' account.
So what do I do? Record ODI, EFS and comorbidity as scores, and ask which one drives the patient's limitation.
slides.notes: Say the summary in about 30 seconds. Then expect these. Does this mean frail patients do fine with surgery? No. Outcomes were not studied, and the authors explicitly avoid claims about perioperative risk. It also does not validate withholding surgery from anyone. Why is frailty so rare when it is so talked about? Selection: this is a complex elective surgical registry, and 27% of the enrolled were dropped for missing data, possibly the frailest, as the authors note. And a different cutoff changes the number. Are frailty and disability the same thing? Not quite. They share a functional factor (the Edmonton functional items load with the ODI items), but EFS also contains non-functional items, and the authors report frailty related more to PhenoAge than to birthday age, though in a 208-patient subset rather than the same patients. The practical point, ours from the authors' framing: a patient whose slowness comes from sagittal imbalance may gain from reconstruction, while physiological frailty may limit recovery. The paper argues that distinction but does not prove which patients are which. Why does continuous versus categorical matter? Thresholds at ODI 40 or EFS 8 put very similar patients on opposite sides of a line, and the choice of threshold is arguable. Be ready to concede the paper's weaknesses: errors in Table 1, the 18% versus 24% denominator, cluster absence judged by eye, and no outcome data. Pair it with this week's question: which disability is reversible and which risk is physiological. This paper shows the labels overlap; it does not sort them for you.

decks.not_reviewed: The deck was drafted from the PubMed abstract of PMID 40980941, when the file papers/PM40980941.pdf held a different paper (Sardi, PMID 42661383). The file now holds the correct Khanna full text, which was used only for targeted checks: group sizes (131 MIS, 973 open), baseline Table 1, the 6-week film defining ideal L1PA, and the authors' limitations. Not yet reviewed in full: Tables 2 and 3 beyond the rows cited, the Discussion, reoperation causes and any supplement. The prior open-surgery L1PA work was not read.

slides.title: Khanna 2026: Ideal L1 pelvic angle in MIS adult deformity correction
slides.lead: Warning: drafted from the abstract. The correct full text is now on file but was used only for targeted checks.
points: Journal club · Adult deformity: alignment targets in MIS
Khanna R, et al, International Spine Study Group. Spine 2026;51(5):E118-E122. PMID 40980941
The PDF first filed under this ID was a different paper (Sardi 2026, PMID 42661383); the correct full text is now on file
Bottom line from the abstract: in MIS cases, ideal L1PA went with fewer reoperations (15% vs 33%) and larger PRO gains; in open cases it did not go with fewer reoperations
slides.notes: Say the limitation first. This deck was drafted from the PubMed abstract of Khanna et al, because the file first stored as PM40980941.pdf was a different paper (Sardi et al, PM42661383). The correct full text is now on file and was used for targeted checks only: the group sizes, baseline table and the authors' limitations. Treat the rest as the authors' summary, not a fully verified result. What the paper is: a retrospective look at a prospectively collected multicenter ISSG deformity database. It asks whether hitting the L1PA target matters when the correction is done with circumferential MIS (lateral or anterior interbody fusion with percutaneous posterior screws), as earlier work suggested it does for open surgery. The deck should be fully re-reviewed against the full text now on file.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: Does reaching the ideal L1PA during MIS deformity correction go with less mechanical failure and better patient-reported outcomes?
points: Ideal L1PA, as the authors define it: 0.5 × pelvic incidence − 21°
Ideal means within ±5° of that target
Background, per the authors: ideal L1PA was linked to lower reoperation risk in open ASD correction
Gap, per the authors: its relevance in MIS had not been well established
slides.notes: The table is our arithmetic from the formula in the abstract, to make the target concrete. Our framing, not the abstract's: L1PA is an angle anchored to the pelvis, so it is less affected by standing compensation than SVA, which is why it appeals as a target that can be planned and checked. Also ours: circumferential MIS corrects mainly through interbody cages with limited posterior release, which is why surgeons ask whether it can reach sagittal targets at all. Two questions sit inside this paper. First, can MIS reach the target as often as open surgery? Second, if it does, does it matter for outcome in MIS? Library comparison: the Hills T4-L1-hip axis record (D14) gives an observational risk-minimizing L1PA target of 0.5 × PI − (19° ± 2°). Khanna uses 0.5 × PI − 21° with a ±5° window. The two targets differ by about 2° at the center, and Khanna's window is wider. We cannot tell from the abstract why the authors chose −21 and ±5, or which prior paper they draw on.

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: Retrospective cohort from a multicenter, prospectively collected ASD database.
points: 1104 ASD patients at 13 centers
Included: scoliosis ≥20°, SVA ≥5 cm, PT ≥25° or TK ≥60°, and ≥2-year follow-up
MIS: circumferential only, meaning LLIF or ALIF with percutaneous posterior fixation; compared with open surgery
Radiographs and PROs: preoperative, 6 weeks and final follow-up
Outcomes: reoperation, SRS-22 total and SF-36 PCS change
Analysis named: linear regression and t tests
slides.notes: What to notice. The inclusion criteria are joined by or, so this is a broad deformity population: a 20° coronal curve with good sagittal balance qualifies alongside a patient with 10 cm of SVA. The abstract does not give group sizes; the full text does: 131 MIS and 973 open. Every MIS result below is a subgroup result in 131 patients, and only about 12% of the cohort. The abstract also does not say how many eligible patients were lost before the 2-year cut, which is a common source of bias in registry work. The full text says the 6-week postoperative film defined whether L1PA was ideal. The objective names mechanical failure, but the results report reoperation, and the abstract does not say whether reoperation was for any cause or only for mechanical failure. On analysis: t tests and linear regression are named. Reoperation is a yes or no outcome, which would usually call for logistic or time-to-event models. That observation is ours. No adjustment for age, frailty, bone density, levels fused or pelvic incidence is reported in the abstract. The full text may address some of this; we could not check.

slides.title: Results
slides.lead: MIS reached ideal L1PA at a similar rate to open surgery. Within MIS, ideal L1PA went with fewer reoperations and larger PRO gains.

rows: Reached ideal L1PA, MIS vs open

points: Open surgery: ideal L1PA was not associated with reduced reoperation
All patients: each 1° deviation from ideal L1PA raised reoperation risk by 1.8% (P=0.04)
slides.notes: Read the first row differently from the rest: it compares MIS against open, while the other rows compare ideal against not ideal within MIS. Our arithmetic: the MIS reoperation gap is 18 percentage points, and the ideal group's rate is under half the other group's. The SRS-22 total gap in improvement is 0.45 points and the SF-36 PCS gap is 4.5 points. Our recomputation, using the full-text group sizes of 131 MIS and 973 open with a two-proportion test: 63% vs 61% gives P of about 0.52 to 0.66 allowing for rounding, not the reported 0.342. A P of 0.342 would need an MIS group of roughly 400 to 700. Within MIS, 63% of 131 is about 83 ideal and 48 not ideal, so 15% vs 33% is about 12 vs 16 reoperations and gives P of about 0.02, not below 0.01; reaching P below 0.01 would need about 150 or more MIS patients. Either a different test was used or the numbers do not match. The full text also says sixty-three patients in the MIS group reached ideal L1PA, which would be 48% of 131, not 63%. This is the main fragility: the MIS result rests on about 28 reoperations in total. The open-surgery result is the key contrast. The authors' own Background says ideal L1PA was linked to lower reoperation in open correction, yet in this cohort it was not, at least on reoperation. The abstract does not report open-group PRO results. The 1.8% per degree estimate is pooled across MIS and open. The abstract does not say whether it is absolute percentage points or relative risk, or whether deviation counts in both directions (under- and overcorrection). Our reading: a linear regression on a binary outcome would give percentage points per degree, which would mean a patient 10° off target carries about 18 points more risk, a large claim that needs the full model. The SF-36 PCS P value of 0.04 is close to the threshold, and no multiplicity correction is reported in the abstract.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: Interesting signal, weak causal footing, and we have only the abstract.
points: Holds up: large multicenter prospectively collected database
Holds up: minimum 2-year follow-up and a clear, reproducible alignment target
Holds up: authors report MIS reached the target at a similar rate to open surgery (not tested for equivalence)
Weakens it: retrospective and not randomized to an alignment target
Weakens it: MIS group is only 131 of 1104, and the reported P values do not recompute from those sizes
Weakens it: no multivariable adjustment (authors' choice, citing limited patient numbers); t tests and linear regression only
Weakens it: reoperation cause and timing not given
Weakens it: the finding did not hold for reoperation in open surgery
slides.notes: Be fair to the authors. Achievability is the cleanest result: ideal L1PA in 63% of MIS and 61% of open cases is a descriptive comparison and less exposed to confounding, although we cannot see whether the patients being compared had similar deformity. The outcome associations are harder. Patients in whom the surgeon reaches the target may be those with less severe or more flexible deformity, better bone or simpler anatomy, and those same traits predict fewer reoperations and better PROs. Our reading: that is confounding by indication, and the authors state they did not adjust for it with a multivariable model. The MIS against open contrast also carries selection: surgeons choose circumferential MIS for particular patients. The authors acknowledge this selection bias but argue that baseline differences were not significant, so it likely does not apply. Our reading: the full text's Table 1 shows MIS patients were older (68 vs 60) with lower baseline SF-36 PCS, and the authors chose not to fit a multivariable model, so comparability is not shown. The open-group null result cuts both ways. It may mean the target matters less once a big posterior release and rigid construct are used. It may also mean the MIS finding is a subgroup result that will not replicate. We cannot say which. The authors' conclusion calls ideal L1PA a key surgical target. Our reading: the data support an association in MIS, not that aiming for the number causes fewer reoperations. The paper is 5 journal pages (E118-E122), so detail may be limited even in full text. Recheck all of this when the correct PDF is in hand.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "In an ISSG cohort, circumferential MIS reached the ideal L1 pelvic angle at a similar rate to open surgery, about 6 in 10 cases. In MIS patients, those within 5° of target had half the reoperation rate, 15 versus 33 percent, and better SRS-22 and SF-36 gains. It was not linked to fewer reoperations after open surgery, and this is an association, not proof."
points: Hills comes from the library record. Populations and endpoints differ.
Abstract-level only: re-review when the correct full text is obtained
slides.notes: Expect these follow-up questions. Should I aim for L1PA in MIS cases? The abstract supports it as a reasonable target that MIS can reach, and reaching it went with better results. It does not show that pushing harder for it, for example adding an osteotomy or converting to open, improves outcome. That step is ours to warn against, not the authors' claim. Why did it not matter in open surgery? The abstract gives no explanation, and the authors' own Background says it mattered in prior open-surgery work. Say that you do not know, and that this is the weak point of the paper. How big was the MIS group? 131 patients, against 973 open (full text). With those sizes, our recomputed P values are weaker than reported: about 0.02 for the MIS reoperation gap. The authors say they did not fit a multivariable model because of the limited number of patients. Is 1.8% per degree absolute? The abstract does not say. How does this fit the T4-L1-hip axis? Hills (D14 record) gives a similar target, 0.5 × PI − (19° ± 2°), and linked deviation to mechanical failure. Khanna's target sits about 2° lower with a wider window. The two are consistent in direction, but neither is a trial of aiming for the target. Finally, this deck was drafted from the abstract; the correct full text is now on file and the deck should be fully re-reviewed against it.

decks.not_reviewed: The four source articles (Rutsch 2023, Cirillo 2025, Singh 2024, Kwon 2007) were not read; every number in this deck is as this review reports it. Published figures or tables were not seen (the reformatted PMC copy omits images; the text cites none). No supplement is cited.

slides.title: AO Spine: subaxial fractures
slides.lead: Four hand-picked studies, one per decision point, each turned into a recommendation.
points: Journal club: subaxial cervical trauma
Camino-Willhuber G, et al. Global Spine J 2026;16(3):1411-1417
AO Spine Knowledge Forum Trauma and Infection. Literature review with clinical recommendations, not a systematic guideline.

Bottom line: CT or MRI, not plain films alone. Consider surgery for the floating lateral mass (conditional, very low certainty). Watch for PLL injury, bilateral facet dislocation and older age when planning ACDF. Anterior fixation is reasonable for unilateral facet injury without cord injury.
slides.notes: Frame this before the content. It is not a guideline built from a systematic search. The Knowledge Forum chose four studies it judged impactful, one per phase of care: imaging, operate or not, when to add posterior fixation, and which approach. For each, the authors give a clinical rationale, a summary, a methods critique and a recommendation. The authors themselves name the selection bias: articles were chosen on the authors' expertise, the subject and the quality of the evidence. The paper gives no search strategy and no formal method for assigning strong or conditional. What was reviewed: the full text of the review in a reformatted PMC copy with images omitted. The four source studies were not read, so every figure here is the review's report of those studies, and errors in transcription from the originals cannot be checked from this PDF. Background the paper gives: cervical injuries occur in 2.4% of trauma cases, and about half of cervical injuries involve C3 to C7. Our note for the room: one author of this review (Joaquim) is also an author of the Cirillo review it selects, and both appear in the same journal. That is not a flaw in itself, but it is worth knowing when a panel rates its own work.

slides.title: The recommendations
slides.lead: Every recommendation rests on a single study.

rows: Against plain films as the sole test when NEXUS calls for imaging
MRI if neurologic deficit and normal CT
Cirillo, systematic review, very low certainty
At index surgery, consider added posterior fixation or posterior-only approach if age over 60, PLL injury or bilateral facet dislocation
Anterior fixation for unilateral facet injury without cord injury

slides.notes: This is the slide to memorize. Seven recommendations, one strong. The abstract gives one sentence per article and states five of them; it leaves out the conditional recommendation against plain films alone and the conditional MRI recommendation. The single strong recommendation comes from a single-center retrospective cohort. Our view: under usual GRADE practice, a strong recommendation from one observational study needs a stated justification, and none is given. The strength labels use GRADE words, but the paper does not describe a GRADE evidence-to-decision process, a vote or a panel. Only the Kwon trial gets an explicit GRADE rating (moderate), and the review notes very low GRADE certainty for Cirillo as that review reported it. Wording matters. The abstract says to add posterior fusion for the Singh risk factors. The body says to consider added posterior fixation, or a posterior-only approach, at index surgery. The second is softer and also widens the options beyond what the study tested. Also note the abstract calls Singh's cases stand-alone ACDF, yet every patient had an anterior plate with bicortical screws. Stand-alone here means anterior only. Note too the fragment-size recommendation: the authors map larger fragment size onto F2 of the AO Spine subaxial classification, inside a review whose source population was non-displaced fractures.

slides.title: Imaging: Rutsch 2023
slides.lead: Retrospective, single center, adult blunt trauma with neck pain meeting NEXUS imaging criteria, over 5 years.
points: 4996 screened; 2321 met NEXUS criteria (73.2% low energy). 186 injured by full case review.
MRI found injury in 14 patients with false-negative CT: 8 treated conservatively, 6 operated (5 with deficits).
CT sensitivity rose to 89.8% with orthopedic surgeon consultation.
slides.notes: How to read it. The reference standard was not a test. It was a full case review, described once as by a senior spine surgeon and once as by a junior researcher and spine surgeon. Every sensitivity is measured against that judgment. Patients were not imaged the same way. CT went to 2120, MRI to 206, plain films to 215, LODOX to 498. Who got MRI was a clinical choice, so the MRI figure is measured in a selected group. The review names two notable limitations: no same-patient comparison of the tests, and no long-term follow-up for missed or misdiagnosed injuries. Our point: this is verification bias, and it can push estimates either way. What is fragile. CT missed about 1 in 9 injuries here, and MRI found 14 of them, 6 needing surgery. That supports the conditional MRI recommendation. It sits awkwardly with calling CT/MRI the gold standard, since neither was the reference standard in this study and CT sensitivity was 88.6%. Our recomputation: low and high energy (1700 and 621) are 73.2% and 26.8% of 2321, and 2135 uninjured plus 186 injured is 2321. Both check. The per-test counts do not fit one convention. The review says injuries were identified in 178 CT, 78 MRI, 22 plain film and 3 LODOX patients. Our reading: as all test positives (true plus false), CT and LODOX reconcile (for example 164 true and 14 false positives among 185 injured gives 88.6% and 99.3%; 3 of 57 injured gives 5.3% and 100%). MRI (69 of 78 is 88.5%) and plain films (8 of 22 is 36.4%) reconcile only if the counts are injured patients per test. So the counts probably use mixed conventions rather than a transcription error. Check the original before quoting the counts. The rates themselves are the paper's. Plain films did poorly here: 36.4% sensitivity, but from about 22 injured patients in a selected subgroup (our approximate 95% CI 20% to 57%), and the review itself cites a literature range of 44% to 93%. LODOX is a low-dose 2D x-ray, and 5.3% sensitivity rules it out as a screen.

slides.title: Facet fractures: Cirillo 2025
slides.lead: Systematic review: what predicts failure of nonoperative care for isolated unilateral non-displaced subaxial facet fractures in neurologically intact adults?
points: 1639 records, 8 studies included. ROBINS-I for bias. GRADE certainty very low.
Failure: pseudarthrosis, posterior translation, new neurologic symptoms or persistent pain.
Floating lateral mass: OR 5.4 (95% CI 1.32 to 22.19) for failure, from 2 studies defining failure as translation over 3.5 mm.
Smaller absolute facet fracture height went with successful conservative care in 2 studies.
Excluded: fracture-dislocation, osteoporosis, low-energy trauma, pathological fracture, RA, AS, DISH.
slides.notes: What to notice. The headline odds ratio comes from 2 studies, and the review gives no patient count. The interval runs from 1.32 to 22.19, so the true effect could be small or very large. Our check: the log midpoint of the interval is 5.41, so the interval is symmetric on the log scale and consistent with OR 5.4. The two studies defined failure more narrowly than the review's primary outcome: translation over 3.5 mm, not the composite of pseudarthrosis, translation, new symptoms or pain. The fragment-size finding has no effect size in this paper, only a direction. A source problem: the review describes the Spector measure as the total vertical height of the facet's articular surface divided by the height of the fracture fragment. Read as written, that ratio gets smaller as the fragment gets bigger. A fragment-size percentage would put the fragment height on top. Our reading is that the description is inverted; check Spector before teaching the formula. The recommendation for surgery in F3 is conditional and built on very low certainty evidence. The F2 recommendation stretches further: the source review studied non-displaced fractures and reported fragment height as a correlate, and the authors map that onto F2. The populations excluded are the ones where you most worry about failure: AS, DISH, osteoporosis and low-energy trauma. Our inference: this applies to adults with a normal spine after higher-energy injury, not to the osteoporotic low-energy fall. The review states no age limit.

slides.title: When ACDF fails: Singh 2024
slides.lead: Retrospective, single center: 341 adults with traumatic subaxial injury treated with ACDF (PEEK cage, plate, bicortical screws).
points: Delayed posterior fixation in 11 of 341 (3.2%), median 20 days after ACDF, all for construct failure with instability.
CT within 24 h, at 4 and 12 weeks. 78% single level, 16% two level, 6.2% three or more.
Excluded: AS, non-traumatic cases, primary posterior or 360 surgery, ACCF, incomplete records.
slides.notes: Read the denominator first. Only 11 events. A multivariable model with 3 retained predictors, after at least 6 were tested univariably, has very few events per variable. Our view: the odds ratios are unstable and probably inflated, and PLL injury at P = .048 is barely over the line. The review gives no confidence intervals. Our approximation, back-calculated from each OR and P: PLL injury about 1.02 to 31, bilateral facet dislocation about 1.6 to 27, age about 1.01 to 1.13 per unit. Our recomputation: 11 of 341 is 3.2%, which checks. Neurologic grades (28, 16, 5.3, 5.3 and 45%) and level counts (78, 16 and 6.2%) each sum to about 100. Age is the slippery one. The model reports OR 1.07, presumably per year, though the review does not state units. The phrase "especially above the age of 60 years" has no supporting number in this review, so the 60 cutoff cannot be checked here. Height was protective on univariable analysis (OR 0.92). What the study cannot show: everyone had ACDF. It identifies who failed ACDF. It does not show that 360 fixation or a posterior-only approach would have done better in those patients. The recommendation to consider posterior-only at index surgery is the authors' extrapolation. The reviewers call 12-week CT follow-up relatively long. Our view: it is short, and late failures would be missed. 87% had an injured anterior longitudinal ligament. Median time to surgery was 2.0 days. Absolute message for the patient: about 97% did not need delayed posterior fixation. Other reoperations are not reported.

slides.title: Approach: Kwon 2007 RCT
slides.lead: Unilateral facet injury C3 to T1, judged surgical by the treating surgeon, approach randomized, no cord injury: 20 anterior vs 22 posterior.

rows: Swallowing or voice change at discharge

points: Anterior: ACDF, iliac crest autograft, locking plate. Posterior: lateral mass screw-plate and/or wiring, iliac crest graft.
No difference in SF-36, NASS cervical or neurologic scores at 12 months. Neck pain VAS slightly lower anterior early (P = .15).
34 fracture-subluxations, 8 purely ligamentous. Block randomization.
slides.notes: The primary outcome was negative. The recommendation for anterior fixation rests on secondary outcomes, which the authors concede: the trial was not powered for them. What the authors cite for anterior: a trend toward less pain (P = .15), fewer infections, higher fusion and better lordosis. Only lordosis was significant. Our Fisher test on infection, 0 of 20 against 4 of 22, gives P = .11, and fusion was P = .49. What costs anterior: 11 of 20 (55%) had swallowing or voice changes at discharge, all resolved by 3 months. The review then says no major complication occurred, alongside 4 wound infections that lengthened stay. Decide for yourself whether those count. Our recomputation on fusion: 2 pseudarthroses of 22 is 91% fusion, not 89%. A Fisher exact test of 20 of 20 against 20 of 22 gives P = .49, which matches the reported P. But a smaller posterior denominator alone does not fit: 20 of 20 against 16 of 18 (89%) gives P = .22. The 89% and P = .49 fit together only if both arms lost patients (for example 18 of 18 against 16 of 18, P = .49) or the 89% is a slip. The review does not report follow-up completeness. Radiculopathy 6 plus 4 is 10, and 34 plus 8 is 42; both check. On the methods critique: the review says allocation concealment and blinding were not possible. Our view: allocation concealment is always possible in a surgical trial. Blinding the surgeon and patient is what is hard. The review grades the trial moderate and also calls it level 1. The trial is from 2007 and used iliac crest graft in both arms, so the donor-site burden fell on both arms. The authors add their own cautions, beyond the trial: be careful going anterior in the elderly, and prefer posterior or combined fixation when the subjacent endplate is fractured (citing Johnson).

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: AO Spine picked four studies and made seven recommendations, one strong, each resting on one study.
points: Spoken summary: In blunt neck trauma that needs imaging, plain films alone missed most injuries in Rutsch's selected subgroup, and CT still missed about one in nine in Rutsch, so get MRI when there is a deficit and a normal CT. A floating lateral mass fails a collar more often, odds ratio 5.4 with a wide interval. After ACDF only 3% needed posterior fixation, and PLL injury, bilateral facet dislocation and age predicted it, from 11 events. In Kwon's 42-patient trial, the primary outcome, time to discharge criteria, showed no significant difference (2.75 vs 3.5 days, P = .096, not powered); anterior had no infections and better lordosis but more early dysphagia.
Expect: Is this a guideline? No. It is an expert-selected review, with no systematic search.
Expect: Why is the one strong recommendation from a retrospective cohort?
Expect: Does Singh show 360 is better for bilateral facet dislocation? No. Everyone had ACDF.
Expect: Kwon's primary outcome was negative. Why recommend anterior?
