Expect: Do the facet data apply to elderly, AS or DISH patients? No. They were excluded.
slides.notes: Keep the summary to the numbers you can defend. Lead with the CT miss rate, about 1 in 9, and the 14 injuries MRI found after a normal CT. Quote plain films at 36.4% as Rutsch's selected subgroup of about 22 injured patients, not a general figure; the review cites 44% to 93% elsewhere. For the floating lateral mass, say the odds ratio with its interval, 1.32 to 22.19, so nobody hears it as a precise five-fold risk. For Singh, give the absolute number first: 11 of 341. Then the predictors. Then the caveat that the age-over-60 cutoff is not supported by a number in this review. For Kwon, say the primary outcome first and the secondary findings second, and mention the 55% early dysphagia so the room hears both sides. Likely pushback and short answers. Why should a GRADE-style strong recommendation come from a retrospective cohort? The authors do not say; our view is that it reflects consensus more than the strength of that one study. Should a bilateral facet dislocation get 360 at index? Singh shows higher failure after ACDF, not benefit from 360. The decision still rests on judgment and on the Dvorak-style algorithms the authors cite. Why isn't LODOX acceptable? 5.3% sensitivity. What would change these recommendations? The authors call for prospective multicenter studies. Our view: a same-patient imaging comparison and a larger approach trial powered for infection and alignment would matter most. Remind the room that every number came through this review, not from the original papers, and two internal inconsistencies (the Rutsch counts and Kwon's fusion percentage) mean the originals should be checked before quoting detail.

decks.not_reviewed: Figure 1 (decision flowchart), omitted from our reformatted PMC copy. The three appraised source studies (Martha 2009, Xu 2010, Tacconi 2020) and the supporting literature (references 2, 9-14) were not read; their numbers are as this paper reports them. No funding or conflict of interest statement appears in our copy. The PDF is the full text of the paper, not a critique.

slides.title: Guiroy 2026: AO Spine recommendations for lumbar synovial cysts
slides.lead: Bottom line: fuse when instability is present or expected after decompression. In a stable segment, decompression alone or interlaminar endoscopy is reasonable. Percutaneous rupture buys time. Every recommendation is conditional and rests on one low or very low quality study.
points: Journal club · Lumbar degeneration
Guiroy A, Gagliardi M, Cabrera JP, Le HV, Feger M, Fisher C, Yoon T. Global Spine J 2026;16(7):2804-2810
AO Spine Degenerative Knowledge Forum, Clinical Practice Recommendations series
Source read: full text reformatted from the open-access PMC version. Figure 1, the decision flowchart, is not in our copy.
slides.notes: This is not a trial and not a systematic review. It is a short AO Spine Knowledge Forum paper that picks three original studies, appraises each one, and attaches a GRADE-style recommendation to each. Read it as expert framing of three papers, not as a pooled estimate. The three studies are Martha 2009 (percutaneous rupture, 101 patients), Xu 2010 (decompression with or without fusion, 167 patients) and Tacconi 2020 (full-endoscopic resection, 35 treated patients). None is randomized and none has a concurrent control except the nonrandom fusion versus decompression comparison in Xu. This deck was prepared from the whole text of the paper as reformatted from PMC. The copy is complete text, not a critique, but images were omitted, so Figure 1, the flowchart the Discussion leans on, was not seen. The three source studies and the supporting literature (references 2, 9 to 14; by title only 2 and 9 are meta-analyses) were not read, so every number about them here is as this paper reports it. The copy also shows no funding or conflict of interest statement; check the published version before quoting either.

slides.title: The question and how they answered it
slides.lead: When a synovial cyst needs treatment, which option, and when does it need a fusion?
points: Background (authors): cysts arise from degenerating facet joints and are linked to disc degeneration, instability and degenerative spondylolisthesis.

Some consider a cyst a definitive sign of instability. The authors call the pathomechanics of that association controversial (and the pathogenesis of cysts too), but say it still drives surgical decisions.
Conservative care first for asymptomatic or mild cysts. Surgery when it fails, symptoms worsen or deficits appear.
Method: a focused narrative review, explicitly not a comprehensive systematic review. Three studies chosen for relevance, methodological quality and fit to the three strategies.
Systematic reviews and meta-analyses were used only as supporting discussion.
Each study was appraised and given a quality rating; recommendations were graded Strong or Conditional with GRADE.
slides.notes: The selection step is the whole paper, so look at it hard. The authors state that the AO Spine method is to pick representative studies rather than to search systematically. No search strategy, databases, dates or selection criteria beyond relevance and quality are given, and no consensus process (such as a vote or Delphi round) is described. So the old record label of consensus is not something the paper states. Note what GRADE is normally for: rating a body of evidence for one outcome across studies. Here it is applied to one study per question, which makes the quality rating close to a rating of a single study design. That is our reading, not the authors'. Also notice the introduction's background figures. It says over 90 percent of cases involve L4-5, yet Martha's series was primarily at L4-5 at only 68.3 percent (the text does not say whether of patients or of cysts). The sentence probably means the lumbar spine accounts for most cases, but as printed the two numbers conflict; that is our inference. The introduction cites a meta-analysis on synovial cyst as a marker of instability (reference 2) but does not report its result, so the deck cannot say what it found.

slides.title: Recommendations, strength and evidence
slides.lead: Three conditional recommendations, each resting on a single study rated low or very low.

rows: Temporary or palliative; consider in patients unfit or unwilling for surgery. Counsel on likely surgery
When mechanical instability is present or expected after decompression
No instability and facets can be preserved; warn about higher recurrence
Stable segment, experienced endoscopic surgeon, cyst reachable interlaminar

points: Instability is the hinge: the authors call it the primary factor once a patient is a surgical candidate.
Fusion is preferred for mobile degenerative spondylolisthesis, disrupted facets or expected instability after decompression.
Other factors named: neurologic deficit, coexisting listhesis or deformity, functional demand and surgeon expertise.
slides.see: Figure 1 is the decision flowchart: surgical candidate or not, then stable or unstable. It was not in our copy.
slides.notes: Read the strength words carefully, because the paper itself is not consistent. Every formal recommendation is Conditional. Yet the Discussion says fusion with decompression is highly recommended when instability is present or likely, and the Conclusion says fusion is recommended. Teach the formal grade: conditional. Second, two recommendation sentences are worded as first-line use. The rupture section gives a conditional recommendation for percutaneous rupture as a first line treatment, then says it could be considered in patients unwilling or unfit for surgery. The endoscopy section gives a conditional recommendation for endoscopic surgery as first line treatment without instability, while Table 1 calls it a good alternative for experienced surgeons and the practice text limits it to interlaminar access. We read both as options for selected patients, not as defaults, which matches the authors' own surrounding text. Third, the decompression-alone recommendation and the fusion recommendation both come from Xu. This paper reports only that patients with instability or advanced facet degeneration were more likely to be fused and that imaging characteristics were not stratified. It does not say whether Xu compared fusion and decompression within stable or within unstable patients; our reading is that neither rule was tested directly. The rule is the authors' clinical logic layered on a confounded comparison.

slides.title: The three studies, by the numbers
slides.lead: All figures are as this paper reports them; the source studies were not read.

rows: 101; 68.3% female; mean age 59.8; 68.3% at L4-5 (same figure twice)
67% immediate relief; 33% lasting at mean 22 months
54% later surgery, mean 0.7 years; 30% had 2 or more injections; 21% non-response or lost
167: 56 instrumented fusion, 18 in situ fusion, 39 laminectomy, 51 hemilaminectomy
Cyst recurrence 0 with fusion; 3 (8%) laminectomy; 2 (4%) hemilaminectomy
Dural tear 16.5% fusion vs 5.8% decompression; radicular pain recurred in 12%
Pain 6.8 to 2.1 at 6 months; 77.2% good or excellent (McNab) at 15 months
4 converted to open; dysesthesia 3 of 11 transforaminal; 2 dural tears, both transforaminal; 3 later fused

slides.notes: Recompute what you can. Martha: 68.3 percent of 101 is 69, but the identical 68.3 percent is given for both female sex and the L4-5 level, possibly a transcription duplication (ours). The 33 percent and 54 percent figures are given without a denominator, and 21 percent were lost or did not respond, so we cannot tell whether they are of 101 or of responders. The paper also says patients with successful rupture had higher ODI scores but similar pain scores; on ODI higher means worse, so as printed this reads as worse disability after a successful rupture. That is unexplained. Xu: the four groups sum to 164, not the 167 stated; 195 is the cyst count. Recurrence 3 of 39 is 7.7 percent and 2 of 51 is 3.9 percent, so 8 and 4 percent check. All 5 recurrences were in decompression-only patients: 5 of 90, about 6 percent overall (our arithmetic). Dural tears: 16.5 percent of 74 fused is 12.2 and 5.8 percent of 90 decompressed is 5.2, so the rates do not reproduce from patient counts. They fit cyst-level denominators summing to the 195 cysts (15 of 91, 6 of 104), so they may be per cyst (ours). On patient counts of 12 or 13 of 74 vs 5 or 6 of 90, Fisher P runs 0.02 to 0.08 (ours): borderline. Median time to recurrence was 12 months; nothing beyond 2 years. The paper says fusion gave more durable axial back pain relief but gives no number. Tacconi: 54 minus 7 declined, 5 with listhesis above grade I, 4 with severe stenosis and 3 with deficits leaves 35, which checks. 11 were transforaminal, so 24 were presumably interlaminar (ours). 77.2 percent fits no denominator from 1 to 54 (27 of 35 is 77.1; 28 followed at 12 months cannot give it), so it is a rounding or transcription slip (ours). Follow-up was 100 percent at 6 months and 80 percent at 12 months; the 15-month denominator is not reported, probably smaller (ours). Whether the 4 conversions are inside the 35 is not stated.

slides.title: Gaps and errors
slides.lead: The recommendations are sensible; the evidence under them is thin and the text overstates it in places.
points: Abstract says over half of rupture patients needed surgery within one year. The study summary says 54% eventually needed surgery, mean 0.7 years. A mean does not show over half within a year.
Conclusion says fusion and laminectomy reduce recurrence compared with decompression only. Laminectomy is decompression only and had the highest recurrence (8%) in Xu.
Discussion says highly recommended; the formal grade is conditional.
Xu group sizes sum to 164, not 167, and the dural tear percentages do not reproduce from patient counts (they may be per cyst).
Abstract says fusion reduces recurrence; no test is reported. Our Fisher test of 0 of 74 vs 5 of 90 gives P about 0.065.
Introduction gives over 90% at L4-5; Martha's series had 68.3%, the same figure given for female sex.
Selection bias in Xu (authors): instability and advanced facet degeneration pushed patients toward fusion, so fusion versus decompression is confounded.
slides.notes: Two of these matter clinically. First, the recurrence argument for fusion. In Xu, fusion was given to the patients with instability or advanced facet degeneration, and the authors of this review say so. Recurrence was 0 in 74 fused patients against 5 in 90 decompressed, a small number of events in a nonrandom comparison, with no imaging stratification and no follow-up past 2 years. Fusion also had about three times the dural tear rate as reported, and adjacent segment disease and pseudarthrosis were not reported. No test is reported. Our Fisher exact test of 0 of 74 against 5 of 90 gives two-sided P about 0.065 (one-sided 0.047), and laminectomy against hemilaminectomy (3 of 39 vs 2 of 51) gives P about 0.65, so the 8 versus 4 percent ranking is noise. So the honest statement is: in one confounded series fusion had no recurrences, a difference that is not significant even there; it has not been shown to be better for a stable segment. Second, the rupture numbers. The abstract's over half within one year is stronger than the study summary supports. Tell patients what the paper actually reports: about two thirds get early relief, about one third keep it, and about half go on to surgery at the treated level. Also note the methodological limits the authors list for each study: Martha had telephone outcomes, recall bias, 21 percent loss and mixed repeat injections; Tacconi had no control arm and is Level IV. Separately, the Tacconi authors emphasized the learning curve and the risk of the transforaminal route, which had a higher dysesthesia rate (3 of 11) and both dural tears. What is missing entirely: any randomized or prospective comparative study, any patient-reported comparison of fusion against decompression in stable cysts, and any definition of instability (translation thresholds, dynamic films, facet effusion). The paper relies on instability but never says how to measure it.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: AO Spine 2026: fuse a synovial cyst for instability, not for the cyst. Everything else is a conditional, low-evidence choice.
points: Spoken summary: an AO Spine Knowledge Forum appraisal of three studies, one per strategy. All recommendations are conditional.
Percutaneous rupture with steroid: very low evidence. About two thirds get early relief, one third keep it, about half go on to surgery. Use for patients unfit or unwilling.
Decompression alone: reasonable in a stable segment with facets preserved; warn about recurrence (4-8% in Xu).

Fusion: when instability is present or expected after decompression. In Xu, no recurrences after fusion (not significant on our test), but unstable or degenerate segments were more likely fused, and fusion had more dural tears.
Endoscopy: stable segment, experienced surgeon, interlaminar route. 77.2% good or excellent at 15 months in a 35-patient case series.

rows: Does a cyst mean the segment is unstable?
Some think so. The authors call the mechanism of the association controversial. They tie fusion to instability, present or expected, not to the cyst.
Is fusion proven to lower recurrence?
No. One retrospective, confounded cohort: 0 of 74 fused vs 5 of 90 decompressed, no test reported; our Fisher test gives P about 0.065.
No. Three studies were hand-picked; no search or consensus process is described.
It is not. The paper names mobile spondylolisthesis, disrupted facets and expected iatrogenic instability.
Interlaminar. Transforaminal had a higher dysesthesia rate (3 of 11) and both dural tears.

slides.notes: If you have 30 seconds: this is expert framing, not new data. One study per option, none randomized, all recommendations conditional. Instability, present or expected after decompression, is the trigger for fusion; otherwise decompression alone or interlaminar endoscopy, with counseling about recurrence. Percutaneous rupture is a bridge. Expect pushback on three points. Someone will say the recurrence data prove fusion. Answer that patients with instability or advanced facet degeneration were more likely to be fused, that 0 of 74 against 5 of 90 is not significant on our own Fisher test (P about 0.065), and that dural tears were reported as more frequent with fusion. Someone will quote the text's highly recommended; answer that the formal GRADE strength is conditional. Someone will ask about the over half within a year figure for rupture; the study summary supports about half eventually, at a mean of 0.7 years, not half within a year. Finally, say what you have not seen: the flowchart figure and the three source papers. If a decision rests on a specific number, such as the dural tear rate, check it in Xu 2010 itself, because the group sizes reported here do not add up.

decks.not_reviewed: No figures appear in our reformatted PMC copy; the text cites none, so only Table 1 is relevant and it is present. The four appraised source studies (Dial 2022, Line 2020, Chen 2023, Safaee 2018) and the supporting literature (references 1-11, 16-39, including the tether review, the tether meta-analysis and the cost analysis) were not read; their numbers are as this paper reports them. No supplement is cited. The PDF is the full text of the paper, not a critique. A funding statement is present; no conflict of interest statement appears in our copy.

slides.title: Sardi 2026: AO Spine recommendations for PJK and PJF prevention
slides.lead: Bottom line: check bone quality, do not overcorrect, and consider junctional protection in high-risk long fusions to the pelvis. One strong recommendation (assess BMD); the rest are conditional and rest on observational data.
points: Journal club · Adult deformity
Sardi JP, Shawky A, Aldebeyan S, Nicholls F, Astur N, Fisher C, Klineberg EO, Smith JS. Global Spine J 2026
AO Spine Knowledge Forum Deformity, Clinical Practice Recommendations series
Source read: full text reformatted from the open-access PMC version, including Table 1. Not a critique.
slides.notes: This is not a trial and not a systematic review. The AO Spine Knowledge Forum Deformity listed 30 articles on PJK and PJF, picked four, had one author appraise each, and agreed GRADE-style recommendations at a consensus meeting. The four are Dial 2022 (alignment targets, 165 patients), Line 2020 (implant prophylaxis and overcorrection, 625 patients), Chen 2023 (bone density meta-analysis, 2,185 patients) and Safaee 2018 (ligament augmentation, 100 versus 100). So read it as expert framing of four papers, plus a Discussion that brings in a wider literature, mainly on tethers and bone drugs. Scope matters: the authors limit the recommendations to adults having long posterior instrumented thoracolumbar fusions ending at the pelvis, upper or lower thoracic UIV. Cervical-to-pelvis constructs and long constructs not ending at the pelvis are excluded. This deck was prepared from the whole text. No figures are cited and none were seen. The four source studies and the Discussion's supporting papers were not read, so every number about them is as this paper reports it. Funding was from AO Spine through the Knowledge Forum; the copy has no conflict of interest statement. The library record was abstract level before this review.

slides.title: The problem and how they answered it
slides.lead: Which risk factors and preventive steps should change practice for PJK and PJF after long fusion to the pelvis?
points: Burden (authors, citing others): radiographic complications are nearly 20% of major ASD complications; PJK and PJF are about two thirds of those.
Incidence 6-60% by definition and follow-up; most series 20-40%. Most occur within 2 years, but about 20% of PJF may occur later.
PJF reoperation 10-47%; revision cost commonly $55,000-195,000 per case.

Definitions: Glattes PJK is a proximal junctional angle of at least 10 degrees and at least 10 degrees beyond baseline. Thresholds of 15 and 20 degrees, and later 28 degrees absolute or 22 degrees change, still predicted revision poorly.
PJF is defined by structure: fracture at UIV to UIV+2, listhesis, ligament disruption, implant failure, stenosis or progression, with pain, deficit or revision.
Method: 30 articles identified by forum members, 4 chosen after discussion for relevance to prevention. No search strategy is given.
slides.notes: Set the stakes with the distinction the authors draw. Radiographic PJK often does not track clinical outcome: the authors say SRS scores were comparable with and without PJK in clinical series, so a 10 degree threshold catches many harmless changes. Surgeons worry about PJF, which drives revision. But the authors also say, citing a long-term cohort of 160 patients (reference 4), that nearly two thirds of initially asymptomatic PJK progressed to PJF within five years, so they suggest PJK and PJF may be points on a disease continuum. Hold both ideas: they are different outcomes, but PJK is not reliably benign. Two other teaching points from the Discussion. First, failure mode differs by UIV level in the authors' account: compression fracture predominates in lower thoracic constructs and ligament disruption with angular progression in upper thoracic constructs. They float cement for lower and hooks or tethers for upper thoracic UIVs, then say direct comparative evidence is lacking. Second, some rise in junctional angle may be physiologic relaxation of compensatory lordosis after lumbar lordosis is restored, not pathologic PJK. Now look at the method. The 30 articles were identified by forum members, not by a described database search, and the four were picked after discussion. There is no list of the 26 not chosen. Our reading: the question set is defined by what the four studies covered, so other levers (UIV choice, rod type, frailty, sarcopenia) get Discussion mention but no graded recommendation.

slides.title: The four studies the recommendations rest on
slides.lead: Three observational cohorts and one meta-analysis of observational studies; none randomized.

rows: Post hoc, multicenter ASLS cohort, 165, at least 2 years
GAP AUC 0.57; LL over 15 deg above GAP ideal raised mechanical complications; overcorrection did not raise PJK
PJF 20.3% no implant vs 10.6% implant; revision similar; overcorrected without implant 24.2% PJF
T-score -2.14 with PJK vs -1.43 without; UIV HU about 32 lower with PJK
Single center, 100 vs 100 historical controls, mean 12 months
PJA rise 6 vs 14 deg; PJF 4 vs 18 (P=0.002)

slides.notes: Read each row for what was actually measured. Dial: mechanical complications occurred in 25%, PJK 12.7% and pseudarthrosis or rod fracture 17%; those sum to 29.7%, so some patients presumably had both (our inference). The hyperlordosis signal was for mechanical complications and pseudarthrosis; no PJK-specific result is reported for hyperlordosis, and the authors themselves report that overcorrection by age-adjusted offsets did not increase PJK. A lumbar distribution index near 90% was linked to fewer complications. Line: overall PJF 13.9%, PJF revision 7.4%. The halving of PJF with implants came with similar revision rates, per the authors. Hooks beat no prophylaxis; cement, hooks and tethers did not differ from each other, and the authors say the subgroups are underpowered, so no difference is not equivalence. Among implant patients, overcorrected and aligned groups had similar PJF and revision rates. So, as reported, avoiding overcorrection added nothing once implants were used, which does not support Table 1's summary of lowest PJF with the combined strategy (our reading). Our arithmetic: 20.3% and 10.6% average to the reported 13.9% only if about a third of the 625 had no implant, so these look like whole-cohort rates rather than 1:1 matched pairs. The paper does not say which. Chen: the outcome is PJK, not PJF, though the recommendation says PJK/F. The HU values are printed as 169.62 vs 137.40, respectively, after naming PJK first; the higher value must be the no-PJK group, and the gap computes to 32.22, not the printed 32.35. Safaee: our Fisher test on 4 of 100 vs 18 of 100 gives P about 0.003, in line with the reported 0.002. Controls came from the era just before the technique, while vertebroplasty use was higher in the augmented cohort, so co-interventions differ.

slides.title: Recommendations, strength and evidence
slides.lead: One strong recommendation, about measuring bone density. Everything about what to do is conditional.

rows: Assess BMD before ASD correction: DEXA and/or CT HU at the UIV
Consider perioperative BMD optimization with anabolic agents
Combine prophylactic implants with avoiding sagittal overcorrection
Avoid lumbar hyperlordosis; optimize lordosis distribution rather than chase GAP or age-adjusted ideals
Ligament augmentation in higher-risk patients: long constructs, revision, 3-column osteotomy

slides.notes: The abstract's summary is fair: assess bone quality, avoid overcorrection, consider junctional protection in high-risk patients, mostly conditional because the data are observational. Check the details, though. The strong recommendation is to measure, not to treat. The authors say plainly that Chen did not study treatment of low BMD; the anabolic recommendation is conditional and extrapolated from the strength of the association. Table 1 folds the anabolic advice into the strong recommendation, while the text separates it as conditional; use the text. The imaging wording also drifts: Table 1 says DEXA and CT HU, the Article 3 text says DEXA and/or CT HU, and the Discussion says both, at or above the UIV. The Discussion adds a practical reference point, HU below roughly 160 at the UIV or UIV+1, from three cited studies that were not appraised. Next, the rating of Line and Chen as moderate. Under GRADE, observational evidence usually starts low. The authors upgrade Line for size and propensity matching and Chen for size and a consistent signal. That is a judgment call, and ours is that moderate is generous for both, especially since Line's PJF reduction did not change revision rates. The combined implant-plus-alignment recommendation has a gap too: in Line, among implant patients, PJF and revision were similar whether overcorrected or aligned, so no additive effect of avoiding overcorrection is shown. The Safaee recommendation cites a reduction in radiographic PJK, but the summary reports only PJA change and PJF, no PJK incidence. And the Introduction says the aim is conditional recommendations only, yet the BMD recommendation is strong. For ligament augmentation, the high-risk list (long constructs, revision, 3-column osteotomy) is the authors' choice. About half of Safaee's patients were revisions, but no subgroup result for revision or osteotomy is reported. Note what is not recommended: no specific implant type, no UIV level rule, and no alignment formula. The Discussion's four practical principles restate these five.

slides.title: What the Discussion adds beyond the four studies
slides.lead: The strongest clinical claims about tethers and bone drugs come from papers that were cited, not appraised.
points: Tethers: a review found 15 clinical studies, 14 reporting less PJK and/or PJF. A meta-analysis gave OR 0.44 for PJK and 0.36 for PJF.
Cost: tethering adds about $1,100 per case in the US. One series: PJF down about 10.5%, NNT 9.5 to prevent one revision, projected savings over $1.1 million per 100 patients.
Bone drugs: teriparatide the most studied; benefit may hold even if started after surgery. Romosozumab raised UIV+1 HU and lowered PJK in short-term use.
Alignment: both undercorrection and overcorrection relative to a patient's ideal are said to raise risk; T4-L1-hip axis offered as a continuous framework.
Risk factors named: older age, frailty, sarcopenia, obesity and especially low BMD.
slides.notes: This slide is where the paper moves from graded to ungraded. The authors write that tether-based ligamentous augmentation currently has the strongest clinical support among junctional protection options. That claim comes from a review (reference 37, on which Sardi and Smith are authors) and a 2025 meta-analysis (reference 38), not from the four appraised studies. Three tensions to notice, all our reading. First, the appraised augmentation study, Safaee, used sublaminar cables at UIV-1 to UIV+1, which the paper groups with tethers; the materials and constructs differ. Second, in Line, the one appraised study comparing implant types, only hooks were reported as lower than no prophylaxis, and cement, hooks and tethers did not differ, underpowered. So the appraised evidence does not single out tethers. Third, the cost argument converts a 10.5% fall in PJF into an NNT to prevent one revision. 1 divided by 0.105 is 9.5, so the arithmetic holds, but it treats every prevented PJF as a prevented revision. In Line, PJF fell with implants while revision rates were similar. The authors also say no consensus exists on the best bone drug or duration. The library has a related trial: in O07, from its abstract-level master record, perioperative teriparatide reduced PJF versus denosumab in 64 osteoporotic patients (3.4% vs 22.2%, modified ITT), while PJK was not significantly different (17.2% vs 33.3%, P=.165). This paper does not cite that trial. The undercorrection and overcorrection sentence carries no citation and no numbers.

slides.title: Critical appraisal: gaps and errors
points: Holds up: explicit scope, a stated appraisal framework, quality and strength separated, limitations of each study named.
Holds up: authors avoid overclaiming implant subgroups and say no single measure can prevent PJK or PJF.
Weak: 4 of 30 hand-picked studies, no search, no list of exclusions, grading criteria cited but no voting or agreement rules described.
Weak: evidence populations wider than the scope; Line took fusions of at least 5 levels, not only to the pelvis.
Weak: PJK and PJF definitions differ across the four studies.
Errors: HU gap printed 32.35, values give 32.22, labels reversed; Safaee review says 12 months captures most events, but the Introduction says events occur within 2 years and about 20% of PJF later.
Errors: Table 1 calls anabolic optimization strong; text says conditional. Abstract typo: assessment and of bone quality.
slides.notes: Be fair first. The paper states its scope, separates quality of evidence from strength of recommendation, and its appraisals are candid: it says Line is underpowered for implant subgroups and that Dial inadequately assessed contributing factors such as bone density. Now the weaknesses. Selection: the forum identified 30 articles and chose four after discussion and consensus review. No database, dates or criteria are given, and while quality and strength were graded against predefined criteria (GRADE handbook), no voting or agreement rule for the consensus meeting is described. Our concern is that the four studies define the questions. Scope: the recommendations are limited to fusions ending at the pelvis, but Line included posterior fusions of at least five levels, Dial was adult lumbar scoliosis, and Chen pooled any ASD correction; the paper does not say how many patients matched the stated scope. Outcomes: Dial counted symptomatic PJK, Line used region-specific angular and anterolisthesis thresholds for PJF, Chen pooled PJK by varying definitions, and Safaee measured PJA change and PJF. Alignment: Dial found overcorrection by age-adjusted offsets did not increase PJK, while Line found overcorrection without implants had the highest PJF. Different outcomes and definitions, but the paper does not reconcile the two before recommending against overcorrection. Internal problems: the Safaee review says its 12-month follow-up captures the period when most events occur, while the Introduction says events occur within 2 years and about 20% of PJF later, so the paper contradicts itself; the Safaee recommendation cites a reduction in radiographic PJK that the summary never reports (only PJA change and PJF); the Introduction promises conditional recommendations only, yet the BMD recommendation is strong; and the cable description, sublaminar cables placed through the spinous processes, is hard to picture as written. Our arithmetic: Dial's percentages, Line's 625 of 834 (75%) and the NNT of 9.5 all recompute. Chen's 537 of 2,185 is 24.6% PJK.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: AO Spine 2026: PJK prevention is multimodal. Measure bone, do not overcorrect, protect the junction in high-risk long fusions to the pelvis.
points: Spoken summary: an AO Spine forum appraisal of four studies, none randomized. Strong recommendation only to assess BMD with DEXA and/or UIV CT HU.
Conditional: consider anabolic optimization; combine implant prophylaxis with avoiding overcorrection; avoid lumbar hyperlordosis; use ligament augmentation in higher-risk cases.
Best numbers: Line PJF 10.6% with implants vs 20.3% without, revision similar; Safaee PJF 4 vs 18 of 100 with historical controls.

rows: Not shown in Line: PJF halved, revision rates similar.
Unknown. Types did not differ, underpowered; only hooks beat none. Tether preference comes from cited, not appraised, work.
About 160 at UIV or UIV+1, from cited studies, offered as a practical reference.
Does an ideal alignment score prevent PJK?
Not shown. GAP predicted mechanical complications poorly in Dial (AUC 0.57). Individualize and avoid hyperlordosis.
Not tested in Chen. Conditional, by extrapolation.

slides.notes: If you have 30 seconds: this is expert framing of four observational studies, not new data. The one strong recommendation is to measure bone density, by DEXA and or CT Hounsfield units at the UIV. Everything about intervention is conditional: consider anabolic therapy, avoid overcorrection and lumbar hyperlordosis, and use junctional protection in high-risk long fusions to the pelvis. Expect four pushbacks. Someone will say implants are proven. Answer that Line found PJF 10.6% with implants against 20.3% without in a propensity-matched observational cohort, but revision rates were similar, and Safaee's 4 against 18 PJF used historical controls with more vertebroplasty in the later cohort. Someone will say tethers are best. Answer that this is the authors' Discussion, based on a review and meta-analysis they cite, while in the one appraised comparison of implant types only hooks were reported to beat no prophylaxis. Someone will cite an alignment target. Answer that Dial found GAP predicted mechanical complications poorly, AUC 0.57, and that the library's GAP records point the same way: D05 reported an internal split-sample validation AUC of 0.92, while external validation in D06 gave 0.60 (both from abstract-level master records). Someone will ask whether bone treatment works. Chen did not test it; the library's O07 trial, from its abstract-level record, found teriparatide lowered PJF versus denosumab, while the PJK difference was not significant. Finally, say what you have not seen: the four source papers and the Discussion's cited literature. Also remember the scope: not cervical-to-pelvis and not long constructs that stop short of the pelvis.

decks.not_reviewed: Figure 1 (clinical decision algorithm; omitted from the reformatted PMC text we read). The typeset journal version, including any funding and conflict-of-interest statements, which are not in this PDF. The six reviewed source papers themselves (Kim 2021, Lurie 2014, Peul 2007, Bailey 2020, Petr 2019, Thomé 2022) and reference 10.

slides.title: AO Spine: when to operate in disc herniation
slides.lead: Consensus recommendations built on six selected studies, ordered from elective to urgent.
points: Journal club · Timing of disc surgery
Vadalà G, et al. Global Spine J 2026 (AO Spine Knowledge Forum Degenerative)
Source: the full open-access PMC text, reformatted. Figure 1, the decision algorithm, is not in the PDF; Table 1 is.

Bottom line: without a motor deficit, preference and symptom duration decide. With a deficit, the authors want decompression within 3 days for MRC 3/5 or worse, and within 8 days for MRC 4/5. Every recommendation is conditional.
slides.notes: This is not a trial and not a systematic review. It belongs to a Global Spine Journal series in which a Knowledge Forum picks a few key papers, summarizes and grades each one, and attaches a recommendation. Here the steering committee chose six papers: Kim 2021, SPORT at 8 years (Lurie 2014), Peul 2007, Bailey 2020, Petr 2019 and Thomé 2022. They are presented in order of rising urgency. The source we read is the complete PMC text reformatted for phone reading. Figure 1, a clinical decision algorithm, was left out of that version, so we have not seen it; its caption says the timing thresholds should not override immediate decompression for cauda equina syndrome or rapidly progressive deficit. The PDF also has no funding or conflict-of-interest statement, so we cannot comment on either. Nothing in the deck comes from the six original papers except where it compares with our library record of Peul (L02). Our library also holds Bailey (L03), Thomé (PM35040807) and the 2-year SPORT randomized report (L01, Weinstein 2006, not the 8-year paper reviewed here); we did not compare against those. The value of the paper is the framework, not new data. The authors' central move: stop asking whether surgery beats conservative care and ask how urgent surgery is and what is lost by waiting. Read every number in this deck as the review's summary of someone else's paper.

slides.title: The question and how the evidence was chosen
slides.lead: Given the presentation, how urgently is surgery needed, and what is lost by waiting?
points: Panel: steering committee of the AO Spine Knowledge Forum Degenerative.
Selection: 6 articles chosen for quality of evidence, recency and clinical relevance. No search strategy is reported.
Mix: 2 RCTs (Peul, Bailey), 2 RCTs with observational cohorts (Kim, SPORT), 1 prospective series (Thomé), 1 retrospective series (Petr).
Process: working groups of 2 to 4 members summarized and appraised each paper; the committee reviewed; consensus by virtual review.
Grading: modified GRADE. Quality high, moderate, low or very low; recommendation strong or conditional.
slides.notes: Methods matter here because they set how far the conclusions can travel. The six papers were hand-picked. There is no search, no inclusion criteria and no list of what was considered and left out, so we cannot know whether contrary evidence exists. Our comment: that is acceptable for a teaching framework but it is not a guideline in the formal sense, and it should not be quoted as one. The grading is called a modified GRADE approach, but the modification is not described. GRADE was applied per paper, not across a body of evidence for each question, so most recommendations rest on one study; only Table 1's moderate-to-severe deficit row combines two (Petr and Thomé), with a merged Low–Moderate rating. Consensus was reached by virtual review and agreement; no voting, threshold or Delphi rounds are reported. Note a small inconsistency in the boilerplate: the series disclaimer says authors select 3 to 4 articles, and this review selected 6. Ask the room: the two motor-deficit papers came from the same institution over the same years. The authors raise this themselves in the Discussion. Hold that thought for slide 6.

slides.title: Without a motor deficit: preference and duration decide
slides.lead: Four recommendations, all conditional, for sciatica without a major deficit.

rows: Surgical candidate, prefers to avoid surgery, 6+ weeks
Continued nonoperative care may be offered; slower relief, similar long-term outcomes possible
Early (<2 weeks) surgery for faster leg-pain relief
Discectomy for greater, durable gains; conservative care also improves

points: Authors' gradient: the benefit of surgery grows as symptoms last longer.
The Kim-based recommendation excludes MRC 3/5 or worse, cauda equina syndrome and instability from the wait-and-see option.
slides.notes: Read the table as a timeline. Early on, waiting costs time in pain but, on the review's account of Peul, not the 1-year result. Later, at 4 to 12 months, Bailey shows waiting longer costs outcome at 6 months. Two points to notice. First, 'early surgery' in Peul means within about 2 weeks of randomization, in patients who already had 6 to 12 weeks of sciatica. It does not mean surgery within 2 weeks of onset. Our comment: the recommendation label '<2 weeks' invites that misreading. Second, quality ratings of High for Peul and Bailey are generous. Both were open label with subjective primary outcomes, Bailey was single center and up to 20% of its primary outcome data were imputed. The authors list these limits and still rate High; ours is that a standard GRADE reading would likely downgrade for risk of bias. All four recommendations are conditional even where quality is High. The authors do not say why; our reading is that the choice depends on how a patient weighs pain now against the risk of an operation. The SPORT row sits awkwardly. The authors call its handling of crossover methodologically rigorous; our comment is that its as-treated analysis is observational in character, and the randomized analysis did not reach significance on primary outcomes, yet it carries Moderate quality and a recommendation to operate. Kim's row is the weakest: an interim analysis, 128 of 169 consented patients (76%, our arithmetic), crossover of about half in one direction and 27% in the other, and individualized conservative care.

slides.title: With a motor deficit: timing becomes urgent
slides.lead: Two observational series from one institution drive the time windows.

rows: Any paresis: emergency evaluation and imaging. MRC 0-3: decompress within 48 hours

points: Table 1 merges them: 3 days ideal, 48 hours preferred, quality low to moderate.
Authors: treat moderate-to-severe weakness like cauda equina syndrome.
Examine after adequate analgesia, because pain inhibition can mimic weakness.
slides.see: Figure 1 (not in our PDF) is the authors' decision algorithm; its caption says the thresholds never delay decompression for cauda equina syndrome or rapidly progressive deficit.
slides.notes: This is the part of the paper most likely to change practice, and the part with the thinnest evidence. Both studies enrolled only patients who had surgery, so neither can say whether surgery beats no surgery for a deficit. They can only say that, among operated patients, earlier operation went with better recovery. Timing was not assigned. In Thomé, the review says timing was largely determined by extramural factors (time to presentation and operating room availability), which the authors note may introduce confounding: patients who present late may differ in ways that also affect recovery. The 48-hour cut in Petr was chosen without stated justification, per the authors. The 3-day cut in Thomé was found by recursive partitioning in the same data it was tested on; the authors call this unbiased, but a cut point found in one data set needs confirming in another. Watch the clock definition. Petr grouped patients by duration of motor deficit before surgery, yet both recommendations say 'of symptom onset'. Our reading: the clock should start at onset of weakness, not of pain, but the review does not say. The analgesia point is practical and the authors make it three times: MRC grading is subjective, inter-rater reliability was not reported in either study, and pain-inhibited weakness can inflate urgency.

slides.title: The numbers behind the recommendations
slides.lead: As the review reports them; we rechecked the arithmetic.

rows: Recovery median 4.0 vs 12.1 weeks; HR 1.97 (1.72-2.22); about 95% recovered by 1 year in both
Full strength 90.5% within 3 days vs 36% later

slides.notes: Our checks. Peul: 125 of 141 is 88.7% and 55 of 142 is 38.7%, as stated. The hazard ratio interval, 1.97 (1.72-2.22), fails our check. It is symmetric on the arithmetic scale, where ratio intervals are usually symmetric on the log scale, but the bigger problem is width. It implies a standard error of log HR of about 0.065, which would need roughly 470 events per arm. Peul had about 140 per arm and about 95% recovered, so about 130 events each; that predicts an interval of roughly 1.55-2.51. Our library record of Peul (L02) reports the same interval and already flags it as too narrow (our estimate there about 1.55-2.50), unresolved. Treat the HR as right in direction but its precision as overstated. That record, from the full Peul paper, gives timing as means of 2.2 and 18.7 weeks; this review gives medians of 1.9 and 14.6 weeks. These may both be right, but we cannot check from here. Bailey: the review says 56 of 64 had surgery and 7 cancelled because they improved. That accounts for 63, so one patient is missing. The 2.8 and 5.2 are given with plus or minus 0.4 and no label; with about 64 per arm that must be a standard error, not a standard deviation. 22 of 64 is 34%, correct. SPORT: all three as-treated intervals are centered on their estimates. Petr: 126 + 204 = 330; 11.1% of 126 is 14 and 14.2% of 204 is 29, so the complication rates fit whole numbers. Thomé: 90.5% vs 36% is an absolute difference of 54.5 points, NNT about 1.8, and 61% vs 0% gives about 1.6, consistent with 'fewer than 2'. But note the 90.5% vs 36% comparison covers all severities, not only moderate to severe. Now compare Petr and Thomé for severe deficits: 96.2% complete remission with early surgery in Petr (MRC 0-2, within 48 hours, at 3 months) against 61% complete recovery in Thomé (MRC 2/5 or worse, within 3 days, at final follow-up, mean 43.4 months), in cohorts the authors say may partly overlap. Thomé's full strength is defined as MRC 5/5; Petr's complete remission is not defined. The windows and time points differ, but a higher rate at 3 months than at long-term follow-up is hard to explain. Treat both numbers cautiously.

slides.title: Critical appraisal: gaps and errors
slides.lead: A useful framework; its most urgent advice rests on its weakest evidence.
points: Six hand-picked studies, no search and an undescribed modified GRADE.
Petr and Thomé come from one institution over January 2013 to December 2015. The authors say their agreement may partly reflect overlapping cohorts.
No nonoperative control for motor deficit; timing was not assigned.
Peul's 1-year result is called 'equivalent'; a P of 0.13 is not a test of equivalence.
Table 1 labels the Kim scenario 'no motor deficit', but the Kim-based recommendation excludes only MRC 3/5 or worse.
The Conclusion says surgery for acute sciatica (6-12 weeks) gives similar long-term outcomes, while the SPORT section reports an as-treated advantage lasting 8 years.
Authors' own gaps: approach (open, tubular, endoscopic), disc morphology, stenosis and endplate changes are untested against timing.
slides.notes: Start with the overlap, because it is the most important weakness. Petr analyzed 330 patients operated from January 2013 to December 2015; Thomé followed 390 consecutive patients operated over the same dates. The review lists Thomé C as an author of both. The authors write that the convergent findings may partly reflect overlapping cohorts and call for cautious interpretation. Our comment: if the cohorts overlap heavily, the two papers are close to one observational data set analyzed twice, so the agreement between 48 hours and 3 days is not independent confirmation. Next, wording. The Abstract says Peul showed equivalent 1-year outcomes. The review reports P = 0.13 for disability; a nonsignificant difference is not equivalence. The Discussion also says the 1-year endpoint is 'equivalent', though it adds that surgery and conservative care are not themselves equivalent. Table 1 and the Conclusion use 'similar', which is fairer. Then the deficit labels. Table 1 labels the Kim scenario 'no motor deficit', while the Kim-based recommendation excludes only major deficit (MRC 3/5 or worse), so the two do not match. The review does not report Kim's eligibility criteria. Our Peul record says Peul excluded paralysis and strength below antigravity, not all weakness. Our comment: patients with mild weakness could have been eligible for the 'no deficit' studies, but we have no count of how many were enrolled. Internal tension: the Conclusion says surgery for acute sciatica offers faster relief but similar long-term outcomes, while the SPORT summary reports as-treated advantages sustained over 8 years and the Discussion calls that evidence against surgery merely accelerating recovery. These can be reconciled (different populations, as-treated versus randomized), but the paper does not do it. Smaller errors: Bailey's timing paradigm says surgery within 3 weeks while its median was 3.1 weeks; one Bailey surgical patient is unaccounted for; Kim's summary uses P < 0.05 and then P > 0.01 as the no-difference threshold. On technique the authors are sensible: timing is approach-agnostic in principle, but use whatever decompresses fastest and most completely.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: Triage disc herniation by neurological urgency, then by duration and preference.
points: Spoken summary: AO Spine reviewed six key studies and made conditional recommendations. Without a real motor deficit, surgery and continued conservative care are both reasonable at 6 to 12 weeks; surgery gives faster leg-pain relief. By 4 to 12 months, discectomy does better. With weakness of MRC 3/5 or worse, they advise decompression ideally within 3 days, 48 hours preferred, and within 8 days for MRC 4/5. Those windows come from two observational series from one center, with no nonoperative control.
Expect: is this a guideline? Consensus on six chosen papers, not a systematic review.
Expect: where does 3 days come from? A data-derived cut point in operated patients only.
Expect: does 'early' in Peul mean 2 weeks from onset? No, 2 weeks from randomization after 6-12 weeks of sciatica.
Expect: what about foot drop of MRC 4? 8 days, close watch, after adequate analgesia.
slides.notes: Say the framework in one breath: urgency first, then duration, then preference. The strongest evidence, Peul and Bailey, is randomized and concerns pain, which is preference-sensitive. The most urgent advice, the 48-hour and 3-day windows, concerns motor recovery and rests on observational data from one institution. That is the inversion to remember. Likely questions and short answers. Why are all recommendations conditional? The authors do not say. Our reading: for the no-deficit questions the choice depends on patient values, even where quality is rated High; for the deficit questions the evidence is low to moderate and observational. Is 48 hours or 3 days the target? The authors' Table 1 says 3 days ideal and 48 hours preferred. Why not randomize timing? The authors say random assignment to delayed decompression may be unethical for moderate-to-severe deficits, and call for registries and pathway studies instead. Where do delays happen? Often before the surgeon: primary care, emergency departments and imaging, per the authors, who want fast-track pathways with prompt MRI, repeat motor examination and protected operating time. Does endoscopic surgery change timing? The authors say the evidence cannot tell; choose the approach that decompresses without delay. If pressed on numbers, the one to know is Thomé: full strength 90.5% when operated within 3 days against 36% after, in operated patients, as the review reports it.

decks.not_reviewed: The six source articles themselves (Laiwalla 2024, Farber 2023, Zhang 2025, Polly 2024, Durand 2025, Lightsey 2022) were not read; every study number here is as this paper reports it. The PDF is the complete article, reformatted from the open-access PMC text with images omitted. The text refers only to Tables 1 and 2, which are present. No supplement is cited.

slides.title: Martin 2026: AO Spine recommendations for interbody fusion at the lumbosacral junction
slides.lead: Bottom line: for a large lordotic correction the panel favors ALIF, a TLIF needs extra technical steps to reach alignment goals, and stand-alone ALIF suits only selected patients.
points: Journal club · Lumbosacral interbody fusion
Martin CT, et al. Global Spine J 2026. PMID 42925017
AO Spine Knowledge Forum Degenerative: 6 selected studies, each GRADE-rated, with unanimous consensus
All six recommendations are conditional
slides.notes: Be clear about what kind of paper this is. It is an expert-panel review, not a systematic review and not a formal guideline. The steering committee picked six recent articles. Small groups of three members summarized each one, evidence and recommendation strength were set with GRADE (the paper does not say who assigned the grades), and all 23 Forum members agreed on the wording of a conditional recommendation for each. The deck comes from the full reformatted PMC text. Images were omitted, but the text cites only Tables 1 and 2, which are present. We did not read the six source papers, so every study number here is the panel's account of it, not a check against the original. The authors build their case on one premise: segmental lordosis matters even in short constructs, especially at L5-S1. They support it with cadaveric strain work and with adjacent-segment and pain data (references 1 and 2), and this paper does not test that premise. Three things to hold onto. First, the core claim is radiographic: ALIF gains more lordosis than TLIF. Second, the patient-reported benefit is inconsistent across the studies. Third, the TLIF comparators were often under-built, and the panel says so itself.

slides.title: How the panel worked
slides.lead: Question: which interbody approach, how much lordosis, and whether ALIF needs posterior fixation at L4-S1.
points: Articles chosen at the steering committee's discretion for quality, recency and relevance. No search strategy is reported.
Each article was summarized by 3 members. Evidence and recommendation strength were set with GRADE.
All 23 Forum members reviewed the manuscript, and the wording was revised until consensus was unanimous.
All six studies are observational. Only one (Polly) is prospective.

rows: Single center, retrospective: L5-S1 ALIF vs MIS-TLIF
Single center, retrospective: L4-S1 ALIF vs TLIF with osteotomy
Prospective: TLIF with SPO on a hinged table
Retrospective: L5-S1 isthmic ALIF vs TLIF

slides.notes: Read the method before the recommendations. The committee chose the six articles, so this is a curated reading list, not a sweep of the literature. Another panel could pick six different papers. The abstract says the literature was graded by integrating scientific method with expert opinion, and the Methods name GRADE. Our point, not the paper's: GRADE rates a body of evidence for an outcome, and observational evidence usually starts at low. Here each paper got its own grade, and three single-center, single-system or claims studies were rated moderate. That is generous. Watch the authorship too. Polly 2024 lists Martin CT, the lead author of this review. Zhang 2025 lists Yoon ST, who is also an author here. Durand 2025 is the Forum's own paper, and seven of its authors (Yoon, Hsieh, Le, Corluka, Muthu, Hamouda, Jain) are among this paper's authors. So at least three of the six graded studies (Zhang, Polly, Durand) have authors on this panel, and Zhang and Durand were rated moderate. No conflict-of-interest statement appears in the reformatted text. Sample sizes run from 50 to 1,377. The Laiwalla count is 307 plus 1,070 procedures, which checks, but its title calls it a 1,377-patient cohort, so the unit (patients or procedures) is unclear. Follow-up ranges from intraoperative only (Polly) to a mean of about 6 years (Laiwalla, ALIF+PSF arm).

slides.title: ALIF vs TLIF: lordosis and outcomes
slides.lead: Panel: use ALIF when more lordosis correction is needed (Articles 2, 3 and 6).
points: Farber, L5-S1: ALIF gained more segmental lordosis, disc angle and foraminal height. MIS-TLIF had a shorter stay. PROMs, subsidence, revision and complications were comparable.
Farber cages: 96% of ALIFs used hyperlordotic cages of 15 degrees or more, while the MIS-TLIFs used 6-degree cages.
Zhang, L4-S1: ASD 3.8% vs 15.7% (P = 0.034) and reoperation 7.5% vs 25.5% (P = 0.009), ALIF vs TLIF.
Lightsey: ALIF patients also gained in PROMIS Physical Function and Global Health-Physical. Pain domains improved in both groups.
slides.notes: The direction is consistent: in all three comparisons, ALIF gained more lordosis. Now look at the comparators. In Farber, ALIF used hyperlordotic cages and MIS-TLIF used 6-degree cages, and the panel calls that a significant confounder. Zhang's TLIF group mixed grade 1 and grade 2 osteotomies with static cages, and the panel suspects this underestimates what a TLIF can do. Lightsey pooled open and MIS TLIF and did not report the facet resection. Our reading: part of the result is ALIF against an under-built TLIF. Zhang numbers. We recomputed 2 of 53 vs 16 of 102 for ASD and 4 of 53 vs 26 of 102 for reoperation. The percentages match, and Fisher's exact test gives P = 0.034 and 0.009, matching the printed values. Note how ASD was defined: symptomatic disease at L3-L4 that needed surgery. There is a time-point problem. The paper says both groups gained L4-S1 lordosis, then says TLIF lordosis at final follow-up was 1.2 degrees below its preoperative value. It never says whether the 6.5 vs 1.3 gain is immediate or final. ALIF kept 72% of its immediate gain. Lightsey: all ALIFs had posterior fixation, because stand-alone ALIFs were excluded. A single rater did the measurements. Final follow-up is given as more than 1 year in one place and as one year in another. PROMs: Farber found no difference and Lightsey found an ALIF benefit in two domains. The paper reports no numbers or effect sizes for those domains. Lordosis gain alone is not proof of better patient outcomes. No complication data are given for Lightsey. Farber found overall complication rates comparable, but no study, as reported here, breaks out ALIF access-specific complications such as vascular injury or retrograde ejaculation.

slides.title: Making a TLIF lordotic
slides.lead: Panel: if you go posterior, take extra steps to reach segmental alignment goals (Articles 2, 3 and 4).
points: Steps the panel names: grade 2 osteotomy or wide facet release, higher-lordosis cages, anterior cage placement, rod compression and table extension.
Polly: 61 enrolled, 50 analyzed (24 male, 26 female), 73 osteotomy levels, all bilateral TLIF with SPO.
After the cage was placed, extending the table from 10° of flexion to 10° of extension added a mean 5.6° of segmental lordosis.
The first 5° of table motion gave about 1.9°, and rod placement with compression added 1.8°.
ICC was 0.97 to 0.98. No intraoperative neurologic injury or hardware failure occurred.
slides.notes: This is the only prospective study in the set, and its endpoint is purely intraoperative and radiographic, with no clinical outcome. Read the numbers carefully. The Study Summary gives 5.6 degrees from table extension and then another 1.8 degrees from rod placement and compression. The panel's recommendation later says the table and rod compression together gave 5.6 degrees. Those two statements conflict, so we quote the Study Summary and flag the error. Each table step gave only 1 to 2 degrees, and the panel itself notes that lordosis measurement error is about 1 to 3 degrees. The measurers were the operating surgeons, and the measurements were not blinded. Patients whose osteotomy closed fully before the table reached full extension were excluded, which selects the cases. There was no control group using manual compression alone. So the study cannot show that the table adds correction, or safety, beyond what compression alone gives. The panel makes that point too. Anterior cage placement appears in the Article 4 recommendation in the abstract and Table 2, but this study did not test it. The idea comes from the panel's Article 2 discussion. That reading is ours. Remember that Martin CT is an author of both this review and Polly 2024. Quality was rated low, and the recommendation is conditional.

slides.title: Supplemental fixation and isthmic spondylolisthesis
slides.lead: Panel: stand-alone ALIF suits selected patients, and in isthmic slips interbody or 360 fusion is preferred over ALIF alone or PLF alone (Articles 1, 5 and 6).
points: Laiwalla: 307 stand-alone ALIF vs 1,070 ALIF+PSF. Mean follow-up was 4.5 vs 5.9 years. There were only 13 reoperations for nonunion.
Durand, isthmic claims: n = 1,014, and 4.2% (43) had revision. ALIF alone had higher unadjusted revision risk than ALIF+PSF (HR 4.8), PLIF/TLIF (5.5) and PLF alone (2.6).
Durand after adjustment: ALIF alone was still higher. PLF alone was higher than PLIF/TLIF (HR 2.4), and the other comparisons were not significant.
Lightsey: ALIF with posterior fixation is preferred for L5-S1 isthmic slips when feasible.
slides.notes: Laiwalla first. Only the reoperation rates are 5-year figures; operative time and stay are index-admission values, and the ED and readmission figures are 90-day adjusted odds. The crude rates fit 13 events: 2.4% of 307 is about 7, and 0.5% of 1,070 is about 5. Both hazard-ratio intervals are symmetric on the log scale, so they look plausible. The absolute gain is small: about 2 fewer nonunion reoperations per 100 at 5 years. Only reoperations were counted, so nonoperative nonunion and ASD were missed. More than 75% of patients got BMP, and 80% of fusions were at L5-S1. Surgeons chose who got PSF, and bone density and alignment were not adjusted for. The ED and readmission odds ratios are printed without intervals or P values. Lower odds after a bigger operation is unexpected, so do not lean on them (our reading). Durand next. The four group counts add to 1,014, and the percentages check. No intervals are printed for any hazard ratio, and only 66 patients had ALIF alone. Revision was defined by CPT code at any level, so the level and cause are unknown. The panel infers nonunion because arthrodesis was more common than decompression alone. That is the panel's inference, not a measured result. Mean follow-up was 637.6 days. Kaplan-Meier revision rose from 1.4% at 6 months to 11.0% at 5 years. Durand and Laiwalla point the same way on ALIF alone. Durand did not show ALIF+PSF beating PLIF/TLIF. The panel's own summaries do not match. The abstract says fixation reduces nonunion in anterior fusions, except in stable slips with good bone. The Discussion limits it to isthmic slips without instability. Table 2 calls stand-alone ALIF comparable to 360 fusion, although Laiwalla's nonunion hazard ratio was 0.22.

slides.title: Critical appraisal: strength, gaps and errors
points: Holds up: the direction is consistent (ALIF gains more lordosis), the panel's critiques of each study are candid, and the recommendations are conditional.
Weakens it: six hand-picked observational studies, generous grades, the panel grading its own studies, a radiographic-dominant evidence base and TLIF comparators that were under-built.
Gaps: ALIF access-specific complications are not reported (Farber found overall complications comparable), PROM effects have no sizes, and there is no randomized comparison.
Errors: Polly's 5.6° is misattributed, Durand's revision-coding percentages do not add up, and Durand's SD of 574 days does not fit its own CI or Table 1.
Table 2 says 'ALIF+Perc screws' for Article 6. The Article 6 text says only posterior instrumentation.
slides.notes: Be fair first. The panel's appraisal of each study is honest: it names the cage confounder in Farber, unblinded measurement in Polly, coding limits in Durand and the pooled TLIFs in Lightsey. Every recommendation is conditional. The Discussion says the agreement across studies increases confidence. Our counterpoint: when the TLIF comparators share the same weakness, agreement can reflect a shared bias. Errors we found by recomputing. First, Durand: 21% decompression alone and 56% fusion alone leave 23% with both, so any decompression is 44%, not the printed 49%. The 79% for arthrodesis does check. Second, Durand's revision timing: the mean is 441 days with SD 574 over 43 revisions, and the printed 95% CI is about 326 to 558 days. That CI implies an SD of about 390 days. Table 1's month bins give a mean of about 15 months (about 456 days, close to 441) and an SD of about 370 days, and even pushing every revision to the edge of its bin cannot reach 574. So the SD of 574 is the likely error, and the CI is plausible. Its Table 1 also has overlapping bins (48-53 and 53-59), although the counts add to 43. Third, Polly's 5.6 degrees is given to the table alone in the summary but to the table plus rod compression in the recommendation. Fourth, Zhang's time point is ambiguous, as covered earlier. Fifth, Table 2 and the abstract recommend ALIF with percutaneous screws for Article 6. Lightsey included open and MIS techniques, and the panel's own recommendation for it says only supplemental posterior instrumentation. Sixth, Table 2 uses causal wording ('decrease revision rates') for a claims-data association. What is missing: Farber compared overall complications and found them comparable, but none of the six studies, as reported here, breaks out ALIF access-specific complications, and harms barely appear. None reports bone density as summarized here (Laiwalla did not record it), and none is randomized. Laiwalla's unit is also unclear: the title says 1,377 patients, the text says 1,377 procedures.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: A spoken summary, then the questions to expect.
points: "AO Spine's 2026 panel graded six observational studies. When I need a big lordotic correction at L5-S1, an ALIF gets it more reliably. If I go posterior, I need grade 2 osteotomies, a lordotic cage placed anteriorly and compression. Stand-alone ALIF is reasonable in selected patients, but posterior fixation lowers the small nonunion reoperation risk. In isthmic slips I avoid ALIF alone and PLF alone. All of these recommendations are conditional."
Expect: Does more lordosis mean better patients? Not proven here.
Expect: Is stand-alone ALIF safe? Nonunion reoperation was 2.4% vs 0.5% at 5 years.
Expect: Is this a guideline? It is an expert consensus built on 6 selected studies.
slides.notes: Expect these questions. First: does more lordosis mean better patients? Not proven here. Farber found comparable PROMs. Lightsey found ALIF gains in two PROMIS domains, with no sizes reported. Zhang's lower ASD and reoperation rates are the strongest clinical signal, but they come from a single-center retrospective study with an under-built TLIF comparator. Second: should every L5-S1 ALIF get posterior screws? Laiwalla's absolute difference was about 2 nonunion reoperations per 100 at 5 years, with no difference in ASD. In the panel's words, stand-alone ALIF needs adequate anterior column support, favorable bone and minimal instability. Supplemental posterior fixation may be considered for osteoporosis, multilevel constructs, high shear, smoking or revision. For isthmic slips, Durand's claims data favor not leaving an ALIF alone. Third: ALIF or TLIF for an isthmic slip? The panel prefers ALIF with posterior fixation when an anterior approach is feasible, based mainly on Lightsey. Durand found no significant revision difference between PLIF/TLIF and ALIF+PSF, so a well-built TLIF remains defensible. That reading is ours. Fourth: how strong is this? The six articles were hand-picked, and at least three (Zhang, Polly, Durand) have authors on this panel. ALIF access-specific complications are not reported. Cite the direction, not the precision, and quote numbers as the panel reports them, since the source papers were not reviewed here.

decks.not_reviewed: Published figures (the reformatted PMC copy omits images, so Figures 1-3, the reducible disc height measurement and MRI success and failure examples, were not seen). No supplement is cited. Cited studies, including the Kirnaz systematic review and the Gabel and Lim series, were not read; their numbers are as quoted in this paper. The copy is otherwise complete full text, read end to end.

slides.title: LLIF indirect decompression criteria
slides.lead: Who can skip direct decompression when an LLIF cage does the work?
points: Journal club: MIS and technique selection
Yingsakmongkol W, et al. Neurospine 2022;19(3):805-815
Retrospective single-center cohort, 191 patients, 235 levels, King Chulalongkorn Memorial Hospital, 2014-2020

Bottom line: in patients who met four selection criteria, 13 of 191 (6.8%) later needed direct decompression. Low reducible disc height and high-grade cage subsidence were the strongest adjusted risk factors.
slides.notes: Reviewed from a reformatted open-access PMC copy of the full text, read end to end. The copy says images are omitted, so Figures 1 to 3 (the reducible disc height measurement and the success and failure MRI examples) were not seen. All four tables are present as text. No supplement is cited. Frame it first: this is a single-arm cohort. Every patient met the authors' four criteria, so the paper reports how often selected patients failed. It cannot show that the criteria select better than no criteria, because nobody who failed the criteria was studied. The second half of the paper is a risk-factor analysis inside that selected group, with only 13 failing patients (14 failing levels). Keep both numbers in mind; most of what is fragile comes from that small event count. The master record already says the abstract drops the minus sign on the BMD T-score cutoff (abstract: T-score < 2.1; full text: < -2.1). That is confirmed, and there are several more internal inconsistencies covered on slide 5.

slides.title: The question, patients and methods
slides.lead: All four criteria had to be met to enter the cohort.
points: Consecutive 1-2 level XLIF or OLIF, one institution, 3 senior surgeons
217 eligible; 191 with complete data and follow-up through 12 months (26 excluded, 12%)
Excluded: planned combined direct and indirect decompression, incomplete 1-year follow-up
Failure: persistent pain needing direct decompression at the index level within 6 months
Analysis: ROC (Youden) cutoffs, then GEE logistic models by level; p<0.1 entered the multivariable model

rows: Pain standing or walking, subsiding by more than 50% supine
Disc height recovers at least 1 mm from upright to supine
Excluded if motor power below grade IV
No facet cyst (MRI) or bony lateral recess stenosis (CT)

slides.notes: Two aims: the success rate under the criteria, and risk factors for failure. Patients: median age 65 (59-73). The text says 93% were women, which is unusual and has an arithmetic problem (slide 5). Diagnoses were mixed: degenerative spondylolisthesis 32.5%, adjacent segment disease 26.7%, DDD/HNP 14.1%, stenosis 10.5%, scoliosis 7.3%, FBSS 4.7%, isthmic 4.2%. 147 had one level and 44 two levels. 109 XLIF and 82 OLIF. Fixation was mostly percutaneous posterior screws (169 of 235 levels), with 40 anterolateral plates, 19 standalone and 7 lateral screw-rod. The paper says instrumentation used 'selected fixation' in most cases and standalone LLIF 'in some cases'. It gives no rule for the choice and does not say who made it. How to read the definitions: reducible disc height is an inclusion criterion (at least 1 mm) and also a continuous predictor (percent change supine versus standing). So the 13% cutoff is measured inside a group that already had some reducibility. What to notice: the failure definition is a decision to reoperate, not a symptom measure. A patient with persistent pain who declined or was not offered surgery counts as a success, and so does a patient reoperated after 6 months. The paper does not say whether the criteria were applied prospectively when choosing surgery or retrospectively when assembling the cohort. Methods call them inclusion criteria; the Discussion says all criteria must be met to be eligible for the surgery. Our reading: we cannot tell how many patients were turned away by the criteria, so the criteria's effect on case selection is unknown. Follow-up visits were scheduled at 1, 3, 6, 12 and 24 months; median follow-up was 24 months (12-40).

slides.title: Primary outcome: failure rate
slides.lead: 13 of 191 patients (6.8%) needed direct decompression; success 178 of 191 (93.2%).
points: Median time to reoperation 4.5 months (range 2.5-6.0)
All 13 had posterior direct decompression; authors report buckled ligamentum flavum at surgery and relief afterwards in all
Fusion rate 93.2% overall, not different between groups (no counts or p value given)
PROs: authors report significant gains in the success group versus the failure group at all visits, without p values
slides.notes: The headline is 13 of 191, which recomputes to 6.8%, and 178 of 191, 93.2%. Our calculation: an exact 95% CI on 13/191 is roughly 3.7% to 11.4%, so the true rate in similar selected patients could plausibly be as high as the 9% pooled estimate the authors cite from Kirnaz. The paper gives no CI. The PRO table is not an outcome result in the usual sense. The groups are defined by whether the patient was reoperated for persistent pain, so of course the success group improved more. Read it as a check on the failure definition, not as evidence the procedure works. The change scores have no time point stated, so we do not know whether they are final, 12-month or reoperation-time values. Leg and back VAS changes in the success group are identical (-4.6 ± 3.5), which may be a copy error. The failure group's baseline leg VAS is 8 with an IQR of 0 to 9, so at least a quarter of the 13 scored 0 for leg pain before surgery. The criteria require pain standing or walking that eases supine, not leg-dominant pain, but a lower quartile of 0 is still worth noticing in a study of decompression. Fusion: the 93.2% fusion rate equals the 93.2% success rate. That may be coincidence, but the paper gives no fusion counts, so we could not check it. Compare with the literature as the authors do in Table 5: Oliveira 9.5% (2/21), Malham 9% (11/122), Gabel 3.5% (1/28, which is 3.6%; Table 5 misprints it), Wang 29% (13/45), Lim 2% (1/50), Rentenberger 19% (25/133), Park 72% (62/86). The authors say their rate is lower than previous studies, but two series in their own table, Gabel and Lim, report lower rates, and both also selected patients.

slides.title: Secondary: risk factors for failure
slides.lead: Adjusted analysis by level, 14 failing levels of 235.

rows: Anterolateral plate vs posterior or lateral rod

points: Cutoffs from ROC: reducible <13% AUC 0.71, postop disc height AUC 0.69, BMD AUC 0.84 (0.64-1.0)
Predicted failure: 0.3% with none of the three adjusted factors; 71.7% (44.9-98.5) with all three
Cage size, lordosis, OLIF vs XLIF and number of levels did not differ
slides.see: Table 2: Grade III subsidence occurred at 7 of 14 failing levels (50%) and 4 of 221 successful levels (1.8%).
slides.notes: Read the sizes before the effects. 14 failing levels, about 6 model parameters (O-arm, two cutoffs, fixation with 2 contrasts, subsidence). Our inference: roughly 2 events per parameter is far below what stable logistic regression needs, so the adjusted ORs are imprecise and probably inflated. The interval on reducible disc height, 18.9 (3.8-93.9), is wide: the effect could be as small as about 4. The cutoffs were chosen on this same data with the Youden index, then tested on the same data, so they are optimistic and need outside validation. BMD: the strongest univariable signal, but measured in only 66 of 191 patients (the text says 67, and 35%), with 5 failures. It could not be adjusted. Who got a DEXA was not described, so the missing two-thirds may not be random. Fixation: the abstract and conclusion list the anterolateral plate as a risk factor. The adjusted CI crosses 1 and the overall fixation p was 0.21. The Discussion says both that the plate was not an independent predictor and that it raised risk after adjustment. Say it as a univariable association only. Subsidence is a postoperative event, so it explains failure rather than predicting it before surgery. Our reading: it may be on the causal path from low BMD and stiff segments to failure, so adjusting for it can hide those upstream effects. The predicted probabilities assume equal numbers in each category; 71.7% with a CI of 44.9-98.5 rests on very few patients. The CIs on the ORs are log-symmetric, which we checked; they look internally consistent.

slides.title: What does not add up
slides.lead: Our recomputation found errors in direction, counts and p values.

rows: Higher in success group, 2.0 vs 5.1 mm
Direction reversed; Table 2 shows failure higher
Table 1: 41% vs 7.7%; our Fisher p about 0.018

slides.notes: These are checks we ran, not claims made by the authors. Most Table 1 and Table 2 percentages recompute correctly, and the diagnosis rows sum to 191 and 13. One-level plus two-level counts give 235 levels, and the failure group's 12 one-level and 1 two-level patients give the 14 failing levels. The problems: (1) the Results text says subsidence was higher in the success group, but its own numbers and Table 2 show the failure group subsided more. Read Table 2. (2) Women: the total of 178 equals the success group size, and the parts sum to 171. The true proportion of women is uncertain, between about 90% and 93%. (3) Two p values in the text are stronger than the tables. (4) BMD specificity of 88.9% cannot come from 61 successful patients with BMD; no whole number of 61 gives 88.9%. Reducible disc height specificity of 56.0% does not match any whole number of 221 levels either (124/221 is 56.1%). (5) Fixation counts in Table 1 are levels (235), though the table header says patients. (6) Three Table 1 percentages in the success group are misrounded: smokers 6/178 is 3.4% (printed 3.5), degenerative spondylolisthesis 59/178 is 33.1% (printed 33.2), OLIF 77/178 is 43.3% (printed 43.2). The smoker Fisher p recomputes to 0.39, not the printed 0.35. Levels (0.30 vs 0.31), LLIF type and female p values reproduce. (7) Table 5 labels this study 2021, calls Oliveira 'Oliviera', and prints Gabel 1/28 as 3.5% (it is 3.6%). The other Table 5 rates recompute. (8) The Discussion says the success group had demographics similar to the failure group, but fixation and BMD differed. So did O-arm navigation: Table 1 prints 73/178 (41%) in the success group versus 1/13 (7.7%) in the failure group, with no p value. Our Fisher exact test gives p of about 0.018, yet the Results text says O-arm use did not differ. O-arm (univariable p=0.09) was then entered in the multivariable model. (9) Our check of the AUC CI for reducible disc height, 0.61-0.80, with 14 positives: a standard Hanley-McNeil estimate gives a wider interval, about 0.55-0.87. The reported CI is narrower, and the cause is unknown. Accounting for clustering by patient would widen an interval, not narrow it, so clustering does not explain it. (10) Cage width in Table 1 is 18 (18-45) mm in the total and success groups. Our reading: an upper quartile of 45 mm overlaps the lengths (50-55 mm), probably a data or column error. None of these change the headline 13/191. Several weaken the risk-factor story.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
