points: No comparator: no patients failing the criteria, no direct-decompression group
The criteria were proposed, not tested; the authors' claim that each criterion had a significant impact is not shown by these data
Failure is a surgeon's reoperation decision within 6 months, not a measured symptom threshold
26 of 217 eligible (12%) excluded for incomplete data; their outcomes are unknown
14 failing levels support only a few predictors; cutoffs derived and tested on the same data
BMD missing in about two-thirds; subsidence is a postoperative mediator
Single center, 3 surgeons, 93% women by the paper's count, mixed diagnoses
slides.notes: Strengths the authors claim: larger than earlier series, one center, the same protocol and care. Fair, and the criteria are simple and easy to apply in clinic. The core weakness: a success rate in selected patients tells you the selected patients did well. It does not tell you the selection did it. Gabel's 28 patients and Lim's 50 patients, also selected, did as well or better. Our inference: the criteria are a sensible synthesis of earlier work (Gabel's algorithm and Lim's postural-pain criterion), with reducible disc height and the motor grade added. They are reasonable to adopt as a clinical checklist, not as a validated rule. Modifiable or not: the authors call the four criteria nonmodifiable and the risk factors modifiable. Reducible disc height is a preoperative patient trait, not modifiable. Postoperative disc height and subsidence are partly in the surgeon's hands (cage height, endplate care) and partly not (bone quality). BMD can be treated before surgery, but this paper does not show that treating it reduces failure. Ascertainment: failure was counted only to 6 months. Late subsidence or loss of indirect decompression after 6 months would not count as failure under the 6-month definition, even though median follow-up was 24 months. Missing items the paper does not report: complication counts beyond reoperation, how many patients had persistent pain without reoperation, and what proportion of the clinic's LLIF patients met the criteria. Bias direction, our reading: counting only reoperations pushes the failure rate down, because persistent pain without reoperation counts as success. The 26 excluded patients are not described, so the direction of that exclusion is unknown. It could even raise the rate, since reoperated patients may be more likely to complete follow-up (failure-group median follow-up 34 vs 24 months overall, Table 1).

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "In 191 selected patients who met four criteria (dynamic symptoms relieved supine, reducible disc height, no weakness below grade IV, no facet cyst or bony lateral recess stenosis), 6.8% needed direct decompression within 6 months. Failure was linked to low reducible disc height, high-grade subsidence and low postoperative disc height, and, among the third with a BMD measurement, to low BMD. There was no comparison group, so it describes a sensible checklist, not a proven rule."
points: Expect: does this mean indirect decompression works? Only in selected patients; no comparator
Expect: what is the 13% reducible disc height? Percent disc height gained supine versus standing; derived on this data
Expect: should I get a DEXA first? The BMD signal is strong but rests on 66 patients and 5 failures
Expect: should I avoid lateral plates? Univariable signal only; adjusted CI crosses 1

rows: Bone-health testing and considering teriparatide before instrumentation
MIS less blood loss; PROs and reoperation not significantly different

slides.notes: Lead with the selection, then the number, then the limit. If asked whether this beats direct decompression: it does not address that. No patient had planned direct decompression, and the authors list applying their criteria to posterior direct decompression as future work. If asked how to measure reducible disc height: compare standing radiograph disc height with supine imaging (the example in Figure 1 uses supine MRI), mean of anterior and posterior heights. The figure was not in our copy. If asked about BMD: the paper's own data suggest low BMD matters, with a T-score cutoff of -2.1, but it was measured in about a third, could not be adjusted, and the paper does not test treatment. O05, per its library record, supports bone-health testing before instrumentation and considering teriparatide in osteoporosis, with Grade B recommendations; it is a separate guideline, not evidence from this cohort. T02, per its record, is an MIS versus open TLIF registry comparison and does not test indirect decompression; it is a pairing on MIS technique choice. If asked about subsidence: the authors advise avoiding endplate injury, especially with older age, osteoporosis and specific endplate morphology. That is their recommendation, not a tested intervention. If asked what is wrong with the paper: the results text reverses the direction of subsidence, the female count does not add up, and two p values in the text are stronger than in the tables. The headline 13/191 is internally consistent.

decks.not_reviewed: The 24-month QOD paper on this cohort (reference 7), the QOD inclusion-criteria and MCID papers (references 29-36), and the Kwon 10-year study (reference 40). Figure 1 is an operative illustration only. The PDF cites no supplement.

slides.title: Chan 2023: MI versus open TLIF for grade I spondylolisthesis at 5 years
slides.lead: Bottom line: MI-TLIF had less blood loss and longer operations. At 60 months, adjusted disability, pain, quality of life and satisfaction did not differ significantly from open TLIF.
points: Journal club · MIS and technique selection
Chan AK, et al. Neurosurg Focus 2023;54(1):E2
Quality Outcomes Database (QOD) spondylolisthesis module, 12 sites
297 patients: 72 MI-TLIF, 225 open TLIF
slides.notes: This deck was prepared from the full text of the paper, not from a critique or abstract. The PDF is complete: methods, four tables, discussion, limitations and references. No supplement is cited. Not reviewed: the 24-month paper on the same cohort (reference 7) and the Kwon 10-year study (reference 40); their results are quoted only as this paper reports them. Frame the paper before the numbers. This is not a trial. Surgeons chose the technique, so this is a registry comparison with regression adjustment, and the authors themselves call it a retrospective analysis of prospectively collected data. The interesting story is the change over time in the same cohort. The authors report that at 24 months MI-TLIF was associated with better disability, quality of life and satisfaction. At 60 months, after adjustment, those differences were not significant. So the question for the room is whether the early MIS advantage fades, or whether it was never robust. The paper cannot tell you which, and that is worth saying out loud.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: Does the short-term advantage claimed for MI-TLIF translate into better 5-year patient-reported outcomes in grade I degenerative spondylolisthesis?
points: Background: MI-TLIF uses a paramedian Wiltse approach with percutaneous screws to limit muscle dissection.
Known: less blood loss and, in some studies, faster recovery and shorter stays.
Gap: spondylolisthesis-only comparisons are mostly small, single-center and 12 to 24 months long, per the authors.
Same cohort at 24 months: MI-TLIF was associated with better ODI, EQ-5D and satisfaction, per the authors' earlier paper.
This paper: the same 297 patients, outcomes at 60 months.

rows: Meyerding grade I degenerative listhesis, single-level TLIF
MI-TLIF: percutaneous screws and Wiltse-plane interbody

slides.notes: The authors cite a prevalence of degenerative spondylolisthesis of 13.6 percent of the US population. Their stated motivation is durability: MI-TLIF is relatively new, so long-term comparison matters. Note the definition of MI. A case counted as MI only if both screws were percutaneous and the interbody graft went in through the Wiltse plane. Mini-open and other partly open procedures were excluded, not counted as open. That makes the MI group a fairly pure technique, but it also means the comparison is between two ends of a spectrum chosen by the surgeon. The open group is a standard midline approach with paraspinal dissection. What the paper does not compare: cost, opioid use and sagittal alignment are all named by the authors as outside scope. When a surgeon asks whether MIS is worth learning, this paper speaks mainly to 5-year patient-reported outcomes and reoperation. It reports a few perioperative recovery measures, length of stay 2.9 vs 3.3 days (p = 0.08), discharge home 93.1% vs 91.1%, and 24-month return to work 100% vs 80% (p = 0.02), but not cost, opioid use or alignment.

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: A registry cohort where the surgeon chose the approach, with clear imbalances at baseline.
points: Enrolled July 2014 to June 2016 at 12 high-enrolling QOD sites; data audited centrally and by sites.
Grade I listhesis confirmed by site surgeons on standing or dynamic radiographs.
Excluded: grade II or higher, and partly MI procedures such as mini-open.
Analysis: t-tests and chi-square; multivariable linear, logistic and ordinal models.
Covariates: any baseline factor with p below 0.20, plus the baseline value of that outcome.
Missing values imputed with missForest, per Methods.
Follow-up at 60 months: 62 of 72 MI-TLIF (86.1%) and 170 of 225 open (75.6%), p = 0.06.
slides.notes: Read the baseline table for clues about selection. Open patients had motor deficit four times as often, 23.6 versus 5.6 percent. That is a surgeon decision signal: our reading is that surgeons may have preferred open decompression when there was a deficit. MI patients used workers' compensation far more often, 11.1 versus 1.3 percent; the authors report this imbalance and say they adjusted for it. Our reading, not the paper's: workers' compensation is usually linked to worse outcomes, so if anything this would bias against MI. Baseline ODI, back pain, leg pain and EQ-5D did not differ significantly. We recomputed the baseline P values from the means and SDs and the counts. Age, BMI, EQ-5D, ODI, motor deficit, follow-up and insurance all reproduce. Baseline listhesis did not: 6.5 versus 5.9 mm with SDs of 3.2 and 3.4 gives p about 0.17 on all 297, not the 0.42 printed. Fewer patients may have had measurements, but the table does not say so. Dynamic films existed for only 78 open and 32 MI patients. Two design points matter. First, covariate choice by baseline p value below 0.20 is a weak rule: it picks what happened to differ, not what is known to confound. Second, nothing in Methods mentions adjustment for site or surgeon, and with 12 sites and surgeon-chosen technique, clustering is likely. The paper does not report how many surgeons did MI cases. Follow-up differed by 10.5 points; the authors call it similar because p = 0.06.

slides.title: Primary outcome: ODI at 60 months
slides.lead: Unadjusted ODI favored MI-TLIF by about 6 points; after adjustment the difference was 2.4 points and not significant.
points: Both groups improved from baseline (p < 0.001 within each group).
Unadjusted change in ODI and ODI MCID (14.3 points) did not differ.
Adjusted: no outcome in Table 4 reached significance.
Adjusted effects are reported as MI minus open; negative ODI favors MI.
slides.notes: How to read this slide. The unadjusted 60-month ODI favored MI by about 6 points with p = 0.04, but change from baseline did not differ, and once baseline and imbalanced covariates entered the model the gap shrank to 2.4 points. The useful number is the confidence interval: minus 7.0 to plus 2.2. Our reading: this interval excludes a mean group difference as large as 14.3 points, so a very large mean difference is unlikely in this sample, unless there is confounding the model did not capture. Be careful with that yardstick. The 14.3-point MCID is a threshold for change in an individual patient, not a margin for a difference between group means, so clearing it is weaker reassurance than it sounds. The interval allows an MI advantage of up to 7 points, about half the individual MCID, which a group-level comparison could still care about. That is the honest summary: no large difference, small difference not ruled out. The authors go further and call the techniques equivalent. No equivalence margin or power calculation was set, so that word is theirs and is not supported by a formal test. Three recomputation checks. First, the unadjusted ODI p of 0.04 reproduces with 169 open and 62 MI patients (our p about 0.036), not with 225 and 72 (about 0.02). So the univariable outcomes look like complete cases even though Methods says missing values were imputed. Second, with baseline ODI as a covariate, a model for the 60-month score and a model for change should give the same treatment coefficient. Table 4 gives minus 2.4 and minus 1.9, and the same mismatch appears for back and leg pain, so the two models were not specified as described or used different samples. Third, the published intervals are close to symmetric and their p values reproduce. The MCID odds ratio direction is not defined in the footnote; we assume above 1 favors MI.

slides.title: Secondary outcomes and harms
slides.lead: Perioperative differences were real; at 60 months, unadjusted back and leg pain were lower with MI-TLIF, but adjusted pain, EQ-5D and satisfaction did not differ, nor did unadjusted reoperation.
points: Unadjusted 60-month pain favored MI: NRS back 2.8 vs 3.7 (p = 0.048), leg 1.8 vs 2.8 (p = 0.03); change scores did not differ (p = 0.21 and 0.40).
Adjusted beta, MI versus open: NRS back pain -0.5 (-1.3 to 0.3), leg pain -0.5 (-1.3 to 0.2), EQ-5D -0.01 (-0.07 to 0.04).
Adjusted NASS satisfaction OR 1.0 (0.5 to 1.8), p = 0.99.
30-day complications: MI 5 events (2 durotomies); open 18 events in 17 patients (7 durotomies, 5 infections).
Related reoperation: MI 4 patients with 6 operations; open 26 patients with 29 operations, adjacent segment disease most common.
At 24 months, per this paper: fusion 100% vs 96.4% (p = 0.21); return to work 100% vs 80% (p = 0.02).
slides.notes: MI-TLIF cost about 39 minutes more operating time and saved about 190 mL of blood. Length of stay did not differ significantly, which the authors attribute to local practice patterns. Reoperation: 5.6 versus 11.6 percent, p = 0.14. Our rough 95 percent interval for that 6-point difference runs from about minus 1 to plus 13 points, so a clinically meaningful reduction with MI is neither shown nor excluded. Those rates use all 225 and 72 patients as denominators, including those lost to follow-up, and there is no time-to-event analysis. Reoperation was not adjusted; it appears only in the univariable table. Pain follows the same pattern as ODI. Unadjusted 60-month back pain (2.8 vs 3.7, p = 0.048) and leg pain (1.8 vs 2.8, p = 0.03) were lower with MI-TLIF, but change from baseline did not differ and the adjusted betas were not significant. Our recomputation with completer denominators reproduces both p values. The NASS result needs care. The distribution differed, p = 0.04, and the authors say this was largely driven by the open group having more score 4 responses, 10.7 versus 4.8 percent. We reran the chi-square on the Table 2 counts and got p about 0.036, but about three quarters of the statistic comes from score 3, where MI had 4 of 63 against open 1 of 159. Score 3 means surgery helped but the patient would not have it again. Two cells have expected counts under 5, so the test is shaky either way, and after adjustment the odds ratio was 1.0. A second NASS problem: 63 MI patients answered NASS, but only 62 MI patients had 60-month follow-up. One MI patient listed as reoperated had an aborted MI-TLIF because of air embolism and returned at 1 month for instrumentation, and was kept in the MI group. EQ-5D adjusted beta is negative, which by the table footnote is in the direction of open, but it is tiny.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: A useful long-term registry signal with selection, follow-up and reporting problems that limit it to: no large difference found.
points: Strengths: prospective multicenter collection, audited data, strict MI definition, 5-year follow-up.
Selection: surgeon choice, with motor deficit four times as common in the open group.
Adjustment: covariates chosen by p below 0.20; no stated site or surgeon adjustment.
Attrition: 24.4% of open and 13.9% of MI patients missing at 60 months.
Size: only 72 MI patients; no power or equivalence margin.
Internal inconsistencies: NASS denominator, model coefficients, listhesis p value, imputation.
slides.notes: Authors' limitations: retrospective analysis of a prospective cohort; no control of surgeon and patient selection; variation in technique such as unilateral versus bilateral facetectomy; baseline differences in BMI, motor deficit and workers' compensation, which they adjusted for; loss to follow-up, which they defend by comparison with SPORT, where in their account only 69 percent of the randomized and 57 percent of the observational cohorts had 8-year data; and no segmental alignment, cost or opioid data. Our additional points. Confounding by indication is the core problem. Adjustment can only handle what was measured, and the reason a surgeon chose open surgery for a given patient was not recorded. Differential attrition matters because patients who do poorly may be less likely to return questionnaires, and the open group lost more. The authors read the high follow-up as evidence that long-term parity is real. That is reasonable but not proof. The model approach selects covariates by baseline p value, ignores clustering, and the final-value and change models disagree when they should match. The 24-month superiority reported in the earlier paper and the 60-month null here come from one cohort; the paper does not show the trajectory, so we cannot say whether the MI advantage faded or was always fragile. Interpretation: the Discussion calls MI and open TLIF equivalent and concludes there is no compelling evidence for either. The second statement is supported; equivalence was never tested. Funding was from NeuroPoint Alliance, NREF and the Spine Section; several authors report industry fees outside the submitted work, and two authors report Medtronic patents with royalties: Dr. Glassman a patent for Medtronic, and Dr. Foley a patent for instruments for stabilization of bony structures.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "In 297 registry patients with grade I degenerative spondylolisthesis, MI-TLIF had less blood loss and longer operations. At 5 years, adjusted disability, pain, EQ-5D and satisfaction did not differ significantly, and reoperation was 5.6 versus 11.6 percent, not significant."
points: Adjusted ODI difference 2.4 points favoring MI, 95% CI -7.0 to 2.2: large differences unlikely, small ones not excluded.
Not randomized: surgeons chose the approach, and open patients had more motor deficits.
Do not say equivalent: no equivalence margin or power was set.
Choose by surgeon skill, patient factors and perioperative goals, as the authors suggest.
slides.notes: Expect these questions. Does MI-TLIF give better long-term outcomes? This paper says no detectable difference at 5 years after adjustment. The 24-month advantage the authors report from the same cohort did not hold at 60 months. Is the lower reoperation rate real? 5.6 versus 11.6 percent is a 6-point gap, but p = 0.14 and the analysis was unadjusted with incomplete follow-up; our rough interval spans from no benefit to a 13-point reduction. It is a hypothesis, not a finding. Adjacent segment disease made up most open reoperations, 16 of 26 patients. Is MI-TLIF safe in this cohort? 30-day complications were 6.9 versus 7.6 percent, with fewer durotomies and no 30-day infections in the MI group, but the counts are small and the groups were selected differently. Should I switch to MIS? The authors say either technique is acceptable and that surgeons who perform only one approach can reasonably continue. What the paper supports is narrower: if you are good at open TLIF, these data do not show your patients do worse at 5 years. What about motor deficit? Few MI patients had one, 4 of 72, so this paper says little about MI-TLIF in patients with weakness. How does it compare with Kwon? The authors cite Kwon's single-surgeon Korean series with 10-year follow-up: early MI superiority at 2 years and similar ODI and pain at 10 years, reoperation 4.6 versus 5.7 percent. Those figures are as quoted in this paper; Kwon was not reviewed here.

decks.not_reviewed: Supplementary tables A to I (outcome overview, learning-curve case distribution and outcomes, time-point detail, regression, per protocol and learning-curve sensitivity analyses, NRS results), the protocol paper, the 24- and 60-month follow-up and the separate cost-effectiveness paper. The PDF is the complete article text reformatted from PMC, not a critique, but it omits Figures 1 to 3 and truncates Table 2 at the right: the open-arm 6-month medians are visible, but their IQRs, the open-arm 6-month n, the 6-month between-group differences and the 12-month columns are cut off.

slides.title: Gadjradj 2022: Full endoscopic versus open discectomy for sciatica (PTED-study)
slides.lead: Bottom line: transforaminal endoscopic discectomy (PTED) was noninferior to open microdiscectomy for leg pain at 12 months; the difference favored PTED by 7.1 points on a 0 to 100 scale, which the authors say may not be clinically relevant.
points: Journal club · MIS and technique selection
Gadjradj PS, et al. BMJ 2022;376:e065846
Four Dutch hospitals. 613 randomized: 304 PTED, 309 open microdiscectomy.
Prepared from a reformatted copy of the full PMC text. Figures were not included, Table 2 is cut off at the right, and the supplementary tables were not reviewed.
slides.notes: This is a government-funded Dutch noninferiority trial (ZonMw, no medical technology industry involvement). PTED was not reimbursed in the Netherlands, so insurers paid for it only inside this trial; the authors say the result led the Dutch government to reimburse it. That context explains the design: three of the four surgeons learned PTED during the trial, and their first 50 cases each were set aside as learning-curve cases. The question is technique, not whether to operate. Every patient already had a surgical indication under Dutch consensus. Source note: the PDF is the complete article text reformatted for phone reading, not a critique. It omits Figures 1 to 3 (flowchart, outcome curves, forest plot of the primary analyses). Table 2 is truncated: the open-arm 6-month medians show, but their IQRs, the 6-month between-group differences and the 12-month columns are cut off, so 12-month figures here come from the Results text. Supplementary tables A to I, which hold the learning-curve results, the per protocol tables and the sensitivity analysis that includes the learning-curve patients, were not reviewed. The 24-month and 60-month follow-up and the separate cost-effectiveness paper were not reviewed either.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: Can a less invasive transforaminal endoscopic discectomy match open microdiscectomy for leg pain, so that it can be offered as an alternative?
points: Claimed PTED advantages: no muscle detachment, no bony change, no general anesthesia, so less back pain and faster recovery.
Concerns the authors cite: leg-pain effectiveness, a learning curve, more radiation, and earlier studies possibly influenced by industry.
Earlier comparisons were small, nonrandomized or single-surgeon, per the authors.

rows: Age 18–70, at least 6 weeks of disabling radiating leg pain from MRI-confirmed lumbar disc herniation, no improvement with conservative care
PTED under local anesthesia and conscious sedation, outpatient
Open transflaval microdiscectomy under general anesthesia
Leg pain, 0–100 VAS, at 12 months; noninferiority margin 5.0

slides.notes: Frame it as a noninferiority question. The authors hypothesized that PTED's claimed advantages, less back pain and shorter stay, would justify offering it only if it was not worse for leg pain, the main goal of surgery. So the bar was set on leg pain, with a margin of 5.0 points on 0 to 100. That margin is small: the authors themselves later say a 7.1-point difference is below commonly recognized MCID thresholds, so, by our inference, the margin is tighter than what a patient would notice. The authors list as a strength that the margin was agreed in writing before the trial by the research group, the patients' organization, professional organizations and the Dutch Health Care Institute. Note the eligibility. Patients could have motor or sensory loss. Excluded were prior surgery at the same or adjacent level, cauda equina syndrome, isthmic or degenerative spondylolisthesis, ASA above 2, and severe cranial or caudal sequestration beyond half the adjacent vertebra. That last exclusion matters for a transforaminal approach and limits generalization to large migrated fragments. L5-S1 was 52 percent of the primary PTED group, so the approach was used at the level where iliac anatomy is often cited as a hurdle; that comment is ours, the paper does not discuss it.

slides.title: Patients and methods
points: Randomized 1:1, computer-generated variable blocks of 4, 6 or 8, stratified by centre
Patients not blinded; research nurse doing the neurologic exam knew allocation
Surgeons spine-dedicated, 8–11 years' experience; one already proficient in PTED, three trained during the trial
Learning curve: each trainee's first 50 PTED cases, including 10–15 supervised; excluded from the primary analysis
Primary analysis: intention to treat without learning-curve cases, linear mixed model adjusted for baseline and centre, bootstrap CIs
Sample size: 306 for 90% power, SD 14.9, one-sided alpha 0.05; 382 with 20% attrition; target 682 with learning-curve cases and matching open patients
slides.notes: Walk the flow, because this is where the trial is fragile. 711 were assessed and 613 enrolled. The target of 682 was not reached because the enrollment period, already extended from two to three years, ran out. The plan was 150 learning-curve PTED cases plus 150 open patients randomized alongside them; only 125 learning-curve cases accrued. The primary analysis drops those 125 PTED patients but keeps all 309 open patients. Our reading, not the authors': learning-curve status depended on when a patient was operated on and by whom, so the primary comparison sets later PTED patients, mostly from experienced hands, against open patients from the whole enrollment period. It is no longer a purely randomized comparison. The authors' sensitivity analysis with all 613 is reported as comparable, but its numbers sit in supplementary table H, which we did not see. Second, look at who got surgery. In the primary groups, 171 of 179 PTED patients (96 percent) were operated on, against 249 of 309 open patients (81 percent). By our chi-square that gap has P below 0.001. The authors say some patients with a strong PTED preference who were randomized to open surgery left the study immediately. Missing data were handled by mixed models with maximum likelihood, which assumes they are missing at random. Check the power arithmetic: 2 x (1.645 + 1.282) squared x 14.9 squared / 5 squared gives about 152 per group, so 306 assumes no true difference. The paper says the expected difference was 5, which does not fit that number. Table 1 shows only the primary groups. Baseline leg pain median 71 versus 74, ODI 44 in both. Preference for PTED was 85 versus 78 percent, and our chi-square gives P about 0.04. Weakness was 51 versus 59 percent, P about 0.09. The authors call the groups similar.

slides.title: Primary outcome: leg pain
slides.lead: At 12 months the mean difference was 7.1 points (95% CI 2.8 to 11.3) in favor of PTED, which is entirely above zero and well clear of the 5.0 margin.
points: Median leg pain at 12 months: 7.0 (IQR 1.0–30.0) PTED versus 16.0 (2.0–53.5) open
Little difference early; the gap widened at 6, 9 and 12 months, per the authors
Per protocol and learning-curve sensitivity analyses agreed, per the authors
slides.see: Figure 2 has the median score curves over time and Figure 3 the forest plot of all primary analyses, including the 613-patient analysis; neither figure was in our copy, and the text says only that both groups improved similarly.
slides.notes: Read the sign. For leg pain, back pain and ODI a positive difference favors PTED; for quality of life and SF-36 a negative difference favors PTED, because higher is better on those scales. So the table differences are open minus PTED. Noninferiority asks whether the lower CI bound stays above minus 5. Here the whole interval is above zero, so the result is noninferior and also statistically in favor of PTED. The authors say statistically significantly lower but frame the conclusion as noninferiority, and they say 7.1 is below commonly recognized MCID thresholds. The time pattern is the teaching point. At 2 and 6 weeks there was essentially no difference. Patients who had the procedure promoted as less invasive did not report less leg pain early. The gap appeared at 6 to 12 months. The authors suggest scar tissue after open surgery as one hypothesis and label it as such. Our caution: at 12 months both medians are low and the distributions are skewed, with the open arm's upper quartile at 53.5 against 30.0. A mean difference of 7 is likely driven by a tail of patients doing poorly after open surgery. The authors used bootstrap intervals to account for skewed residuals. The authors also note that the mixed model draws on earlier time points, so it differs subtly from the planned change at 12 months; linear regression gives 7.9. The primary outcome was switched mid-trial to an 11-point NRS because VAS length varies across devices, then switched back to VAS. The NRS result, 0.6 on 0 to 10, matches, which reassures. We could not check the 613-patient sensitivity analysis or Figure 3.

slides.title: Secondary outcomes and harms
slides.lead: Every 12-month patient-reported outcome favored PTED by small margins; PTED had no dural tears and same-day discharge, but learning-curve patients had roughly twice the reoperation rate, a difference the paper did not test.
points: SF-36 at 12 months: PCS −2.8 (−4.1 to −1.6), MCS −2.1 (−3.4 to −0.9), favoring PTED
Learning-curve PTED: 14 of 125 (11%) repeat surgery within 1 year, 4 converted to open
Opioid use: 13% versus 29% at 2 weeks (our P below 0.001); 5% versus 10% at 12 months (our P about 0.10); no tests reported
slides.notes: The authors write that secondary outcomes followed the same course as leg pain: small in the first three months, larger at 6 to 12 months. Table 2 disagrees. ODI favored PTED by 6.5 at 2 weeks and 3.4 at 6 weeks against 5.3 at 12 months; QoL by −6.8 and −7.8 against −6.2. Only back pain (1.8, 0.9, then 6.0) and SF-36 PCS follow the stated pattern, so PTED showed early ODI and QoL advantages. The ODI difference of 5.3 points and back pain of 6.0 are small; the authors say these may not reach clinical relevance. The odds ratios come from logistic mixed models. Our caution: those are patient-level odds ratios, which run larger than a crude comparison of proportions. At 6 weeks, for example, 66 versus 59 percent recovered gives a crude odds ratio of about 1.35 by our arithmetic, against 1.5 in the table. Twelve-month proportions were in the truncated part of Table 2. Harms favor PTED in the primary groups. Open surgery had 8 dural tears, 1 nerve root injury, 3 wound infections, 2 CSF leaks and 1 DVT. PTED had 1 wrong-level exploration and 2 transient increases in neurologic deficit. Operating time was the same, median 30 minutes. Scar length was 11.7 versus 38.4 mm. Discharge and mobilization differences partly reflect the protocol: PTED was planned as outpatient surgery, and open patients usually went home on day 1. Reoperation within a year was 5.3 versus 5.6 percent, but only after the learning curve. The 125 learning-curve patients had 14 repeat operations, 11 percent, for recurrent herniation, roughly twice the 5.3 percent of the primary PTED group. The paper gives no test; our chi-square P is about 0.06 (Yates 0.10), and the denominators differ (all randomized learning-curve cases versus operated primary-group patients). The Discussion says the learning-curve analysis shows PTED can safely be adopted, while the policy section says it has a learning curve with a higher rate of repeat surgery. Our arithmetic, approximate because supplementary table C was not seen: including learning-curve cases, PTED reoperation is about 23 of roughly 290 operated, near 8 percent. No statistical tests on complications or reoperation are reported. The authors say opioid use was lower with PTED at 2 weeks, 6 months and 12 months, but report no test. By our chi-square, 2 weeks (13 versus 29 percent) gives P below 0.001; 6 months (5 versus 9 percent) P about 0.13 and 12 months (5 versus 10 percent) P about 0.10, so only the 2-week difference is statistically supported.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: Holds up: large multicentre randomized trial, 4 centres, several surgeons
Holds up: no industry funding; margin signed in advance by the research group, patients’ organisation, professional organisations and the Dutch Health Care Institute
Holds up: per protocol, regression, NRS and 613-patient analyses all agree, per the authors
Weakens: learning-curve PTED cases removed but their concurrent open controls kept (our reading)
Weakens: 19% of open patients versus 4% of PTED patients had no trial surgery; PTED preference drove some dropout
Weakens: unblinded patients, 78–85% preferring PTED, all patient-reported outcomes self-reported
Weakens: primary outcome switched to NRS and back to VAS during the trial
Weakens: 12-month follow-up only; ASA 2 or less, no large migrated fragments
Errors: Table 3 open-arm herniation positions add to 250 of 249; a Table 2 median lies outside its IQR
slides.notes: Be fair: this is a large multicentre randomized comparison of PTED with open microdiscectomy, government funded with a margin agreed before the start. The authors' own limitations are participation bias from PTED-preferring patients who dropped out after randomization to open surgery, no patient blinding, missing the 682 target, and the VAS device question. The rest are our reading. The biggest issue is the learning-curve handling. It protects PTED from its early cases, which is a fair question to ask about a mature technique, but it breaks the randomized balance in time and surgeon. The 613-patient analysis is the real randomized comparison, and the authors say it agreed; we could not see the numbers. Next, differential attrition. 60 of 309 open patients had no surgery in the trial, against 8 of 179 PTED. Patients were told both techniques were equally effective, yet 81 percent preferred PTED. Patients who wanted PTED and got open surgery may report worse pain; the patients who stayed may differ from those who left. Both effects push self-reported outcomes toward PTED, and the gap only needs to be about 5 points to matter here. Noninferiority survives this easily, because the lower bound is 2.8 and the margin is minus 5. The favorable direction is less secure. Recompute what you can. Table 1 percentages check. Table 3 percentages check, but open-arm herniation positions sum to 250 for 249 patients. Table 2 shows the open SF-36 MCS at 2 weeks as 42.7 with IQR 42.9 to 53.4, which is impossible. The text counts the 10 tubular cases within the 244 who had microdiscectomy as assigned, while Table 3 lists tubular discectomy as a procedure other than assigned. The sample-size text gives an expected difference of 5, but 306 only fits an assumed difference of zero. Odds ratio intervals are symmetric on the log scale, as they should be.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "In patients needing discectomy, PTED was noninferior to open microdiscectomy for 12-month leg pain, 7 points better on 0 to 100. That is less than a patient would likely notice, with no dural tears and same-day discharge. Reoperation matched open surgery only after each newly trained surgeon's first cases (up to 50)."

rows: Is PTED better for leg pain?
Statistically yes at 12 months, 7.1 points; clinically small, per the authors
No dural tears versus 8; same reoperation after the learning curve
11% repeat surgery in the first 125 cases
Does it apply to every herniation?
Not tested for large migrated fragments, ASA above 2, prior surgery

slides.notes: Expect four follow-up questions. First, should I switch to PTED? This trial supports PTED as an alternative in trained hands. It does not show a clinically meaningful advantage in pain or function. The authors say decisions should weigh patient preference, burden and cost, and that cost-effectiveness is reported separately. Second, is PTED superior? The 95 percent interval for leg pain lies above zero, but the trial was designed for noninferiority, the margin sits below a noticeable difference (our inference from the authors' MCID comment), and patients were unblinded with a strong preference for PTED. Say superior only with those qualifiers. Third, what does the learning curve cost? In this trial, three surgeons with 8 to 11 years of experience did a course and 10 to 15 supervised cases. Their first 125 cases carried an 11 percent one-year reoperation rate, roughly twice the 5 percent in the primary PTED group, though the paper did not test this (our P about 0.06), and 4 conversions to open surgery. The authors also cite more radiation exposure, which this paper did not measure. Fourth, does this tell me whether to operate? No. Every patient already met the Dutch surgical indication. Timing and whether to operate are the questions of Peul and Bailey in the library. Bailey's record, for comparison, reports leg pain 2.8 versus 5.2 on 0 to 10 at 6 months with microdiscectomy against continued nonsurgical care. This trial compares two techniques after that decision. Durability beyond 12 months was added by amendment and is not reported in this paper.

decks.not_reviewed: Nothing beyond the 6-page article. The PDF is the complete Lancet paper (pages 643-648, Figures 1-3, Tables 1-2). The linked Comment (page 609), the protocol, the DSMB interim report and the cited uncontrolled series and meta-analysis were not reviewed. Figure 2 and 3 curves were read from the number-at-risk rows only, because pdftotext does not render the plotted lines.

slides.title: Patchell 2005
slides.lead: Direct decompressive surgery plus radiotherapy versus radiotherapy alone for metastatic spinal cord compression.
points: Journal club: metastatic cord compression
Patchell RA, et al. Lancet 2005;366:643-48

Bottom line: in selected surgical candidates, more patients were walking after treatment with surgery first (84% vs 57%), and they walked longer (median 122 vs 13 days). The trial was small and stopped early at 101 of a planned 200 patients.
slides.notes: This deck was built from the full article, all six pages, including Figure 1 (trial profile), Figures 2 and 3 (Kaplan-Meier ambulatory time) and Tables 1 and 2. It is not a critique or abstract. Not reviewed: the accompanying Lancet Comment, the protocol and the cited earlier series. The trial is the Bluegrass Neuro-Oncology Consortium study, run from Kentucky, which enrolled 70 of the 101 patients. Frame it this way: before this paper, steroids plus radiotherapy was standard, laminectomy had not shown any benefit in retrospective studies and one small randomized trial, and direct decompression, developed in the 1980s, was supported only by uncontrolled series and a meta-analysis. Patchell tests a different operation, direct circumferential decompression aimed at the tumour, usually in front of the cord, with stabilization when needed. So the question is not laminectomy again. It is whether removing the tumour and decompressing the cord directly, before radiotherapy, changes walking. Keep two numbers in your head for recall: 84 versus 57 percent walking, and 10 of 16 versus 3 of 16 regaining walking. Keep one caveat with them: stopped early, 101 patients.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: Does direct decompressive surgery before radiotherapy keep patients with MESCC walking better than radiotherapy alone?
points: Standard care: corticosteroids and radiotherapy; the authors cite about 50% walking and few non-ambulatory patients walking again
Laminectomy, with or without radiation, had shown no benefit in retrospective series and one small randomized trial
Most compressing metastases sit in the vertebral body, in front of the cord, so laminectomy often fails to decompress and can destabilize
Uncontrolled direct-decompression series and a meta-analysis favored surgery but carried selection bias

rows: MRI-proven MESCC at one area, surgical candidates, expected survival at least 3 months
Direct decompressive surgery within 24 h, then 30 Gy in 10 fractions within 14 days
30 Gy in 10 fractions started within 24 h
Walking after treatment, and time spent walking

slides.notes: The authors' argument for a new trial rests on anatomy. Metastases usually arise in the vertebral body and compress the cord from the front. Laminectomy removes the back of the canal, leaves the tumour, often does not decompress, and can destabilize a spine whose posterior elements were the only intact column. That is why the old negative laminectomy evidence does not answer the question. The authors also argue that the positive uncontrolled surgical series were weakened by selection bias, mixed tumour types, unclear inclusion criteria and imprecise endpoints. Their expected rates for the power calculation came from those sources: about 45 percent walking with radiation alone and about 75 percent with direct surgery. They planned conservatively for a 20-point difference. Note the comparator carefully. Both arms got the same steroid schedule: 100 mg dexamethasone at diagnosis, then 24 mg every 6 hours until treatment started, then a taper during radiotherapy. Both arms got the same radiotherapy dose, 30 Gy in ten 3 Gy fractions, to one vertebra above and below the lesion. So the planned differences were the operation and the timing of radiotherapy: within 24 h of randomisation in the radiation arm, within 14 days after surgery in the surgery arm. The paper does not test other radiation schedules or techniques. That observation is ours.

slides.title: Patients and methods
points: Seven institutions, Sept 1992 to Dec 2002; Kentucky enrolled 70 of 101

Excluded: radiosensitive tumours (lymphoma, leukaemia, myeloma, germ-cell), paraplegia over 48 h, multiple discrete compressive lesions, cauda equina or root compression only, prior MESCC, brain metastases
Stratified by institution, tumour type, walking status and spinal stability (Cybulski guidelines, plus pathological fracture or bone in canal)
Operation not specified; aim was immediate circumferential decompression, approach by tumour position, fixation if unstable
Non-blinded. Intention to treat. O'Brien-Fleming interim analysis at the halfway point
slides.see: Figure 1: 123 assessed, 22 excluded (9 ineligible, 5 patient refusals, 8 physician refusals), 101 randomized, none lost, all analysed.
slides.notes: Flow arithmetic checks: 123 minus 22 is 101, and 9 plus 5 plus 8 is 22. Table 1 columns sum correctly for sex, tumour type, spinal level and tumour position. The institution counts in Methods also sum to 101. Two selection points matter. First, 123 assessed over ten years at seven centres is about 12 a year, so these were patients already judged plausible for surgery. Eight were refused by physicians. That is our reading, not the authors'. Second, the population was deliberately operable: expected survival of 3 months or more, fit for surgery, a single compressive area, and not paraplegic for more than 48 hours. Table 1 gives no P values. Two imbalances are worth naming. Posterior tumours were 13 versus 7. Our Fisher test gives P about 0.14. Median time from primary diagnosis to MESCC was 3 months in the surgery group versus 7 in radiation, with no spread given. Neither clearly favors one arm. Walking at entry and stability were stratification factors and are close. Note there is no lumbar row in the spinal level table; the levels run cervical, T1-T6, T7-T12, and they sum to the full groups. Ambulatory means at least two steps with each foot unassisted, cane or walker allowed. It was measured immediately after radiotherapy finished. In the surgery arm that is after surgery plus up to 14 days plus the radiotherapy course, so the arms were assessed at different times after randomization. That point is ours. The paper says the trial was non-blinded and does not say who assessed walking. The stated power was 82% for a 20-point difference with 100 per group. Our recalculation for 45% versus 65% gives about 82%, matching the paper.

slides.title: Primary outcome: walking
slides.lead: Surgery won on both prespecified walking measures, in every entry subgroup.

rows: Not walking at entry, median days

points: Overall odds ratio 6.2 (95% CI 2.0 to 19.8), Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel stratified by entry walking status
Stopped at the interim: P 0.001 against the O'Brien-Fleming boundary of 0.0054
Our arithmetic: absolute difference 27 points, about 4 patients treated per extra patient walking
slides.see: Figure 2: number at risk at 250 days is 16 surgery versus 7 radiation, and at 500 days 10 versus 2, so the long tail rests on a handful of patients.
slides.notes: Recompute what you can. 42 of 50 is 84 percent and 29 of 51 is 57 percent. The subgroups add back: 32 plus 10 is 42, and 26 plus 3 is 29. Our Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio from those strata is 6.3, matching the printed 6.2, and the interval is symmetric on the log scale. Note the crude odds ratio is only about 4.0. The stratified 6.2 is the honest analysis for this design, but quote the absolute numbers, not the odds ratio, which overstates the effect to a listener when outcomes are common. The 62 percent for 10 of 16 is 62.5 percent, so 63 would be the usual rounding. Two fragile points. First, the subgroup P values. For 32 of 34 versus 26 of 35, the printed 0.024 matches an uncorrected chi-square. Fisher's exact test, more usual with cells of 2, gives about 0.045. For 10 of 16 versus 3 of 16, the printed 0.012 again matches uncorrected chi-square, and Fisher gives about 0.029. The paper does not name the test. These are our calculations. Both stay below 0.05, but they are weaker than printed. Second, the walking-at-entry time result is printed as odds ratio 1.82 (1.08 to 3.12), P 0.024. A time-to-event comparison would normally give a hazard ratio, it runs in the opposite direction to the relative risks in Table 2, and its P is identical to the proportion test. We would not quote that 1.82. 22 of 51 radiation patients were not walking after treatment (13 entry non-walkers who never walked and 9 entry walkers who lost walking), which pulls the overall median down. That reading is ours; the paper does not explain the 13-day median. The multivariable Cox models kept surgery significant, P 0.0017 overall, with pretreatment Frankel score the other predictor. Early stopping on a large effect tends to overstate it. That is a general point, ours, not the authors'.

slides.title: Secondary outcomes and harms
points: Median hospital stay 10 days in both groups; stays over 20 days 7 surgery vs 11 radiation
10 radiation patients (20%) lost strength during radiotherapy and crossed to surgery; none could walk then, 3 regained walking, 4 had surgical complications
Complications of the planned surgery in the surgery arm are not reported
slides.notes: Relative risks below 1 favor surgery here. They come from a Cox model with all covariates. The intervals are log-symmetric and match their P values on our check. Survival is the one to handle carefully: 126 versus 100 days, adjusted RR 0.60, P 0.033. The authors think it reflects more patients staying ambulatory and avoiding infection and clots. That is their explanation, not a tested finding. No unadjusted survival comparison is given. The identical medians for ASIA and Frankel maintenance, 72 and 566 days, are possible but we could not verify them. Harms are the weak part of the reporting. Morbidity at 30 days was defined only as deterioration in ASIA or Frankel scores. Patients maintaining or improving were 86 versus 60 percent for ASIA (P 0.0064) and 91 versus 61 percent for Frankel (P 0.0008). Denominators are not stated. Our check: no single denominator of 50 or 47 (surgery), or 51 or 44 (radiation), yields both reported percentages. 86 percent fits 43 of 50 and 91 percent fits 43 of 47, but no one count gives both, and 60 percent cannot come from 51 or 44 at all. So both arms' denominators are unstated and are not the full arms. Wound infection, fixation failure, CSF leak, reoperation and surgical death in the primary surgery arm are not reported. The only surgical complications given are in the 10 crossovers: 3 wound infections and 1 fixation failure needing more surgery. The 30-day mortality, 3 of 50 versus about 7 of 51 by our back-calculation, has a Fisher P of 0.32, matching the paper. With 101 patients, this cannot exclude a real surgical mortality cost. That reading is ours. The authors conclude there was no excess morbidity or mortality from surgery. Steroid and morphine doses are medians of each patient's mean daily dose, with what are labelled IQRs such as 0.1 to 44.0 mg. Several IQRs in the paper start at 0 and look like ranges.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: Holds up: randomized within strata, central MRI review, central review of radiotherapy plans and operative reports
Holds up: no loss to follow-up, intention to treat, prespecified endpoints and covariates, DSMB stopping rule
Holds up: a clearly defined primary endpoint and a large effect in both entry subgroups
Holds up: 11 of 51 radiation patients had surgery, and intention to treat makes that conservative
Weakens it: stopped at 101 of 200 planned; early stops on benefit tend to overstate effects
Weakens it: non-blinded, walking assessor not described, assessment timing differs by arm
Weakens it: 70 of 101 from one centre; 10 years to accrue; heavily selected
Weakens it: surgery not standardized and its complications not reported
slides.notes: Be fair: for its time this was an ambitious surgical trial, and the walking result is large enough that small biases are unlikely to erase it. The authors name one limitation: patient selection bias. They say the results apply only to patients like those enrolled and that clinical judgment should still be used. Everything else on the weakens list is our reading. Allocation: the paper says permuted blocks within strata at each institution with a computerized technique, but does not describe concealment beyond that. Crossovers: ten radiation patients crossed when they lost strength, and one more was treated with surgery from the start, counted as a protocol violation. All 11 are analysed as radiation, so if anything the comparison is conservative. The authors use the crossovers as further evidence: 3 of 10 walked again after salvage surgery, versus 10 of 16 non-walkers operated first. That comparison is not randomized. Crossovers had failed radiation and had already lost walking, so they are a worse-prognosis group. It supports the direction but not the size. That point is ours. Internal errors to flag: in Table 2, the cervical level predictor reads RR 0.53 with interval 0.74 to 0.98, which excludes its own estimate. Baseline Frankel reads 0.56 (0.3 to 0.73), off-centre on the log scale. The acknowledgments thank the University of Indiana for contributing patients, but Methods lists seven institutions without Indiana that already sum to 101. Follow-up is given as median 102 days, IQR 0 to 1940. An IQR beginning at 0 is implausible, but it cannot be the range either: Figure 2 still shows 1 surgery patient at risk at 2000 days. Radiation, 0 to 1117, fits its last patient at risk at 1000 days. Our check. The reference list misspells O'Brien as 'O'Brian' (ref 21). Spinal stability used Cybulski's guidelines, not a modern score.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "In operable patients with a single area of metastatic cord compression, direct decompressive surgery and then radiotherapy left 84% walking after treatment versus 57% with radiotherapy alone, and walking lasted a median 122 versus 13 days. Of non-walkers, 10 of 16 walked again versus 3 of 16. It was 101 patients, non-blinded and stopped early."

rows: Four domains: N, O, M and S

points: SINS and NOMS rows come from the library records, not from this paper
Do not stretch it: radiosensitive tumours, paraplegia over 48 h, multiple compressive lesions and short expected survival were excluded
slides.notes: Expect these questions. Should ambulatory patients get radiotherapy first and surgery only if they worsen? The authors raise this and say no: in walkers, 94 versus 74 percent kept walking with surgery first, and salvage surgery after failed radiation restored walking in only 3 of 10. Remember that the walker subgroup P is fragile, about 0.045 by Fisher's test on our calculation, and the crossover comparison is not randomized. Does it apply to lymphoma, myeloma or a patient paraplegic for days? No. Those patients were excluded, and the authors say the results cannot justify surgery for all MESCC. Does surgery prolong life? Median survival was 126 versus 100 days in a Cox-adjusted analysis. The authors attribute it to staying ambulatory. Treat it as a secondary finding from a small, early-stopped trial. What did surgery cost? The paper reports equal hospital stays and 30-day mortality of 6 versus 14 percent, not significant, but it does not report the complication rate of the planned operations. The only listed complications are 4 of 10 crossovers. What was the operation? Not standardized: anterior, lateral or posterior by tumour position, aiming at circumferential decompression with fixation if unstable. In general, posterior tumours had a laminectomy with removal of any other involved posterior elements, and any location was stabilised if unstable. What about modern radiotherapy? This trial used 30 Gy in 10 fractions in both arms. It says nothing about other radiation schedules. That is our boundary, not a finding. How does it fit with SINS and NOMS? Those library records describe stability and decision frameworks. This trial judged stability with Cybulski's guidelines plus fracture or bone in the canal, not with SINS, and it selected patients by operability, not by NOMS. Linking them is our framing.

decks.not_reviewed: The two underlying SOSG systematic reviews (references 5 and 6, cited as in press), the questionnaires themselves, the full list of 40 rated factors with their scores, and the representative cases used to test the draft score. Figures 1 to 3 are CT and MRI images of the worked cases; their captions were read. No supplement is cited in the PDF.

slides.title: SINS: the paper
slides.lead: How the Spine Oncology Study Group built a score for neoplastic spinal instability.
points: Journal club: spinal metastases and instability
Fisher CG, et al. Spine 2010;35(22):E1221-9
Design: 2 systematic reviews plus a modified Delphi expert consensus. No patient cohort.
Bottom line: six components summed to 0-18. 0-6 stable, 7-12 indeterminate, 13-18 unstable. A score of 7 or more warrants surgical consultation.
slides.notes: This is a derivation paper, not a validation study. The 33 authors, writing for the SOSG, took two systematic reviews that could not define neoplastic instability and used expert opinion to fill the gap. The output is the Spine Instability Neoplastic Score. The paper contains no patients except three illustrative cases. So it can tell you what experts agreed matters. It cannot tell you how well the score predicts collapse, pain or neurologic decline, or how reliably two readers agree. The authors say so: their conclusion says SINS should be useful 'after further validation and reliability testing'. What was reviewed: the full 9-page article, E1221 to E1229, including all 8 tables and the figure captions. Not reviewed: the two systematic reviews it rests on (cited as in press), the questionnaires, the full 40-factor ranking list and the test cases used for clarity checks. The paper says corporate or industry funds supported the work but does not name the source. Keep it next to Patchell (X01) and NOMS (X03) in this library. Our framing, not the paper's: SINS can be read as the M in NOMS, the mechanical axis. This 2010 paper does not place itself inside NOMS; it criticizes the NOMS mechanical criterion of the time.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: When should a patient with a spinal tumor see a surgeon for instability?
points: Instability was poorly defined. Trauma criteria do not fit tumors: different bone and ligament patterns, healing, neurology and bone quality.
Non-surgeons find it hard to judge, which the authors say often leads to inappropriate referrals of patients without instability or undertreatment of patients with instability.
SOSG definition: loss of spinal integrity from a neoplastic process, with movement-related pain, symptomatic or progressive deformity, and/or neural compromise under physiologic loads.
Goal: a simple shared language for oncologists, radiologists and spine surgeons.
slides.notes: Set the stakes the way the authors do. They argue that neurologic status is only one input into surgical decisions, and that for metastatic disease it is not established when patients should be referred. They cite Patchell (their reference 2, X01 in this library) for the benefit of surgery plus radiation in cord compression. In our record, Patchell reported 84% ambulatory after surgery plus RT versus 57% with RT alone. That number is from the X01 record, not from this paper. The real gap is the patient without deficit: who has a mechanically failing spine, and who just has a painful lesion that radiation will treat? The authors cite White and Panjabi's definition of stability (their reference 12, on the lower cervical spine) and then say neoplastic instability 'appears to be different from that associated with traumatic injuries'. Our reading is that White's definition comes from the trauma setting; the paper does not say so directly. Their own definition combines three things: pain with movement, deformity, and neural compromise under load. Notice that the definition includes neural compromise, but the score itself has no neurologic item. The paper never explains why. 'Character of neurologic changes (with motion)' was one of the four top-rated factors (77.71, SD 19.89) and still did not become an item. What the authors do say is a neurologic deficit or high-grade cord compression is a surgical indication regardless of the score. Also note their critique of NOMS as it stood in 2010. They say its mechanical component rested only on movement-related pain, ignored imaging and was not validated. That is the authors' view of earlier NOMS reports, not of the 2013 NOMS paper (X03), which came later.

slides.title: How it was built
slides.lead: Selection and measurement: who voted, on what, and how.
points: Round-table meeting listed candidate factors. A survey followed: 12 clinical, 12 radiographic, 9 location items, plus open-ended.
Each factor rated 0 (irrelevant) to 100 (absolute importance). Grouped as above 70, 40-70, below 40.
Round 2 by e-mail; paired t tests compared each respondent's ratings with round 1.
Draft score applied to representative cases by a subgroup for clarity, then refined.
slides.notes: This slide is where the validity question lives. The panel is the sample, and the paper is loose about who was on it. Methods says SOSG has 30 members. Results says 24 fellowship-trained spine surgeons out of the 26 in the group completed round 1. Methods step 1 has 24 'spine surgeons and oncologists' listing factors at the round-table stage, and Results later calls the round 1 group 'physicians'. Whether both 24s are the same people is not stated. Round 2 had 20 respondents. So we cannot tell whether any non-surgeon voted, which matters for a score meant to guide oncologists. The survey had 12 plus 12 plus 9, which is 33 listed items, but 40 factors were ranked. Methods step 3 says the open-ended responses 'were compiled and included in the final results', so that is the likely source of the other 7, but the paper never gives the count. Top-rated factors: subluxation or translation 86.67 (SD 11.95), progression of deformity 86.52 (13.60), bilateral facet destruction 78.75 (13.85), and neurologic change with motion 77.71 (19.89). Of locations, cervicothoracic 72.29 (SD 21.01) and occipitocervical 70.83 (SD 16.33) rated highest. Our checks: 86.52 cannot come from 24 whole-number ratings (86.50 or 86.54) but fits 23, so a response may be missing; the other five means fit 24. Ratings bunch at the 100 ceiling (86.52 + 13.60 is over 100), so mean and SD summarize them poorly. Table 1's footnote reverses the usual skewness convention and calls skewness 'pointed', which is kurtosis. The paper never shows how ratings became point values. The authors say weights came from relative importance in the literature, refined by consensus. Our observation: there is no formula. Also note a direct contradiction. Methods step 5 says there were no significant changes between rounds. Results and Table 1 report three: pain with percussion rated higher (P = 0.034), and midcervical location (P = 0.031) and unilateral pedicle involvement (P = 0.037) rated lower. Our view: these are paired t tests across 40 factors in 20 people with no stated multiplicity correction. At P below 0.05, about 2 changes (40 x 0.05) are expected by chance alone, and the chance of 3 or more under no true change is about 0.32. The 3 reported changes are consistent with chance. Table 1's footnote opens with a stray phrase about ECOG/Karnofsky that does not belong there.

slides.title: The score
slides.lead: Six components, scored per lesion and summed to 0-18.

rows: Mechanical: relief lying down, or pain with movement or loading
No collapse, over 50% of body involved
Bilateral facet, pedicle or CV joint

points: 0-6 stable. 7-12 indeterminate, possibly impending. 13-18 unstable.
7 or more: surgical consultation.
slides.notes: How to read it. Subluxation or translation is the only 4-point item in the whole score, matching its top expert rating. Bilateral posterolateral involvement gets 3 against 1 for unilateral. The authors call that 'greater than double' the weight; it is triple. Junctional levels score highest because of transitional forces and, the authors say, blood supply. Rib-supported thoracic levels and the sacrum get the least. CT is the authors' preferred test for lesion quality; they say MRI alone defines it less well. De novo deformity needs prior images or supine-to-upright films. That is a practical trap: a supine CT alone can miss it. The authors admit the 50% vertebral body threshold may be arbitrary because the literature shows no clear cutoff. Score each lesion or region separately and never add lesions together. SINS has no global score and does not model interactions between lesions. Things outside the score that the authors say still matter: contiguous multilevel disease, prior laminectomy or other surgery, prior radiation or radiosurgery, diffuse bony disease and poor bone density, body weight and activity. Two errors to know. First, the text says blastic lesions score 1, but Tables 4 and 8 give blastic 0 and mixed 1. Use the tables. Second, the paper states the minimum score both as 0 (Results) and 2 (Discussion). Table 8 allows 0, for example a pain-free blastic sacral lesion with normal alignment. Also, the Table 2 legend says the rigid segment is S2-S4 while Tables 2 and 8 say S2-S5. Our view: the 7-point consultation threshold and the 13-point instability threshold are consensus cutoffs. No data in this paper tests them.

slides.title: The three cases
slides.lead: Recompute them, and one label does not match its own score.
slides.see: Figure 1 shows the T10 fracture with over 50% height loss and bilateral pedicle and costovertebral involvement; Figure 2 shows the lytic C2 lateral mass with C1-C2 subluxation.
slides.notes: All three sums are correct; we recomputed them. The problem is case 1. It scores 14, which the paper's own rules put in the 13-18 unstable band, yet the text calls it 'indeterminate instability'. Case 2 also scores 14 and is called unstable. Same score, different label. Treat case 1 as unstable by the published bands. Case 1 also teaches modifiers. She had diffuse disease, an old T11 vertebra plana and a 20-degree increase in kyphosis from supine to upright. That increase earned the 2 for de novo deformity. The authors use her later as an example of poor bone quality that should weigh in the decision even though SINS does not score it. Case 2 shows how a C2 lesion is split. The lytic lateral mass with fracture scored 1 under vertebral body (over 50% involvement, no collapse) and 1 for unilateral posterolateral involvement. Our view: it is not obvious that a lateral mass fracture should count as 'no collapse'. This is the kind of call where two readers could differ by a point or two. Case 3 is the authors' warning that stability is not the whole decision. A score of 6 is stable, but he has renal cell carcinoma. The authors cite survival benefit from surgery for solitary renal metastasis, and he was worked up for surgery anyway. Surgery was abandoned because the tumor shared blood supply with the artery of Adamkiewicz. Figure 3 caption says severe destruction of the right pedicle, scored as unilateral, 1 point.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: A consensus tool with content validity only, untested in this paper.
points: Strength: international, multidisciplinary authorship, explicit definition, simple additive score, worked examples.
No reliability data: no inter- or intra-observer agreement.
No criterion validity: score never tested against collapse, pain, neurologic decline or surgeon judgment.
Cutoffs (7 and 13) and point weights set by consensus, with no stated method.
Internal errors: rounds-change contradiction, blastic score, minimum score, case 1 label, panel counts.
slides.notes: Read the abstract's claim carefully: 'content validity'. That means experts agree the items cover the concept. Our view: content validity by expert consensus is a low bar, well short of reliability or criterion validity, and the paper shows no formal content-validity index. It shows mean ratings for a few top items and skewness flags. Our view of what is fragile. One: the panel was drawn from the SOSG, the group the authors write for, so the score's builders and its judges overlap heavily. They are not identical: 33 authors against 24 round 1 and 20 round 2 respondents, and the panel is never named. Two: the respondents were mostly or entirely surgeons, depending on which sentence you believe, yet the tool is aimed at oncologists. Three: the jump from 0-100 ratings to 0-4 points is not explained, so the weights cannot be reproduced. Four: the thresholds are untested. Five: mechanical pain carries 3 of 18 points and depends on history, which may be the least reproducible item. That last point is our inference; the paper has no agreement data. The authors do make good points of their own. Instability from tumor differs from trauma. Static deformity can settle and stay stable. Pain from periosteal stretch or nerve compression is not instability, even though it can coexist. And in their words: 'If a patient has neurologic deficit or high-grade spinal cord compression without deficit, surgery is certainly indicated regardless of the SINS score.' There are also citation slips. Reference 41, cited for posterolateral elements as a separate stability factor, is an ATS statement on grading evidence. Reference 7, cited for lytic lesions carrying greater collapse risk, is Mirels on long bones: an extrapolation from long bones to the spine rather than an outright mis-citation. Reference 7 is also cited among the '2 systematic reviews' done by the SOSG, which it is not. Neither error changes the score. Our inference: the literature support is thinner than the citations suggest.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: SINS is a consensus score for mechanical instability, not a surgical indication by itself.
points: Spoken summary: the SOSG built SINS from two inconclusive systematic reviews and a two-round expert survey. Six items score 0-18; 7 or more means call a spine surgeon, 13 or more is unstable. This paper shows content validity only, with no reliability or outcome data. Score each lesion alone, and remember neurology, histology, prognosis and patient choice sit outside it.
Expect: what are the six components and the bands?
Expect: what is the only 4-point item? Subluxation or translation.
Expect: does SINS decide surgery? No. The authors call it one component.
Expect: what validity did this paper show? Content only, by consensus.
Expect: how do you score multiple lesions? Separately, never summed.
slides.notes: Practice the summary aloud in under 40 seconds. Then be ready for the harder follow-ups. 'A patient scores 14. Unstable or indeterminate?' Unstable by the published bands; the paper mislabeled its own case 1. 'A blastic lesion, how many points?' Zero per the tables; the text's 1 is an error. 'Why no neurology item?' The paper does not say why. The authors keep neurologic deficit and cord compression as separate surgical indications that apply regardless of the score. 'How does SINS relate to NOMS?' Our framing: SINS gives a structured answer for the M in NOMS (X03), the mechanical axis, while NOMS adds neurologic, oncologic and systemic axes. The authors in 2010 criticized earlier NOMS reports for judging mechanical instability by pain alone. 'What would you want before trusting the 7-point cutoff?' Our answer: interobserver agreement and outcome data showing that scores of 7 or more predict collapse, deformity or failed nonoperative care. This paper does not provide either. 'Can a radiation oncologist use it?' That is the authors' intent, but the panel appears to have been mostly surgeons, and the history-based pain item and the need for upright films make it harder outside a spine clinic. That last point is our inference.

decks.not_reviewed: The full 8-page article (pages 744-751) was read, including Tables 1-3 and Figures 1-6. None of the cited studies were read, including the SINS paper (ref 35), the ESCC reliability study (ref 5) and Patchell (ref 31); their numbers here are as this paper reports them. The article cites no supplement. Despite the abstract, the paper contains no implementation cohort to review.

slides.title: Laufer 2013: The NOMS framework for spinal metastases
slides.lead: Bottom line: the four assessments give one decision rule. Radiosensitivity and epidural compression choose the radiation and decide if decompression comes first. Instability is a separate reason to stabilize. Systemic status decides if surgery is tolerable.
points: Journal club · Spine tumor decision making
Laufer I, Rubin DG, Lis E, et al. Oncologist 2013;18:744-51
Type: an expert framework from one center (Memorial Sloan-Kettering) with a narrative literature review
Full text read. The abstract promises results of implementing NOMS, but the paper reports none.

rows: How much epidural cord compression, and is there myelopathy?
ESCC grade on axial T2 MRI
How will the tumor respond to treatment?
Can the patient tolerate treatment, and for how long will they live?

slides.notes: Say clearly what kind of paper this is. It is not a trial, a cohort or a validation study. It describes the decision framework the MSKCC spine team says it has used for 15 years, then sums up the literature behind each step. The opening gives the stakes: spinal metastases occur in 20 percent of cancer patients, and 5 to 10 percent develop cord compression. Treatment is palliative. The goals the paper lists are pain relief, keeping or recovering neurologic function, durable local control, stability and quality of life. The abstract's Methods says the authors report the results of systematic implementation of NOMS-guided treatment. We read the full text and found no such results: no patient count, no outcome table and no comparison. There are four illustrative case figures (Figures 2 to 5), and the rest is cited literature. So judge it as a thinking tool with reasoning you can check, not as evidence that NOMS improves outcomes. The authors say the four assessments have stayed the same while the treatments have changed a lot, and they expect the indications to keep changing. Our reading, not the authors' ranking: the lasting lesson is that the questions outlast the answers. The paper's main clinical claim is about separation surgery and SRS. Disclosures: Laufer consulted for SpineWave, Yamada for Varian Medical Systems, and Bilsky holds intellectual property with DePuy Spine. Received July 2012, published online May 2013.

slides.title: Neurologic and oncologic: read them together
slides.lead: ESCC grade and radiosensitivity together decide whether radiation can go first.
points: ESCC scale (SOSG, 6 grades): 0 bone only; 1a epidural, no thecal sac deformation; 1b thecal sac deformed, no cord contact; 1c cord abutted, not compressed; 2 cord compressed, CSF visible; 3 cord compressed, no CSF visible.
Without instability, grades 0, 1a and 1b go to radiation first. Grades 2 and 3 need decompression first unless the tumor is highly radiosensitive. Grade 1c is undecided.
Myelopathy matters, but the authors base most of the neurologic decision on ESCC grade.
Radiosensitive: lymphoma, seminoma, myeloma; and among solid tumors, breast, prostate, ovarian, neuroendocrine.
Radioresistant: renal, thyroid, hepatocellular, colon, NSCLC, sarcoma, melanoma.
slides.see: Figure 1 shows the ESCC grades drawn on axial T2 images. Figure 2 shows myeloma epidural tumor resolving 11 weeks after cEBRT.
slides.notes: Reading the ESCC scale: the hinge is the cord. Grades 1a to 1c describe how close the tumor gets to the cord; grades 2 and 3 mean it is compressed. The authors say only patients with radiographic cord compression risk deficits from epidural tumor, which is why the image grade carries most of the neurologic decision. Radiosensitivity here means response to conventional external beam radiation (cEBRT). We counted the Table 1 cells ourselves. The table pools 7 cEBRT studies and was adapted from reference 7. All 7 call lymphoma, seminoma and myeloma favorable, and the text says so. Breast and prostate are less clean than the text suggests: two of the three Rades studies (references 13 and 14) rate both as intermediate, Rades 12 rates both favorable, and Gilbert rates prostate unfavorable. Ovarian, neuroendocrine, thyroid and hepatocellular are classed in the text but do not appear in the table. The cEBRT numbers the paper cites: mean ambulation rate 81 percent (range 58 to 100) after cEBRT, but only 6 to 67 percent of nonambulatory patients walked again. In Maranzano and Latini's prospective study, responses lasted 16, 12 and 10 months for myeloma, breast and prostate, and 67 percent of nonambulatory breast patients walked again. Katagiri found combined improvement in 72 percent of favorable histologies and 33 percent success in radioresistant ones. Maranzano reported only 20 percent response for tumors such as hepatocellular, lasting 1 to 3 months. Short courses (800 cGy x 1, 400 cGy x 5) give short-term palliation. Longer, higher-dose courses give more durable control. For radiosensitive tumors, the authors support cEBRT even with high-grade ESCC, because tumor cell death decompresses the cord. Teaching point, ours: a grade 3 myeloma is not a surgical emergency in this framework unless it is unstable.

slides.title: Radiation, and surgery as separation
slides.lead: SRS changed the job of surgery from maximal resection to clearing the cord so the full tumor dose can be given.
points: Radioresistant with ESCC 0, 1a or 1b: image-guided radiation or SRS, no decompression.
Radioresistant with ESCC 2 or 3: decompression and stabilization, then SRS.
The logic: cord Dmax taken as 14 Gy; all SRS failures had under 15 Gy to part of the target, so about 2 mm of tumor-cord separation is needed.
Separation surgery: remove only enough tumor to separate it from the cord, and leave the rest to radiation.
No study has compared separation with maximal resection, as the authors say.

rows: Local control 92% at median follow-up 16 months
413 in review; subgroup size not given
1-yr progression 4.1% (24 Gy x1) vs 9.0% (8-10 Gy x3)

slides.see: Figure 3 shows renal cell T12 pain gone 2 weeks after 2400 cGy SRS. Figure 4 shows a T10 grade 3 renal metastasis before and after posterolateral separation surgery.
slides.notes: This slide is the heart of the paper. Follow the dose chain. The authors take 14 Gy as the maximum safe dose to a single cord voxel. Every SRS failure in one analysis had under 15 Gy to some part of the planning target. If tumor touches the cord, you cannot give 15 Gy to its edge without exceeding cord tolerance. So surgery's job is to make about 2 mm of space. That is an engineering argument, and it is the reason for separation surgery. They credit the term to Benzel and Angelov but give no citation for it. Patchell is the one randomized trial cited for decompression. The paper says surgery plus cEBRT beat cEBRT alone on survival, ambulation, keeping and regaining ambulation, narcotic use and continence, with no difference in length of stay. The library record for Patchell (X01) gives ambulation after treatment of 84 versus 57 percent. Note that Patchell paired surgery with cEBRT, not SRS. The case for surgery followed by SRS rests on case series. Look at the evidence quality. The 413-patient 3 percent figure comes from reference 24, which the paper calls a recent review. Its citation is a journal supplement (Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys 2011;81:S132-S133), so it is likely a meeting abstract; that is our inference. The 3 percent applies to the 24 Gy subgroup, whose size is not given. The 186-patient series and the 2.8 percent symptomatic fixation failure rate after separation surgery have no citation at all. In that 186-patient series, single-fraction 24 Gy had lower 1-year progression than hypofractionated 8 to 10 Gy x 3 (4.1 versus 9.0 percent). The paper gives no per-arm counts and does not say whether the groups were comparable or the difference significant. Our arithmetic on Moulding: with 21 patients a crude rate could only be 4.8 (1 of 21) or 9.5 percent (2 of 21), so the estimated 6.3 percent must be an actuarial figure. Rock reported 92 percent local control with radiosurgery after open surgery. The authors claim SRS responses over 85 percent regardless of histology and pain response in 85 to 92 percent. SRS side effects are mostly mild. The most serious named is radiation-induced cord injury, which is exceedingly rare. Delayed vertebral body fracture is described as another complication that is becoming apparent. Finally, the authors say patients tolerate limited decompression better than attempts at gross total resection. That is their experience, not a comparison.
