slides.title: Mechanical and systemic
slides.lead: Instability is its own indication, whatever the ESCC grade or histology, because radiation does not restore stability.
points: SOSG definition: loss of spinal integrity from tumor with movement-related pain, symptomatic or progressive deformity, or neural compromise under physiologic loads.
Mechanical pain worsens with movement or loading. Biologic pain comes in the evenings and mornings and responds to steroids and radiation.
Clues by level: C1-C2 pain on rotation, flexion and extension; subaxial cervical pain on flexion-extension; thoracic pain on extension (straightening a kyphosis); lumbar radicular pain on standing.
Painful compression fractures without gross instability or major posterior element involvement: vertebroplasty or kyphoplasty.
Systemic: can the patient recover from surgery or radiation and go on with systemic therapy?

rows: Collapse: over 50% 3, under 50% 2, none with over 50% body involved 1

slides.see: Figure 5 shows an L2 colon metastasis with mechanical radiculopathy relieved by laminectomy and T12-L4 fusion.
slides.notes: Mechanical first. The item maxima add to 18 (3+3+2+4+3+3), which matches the stated 18-point scale. The authors say 0 to 6 is generally stable, 13 to 18 reliably predicts the need for stabilization, and 7 to 12 needs further assessment. SINS is the library's X02 paper; that record is abstract-level. Clinical pain is the key history: the authors say all patients with clear cervical, thoracic or lumbar mechanical instability need surgical stabilization, because mechanical pain does not get better with steroids or radiation. C2 details as given: fractures with normal alignment or minimal subluxation often heal in a hard collar worn during radiation and for 6 weeks after, with a 95 percent chance of healing. Fixation is advised for subluxation over 5 mm, or over 3.5 mm with 11 degrees of C1-C2 angulation, with movement-related pain. The printed wording is ambiguous, and that reading is ours. Cement: Fourney reported marked or complete pain relief in 84 percent at a median of 4.5 months, durable at 1 year. An SOSG review gave a strong recommendation for vertebroplasty or kyphoplasty in symptomatic osteolytic tumors. A randomized trial of kyphoplasty against nonsurgical care showed Roland-Morris improvement at 1 month that lasted to 6 months but was no longer significant at 1 year. Systemic: the authors cite median survival of about 4 months after surgery for NSCLC, colon and unknown primary. They avoid rigid survival scores, saying physicians tend to overestimate survival and new drugs keep changing it. Their test: is reasonable systemic therapy available after surgery, and is systemic progression slow enough to allow recovery? If yes, surgery is considered. If surgery is too risky, radiation and medical treatment can often still be given.

slides.title: The decision grid
slides.lead: Table 3 combines the four assessments. Only radioresistant tumors with high-grade ESCC need decompression before radiation.

rows: High grade (with or without myelopathy), radiosensitive
High grade, radioresistant, fit for surgery
High grade, radioresistant, unfit for surgery

points: Table 3 rows are low-grade ESCC (0 or 1) without myelopathy, and high-grade ESCC (2 or 3) with or without myelopathy.
Stabilization can mean cement, percutaneous screws or open instrumentation; for frail patients, it may be limited to cement or percutaneous screws.
Surgery is also advised if the tumor or deficit progresses during radiation, or if the area was already radiated.
slides.see: Figure 6 draws the same logic as arrows and adds previously radiated tumors alongside radioresistant ones.
slides.notes: We rearranged Table 3 into stable and unstable columns to fit a phone; the cells are the paper's. Read it in order. First, ESCC grade and radiosensitivity pick the radiation, and say whether decompression must come first. Then instability adds stabilization to any row. Systemic fitness only changes the plan in the high-grade radioresistant rows, as the table is printed. Two inconsistencies to notice. First, the footnote defines low grade as ESCC 0 or 1, which puts 1c with the radiation-first group. The text says only 0, 1a and 1b go to radiation first and calls 1c undecided. Second, Figure 6 groups previously radiated tumors with radioresistant ones, and the text names prior radiation to overlapping ports as a reason for surgery. Table 3 has no row for prior radiation. Our reading of the unfit row: a high-grade radioresistant tumor in a patient who cannot have surgery gets cEBRT, even though the paper describes poor cEBRT response in such tumors. That is palliation by default, not a claim that cEBRT works well there. The grid does use myelopathy: the low-grade rows are low grade without myelopathy, and the high-grade rows are with or without myelopathy. There is no row for low-grade ESCC with myelopathy or functional radiculopathy, although the neurologic assessment names both. The paper does address neurologic deficit: it cites support for cEBRT in radiosensitive tumors regardless of deficit, and advises surgery if the deficit progresses during radiation. What it does not address, our point, is how fast the deficit was worsening before treatment. Ask the room whether a patient with rapidly worsening weakness from a radiosensitive tumor would really go straight to cEBRT.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: What holds up: a clear, teachable structure that separates four questions often mixed together.
The dose logic for separation surgery is explicit and can be checked.
Instability is treated as independent of ESCC and histology, which matches how radiation works.
Built for change: the authors expect the treatments in each box to change.
What weakens it: a single-center expert view, not a systematic review; there is no search strategy or grading of evidence.
No implementation results, although the abstract says it reports them.
Never tested against another strategy, and it reports no reliability or outcomes for the grid itself.
Key numbers come from uncited series (186 patients; 2.8% fixation failure) or a journal supplement citation that is likely a meeting abstract, our inference (413 patients).
Grade 1c is placed differently in the text and Table 3; prior radiation is in Figure 6 but not Table 3.
Authors are the developers, from the center that uses NOMS; industry ties disclosed.
slides.notes: Be fair about the purpose. A framework paper is meant to organize decisions and give teams a common language, and that is the authors' stated goal. It does that well. The ESCC scale it uses was validated for reliability by the same group (reference 5), and SINS by SOSG (references 35 and 46), but we did not read those papers. Here is the weak point. The paper reads as evidence-based, yet the literature is chosen to support the framework, with no search method. The strongest new claim, that separation surgery plus SRS gives durable control regardless of histology and ESCC grade, rests on case series, partly uncited. The comparison that matters, separation surgery against more aggressive resection, has not been done, as the authors say. Patchell supports surgery before radiation for compression from solid tumors, but with cEBRT. Its relevance to SRS is an inference. Our further point: SRS dosing details (24 Gy single fraction, 2 mm separation, 14 Gy cord Dmax) come from one center's technology and planning in that era. Treat them as that center's working parameters, not universal thresholds. Histology alone is also a crude stand-in for radiosensitivity, and Table 1 shows that the studies disagree for breast and prostate. Systemic assessment is deliberately informal. That is honest, but it means the S step is not reproducible across teams. Finally, conflicts: three authors disclose industry ties relevant to spine implants or radiation equipment. That is disclosed, and we note it as context only.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: “NOMS asks four separate questions: cord compression, tumor radiosensitivity, stability and systemic fitness. Radiation comes first unless a radioresistant tumor is compressing the cord, which calls for separation surgery and then SRS. Instability is its own reason to stabilize. It is a single-center expert framework, not a tested rule.”

rows: Ambulatory after treatment 84% vs 57%, surgery plus RT vs RT
Puts N, O, M and S together into one decision

points: X01 and X02 details come from the library's abstract-level records.
Do not stretch it: NOMS has not been shown to improve outcomes in this paper.
slides.notes: Spoken summary: NOMS is how one experienced team splits the metastatic spine decision. ESCC grade and radiosensitivity decide the radiation and whether decompression goes first. Instability, judged mostly by mechanical pain and summed up by SINS, adds stabilization at any grade. Systemic status decides whether surgery is worth it. Since SRS, surgery is about separation, not resection. Expect these follow-up questions. First: what about ESCC 1c? The paper leaves it open, and its own Table 3 footnote and text disagree. Second: why not decompress every grade 3 lesion? For radiosensitive histologies like myeloma or lymphoma, the authors support cEBRT even with high-grade compression if the spine is stable. Third: does Patchell support separation surgery plus SRS? Only indirectly. Patchell combined surgery with cEBRT, and the SRS-era results here are case series, some uncited. Fourth: how is S judged? Informally, by talking with the oncologist about whether the patient can recover and continue systemic treatment. The authors avoid rigid survival scores. Fifth: what if the area was radiated before? Figure 6 sends previously radiated tumors down the radioresistant path, and the text lists prior overlapping radiation as a reason for surgery. Sixth: is this evidence that NOMS improves care? No. The abstract mentions implementation results, but the paper reports none.

decks.not_reviewed: The PDF is a complete reformatted copy of the open-access PMC article text with all seven tables, not a critique, but its images are omitted: Figure 1 (patient flow diagram) and Figure 2 (AIS improvement chart) were not seen, so the flow numbers here come from the Results text. The Footnotes section is empty in this copy, so funding and competing-interest statements were not reviewed. Also not reviewed: the published comment (PMID 22857647), any supporting information, and the cited systematic reviews (references 20 and 34) and Spine Trauma Study Group survey (reference 21).

slides.title: STASCIS: early vs late decompression
slides.lead: The largest prospective multicenter study of surgical timing in cervical spinal cord injury, in the authors' description.
points: Journal club: spinal cord injury
Fehlings MG, et al. PLoS One 2012;7(2):e32037
Question: after traumatic cervical cord injury, is decompression before 24 hours linked to better neurological recovery than decompression at 24 hours or later?

Bottom line: 19.8% of early patients vs 8.8% of late patients improved at least 2 AIS grades at 6 months (adjusted OR 2.83, 95% CI 1.10 to 7.28). At least 1-grade improvement did not differ significantly. Timing was not randomized.
Source: full article text with tables; Figures 1 and 2 were not available in this copy

rows: Age 16-80, cervical cord injury C2-T1, AIS A-D, cord compression, GCS above 13
Change in AIS grade at 6 months

slides.notes: Set the scene. The authors say the balance of laboratory evidence supports early decompression: in the preclinical review they cite, 11 of 19 animal studies found a time-dependent effect favoring early surgery. Clinical studies had not shown it. One small randomized trial and several prospective studies found no benefit, but they defined early as within 72 hours. A systematic review favored decompression within 24 hours, and the Spine Trauma Study Group adopted the 24-hour cutoff. STASCIS was built to test that cutoff prospectively. Say what kind of study this is before anything else: a cohort. Patients were not assigned to timing. The surgeon's discretion, arrival time and imaging time decided it. Every result here is an association, and the authors say so in their conclusion, where they ask for the findings to be tempered by the cohort design. Source note: this deck was prepared from a full-text copy of the PMC article. The images were omitted from that copy, so the flow diagram (Figure 1) and the improvement chart (Figure 2) were not seen. The tables were complete, and we checked them against the text. Funding and conflict-of-interest statements were not in this copy. This paper pairs with the 2024 timing guideline (X05) in the library.

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: Six North American spine trauma centers, enrolment August 2002 to September 2009.
points: Excluded: cognitive impairment, penetrating neck injury, pregnancy, prior major neurologic disease, life-threatening injuries preventing early decompression, arrival more than 24 hours after injury, surgery more than 7 days after injury
Timing decided by arrival time, time to complete imaging and surgeon discretion; approach and levels also by surgeon
Every decompression included instrumented fusion; closed reduction counted as decompression if MRI showed the cord fully decompressed
Medical care per 2002 AANS guidelines, including mean BP above 85 mm Hg; methylprednisolone at the team's discretion
6-month examination by a research assistant blinded to surgical timing
Analysis: generalized ordinal logistic regression with backward elimination at P above 0.05; no sample size calculation reported
slides.notes: Three design points to say aloud. First, the inclusion criteria selected a fairly clean population: GCS above 13, no life-threatening injuries that prevented early surgery, and arrival within 24 hours. The paper names arrival time, time to complete investigations and surgeon discretion as what decided timing. It does not rule out delay for resuscitation or instability short of life-threatening, and the authors themselves suggest younger patients reached surgery faster because they were easier to resuscitate. The selection makes the comparison cleaner than a registry, but it also means the result does not tell you about polytrauma patients. Second, look at what counted as decompression. For facet dislocations, the time of closed reduction was recorded as the time of decompression if MRI showed full resolution of compression. So some early patients may have been reduced early and fused later. The paper does not say how many. Third, the outcome examiner at 6 months was blinded to timing, which is a real strength for an exam-based endpoint. The anchor for 6 months is stated inconsistently: Methods say 6 months post-operatively, the primary outcome says 6 months follow-up, and Results say patients were followed until 6 months post injury. With late surgery up to 7 days after injury, the gap is small but unexplained. The baseline exam was done within 24 hours on everyone, but the paper does not say who did it or whether that person was blinded. Flow arithmetic checks: 182 minus 4 deaths and 47 lost is 131, and 131 minus 1 death and 39 lost is 91, giving 222. Missing 6-month data: 51 of 182 early (28%) and 40 of 131 late (31%), similar between groups by our count. The authors quote 27% lost, which is 86 of 313. Counting deaths, 91 of 313 (29%) had no 6-month exam. No sample size or power calculation is reported, so we cannot say what effect the study was designed to detect. Note the late group is not very late: mean 48.3 hours, SD 29.3, and surgery after 7 days was excluded.

slides.title: Who was compared
slides.lead: The groups differed at baseline in age, injury severity and steroid use.
points: Early patients were younger and more often AIS A or B; late patients more often AIS C or D
Steroids at admission: 194 of 313 (62.0%), more often in the early group (P=0.04); group counts not reported
Sex, mechanism, comorbidity index and GCS did not differ significantly
slides.notes: This slide is the key to reading the result. The surgeons operated sooner on the more severe injuries: 57.7% of early patients were AIS A or B against 38.2% of late patients (our sums from Table 2). The authors offer two explanations: surgeons being more aggressive with younger, more severe patients, or younger patients being easier to resuscitate. Our recomputation agrees with the printed P values: age t-test P about 0.003, and AIS distribution chi-square P about 0.005. Why the AIS mix matters so much here: the headline endpoint is a gain of at least 2 grades. A patient who starts at AIS D can only move to E, a 1-grade gain, so D patients can never meet that endpoint. A patient at C can meet it only by reaching E. So a group with more D patients is structurally less likely to reach a 2-grade gain, whatever the timing. That is our reading, and the paper does not discuss it. Among the patients analyzed at 6 months, AIS D was 34 of 131 early (26%) and 32 of 91 late (35%). The model adjusted for complete versus incomplete injury, not for the full AIS grade, so it does not remove this imbalance. Table 2 has errors. The overall counts for sports and other mechanisms are both printed as 3 (9.6%), but the group counts sum to 28 and 32. The comorbidity row gives the late group 30 (26.0%), but 30 of 131 is 22.9%, and the overall 74 implies 34. Fall in the early group is printed as 64 (35.1%), but 64 of 182 is 35.2%. Every other Table 2 percentage checks. GCS is given as 14.9 SD 0.4 in all three columns. With GCS above 13 required, scores could only be 14 or 15, and an SD of at least 0.35 then needs a mean of 14.85 to 14.857 in every column, so the SD is borderline implausible (our check). None of these changes a conclusion. They may be errors in this reformatted copy, and the published version should be checked. Steroid use differed, and steroids stayed in the final model, but the paper gives no counts by group.

slides.title: Primary outcome: AIS change at 6 months
slides.lead: More early patients gained 2 grades. The 1-grade result was not significant.
points: Unadjusted absolute difference in 2-grade improvement: 11.0 percentage points (our arithmetic)
Adjusted model kept only complete vs incomplete injury and steroid use; age dropped out
One early patient worsened by 1 grade (B to A); no late patient worsened
All 222 analyzed patients together improved significantly from baseline (P=0.02)
slides.see: Tables 4 and 5 give the full shift tables by baseline grade; they show where the 2-grade gains came from.
slides.notes: Read the endpoint carefully. The stated primary outcome is ordinal change in AIS grade. The paper reports it as two cut points from a generalized ordinal model: at least 1 grade and at least 2 grades. Only the 2-grade cut point was significant. The authors justify the 2-grade definition with the Sygen trial, which used it to define significant recovery. That is reasonable, but the 1-grade result is part of the same primary outcome and should be quoted alongside it. We recomputed the unadjusted results from the counts and they match: OR 2.57 with interval 1.11 to 5.97, and 1.33 with 0.78 to 2.27. Our Fisher exact P for the 2-grade comparison is about 0.04, which is close to the threshold. Both adjusted intervals are symmetric on the log scale, as they should be. The text gives the adjusted 1-grade result as 1.37 (0.80 to 2.57), while Table 6 gives 1.38 (0.74 to 2.57), P=0.31. The table version is internally consistent. Quote it. The adjusted 2-grade interval is wide, from 1.10 to 7.28, so the true effect could be very small. How to read the size: 11 of every 100 patients, unadjusted, or roughly one extra 2-grade improvement per 9 treated early. That is our arithmetic, it is unadjusted, and it is not a causal number. The shift tables add up: Table 3 is the sum of Tables 4 and 5. One text percentage is off: the late group's no-improvement count is given as 46 (50.6%), but 46 of 91 is 50.5%. The others check. The authors also report that 40% of AIS A patients gained at least 1 grade (43% early, 37% late), which they compare favorably with historical rates of 15-25%. They credit careful selection, blood pressure management and the cervical-only cohort.

slides.title: Secondary outcomes and harms
slides.lead: Complications were not higher with early surgery: 24.2% vs 30.5% of patients, P=0.21.
points: Complication analysis included all 313 enrolled patients, because inpatient data were complete
97 major inpatient complications occurred in 84 patients; table percentages are shares of complications, not of patients
No patient in either group needed repeat surgery for inadequate decompression on postoperative imaging
slides.notes: The authors conclude that early decompression can be performed safely. Read that as no signal of excess harm, not as proven safety. The complication comparison is not significant, and our uncorrected chi-square gives the same P of 0.21. The study was not sized for harms. Look at the small numbers that point the other way. Neurologic deterioration was 4 events early against 1 late, construct failure needing surgery 3 against 1, and deaths 4 against 1 overall. All 3 deaths after 30 days were in the early group, from cardio-respiratory causes. These are counts too small to test meaningfully. Our Fisher exact P for deaths is about 0.40. They are worth naming because a safety claim rests on them. The neurologic deterioration counts are events, so we cannot tell if they were 4 patients. Our inference, not the authors': the early group was more severely injured, with more AIS A and B, which might be expected to raise cardiopulmonary risk, yet it had fewer complications. Against that, the early group was younger (45.0 vs 50.7 years), and the authors suggest younger patients have fewer comorbidities. The paper does not adjust the complication analysis for anything. The Table 7 columns add up for each group, 48 and 49. In the total column, wound dehiscence is printed as 1 although each group has 1, and that column sums to 96, not the stated 97. The paper does not report length of stay, ICU time or functional outcomes beyond AIS grade. The secondary outcomes named in the abstract are complications and mortality only.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: Holds up: prospective, multicenter, predefined criteria
Holds up: blinded 6-month neurological examination
Holds up: missing follow-up similar between groups, 28% and 31%
Holds up: unadjusted and adjusted results point the same way
Weakens it: timing chosen by surgeons and logistics, not randomized
Weakens it: early group had more AIS A and B, late group more AIS D, who cannot gain 2 grades
Weakens it: model adjusted only for complete vs incomplete injury
Weakens it: 29% had no 6-month exam
Weakens it: only the 2-grade cut point was significant, with a wide interval
Weakens it: no sample size calculation; harms underpowered
slides.notes: Be fair first. This was a serious prospective study with a blinded outcome examiner, and the authors explain why they did not randomize. In their account, only 23.5% to 51.4% of patients can be operated on within 24 hours, so a trial would enroll an unrepresentative minority, and surgeons would not accept withholding decompression from a deteriorating patient. The authors name two limitations: the baseline imbalance in age and severity, and 27% loss to follow-up, which they compare with 31% in NASCIS I. The rest is our reading. The table is our breakdown from Tables 4 and 5. It shows where the 2-grade difference came from. In AIS B the rates were identical. The gap came from AIS A and AIS C, and the C contrast is 4 of 22 against 0 of 21. These are small cells, so treat this as a description, not a subgroup finding. If we leave out AIS D patients, who could not reach the endpoint, 26 of 97 early (26.8%) and 8 of 59 late (13.6%) gained 2 grades. Our Fisher P is about 0.07. The direction holds, but the result becomes borderline. The adjusted model controlled for complete versus incomplete injury and steroid use, but not for the full grade, so it does not fix the ceiling problem. Residual confounding by surgeon choice also remains. Surgeons who operated faster on more severe injuries may differ in other ways that the data do not capture. Missing data were similar in the two arms, but 91 patients without a 6-month exam is a large share of a result that rests on 34 events. The study was not designed to find the best time window. It tested one cutoff. The authors themselves say further study is needed to define who benefits most. Small text problems are listed in the patch: Table 2 mechanism, fall and comorbidity rows and a borderline GCS SD, a 50.6% that should be 50.5%, the text-table mismatch for the adjusted 1-grade OR, a Table 7 total, a 22-study count that sums to 21, an inconsistent 6-month anchor, and reference list errors including a duplicate.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "In STASCIS, a prospective cohort of cervical cord injuries, 20% of patients decompressed before 24 hours improved 2 or more AIS grades by 6 months, against 9% decompressed later, with no excess in complications. Timing was not randomized, the early group had more severe injuries, and 1-grade improvement did not differ."
points: Do not call it proof that early surgery causes recovery: it is an association in a non-randomized cohort
Do not apply it to polytrauma, head injury (GCS 13 or below) or patients arriving after 24 hours: they were excluded
Do not quote it for an ultra-early window: it tested one 24-hour cutoff

rows: Decompression within 24 hours when medically feasible; no supported universal under-12-hour threshold

slides.notes: The X05 entry comes from the library's abstract-level record, not from a full-text review here. Expect these questions. Does this prove I must operate within 24 hours? No. It shows that patients operated on sooner did better on one cut point of the outcome, in a cohort where surgeons chose the timing and the early group had more severe injuries. The 2024 guideline in the library now recommends decompression within 24 hours when medically feasible. The library record does not say which studies it relied on, so do not claim STASCIS was part of its evidence base. What about AIS D patients? In this design they cannot show a 2-grade gain, so STASCIS says little about them for its headline endpoint. Among D patients, the share reaching E was 12 of 34 early and 12 of 32 late, about the same (our count from Tables 4 and 5). Is early surgery dangerous? No excess of complications was seen, 24.2% against 30.5%, but deaths and neurologic deterioration were few and numerically more frequent early, so the study cannot exclude small harms. What about the patient who arrives at 30 hours? Arrival after 24 hours was an exclusion criterion, so this study does not address them. Does earlier than 24 hours help more? STASCIS did not test that. The early group averaged 14.2 hours. The guideline record says evidence was insufficient for a universal under-12-hour threshold. What about steroids? Methylprednisolone was given at the team's discretion. It was used more in the early group and stayed in the final model, but the paper reports no steroid effect estimate, so do not quote one.

decks.not_reviewed: The systematic review behind this guideline and its evidence tables were not read; the paper says they were presented to the guideline group but does not cite where they are published. The separate methods article in the same focus issue, which the paper cites for protocol, methods and conflicts of interest, was not read. The PDF is a reformatted copy of the PMC full text with images omitted; the text itself refers to no figures or tables. None of the cited primary studies were read.

slides.title: Fehlings 2024: AO Spine/Praxis guideline on timing of decompression after acute SCI
slides.lead: Bottom line: a strong recommendation, on moderate evidence, to offer decompression within 24 hours of injury to adults with acute SCI at any level. No recommendation could be made for ultra-early surgery.
points: Journal club · Trauma: timing of surgery for spinal cord injury
Fehlings MG, Tetreault LA, Hachem L, et al. Global Spine J 2024;14(3 Suppl):174S-186S
Type: GRADE clinical practice guideline, an update of the 2017 guideline
Read from the full text (reformatted PMC copy, images omitted). The underlying systematic review was not read; this paper does not cite where it is published.
slides.notes: This is a guideline, not a trial, so the questions change. Instead of asking whether randomization worked, ask three things: what evidence fed it, how the panel moved from evidence to a recommendation, and whether the wording of the recommendation matches the strength of the evidence. Sponsors were AO Spine and the Praxis Spinal Cord Institute. The guideline development group included neurosurgeons, orthopedic surgeons, neurologists, critical care and emergency doctors, first responders, rehabilitation professionals and people living with SCI. Methodologists from Aggregate Analytics ran the systematic review. The headline change from 2017: the 2017 guideline made a weak recommendation to suggest early surgery be offered as an option; this update makes it strong. The 24-hour cutoff is unchanged. The new question was ultra-early surgery, and the answer is that the evidence cannot support a recommendation either way. Source of this deck: the full guideline text. The study-by-study data and evidence tables come from a systematic review that was presented to the panel; this paper does not cite where they are published, and we did not read them, so we cannot check which studies went into each pooled estimate beyond the citation numbers in this paper. Where those citations disagree with themselves, we say so on the appraisal slide.

slides.title: The questions and how the guideline was built
slides.lead: Two key questions: should we recommend surgery within 24 hours, and should we recommend ultra-early surgery, regardless of severity and level?
points: Population: adults with acute SCI, any level and severity
Early: decompression within 24 hours. Late: after 24 hours
Ultra-early: not fixed; studies used 4, 5, 8 and 12 hour cutoffs, compared with the rest of the first 24 hours

Outcomes ranked critical: at least 2-grade AIS improvement, ASIA motor score, FIM, major complications, mortality, device failure, sepsis, pressure ulcers, neurological deterioration, cardiopulmonary events, tracheostomy
GRADE for certainty; evidence-to-recommendation framework for benefits, harms, cost, equity, acceptability and feasibility
Internal appraisal with AGREE II; external review by clinicians and spine societies

rows: Early vs late or conservative care on neurological change; ultra-early vs other early windows

slides.notes: The outcome choices drive everything, so slow down here. The panel made a 2-grade AIS improvement the main critical outcome and called a 1-grade change important but not critical. Their reasoning: A to B, or B to C with only a flicker of leg movement, may not change function, while in C or D a single grade can. They also judged outcomes at more than 6 to 12 months more relevant than those before 6 months, because patients often keep improving up to, and sometimes after, a year. For the ASIA motor score there is no agreed MCID. The paper reviews distribution-based estimates from one study (total motor score 4.48 overall, 2.22 to 4.16 by AIS grade) and then reports a panel vote: 45 percent said any change matters, 18 percent 2 points, 5 percent 3 points, 23 percent 4 points, 9 percent 5 points. Those sum to 100. The authors say there was a lack of consensus, then summarize this as 91 percent agreeing that 4 points (and sometimes less) is likely meaningful, and they concede it is opinion, not a statistical derivation. Ours: 68 percent chose 3 points or fewer, so 4 is the top of the range, not an agreed threshold. Keep that in mind when you see a pooled gain of 4.50 on the next slide. The systematic review also asked about conservative care, but this paper reports no comparison with nonoperative treatment. Every Part 1 result is early (within 24 hours) versus late (after 24 hours) surgery, and every Part 2 result is ultra-early versus later surgery still within 24 hours. The 2017 guideline is reference 10 and was not read.

slides.title: Recommendation 1: surgery within 24 hours
slides.lead: Wording: we recommend that early surgery be offered as an option for adult patients with acute SCI regardless of level. Quality of evidence moderate; strength strong.
points: Benefit estimates are early (within 24 hours) compared with late (after 24 hours)
Injury severity: complete and incomplete groups both favored early surgery; interaction test not significant
Injury level: the authors say data were insufficient, but point estimates were similar, so they did not split by level
Panel votes: 95% said desirable consequences clearly outweigh undesirable; 100% for a strong recommendation; over 90% approved the final wording
slides.notes: How to read the numbers. RR 2.76 at 6 months means a 2-grade AIS gain was 2.76 times as likely after early surgery. The abstract calls this 2 times more likely, which understates the 6-month figure; the 12-month RR of 1.95 is the one that is about 2. The panel weighted the 12-month results more, so 1.95 is the better number to quote. The paper gives only ratios, not event rates, so we cannot turn these into absolute differences or a number needed to treat. Ours: the CIs are slightly wider above the estimate than below on the log scale, which fits a random-effects or small-sample method; nothing looks implausible. The motor gain is 4.50 points with a CI of 1.70 to 7.29. That point estimate sits just above 4 points, the top of the range the panel voted meaningful (no consensus; 68 percent chose 3 or fewer), and the lower bound sits below it. Ours: the data are compatible with a gain too small to matter. The FIM result comes from one prospective study of central cord syndrome; the P value of .0474 matches the printed CI on our recalculation, and the lower bound of 0.09 is barely above zero. On subgroups, the authors conclude that severity does not modify the effect because the interaction test was not significant. Ours: a nonsignificant interaction test is weak evidence of no difference. The 2 unpooled motor studies are labeled 'at 6 months' and then 'short term (<6 months)'; we use the first. The recommendation still says 'regardless of level' even though the authors say level data were insufficient. One panel member dissented that the recommendation should be stronger. STASCIS (reference 29; library record X04) is one of the studies pooled for the 6-month AIS outcome.

slides.title: Harms, cost and length of stay
slides.lead: No harm outcome differed significantly between early and late surgery, but the authors say most studies were underpowered to show one.
points: Most complication rates tended to be higher with late surgery; neurological deterioration and sepsis tended to be higher with early surgery
Length of stay, 5 studies pooled: early surgery shorter by 3.52 days (2.95 to 4.08); low certainty

Cost: Mac-Thiong 2012 hospitalization costs $20,525 vs $25,036 (under vs 24 hours or more), confounded by baseline differences; one cost-utility study in cervical SCI showed no clearly dominant strategy in Monte Carlo runs
Panel: 55% judged harms of early surgery trivial and 45% small, meaning no added risk, not that the complications are minor
slides.notes: The panel decided harms should not drive the recommendation, because early surgery did not increase major complications or mortality and because the studies were underpowered. Hold both halves of that sentence together: absence of a significant difference in underpowered studies is not proof of safety. The one signal worth pausing on is neurological deterioration in cervical SCI: 4.7 percent early against 0.7 percent late, RR 3.51 with a CI from 0.73 to 17.23. That is very low certainty and not significant, but the direction is against early surgery and the upper bound is large. Sepsis also leaned the same way. Ours on the arithmetic: the single-study RRs match their percentages (24.2 over 30.5 is 0.79; 17.6 over 25.9 is 0.68; tracheostomy 45 over 55 is 0.82). The pooled RRs differ from the crude ratio of the printed percentages, as pooled estimates can. The biggest gap is neurological deterioration: 4.7 over 0.7 is about 6.7 against a pooled 3.51, larger on the log scale than pressure ulcers (0.55 against 0.81). Each pooled RR sits near the center of its own CI. The text also says those 4 studies 'concluded' early patients had fewer ulcers, then says the difference was not significant. Also not tabled: construct failure 1.5% vs 1.4%, screw revision 8.1% vs 8.3%, tracheostomy 45% vs 55%, all non-significant. On cost, Mac-Thiong found lower hospital costs with early surgery, but the authors flag that early patients were younger, more often had a lower AIS and more often thoracolumbar injury. Furlan 2016 gives cost per QALY early vs late of 524,484 vs 544,852 USD in motor complete and 83,009 vs 81,233 USD in motor incomplete injury. Ours: early costs more per QALY in incomplete injury, yet the paper says it saves 536,217 USD/QALY there, and the 58,368,024 USD/QALY saving in complete injury does not follow from a 20,368 difference. Ours: the length of stay CI is narrow for 5 pooled studies (ref 50 is an RCT by its title), which suggests one or two large studies dominate; we cannot check without the review. The authors call 3.5 days a minor saving.

slides.title: Question 2: ultra-early surgery
slides.lead: Statement: a recommendation for ultra-early surgery could not be made, because of small samples, variable definitions of ultra-early and inconsistent results.
points: Four cutoffs, one study each for the AIS outcomes; all certainty very low
One newer study at 12 hours (Hosman 2023) appeared after the review; the authors judge it would not have changed the conclusion, citing baseline ASIA differences between groups, low power and no UEMS
Harms: mortality 0 in both groups at 4 hours; 2/26 vs 1/22 at 8 hours. Neurological deterioration 2 vs 1 of 57 at 12 hours
Feasibility: in one Canadian cohort, mean time to surgery was 49.4 hours and only 34.2% reached the operating room within 12 hours
Panel: 100% voted the balance closely balanced or uncertain; over 80% approved the no-recommendation wording

columns: Ultra-early vs rest of first 24 hours

slides.notes: Read this table as the reason the panel stopped. Two single studies point opposite ways, and the other two show nothing. The 8-hour study (Jug 2015) favored ultra-early surgery with an RR of 4.55, but its CI runs from 1.13 to 18.29, which is what a small sample looks like. The 5-hour study (Mattiassich 2017) found ultra-early patients less likely to gain 2 grades. Every comparison here is ultra-early against later surgery still within 24 hours, not against late surgery. The 8-hour study also reported median motor gains of 38.5 vs 15.0 points; the paper gives no test for that difference. The authors raise a point that matters for any future study: patients operated within a few hours are examined within a few hours, often in spinal shock, so an AIS A at 2 hours is not the same patient as an AIS A at 14 hours. Ours: that bias could make ultra-early groups look better or worse depending on who converts, and it applies partly to the 24-hour comparison too. Feasibility votes were split: 21% no, 21% probably no, 50% uncertain, 7% varies. The Wilson 2016 transfer times are given as means with SDs larger than the means (8.1 plus or minus 25.5 hours to arrival; 49.4 plus or minus 65.0 hours to surgery). Ours: times cannot be negative, so the distribution must be strongly skewed and the mean overstates the typical patient. Ours: no recommendation is not a recommendation against. The authors also note the length of stay result at 8 hours was not significant; see the appraisal slide for a sign error there.

slides.title: Critical appraisal: gaps and errors
slides.lead: The process is careful and transparent about votes. The weak points are what the pooled evidence can bear and several internal inconsistencies.
points: Strengths: GRADE, explicit evidence-to-recommendation votes, people with SCI on the panel, AGREE II, external society review
Wording varies: 'offered as an option' in the formal recommendation, 'the preferred option' in the abstract, 'undergo surgery within 24 hours when medically feasible' in the conclusions

Not stated in this paper: the design mix behind most pooled estimates (given only for mortality: 2 RCTs and 4 observational studies), so how many randomized studies support the moderate-certainty pools cannot be checked
Funding: AO Spine and Praxis; members disclosed conflicts; the conflict details are in the methods article, not this one
Authors' gaps: central cord syndrome, severity and level subgroups, consistent ultra-early cutoffs, MCIDs, cost-effectiveness, what counts as adequate decompression

rows: 38.8 vs 48.8 days printed as MD 10.0 with CI -30.31 to 10.31; the CI centers on -10.0
3 pooled studies cited as refs 14, 16, 31, but ref 31 is also one of the 2 short-term studies; ref 12 is left out
9 studies listed as refs 13, 15, 16, 19-21, 29-31; the 6- and 12-month subsets use ref 32, not 31
Text says 2 RCTs and 4 observational studies; 5 references are cited
RR 2.76 described as 2 times more likely; a 91% vote sum (48 + 43) reported as 90%

slides.notes: None of these errors changes the direction of the main recommendation, but together they mean you cannot trace each pooled number back to its studies from this paper alone. The length of stay error is clear arithmetic: ultra-early minus early is 38.8 minus 48.8, which is minus 10.0, and the printed CI is symmetric around minus 10.0, so the sign of the point estimate is wrong. The citation slips matter more for a reader trying to check the work. In the motor score paragraph, five studies are listed (refs 12, 14, 16, 31, 32), two short-term studies are refs 31 and 32, and the remaining three are then cited as 14, 16 and 31; by subtraction they should be 12, 14 and 16. Ref 12 is the Badhiwala individual patient data analysis, so whether it is in the 4.50-point estimate matters. Ours: the recommendation wording is a real issue. 'Offered as an option' is the language of the 2017 weak recommendation, yet this one is graded strong, and the abstract and conclusions say something firmer. The 'when medically feasible' qualifier appears in the abstract conclusions, not in the formal recommendation. Ours on certainty: the paper reports moderate certainty for the main benefit outcomes but does not say how many pooled studies were randomized; reference titles show at least one RCT (Haghnegahdar 2020, ref 16), which is in both the 12-month AIS pool and the motor score pool. Panel comments call the AIS outcome a '2-point' improvement though AIS is graded A to E. The panel also calls an effect size above 2 large, yet the 12-month RR it weighted most is 1.95. The authors themselves note two high-quality studies published after the review (Badhiwala 2022 on central cord syndrome; the OSCIS trial, 2021) that a future update must include. Ours: OSCIS is a randomized trial in incomplete cervical SCI with stenosis, so check what it found before using this guideline to argue for urgent surgery in central cord patients.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: Spoken summary: the 2024 AO Spine/Praxis guideline makes a strong recommendation, on moderate evidence, to offer decompression within 24 hours of injury to adults with acute SCI at any level. Early patients were about twice as likely to gain 2 AIS grades at a year, RR 1.95, and gained about 4.5 more motor points. Harms did not differ significantly, but the studies were underpowered. Under 24 hours, the evidence on ultra-early surgery is inconsistent, so there is no recommendation for any shorter cutoff.
points: Expect: why strong if the evidence is only moderate? Panel votes on balance, values, cost and feasibility; 95% said benefits clearly outweigh harms
Expect: is 4.5 motor points meaningful? Just above 4 points, the top of the panel's range, with no consensus (68% chose 3 or fewer); the CI lower bound of 1.70 is below it
Expect: does this apply to central cord syndrome? Authors extrapolate and call it a gap; newer studies came after the review

Expect: should we push for under 8 hours? The guideline makes no recommendation either way: four cutoffs, inconsistent results, very low certainty; some dissenters thought the evidence supported ultra-early surgery
Expect: does early surgery cause neurological worsening? Not significant, 4.7% vs 0.7% in cervical injury, very low certainty
slides.notes: Keep the summary tied to the 12-month figure, RR 1.95, rather than the 6-month 2.76, because the panel weighted later outcomes more and 1.95 is the honest 'about twice as likely'. Say 'offer within 24 hours when medically feasible'; the feasibility qualifier comes from the guideline's own conclusions, and the authors note some patients need hemodynamic stabilization first. If asked how this fits with STASCIS (X04): STASCIS is one of the pooled cohorts, and the library record gives its own result as a 2-grade improvement in 19.8% early vs 8.8% late among 222 followed, adjusted OR 2.83. Ours: the guideline adds pooled estimates and a formal grade, but it rests partly on the same kind of nonrandomized timing data. If asked what 'effective decompression' means, the authors list duroplasty, extent of laminectomy, approach and intraoperative ultrasound as open questions, so the guideline sets a clock, not a technique. If someone quotes the abstract's '2 times more likely' for the 6-month RR of 2.76, note that it understates that figure. If someone says ultra-early surgery is proven harmful, point out that no ultra-early result was significant for harm. The 5-hour study's RR of 0.24 means less chance of a 2-grade gain, not harm; mortality (2/26 vs 1/22 at 8 hours, RR 1.69, 0.16 to 17.44) and neurological deterioration (2 vs 1 at 12 hours, RR 1.56, 0.15 to 16.27) leaned against it non-significantly. The authors made no recommendation either way. Finally, the guideline is due for review 3 to 5 years after publication, so check whether a newer version exists before quoting it as current.

decks.not_reviewed: The linked commentary by Paul A. Anderson (online only, not in this PDF), the original 2003 report of this trial (reference 16), and the online conflict-of-interest disclosures. The full 7-page paper was read, including Tables I to IV and the Figure 1 CONSORT diagram.

slides.title: Wood 2015: burst fracture at 18 years
slides.lead: Operative versus nonoperative care of a stable thoracolumbar burst fracture without neurological deficit, followed 16 to 22 years.
points: Journal club: thoracolumbar trauma
Wood KB, et al. J Bone Joint Surg Am 2015;97:3-9
Long-term follow-up of the randomized trial first reported in 2003

Bottom line: at a mean 18.6 years, the 18 nonoperative patients reported less pain and disability than the 19 operative patients (median ODI 2 vs 20). Kyphosis was 19 vs 13 degrees and was not linked to symptoms.
slides.notes: This is the long-term report of the Minnesota trial that randomized 47 neurologically intact patients with a stable thoracolumbar burst fracture to fusion or a cast or brace between 1992 and 1998. The 2003 report, at an average of 44 months, found no significant differences in return to work, pain or disability; this paper says the main early differences were hospital cost and more complications with surgery. Here the authors brought back 37 of the 47 at 16 to 22 years. Frame the question for the room: if surgery and bracing look similar at 4 years, does the picture change after two decades of adjacent-segment wear, hardware and aging? The authors' answer is yes, in favor of nonoperative care. Our job is to decide how much 37 patients, no power calculation and no blinding can carry. What was reviewed: the full paper, all four tables and the CONSORT figure. Not reviewed: the linked commentary by Paul Anderson, which is online only, and the original 2003 paper. Every reported number in this deck comes from the 2015 paper. Our own calculations (Fisher and Pearson P values, the 257-month maximum and the multiplicity check) are labeled as ours where they appear.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: Does surgery for a neurologically intact stable burst fracture help or hurt over 20 years?
points: Patients: isolated T10-L2 burst fracture with retropulsion on CT, no new neurological deficit, age 18-66, within 3 weeks of injury
Intervention: short-segment posterior (2-4 level) pedicle screw-hook fusion, or anterior 2-level strut fusion
Comparison: cast for 8 weeks then orthosis for 4, or orthosis alone for 12 weeks
Outcome: pain VAS, Oswestry, Roland-Morris, SF-36, work, medication and radiographs. No primary outcome is named.
Authors' hypothesis: nonoperative patients would function at least as well as operative patients
slides.notes: Set the stakes. The authors frame surgery as offering immediate stability, deformity correction, earlier walking and less reliance on a brace, and nonoperative care as avoiding surgical risk. They cite opposing literature: Denis 1984, a retrospective series in which 25 percent of nonoperative patients could not return to full-time work and 17 percent developed neurological problems, and Siebenga's randomized trial of 34 patients, which found better functional scores with surgery at 4 years; a later Siebenga article concluded surgery was also more cost-effective. Those figures are as reported in this paper. The authors argue that follow-up length explains some of the disagreement, since many comparative studies had only 5 to 6 years of follow-up at most, and some as little as 1 year. Notice what stable means here. The eligibility list defines a burst fracture with retropulsion and no deficit, but this paper does not say how stability or the posterior ligaments were judged. No MRI is mentioned. That definition may be in the 2003 paper, which we did not review. Also note the hypothesis is one of noninferiority in plain words (at least as well), yet there is no margin and no power calculation, so the trial cannot formally test it. The conclusion goes further than the hypothesis: the authors now call nonoperative care optimal.

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: 53 assessed, 47 randomized, 37 analyzed at a mean 223 months.
points: Computer-generated randomization; surgeons got assignments from administrative assistants
The paper states the study was unblinded after assignment
All 47 received the allocated treatment; no crossovers in the CONSORT diagram
Lost: operative 1 died, 4 not contacted; nonoperative 2 died, 3 not contacted
Tests listed: paired t test, Wilcoxon signed-rank, Shapiro-Wilk normality and Mann-Whitney; the paper does not say which was used for which comparison. No power analysis.
slides.notes: Read the CONSORT diagram: 53 assessed, 2 declined and 4 excluded for other reasons, leaving 47 randomized. The abstract calls them consecutive. Flow arithmetic checks: 24 minus 5 is 19, 23 minus 5 is 18, and 19 of 24 and 18 of 23 match the 79 and 78 percent in the text. Allocation looks reasonably concealed: computer-generated sequence, held by administrative assistants. After assignment, the paper says it became an unblinded study. Outcomes are patient-reported, so patients knew what they had. The paper does not say whether radiograph readers were blinded. Table I describes only the 37 patients with follow-up data (3 of the 10 missing had died, 7 could not be located), not the randomized 47, so it cannot show the randomized groups were balanced. Our check: men 13 of 19 versus 15 of 18 gives Fisher P about 0.45; cause of injury differs: motor vehicle accidents 11 of 19 vs 6 of 18 (our Fisher P about 0.19, against all other causes) and falls 4 of 19 vs 9 of 18 (our Fisher P about 0.09); motor vehicle accident vs fall alone gives about 0.14. Fracture level is balanced (T12/L1/L2 4/12/3 vs 5/10/3, our chi-square P about 0.88). Small groups, so imbalance is easy to miss and hard to detect. The authors state that those lost and those retained did not differ at baseline or at 4 years, but show no data. One more thing: the text gives injury causes as 43, 34, 13 and 9 percent. Those do not match Table I's 37 patients (about 46, 35, 5 and 11 percent). They do fit 20, 16, 6 and 4 of the original 47, so the text probably describes the original cohort without saying so. That is our inference. Ages are at follow-up; subtract about 18.6 years for age at injury.

slides.title: Main outcomes at 18.6 years
slides.lead: All three patient-reported scores favored nonoperative care.
points: Medians with ranges; no confidence intervals or effect sizes
Per the paper, ODI 0-20 is minimal disability and 21-40 moderate
Kyphosis: 13 degrees operative vs 19 nonoperative; called not significant, but no test or P value is shown
slides.notes: No primary outcome is named, so treat these three as the main ones; they are the ones in the abstract. How to read them: these are medians with ranges. The paper lists Mann-Whitney among its tests but does not say which test produced these P values; Mann-Whitney is the likely one (our inference). There are no confidence intervals, so you cannot see how precise the difference is. The ranges overlap heavily (operative ODI 0 to 48, nonoperative 0 to 22). Put the operative median in context: using the scale the paper quotes, ODI 20 is still the top of minimal disability. So the operative group is not doing badly; the nonoperative group is doing very well. All three, VAS (0.003), ODI (<0.001) and Roland-Morris (0.001), would survive a strict Bonferroni correction for the 11 outcomes tested (3 scores plus 8 SF-36 domains, threshold 0.0045), as would SF-36 pain, general health and social function; that is our check, as the paper made no correction. Direction is clear and consistent. Kyphosis: operative patients went from 10 degrees on admission to 5 at discharge, 13 at 4 years and 13 at long-term follow-up. Nonoperative patients went from 11.3 to 9, then 14, then 19. The abstract says the 13 versus 19 difference was not significant, but no test or P value appears anywhere, so take that on trust. The authors found no correlation between final kyphosis and pain or disability. Be careful here: in the operative group, kyphosis and ODI gave r 0.45, P 0.1. That is a moderate correlation in a small sample, not proof of none. The paper gives neither the test nor the number of patients in the correlation. Our Pearson check: P about 0.05 if all 19 were included, but about 0.09 to 0.11 with 14 or 15, so the reported P fits a smaller radiographic sample. The Roland-Morris figure (r 0.05, P 0.6) does not fit at any plausible sample size; our Pearson P is about 0.84 at 19 and higher with fewer.

slides.title: Secondary outcomes and harms
points: SF-36: 6 of 8 domains significantly favored nonoperative care; role-emotional and mental health did not
Subjacent-segment degeneration: 64% operative vs 70% nonoperative
No new neurological deficits related to the fracture in either group
All patients kept C7 plumb line within 5 cm of the posterior corner of S1
slides.notes: SF-36 domain medians, operative vs nonoperative: physical function 70 vs 89.5, role-physical 75 vs 100, energy 56 vs 75, social 75 vs 100, pain 50 vs 87, general health 70 vs 95, all significant. Role-emotional (100 vs 100) and mental health were not. Watch the wording: the abstract says seven of eight scores favored nonoperative care. That matches Table IV (seven higher medians, role-emotional tied), but it means direction, not significance; six of eight were significant. The Discussion's all strongly favoring refers to the instruments together, not every domain. Work: 9 of 19 operative and 13 of 18 nonoperative were still working; 6 and 3 had retired, 4 and 2 had lost jobs. No test is reported; our Fisher test gives P about 0.18. Median age is 62, so retirement is a big part of this. Narcotics: 3 operative patients took them regularly, none of the nonoperative patients did (our Fisher P about 0.23). The authors present both as favoring nonoperative care; in numbers this small they are not significant. Degeneration: the authors expected more adjacent-segment change after fusion and did not find it at the next segment (64 vs 70 percent). They suggest anterior bony bridging after nonoperative healing stiffens the segment too. Lower down, L3 to S1, degeneration was 75 vs 55 percent, P 0.02. We could not reproduce that P: with 19 and 18 patients, 64, 75 and 70 percent are not possible whole-number results, and neither is 55 (10 of 18 is 56), and our Fisher test on the nearest counts gives P 0.17 to 0.31. The radiograph denominators are not reported. Harms missing: the paper does not report reoperations, hardware removal or later spine surgery, though it says this was collected.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: Consistent direction, but a small retained cohort, no blinding and no power calculation.
points: In Table II the gap between groups is already present at 4 years
Follow-up range does not fit the stated dates
Level I label despite 21% loss, no power calculation and an unblinded design
Surgery reflects 1990s technique: pedicle screw-hook constructs and fibula or rib strut grafts
slides.see: Table II shows the 4-year and 20-year medians side by side for each group.
slides.notes: The key teaching point is Table II. The story in the abstract is that groups looked similar at 4 years and diverged later. But in Table II the 4-year medians already favor nonoperative care (ODI 20 vs 4, Roland-Morris 6 vs 2, VAS 3 vs 1.5). Within each group, scores barely moved over 16 years; only nonoperative Roland-Morris improved significantly. So the long-term gap mostly reflects a difference already present at 4 years in these 37, not a late divergence. That is our reading. Possible reasons: the 2003 analysis had more patients and wider spread, or the 37 who returned are not typical of the 47. Paired tests imply Table II uses only the 37, but the paper does not say. The operative ODI is identical at both times, 20 (0-48), median and range; that may be real or a copying error. Dates: enrollment 1992 to 1998 and follow-up January 2012 to June 2013 allow at most about 257 months, yet the maximum reported is 268 months. The minimum, 204 months, is 17 years, not the 16 in the title. Fragility: 37 patients, medians only, no confidence intervals, no correction for many outcomes, no adjustment for the injury-cause imbalance, and the authors themselves say hundreds of patients would be needed. Unblinded patient-reported outcomes can drift toward expectation. What holds up: randomization, no crossovers, similar loss in both arms, and every patient-reported score pointing the same way. Not every outcome did: final kyphosis was numerically better with surgery (13 vs 19 degrees), subjacent-segment degeneration was 64 vs 70 percent, and SF-36 role-emotional was tied. At minimum, surgery did not show long-term benefit.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: In 47 neurologically intact patients with a stable thoracolumbar burst fracture randomized to fusion or a cast or brace, 37 were seen at a mean 18.6 years. The nonoperative group reported less pain and disability, median ODI 2 vs 20, with kyphosis 19 vs 13 degrees that did not track with symptoms. The gap was already visible at 4 years in these patients, and the trial is small and unblinded, so read it as no long-term benefit from surgery rather than proof of harm.
points: Expect: does this apply to a PLC injury? Is ODI 20 a bad outcome? Was the difference there at 4 years? Would modern percutaneous fixation change it?
Library link: the TLICS record (X09) adds posterior ligamentous complex integrity to morphology and neurology; this paper does not report PLC assessment
slides.notes: Expect four follow-up questions. Does this apply to a posterior ligament injury? This paper does not say how stability was judged and mentions no MRI, so you cannot use it for a tension-band injury. The TLICS record in our library integrates posterior ligamentous complex integrity with morphology and neurological status; this trial does not report that domain. Is ODI 20 a bad outcome? By the scale the paper quotes, 20 is minimal disability. The operative group did reasonably well; the nonoperative group did better. Was the difference there all along? In the retained 37, yes, on Table II medians the gap existed at 4 years, while, per this paper, the 2003 report found no significant difference at 44 months. This paper does not say how many patients that analysis included. So do not say surgery causes late deterioration; that is not what the within-group data show. Would modern surgery change this? Unknown. These were open fusions with autograft, posterior screw-hook or anterior strut constructs. The trial says nothing about percutaneous fixation without fusion. Two numbers to have ready: 37 of 47 analyzed, and median ODI 2 vs 20. Also be ready to say what is missing: no reoperation data, no confidence intervals, no power calculation. The authors conclude nonoperative care is optimal; a fair summary is that bracing is at least as good, and surgery bought no long-term advantage in function or pain.

decks.not_reviewed: None of the paper itself; the full 7-page article was read, and the flow diagram (an image) was read from the rendered page. The PDF cites no supplement. Cited works were not reviewed, including Heusner's original classification (ref 3) and the methods sources (refs 25 and 26).

slides.title: Kim 2014: Predictors of failed nonoperative care of spinal epidural abscess
slides.lead: Bottom line: among patients started on antibiotics alone, a cord-level deficit was the strongest predictor of failure. Age over 65, diabetes and MRSA each added risk.
points: Journal club · Spinal epidural abscess
Kim SD, et al. Spine J 2014;14:1673-9
Retrospective, two academic centers, 1993–2011. 355 patients; 127 in the failure analysis
54 of 127 failed (our arithmetic: 43%). 12 of the 54 failures were deaths from sepsis
slides.notes: What this deck covers: the full paper, 7 pages, read end to end. The flow diagram is an image, and we read it from the rendered page. It is a complete article, not a critique or abstract. The question is narrow. It does not ask whether surgery beats antibiotics. It asks which patients, once a surgeon has chosen to try antibiotics, go on to fail. Frame it for the room early: the denominator is 127 patients started on antibiotics with at least 2 months of follow-up, not all 355. Say the failure rate aloud, because the paper never puts it as one number. 54 of 127 is 43 percent, our arithmetic. Then say what failure means here. 42 were operated after failed medical care, and 12 died of overwhelming sepsis despite IV antibiotics. So nearly one in four failures was a death. That is the stake when a surgeon defers decompression. The authors present a probability table built from four predictors and say it gives concrete numbers to discuss with patients. Treat that table as a model output from one retrospective sample, never validated in other patients. The paper reports no validation. Study funding is not stated. Two authors disclose industry relationships, and one serves on the NASS board. The editors' box flags potential biases in the method and says the authors' limitations should be noted.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: Surgery has been the default for SEA. Some selected patients do well on antibiotics. Who fails?
points: Background, per the authors: incidence once under 2 per 10,000 admissions, now reported above 10
Mortality reported at 12% to 34% in earlier series; 34% presented with paralysis in one meta-analysis
Accepted reasons for surgery: evolving deficit, instability, infection persisting despite antibiotics
The gap, per the authors: no study had identified the variables that predict failure of medical care

rows: Adults with SEA on MRI or CT myelogram, started on antibiotics alone
Age, comorbidity, neurologic phase, labs, organism, abscess level and extent
Failure: worse pain or deficit, imaging progression, ongoing sepsis or death after over 1 week of antibiotics

slides.notes: Set the stakes. The authors cite a rising incidence and earlier mortality of 12 to 34 percent. They frame surgery as needed for evolving neurologic deterioration, instability or persistent infection, and say that outside those settings the need for surgery has been challenged. They cite older relative indications for medical care: Leys proposed multilevel abscess, intact neurology, or complete cord injury for over 72 hours; Darouiche added refusal and narrowed the paralysis window to 24 to 36 hours. Those come from the authors' review, not from papers we read. Now the definitions, because the result depends on them. Success was eradication of infection without progression of the neurologic exam. Failure was increasing back pain or deficit, abscess progression on serial imaging, ongoing sepsis, or death despite more than 1 week of IV antibiotics. The 1-week window was borrowed from endocarditis surgery timing. Notice two things. First, increasing back pain alone counts as failure, which is soft and was judged by the treating team. Second, 42 of the 54 failures are defined by a surgeon's decision to operate. So the outcome is partly a clinical choice, not only a biological event. That is our reading. Neurologic status used a modified Heusner scale: phase I pain, phase II radicular weakness, phase III incomplete cord injury including conus, cauda equina and myelopathy, phase IV complete cord injury.

slides.title: Patients and methods
slides.lead: Selection happened twice: the surgeon chose who got antibiotics, then follow-up decided who was analyzed.
points: Two tertiary academic centers, 1993–2011; chart and imaging-report review by three authors
Excluded: phlegmon without abscess, SEA at a prior laminectomy level, complete cord injury over 48 hours
Initial treatment chosen by the consulted spine surgeon, with the patient's wishes
Generally IV antibiotics for at least 6 to 8 weeks, then possibly oral, guided by infectious disease
Most imaging findings taken from radiologist reports; most images before 2007 were not accessible
Logistic regression with five candidates from univariate P under .10; 80% power claimed for 20% differences
slides.notes: Walk the flow diagram; it adds up. 355 = 142 + 213. 142 - 42 = 100 nonoperative. 100 - 13 - 2 = 85, and 85 = 73 successes + 12 sepsis deaths. 42 + 12 = 54 failures. On the surgical side, 213 + 42 = 255, of whom 39 had under 2 months of follow-up. The authors say all 127 had at least 2 months. The paper does not say how the follow-up rule was applied to the 42 who crossed to surgery. The authors call it a case-control study. Our reading: it behaves like a retrospective cohort of everyone started on antibiotics, which is why absolute failure probabilities can be estimated at all. In a true case-control sample they could not. Now selection. The surgeon picked the 142. Table 1 shows who ended up nonoperative: 73 percent had pain only and none had complete cord injury, against 9.6 percent complete in the operative group. Patients with cord-level abscess, over 5 levels, staphylococcus and diabetes were more often operated. Immunosuppression and malignancy were more common in the nonoperative group. So these predictors describe failure in a group already filtered by surgical judgment. Measurement: three authors abstracted charts, and the paper does not say they were blinded to outcome. Imaging relied on radiologist reports. A delay-in-diagnosis variable is defined in Methods but never reported. The 80 percent power claim is fragile. Our calculation for 54 against 73 gives about 80 percent only when proportions are near 10 against 30 percent. For 30 against 50 percent it is closer to 60 percent. About 15 percent of the whole cohort was lost before 2 months, which the authors tie to transfers.

slides.title: Who failed
slides.lead: A cord-level deficit dominated. Age, diabetes and MRSA each roughly doubled to quadrupled the odds.
points: Our arithmetic: 20 of the 22 patients with a cord deficit failed (91%)
Radicular weakness alone: 6 failed, 12 succeeded
Circumferential abscess 16% vs 2.5% on univariate testing, not entered in the model
slides.see: Table 2 gives every univariate comparison, including labs and abscess position.
slides.notes: Read the left columns before the odds ratios. Only 22 analyzed patients had a cord-level deficit, and 20 failed. The odds ratio of 15.2 rests on 2 successes, which is why its interval runs from 3.2 to 71.9. Our check: the crude odds ratio from those counts is about 21. The point is robust in direction and fragile in size. Root-level weakness is different. 6 of 18 with radicular weakness failed, which is the authors' central teaching point: a deficit at the cord is worse than one at the root. Failure patients were about 8 years older on average, 68.4 against 60.1, and our t test reproduces P of about .001. Diabetes, MRSA and age over 65 reproduce on our two-proportion tests. Labs did little. WBC and CRP did not differ. ESR was borderline at P=.05, and the authors say many patients lacked an early ESR and many arrived already on antibiotics. Abscess level above the conus was significant alone but not after adjustment, which the authors attribute to small asymptomatic cord-level abscesses. Now the model building. The rule was univariate P under .10. Hemodialysis (.07), circumferential abscess (.01), ventral (.06), dorsal (.08) and ESR (.05) all met it, yet only five candidates entered. The authors cite convergence with five variables; they do not say how the five were chosen. Ventral and dorsal did meet the rule: our tests reproduce the printed .06 and .08 from the counts, which makes the departure from the stated rule clearer, not weaker. A footnote to Table 3 calls the neurologic variable incomplete or complete deterioration. If that meant worsening during treatment, it would overlap the outcome. The Discussion says present with, so we read it as status at presentation, but the wording is unclear.

slides.title: The probability table
slides.lead: The authors turn the four predictors into a predicted failure risk for each of 16 combinations.

rows: Age, diabetes and MRSA, no deficit

points: Our check: these values follow from the Table 3 odds ratios applied to a 17% baseline
The paper gives no count of patients in each combination
No discrimination, calibration or validation is reported
slides.see: Table 4 lists all 16 combinations with intervals.
slides.notes: This is the table people quote, so teach how it was made. The authors say each combination was determined by maximum likelihood estimation. Our check: if you take the 17 percent no-risk-factor probability and multiply the odds by 2.5 for age, 2.5 for diabetes, 3.8 for MRSA and 15.2 for a cord deficit, you reproduce almost every row within a point. All four gives about 98.7, printed 99. So the table is a main-effects logistic model, not observed failure rates in each group. Some combinations may contain very few patients or none; the paper does not say. The intervals tell you that. Age, diabetes and MRSA without a deficit is 83 percent, but the interval runs from 46 to 97. Now the two ends. With no risk factors, predicted failure is still 17 percent, 10 to 28. The authors themselves say that 17 percent risk exists even without the four factors. Single non-neurologic factors give 33 to 44 percent. That is the honest reading for an older diabetic patient without a deficit: the model predicts roughly a coin flip, 56 percent for age plus diabetes. Contrast that with the abstract's conclusion, which says medical management has a very high risk of failure if the patient is older than 65 with diabetes, MRSA or neurologic compromise. Our reading: the table supports very high risk for a cord deficit or for three or more factors, not for any single factor other than deficit. Also remember what the model is not. It predicts failure only in patients a surgeon already judged suitable for antibiotics. It was fitted on the same 127 patients with 54 events, and the paper reports no test of its performance: no discrimination, calibration, or internal or external validation. So treat the percentages as a starting point for the conversation, as the authors intend, not as a calibrated risk score.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
slides.lead: Useful direction, calibration not reported, and several internal inconsistencies.
points: Holds up: large two-center series, flow diagram that adds up, explicit failure definition
Holds up: cord-deficit effect is large and reproduces from the counts
Weakens it: treatment chosen by surgeons, so predictors apply to a preselected group
Weakens it: failure partly defined by the decision to operate; soft criteria such as back pain
Weakens it: 19-year span, imaging from radiologist reports, about 15% lost before 2 months
Weakens it: candidate selection departs from the stated P under .10 rule; no validation
Not reported: time to failure, neurologic outcome of the failures, outcomes of the 42 operated
slides.notes: Credit the authors' own limitations first. They name the retrospective design, say ethics bar randomizing, admit there were no specific deciding factors for initial treatment, note that imaging came from radiologist reports because older images were not accessible, and link the near 15 percent lost to follow-up to transfers. The rest is our reading. Confounding by indication is the core problem. The surgeon chose antibiotics for the least sick, so every estimate is conditional on that choice. The outcome is also partly a decision. A patient with a deficit who worsens slightly is more likely to be taken to surgery, so a predictor and the trigger for failure can overlap. Nothing is said about when failures happened, whether operated failures recovered neurologically, or how they compared with immediate surgery. So the paper cannot tell you what delay costs. The internal checks matter for trust. In Table 2, the success-group percentages for over 5 levels, skip lesions, dorsal, ventral and circumferential fit a denominator of 79, larger than the 73 patients; the failure group fits 50. The printed P values do reproduce from the counts over 54 and 73, so the percentages are what is off. Table 1: in-hospital deaths are 30 overall but 12 + 19 = 31, and 90-day deaths are 41 overall but 14 + 26 = 40. The operative mortality percentages use 216, not 255, yet the printed P values (.17, .31) reproduce only with 255; neither is significant either way. Staphylococcus subtypes add to 208 against 204 in the operative column and 269 against 265 overall. 'Other' organisms, 7 of 100 against 6 of 255, gives P about .036 on our test, printed .02. In Table 3 the MRSA interval, 1.1 to 15.1 around 3.8, is lopsided on the log scale where the others are symmetric, so one number may be misprinted; it does not change the conclusion. The footnote expands CNS as central nervous system for what is presumably coagulase-negative staphylococcus. Results give a follow-up range starting at 2 months although 52 patients had less. Table 1 compares groups by final treatment: the 42 crossovers are counted in the operative 255, so the mortality comparison is by treatment received, not initial intent. None of these errors overturns the main finding, but they lower confidence in the fine print.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "In patients a surgeon has chosen to try on antibiotics, 20 of 22 with a cord-level deficit failed. Age over 65, diabetes and MRSA each added risk. Even with none of these, predicted failure was 17%."

rows: 54 of 127 failed antibiotics; cord deficit OR 15.2
6 weeks of antibiotics noninferior to 12; cure 90.9% both

points: Bernard comes from the library record (X08). It studied vertebral osteomyelitis and antibiotic duration, not surgery for SEA.
Do not stretch it: the model was not validated and applies only to patients selected for antibiotics.
slides.notes: Spoken summary: in a two-center retrospective series, 142 of 355 adults with spinal epidural abscess were started on antibiotics alone. Of the 127 with follow-up, 54 failed: 42 went to surgery and 12 died of sepsis. A cord-level deficit was the dominant predictor, with an adjusted odds ratio of 15.2, and 20 of 22 such patients failed. Age over 65, diabetes and MRSA had odds ratios of 2.5 to 3.8. The authors' model gives 17 percent failure with none of the four and 99 percent with all four. Expect these questions. Does this mean a neurologically intact young patient can safely have antibiotics? The authors say nonoperative care may be considered with close monitoring by a spine surgeon. But predicted failure is still 17 percent, up to 28 percent, and 12 of the 54 failures were sepsis deaths. What about isolated radicular weakness? The authors separate root from cord deficits and say only a study comparing surgery and medical care in isolated radicular weakness would show equipoise. In their data 6 of 18 such patients failed. Can I use Table 4 as a risk calculator? Only loosely. It is a model fitted on the same 127 patients, with no reported test of its performance, with no reported validation and wide intervals. Does Bernard tell us how long to treat SEA? Not directly. The library record for Bernard is a trial of 6 against 12 weeks of antibiotics in pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis, and its own caveat says it is not a trial of decompression indications. Here, patients were generally given IV antibiotics for at least 6 to 8 weeks; duration per patient is not reported.

decks.not_reviewed: The online appendix (study group list, protocol, timing of randomisation, reasons for protocol violations, causes of probable failure, subgroup results, multivariable model, time courses of fever, pain, CRP and creatinine, EQ-5D by group, antibiotics by organism) and the linked Comment (Lancet page 836) and later letters. The main article PDF was read in full and is complete.

slides.title: Bernard 2015
slides.lead: Six versus twelve weeks of antibiotics for pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis.
points: Journal club: spinal infection
Bernard L, et al. Lancet 2015;385:875-82 (DTS trial)

Bottom line: in 351 adults with culture-proven pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis, 6 weeks of antibiotics cured as many patients at 1 year as 12 weeks, 90.9% in each arm (160/176 and 159/175), well inside a 10-point noninferiority margin.
slides.notes: This is the French Duration of Treatment for Spondylodiscitis trial: 71 infectious diseases, rheumatology and internal medicine centres, enrolment November 2006 to March 2011, funded by the French Ministry of Health, no competing interests declared. It is a medical trial. It tests how long to give antibiotics, not whether or when to operate. Hold that frame for the whole deck. This deck was prepared from the full text of the main article, which is complete. The online appendix was not available, and much of the detail the authors point to lives there: subgroup results, causes of failure, reasons for protocol violations and the multivariable model. Where a slide depends on the appendix, it says so. The linked Comment and later letters were not read.
