One point to set up early: the 1-year clock starts at the end of antibiotics, not at randomisation. So both groups had 12 months off treatment before the cure assessment, which is the right design for a relapse question.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: Guidelines gave 6 to 12 weeks, and some experts 3 months, without trial evidence. Is 6 weeks enough?
points: Patients: adults with microbiologically confirmed pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis and typical MRI or CT findings
Intervention: 6 weeks of effective antibiotics, intravenous and oral periods combined
Comparison: 12 weeks
Outcome: cure 1 year after the end of treatment, judged by a masked committee
Design: open-label noninferiority trial, absolute margin 10 percentage points
slides.notes: The authors' case: incidence of 4 to 10 per 100 000 a year in high-income countries and rising, and longer antibiotic exposure brings more adverse events, health-care infections, cost and resistance. Most guidelines regard about 6 to 12 weeks as standard, others say at least 3 months, and the authors call this not evidence based. Note what noninferiority means here. The question is not whether 12 weeks is better. It is whether 6 weeks loses no more than 10 percentage points of cure. A 10-point loss of cure is a lot for a disease with this mortality, and the authors concede the margin is arbitrary and debatable. Their defence: 10% is commonly used for antibiotic trials, and the observed lower bound, minus 6.2, would have passed a much smaller margin. Keep that in mind when you appraise. The surgeon's question, which patients need decompression or stabilisation, is not asked here.

slides.title: Patients and methods
points: Confirmation: same organism in at least 2 blood cultures or biopsy samples, 3 for skin organisms
Excluded: vertebral implant, recurrence, fungal, brucellar or mycobacterial infection, no organism, life expectancy under 1 year
Randomised within the first 3 weeks of antibiotics; permuted blocks by centre, central voice server
Drugs at the physician's choice under French guidelines; oral fluoroquinolone plus rifampicin favoured
Patients and treating staff not masked; adjudication committee masked
Planned 200 per group; 359 randomised
slides.see: The Figure, trial profile, lists why each of the 8 post-randomisation exclusions occurred.
slides.notes: This is a sick, mostly bacteraemic group: mean age 61, 68% positive blood cultures, S aureus in 41% (only 8 MRSA), CRP above 10 in 91%, lumbar involvement in 70%, Duke definite endocarditis in 51 of 257 with data. 57 (16%) had neurological signs, of whom 17 had major motor deficit. 34 had post-surgical infection without an implant. Groups were similar except diabetes, 20% versus 10%, more in the 6-week arm. The flow arithmetic adds up: 182 minus 6 is 176, 177 minus 2 is 175, and 30 plus 38 gives the 68 violations. One label is off: the Figure prints 176 as 98% of 182, which is 97%. The 8 exclusions include a diagnostic error and a death, so the analysis is a modified intention to treat. Antibiotics were pragmatic. Median intravenous time was 14 days overall, 52% had under 14 days intravenously, and 72% received oral fluoroquinolones, rifampicin or both. Intravenous duration was not standardised, which the authors list as a limitation. Sample size: 85% cure assumed, one-sided alpha 0.025, 80% power, 20% dropout, 200 per group. Our arithmetic, not the paper's: those inputs give about 200 per group before dropout and about 250 after, so the stated figure does not account for the dropout it names. The trial also stopped at 359 of a planned 400, and the paper does not say why. Our reading: the higher than expected cure rate, 91%, narrowed the interval and made up for the shortfall.

slides.title: Primary outcome
slides.lead: Cure at 1 year after treatment; difference is 6 weeks minus 12 weeks, in percentage points.
points: Noninferior if the lower 95% bound stays above -10
169 met cure criteria outright; the masked committee reviewed the other 182
32 probable failures, 16 in each group
slides.notes: Read the lower bounds, not the point estimates. Every analysis keeps the lower bound above -10, so every one passes. The lowest bound is -8.6, when the 8 post-randomisation exclusions are counted as failures, then -8.3 for cure without further antibiotics and -8.2 per protocol. Per protocol matters most in noninferiority, because intention to treat can blur differences toward zero, and its point estimate, -2.5, favours 12 weeks more than any other analysis. It still passes, with less room. We recomputed the intervals. Newcombe intervals on the printed counts reproduce -6.2 to 6.3, -4.2 to 10.0, -8.5 to 4.7 and -8.1 to 2.9, so the published exact intervals are plausible. 159/175 is 90.86%, which rounds to 90.9% as the abstract and Table 2 print it; Results misprints it as 90.8%. Know how cure was defined. Cure meant no fever, no pain and CRP 10 or less at 12 months off treatment. Only 169 met that outright. The committee judged the other 182, including the 62 who died, were lost or withdrew, and classed 150 of them as cured. So a patient lost to follow-up, or with residual pain, could be counted as cured. At 1 year, 30% still had back pain in each arm, so cure here is not pain-free. Deaths: only 13 of 26 were classed as failures. Our arithmetic from Table 2: 4 deaths in the 6-week group and 9 in the 12-week group were counted as cures, which is why 'cured and alive' moves in favour of 6 weeks. The 'no further antibiotics' row is about 80% in both arms. This is the prespecified sensitivity analysis that counts any extension of treatment beyond 6 days as a failure; the authors explain that a cure after an extension might be due to the extra antibiotics. The Figure gives 22 extensions of at least 1 week in each arm. Our arithmetic: 18 cured patients in each arm had their treatment extended, so roughly 10 points of each cure rate include patients given more antibiotics. Per-patient reasons for the extensions are in the appendix, which was not read.

slides.title: Secondary outcomes and harms
points: No acquired antibiotic resistance was reported
No relapse with the same organism among patients with back pain; 2 reinfections with other bacteria
Failure linked to age 75 or older and S aureus, regardless of duration (model in the appendix)
Quality of life (EQ-5D) did not differ between groups (data in the appendix)
slides.notes: No secondary outcome differed. Fever, pain, CRP, creatinine and failure at 6 months were all similar; the time courses are in the appendix. The harms result is the surprise. The authors' premise was that longer antibiotics cause more harm, yet twice the duration produced no visible excess here: intolerance 12 versus 9, C difficile 2 versus 2. Our reading: the trial was not powered for harms, and patients were randomised up to 3 weeks into treatment, so early intolerance may have occurred before entry. Mortality was 26 of 351, 11 in the first month. Predictors of failure: failures were older, mean 67.4 versus 60.5 years, and more often had S aureus, 22 of 32 versus 123 of 319 (our Fisher test agrees, P about 0.001). Subgroups were post hoc and their data are in the appendix. Noninferiority was not shown in half of them: age 75 or older, non-S aureus organisms, immunodepression or diabetes, endocarditis, neurological signs, abscesses, fluoroquinolone plus rifampicin, and post-surgical infection. The authors put this down to small subgroups and say 12 weeks was superior in none. That is fair as far as it goes, but absence of proof is not proof of noninferiority, and these are exactly the patients a surgeon sees: abscess, neurological signs, prior surgery. Also note that the abstract and Results give adverse events as 50 versus 51 patients, while Table 3 gives 51 versus 50.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: Holds up: individual randomisation in permuted blocks stratified by centre, masked adjudication, strict microbiological entry criteria
Holds up: all analyses pass, including per protocol and failure-imputed sensitivity
Holds up: relapse window is 12 months off treatment in both arms
Weakens: open label; cure for 182 patients was a committee judgment, with lost and dead patients classified case by case
Weakens: 10-point margin is wide for a disease with 7% mortality
Weakens: enrolled 359 of 400 planned; lowest bound -8.6 (exclusions as failures), per protocol -8.2
Weakens: no data on surgery for the infection; implants excluded and only 8 MRSA enrolled
Weakens: several internal number errors
slides.notes: Be fair: for an infection trial this is large and careful. The authors name two limitations themselves, the open-label design (offset, they argue, by masked adjudication and the impracticality of placebo for physician-chosen drugs) and unstandardised intravenous duration. The rest is our reading. Open label matters because pain was part of the cure definition, and investigators knew the arm. Lost-to-follow-up patients were not automatically failures, which in a noninferiority trial pushes results toward similarity. The 'cured and alive' and 'failure-imputed' analyses partly answer this. Our recomputation found several problems. Diabetes P is printed 0.024, but Fisher gives 0.011 and chi-square 0.008 to 0.013; the imbalance is real either way. Methods say Fisher tests, but many printed P values match a continuity-corrected chi-square instead: cardiorespiratory failure 0.33, intravenous duration 0.204, death 0.85, antibiotic intolerance 0.66, other infection 0.76 (Fisher 0.57) and oral fluoroquinolone plus rifampicin 0.793 (Fisher 0.748). The last two cannot be Fisher P values. The Discussion says coagulase-negative staphylococci caused 61 (71%) of 351 infections; that is 17%, as Table 1 says. Table 4 labels intravenous duration in weeks; the values are days. The 12-week arm lists 16 discontinuations but the reasons add to 12. Intolerance is given as 29 reports in 21 patients, 15 versus 14, but the itemised list adds to 25 reports, 10 versus 15. Deaths classed as failure are 10 versus 3, yet the itemised causes split 5 versus 8. Table 1 says 227 had echocardiography; the endocarditis denominators add to 257. The Panel says results are valid for patients aged 75 or older, while Results say noninferiority was not shown in that subgroup. None of these touches the primary counts, which check out.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: 'For culture-proven pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis without an implant, 6 weeks of antibiotics cured as many patients as 12 weeks at 1 year off treatment, about 91% in each arm, with the lower bound at -6.2 against a 10-point margin. It is a duration trial, not a surgery trial.'
points: Do not stretch it: implants, MRSA (8 patients), TB, brucella, fungi and culture-negative disease are outside it
Abscess, neurological signs, endocarditis and age 75 or older: noninferiority not shown in post-hoc subgroups
Older age and S aureus predicted failure whatever the duration
Kim (X07, library record) addresses a different question: failure of nonoperative care for epidural abscess, 54 of 127
slides.notes: Expect three follow-up questions. First, does this tell me when to operate? No. The trial reports no numbers on decompression, drainage or stabilisation, and its centres were medical departments. Use it for the antibiotic duration after your surgical decision, not to make that decision. Kim, from the library record at abstract level, looks at medical failure in spinal epidural abscess, 54 failures among 127 initially nonoperative patients, and is a separate question. Second, does 6 weeks apply to my patient with an epidural abscess, a deficit or endocarditis? The trial included such patients, 16% had neurological signs, but in post-hoc subgroups with abscesses, neurological signs or endocarditis, noninferiority was not shown. The authors attribute that to low power and note 12 weeks was not superior in any subgroup. So the honest answer is that 6 weeks is supported overall and unproven in those subgroups. Third, what about hardware? Patients with a vertebral implant were excluded, so this says nothing about infected instrumentation; the 34 post-surgical infections had no implant. The authors themselves warn against extending the result to non-pyogenic organisms, MRSA or infection without microbiological identification. Also say aloud what the trial counted as cure: no fever, pain or CRP rise at 12 months, with a masked committee deciding unclear cases, and 30% of patients still had back pain at 1 year in both arms. Finally, 18 of the cured patients in each arm had their antibiotics extended beyond 6 days of the allocated duration (our arithmetic from Table 2). The prespecified 'no further antibiotics' analysis counts them as failures and still passes; the per-patient reasons are in the appendix.

decks.not_reviewed: Figures 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and 13, which the paper says are online only through ArticlePlus. The earlier TLISS paper (reference 21) and the validation survey data it may hold. Any later TLICS reliability or outcome studies. The PDF itself is complete: all 9 printed pages (2325-2333) with tables, figures in print, and references.

slides.title: Vaccaro 2005: A new classification of thoracolumbar injuries (TLICS)
slides.lead: Bottom line: TLICS adds points for injury morphology, posterior ligamentous complex (PLC) integrity and neurologic status; 3 or less suggests nonoperative care, 5 or more suggests surgery may be considered, and 4 is either.
points: Journal club · Thoracolumbar trauma classification
Vaccaro AR, Lehman RA, Hurlbert RJ, et al. Spine 2005;30:2325-33
Spine Trauma Study Group; funded by an educational/research grant from Medtronic Sofamor Danek
Type: expert-consensus classification and treatment proposal. No patient series and no outcome data.
slides.notes: Prepared from the full printed paper, all 9 pages. Six figures (2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and 13) were online only and were not reviewed; the text describes what they show. Frame it before you start: this is not a trial and not a cohort. It is a proposal written by the Spine Trauma Study Group. The paper reports no patients, no reliability statistics for TLICS, and no outcomes. Read it as a structured statement of expert opinion about what should drive the decision to operate on a thoracolumbar injury and from which side. The core idea is still worth learning: the authors move away from mechanism, which surgeons disagreed on, toward what the images show, and they add two things many older systems left out, in the authors' words, the posterior tension band and the neurologic exam. Its value as a score depends on later validation work that this paper does not contain. The library pairs it with X06, the Wood stable burst trial, which we use on the last slide.

slides.title: The question
slides.lead: Thoracolumbar classifications were descriptors, not decision tools. Can one system guide whether to operate and which approach to use?
points: The authors' complaint: existing systems are too complex for routine use, omit the PLC and neurology, and do not suggest treatment.
AO (Blauth, 14 lumbar fractures, 22 institutions): 67% mean interobserver agreement on A/B/C, kappa 0.33.
Oner, 53 patients: AO main categories kappa 0.34 on CT, 0.42 on MRI.
Denis (same thesis, as the paper presents it): CT major type kappa 0.60, entire system 0.45; MRI 0.52 and 0.39.
Their design brief: describe morphology, grade severity, include mechanical and neurologic aspects, be reproducible, useful for research, and able to evolve.
slides.notes: The background is a fair summary of the problem in 2005. AO preserves detail but is hard to use and only fair in agreement. Denis is simpler but leaves injury patterns without a home. The authors frame this as the trade-off every classification faces: more categories, less reproducibility; fewer categories, lost information. Note what they want TLICS to do that the others do not: suggest treatment. That is a big step from description to prescription, and it raises the bar for evidence, because a treatment rule needs outcome data behind it, not just agreement. The reliability numbers on this slide are for AO and Denis, quoted by the authors from other work. The Denis kappas follow the Oner paragraph without their own citation, so we assume they come from the same thesis (reference 20); that link is ours. None of these numbers describe TLICS. The authors also offer a reframing of instability as three categories: immediate mechanical stability, shown by morphology; long-term stability, shown by the PLC; and neurologic stability, shown by the deficit. That is the logic of the three score domains, and it is the most teachable idea in the paper.

slides.title: How it was built: selection, measurement and validity
points: Literature review, then meetings and teleconferences of 40 spine surgeons from 15 level I trauma centers in 9 countries.
Experts polled for injury features pivotal to decisions; limitations of old systems tabulated.
Two preliminary validation surveys: one institution (71 cases) and the Spine Trauma Study Group (56 cases).
Those surveys tested the earlier version, TLISS, which scored mechanism. Surgeons disagreed on mechanism, so it was replaced by morphology.
No rater numbers, kappa values, agreement rates or patient outcomes are reported for either version.
Final check: applied to a shared set of clinical scenarios discussed by the investigators.
slides.notes: This is the slide to slow down on. For a classification you ask three things: who were the cases, how was each element measured, and is there evidence it is reliable and valid. Here the cases are not patients in a study. The inputs were literature selected by level of evidence, soundness and popular acceptance, plus expert opinion. Agreement was unanimous on the design constraints, but the paper does not describe a formal consensus method or voting. The validation surveys of 71 and 56 cases are mentioned in Methods with no results. The Discussion says the score was validated several times to see if it was reliable and reproducible, but that sentence sits in the paragraph about the earlier TLISS, and the next sentence says the results led to the final TLICS; the Abstract also says the initial validation was of an earlier version. So that claim is about TLISS, and the problem is that no validation results are reported. The Conclusion says TLICS is based on objective clinical indicators linked to patient outcome. That one does sit in tension with the Abstract, which says further studies are underway to determine reliability and validity, and with the Discussion, which says it remains imperative that the score be validated. Our reading: the paper contains no data that support the outcome-link statement. The point values and the 3, 4 and 5 thresholds are presented without derivation; the Discussion says scoring outcomes were reviewed against best treatment options for TLISS, but gives no numbers. Measurement is also soft in places. PLC status comes from splaying, facet diastasis, perch or subluxation, with translation or rotation as indirect signs, and a palpable gap as a clinical clue. No criteria for MRI signal are given, and no definitions separate indeterminate from injured except that the evidence is subtle.

slides.title: The score
slides.lead: Score the worst level only, and only the highest morphology; then add the three domains.
slides.see: Figure 11 (L1 axial burst, total 2): the caption notes PLC edema on MRI but scores the PLC 0 because no rotation, translation or distraction was seen.
slides.notes: Teach the rules, not just the table. First, multiple levels: only the most severe level is scored. Second, multiple morphologies: only the highest is scored, so a translation with a lateral burst scores 3 for morphology, not 5. Third, morphology must be clearly present. If distraction is suspected but the PLC is indeterminate, distraction is not listed or scored. The paper does not say what morphology is scored instead; our reading is that you fall back to the next one clearly seen. Fourth, the neurologic scale is ordered by urgency, not severity. Incomplete cord and cauda equina injuries score 3; a complete cord injury scores 2, the same as a root injury. The authors give no reason beyond urgency, noting that incomplete injury is generally accepted as an indication for decompression. Check the worked examples, which all add up. Intact compression fracture: 1. Intact axial burst with intact PLC: 2. Flexion burst, complete cord, disrupted PLC: 7. Translation with lateral burst, complete cord, disrupted PLC: 8. T12 flexion burst, incomplete cord, injured PLC: 8. Flexion distraction at T12-L1, ASIA A, injured PLC: 9. The range is 1 to 10, our arithmetic. Two printed slips: the Results say one to four points are assigned to each subgroup, but PLC and neurology use 0 to 3; and Table 1 lists lateral burst twice. A larger conflict: Table 1 places flexion compression or burst with distraction of posterior elements under Compression (1 or 2 points), but the Results say that in a compression burst injury with distraction of the posterior elements only distraction is scored, 4 points. Follow the Results text; the 2-point difference can move an intact patient across the 3 and 5 thresholds (our arithmetic). Figure 11 is worth a look, as an internal inconsistency. The caption scores the PLC 0 despite edema on MRI and justifies it with morphology criteria (no rotation, translation or distraction). But the paper's own PLC criteria are splaying, facet diastasis and perch or subluxation, and subtle evidence of disruption is to be called indeterminate, 2 points. Our reading: by that rule edema could reasonably score 2, making the total 4, not 2. Do not take the figure as clear guidance that edema does not count.

slides.title: From score to treatment
slides.lead: 3 or less suggests nonoperative care, 4 is either, 5 or more suggests surgery may be considered.
points: Approach rules: incomplete deficit with anterior compression after reduction attempts favors anterior; PLC disruption favors posterior; both favors combined.
*Aggressive decompression in ASIA A is practiced in many institutions (Table 5 footnote).

Qualifiers can override the score: extreme kyphosis or collapse, lateral angulation, open fracture, burns, rib fractures, inability to brace, head injury, polytrauma, ankylosing spondylitis, osteoporosis, age.
slides.notes: The thresholds are worded more firmly in the Key Points than in the Results. Results: a score of 5 or more suggests that surgery may be considered. Key Points: 5 or greater are considered surgical cases. Quote the Results wording. Now look at what the arithmetic forces, which is our reading, not the authors'. A distraction injury scores 4 before anything else, so with any PLC points it is surgical. Translation scores 3, and translation is also listed as an indirect sign of PLC disruption, so most translation injuries will reach 5 or more. A burst in an intact patient scores 2 with an intact PLC, 4 with an indeterminate PLC, and 5 with an injured PLC. So for the common neurologically intact burst fracture, the whole decision turns on how the PLC is read, the softest measurement in the system. Table 5 has two internal problems. It lists cauda equina under both complete and incomplete rows, but Table 4 does not split cauda equina and scores it 3 regardless. And the anterior recommendation in Table 5 drops the condition stated in the text, that anterior compression remains after postural or open reduction. The authors close the section firmly: no algorithm supersedes a surgeon's judgment, and various approaches can succeed.

slides.title: Critical appraisal
points: Holds up: simple, three domains, easy to recall and teach; adds the PLC and neurology that many older systems omitted.
Holds up: morphology replaced mechanism after surgeons disagreed on mechanism.
Holds up: authors state that qualifiers and surgeon judgment can override the score.
Weak: no reliability data for TLICS; TLISS surveys reported without results.
Weak: no derivation of point values or thresholds from outcome data, and no patients managed by the score, are reported.
Weak: PLC indeterminate versus injured is undefined beyond subtle evidence.
Weak: Conclusion claims a link to patient outcome the paper does not show; TLISS validation is mentioned without results.
Weak: industry grant; several authors also wrote TLISS.
slides.notes: Be fair to it. As a teaching framework it is clear, and the three-domain idea of instability is sound, in our view. The authors themselves say it must be further validated and its reliability established, and they invite modification as new factors come to light. The problems are in how strongly the paper speaks. Our reading of the internal tensions: the Conclusion says the system is based on objective indicators linked to patient outcome, while the same paper says reliability and validity studies are still underway. The domains are called largely independent predictors, but translation and distraction morphologies are themselves evidence of PLC disruption, so the same finding can score twice. The Discussion says combinations of morphology represent more severe injuries, but the rules score only the highest morphology, so combinations add nothing. A complete cord injury scores less than an incomplete one by design, so the total is not a severity scale in the ordinary sense; it is a surgical urgency scale. Some smaller slips: Figure 14 caption says PCL for PLC; Table 1 repeats lateral burst; reference 21 lists Hubert RJ where the co-author is Hurlbert RJ, likely a typo. Funding was a Medtronic educational grant; the paper states no commercial benefit to the authors. None of this makes TLICS wrong. It makes this paper the proposal, and the evidence a separate question.

slides.title: How to say it
slides.lead: "TLICS adds morphology, PLC and neurology: 3 or less nonoperative, 5 or more surgery may be considered, 4 either. In this paper it is an expert-consensus proposal with no reliability or outcome data."

rows: Intact burst, intact PLC scores 2: nonoperative
37/47 followed; median ODI 2 nonop vs 20 op

points: Wood numbers are from the library record (abstract level), not this paper.
Do not stretch it: the score is a guide and the thresholds are opinion. For the neurologically intact burst fracture, the PLC read decides between 2, 4 and 5 (our arithmetic).
slides.notes: Spoken summary, about 20 seconds: TLICS scores three things. Morphology, 1 to 4, highest only. PLC, 0, 2 or 3. Neurology, 0 to 3, with incomplete injuries scoring highest. Add them; 3 or less nonoperative, 5 or more surgery may be considered, 4 is your call. Approach follows the PLC and the neuro exam: posterior for a torn tension band, anterior for an incomplete deficit with anterior compression, combined for both. Expected questions. Is TLICS validated? Not in this paper. It reports validation surveys of the earlier TLISS without results and says reliability studies were underway. Why does a complete cord injury score lower than an incomplete one? Because the scale ranks urgency of decompression, not severity, in the authors' framing. What about the neurologically intact burst fracture? With an intact PLC it scores 2 and falls into nonoperative care, which fits the Wood long-term trial in the library record of stable bursts without deficit, where nonoperative patients reported less pain and better function. That link is ours; the trial did not use TLICS. With an indeterminate PLC the same fracture scores 4, so it is the PLC read that decides. Is MRI edema enough to call the PLC injured? The paper does not settle it. Figure 11 scores edema 0, but by the paper's own rule subtle evidence is indeterminate, 2 points, which would make that case 4. That reading is ours. When should the score be overridden? The authors do not say it stops applying; they say qualifiers can significantly influence treatment and must be considered before blindly acting on the score, for example ankylosing spondylitis, osteoporosis, open fractures, multisystem trauma or inability to brace.
